summary: A primer arguing that behaviour comes from system structure: stocks, flows and feedback explain how systems work, why they surprise and trap us, where to intervene, and how to live with them.

unitSummaries.Introduction: Meadows shows with a Slinky that a system's behaviour comes from its own structure, not from outside pushes, and sets out why seeing systems matters.
unitSummaries.Chapter 1: Defines a system as elements, interconnections and a purpose, then builds the tools: stocks and flows, behaviour over time, and balancing and reinforcing feedback loops.
unitSummaries.Chapter 2: Walks through simple one-stock and two-stock systems (thermostat, population, inventory, oil, fishing) to show how feedback structure produces characteristic behaviour.
unitSummaries.Chapter 3: Names three properties of highly functional systems: resilience, self-organization and hierarchy, and says why each makes systems work and how they are lost.
unitSummaries.Chapter 4: Explains why dynamic systems baffle us: events hide structure, minds are linear, boundaries are artificial, limits and delays are everywhere, and rationality is bounded.
unitSummaries.Chapter 5: Presents eight archetypal system structures that produce poor results, each with the trap, examples and the way out.
unitSummaries.Chapter 6: Ranks twelve places to intervene in a system, from adjusting numbers up to transcending paradigms, and argues that the highest points are the hardest to use.
unitSummaries.Chapter 7: Offers fifteen guidelines for living with systems, from getting the beat of the system to not eroding the goal of goodness, drawn from the author's own failures.
unitSummaries.Reading the book as a whole: How the book's seven chapters build from defining systems to changing how we live in them, and what Meadows' whole argument concludes.

concepts.title: The Slinky and the box
concepts.question: What does the Slinky show about where a system's behavior comes from?

paragraphs: Meadows perches a Slinky on one upturned palm and holds it from above with the fingers of her other hand. When she pulls the lower hand away, the lower end drops, bounces back up and yo-yos up and down. Asked what made it bounce, students say it was her hand.

She then holds the box the Slinky came in the same way and pulls the lower hand away. Nothing happens: the box just hangs there. The same hands and the same movement give a bounce in one case and none in the other.

So the answer lies within the Slinky itself. The hands suppress or release a behavior that is latent, meaning stored but not yet showing, in the structure of the spring. Meadows calls this a central insight of systems theory.
card.rule: When the same push gives different results on different things, look for the cause in the structure of the thing pushed.
card.limits: The hands still matter as the trigger that suppresses or releases the behavior. Our reading: a toy shows the principle, not how far it reaches.

concepts.title: A system largely causes its own behavior
concepts.question: How much of a system's behavior does Meadows say comes from outside events?

paragraphs: Meadows defines a system as a set of things, such as people, cells or molecules, interconnected so that they produce their own pattern of behavior over time. Outside forces can buffet, constrict, trigger or drive it, but the system's response is characteristic of itself and is seldom simple in the real world.

Her claim follows: a system, to a large extent, causes its own behavior. An outside event may unleash that behavior, but the same event applied to a different system is likely to produce a different result.

She draws uncomfortable implications. Political leaders do not cause recessions or booms, because ups and downs are inherent in the market economy. Competitors rarely cause a company to lose market share. Oil exporters are not solely responsible for price rises, because importing nations built economies vulnerable to supply interruptions.
card.rule: Before blaming the event that set a pattern off, ask how the system's own structure made it respond that way.
card.limits: Meadows hedges on purpose, with phrases such as to a large extent, rarely, at least in part and not solely. She does not say outside events are irrelevant.

concepts.title: Why the idea unsettles and also feels true
concepts.question: Why does the claim that systems cause their own behavior feel both unsettling and like common sense?

paragraphs: Meadows says statements like these are deeply unsettling, yet also purest common sense. She submits that the two reactions come from two kinds of experience that everyone has had. One produces resistance to systems ideas; the other produces recognition of them.

The first experience is training in analysis. We learn to use our rational ability, trace direct paths from cause to effect, look at things in small understandable pieces and solve problems by acting on or controlling the world. This brings much power, but leads us to name presidents, competitors, oil producers, viruses and drugs as the causes of our problems.
The second is lived experience. Long before formal education we dealt with complex systems, and we built up a practical understanding of how they work, often without analysis and often without words.
card.rule: Expect two pulls at once: training says find the cause and control it, while lived experience says the parts are connected.
card.limits: This is Meadows' own explanation, offered as a submission, not a tested finding. She does not call analytical training wrong: she credits it with much personal and societal power.

concepts.title: Systems jargon as traditional wisdom
concepts.question: How are technical systems principles related to sayings people already know?

paragraphs: Meadows notes that modern systems theory, tied up with computers and equations, hides a fact: it deals in truths that everyone knows at some level. So it is often possible to translate systems jargon directly into traditional wisdom.

She gives pairs. Feedback delays make a problem hard to solve by the time it shows: a stitch in time saves nine. A reinforcing loop, where winning gives the means to win again, fits the rich get richer. A diverse system with many pathways and spare capacity is more stable: do not put all your eggs in one basket.
card.rule: Translate a systems principle into a saying you know, and the saying back into the principle.
card.limits: Our reading: a proverb is a compact reminder and leaves out the mechanism, such as the loop or the delay behind it, so use it as a bridge, not a proof.

concepts.title: Why real messes refuse to go away
concepts.question: Why do some problems persist despite great analytical and technical effort?

paragraphs: Since the Industrial Revolution, Western society has favored science, logic and reductionism over intuition and holism. Reductionism explains things by breaking them into parts; holism looks at wholes. Meadows says we would rather assume a problem's cause is out there than in here, so we shift responsibility and look for a control knob, a pill or a technical fix.

Looking outward has solved serious problems, such as smallpox and food production. But some problems, the real messes, are rooted in the internal structure of complex systems and have refused to go away: hunger, poverty, environmental degradation, unemployment, chronic disease, addiction and war.

No one deliberately creates these problems or wants them to persist. They are intrinsically systems problems, undesirable behaviors characteristic of the structures that produce them. They yield only as we reclaim intuition, stop casting blame, see the system as the source of its own problems, and restructure it.
card.rule: When a problem persists despite repeated technical fixes, examine the structure that produces it instead of looking for someone to blame.
card.limits: Meadows grants that focusing on external agents has solved serious problems. Her claim concerns the messes rooted in internal structure, not every problem.

concepts.title: What the systems lens gives us
concepts.question: What does Meadows say systems thinking gives us in a complex, fast-changing world?

paragraphs: Meadows says that as the world grows more complex, systems thinking helps us manage, adapt and see the wide range of choices open to us. It gives us the freedom to identify root causes of problems and to see new opportunities.

The systems lens lets us reclaim our intuition about whole systems. It also helps us hone our abilities to understand parts, see interconnections, ask what-if questions about possible future behaviors, and be creative and courageous about redesigning systems.
Then, she says, we can use our insights to make a difference in ourselves and in our world.
card.rule: Use the systems lens to look for root causes and to ask what-if questions about redesign, not only to find someone to blame.
card.limits: Meadows offers understanding and choices, not a technical fix. She says restructuring takes courage and wisdom.

concepts.section: Purpose and method of the book
concepts.title: What the book is for and how it is written
concepts.question: Who is Meadows writing for, and why does she rely on diagrams?

paragraphs: Meadows says the book is about a different way of seeing and thinking. She wrote it for people who may be wary of the word systems and of systems analysis, even though they may have done systems thinking all their lives.

She keeps the discussion nontechnical to show how far you can go toward understanding systems without mathematics or computers. She uses diagrams and time graphs because words come one at a time in linear order, while systems happen all at once and connect in many directions.
card.rule: Ask what the author is trying to do and for whom, then read the book as that kind of attempt.
card.limits: Our reading: an author's stated aims are a guide, so check them against what the chapters actually do.

concepts.title: The road map of the book
concepts.question: In what order does the book move from the basics to its largest lessons?

paragraphs: Meadows starts with the basics: the definition of a system and a dissection of its parts. Then she puts the parts back together into the basic operating unit of a system, the feedback loop. Next comes a systems zoo, a collection of common and interesting types of systems whose behavior she explains.

With zoo examples as a foundation, she steps back to ask how and why systems work so well and why they so often surprise us. Then she turns to archetypes, common structures that produce characteristic behaviors. She calls them system traps and opportunities.

From there she moves to restructuring the systems we live within, looking for leverage points for change, and concludes with the largest lessons from systems thinkers' shared wisdom. The Appendix offers a glossary, a bibliography, a list of systems principles and the model equations from Part One.
card.rule: Outline a book by its movement: basics, examples, why systems work and surprise us, traps, leverage, then lessons.
card.limits: This is the author's plan as announced in the introduction. Our reading: check it against the chapters themselves.

concepts.title: A complementary way of seeing
concepts.question: Does Meadows say the systems way of seeing is better than reductionism?

paragraphs: Meadows does not think the systems way of seeing is better than the reductionist way of thinking, which explains things by breaking them into parts. She thinks the two are complementary, and therefore revealing.

Her comparison is with lenses. You see some things through the human eye, others through a microscope, others through a telescope, and still others through systems theory. Everything seen through each kind of lens is actually there, and each way of seeing makes our knowledge of the world a little more complete.
In a world more messy, crowded, interconnected, interdependent and rapidly changing than ever, she says, the more ways of seeing, the better.
card.rule: Add the systems lens to analysis rather than replacing one with the other, since each shows real things the other misses.
card.limits: Our reading: this is Meadows' stated position, offered as what she thinks and hopes to convey, not a tested comparison of the lenses.

concepts.section: Interlude • The Blind Men and the Matter of the Elephant
concepts.title: The blind men and the elephant
concepts.question: What does the story of the blind men and the elephant show about knowing a system?

paragraphs: The Interlude retells an ancient Sufi story. In a city beyond Ghor all the people were blind. A king camped nearby with a mighty elephant, and some of the blind townspeople ran to find it, learning about it only by touching a part.

One touched an ear and called it a large, rough thing like a rug. Another felt the trunk and called it a hollow pipe. A third felt the legs and called it a pillar. Each had felt one part out of many and perceived the elephant wrongly.
Meadows says the story teaches a simple lesson we often ignore: the behavior of a system cannot be known just by knowing the elements of which the system is made.
card.rule: Knowing every part separately is not enough to know how the whole behaves, so study how the parts connect.
card.limits: Meadows does not dismiss parts: the introduction also says to hone our abilities to understand them. The story warns against stopping at the parts.

concepts.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
concepts.title: What a system is
concepts.question: What three kinds of things must every system contain?

paragraphs: Meadows defines a system as an interconnected set of elements that is coherently organized in a way that achieves something. Read closely, the definition names three kinds of ingredient: elements, interconnections, and a function or purpose.

Take the digestive system. Its elements are teeth, enzymes, stomach and intestines. Its interconnections are the physical flow of food and a set of regulating chemical signals. Its function is to break food down into nutrients and move them into the bloodstream while discarding waste.

A football team has players, a coach, a field and a ball as elements. Its interconnections are the rules of the game, the coach’s strategy, the players’ communications and the laws of physics acting on ball and players.
card.rule: A system is elements plus interconnections plus a function or purpose, organized so that together they achieve something.
card.limits: Naming a system means choosing which elements and links to look at; Meadows later stresses that every system description is a simplification of the real world.

concepts.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
concepts.title: A system or a heap?
concepts.question: How can you tell a real system from a loose pile of things?

paragraphs: Not everything is a system. Meadows says a conglomeration with no particular interconnections or function is not one. Sand scattered on a road by happenstance is her example: add sand or take sand away and you still have sand on the road.
A real system reacts differently. Arbitrarily add or remove football players, or pieces of a digestive system, and you quickly no longer have the same system.

She offers four questions. Can you identify parts? Do the parts affect each other? Do the parts together produce an effect different from the effect of each part alone? And perhaps: does that effect, the behavior over time, persist in a variety of circumstances?
card.rule: To test for a system, ask whether there are identifiable parts, whether they affect each other, and whether together they do something none does alone.
card.limits: The fourth question is offered only as a perhaps, so treat persistence across circumstances as a further check rather than a required test.

concepts.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
concepts.title: Systems behave in lifelike ways
concepts.question: What lifelike behaviors can a system show even when its parts are nonliving?

paragraphs: Meadows says a system is more than the sum of its parts. It may be adaptive, dynamic, goal-seeking, self-preserving, and sometimes evolutionary. A system has an integrity or wholeness, and active mechanisms to maintain it.

Systems can change, adapt, respond to events, seek goals, mend injuries and attend to their own survival, although they may contain or consist of nonliving things. They can be self-organizing, and often self-repairing over at least some range of disruptions. They are resilient.

Systems can also be nested. A forest is a larger system that encompasses subsystems of trees and animals, and the earth, the solar system and a galaxy are systems too: systems can be embedded in systems, which are embedded in yet other systems.
card.rule: Expect a system to maintain its wholeness, responding, adapting and repairing itself, because the whole does things the parts alone do not.
card.limits: Self-repair works only over some range of disruptions; beyond that range a system can lose its system-ness, as a dying creature does.

concepts.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
concepts.title: Elements are the easy part to see
concepts.question: Why is it easy to list a system’s elements, and where should you stop listing?

paragraphs: The elements of a system are often the easiest parts to notice, because many are visible, tangible things. A tree has roots, trunk, branches and leaves. A university has buildings, students, professors, administrators, libraries, books and computers.
Elements need not be physical. Intangibles count too: in a university, school pride and academic prowess can be very important elements.

Listing has no natural end, because you can divide elements into sub-elements and sub-sub-elements. Pretty soon you lose sight of the system, as the saying goes: you cannot see the forest for the trees. So stop dissecting and start looking for the interconnections.
card.rule: List the elements, physical and intangible, but stop before you lose the system and turn to the relationships between them.
card.limits: Elements still matter: particular elements, such as the players on a team, can be important to how well a system does.

concepts.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
concepts.title: Interconnections hold elements together
concepts.question: What are interconnections, and what do a tree and a university show about them?

paragraphs: Interconnections are the relationships that hold a system’s elements together. In a tree they are the physical flows and chemical reactions of metabolism, the signals that let one part respond to what is happening in another.

On a sunny day the leaves lose water, and a drop in pressure in the water-carrying vessels lets the roots take in more water. If the roots meet dry soil, the loss of water pressure signals the leaves to close their pores.
In a university the interconnections include admission standards, degree requirements, examinations and grades, budgets and money flows, gossip and, most important, the communication of knowledge.
card.rule: To understand a system, look for the signals, flows and rules that link its elements.
card.limits: Our knowledge of them is often partial: Meadows notes no one understands all the relationships that let a tree do what it does.

concepts.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
concepts.title: Information as an interconnection
concepts.question: Why are so many interconnections flows of information, and what does information alone not guarantee?

paragraphs: Many interconnections operate through the flow of information. Information holds a system together and plays a great part in determining how it operates.

Some interconnections are physical flows, such as water in a tree trunk or students progressing through a university. Many are signals that go to decision points or action points. These are often harder to see, though the system reveals them to those who look.

Students may use informal information about the chance of a good grade to choose courses. A consumer decides what to buy using information about income, savings, credit rating, stock of goods at home, prices and availability.
card.rule: Look for the signals that reach decision points; they are often the hidden connections that explain what a system does.
card.limits: Information links are harder to see than physical flows, so they are easy to miss when you map a system.

concepts.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
concepts.title: Purpose shows in behavior
concepts.question: How can you tell what a system is really for?

paragraphs: A system’s function or purpose is even harder to see than its information links. It need not be spoken or written down, except through how the system operates. The best way to deduce it is to watch how the system behaves for a while.
If a frog turns right and catches a fly, then turns left and catches a fly, then turns around backward and catches a fly, its purpose has to do with catching flies, not with turning in any direction.

A government that proclaims its interest in protecting the environment but allocates little money or effort to it does not have environmental protection as its purpose. Purposes are deduced from behavior, not from rhetoric or stated goals.
card.rule: Judge a system’s purpose by what it consistently does, not by what it says.
card.limits: The purpose of the whole system may differ from what any single actor inside it intends.

concepts.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
concepts.title: Purposes that add up to what no one wants
concepts.question: How can every actor’s purpose be reasonable while the whole system acts in a way no one wants?

paragraphs: System purposes need not be human purposes and are not necessarily those intended by any single actor. One of the most frustrating aspects of systems is that the purposes of subunits may add up to an overall behavior that no one wants.

Meadows’ example is drug addiction and crime. No one intends to produce them. But consider the combined purposes: desperate people who want quick relief from psychological pain, and farmers, dealers and bankers who want to earn money.
Altogether, she says, the actors make up a system from which it is extremely difficult to eradicate addiction and crime.
card.rule: To explain a stubborn result, look at how all the actors’ separate purposes combine, rather than for one villain’s intent.
card.limits: This explains why change is hard; it does not say that no actor has any responsibility (our reading).

concepts.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
concepts.title: Purposes within purposes
concepts.question: What happens when a sub-purpose conflicts with the purpose of the whole system?

paragraphs: Systems can be nested within systems, so there can be purposes within purposes. The purpose of a university is to discover and preserve knowledge and pass it on to new generations.

Inside it, a student may want good grades, a professor may want tenure, and an administrator may want to balance the budget. Any of these sub-purposes could come into conflict with the overall purpose: the student could cheat.
Keeping sub-purposes and overall system purposes in harmony is an essential function of successful systems.
card.rule: Check whether the sub-purposes of the parts serve or undermine the purpose of the whole.
card.limits: Meadows says she will return to this point when she reaches hierarchies; this chapter only introduces it.

concepts.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
concepts.title: Swap the players, keep the system
concepts.question: What happens to a system when its elements are replaced but its links and purpose stay?

paragraphs: To see how much each ingredient matters, imagine changing them one at a time. Changing elements usually has the least effect. Replace every player on a football team and it is still recognizably a football team, though it may play much better or much worse.

A tree changes its cells constantly and its leaves every year or so, yet it is the same tree. Your body replaces most of its cells every few weeks and goes on being your body. A university has a constant flow of students and a slower flow of professors, and remains a university.
A system generally goes on being itself, changing only slowly if at all, even when its elements are completely replaced, as long as its interconnections and purposes remain intact.
card.rule: Swapping elements rarely changes what a system is, provided the links and purpose survive.
card.limits: Particular elements can matter, as a team’s quality shows, and replacing an element that also changes relationships or purpose does change the system.

concepts.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
concepts.title: Change the rules, change the system
concepts.question: How much can a system change when its interconnections change but its players stay?

paragraphs: If the interconnections change, the system may be greatly altered. It may even become unrecognizable though the same players are on the team.
Change the rules from football to basketball and you have, as they say, a whole new ball game.

In a university, if students graded the professors, or if arguments were won by force instead of reason, the place would need a different name. It might be an interesting organization, but it would not be a university.
card.rule: Changing relationships usually changes system behavior, sometimes dramatically.
card.limits: Links matter greatly, yet Meadows ranks purpose, the least obvious part, as often the most crucial determinant.

concepts.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
concepts.title: A new purpose, a new system
concepts.question: Why is a system’s purpose often the most crucial determinant of its behavior?

paragraphs: Changes in function or purpose can be drastic. Keep the players and the rules but change the purpose from winning to losing, and the team is a different thing.

Imagine a tree whose function were not to survive and reproduce but to capture all the nutrients in the soil and grow to unlimited size. A change in purpose changes a system profoundly even if every element and interconnection stays the same.
That is why the least obvious part of the system, its function or purpose, is often the most crucial determinant of the system’s behavior.
card.rule: When behavior needs explaining, ask first what the system is for.
card.limits: Meadows says often, not always; the three ingredients all interact and all are essential.

concepts.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
concepts.title: All three matter, and leaders have limits
concepts.question: Why is asking which ingredient matters most the wrong kind of question?

paragraphs: To ask whether elements, interconnections or purposes are most important is, Meadows says, an unsystemic question. All are essential, all interact, all have their roles.
Elements, the parts we notice most, are often (not always) least important in defining a system’s unique character, unless changing an element also changes relationships or purpose.

Changing one leader at the top, from a Brezhnev to a Gorbachev or a Carter to a Reagan, may or may not turn a nation in a new direction. A leader can make the same land, factories and people play a different game with new rules, or direct the play toward a new purpose.
card.rule: Ask how elements, links and purpose work together; do not rank them in isolation.
card.limits: The ranking is a tendency: elements are often, not always, least important.

concepts.title: Stocks: accumulations that remember
concepts.question: What is a stock, and why does Meadows call it the memory of a system’s history?

paragraphs: A stock is the foundation of any system. It is the part of a system you can see, feel, count or measure at a given time: a store, a quantity, an accumulation of material or information built up over time. Examples are the water in a bathtub, a population, the books in a bookstore, the wood in a tree and the money in a bank.
A stock need not be physical. Your self-confidence, your reserve of good will, or your supply of hope that the world can be better are stocks too.

Stocks change over time through the actions of flows: filling and draining, births and deaths, purchases and sales, deposits and withdrawals. So a stock is the present memory of the history of changing flows within the system.
card.rule: A stock is an accumulation at one moment, and it records everything its flows have done so far.
card.limits: A stock tells you where the system stands now; it does not by itself tell you which flows will move it next.

concepts.title: Reading stock-and-flow diagrams
concepts.question: How do stock-and-flow diagrams show stocks, flows, faucets and clouds?

paragraphs: Meadows draws a stock as a box. A flow is an arrow-headed pipe leading into the box (an inflow) or out of it (an outflow).
A small T on each pipe stands for a faucet: the flow it controls can be turned higher or lower, or on or off.
The convention gives a quick picture of a system as boxes joined by pipes with taps. In the book these diagrams are figures; here each is described in words.
card.rule: Read a stock as a box, a flow as a pipe with a tap, and ask what each tap controls.
card.limits: A diagram shows only what its drawer chose to include; it is a simplification of the real system.

media.alt: A box labelled stock sits in the middle. A pipe with a tap, labelled inflow, runs from a cloud on the left into the box. A second pipe with a tap, labelled outflow, runs from the box out to a cloud on the right. Arrowheads on the pipes show the direction of flow.

A box labelled water in tub has an inflow pipe with a tap arriving from a cloud on the left and an outflow pipe with a tap leaving to a cloud on the right. Both arrows point left to right through the box: one stock, one inflow, one outflow.

concepts.title: Stocks in real systems
concepts.question: What are the stocks, inflows and outflows in a reservoir and in a mineral deposit?

paragraphs: An underground mineral deposit is a stock, and the flow of ore out through mining drains it. Its inflow is minute over any period shorter than eons, so Meadows draws the picture with no inflow at all.
Water in a reservoir behind a dam is a stock. Rain and river water flow in; evaporation from the surface and water discharged through the dam flow out.
The same bathtub logic fits both. Each has a store that builds up or runs down as its flows change.
card.rule: For any system, name the stock first, then list what flows into it and what flows out.
card.limits: Dropping a tiny flow from the picture, as with the deposit’s inflow, is a choice that depends on the time period you care about.

media.alt: A box labelled mineral deposit has one pipe leaving it to the right. The pipe has a tap labelled mining and ends at a cloud. No pipe enters the box, so the picture shows an outflow and no inflow.

A box labelled water in reservoir has two pipes with taps arriving from clouds on the left, labelled rain and river inflow, and two pipes with taps leaving to clouds on the right, labelled evaporation and discharge. Two inflows and two outflows surround one stock.

From left to right: a cloud feeds a box of wood in living trees through a tree growth tap. A logging pipe runs from that box into a second box, lumber inventory. A separate tree deaths pipe turns downward from the trees into its own cloud. Lumber sales then drain the inventory to a cloud on the right.

concepts.title: Reading graphs of behavior over time
concepts.question: What should you look at when reading a graph of a system’s behavior over time?

paragraphs: Systems thinkers use graphs of behavior to understand trends over time, rather than focusing on individual events. They also use them to learn whether the system is approaching a goal or a limit, and how quickly.

The variable on the graph may be a stock or a flow. The pattern, the shape of the line, is important, as are the points where the line changes shape or direction. The precise numbers on the axes are often less important.
card.rule: Read the shape and the turning points of a line first, and the exact numbers afterward.
card.limits: Shape is a guide, not a replacement for numbers; some questions need the exact figures (our reading).

media.alt: A graph of the water stock in a tub over ten minutes. The line begins at fifty gallons at minute zero and falls in one straight diagonal to zero gallons at minute ten, showing steady draining with no water coming in.

concepts.title: Inflows, outflows and dynamic equilibrium
concepts.question: What happens to a stock when inflows exceed, equal, or fall below outflows?

paragraphs: Picture a tub filled with water, plug in and taps off: an unchanging, boring system. Pull the plug and the water runs out until the tub is empty. If you start again from a full tub and, when it is half empty, turn on the inflow so that it just equals the outflow, the level stays constant.

Meadows calls this dynamic equilibrium: the level does not change although water is continuously flowing through. From the bathtub she draws three rules. If inflows exceed outflows, the stock rises. If outflows exceed inflows, it falls. If they are equal, it holds steady.
The same rules extend to more complicated systems, which is why a bathtub is such a useful model.
card.rule: A stock rises when inflows exceed outflows, falls when outflows exceed inflows, and holds when they match.
card.limits: The rules are exact for a stock with only these flows; a real system may have flows you left out, such as evaporation from the tub.

media.alt: A graph of flows in gallons per minute over ten minutes. A dashed horizontal line at five marks a constant outflow. The inflow line lies at zero until about minute four, rises steeply to five by minute five, then runs level with the outflow line to minute ten.

A graph of the tub's water stock over ten minutes. The line starts at fifty gallons and falls in a straight line to about twenty-five gallons at minute five, then continues as a flat horizontal line at that level through minute ten.

concepts.title: More than one way to fill a bathtub
concepts.question: Why can a stock be raised by cutting an outflow as well as by increasing an inflow?

paragraphs: Meadows notes that the human mind seems to focus more easily on stocks than on flows, and, when it does focus on flows, more easily on inflows than on outflows. So we sometimes miss that a tub can be filled by shrinking the outflow as well as by opening the tap.

Everyone understands that finding new oil deposits prolongs the life of an oil-based economy. It is harder to see that burning less oil achieves the same result. A breakthrough in energy efficiency has the same effect on the stock of available oil as discovering a new oil field, although different people profit.
In her words: “There’s more than one way to fill a bathtub!”
card.rule: To raise a stock, consider lowering its outflows as well as raising its inflows.
card.limits: The two routes can differ greatly in cost and in who benefits, so an equal effect on the stock does not mean equal merit.

concepts.title: Every model is a simplification
concepts.question: Why does Meadows leave evaporation out of the bathtub, and what does that say about models?

paragraphs: The bathtub is a very simple system with one stock, one inflow and one outflow. Over the minutes that matter, Meadows assumes evaporation from the tub is insignificant, so she leaves that outflow out.

She says all models, whether mental models or mathematical models, are simplifications of the real world. A model is useful when you know all its dynamic possibilities, as you do for the bathtub, and can deduce principles that extend to more complicated systems.
card.rule: Decide which flows matter over your time period, include those, and remember the model leaves the rest out.
card.limits: A simplification that is fine for minutes may be wrong for days; a flow you drop at one time scale can matter at another.

concepts.title: Stocks change slowly
concepts.question: Why can a faucet be changed at once while the water level cannot?

paragraphs: You can adjust the drain or faucet of a tub abruptly, but it is much harder to change the level of water quickly. Water cannot run out instantly even with the drain wide open, and the tub cannot fill at once with the faucet on full.

A stock takes time to change because flows take time to flow. Meadows calls this a vital point and a key to understanding why systems behave as they do. Stocks, especially large ones, respond to change, even sudden change, only by gradual filling or emptying.

So stocks act as delays, lags, buffers, ballast and sources of momentum. People often underestimate the momentum of a stock: populations take a long time to grow or stop growing, wood takes a long time to accumulate in a forest, and a mine takes a long time to be depleted.
card.rule: Flows can change suddenly but stocks change gradually, so stocks act as delays, buffers and momentum.
card.limits: Slowness is relative to the size of the stock and the flows; a small stock with big flows can change quickly.

concepts.title: Lags as stability and as opportunity
concepts.question: How can the time lags that stocks impose both cause problems and give room to maneuver?

paragraphs: Changes in stocks set the pace of a system’s dynamics. Industrialization cannot go faster than factories and machines can be built and people educated to run them. Forests cannot grow overnight.

The lags from slowly changing stocks can cause problems, but they are also sources of stability. Soil that has built up over centuries rarely erodes all at once, and a population that has learned many skills does not forget them immediately. These lags allow room to maneuver, to experiment and to revise policies that are not working.

If you know the rates at which stocks change, you do not expect things to happen faster than they can, and you do not give up too soon. You can use a system’s momentum to guide it toward a good outcome, as a judo expert uses an opponent’s momentum.
card.rule: Know how fast your stocks can change: it keeps you from expecting miracles, from giving up early, and from wasting the room that lags give you.
card.limits: The same lag that protects can also hide damage until it is hard to undo.

concepts.title: Stocks decouple flows and invite regulation
concepts.question: How do stocks let inflows and outflows differ, and how do people regulate stocks?

paragraphs: Stocks allow inflows and outflows to be independent of each other and temporarily out of balance. An oil company could hardly run if gasoline had to be produced at exactly the rate cars burn it, and a forest cannot be harvested at exactly the rate trees grow. Stored gasoline and standing wood give life certainty and continuity even though flows vary.

People have invented hundreds of stock-maintaining mechanisms for this: reservoirs let downstream farmers live without constantly adjusting to a river’s droughts and floods, and banks let you earn at a rate different from how you spend.

Most decisions are designed to regulate the levels in stocks. If inventories rise too high, prices are cut so sales go up. If the food stock in your kitchen gets low, you go to the store. Systems thinkers therefore see the world as stocks plus mechanisms that regulate them by manipulating flows: feedback processes.
card.rule: A stock lets flows differ for a while, and people watch stocks and adjust flows to keep levels acceptable.
card.limits: The buffer works only within the stock’s capacity: an empty or overflowing stock can no longer decouple the flows.

concepts.title: Persistent behavior hints at a feedback loop
concepts.question: What does it suggest when a stock keeps growing, falling or holding steady whatever else happens?

paragraphs: When a stock grows by leaps and bounds, declines swiftly, or is held within a certain range no matter what else is going on, a control mechanism is probably at work.
In Meadows’ words, a behavior that persists over time is probably produced by a mechanism, and that mechanism operates through a feedback loop.
card.rule: Treat a persistent pattern in a stock as a clue to look for the loop that produces it.
card.limits: A clue is not proof: persistence suggests a mechanism, but you still have to find and check it.

concepts.title: What a feedback loop is
concepts.question: When does a change in a stock feed back on the stock itself?

paragraphs: A feedback loop is formed when changes in a stock affect the flows into or out of that same stock. The simplest case is an interest-bearing savings account. The balance is the stock, and the bank’s rule pays a percent of it each year, so the interest flowing in varies with the size of the balance rather than being a fixed amount.

A checking account shows a loop you run yourself. As your available cash falls, you may work more hours and earn more. If the balance grows very large, you may feel free to work less. This keeps your cash within a range you find acceptable.
card.rule: Look for a stock whose level changes the flow that changes it.
card.limits: A link between a stock and a flow is only a loop if the flow actually responds to the stock’s level; a fixed payment is not a loop.

concepts.title: Anatomy of a loop, and chains without one
concepts.question: What parts make a feedback loop, and which systems have none?

paragraphs: Meadows defines a feedback loop as a closed chain of causal connections. It starts at a stock, passes through decisions, rules, physical laws or actions that depend on the stock’s level, and returns through a flow to change the stock. The stock level feeds back through a chain of signals and actions to control itself.
In her diagrams a loop has three parts: the stock, the flow that changes it, and an information link, a thin curved arrow that carries the stock’s level to the point of action.
Not all systems have loops. Some are open-ended chains of stocks and flows, which outside factors may affect but where the levels of the stocks do not affect the flows.
card.rule: To test for a loop, ask whether the stock’s level reaches a decision that changes a flow back into the same stock.
card.limits: Loops that exist are common and can be elegant or surprising, but not every system has one.

media.alt: Two small stock-and-flow diagrams. In the upper one a cloud feeds a tap that fills a stock box, and a curved information arrow runs from the stock back to that tap. In the lower one a stock empties through a tap to a cloud, with a curved arrow from the stock back to that tap.

concepts.title: Balancing loops seek a goal
concepts.question: How does a balancing loop keep a stock near a goal, in whichever direction it is pushed?

paragraphs: One common kind of loop stabilizes a stock. The level may not stay completely fixed, but it stays within an acceptable range. A coffee drinker holds a desired level of energy in mind, and the purpose of the coffee-delivery system is to keep the actual level near it.
It is the gap between actual and desired energy that drives the decision to drink more or less coffee.

Meadows calls this a balancing feedback loop and marks it with a B. Balancing loops are goal-seeking or stability-seeking. A balancing loop opposes whatever direction of change is imposed: push the stock too far up and it pulls down, shove it too far down and it brings it up.
card.rule: A balancing loop compares the stock with a goal and acts on the gap to push the stock back toward it.
card.limits: The stock need not stay exactly at the goal; a balancing loop keeps it near the goal or within a range.

media.alt: A box of stored energy in the body feeds, through a tap for metabolic mobilization, a box of energy available for work, which drains through an expenditure tap to a cloud. Curved information links run from available energy and from the desired energy level into discrepancy, then to coffee intake, then to the mobilization tap. A B marks the loop.

Two side-by-side diagrams, each with a box of coffee temperature and a tap joined to a cloud: cooling on the left, heating on the right. In each, information links carry coffee temperature and room temperature into a discrepancy, which links back to the tap. Both loops are marked B.

concepts.title: Homing: fast at first, then slower
concepts.question: How does a stock approach its goal when the gap itself sets the speed of correction?

paragraphs: A hot cup of coffee cools gradually to room temperature, and here the loop works through physical law rather than a human decision. The rate of cooling depends on the difference between the coffee and the room: the greater the difference, the faster it cools. The loop also works the other way, since iced coffee on a hot day warms until it matches the room.
The function of this system is to bring the discrepancy to zero, whichever way it points.

Graphs of coffee starting anywhere from just below boiling to just above freezing show the homing behavior. Whatever the starting value, above or below the goal, the loop brings it toward the goal. The change is faster at first and then slower, as the gap shrinks.
card.rule: When correction is proportional to the gap, a stock closes in on its goal quickly at first and ever more slowly near the end.
card.limits: Homing in this smooth way is the simple case; real loops with delays or weak actions can behave differently.

media.alt: A graph of temperature in degrees Celsius over eight minutes, with a dashed line marking room temperature at 18. Three hot-coffee curves start high, near 100, 80 and 60, and fall steeply at first, then flatten toward the dashed line. Three iced-coffee curves start near the bottom, between about 0 and 10, and rise steeply, then level off toward the same line.

concepts.title: A loop’s presence does not mean it works
concepts.question: Why can a system have a feedback loop and still fail to reach its goal?

paragraphs: A feedback mechanism does not necessarily work well. It may not be strong enough to bring the stock to the desired level.

Meadows lists many ways feedback can fail. Information can arrive too late or at the wrong place. It can be unclear, incomplete or hard to interpret. The action it triggers may be too weak, delayed, resource-constrained or simply ineffective. As a result the actual stock may never reach the loop’s goal.
card.rule: When a goal is missed, check the loop’s information and action for lateness, weakness or confusion.
card.limits: The coffee-cooling loop is simple and always reaches room temperature; weaker, delayed or confused loops may not reach their goals.

concepts.title: Reinforcing loops amplify
concepts.question: How does a reinforcing loop make a stock grow or collapse by feeding on itself?

paragraphs: The second kind of loop is amplifying, reinforcing, self-multiplying, snowballing: a vicious or virtuous circle that can cause healthy growth or runaway destruction. Meadows marks it with an R. It generates more input to a stock the more is already there, and less input the less is there. It enhances whatever direction of change is imposed on it.

The more rabbits there are, the more rabbit parents there are to make baby rabbits, and the more baby rabbits there are, the more grow up to be parents. The more soil is eroded, the fewer plants grow, so the fewer roots hold the soil, and the more soil is eroded.
card.rule: A reinforcing loop makes more of whatever is already happening to a stock, upward or downward.
card.limits: A reinforcing loop does not run forever on its own in a real system; in practice it is joined by other loops.

media.alt: A box labelled money in bank account receives an inflow pipe with a tap, labelled interest added, from a cloud. A curved information arrow runs from the account balance back to that tap, forming a loop marked R. A second arrow from the interest rate also points to the tap.

concepts.title: Reinforcing loops and exponential growth
concepts.question: Why does growth through a reinforcing loop speed up rather than rise by a fixed amount?

paragraphs: In an interest-bearing account, the more money you have, the more interest you earn, and that interest is added to the money already there, where it earns still more. Meadows shows $100 over twelve years with no deposits or withdrawals, at five different rates from 2 to 10 percent a year.

This is not simple linear growth, which would add a constant amount each year. In a reinforcing loop growth goes faster and faster, because the more is there, the more is added. This is called exponential growth. It is good or bad news depending on what grows: money, a pest in a cornfield, an economy, or weapons in an arms race.
card.rule: Where a stock feeds its own growth, the amount added each period grows too, so growth is exponential, not linear.
card.limits: Exponential growth in real systems eventually meets other loops that limit it; the arithmetic alone does not say how long it lasts.

media.alt: A graph of dollars over twelve years with five curves, one for each interest rate from two to ten percent. All start together at one hundred dollars and fan out, each bending upward. The highest rate ends near 314 dollars and the lowest near 127, with the other three ordered between.

concepts.title: The rule of 70
concepts.question: About how long does an exponentially growing stock take to double?

paragraphs: Because reinforcing loops turn up so often, Meadows offers a shortcut. The time it takes an exponentially growing stock to double, the doubling time, is approximately 70 divided by the growth rate expressed as a percentage.
Her example: put $100 in the bank at 7 percent interest a year, and you double your money in 10 years, since 70 divided by 7 is 10.
card.rule: Doubling time is about 70 divided by the percentage growth rate.
card.limits: It is an approximation, and it applies only to steady exponential growth with a constant percentage rate.

concepts.title: Reinvestment: the engine of growth
concepts.question: How does a reinforcing loop turn capital into more capital?

paragraphs: Meadows’ diagram of reinvestment links two quantities. The more machines and factories, collectively called capital, an economy has, the more goods and services, called output, it can produce.

The more output it can produce, the more it can invest in new machines and factories. The more it makes, the more capacity it has to make even more. Capital is the stock, and investment is the inflow that adds to it.
card.rule: When output is reinvested to raise capacity, the capital stock feeds its own growth.
card.limits: Capital also wears out and is discarded, so the loop is joined by an outflow; the reinvestment loop alone describes growth, not the whole story.

media.alt: A box labelled capital receives an inflow pipe with a tap, labelled investment, from a cloud. A curved information arrow runs from capital to output. Another arrow from output, together with a fraction of output invested, points to the investment tap, closing a loop marked R.

concepts.title: Seeing loops everywhere
concepts.question: What habit of thought does the feedback concept build, and what does it replace?

paragraphs: Meadows sometimes challenges students to think of any human decision made without regard to the level of the stock it influences. The more you try, the more you begin to see feedback loops everywhere.

Instead of seeing only how A causes B, you begin to wonder how B may also influence A, and how A might reinforce or reverse itself. When someone says population growth causes poverty, you ask how poverty may cause population growth. If A causes B, is it possible that B also causes A?

You think not in terms of a static world but a dynamic one. You stop looking for who is to blame and start asking what the system is. The concept of feedback opens up the idea that a system can cause its own behavior.
card.rule: Ask what B does back to A, and replace the hunt for blame with the question of what the system is.
card.limits: Seeing a loop does not show which direction is stronger; that has to be found out, not assumed.

concepts.title: Real systems hold many loops
concepts.question: What happens when several reinforcing and balancing loops pull on the same stock?

paragraphs: In real systems feedback loops rarely come singly. They are linked together, often in fantastically complex patterns. A single stock is likely to have several reinforcing and balancing loops of differing strengths pulling it in several directions.

The many loops tug against each other, trying to make stocks grow, die off or come into balance with each other. As a result, complex systems do much more than stay steady, explode exponentially, or approach goals smoothly.
card.rule: When loops compete, predict the stock’s behavior from their relative strengths, not from any one loop.
card.limits: Our reading: this idea warns that single-loop patterns are only a first model; Meadows leaves the richer behaviors for later chapters.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.title: The systems zoo: learning from examples
concepts.question: Why tour simple systems one at a time, and what does a tidy tour leave out?

paragraphs: Meadows says a good way to learn something new is through specific examples rather than abstractions. The chapter therefore presents several simple but important systems, each worth understanding in its own right, that illustrate general principles of complex systems.

She likens the collection to a zoo. It shows the variety of systems and groups the animals by family, single-stock systems here and two-stock systems there, so you can see each family's characteristic behavior.

But a zoo is too neat. It pulls animals apart from each other and from the environment that normally hides them. Real systems interact with one another and with others not shown, in a buzzing, changing complexity.
card.rule: Study systems one at a time to see their characteristic behavior, and remember that real systems are mixed together.
card.limits: The zoo is far from a complete list of systems, and its tidy separation is an aid to seeing, not a fact about the world.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
concepts.title: Two balancing loops on one stock
concepts.question: What happens when two balancing loops pull one stock toward two different goals?

paragraphs: In the thermostat model the stock is the room's heat, seen as its temperature. One balancing loop compares the temperature with the thermostat setting. When the room is too cold, it turns the furnace on and heat flows in; when the room is warm enough, it turns the flow off.
A second balancing loop is heat leaking to the outside. It tries to make the room equal to the outdoor temperature, as a cooling coffee cup does.

Alone, the furnace loop would warm a cold room quickly to the setting (18°C in the book) and hold it there. Alone, the leak loop would let a warm room cool very slowly toward the outside (10°C in the book's run). Better insulation means a slower drop.
card.rule: A stock with two balancing loops is pulled toward two goals at once: the thermostat setting and the outside temperature.
card.limits: Describing each loop alone is a way to understand it; in a real room both run together, so neither alone predicts the temperature.

media.alt: Stock-and-flow diagram with one box, room temperature. A valved pipe brings heat in from a cloud on the left; another valved pipe carries heat out to a cloud on the right. Thin arrows show the inflow valve driven by the gap between thermostat setting and room temperature, and the outflow valve driven by the gap between inside and outside temperature. Both loops are marked balancing.

Line graph over eight hours, temperature in degrees Celsius. A flat horizontal line marks the thermostat setting near 18. The room temperature curve starts near 10, climbs steeply at first, then flattens and meets the setting line after about four hours, staying there.

Line graph over eight hours. A flat line marks the outside temperature at 10 degrees Celsius. The room temperature curve starts near 17.5 and slopes gently downward, reaching roughly 13 by hour eight, still above the outside line and heading toward it.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
concepts.title: Why the room settles below the setting
concepts.question: When both loops run together, where does the room temperature settle, and why?

paragraphs: With enough insulation and a properly sized furnace, the heating loop dominates the cooling loop, so the room ends up warm even when it starts cold on a cold day. As the room warms, the gap with the outside widens and more heat leaks out.
Still, the furnace puts in more heat than leaks out, so the room warms nearly to the target. Then the furnace cycles on and off to make up for the heat constantly flowing out.

The temperature levels off slightly below the 18°C setting. The leak drains heat even while the furnace is being told to replace it. The book compares this to keeping a bucket full when there is a hole in the bottom, where the fuller the bucket the faster the outflow.
card.example: In the bucket picture the water pressure at the hole rises as the bucket fills, so the outflow rises, just as a warmer room loses heat faster.
card.rule: When a leak runs alongside a maintaining loop, the stock levels off a little short of the goal.
card.limits: This describes a well-insulated room with a properly sized furnace; if the leak overwhelms the furnace, the result is different (see breakdown point).

media.alt: Line graph over eight hours with a flat thermostat setting near 18 degrees Celsius. The room temperature curve starts at 10, rises quickly for about two hours, then runs flat just under the setting line, near 17, and never quite reaches it.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
concepts.title: Set the goal to cover the drain
concepts.question: How should you set a stock-maintaining loop's goal when something drains or fills the stock as you work?

paragraphs: From the thermostat Meadows draws a specific principle: in thermostat-like systems you must take account of whatever draining or filling processes are going on, or you will not reach the target level of the stock.

To hold a room at 18°C you set the thermostat a little above it. To pay off a credit card, or the national debt, you must raise your repayment rate high enough to cover the charges you incur while you are paying, interest included.
In other words, your mental model of the system must include all the important flows, or the system's behavior will surprise you.
card.rule: Set a stock-maintaining loop's goal to allow for the drains and inflows acting on the stock, or it will fall short of or exceed the target.
card.limits: Our reading: the principle says to compensate, not by how much; the size of the adjustment must be judged from the size of the flows.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
concepts.title: Feedback can only change the future
concepts.question: Why can a feedback loop never correct the behavior that produced its own signal?

paragraphs: Meadows draws a general principle: the information a feedback loop delivers can affect only future behavior. It cannot deliver a signal fast enough to correct the behavior that drove the current feedback, and even nonphysical information takes time to feed back into the system.
A person who decides on the basis of feedback cannot change the behavior that produced it; the decision affects only what comes next. So there will always be delays in responding.

A flow cannot react instantly to a flow. It can react only to a change in a stock, and only after a slight delay to register the information. In a bathtub it takes a split second to read the depth and decide to adjust the taps.
card.rule: Feedback can change only future behavior: a flow responds to a stock after a delay, never instantly to another flow.
card.limits: Our reading: the delay may be a split second and harmless in a bathtub; it matters most where it is long compared with how fast the stock changes.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
concepts.title: A stock that keeps changing while you control it
concepts.question: Why can the thermostat structure cause real trouble in systems that are less forgiving than a room?

paragraphs: For a thermostat the control problem is not serious. But in other systems with the same competing-loop structure, the fact that the stock goes on changing while you are trying to control it can create real problems.

Take a store trying to hold inventory at a certain level. It cannot order stock instantly to make up a shortfall that is already visible. If it ignores the goods that will be sold while the order is on its way, inventory will never be quite high enough.
The structure is the same as the thermostat: one loop drains the stock, another loop works to refill it, and the stock does not wait.
card.rule: Where a stock keeps changing while you correct it, plan for what will drain or fill it during the correction.
card.limits: Our reading: the card names where the trap occurs but gives no formula; the size of the allowance depends on the flows involved.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
concepts.title: Every balancing loop has a breakdown point
concepts.question: What makes a balancing loop lose its hold on the goal?

paragraphs: Every balancing feedback loop has its breakdown point: the place where other loops pull the stock away from its goal more strongly than it can pull back.

In the thermostat system this happens if the heating loop is weakened, with a smaller furnace that cannot put out as much heat, or if the cooling loop is strengthened, with colder outside air, less insulation or larger leaks.

In the book's second run the outside temperature falls far below freezing and the house is leaky. At the coldest times the furnace cannot keep up, the loop pulling the room toward the outside dominates for a while, and the room gets uncomfortable.
card.rule: A balancing loop holds its goal only while it is stronger than the forces pulling the stock away.
card.limits: Our reading: strength is relative; the same furnace may be adequate in one house and overwhelmed in a leakier one.

media.alt: Line graph over 24 hours. The thermostat setting is a flat line near 18 degrees Celsius. Outside temperature starts at 10, sinks to about minus 5 around hour 12, then climbs back toward 10. The room warms from 10 to about 17 within a few hours and then stays within about a degree of that level all day.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
concepts.title: Reading behavior over time with the bathtub rule
concepts.question: How do you explain each rise and fall of the room temperature in the leaky-house run?

paragraphs: Meadows asks you to follow how the variables in the leaky-house run relate as time unfolds. At first both the room and the outside are cool, the furnace's inflow exceeds the leak, and the room warms. For an hour or two the outside is mild enough that the furnace replaces most of the lost heat and the room stays near the desired temperature.

Then the outside temperature falls and the leak grows. The furnace cannot replace the heat fast enough, so with less heat arriving than leaking out, the room cools. Finally the outside warms, the leak slows, and the furnace, still at full tilt, pulls ahead and warms the room.
The bathtub rule explains every turn: whenever the furnace puts in more heat than leaks out, the temperature rises; whenever inflow falls behind outflow, it falls.
card.rule: To explain behavior over time, ask at each moment whether the inflow is ahead of or behind the outflow.
card.limits: The rule gives the direction of change, not its size; sizes depend on the strengths of the two loops.

media.alt: Line graph over 24 hours. The thermostat setting is flat near 18 degrees Celsius. Outside temperature falls from 10 to about minus 5 around hour 12, then recovers toward 10. The room warms to about 16 within two hours, slides down to about 12 near hour 13, then climbs back to about 16 by hour 24.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: Births and deaths: a reinforcing and a balancing loop
concepts.question: What does a stock do when one reinforcing loop and one balancing loop act on it?

paragraphs: A population has a reinforcing loop that makes it grow through its birth rate and a balancing loop that makes it shrink through its death rate. Meadows calls this pairing one of the most common and important system structures.

While fertility and mortality are constant, which in real systems they rarely are, the behavior is simple. The population grows exponentially or dies off, depending on whether the births loop is stronger than the deaths loop.
card.rule: With constant fertility and mortality, the stronger loop decides: births ahead means exponential growth, deaths ahead means decline.
card.limits: This is the simple case; real fertility and mortality rarely stay constant.

media.alt: Stock-and-flow diagram with one box, population. Births flow in from a cloud through a valve; deaths flow out to a cloud through a valve. Fertility is an arrow into the births valve, mortality an arrow into the deaths valve. A loop from population to births is marked R for reinforcing; a loop from population to deaths is marked B for balancing.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: Worked numbers: the 2007 world population
concepts.question: How do you tell from birth and death rates whether a population grows or declines?

paragraphs: In 2007 world population was 6.6 billion. Fertility was roughly 21 births a year for every 1,000 people and mortality was 9 deaths per 1,000. Fertility was higher, so the reinforcing loop dominated.
If those rates continued unchanged, a child born then would see the world population more than double by the age of 60. The net gain is the gap between the two flows, 12 per 1,000 a year.
card.rule: Compare the two flows: whichever is larger decides whether the stock grows or falls.
card.limits: The rates are scenario assumptions; the projection holds only if they stay unchanged, which real rates rarely do.

media.alt: Line graph of population in billions from about 2005 to 2107, with birth and death rates per person held constant and births above deaths. The curve starts near 6.5 billion and rises throughout, bending upward so that it climbs more steeply in later decades, reaching about 22 billion at the end.

Line graph of population in billions from about 2005 to 2105, with birth and death rates per person held constant and deaths well above births. The curve starts near 6.5 billion and slopes steadily downward, flattening gradually as it goes, and ends below 3 billion.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: When the flows change, the line bends
concepts.question: What happens to a population's course when fertility falls until it equals mortality?

paragraphs: Things get more interesting when fertility and mortality change over time. Changing flows bend the line of the stock's behavior.

When the UN makes long-range projections, it generally assumes that as countries develop, average fertility declines toward replacement, where on average each woman has 1.85 children. Mortality was assumed to decline too, but more slowly, since it is already low in most places.
If world fertility fell steadily to equal mortality by 2035 and both stayed constant after that, the population would level off. Births would exactly balance deaths in dynamic equilibrium.
card.rule: When the flows change, the stock's line bends; if inflow comes to equal outflow, the stock levels off in dynamic equilibrium.
card.limits: A levelling-off scenario depends on an assumed path for fertility and mortality, which no one can prove in advance.

media.alt: Line graph of population in billions, 2005 to 2107. The curve rises gently from about 6.5 billion for the first twenty years, then runs perfectly flat at about 7.5 billion for the rest of the period.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: Dominance: which loop sets the behavior
concepts.question: What does it mean for one feedback loop to dominate another?

paragraphs: When one loop dominates another, it has a stronger impact on behavior. Dominance is an important concept in systems thinking because systems often have several competing feedback loops at the same time, and the loops that dominate determine the behavior.

In the population run, at first fertility is higher than mortality, so the reinforcing growth loop dominates and growth is exponential. That loop gradually weakens as fertility falls, until it exactly equals the balancing loop. Then neither loop dominates and the system is in dynamic equilibrium.
card.rule: Complex behaviors often arise as the relative strengths of feedback loops shift, so that first one loop and then another dominates.
card.limits: Our reading: equal strength is a balance, not an absence of loops; if either loop strengthens again, dominance shifts again.

media.alt: Line graph of population in billions, 2005 to 2107, with bracketed labels. The curve rises from 6.5 to about 8, flattens from roughly 2030 to 2050, then climbs steeply to about 18.5. Brackets mark the first and last stretches as fertility above mortality, and the flat middle as the two equal.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: The repertoire of a reinforcing and a balancing loop
concepts.question: What behaviors can a stock show when one reinforcing and one balancing loop act on it?

paragraphs: For a simple system of one reinforcing and one balancing loop, the possible behaviors depend on what happens to the driving variables, here fertility and mortality.

A stock governed by linked reinforcing and balancing loops will grow exponentially if the reinforcing loop dominates. It will die off if the balancing loop dominates, and level off if the two are equal in strength. Or it will do a sequence of these things, one after another, if the relative strengths of the loops change over time.
card.example: The book shows growth, decline and stabilization as three separate curves, then a fourth picture in which dominance shifts so one behavior follows another.
card.rule: A reinforcing loop plus a balancing loop on one stock gives growth, decline, levelling off, or a sequence of these.
card.limits: These are the possibilities for the two-loop structure without delays; later examples show other structures behaving differently.

media.alt: Small graph of a quantity against time from 2000 to 2120, with a vertical scale up to 25. A single curve starts low, near 7, and rises ever more steeply to about 22 by the end: growth that accelerates.

Small graph of a quantity against time from 2000 to 2120, with a vertical scale up to 25. A single curve starts near 7 and slopes steadily downward, flattening a little, to about 3 by the end: decline.

Small graph of a quantity against time from 2000 to 2120, with a vertical scale up to 25. A single curve starts near 7, rises briefly over the first twenty or thirty years, then runs perfectly flat at about 8: stabilization.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: Testing a model, question one: will the drivers unfold this way?
concepts.question: How should you treat the scenario's assumptions about its driving factors?

paragraphs: Every time you hear an economic prediction, a corporate budget, a weather forecast or a climate projection, you meet a scenario. Meadows gives three questions for judging how well the underlying model represents reality. The first: are the driving factors likely to unfold this way? For the population: what are the birth and death rates likely to do?

This question cannot be answered factually. It is a guess about the future, and the future is inherently uncertain. You may have a strong opinion, but nothing can prove you right until the future happens.
A systems analysis can test a number of scenarios to see what happens if the driving factors do different things. You have to be the judge of which scenario, if any, should be taken seriously.
card.rule: Treat the future of the driving factors as an uncertain guess, test several scenarios, and judge for yourself which deserve to be taken seriously.
card.limits: This question tests the inputs, not the model; a model with believable inputs can still react in the wrong way, which the second question checks.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: Testing a model, question two: does the system react this way?
concepts.question: What makes a model useful if nobody can know its driving scenarios are realistic?

paragraphs: The second question is whether, if the driving factors did unfold that way, the system would react that way. This is the more scientific question: how good is the model, and does it capture the inherent dynamics of the system, regardless of whether you believe in the scenario?

For the population scenarios the answer is roughly yes. The population model is very simple, but it grows under the conditions in which a real population would grow and declines under those in which a real one would decline. The numbers are off, but the basic behavior pattern is realistic.
So model utility depends not on whether the driving scenarios are realistic, since no one can know that for sure, but on whether the model responds with a realistic pattern of behavior.
card.rule: Judge a model by whether it responds to its inputs with a realistic pattern of behavior, not by whether the scenarios come true.
card.limits: A realistic pattern does not mean accurate numbers; the author says the numbers in her population model are off.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: Testing a model, question three: what drives the drivers?
concepts.question: Why must you ask what is driving the driving factors of a model?

paragraphs: The third question is: what is driving the driving factors? In the population model, what adjusts the inflows and outflows? Meadows says this is a question about system boundaries. It needs a hard look at the driving factors to see whether they are really independent or are also embedded in the system.

Does the size of the population feed back to influence fertility or mortality? Do economics, the environment and social trends influence them, and does population size affect those factors? The answer to all of these is yes.

Fertility and mortality are governed by feedback loops too, and at least some of those loops are affected by the size of the population. The population model is only one piece of a much larger system.
card.rule: Ask what drives the model's driving factors, and check whether they are really outside the system or part of it.
card.limits: Our reading: every model needs some boundary; the question asks you to check that the boundary is reasonable, not to remove it.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: Capital: the economy's own births and deaths
concepts.question: Which loops govern an economy's stock of capital, and which population quantities do they match?

paragraphs: At the heart of the economy is another reinforcing-plus-balancing system with the same structure as population. The more physical capital (machines and factories) and the more efficient production (output per unit of capital), the more output the economy produces each year.
The more output, the more can be invested in new capital. This reinforcing loop is like the birth loop. The investment fraction, the share of output invested, is equivalent to fertility.

Physical capital is drained by depreciation: obsolescence and wearing out. This balancing loop is equivalent to the death loop. The mortality of capital is set by the average capital lifetime; a longer lifetime means a smaller fraction to be retired and replaced each year.
card.rule: Capital has a reinforcing loop of investing output, like births, and a balancing loop of depreciation, like deaths.
card.limits: Our reading: the match is in structure, not in how the two systems look.

media.alt: Stock-and-flow diagram with one box, capital stock. Investment flows in from a cloud; depreciation flows out to a cloud. Arrows run from capital to annual output, which depends on output per unit capital, and on to investment, which also depends on the investment fraction: a reinforcing loop. A second loop from capital to depreciation, which also depends on capital lifetime, is balancing.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: Capital lifetime decides growth or decline
concepts.question: With investment share and efficiency fixed, what decides whether capital grows, holds or declines?

paragraphs: Whether capital grows, stays constant or dies off depends on whether the reinforcing growth loop stays stronger than the balancing depreciation loop. That depends on three things: the investment fraction, the efficiency of capital (output per unit of capital) and the average capital lifetime.

Hold the first two constant and the lifetime decides. With a short lifetime, capital wears out faster than it is replaced and the economy slowly declines. When depreciation just balances investment, there is dynamic equilibrium. With a long lifetime, capital grows exponentially, and the longer the lifetime, the faster.

In the book's example output is one third of capital each year and 20 percent is invested, so each year a fifteenth of capital is added. A 15-year lifetime retires a fifteenth, so capital just keeps up.
