card.rule: With investment fraction and efficiency fixed, capital declines, holds or grows as its lifetime is shorter than, equal to or longer than the break-even lifetime.
card.limits: The break-even lifetime depends on the investment fraction and efficiency; change either and it moves.

media.alt: Line graph over 50 years of capital stock, with every curve starting at 100. One curve, labelled 20-year lifetime, climbs steadily to about 230. A flat line, labelled 15-year lifetime, stays at 100. A third curve, labelled 10-year lifetime, falls steadily to about 20.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: Linking population and capital
concepts.question: Why should a long-term economic model link the population and capital structures?

paragraphs: Population and capital influence each other. Population contributes labor to output, and it increases demands on consumption, which lowers the investment fraction. Economic output feeds back to population: a richer economy usually has better health care and a lower death rate, and it also usually has a lower birth rate.

Many factors influence capital's output ratio, investment fraction and lifetime too, such as interest rates, technology, tax policy, consumption habits and prices. So just about any long-term model of a real economy should link the two structures to show how they affect each other.
card.rule: A long-term economic model should link population and capital, because each feeds back on the other.
card.limits: Our reading: the link adds loops and variables, so the model grows more complex than either structure alone.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
concepts.title: Similar structures, similar behaviors
concepts.question: Why do very different-looking systems behave in similar ways?

paragraphs: Meadows calls capital the same kind of zoo animal as population, though factories and shipments look nothing like babies and aging people. From a systems view they share what matters: a stock governed by a reinforcing growth loop and a balancing death loop. Both also age; steel mills and turbines get old and die as people do.

Systems with similar feedback structures produce similar dynamic behaviors, even if their outward appearance is completely dissimilar. This is one of the central insights of systems theory, as central as the observation that systems largely cause their own behavior.

A coffee cup cooling is like a warmed room cooling, like a radioactive substance decaying, and like a population or industrial economy aging and dying. Each declines as the result of a balancing feedback loop.
card.rule: Systems with similar feedback structures produce similar behavior, however different they look.
card.limits: Similar structure gives similar patterns of behavior, not the same numbers or time scales.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.title: A dealership's inventory as a thermostat
concepts.question: What loops hold a car dealer's inventory near the level she wants?

paragraphs: A car dealership's stock of cars has an inflow of deliveries from factories and an outflow of sales. By itself it behaves like water in a bathtub. The dealer wants enough inventory to cover ten days of sales.

She watches perceived sales. If they seem to be rising, she raises orders to bring inventory up to a new desired inventory that gives ten days of coverage at the higher sales rate. Higher sales mean higher perceived sales, a larger gap to desired inventory, more orders, more deliveries and higher inventory.

This is a version of the thermostat system: one balancing loop of sales draining the stock, and a competing balancing loop that resupplies what is lost. With no delays, a 10 percent rise in demand gives a not very surprising result.
card.rule: Inventory is held by two competing balancing loops: sales drain it and orders for deliveries refill it.
card.limits: This version has no delays; the next ideas show how adding them changes the behavior.

media.alt: Stock-and-flow diagram with one box, inventory of cars on the lot. Deliveries flow in through a valve; sales flow out through a valve, set by customer demand. Inventory is compared with desired inventory to give a discrepancy, which sets orders to the factory and so deliveries. Perceived sales, taken from sales, feed desired inventory and orders. Two loops are marked balancing.

Line graph over 100 days of cars on the lot, for a dealer with no delays. Inventory sits flat at 200 until about day 25, then steps quickly up to about 220 and stays flat at that higher level through day 100, with no swings.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.title: Three delays in the inventory loop
concepts.question: Which three delays does Meadows add to the dealer's inventory system?

paragraphs: Meadows adds three delays typical of the real world. First, a perception delay: before ordering, the dealer averages sales over the past five days.
Second, a response delay: she does not make up the whole adjustment in one order. She makes up one third of any shortfall with each order, which means partial adjustments over three days.
Third, a delivery delay: it takes five days for the supplier at the factory to receive an order, process it and deliver it to the dealership.
card.rule: Name each delay in a loop: how long it takes to perceive a change, to respond to it and to deliver the result.
card.limits: Our reading: these numbers belong to this dealer; other systems have delays of other kinds and lengths.

media.alt: Diagram of a car dealer's inventory: one box, cars on the lot, with deliveries flowing in through a valve and sales flowing out, and two loops marked balancing. Three labelled delay markers are added: a delivery delay on the deliveries valve, a response delay on the link into orders to the factory, and a perception delay on the link from sales to perceived sales.

Graph over 100 days in cars per day. A solid line, the sales rate, stays flat at 20, then steps sharply to about 22 on day 25. A dashed line, the dealer's perceived sales, follows it, rising gradually and catching up to about 22 within roughly ten days.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.title: Delays in a balancing loop cause oscillation
concepts.question: Why does a permanent 10 percent jump in sales now make inventory swing up and down?

paragraphs: With the three delays in place, the same permanent 10 percent jump in demand produces oscillations. The system still has only two balancing loops, as the simple thermostat did, but it does not behave like it.

A single step up in sales makes inventory drop. The dealer waits to be sure the rise will last, then orders more to cover the new rate and rebuild stock. Orders take time to arrive, so inventory falls further and orders rise again.

Eventually the large volume of orders arrives and inventory recovers, and more than recovers, because she ordered too much. She cuts back, but high past orders still arrive, so she orders too little, and inventory gets too low again.

This is not because the dealer is stupid. She works in a system where timely information is impossible and physical delays stop her actions from acting at once. A delay in a balancing feedback loop makes a system likely to oscillate.
card.rule: A delay in a balancing feedback loop makes a system likely to oscillate.
card.limits: Delays do not guarantee oscillation: how much delay causes what kind of oscillation, in what circumstances, is not simple.

media.alt: Line graph over 100 days of cars on the lot, for a dealer with three delays. Inventory is flat at 200 until about day 25, then swings around a higher level: dips, rises, falls again, each swing larger than the last. Peaks climb from about 245 to about 290 and troughs fall from about 190 to about 135.

Graph over 100 days in cars per day. A solid line, orders to the factory, and a dashed line, deliveries, both stay at 20 until day 25, then oscillate with growing swings, from about 30 up to about 50 at the peaks and down to nearly zero in the late troughs. Each dashed peak trails the matching solid peak by a few days.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.title: High leverage, wrong direction
concepts.question: Why can speeding up a response make an oscillating system worse?

paragraphs: Finding the oscillations intolerable, the dealer decides to shorten delays. First she averages sales over two days instead of five before adjusting orders. Not much happens; if anything the oscillations are a bit worse.
Then she tries shortening her reaction time, making up perceived shortfalls in two days instead of three. Things get very much worse. She sees it as high leverage in the wrong direction.

Meadows says this perverse result is seen all the time. Someone trying to fix a system is attracted to a policy lever that does have a strong effect, and then pulls it in the wrong direction. It is one example of the counterintuitive behavior of systems when we try to change them.
card.rule: A lever with a strong effect can worsen a system if you pull it the wrong way, so check the direction before acting.
card.limits: Our reading: whether a faster response helps depends on the system's delays; in this system speeding up was harmful.

media.alt: Line graph over 100 days of cars on the lot, for a dealer whose perception delay is shortened. Inventory is flat at 200 until about day 25, then oscillates with swings that grow: peaks near 255, 280 and 310, troughs near 175, 150 and 130.

Line graph over 100 days of cars on the lot, for a dealer whose response time is shortened. Inventory is flat at 200 until about day 25, then swings widely: peaks near 270, 415 and 420, troughs near 125 and 120. Cycles are about 20 days long, and the swings reach well above and below the starting level.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.title: Overreacting and the case for slowing down
concepts.question: How can a longer response delay stabilize a system that is oscillating?

paragraphs: Part of the problem is that the dealer has been reacting not too slowly but too quickly. Given how the system is set up, she has been overreacting. Things go better if she lengthens the response delay from three days to six rather than shortening it to two.
With the six-day response, the oscillations are greatly damped and the system finds its new equilibrium fairly efficiently.

Delays are pervasive in systems and strongly determine behavior. Changing a delay's length may or may not make a large change in behavior, depending on the type of delay and the other delays. Changing delays can make a system much easier or much harder to manage.
card.rule: Slowing a response that overreacts can damp oscillations, so check the delays before speeding anything up.
card.limits: The result holds for this system's delays; another type or mix of delay lengths may respond differently.

media.alt: Line graph over 100 days of cars on the lot, for a dealer whose response delay is lengthened. Inventory is flat at 200 until about day 25, dips to about 185, rises to about 225, and then settles near 220 by about day 70, with only small swings.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.title: From one store to business cycles
concepts.question: What does Meadows say causes business cycles?

paragraphs: Imagine the inventory is that of all the unsold automobiles in America. Orders for more or fewer cars affect production not only at assembly plants and parts factories but at steel mills, rubber and glass plants, textile producers and energy producers. Everywhere there are perception, production, delivery and construction delays.

More production means more jobs, which lets more people buy cars. That reinforcing loop also works in reverse: less production, fewer jobs, fewer car sales, less production. Speculators add another reinforcing loop by trading auto shares on recent performance, so a production upsurge lifts share prices and vice versa.

This large system, with interconnected industries responding through delays, entraining each other's oscillations and amplified by multipliers and speculators, is the primary cause of business cycles. They do not come from presidents, though presidents can ease or intensify the optimism of upturns and the pain of downturns.
card.rule: Business cycles arise mainly from delayed balancing loops, amplified by reinforcing loops, across linked industries, not from leaders.
card.limits: Presidents can ease or intensify the swings; the claim is only that they are not the primary cause.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.title: Growth meets a constraint
concepts.question: Why must a physical, exponentially growing system contain a balancing loop that eventually constrains it?

paragraphs: The systems so far were free of constraints from their surroundings, so we could see their internal dynamics. But any real physical entity exchanges things with its environment: a corporation needs energy, materials, workers and customers; a crop needs water and nutrients; a population needs food, water and living space.

So any physical, growing system runs into some constraint sooner or later. The pattern is so common that systems thinkers call it the limits-to-growth archetype. Seeing a growing population, corporation, rumor, epidemic or product, we look for the reinforcing loops driving it and the balancing loops that will constrain it.
We know those balancing loops are there even when they do not yet dominate, because no physical system can grow forever in a finite environment. A hot new product will eventually saturate its market.

Pollution works the same way as resources. A pollution constraint can be nonrenewable, if the environment cannot absorb the pollutant, or renewable, if it has a finite capacity to remove it. The dynamics are the same with opposite flow directions.
card.rule: In a physical, exponentially growing system there must be at least one reinforcing loop driving growth and at least one balancing loop constraining it.
card.limits: The constraining loop may not dominate yet, so it can stay invisible for a long time while growth looks unlimited.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
concepts.title: The oil company as a capital system
concepts.question: How is an oil company's capital stock built up and drained?

paragraphs: Take a capital system that earns money by extracting a nonrenewable resource, such as an oil company that has found a huge field. It is the earlier capital-growth system with profit instead of output. Depreciation is the familiar balancing loop: oil equipment has a 20-year lifetime, so one twentieth, or 5 percent, of the stock is retired each year.

Capital builds up through investment of profits from extraction: more capital allows more extraction, more profit and more reinvestment, the reinforcing loop. The company has a goal of 5 percent annual growth in its capital; if profit is too small for that, it invests whatever profit it can.
Profit is income minus cost. For now price and operating cost per unit of capital are held constant.
card.rule: The oil company is a capital system: reinvested profit is the reinforcing loop, depreciation the balancing loop, and profit is income minus cost.
card.limits: The constant-price and constant-cost assumptions are simplifications that the author relaxes later.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
concepts.title: The depletion loop
concepts.question: Which new balancing loop eventually controls the growth of the oil company's capital?

paragraphs: What is not constant is the yield of resource per unit of capital. The resource is nonrenewable, so the stock feeding extraction has no input. As it is extracted, the next barrel is harder to get: deeper, more dilute, or under less natural pressure. More costly and sophisticated measures are needed to keep it coming.

This is a new balancing loop that ultimately controls capital growth. The more capital, the higher the extraction rate; the higher the extraction, the lower the resource stock; the lower the stock, the lower the yield per unit of capital; so the lower the profit, the lower the investment and the slower the growth of capital.
card.rule: In a nonrenewable resource system, more capital speeds extraction, which depletes the stock and lowers yield per unit of capital, so profit and investment fall.
card.limits: The loop bites because the resource has no input; the fishing example later shows what changes when the stock is renewed.

media.alt: Stock-and-flow diagram of capital and a resource. Capital has an investment inflow, driven by profit and a growth goal, and a depreciation outflow set by capital lifetime. Below it a resource stock, with no inflow, drains through extraction, set by capital and by yield per unit capital. Yield feeds price and profit, forming a third loop, marked balancing.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
concepts.title: A 200-year supply peaks in 40 years
concepts.question: Why does extraction from a 200-year deposit peak after only about 40 years?

paragraphs: In the model the deposit holds enough oil to supply the initial scale of operation for 200 years. Yet actual extraction peaks at about 40 years, because of the surprising effect of exponential growth in extraction.
Reinvesting 10 percent a year against 5 percent depreciation, capital and extraction grow at 5 percent a year, so they double in the first 14 years.

By year 50 the cost of maintaining the capital has overwhelmed the income from extraction. Profits no longer keep investment ahead of depreciation, the operation shuts down quickly as capital declines, and the last, most expensive part of the resource stays in the ground.
card.rule: Exponential growth in extraction uses up a large deposit far sooner than its size suggests: a 200-year supply peaks near year 40, and by year 50 costs overwhelm income and the operation shuts down quickly.
card.limits: The dates belong to this model's assumptions; the shape, a rise, a peak and a fast fall, is the classic depletion pattern.

media.alt: Line graph of the extraction rate over 100 years. A smooth curve rises slowly from near zero to a rounded peak of about 28 between years 40 and 45, then drops fairly quickly and sits close to zero from about year 65 or 70.

Line graph of the capital stock over 100 years. A curve rises from near zero, accelerating, to a sharp point of about 60 near year 52, then declines steadily and more gradually, reaching a low value near zero by about year 100.

Line graph of the resource stock over 100 years, in a run with constant price and continuing depreciation. The curve starts at 1000 and declines slowly at first, falls fastest between about years 25 and 55, then flattens and sits near zero from about year 65 on. Yield per unit of capital falls as the stock shrinks.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
concepts.title: A bigger deposit buys little time
concepts.question: How much longer does extraction last if the resource turns out to be twice or four times larger?

paragraphs: Suppose the resource is twice as large as geologists thought, or four times. It makes a huge difference to the total oil that can be extracted. But with the same goal of reinvesting 10 percent a year for 5 percent capital growth, each doubling of the resource shifts the peak of extraction by only about 14 years.

A quantity growing exponentially toward a limit reaches it in a surprisingly short time. With exponential growth of extraction, a doubling or quadrupling of a nonrenewable resource gives little added time to develop alternatives.
The higher and faster you grow, the farther and faster you fall when your capital depends on a nonrenewable resource.
card.rule: Each doubling of a nonrenewable resource delays the peak of exponentially growing extraction by only about 14 years, at 5 percent growth.
card.limits: The 14 years follows from the model's 5 percent growth; a different growth rate gives a different doubling time.

media.alt: Line graph of the extraction rate over 100 years with three curves sharing the same slow start. The base curve peaks near 27 between years 40 and 45 and collapses. A doubled-resource curve peaks near 70 around year 56. A quadrupled-resource curve peaks near 165 around year 72. Each falls to near zero soon after its peak.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
concepts.title: Get rich fast or stay rich longer
concepts.question: Which numbers matter for a worker at an oil field, and what is the real choice?

paragraphs: For maximum-rate profit, the resource's ultimate size is the key number. A worker concerned with the job and the community needs two: the size of the resource and the desired growth rate of capital. Here the goal of a feedback loop is crucial to the behavior of the system.
The real choice in managing a nonrenewable resource is whether to get rich very fast or to get less rich but stay that way longer.

In the book's graph of extraction over time, the desired growth rate above depreciation varies from 1 to 3, 5 and 7 percent a year. The more profit is reinvested, the sooner the peak; at 7 percent the 200-year supply peaks within 40 years.
card.rule: How long a nonrenewable resource lasts depends on its size and on the growth rate of the capital extracting it: faster growth gives an earlier peak.
card.limits: Our reading: the model shows the trade-off between speed and duration; it does not say which is better.

media.alt: Line graph of the extraction rate over 100 years with four curves from the same low start, one per capital growth goal. The 7 percent curve peaks highest early, near 37 around year 35, then drops fast. The 5 and 3 percent curves peak lower and later. The 1 percent curve stays low, near 8, almost flat to year 100.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
concepts.title: Rising prices and cheaper technology
concepts.question: What happens to capital and depletion when the oil price rises or costs fall?

paragraphs: Suppose price is not constant. In the short term the resource may be so vital that a higher price will not cut demand, so as the resource gets scarce its price rises steeply. The higher price gives more profit, so investment goes up, capital continues rising, and the more costly remaining resources can be extracted.

Compared with the constant-price run, the main effect of a rising price is to build the capital stock higher before it collapses. The same happens if technology brings operating costs down, as with advanced recovery from oil wells, processing low-grade taconite from exhausted iron mines, and cyanide leaching of gold and silver tailings.
The consequence is that the resource is depleted even faster at the end.
card.rule: Rising prices or falling costs let capital grow larger before it collapses, and the resource then runs out even faster.
card.limits: This assumes demand stays firm despite higher prices, which the author allows only for the short term.

media.alt: Line graph of the extraction rate over 100 years, in a run where price rises as the resource grows scarce. A smooth curve rises slowly from near zero to a rounded peak of about 28 between years 40 and 45, then falls fairly quickly and sits near zero by about year 65 or 70.

Line graph of the capital stock over 100 years, in a run where price rises as the resource grows scarce. A curve rises from near zero, accelerating, to a sharp point of about 110 near year 63, then declines gradually to about 15 at year 100. With constant price, capital peaked near 60 around year 52.

Line graph of the resource stock over 100 years, in a run where price rises as the resource grows scarce. A curve starts at 1000, declines slowly at first, falls fastest between about years 25 and 50, and is near zero from about year 60 onward.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
concepts.title: Renewable resources and how they refill
concepts.question: How do living and nonliving renewable resources regenerate differently?

paragraphs: Assume the same capital system, but now the resource stock has an inflow, making it renewable. The resource could be fish with boats as the capital; trees and sawmills; or pasture and cows.

Living renewable resources such as fish, trees and grass regenerate from themselves through a reinforcing feedback loop. Nonliving renewable resources such as sunlight, wind and river water are not regenerated through a reinforcing loop but through a steady input that refills the stock whatever its current state.

The same structure appears in a cold epidemic, where the virus spares its victims, who can catch another cold, and in sales of a product people buy regularly, where the stock of potential customers is ever regenerated.
card.rule: A renewable resource has an input that refills its stock: living resources regenerate through a reinforcing loop, nonliving ones through a steady input.
card.limits: Our reading: renewable does not mean unlimited; the next ideas show how a renewable resource's regeneration can fail.

media.alt: Stock-and-flow diagram of capital and a renewable resource. Capital has investment and depreciation flows with a growth goal, profit and price. The resource stock has a regeneration inflow from a cloud, influenced by the stock itself and by a regeneration rate, and a harvest outflow set by capital and yield per unit capital. Yield feeds price and profit.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
concepts.title: Regeneration depends on density
concepts.question: How does a fish population's reproduction rate change as its density falls?

paragraphs: In the fishery, capital lasts 20 years and the industry grows at 5 percent a year if it can. As fish get scarce they cost more capital to harvest: bigger boats for longer distances, sonar to find the last schools, miles-long drift nets, on-board refrigeration.

The fish regeneration rate is not constant but depends on fish density. If the fish are very dense, reproduction is near zero, limited by food and habitat. If the population falls a bit, it regenerates faster and faster. At some point reproduction reaches its maximum. Further depletion makes it breed slower and slower, because fish cannot find each other or another species moves into the niche.
card.rule: Regeneration of a living resource is nonlinear: near zero when crowded, fastest at a middle density, and slowing again when depleted.
card.limits: Our reading: this is the shape in the simplified model; real species differ in where the peak and the threshold lie.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
concepts.title: Three fishery outcomes and the technology trap
concepts.question: How can a small gain in fishing efficiency turn a stable fishery into an unstable one?

paragraphs: In the first run, capital and harvest rise exponentially. The fish stock falls but that stimulates reproduction, so for decades the harvest keeps rising. Eventually the stock falls low enough to cut profit, and falling harvest brings investment down fast enough to bring the fleet into equilibrium with the fish. The fleet cannot grow forever but can keep a high and steady harvest forever.

A minor change in the controlling balancing loop, yield per unit of capital, makes a surprising difference. If new technology such as sonar lets boats hold their catch a little longer as fish decline, the system becomes unstable: harvest, capital and fish oscillate around a stable value. This is high leverage, wrong direction again.
With even better technology, boats stay profitable at very low fish density, and the result is overshoot and collapse of fish, capital and harvest.
card.rule: A slight increase in yield per unit of capital can turn a stable fishery into an oscillating one, and a larger one into collapse.
card.limits: These are three runs of one simplified model; the outcome depends on the strength of the balancing loop, as the next idea explains.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
concepts.title: What decides the fishery's outcome
concepts.question: Which two things decide whether a renewable resource system finds equilibrium, oscillates or collapses?

paragraphs: Meadows shows three possible behaviors: overshoot and adjustment to a sustainable equilibrium; overshoot beyond it followed by oscillation around it; and overshoot followed by collapse of the resource and of the industry that depends on it.

Which one occurs depends on two things. The first is the critical threshold beyond which the resource's ability to regenerate itself is damaged. The second is the rapidity and effectiveness of the balancing loop that slows capital growth as the resource is depleted.

If that feedback is fast enough to stop capital growth before the threshold is reached, the system comes smoothly into equilibrium. If it is slower and less effective, it oscillates. If it is very weak, so capital keeps growing after the resource drops below its threshold, resource and industry both collapse.
card.rule: The outcome depends on the resource's critical threshold and on how fast and how well the balancing loop stops capital growth.
card.limits: Our reading: the rule is qualitative; it does not say where the threshold lies for any real resource.

concepts.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
concepts.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
concepts.title: Stock-limited versus flow-limited resources
concepts.question: Why do nonrenewable and renewable resources set different kinds of limits?

paragraphs: Nonrenewable resources are stock-limited. The whole stock is available at once and can be extracted at any rate, limited mainly by extraction capital. But the stock is not renewed, so the faster the extraction, the shorter the resource's lifetime.

Renewable resources are flow-limited. They can support extraction or harvest indefinitely, but only at a finite flow rate equal to their regeneration rate. If they are extracted faster than they regenerate, they may be driven below a critical threshold and become, for all practical purposes, nonrenewable.
card.rule: Nonrenewable resources limit the total that can be taken (stock-limited); renewable ones limit the rate (flow-limited).
card.limits: Our reading: a flow limit can turn into a stock limit once overharvest damages regeneration.

concepts.title: Why systems can work so well
concepts.question: Which three characteristics does Meadows point to when she asks why systems work so well?

paragraphs: Chapter Two showed simple systems that produce their own behavior from their structure. Many of them withstand knocks from outside and, within limits, regain their composure and carry on with their job, such as holding a room at a steady temperature.

Meadows grants that a system pushed too far may fall apart or behave in ways nobody has observed before. By and large, though, she says systems manage quite well, and she sees a kind of harmony in them. A community responding to a storm is her picture: people work long hours, talents and skills emerge, and once the emergency is over life goes back to normal.

To explain this, she looks at highly functional systems, whether machines, human communities or ecosystems. Three characteristics keep turning up: resilience, self-organization and hierarchy. The chapter takes them one at a time.
card.rule: When a system works well, look for resilience, self-organization and hierarchy.
card.limits: Pushed far enough, a system still fails or acts in new ways; the three properties explain good function, not invulnerability.

concepts.title: What resilience means
concepts.question: What does Meadows mean by resilience, and what is its opposite?

paragraphs: Resilience has many definitions, depending on whether engineering, ecology or system science is doing the defining. Meadows chooses the ordinary dictionary sense: the ability to bounce or spring back into shape after being pressed or stretched.
In systems terms she calls it a measure of a system’s ability to survive and persist within a variable environment. Its opposite is brittleness or rigidity.
card.rule: Resilience is the ability to bounce back and persist in a changing environment; brittleness is its opposite.
card.limits: The word has several technical definitions; Meadows picks the plain dictionary sense for this chapter.

concepts.title: Resilience comes from many feedback loops
concepts.question: What structure gives a system resilience, according to Meadows?

paragraphs: Resilience arises from a rich structure of many feedback loops that can work in different ways to restore a system even after a large perturbation. A single balancing loop brings a stock back to its desired state. Resilience comes from several such loops, working through different mechanisms, at different time scales, and with redundancy, so one kicks in if another fails.

A set of loops that can restore or rebuild other loops is resilience at a higher level, which Meadows calls meta-resilience. Loops that can learn, create, design and evolve ever more complex restorative structures give meta-meta-resilience. Systems that do this are self-organizing, the next property.
Her example is the human body. It fends off thousands of kinds of invaders, tolerates wide ranges of temperature and food supply, reallocates blood supply and repairs rips.
card.rule: Look for several balancing loops with different mechanisms, time scales and backup, not one loop.
card.limits: A large enough shock can still overwhelm even a rich set of loops; there are always limits to resilience.

concepts.title: Resilience is not the same as stability
concepts.question: Does a system that never changes count as resilient?

paragraphs: Resilience is not the same as being static or constant over time. Resilient systems can be very dynamic. Short-term oscillations, periodic outbreaks, or long cycles of succession, climax and collapse may be the normal condition, which resilience acts to restore.

In the other direction, a system that is constant over time can be unresilient. Static stability is something you can see, measured by variation in a system’s condition week by week or year by year. Resilience may be very hard to see unless you exceed its limits, overwhelm the balancing loops and the structure breaks down.
Because resilience may not be obvious without a whole-system view, people often give it up for stability, productivity or some other more visible property.
card.rule: Judge resilience by the ability to recover, not by how little a system varies.
card.limits: Resilience is hard to see until its limits are exceeded, so a quiet record does not prove it exists.

concepts.title: Resilience traded away for gains
concepts.question: What do people give up when they push a system for productivity, and what are examples?

paragraphs: Because resilience is hard to see, it is often sacrificed for more visible gains. Meadows gives three examples, each with a gain and a cost.

Injections of a growth hormone raise a cow’s milk output without a matching rise in food, by diverting metabolic energy; the cost is a cow that is less healthy, shorter-lived and more dependent on human management. Just-in-time deliveries cut inventory swings and costs, but leave production more vulnerable to fuel supply, traffic, computer breakdown or labor problems.

European forests managed for centuries became single-age, single-species plantations built to yield wood and pulp at a high rate. Without many interacting species, they lost resilience and seem especially vulnerable to industrial air pollution.
card.rule: Ask what resilience a gain in productivity or stability is costing.
card.limits: Meadows does not call the gains worthless; the delivery model did cut costs and inventory swings.

concepts.title: The plateau picture and managing for resilience
concepts.question: How does Meadows picture resilience and its loss, and what should systems be managed for?

paragraphs: Meadows thinks of resilience as a plateau on which a system can play, doing its normal work in safety. A resilient system has a big plateau with gentle, elastic walls that bounce it back if it nears a dangerous edge.

As resilience is lost, the plateau shrinks and the walls become lower and more rigid, until the system is on a knife edge. Loss can come as a surprise because the system pays more attention to its play than to its playing space. One day it does something it has done a hundred times and crashes.

So systems should be managed for resilience as well as productivity and stability. Awareness of it explains encouraging natural ecosystems on farms so predators control pests, and holistic health care that builds up the body’s own resistance.
card.rule: Manage for resilience as well as productivity and stability, and watch the size of the plateau.
card.limits: Loss of resilience is hard to see, so the warning often comes only when the system crashes.

concepts.title: What self-organization is
concepts.question: What is self-organization, and where do we see it?

paragraphs: Meadows calls the most marvelous characteristic of some complex systems their ability to learn, diversify, complexify and evolve. This capacity of a system to make its own structure more complex is called self-organization.

She sees it in a small, mechanistic way in a snowflake, in ice feathers on a poorly insulated window, or in a supersaturated solution suddenly forming a garden of crystals. She sees it in a more profound way when a seed sprouts, a baby learns to speak, or a neighborhood decides to oppose a toxic waste dump.
It is so common in living systems that we take it for granted. If we noticed it, we would do better at encouraging it rather than destroying it.
card.rule: Self-organization is a system’s ability to make its own structure more complex.
card.limits: Crystal growth and a baby learning to speak are both self-organization, but Meadows calls the first small and mechanistic and the second more profound.

concepts.title: Why self-organization is suppressed
concepts.question: Why is self-organization often sacrificed, and what conditions does it need?

paragraphs: Like resilience, self-organization is often given up for short-term productivity and stability. Meadows lists turning creative people into mechanical adjuncts to production, narrowing the genetic variability of crop plants, and building bureaucracies and theories of knowledge that treat people as numbers.

Self-organization produces heterogeneity and unpredictability, and may come up with whole new ways of doing things. It requires freedom, experimentation and a certain amount of disorder. Those conditions can be scary for individuals and threatening to power structures.

As a result, education systems may restrict children’s creative powers, economic policies may favor established enterprises over upstarts, and many governments prefer their people not to be too self-organizing.
card.rule: To protect self-organization, allow freedom, experimentation and some disorder.
card.limits: The conditions it needs are uncomfortable and can threaten power, so protecting them takes tolerance of unpredictability.

concepts.title: Simple rules can produce complexity
concepts.question: How can simple rules lead to great complexity, and what does science not yet know?

paragraphs: Systems theorists used to think self-organization was too complex ever to be understood, so computers modeled mechanistic systems rather than evolutionary ones. Newer discoveries suggest that a few simple organizing principles can lead to wildly diverse self-organizing structures.

Take a triangle with three equal sides. Add to the middle of each side a new equilateral triangle one-third the size, then do the same to each new side, and so on. The result, a Koch snowflake, has an edge of tremendous length that still fits inside a circle. It is a simple example of fractal geometry, where relatively simple rules form elaborate shapes.

A stylized fern can likewise be generated by a computer from a few fractal rules, and the differentiation of one cell into a person may follow similar rules. Meadows adds that complex self-organization may arise from simple rules, or may not: science does not yet know whether all complexity does.
card.rule: A few simple organizing rules can generate great complexity.
card.limits: Meadows says science does not yet know whether all the complexity of the world arises from simple rules.

media.alt: Four outlines in a row, each a six-pointed star shape. The first is a plain star of straight edges. Each later one adds smaller triangular bumps along every edge, so the outline grows more jagged and intricate, ending as a snowflake-like shape.

concepts.title: What a hierarchy is
concepts.question: What is a hierarchy, and why does Meadows say it is no accident that so many systems have one?

paragraphs: A self-organizing system often generates a hierarchy as it builds new structure. The world, at least the parts humans understand, is organized in subsystems aggregated into larger subsystems, then still larger ones. A liver cell is a subsystem of an organ, which is a subsystem of you as an organism, and you belong to a family, a town, a nation. This arrangement is a hierarchy.

Corporate, military, ecological and economic systems and living organisms are arranged in hierarchies, and Meadows says that is no accident. If subsystems can largely take care of, regulate and maintain themselves while serving the larger system, and the larger system coordinates and enhances them, the result is a stable, resilient and efficient structure.
card.rule: A hierarchy lets subsystems manage themselves while the larger system coordinates them.
card.limits: It works as described only when subsystems serve the larger system and the larger system supports them; the chapter later shows how that fails.

concepts.section: Interlude • Why the Universe Is Organized into Hierarchies—a Fable
concepts.title: The fable of Hora and Tempus
concepts.question: Why did the watchmaker Hora prosper while Tempus became poorer?

paragraphs: Two watchmakers, Hora and Tempus, made watches of about a thousand parts each and were constantly interrupted by phone orders. Tempus assembled his in a way that made a partly built watch fall to pieces if set down, so each interruption sent him back to the start, and finishing a watch grew harder as calls increased.

Hora’s watches were just as complex, but he built stable subassemblies of about ten elements, put ten of these into a larger assembly, and ten of those into the whole watch. When interrupted he lost only a small part of his work, so he made watches much faster.
Meadows draws the lesson: complex systems can evolve from simple ones only if there are stable intermediate forms, and the resulting complex forms will naturally be hierarchic.
card.rule: Complex things get built, and survive interruption, when they are made from stable intermediate forms.
card.limits: It is a fable adapted from Herbert Simon’s argument; it explains why hierarchies are common but is not a measurement.

concepts.title: Hierarchy and information
concepts.question: Why does a hierarchy reduce what each part must keep track of?

paragraphs: Meadows calls hierarchies brilliant inventions, not only because they give a system stability and resilience but because they reduce the amount of information any part has to keep track of.

In a hierarchy, relationships within each subsystem are denser and stronger than relationships between subsystems. Everything is still connected to everything else, but not equally strongly. People in the same university department talk to each other more than to people in other departments.
If the links within and between levels are designed right, feedback delays are minimized and no level is overwhelmed with information, so the system works with efficiency and resilience.
card.rule: Strong links within subsystems and weaker links between them keep information manageable.
card.limits: If the links within and between levels are designed badly, the benefit is lost.

concepts.title: Partial decomposability
concepts.question: What does partial decomposability let us do, and what risk does it carry?

paragraphs: Hierarchical systems are partially decomposable. They can be taken apart, and subsystems with especially dense information links can function, at least partly, as systems in their own right. When hierarchies break down, they usually split along subsystem boundaries.

Much can be learned by taking systems apart at different levels, such as cells or organs, and studying them separately, so the reductionist dissection of regular science teaches a lot. But one should not lose sight of each subsystem’s relationships to the others and to higher levels, or surprises follow.

A doctor can usually treat a liver disease without attention to the heart or the personality. There are enough exceptions, though: a chemical at the patient’s job, or a malfunction in the liver cells’ DNA.
card.rule: Study parts separately, but keep their links to other levels in view.
card.limits: There are exceptions, so a part cannot be treated in total isolation.

concepts.title: Hierarchies grow from the bottom up
concepts.question: In which direction do hierarchies grow, and what is the original purpose of the upper levels?

paragraphs: You can watch self-organizing systems form hierarchies. A self-employed person gets too much work and hires helpers. A small informal nonprofit attracts members and money until someone is needed to organize it. A cluster of dividing cells differentiates and generates a circulatory system and a nervous system.

Hierarchies evolve from the lowest level up: from pieces to the whole, cell to organ to organism, individual to team, production to management. Life started with single-cell bacteria, not with elephants.

The original purpose of a hierarchy is to help its originating subsystems do their jobs better. Both higher and lower levels easily forget this, so many systems fail our goals because of malfunctioning hierarchies.
card.rule: Hierarchies grow from the bottom up, and upper levels exist to serve the levels below.
card.limits: Both levels can forget this purpose, so a hierarchy can drift into malfunction.

concepts.title: Suboptimization and too much control
concepts.question: What two failures must a hierarchy avoid, and how does it balance them?

paragraphs: When a subsystem’s goals dominate at the expense of the total system’s goals, the behavior is called suboptimization. A team member chasing personal glory can make the team lose. A body cell that breaks free and multiplies wildly is a cancer. Students who aim at personal grades rather than knowledge cheat.

Just as damaging is too much central control. If the brain controlled each cell so tightly that it could not maintain itself, the organism could die. Central rules that stop students or faculty exploring freely defeat the university’s purpose. Meadows says overcontrol from the top is behind some of history’s great catastrophes.

A highly functional hierarchy balances the welfare, freedoms and responsibilities of subsystems and whole: enough central control for coordination toward the large goal, and enough autonomy for the subsystems to flourish, function and self-organize.
card.rule: A healthy hierarchy balances enough central control for coordination with enough autonomy for the parts to flourish.
card.limits: The right balance differs from system to system, and both too little and too much central control damage the whole.

concepts.title: Putting the three properties together
concepts.question: How do resilience, self-organization and hierarchy fit together, and what does the chapter conclude?

paragraphs: The three properties are linked. Resilience that includes loops able to learn and evolve is self-organization. A self-organizing system often generates a hierarchy while it builds new structure. And Meadows says a hierarchy gives a system stability and resilience.

That purpose is set from the bottom: hierarchical systems evolve from the bottom up, and the upper layers exist to serve the purposes of the lower layers. Both resilience and self-organization are easily sacrificed for short-term productivity and control.
card.rule: Manage for resilience, self-organization and a hierarchy that serves its parts.
card.limits: These properties can themselves be lost, through the trades and failures the chapter describes.

concepts.title: Everything we know is a model
concepts.question: Why does Meadows say even our best knowledge of the world is a model?

paragraphs: Meadows opens with three truths. First, everything we think we know is a model: words, languages, maps, statistics, books, equations, computer programs and the pictures in our heads. None of them is the real world.
Second, models often fit the world well. That fit is why humans have done so well as a species, and the best ones grow from direct, close experience of nature, people and organizations.

Third, models fall far short of the whole. We can track only a few variables at once, and we draw faulty conclusions from sound assumptions or sound conclusions from faulty ones. So we are regularly surprised.
card.rule: Treat every map, number and mental picture as a useful model that fits the world in places and never fully.
card.limits: The claim is not that models are worthless: Meadows says they are usually well matched to the world. The warning is against mistaking a model for the thing it describes.

concepts.title: A warning list, not a cure
concepts.question: After learning these system properties, will a reader still be surprised?

paragraphs: Meadows says the book rests on a duality: we know a tremendous amount about how the world works, but not nearly enough. She believes both sides.
This chapter is a warning list: a collection of ways our mental models miss the complications of the real world, as seen from a systems perspective. It marks where hidden snags lie.
Her bad news or good news, depending on your wish to control the world, is that understanding all these characteristics lets you be surprised less often, but you will still be surprised.
card.rule: Learn the warning list to be surprised less often, and expect some surprise anyway.
card.limits: The promise is modest: fewer surprises, not none. A reader who treats systems thinking as a way to control the world has missed Meadows' point.

concepts.title: Events are the tip of the iceberg
concepts.question: Why does seeing the world as a series of events leave us surprised?

paragraphs: Systems present themselves as events, or we see the world that way: an election, a flood, a team winning, a stock index hitting a number. Events are the outputs, moment by moment, of the system's black box.

Events can be spectacular and hook our emotions. Following them is endlessly engrossing, yet it has almost no predictive or explanatory value. Like the tip of an iceberg, events are the most visible part of a larger complex, but not necessarily the most important.
card.rule: Treat an event as the visible tip of a pattern, not as the explanation.
card.limits: Events are not worthless: they are the system's outputs and the starting evidence. The failing is to stop at them and explain one event by another.

concepts.title: Behavior is performance over time
concepts.question: What is the behavior of a system, and why do systems thinkers start with history?

paragraphs: Meadows defines the behavior of a system as its performance over time. A team is on a winning streak, a river's floods and droughts are getting more extreme, a stock index has trended up for two years.

If the news set events in historical context, we would have behavior-level understanding, which is deeper than event-level understanding. So when a systems thinker meets a problem, the first step is to look for data, time graphs and the history of the system.
The reason: long-term behavior offers clues to the underlying system structure, and structure is the key to understanding not just what is happening but why.
card.rule: Begin with time graphs and history, because behavior over time gives clues to structure.
card.limits: Behavior is deeper than events but not the end: Meadows shows later that behavior-based analysis also has limits.

concepts.title: Structure is the source of behavior
concepts.question: What is a system's structure, and how does it relate to behavior and events?

paragraphs: Meadows defines structure as a system's interlocking stocks, flows and feedback loops. The boxes-and-arrows diagrams her students call spaghetti-and-meatball diagrams are pictures of structure.

Structure determines which behaviors are latent in the system. A balancing loop approaches or holds a dynamic equilibrium. A reinforcing loop generates exponential growth. Linked together they can produce growth, decay or equilibrium.
So structure is the source of behavior, and behavior shows itself as a series of events over time.
card.rule: Ask what arrangement of stocks, flows and loops could produce the pattern you see.
card.limits: Our reading: structure sets what behaviors are possible, not when each event will arrive, so it explains patterns better than it forecasts dates.

concepts.title: Event, behavior and structure in one picture
concepts.question: How does a Slinky show the difference between events, behavior and structure?

paragraphs: Take a Slinky. The hand releasing it is an event. The oscillations that follow are behavior. The mechanical character of the helical coil is structure. Systems thinking moves back and forth between the three, between diagrams of structure and graphs of behavior.

The Slinky makes the levels seem obvious, but much analysis in the world goes no deeper than events. Each night's market report says stocks rose because the dollar fell, or because interest rates changed, or because an election was won. That is event-event analysis.
Such explanations give you no ability to predict tomorrow.
card.rule: When one event is used to explain another, ask for the pattern over time and the structure beneath.
card.limits: Our reading: the Slinky example is clean; real systems hide their structure, so the levels are rarely labelled for you.

concepts.title: Two flaws in behavior-based models
concepts.question: What two flaws does Meadows find in behavior-based economic models?

paragraphs: Most economic analysis goes one level deeper than events, to behavior over time. Econometric models seek statistical links among past trends in income, savings, investment, output and so on. These are more useful than event-based models, but they have fundamental problems.

First, they overemphasize flows and underemphasize stocks. News reports the national output of goods and services, the GNP, not the stock of factories, farms and businesses that produce it. Without seeing how stocks affect flows through feedback, the dynamics stay hidden.
Second, and more seriously, they hunt for stable links between flows, which do not exist. Flows go up and down in response to stocks, not to other flows.
card.rule: Look for the stocks that drive flows, not for fixed links between one flow and another.
card.limits: Meadows grants that behavior-based models beat event-based ones. Her complaint is aimed at flows, not at the use of past data as such.

concepts.title: The thermostat equation that stops working
concepts.question: Why does an equation fitted to past data fail when the system's structure changes?

paragraphs: Suppose you know nothing about thermostats but hold plenty of data on heat flowing into and out of a room. You can fit an equation showing how the flows varied together, because the same stock, the room temperature, governs both.

The equation holds only until the structure changes: a window is opened, the insulation improved, the furnace tuned, the oil forgotten. It predicts tomorrow's temperature while the system stays as it was. It cannot tell you how to warm the room, how to stop a plunge, or how to cut the fuel bill. For that you must dig into structure.
That is why behavior-based models predict near-term performance fairly well, long-term poorly, and are terrible at telling you how to improve.
card.rule: Use a fitted equation to forecast only while structure holds, and look to structure to change anything.
card.limits: The near-term forecasting skill is real. Our reading: the equation is a record of one structure at work, so it breaks when the structure changes.

concepts.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
concepts.title: Linear and nonlinear relationships
concepts.question: What separates a linear relationship from a nonlinear one, and why does it matter?

paragraphs: A linear relationship between two elements can be drawn as a straight line: it has constant proportions. Meadows' farmer finds 10 pounds of fertilizer adds 2 bushels, 20 pounds adds 4, 30 pounds adds 6.
In a nonlinear relationship the cause does not produce a proportional effect, and the link can be drawn only with curves or wiggles.

Linear systems are easy to think about, can be solved, and are modular: you can take them apart and put them together, because the pieces add up. Nonlinear systems generally cannot be solved or added together, which makes them hard to calculate.
card.rule: Check whether doubling the cause doubles the effect before assuming that it does.
card.limits: Nonlinearity is not a defect: Gleick, quoted by Meadows, says it also creates rich kinds of behavior that never occur in linear systems.

concepts.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
concepts.title: Why nonlinearities foil reasonable expectations
concepts.question: Why does 'a little helped, so a lot will help more' so often fail?

paragraphs: If a small push produced a small response, we expect twice the push to produce twice the response. In a nonlinear system, twice the push could produce one-sixth of the response, the response squared, or none at all.

That is why nonlinearities foil a reasonable expectation: if a little of some cure did a little good, a lot will do a lot of good. The same expectation can run the other way: if a little destruction did tolerable harm, more will do only a bit more. In a nonlinear world these expectations produce classic mistakes.
card.example: Traffic on a highway: as the flow rises, car speed changes only slightly over a large range of density. Eventually small further increases in density cause a rapid drop in speed, and past a certain point a jam drives speed to zero. Soil erosion can likewise run a long time with little effect on yield, then plummet.
card.rule: Do not stretch a result from small doses to large doses without testing for a threshold.
card.limits: Over some ranges a relationship can look almost proportional, so small-dose thinking works for a while. The danger lies at the edges, where one more small step has a large effect.

concepts.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
concepts.title: Nonlinearities shift which loop dominates
concepts.question: Why do nonlinearities matter even more than surprising our expectations?

paragraphs: Nonlinearities matter beyond confounding our sense of cause and effect. They change the relative strengths of feedback loops, and so they can flip a system from one mode of behavior to another.

Meadows calls them the chief cause of the shifting dominance seen in several of the systems in the zoo: a sudden swing from exponential growth under a dominant reinforcing loop to decline under a suddenly dominant balancing loop.
card.rule: When behavior changes sharply, ask which loop gained strength and what nonlinearity shifted it.
card.limits: Our reading: this explains why a trend changes mode; it does not say when the switch will happen.

concepts.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
concepts.title: Spraying the budworm: a short-term fix
concepts.question: Why did decades of spraying fail to end the budworm problem?

paragraphs: Tree rings show the spruce budworm has killed spruce and fir in North America for at least 400 years, and no one much cared, since spruce and fir were seen as weed species. Once the virgin white pine was gone, the lumber industry turned to spruce and fir, and the budworm became a serious pest.

From the 1950s, forests were sprayed with DDT, and then with other insecticides after DDT was banned. The budworm returned every year. By 1980, spraying costs were unmanageable and citizens objected to poisons, while the budworm still killed up to 20 million hectares of trees a year.
card.rule: Judge a control programme by whether the problem leaves, not by whether it is repeated.
card.limits: Our reading: the story shows spraying failed as a lasting remedy; it does not claim a single year's spray did nothing.

concepts.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
concepts.title: The natural budworm-fir-spruce cycle
concepts.question: What natural cycle governed budworm, fir and spruce before the spraying?

paragraphs: C. S. Holling and Gordon Baskerville built a computer model to take a whole-system look. They found that before spraying, the budworm was barely detectable in most years, held in check by predators such as birds, a spider, a parasitic wasp and several diseases.
Every few decades an outbreak ran for six to ten years, then subsided, and later the budworm exploded again.

The budworm prefers balsam fir, the most competitive tree in the northern forest. Left alone, fir would crowd out spruce and birch into a fir monoculture. Each outbreak cuts the fir back, opening space for spruce and birch, until fir returns.
card.rule: Look at the whole cycle of pest, host and predators before judging an outbreak.
card.limits: This is Meadows' account of one northern forest; she does not claim every pest follows the same cycle.

concepts.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
concepts.title: The nonlinearities behind an outbreak
concepts.question: Which nonlinearities drive the budworm's rise and crash?

paragraphs: As fir builds up, the probability of an outbreak rises nonlinearly. The final trigger is two or three warm, dry springs. An event-level analyst would blame the springs alone.

Predators multiply faster as budworms increase, over a wide range. Beyond some point they cannot multiply faster, so a reinforcing relationship becomes a nonrelationship and the budworm takes off unimpeded.

Only one thing stops an outbreak: the insect cuts its own food supply by killing fir. The population crashes, again nonlinearly, as the reinforcing loop of budworm reproduction yields dominance to the balancing loop of starvation.
card.rule: Look past the final trigger for the nonlinear thresholds that made the system ready to flip.
card.limits: The warm, dry springs matter as a trigger. The point is that they act on a system already primed by its structure.

concepts.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
concepts.title: Ecologically stable, economically unstable
concepts.question: How can a system be ecologically stable and economically unstable at once?

paragraphs: The budworm, spruce and fir system oscillates over decades but is ecologically stable within bounds. It could go on forever.
Yet in eastern Canada the economy depends almost entirely on logging, which depends on a steady supply of fir and spruce. What is ecologically stable is economically unstable.
card.rule: Ask who the stability is for, and what steady supply they depend on.
card.limits: This is one case. Our reading: Meadows does not claim that every ecologically stable cycle harms the economy.

concepts.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
concepts.title: How spraying locks in the danger
concepts.question: How does spraying leave the forest permanently near an outbreak?

paragraphs: Spraying shifts the whole system to balance uneasily on different points of its nonlinear relationships. It kills the pest and also its natural enemies, weakening the feedback loop that normally keeps the budworm in check.
It keeps the density of fir high, moving the budworm up its nonlinear reproduction curve to the point where it is perpetually on the edge of explosion.
Holling calls the result persistent semi-outbreak conditions. Managers are locked into a policy: if it fails, the outbreak will be worse than any seen before.
card.rule: Before a control policy starts, ask what else it removes and what loops it weakens.
card.limits: This describes the budworm case. Our reading: it does not say every pest control must fail.

concepts.title: Beware of clouds
concepts.question: Why does Meadows warn: beware of clouds on a system diagram?

paragraphs: The clouds in the diagrams of Chapters One and Two stand for the beginnings and ends of flows. They are stocks, sources and sinks, ignored for now to simplify the discussion. They mark the boundary of the diagram.

They rarely mark a real boundary, because systems rarely have real boundaries. Everything is connected to everything else, and not neatly. There is no clean line between sea and land, between sociology and anthropology, or between a car's exhaust and your nose. There are only boundaries of word, thought, perception and social agreement: artificial, mental-model boundaries.
card.rule: Read each cloud as a stock someone chose to ignore, and ask what lies behind it.
card.limits: Clouds are a useful simplification, not an error in themselves. The warning is against forgetting that they stand for something real.

concepts.title: When a cloud is acceptable
concepts.question: When may a cloud safely stand in for the stocks behind a flow?

paragraphs: In the zoo, cars entered a dealer's inventory from a cloud. In fact cars come from raw materials, capital, labor, energy, technology and management, and leave through sales to households and businesses.
Whether a cloud is legitimate depends on whether those stocks are likely to influence the behavior of the system significantly over the time period of interest.

If raw materials are guaranteed to be abundant and consumers keep demanding the products, clouds will do. If a shortage or a glut is possible and the boundary leaves those stocks out, future events can surprise us.
card.rule: Keep a cloud only if the stock behind it is unlikely to matter over the period you care about.
card.limits: The test depends on the question and the time period, so a cloud fine for one purpose can hide a shortage in another.

media.alt: A chain of three boxes from left to right: raw materials, inventory, consumers' home stocks, joined by pipes with taps labelled production and sales. A raw materials processing pipe enters from a cloud on the left, and a depreciation or discard pipe leaves the last box to a cloud on the right.
A box labelled population. A pipe with a tap labelled births enters it from a cloud on the left, and a pipe with a tap labelled deaths leaves it to a cloud on the right.

concepts.title: There is no single legitimate boundary
concepts.question: Is there one correct boundary to draw around a system?

paragraphs: The lesson of boundaries is hard even for systems thinkers: there is no single, legitimate boundary around a system. There are no separate systems; the world is a continuum.
We have to invent boundaries for clarity and sanity, and they cause trouble when we forget we made them. Where to draw one depends on the purpose of the discussion, the questions we want to ask.
That does not mean a model must follow every connection to the whole planet. To understand anything we must simplify, which means we must make boundaries, and often that is safe.
card.rule: Choose the boundary from the question you are asking, and say that you chose it.
card.limits: Having no single true boundary does not excuse drawing none: simplifying is necessary, and often safe, as with births and deaths from clouds.

concepts.title: Boundaries drawn too narrowly
concepts.question: What goes wrong when we draw a boundary too narrowly around a problem?

paragraphs: Ecologist Garrett Hardin says the popular term side-effects roughly means effects I had not foreseen or do not want to think about. Side effects no more deserve the word side than the principal effect does.

When you draw a boundary too narrowly, the system surprises you. Build highways to ease traffic without thinking about settlement patterns and they attract housing along their length, which puts more cars on the road until it clogs again.
A national park managed only inside its perimeter is crossed by nomads, wildlife, water, acid rain and a changing climate.
card.rule: Widen the boundary until the things that can feed back on your action are inside it.
card.limits: Wider is not always better: the next idea shows the opposite trap of boundaries drawn too large.

concepts.title: Boundaries drawn too large
concepts.question: What is the opposite trap in drawing boundaries?

paragraphs: Systems analysts often fall into the opposite trap and make boundaries too large. They produce diagrams covering several pages in small print, with arrows joining everything to everything. There is the system, they say.
This my-model-is-bigger-than-yours game yields enormously complicated analyses and piles of information that can obscure the answers to the questions at hand.
Modelling the earth's climate in full detail is interesting but may not be needed to work out how to reduce a country's CO2 emissions.
card.rule: Stop widening the boundary once the model answers the question you asked.
card.limits: This does not excuse narrow boundaries. Our reading: the aim is a boundary matched to the question, not the smallest or the largest.

concepts.title: Problems ignore our borders
concepts.question: Why do real problems rarely fit academic or political boundaries?

paragraphs: The right boundary for thinking about a problem rarely matches an academic discipline or a political border. Rivers make handy borders between countries but the worst possible ones for managing water. Air is worse still: national boundaries mean nothing to ozone depletion, greenhouse gases or ocean dumping.

Ideally we would find the right boundary for each new problem, but we get attached to the boundaries our minds are used to. Arguments about national, trade, ethnic and public-private boundaries abound, and universities can dispute for years the boundaries between disciplines.
Boundaries are of our own making and can be reconsidered for each new problem.
card.rule: For each new problem, ask whether the usual border is the one the problem respects.
card.limits: Our reading: familiar borders are not wrong in themselves; they are wrong when used for a problem that crosses them.

media.alt: A box labelled criminals in jail. A pipe with a tap for new sentences enters it from a cloud on the left, and a pipe with a tap for sentence completion leaves it to a cloud on the right.

A box labelled fuel rods in nuclear power plants. A pipe with a tap for new fuel rods enters it from a cloud on the left, and a pipe with a tap for fuel rod replacements leaves it to a cloud on the right.

A box labelled registered unemployed. A layoff rate pipe enters it from a cloud on the left. Two pipes leave it to clouds: a hiring rate pipe to the right, and a registration lapses pipe turning downward to a lower cloud.

concepts.title: Many causes, many effects, all limited
concepts.question: Why do our minds resist thinking about the limits on every input?

paragraphs: Systems surprise us because our minds like to think of single causes neatly producing single effects. We like to consider one or a few things at a time, and we dislike thinking about limits, especially when our own plans and desires are involved.
In the real world many causes come together to produce many effects. Multiple inputs yield multiple outputs, and virtually all of them are limited.

An industrial process needs capital, labor, energy, raw materials, land, water, technology, credit, insurance, customers and management. A patch of grain needs sunlight, air, water, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, minor nutrients and living soil.
card.rule: List every input a process needs, not only the one in front of you, and ask which can run short.
card.limits: The lists are examples, not complete catalogues. Our reading: the point is the habit of listing, not the length of any one list.

concepts.title: The most limiting input matters most
concepts.question: What is a limiting factor, and why does the most limiting input matter most?

paragraphs: Justus von Liebig's law of the minimum, drawn from grain, says it does not matter how much nitrogen is available if phosphorus is short, and it does no good to add more phosphorus if potassium is low.

Bread will not rise without yeast however much flour it has. Children do not thrive without protein however many carbohydrates they eat. A company cannot run without energy however many customers it has, or without customers however much energy.
At any given time the input most important to a system is the one that is most limiting. The idea is simple and widely misunderstood.
card.rule: Find the scarcest needed input and put effort there, not into the plentiful ones.
card.limits: The law applies to inputs that are really needed together. Our reading: it does not say the limiting factor stays the same, which the later cards show.

concepts.title: Which limits economics tracks
concepts.question: Why does traditional economics track only capital and labor, and when does that mislead?

paragraphs: Economics evolved when labor and capital were the most common limiting factors, so most production functions track only those two, and sometimes technology.

As the economy grows relative to the ecosystem, the limiting factors shift to clean water, clean air, dump space and acceptable forms of energy and raw materials. Then a focus on capital and labor alone is increasingly unhelpful.
card.rule: Check whether the limiting factor has moved beyond the ones your measures track.
card.limits: This is Meadows' view of mainstream production functions. The point is about a shift over time: she does not say capital and labor never limit.

concepts.title: Growth changes what limits growth
concepts.question: How does growth itself change which factor limits a growing system?

paragraphs: Jay Forrester's corporate-growth model starts with a successful young company growing quickly. Its problem is to recognize and deal with shifting limits, limits that change in response to the company's own growth.

Insight comes from seeing not only which factor limits but that growth itself depletes or enhances limits and so changes what limits. When one factor stops limiting, growth occurs until another becomes limiting. Shifting attention from the abundant factors to the next possible limit brings real understanding and control.
Any physical entity with multiple inputs and outputs is surrounded by layers of limits, and the growing entity and its limited environment together form a coevolving dynamic system.
card.rule: Look ahead from the present limit to the one that growth will meet next.
card.limits: Our reading: this is the story of growth in a finite setting; it does not promise that watching the next limit lets growth go on without end.

concepts.title: There will always be limits to growth
concepts.question: What does Meadows conclude about perpetual growth?

paragraphs: Keeping an eye on the next limit is not a recipe for perpetual growth. For any physical entity in a finite environment, perpetual growth is impossible. In the end the choice is not whether to grow forever but what limits to live within.

Limits can be self-imposed. If they are not, they will be system-imposed: if managers, city governments or the human population do not choose and enforce their own limits, the environment will choose and enforce them.
card.rule: Choose your limits before the system chooses them for you.
card.limits: This applies to physical entities in a finite environment. Meadows does not say every kind of growth, such as growth of knowledge, must stop.

concepts.title: Delays are everywhere
concepts.question: How long do delays take, and why do we underestimate them?

paragraphs: Plants, forests and democracies take time to grow; letters take time to arrive; consumers take time to absorb price news; power plants take time to build and technologies to spread. We are surprised again and again by how much time things take.
Jay Forrester told modelers to ask everyone in the system how long a delay lasts, make a best guess, and multiply by three.
Delays are ubiquitous: every stock is a delay, and most flows have delays of shipping, perception, processing or maturation.
card.rule: Estimate the delay, then expect it to take longer: Forrester multiplied by three.
card.limits: The rule of three is a rough correction from Forrester's experience, not a law. Our reading: the real size of a delay depends on the system.

concepts.title: Which delays matter depends on the question
concepts.question: Which delays should a model include, and which can it ignore?

paragraphs: Just as the right boundary depends on the purpose of the discussion, so do the important delays. If you worry about oscillations that take weeks, you probably need not think about delays of minutes or years.
If you study the decades-long development of a population and an economy, you can usually ignore oscillations that take weeks.
The world peeps, squawks, bangs and thunders at many frequencies at once. What is a significant delay depends, usually, on which set of frequencies you are trying to understand.
card.rule: Match the delays you model to the time scale of the behavior you want to explain.
card.limits: Meadows hedges with usually: the delays that matter depend on which set of frequencies you are trying to understand.

concepts.title: Delays shape how systems behave
concepts.question: How do delays in feedback loops shape accuracy and stability?

paragraphs: Changing the length of a delay may utterly change behavior, so delays are often sensitive leverage points for policy if they can be made shorter or longer.

A decision point responding to delayed information, or responding with a delay, will be off target: actions will be too much or too little for the decision maker's goals. If action is taken too fast, it may nervously amplify short-term variation and create needless instability.
