Delays determine how fast systems can react, how accurately they hit targets and how timely the information is. Overshoots, oscillations and collapses are always caused by delays.
card.rule: When a system overshoots or oscillates, look first at the delays in its feedback loops.
card.limits: Our reading: the claim that delays always cause these behaviors is Meadows' own strong wording; treat it as a prompt to look at delays first.

concepts.title: Long delays demand foresight
concepts.question: What do long delays in feedback loops demand of decision makers?

paragraphs: Delays help explain why Mikhail Gorbachev could transform the Soviet Union's information system almost overnight but not its physical economy, which takes decades.
They help explain why absorbing East Germany into West Germany caused more hardship, over a longer time, than politicians foresaw.
Because of the long ocean response to warming, emissions have already caused climate changes that will not show fully for a generation or two.
When delays in feedback loops are long, some foresight is essential. To act only when a problem becomes obvious is to miss an important chance to solve it.
card.rule: Where feedback is slow, act on forecasts, not on problems that are already obvious.
card.limits: Foresight is not certainty. Our reading: Meadows pairs it with the warning that acting too fast on short-term variation can create instability.

concepts.title: The invisible hand and the invisible foot
concepts.question: Why don't individually rational choices reliably add up to the common good?

paragraphs: Adam Smith held that individuals pursuing their own gain are led by an invisible hand to promote the public interest. Meadows says it would be nice if this were true, since material selfishness would then be a social virtue.

But the world offers many cases of people acting rationally in their short-term interest and producing results nobody likes. Tourists flock to Waikiki or Zermatt and then complain they are ruined. Farmers produce surpluses and prices plummet. Fishermen overfish and destroy their livelihood.
Herman Daly calls this the invisible foot; Herbert Simon calls it bounded rationality.
card.rule: Do not assume that separately rational decisions add up to a good result.
card.limits: Meadows says the market is self-regulating in some ways and not in others, as the Dutch interlude shows. She does not say all markets fail.

concepts.title: What bounded rationality means
concepts.question: What does bounded rationality say about the decisions people make?

paragraphs: Bounded rationality means people make quite reasonable decisions based on the information they have. But they do not have perfect information, especially about distant parts of the system.

Fishermen do not know how many fish there are, much less how many other fishermen will catch that day. Businessmen do not know what others plan to invest, what consumers will buy, their market share or the market's size. Their information is incomplete and delayed, and their own responses are delayed, so they systematically under- and overinvest.
card.rule: Judge a decision against the information its maker had, not against all the facts.
card.limits: This is not an excuse for any behavior. It explains why reasonable actors produce results they would not choose together.

concepts.title: Satisficers, not optimizers
concepts.question: How do real decision makers differ from the perfect optimizers of economic theory?

paragraphs: Herbert Simon says we are not omniscient, rational optimizers but blundering satisficers: we try to meet our needs well enough, sufficiently, before moving to the next decision.
We further our nearby interests rationally but can take into account only what we know. We do not know what others plan until they act, and we rarely see the full range of possibilities.
We often fail to foresee, or choose to ignore, the effects of our actions on the whole system. Instead of a long-term optimum we find, within our limited view, a choice we can live with for now.
card.rule: Expect a choice that is good enough for now, not the best over the long run.
card.limits: Satisficing is Simon's description of how people actually decide, not advice to decide that way.

concepts.title: The two assumptions that fail
concepts.question: Why does bounded rationality overturn two hundred years of economic thinking?

paragraphs: When the theory of bounded rationality challenged two hundred years of economics built on Smith, controversy followed, and it is far from over.

Meadows says that theory first assumes homo economicus acts with perfect optimality on complete information, and second that when many do so, their actions add up to the best possible outcome for everybody. Neither assumption stands up long against the evidence.
In the next chapter she describes structures that let bounded rationality lead to disaster: addiction, policy resistance, arms races, drift to low performance and the tragedy of the commons.
card.rule: Test an economic claim by asking if it assumes perfect information or automatic harmony.
card.limits: The controversy is ongoing. Our reading: Meadows is arguing her side, so treat her verdict as the author's position.

concepts.title: How we misread the information we have
concepts.question: In what ways do we misinterpret even the imperfect information we have?

paragraphs: Behavioral scientists say we do not even interpret imperfectly the imperfect information we have. We misperceive risk, thinking some things far more dangerous and others far less than they are.
We live in an exaggerated present, paying too much attention to recent experience and too little to the past, focused on current events rather than long-term behavior.
We discount the future at rates that make no economic or ecological sense. So we do not even optimize our own individual good, much less the system's.
card.rule: When reading your own judgment, check for a bias to the present, to the comfortable and to the familiar.
card.limits: These are findings Meadows attributes to behavioral scientists. Our reading: she lists them as tendencies, not as fixed laws.

concepts.title: The role shapes the behavior
concepts.question: Why would you probably behave as the person you criticize does, in their role?

paragraphs: Imagine you are lifted from your place and put in the place of someone whose behavior you have not understood: a critic of government who joins it, a laborer who becomes management. You would then experience that position's information flows, incentives, goals, discrepancies and pressures.

Meadows says you might keep your old view and transform the system, but it is distinctly unlikely. A manager sees labor as a cost, a financier overinvests in booms and underinvests in busts, a very poor person sees the rationality of many children, a fisherman with a mortgage overfishes.
She teaches the point with games: simulated fishermen overfish, ministers favor industry, the upper class feathers its own nest.
card.rule: Before blaming a person, ask what the role's information and incentives make reasonable.
card.limits: The claim is about typical behavior, not every individual. Meadows grants that someone might keep an older view and innovate, though it is distinctly unlikely.

concepts.title: Understanding is not excusing
concepts.question: Does seeing behavior as rational within its bounds excuse narrow-minded behavior?

paragraphs: Seeing that individual decisions are rational within the information available does not excuse narrow-minded behavior. It explains why the behavior arises. Within what a person in that part of the system can see and know, the behavior is reasonable.
Swapping one individual for another in a position of bounded rationality will make little difference, and blaming the individual rarely produces a better outcome.

Change comes first from stepping outside the limited information visible from one place in the system and getting an overview. From there, information flows, goals and incentives can be restructured so that separate, bounded, rational actions add up to results everyone wants.
card.rule: Replace blame with a wider view, then redesign the information and incentives.
card.limits: Understanding does not remove responsibility. Our reading: Meadows says the behavior is understood, not approved.

concepts.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
concepts.title: The Dutch electric meters
concepts.question: What did the Dutch meters show about information and behavior?

paragraphs: In a Dutch suburb of near-identical houses, some had the electric meter in the basement and others in the front hall. During the 1970s energy crisis it emerged that some houses used one-third less electricity, though prices and family types matched.
The difference was the meter's position. High users had the meter in the basement, where it was rarely seen. Low users had it in the front hall, where residents passed it every day.
card.rule: To change behavior, put the feedback where the decision maker sees it.
card.limits: The finding comes from one suburb of near-identical houses. Meadows does not report tests in other settings.

concepts.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
concepts.title: Systems that work despite bounded rationality
concepts.question: Which systems function well despite bounded rationality, and is the free market one?

paragraphs: Some systems are structured to work despite bounded rationality: the right feedback reaches the right place at the right time. Your liver gets the information it needs. In undisturbed ecosystems and traditional cultures, the average individual, species or population, left alone, serves and stabilizes the whole. Such systems are self-regulatory and cause no problems.

Since Smith it has been widely believed that the free market is one of them. In some ways it is: producers and consumers, who hold the best information about production and consumption, can make fairly uninhibited, locally rational decisions.
But those decisions cannot by themselves correct the system's tendency to create monopolies and externalities, discriminate against the poor, or overshoot its sustainable carrying capacity.
card.rule: Ask whether the system's feedback gives each actor what they need to act for the whole.
card.limits: This is Meadows' view of the market, not settled economics. She grants that it works in some ways.

concepts.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
concepts.title: Redesign the system, not the actors
concepts.question: What makes a difference when actors' bounded rationality yields bad outcomes?

paragraphs: Meadows paraphrases a prayer: grant us the serenity to exercise our bounded rationality freely in systems that are structured appropriately, the courage to restructure those that are not, and the wisdom to know the difference.

The bounded rationality of each actor is set by the information, incentives, disincentives, goals, stresses and constraints on that actor. It may or may not lead to decisions that further the whole's welfare.
If it does not, putting new actors into the same system will not improve performance. What makes a difference is redesigning the system to improve those factors for the specific actors.
card.rule: Change the information, incentives and goals the actors face, not only who the actors are.
card.limits: The prayer's third part matters: some systems are already well structured, and leaving them alone is the right choice.

concepts.title: Archetypes: structures that trap us
concepts.question: What is an archetype in this chapter, and why does the author call archetypes traps?

paragraphs: In Chapter Five of Thinking in Systems, Donella Meadows separates systems that merely surprise us from systems that are perverse. A perverse system is built in a way that produces truly problematic behavior. Some of these structures recur so often, in such similar form, that she gives them a name: archetypes.

The damage an archetype causes is usually pinned on particular people or events, although it comes from the structure. Blaming, disciplining, firing, pushing policy levers harder, hoping for luckier events and tinkering at the margins leave a structural problem in place. This is why she calls the archetypes traps.

A trap can be escaped, either by seeing it coming and staying out, or by changing the structure: reformulating goals, weakening, strengthening or altering feedback loops, or adding new loops. This is why she calls them opportunities as well.
card.rule: When bad behavior keeps recurring, look for the system structure behind it and change that, instead of blaming people or pushing harder.
card.limits: Our reading: the chapter names eight archetypes, and not every bad outcome fits one of them. Meadows also says understanding a trap is not enough; the structure has to be changed.
card.example: A hospital's waiting times stay long under three successive managers. Firing the third manager, as the first two were fired, treats the problem as personal. The archetype view asks what structure of goals and feedback keeps producing the delay.

concepts.title: Fixes that fail: a stuck balancing loop
concepts.question: Why can energetic policy effort leave a problem exactly where it was?

paragraphs: Balancing feedback loops stabilize a system, so behavior patterns persist. That is good when you want body temperature held at 37 degrees Celsius. It is bad when the pattern that persists is undesirable.

Meadows calls the resulting trap fixes that fail, or policy resistance. Technological or policy fixes are invented, yet the system seems stuck, producing the same behavior year after year. She lists farm programs that fail to end gluts, wars on drugs after which drugs are as prevalent as ever, and decades of job-creation efforts that have not kept unemployment low.
card.rule: If effort year after year produces no change, suspect a balancing structure that holds the unwanted state in place.
card.limits: Persistence alone does not prove the trap. Stability is the goal in some systems, such as body temperature, and Meadows treats the trap as a persistent state that people do not want.
card.example: Subsidies are raised again and again to cut a crop surplus, and the surplus remains. The repeated effort with unchanged results is the signature of this trap.

concepts.title: Why resistance arises: actors with their own goals
concepts.question: How do the goals of separate actors produce resistance to a policy?

paragraphs: Meadows says policy resistance comes from the bounded rationalities of the actors, each pursuing a goal of his, her or its own. Each actor watches some variable, such as income, prices, housing, drugs or investment, and compares its state with a goal.
When there is a gap, the actor acts to close it, and usually the bigger the gap, the stronger the action. Every actor therefore forms its own balancing loop around the same system.
card.rule: Look for each actor's own goal and its own corrective response to find the source of resistance.
card.limits: This explains resistance only where actors respond to the state of the system. Our reading: it says little about systems with a single actor.
card.example: In a housing market, a city wants lower rents, landlords want higher ones, and tenants want security. Each watches rent levels and acts on its own gap.

concepts.title: The standoff and the ratchet
concepts.question: What happens to a stock when several actors pull it in different directions?

paragraphs: Meadows pictures one stock, such as the drug supply on city streets, with several actors pulling it in different directions. Addicts want it high, enforcement agencies want it low, pushers want it in the middle so prices do not swing, and citizens mainly want safety from crime.

If one actor gains ground, the others double their efforts to pull it back. When border enforcement cuts imports, prices rise, addicts commit more crimes, higher profits buy suppliers planes and boats. Together the countermoves produce a standoff: the stock is not much different, and nobody wanted that.
The structure can also work as a ratchet: more effort by one raises effort by all, and reducing it takes mutual trust.
card.rule: In a standoff, everyone works hard to hold the system where no one wants it, and each escalation draws a response.
card.limits: Our reading: the picture covers cases where several actors act on the same stock; it does not say the actors are equally powerful.
card.example: If border agents cut imports, higher prices attract more suppliers and push addicts to more crime. The stock ends up near where it began.

concepts.title: Romania: resistance at tragic cost
concepts.question: What happened when Romania used a ban to raise its birth rate, and why?

paragraphs: In 1967 the Romanian government wanted more people and banned abortions for women under forty-five. The birth rate tripled at first. Then the resistance of the people set in, and the birth rate slowly fell back close to its earlier level.

Mostly this happened through dangerous illegal abortions, which tripled the maternal mortality rate, and many unwanted children were left in orphanages. Families were too poor to raise the many children the government desired, and they knew it, so they pulled against the government's aim at great cost to themselves and the children.
card.rule: A policy that goes against the goals people hold may win briefly and then be undone by their response, at great human cost.
card.limits: This is one case of policy resistance, and Meadows presents it as a tragic one; resistance does not always cost so much.
card.example: A ban that raises births for a short time but pushes families toward hidden, unsafe workarounds shows a policy and a population pulling in opposite directions.

concepts.title: Overpower the resistance, or let go
concepts.question: What are the two responses to policy resistance, and what does each cost?

paragraphs: One response is to overpower the resistance. With enough power, kept up, this can work, at the price of monumental resentment and a risk of explosion if the power ever lapses. Ceausescu tried long and hard to overpower resistance to his policy; when his government was overturned he was executed, and the first law the new government repealed was the ban.

The counterintuitive alternative is to let go: give up ineffective policies and let the energy spent on enforcing and resisting go to more constructive uses. You will not get your way, but the system will not go as far wrong as you fear, since much of what you were correcting was a response to your own action. Prohibition's end in 1933 brought calm.
card.rule: When a policy is met by equal resistance, consider letting go, because much of the trouble is a reaction to the policy itself.
card.limits: Letting go is not the end of the matter: Meadows treats it as the opening for a better approach, and she calls it unthinkable to most.
card.example: A company that tightens control over a team that keeps working around it may find, after relaxing, that the workarounds ease too.

concepts.title: Hungary: ask why before you push
concepts.question: How did Hungary approach a low birth rate differently from Romania?

paragraphs: Hungary, at the same time as Romania, worried about a low birth rate and fears of an economic downturn from fewer workers. Instead of banning something, the Hungarian government asked why families were small and found that cramped housing was one reason.
It rewarded larger families with more living space. The policy was only partly successful because housing was not the only problem, but it did far better than Romania's and avoided its disasters.
card.rule: Before applying force, ask why people behave as they do, and use the answer to shape the policy.
card.limits: Meadows notes the Hungarian policy worked only in part, since housing was not the only obstacle.
card.example: A firm with high staff turnover could ask people why they leave, and find that long commutes matter, rather than ordering them to stay.

concepts.title: Aligning goals: the most effective way out
concepts.question: How can an overarching goal remove policy resistance, and how did Sweden use one?

paragraphs: Meadows calls the most effective way to deal with policy resistance aligning the goals of the subsystems, usually through an overarching goal that lets all actors break out of their bounded rationality. If all feedback loops serve one goal, results can be amazing. Wartime mobilization and recovery after a disaster are the familiar examples.

Sweden's birth rate dropped sharply in the 1930s. Instead of arguing over family size, the government and people agreed on the quality of child care: every child wanted, nurtured and out of material need, with excellent education and health care. The policy included free contraceptives, sex education, free obstetrical care, family support and more spending on education and health. The rate has since risen and fallen without panic.
card.rule: Where actors pull apart, search for a larger goal they can all pull toward and let go of the narrower goals.
card.limits: Meadows says harmonizing goals is not always possible; it can be found only by letting go of narrower goals and considering the long-term welfare of the whole system.
card.example: Neighbors fighting over parking might agree on a shared goal, such as safe, easy access for everyone, and design a scheme that serves it.

concepts.title: Policy resistance: the trap and the way out
concepts.question: What is the policy resistance trap, and what is its way out?

paragraphs: Meadows states the trap this way: when various actors try to pull a system stock toward various goals, the result can be policy resistance. Any new policy, especially an effective one, pulls the stock farther from other actors' goals and produces more resistance, leaving a result no one likes but everyone works to maintain.

The way out: let go. Bring in all the actors and use the energy once spent on resistance to find mutually satisfactory ways for all goals to be realized, or to redefine larger goals that everyone can pull toward together.
card.rule: Policy resistance: many actors pulling one stock; the way out is to let go and seek shared or larger goals.
card.limits: It applies to stocks that several actors with different goals act on; it is not a recipe for every persistent problem.
card.example: A neighborhood with competing demands on a park might settle on a shared aim for the park rather than keep countering each other's plans.

concepts.title: The herdsman's logic
concepts.question: Why does each herdsman add another animal to a pasture that is already limited?

paragraphs: Meadows draws on ecologist Garrett Hardin's 1968 article. A pasture is open to all, and each herdsman asks what it is worth to him to add one more animal. He sells that animal and keeps all the proceeds, so the gain to him is nearly +1.

The harm from overgrazing is shared among everyone, so the loss to him is only a fraction of -1. The sensible choice for him is to add another animal, and another. Every herdsman reasons the same way, so each is locked into increasing his herd in a world that is limited. Ruin is where all rush, each pursuing his own best interest.
Meadows calls it bounded rationality in a nutshell.
card.rule: When one user keeps the whole gain and shares the cost, each user's best move is to take more, and all are ruined together.
card.limits: The logic needs the other conditions the next ideas set out: a limited, erodable resource and users whose growth does not respond to its condition.
card.example: Ten fishing boats share a bay. A skipper who adds a net keeps all the extra fish but pays only a tenth of the damage to the stock.

concepts.title: A limited resource that erodes
concepts.question: What must be true of the shared resource for a commons to end in tragedy?

paragraphs: For a commons to be subject to tragedy, the resource must be limited and also erodable under overuse. Beyond some threshold, the less resource there is, the less able it is to regenerate, or the more likely it is to be destroyed.

On the pasture: as grass thins, cows eat down to the stems from which new grass grows. Roots stop holding the soil against the rain, soil washes away, and grass grows worse. Meadows calls this another reinforcing feedback loop running downhill.
card.rule: A commons fails when overuse pushes the resource past a threshold where it loses the ability to renew itself.
card.limits: A resource that renews itself no matter how it is used would not fit this structure.
card.example: A reef damaged past a threshold has fewer fish to breed, so fewer fish return, and the reef declines further.

concepts.title: Missing feedback from the resource to its users
concepts.question: Which missing link in the structure lets users keep overusing the commons?

paragraphs: A commons needs users who have reason to increase, and who increase at a rate not influenced by the condition of the commons. The herdsman has no incentive, no strong feedback, to let the risk of overgrazing stop him from adding a cow. He has everything to gain.

Meadows sums it up: the tragedy arises from missing, or too long delayed, feedback from the resource to the growth of its users. More users use more resource, which leaves less per user, yet no user has reason to cut back.

She gives the example of the hopeful immigrant to Germany, who expects only benefit from generous asylum laws and has no reason to weigh that too many immigrants will force the laws to tighten; hearing of tightening is a reason to hurry.
card.rule: A commons fails when the state of the resource does not feed back into the decisions of its users, or does so too late.
card.limits: Our reading: the weak feedback is the cause; where users feel the damage quickly, the structure differs.
card.example: A farmer who draws more water from a shared river feels no change in his own supply until the river runs dry.

concepts.title: Commons of sources and sinks
concepts.question: How can a shared dumping place be a commons, too?

paragraphs: Meadows lists commonplace commons driven toward disaster: a popular national park with uncontrolled access, fossil fuels whose carbon dioxide causes climate change, and the number of children when society bears the costs. These are examples of overuse of a shared resource.

Tragedy can also occur with common sinks, shared places where pollution is dumped. A family, company or nation lowers its costs or grows faster if the whole community absorbs its waste, so it gets a large gain and lives with only a fraction of its pollution. The feedback on the rate of use is weak for sources and sinks alike.
card.rule: Whether a commons is a source or a sink, it fails when users gain in full and bear only a fraction of the damage.
card.limits: Meadows applies the label to resources and sinks that are shared; it does not apply to what a user alone pays for.
card.example: A factory dumping waste into a river keeps the savings and shares the harm with everyone downstream.

concepts.title: Three ways out of the commons trap
concepts.question: What three ways does Meadows give for avoiding the tragedy of the commons?

paragraphs: Meadows names three ways. Educate and exhort: help people see the consequences and appeal to morality, with social disapproval or hellfire for transgressors. Privatize: divide the commons so each person bears the results of their own actions. Regulate: Hardin's term is mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon, backed by policing and penalties.

She explains each by its feedback. Exhortation tries to hold use down by moral pressure. Privatization makes a direct link from the resource's condition to its users, since gains and losses fall on the same decision maker. Regulation makes an indirect link, through regulators.
card.rule: Match the remedy to the feedback it supplies: moral pressure, direct feedback through ownership, or indirect feedback through regulators.
card.limits: No one remedy fits every commons, as the next ideas show.
card.example: A fishing ground could be handled by teaching fishers about stocks, giving each a fixed zone, or setting seasons with inspectors.

concepts.title: Why exhortation alone is not dependable
concepts.question: Why does Hardin doubt that moral appeals can protect a commons?

paragraphs: Some so-called primitive cultures have managed common resources for generations through education and exhortation. Hardin does not think the option is dependable, though. Resources protected only by tradition or an honor system can attract those who do not respect the tradition or have no honor.
card.rule: An honor system works only as long as everyone honors it, so exhortation alone is a fragile defense.
card.limits: Meadows does not say exhortation fails everywhere, only that Hardin sees it as undependable.
card.example: A trust-based shared tool library can run for years until one newcomer keeps a tool and takes no notice of the custom.

concepts.title: Drift begins with a gloomy view of the facts
concepts.question: What distorts the actor's picture of performance in the drift to low performance?

paragraphs: Some systems do worse than resist a policy: they keep getting worse. Meadows calls this archetype drift to low performance. Her examples include falling market share, eroding hospital service, and her own jogging program, which faded away.

The actor has a performance goal and compares it with the actual state, as in any balancing loop. But the actor works from a perceived state, not the actual one, and tends to believe bad news more than good. The best results get dismissed as aberrations while the worst stay in memory, so things look worse than they are.
card.rule: Check whether the actor's perception of performance is biased toward bad news before trusting the gap it reacts to.
card.limits: Our reading: the bias is part of the structure here; accurate perception would restore an ordinary balancing loop.
card.example: A manager recalls the two bad quarters and treats the three good ones as flukes, so the team's performance seems weaker than the figures show.

concepts.title: The goal slides with perceived performance
concepts.question: How does a slipping goal turn a balancing loop into a downhill spiral?

paragraphs: The second twist is that the desired state is influenced by the perceived state. Standards stop being absolute: when performance seems to slip, the goal is allowed to slip with it. People say that is about all you can expect, or that things are no worse than last year, or that everyone else has trouble too.

The balancing loop meant to hold performance up is then overwhelmed by a reinforcing loop heading downhill. The lower the perceived state, the lower the desired state; the lower the desired state, the smaller the gap and the less corrective action; the less action, the lower the state.
card.rule: If the standard falls whenever performance falls, the gap never gets large enough to trigger correction.
card.limits: The spiral needs goals tied to past performance; fixed standards break it.
card.example: A school accepts weaker results each year as the new normal, so the gap that would prompt action stays small.

concepts.title: Gradual decline and the boiled frog
concepts.question: Why does a slow decline go unchecked when a sudden one would not?

paragraphs: Meadows says this trap has another name, eroding goals, and is also called the boiled frog syndrome, from the old story that a frog dropped into hot water leaps out, while one in cold water slowly heated stays until it boils. She adds that she does not know if the story is true.
Drift is gradual. A sudden plunge would trigger an agitated corrective response. A slow drift erases the memory of, or belief in, how much better things used to be.
card.rule: Slow declines escape correction because the memory of better times fades along with the performance.
card.limits: Meadows does not vouch for the frog story; it is an illustration of the structure.
card.example: A neighborhood where litter creeps up a little each month stops noticing it, while a sudden dump would draw a response.

concepts.title: Two antidotes: absolute standards, best-based goals
concepts.question: What two antidotes does Meadows give for eroding goals, and how does the second one work?

paragraphs: There are two antidotes to eroding goals. One is to keep standards absolute, whatever the performance. The other is to make goals sensitive to the best performances of the past rather than the worst.

If perception has an upbeat bias, the best results become the standard and the worst only temporary setbacks. The same structure then pulls the system up, and the downhill loop that said the worse things get, the worse I let them get becomes an uphill loop: the better things get, the harder I work to improve them.
card.rule: Fix the standard, or anchor it to the best results, so the same loop pulls performance up instead of down.
card.limits: Our reading: the second antidote needs the actor to adopt the upbeat bias on purpose.
card.example: A coach sets next season's target from the best season on record, not the worst, so the team aims higher after each strong year.

concepts.title: Drift to low performance versus policy resistance
concepts.question: How does drift to low performance differ from policy resistance?

paragraphs: Policy resistance keeps a system in a normal bad state: the system stays stuck. Drift to low performance goes further, as the system keeps getting worse. In resistance the goals of several actors are pitted against each other; in drift a single actor's goal erodes with perceived results.

The trap is: allowing standards to be influenced by past performance, especially if there is a negative bias in perceiving it, sets up a reinforcing loop of eroding goals. The way out: keep standards absolute, or let them be raised by the best actual performances, and use the same structure to drift toward high performance.
card.rule: Persistent bad is resistance; steadily worsening with a slipping goal is drift.
card.limits: Our reading: the chapter lets the two be combined in real cases.
card.example: A hospital whose waiting time stays at ten hours despite reforms suggests resistance; one whose standard slips each year suggests drift.

concepts.title: I'll raise you one: goals that chase a rival
concepts.question: What decision rule sets escalation going, and what makes it differ from a thermostat?

paragraphs: Meadows introduces escalation with the kids' fight: you hit me, I hit you back a little harder, you hit back harder still. The decision rule is I'll raise you one. Escalation comes from a reinforcing loop set up by competing actors trying to get ahead of each other.

A thermostat's goal is absolute, such as 18 degrees Celsius. In escalation one actor's goal is tied to the state of another. Each takes its desired state from the other's perceived state, and ups it. It is not keeping up with the Joneses but keeping slightly ahead of them.
card.rule: In escalation each actor sets its goal by the rival's state and adds a little more, so the loop reinforces.
card.limits: Escalation is not always bad: competition over a desirable goal can hasten progress.
card.example: Two retailers each advertise a bigger discount than the other, and the discounts grow week by week.

concepts.title: Escalation in arms, campaigns, prices and ads
concepts.question: Where does escalation show up, and what do the cases share?

paragraphs: Meadows lists many cases. The United States and the Soviet Union exaggerated each other's arms to justify their own, so each weapons increase set off a scramble to surpass it. She says each side was escalating itself, and the race cost trillions and degraded two economies.

In negative campaigning, one candidate smears another who smears back. Price wars cut prices until both lose money, and one rival may go bankrupt. In advertising, one firm does something loud, the next something louder, until consumers' senses are dulled.
card.rule: Look for two actors who each set their level by the other's, and find the reinforcing loop.
card.limits: Our reading: the cases share the pattern, but their costs and exits differ.
card.example: Two phone makers keep adding cameras to match each other's latest model, whether or not buyers want more.

concepts.title: Exponential build-up and breakdown
concepts.question: Why can escalation reach extremes faster than anyone expects, and how does it end?

paragraphs: Escalation is a reinforcing feedback loop, so it builds exponentially. That is why it can carry a competition to extremes faster than anyone would believe. If nothing breaks the loop, the process usually ends with one or both competitors breaking down.
card.rule: A reinforcing race does not level off by itself; it ends when someone breaks.
card.limits: The text says usually; negotiated or unilateral exits can interrupt the loop.
card.example: A subsidy race between two states ends when one runs out of budget.

concepts.title: Ways out of escalation
concepts.question: What two exits does Meadows give from an escalation trap?

paragraphs: The best way out is to avoid getting into the trap. If you are in it, one exit is unilateral disarmament: deliberately reduce your own state so as to induce reductions in the other's. Within the system's logic this is almost unthinkable, but it can work if done with determination and if you can survive the competitor's short-term advantage.

The only other graceful exit is to negotiate a disarmament, a structural change that creates balancing loops to hold the competition in bounds: parents stopping the kids' fight, rules on advertising size, peacekeepers in violent areas.
card.rule: Interrupt the reinforcing loop, either by backing off yourself or by negotiating new balancing controls.
card.limits: Unilateral disarmament carries a risk: you must survive the rival's short-term advantage.
card.example: Two stores in a price war could agree to publish fixed sale periods, which adds a balancing control.

concepts.title: Privatizing: direct feedback, with a limit
concepts.question: How does privatizing a commons restore feedback, and where does it fail?

paragraphs: Privatizing divides the commons so that each person reaps the consequences of his or her own actions. Gains and losses fall on the same decision maker. An owner may still abuse the resource, but now it takes ignorance or irrationality to do so, and a person who lacks the self-control to stay below carrying capacity harms only themselves.

Meadows says privatization works more reliably than exhortation, if society will let some individuals learn the hard way. But many resources, such as the atmosphere and the fish of the sea, cannot be privatized.
card.rule: Privatize where a resource can be divided, so users feel the cost of their own overuse.
card.limits: Resources like the atmosphere and ocean fish cannot be divided, so privatization is not open for them.
card.example: A shared woodlot split into family plots makes each family bear the loss of its own over-cutting.

concepts.title: Regulation: indirect feedback through regulators
concepts.question: What must regulators be and do for regulation to restore feedback?

paragraphs: Hardin calls regulation, bluntly, mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon. It can take many forms, from outright bans to quotas, permits, taxes and incentives, and to be effective it must be enforced by policing and penalties.

Regulation links the resource's condition to users indirectly, through regulators. For the link to work, regulators must have the expertise to monitor and interpret the commons correctly, effective means of deterrence, and the good of the whole community at heart. They cannot be uninformed, weak or corrupt.
card.rule: Regulation works only if regulators can read the resource, deter abuse, and serve the whole community.
card.limits: Regulation fails when the regulators are uninformed, weak or corrupt; the feedback it supplies is only as good as they are.
card.example: A fishing quota fails if inspectors cannot count the catch or can be bribed.

concepts.title: Everyday mutual coercion and what each restores
concepts.question: How do traffic lights, meters and garbage fees each regulate a commons?

paragraphs: Meadows says life is full of mutual-coercion arrangements. Each limits the freedom to abuse a commons while preserving the freedom to use it. Traffic lights ration the shared intersection by turns, parking meters charge and limit time, bank safes and police protect money from treating the bank as a commons, and permits ration broadcast frequencies.
Garbage fees charge households by the amount they throw away, which directly restores the missing feedback by letting each household feel the cost of its own use.
card.rule: Good regulation limits the freedom to abuse while keeping the freedom to use.
card.limits: The examples show the forms; the effectiveness still rests on enforcement.
card.example: Charging by the bag turns a free dumping commons into a pay-as-you-go system.

concepts.title: Winners get the means to win again
concepts.question: What loop makes winners go on winning and losers go on losing?

paragraphs: Meadows names the archetype success to the successful: using accumulated wealth, privilege, special access or inside information to gain more of the same. It appears whenever the winners of a competition receive, as part of the reward, the means to compete even better in future.
That is a reinforcing feedback loop, which rapidly divides a system into winners who keep winning and losers who keep losing. To him that hath shall be given.
card.rule: When a win brings the means to win again, the gap between winners and losers widens.
card.limits: The loop needs a competition where the reward feeds the next round.
card.example: A town holds a yearly prize that the winner spends on better equipment for next year's contest.

concepts.title: Competitive exclusion in ecology and markets
concepts.question: What does the competitive exclusion principle say, and how does it apply to firms?

paragraphs: In ecology success to the successful is the competitive exclusion principle: two different species cannot live in exactly the same niche, competing for exactly the same resources. One will reproduce faster or use the resource better, win a bigger share, and multiply further. It drives the other to extinction, usually not by direct confrontation but by taking all the resource.

Meadows says Marx's critique of capitalism holds the same structure: two firms in one market behave like two species in a niche, and the one with a slight edge reinvests faster. With a finite market and no antitrust law, one firm can take over everything as long as it keeps reinvesting.
card.rule: Two competitors for the same resource cannot coexist if one's advantage compounds.
card.limits: Antitrust laws, among other things, can prevent the full takeover.
card.example: Two stalls selling the same goods in a small market: the one with slightly better margins can expand and push out the other.

concepts.title: How the loop makes the rich richer
concepts.question: Which feedbacks keep the poor poor and the rich rich?

paragraphs: The trap does its greatest damage in the many ways it makes the rich richer and the poor poorer. Poor children get the worst schools, if any, and with few skills qualify for low-paid jobs. People with low income cannot borrow from most banks, so cannot invest in improvements or must pay moneylenders high rates; even at reasonable rates, the poor pay and the rich collect.

Tenant farmers pay part of their crops to landowners and never buy land of their own, while landowners use that income to buy more land. Meadows adds that the poor pay the highest prices because they buy small quantities, get a small share of government spending, receive new technologies last, and meet disease and pollution first.
card.rule: Look for a link where having more makes getting more easier and having less makes it harder.
card.limits: Meadows presents these as feedbacks that perpetuate inequity, not as the only causes of it.
card.example: A small shop pays more per unit than a chain because it buys in small quantities, which hurts its margins.

concepts.title: Diversification as an escape, and its limit
concepts.question: How can losers escape competitive exclusion, and when does that fail?

paragraphs: Species and companies sometimes escape by diversifying. A species can learn or evolve to use new resources, and a company can create a product that does not directly compete. Markets tend toward monopoly and niches toward monotony, yet they also create offshoots of diversity that may later attract competitors and start the cycle again.
Diversification does not work as a strategy for the poor.
card.rule: Losers can leave the contested game and start another, if the winner cannot crush the new one.
card.limits: It fails against a winner who can crush or buy up offshoots, and it does not work as a strategy for the poor.
card.example: A small bakery that cannot beat a chain on bread starts selling specialty pastries the chain does not make.

concepts.title: Antitrust and leveling the playing field
concepts.question: What feedback controls and equalizing devices break the loop of success to the successful?

paragraphs: The loop can be kept under control by feedback that stops any competitor from taking over entirely, as antitrust laws do in theory and sometimes in practice. A catch: big firms can win the power to weaken the administration of antitrust law.

The most obvious way out is periodically leveling the playing field. Game designers and traditional societies build in equalizers: Monopoly restarts everyone equal, many sports have handicaps, and the potlatch has the richest give away goods. Societies also use taxes on the rich, charity, welfare, unions, universal health care and education, and inheritance tax, a way of restarting the game with each generation.
card.rule: Cap the winners' share, level the field, or reward success without biasing the next round.
card.limits: The equalizers may be weakened by the very winners they restrain.
card.example: A tournament that seeds the weakest players against the strongest only in later rounds keeps the contest interesting.

concepts.title: Success to the successful: trap and way out
concepts.question: Which ways out apply to which cause in the success-to-the-successful trap?

paragraphs: Meadows states the trap: if the winners of a competition are systematically rewarded with the means to win again, a reinforcing loop forms, and if it runs unchecked the winners eventually take all while the losers are eliminated.

Her ways out: diversification, which lets losers leave and start another game; strict limits on any winner's share of the pie; policies that level the playing field by reducing the strongest players' advantage or raising the weakest; and rewards for success that do not bias the next round.
card.rule: Break the loop by diversifying, capping shares, leveling the field, or unbiased rewards.
card.limits: These exits assume someone can enforce them.
card.example: A prize that pays in trophies rather than equipment does not tilt the next contest.

concepts.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
concepts.title: Addiction as a system structure
concepts.question: What is the structure of shifting the burden to the intervenor, and who can be addicted?

paragraphs: Meadows says addiction also appears in larger systems: industry depending on government subsidy, farmers on fertilizer, Western economies on cheap oil, weapons makers on government contracts. The trap goes by several names: addiction, dependence, shifting the burden to the intervenor.

The structure has a stock with inflows and outflows, which may be physical, like a corn crop, or metaphysical, like a sense of self-worth. An actor keeps the stock in line by adjusting a balancing loop, with a goal compared to a perception of the actual state.
card.rule: Addiction is a pattern, not just a chemical: any actor can come to depend on an outside fix.
card.limits: Our reading: the label covers dependence in systems of any size, but needs an intervention that takes the load.
card.example: A town that relies on one factory's tax payments to fund its services has a dependence of the same kind.

concepts.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
concepts.title: A fix that changes perception, not the problem
concepts.question: How can an intervention feel like a solution while leaving the real situation unchanged or worse?

paragraphs: Meadows gives three cases. A boy in a land of famine and war wants to feel happy and energetic, with a huge gap and few options. Drugs do nothing for his real situation, and probably worsen it, but they quickly change his perception of it: numb, tireless, brave.

An ineffective company that gets a government subsidy goes on making a profit and stays a respected member of society. A farmer on overworked land applies fertilizer and gets a bumper crop without improving the soil. The trouble is that the states created by such interventions do not last: the intoxication wears off, the subsidy is spent, the fertilizer is consumed or washed away.
card.rule: A fix that hides the symptom leaves the cause untouched, and the symptom returns when the fix wears off.
card.limits: Our reading: the same intervention can be useful when the underlying capacity is also being repaired.
card.example: Painkillers can let a person work on an injured back, but if the injury is untreated the pain returns.

concepts.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
concepts.title: The loop of atrophy and ever more help
concepts.question: Why does the intervenor have to do more and more?

paragraphs: Meadows describes how the trap forms. A corrective process in the system does a poor job of maintaining its state. A well-meaning intervenor steps in, takes some of the load and quickly brings the system to the desired state. But the root problem was never addressed, so it reappears. The intervenor applies more of the solution, which again disguises the real state of the system.

The trap is closed if the intervention, by active damage or just neglect, undermines the system's own capacity to maintain itself. If that capacity atrophies, more intervention is needed. That weakens the capacity further, and the intervenor picks up more slack.
card.rule: If help weakens the capacity it replaces, the need for help grows in a reinforcing loop.
card.limits: The loop only forms if the intervention undermines the system's own capacity.
card.example: A parent who always finishes a child's homework finds the child less and less able to do it alone.

concepts.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
concepts.title: When shifting a burden is fine
concepts.question: When is handing a burden to an intervenor a good idea, and when is it a trap?

paragraphs: Meadows gives examples: freight once moved by rail until highways; children did sums in their heads before calculators; populations held partial immunity until vaccines; modern medicine moved responsibility for health from individual habits to doctors and drugs.

Shifting a burden can be a good thing and is often done on purpose. She notes that 100 percent protection from smallpox vaccines, if it lasts, beats partial natural immunity, and some systems really need an intervenor. It becomes a trap when the intervention weakens the system's capacity to keep itself in a desirable state.
card.rule: Shifting a burden is fine when it works and lasts; it is a trap when it erodes the system's own capacity.
card.limits: Meadows gives no formula; the test is whether the system's own capacity is undermined.
card.example: A hospital's backup generator is a sound outside help; a school that stops teaching reading because tutors are available is not.

concepts.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
concepts.title: Why anyone enters the addiction trap
concepts.question: What two failures of foresight lead intervenors and the helped into the trap?

paragraphs: Meadows gives two reasons for entering the trap. First, the intervenor may not foresee that the initial urge to help a bit can set off a chain of events leading to ever-increasing dependency, which finally strains the intervenor's own capacity. She says the American health-care system is feeling that strain.

Second, the person or community being helped may not think through the long-term loss of control and increased vulnerability that come with shifting a burden to an able, powerful helper. In the drug case, the more you are sucked into an addictive action, the more you are sucked into it again.
card.rule: Both sides can fail to foresee the dependency that begins with small help.
card.limits: Our reading: these are the two reasons she names; others may exist.
card.example: A company hands payroll to an outside firm and later cannot run it, while the outside firm cannot meet the demands.

concepts.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
concepts.title: Addictive policies: pesticides and oil prices
concepts.question: Why are addictive policies so easy to adopt, and how do the pesticide and oil cases show the loop?

paragraphs: Addiction, Meadows says, is finding a quick and dirty solution to the symptom that prevents or distracts from the harder, longer task of solving the real problem. Addictive policies are insidious because they are easy to sell and simple to fall for.

Insects threaten crops: instead of examining monoculture and destroyed natural controls, apply pesticide. The bugs go, and more monoculture and ecosystem destruction follow, so the bugs return in bigger outbursts and need more pesticide. Oil price rises: instead of accepting depletion and raising efficiency, fix the price. Then pretend nothing is happening, burn more oil, and when that fails go to war for it or search more places for deposits.
card.rule: A policy that hides the symptom is easy to adopt and makes the cause worse.
card.limits: The cases show the pattern in agriculture and energy; other contexts may differ.
card.example: Printing money to cover a deficit hides the budget problem and builds the need for more.

concepts.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
concepts.title: Withdrawal: confronting the real state
concepts.question: What does breaking an addiction require, and what options exist?

paragraphs: Breaking an addiction is painful, whether physically, as in heroin withdrawal, economically, as with an oil price increase to cut use, or through pest damage while predators return. Withdrawal means finally confronting the real, often much-deteriorated state of the system and taking the actions the addiction let you put off.

Sometimes it can be gradual. Sometimes a nonaddictive policy first restores the degraded system with minimal turbulence: home insulation and efficient cars for oil, polyculture and crop rotation for pests. Sometimes the only way is cold turkey. It is worth the pain, but far better to avoid addiction in the first place.
card.rule: Withdrawal means facing the real state; a replacement policy can ease the pain.
card.limits: No way is painless, and Meadows says sometimes cold turkey is the only way out.
card.example: Insulating homes before an oil price rise lessens the shock of the price increase.

concepts.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
concepts.title: Avoiding the trap: help the system help itself
concepts.question: What should an intervenor do to avoid the trap, and what questions begin the effort?

paragraphs: The best way out is not to get in. Intervene so as to strengthen the system's ability to shoulder its own burdens. That can be far cheaper and easier than taking the system over. The start is not a heroic takeover but three questions: why are the natural correction mechanisms failing, how can obstacles to their success be removed, and how can they be made more effective?

The trap statement and way out add: beware symptom-relieving or signal-denying policies, and focus on long-term restructuring. An intervenor should restore or enhance the system's own ability to solve its problems, then remove itself. If you are dependent, rebuild your own capability before removing the intervention, at once, since waiting makes withdrawal harder.
card.rule: Help the system help itself, then step back.
card.limits: Meadows notes liberal politicians seem not to understand how cheap this route can be.
card.example: A development agency trains local mechanics and leaves, rather than running the repair shop itself.

concepts.title: Rule beating: the letter, not the spirit
concepts.question: What is rule beating, and when does it become a problem?

paragraphs: Meadows says wherever there are rules, there is likely to be rule beating: evasive action that gets around the intent of a system's rules, keeping to the letter but not the spirit. It becomes a problem only when it leads the system into large distortions, unnatural behavior that would make no sense without the rules.
Out of hand, it can make a system produce very damaging behavior, distorting nature, the economy, organizations and the human spirit.
card.rule: Rule beating is evasion that keeps the letter of a rule and defeats its purpose.
card.limits: Small evasions are not the trap; the problem is large distortion that would make no sense without the rule.
card.example: A shop sets a dress code that bans logos, and staff wear the same logos in a pattern too small to see.

concepts.title: Four cases of rule beating
concepts.question: What do the year-end spending, Vermont lots, cassava and endangered-species cases have in common?

paragraphs: Departments in governments, universities and corporations often spend pointlessly at year end, because unspent budgets mean smaller ones next year. Vermont's Act 250 requires complex approvals for subdivisions creating lots of ten acres or less, and now Vermont has many lots just over ten acres.

European import limits on feed grains in the 1960s left out cassava, a starchy root that is also animal feed, so corn imports from North America were replaced by cassava from Asia. The U.S. Endangered Species Act limits development where an endangered species lives, and some landowners who find one on their land hunt or poison it so they can develop.
card.rule: Find the rule's edge, and see what behavior piles up just past it.
card.limits: These show the pattern; they do not show how common each type is.
card.example: A law taxing companies above fifty staff may produce many firms with forty-nine.

concepts.title: The look of compliance hides the spirit
concepts.question: What does rule beating produce, and what warning does it carry for rule designers?

paragraphs: Rule beating produces the appearance of rules being followed. Drivers obey speed limits near a police car. Feed grains are no longer imported into Europe. Development does not proceed where an endangered species is documented. The letter of the law is met; the spirit is not.
Meadows takes this as a warning: design the law with the whole system in mind, including its self-organizing evasive possibilities.
card.rule: Design rules with the system's evasive responses in mind.
card.limits: Meadows does not say rules should be dropped, only designed with evasion in view.
card.example: A school ranking that counts attendance leads to students being marked present who are not learning.

concepts.title: Rule beating as feedback: redesign, don't crack down
concepts.question: What are the two responses to rule beating, and which does Meadows recommend?

paragraphs: Rule beating is usually a response of the lower levels of a hierarchy to rules from above that are overrigid, deleterious, unworkable or ill-defined. Meadows names two generic responses. One is to stamp out the self-organizing response by strengthening the rules or enforcement, which usually brings still greater distortion: the way further into the trap.
The way out is to understand rule beating as useful feedback and to revise, improve, rescind or better explain the rules.
card.rule: Treat evasion as a message about the rule, and redesign the rule to point creativity at its purpose.
card.limits: Our reading: some rules may still need enforcement; Meadows says tightening usually deepens distortion.
card.example: If a speed trap is avoided, redesign the road so drivers naturally slow down.

concepts.title: A system produces what you ask it to
concepts.question: Why can a system obey its goal perfectly and still fail?

paragraphs: Back in Chapter One, Meadows says, she described purpose as one of the most powerful influences on behavior. The goal sets direction, defines the gaps that require action, and indicates compliance, failure or success. If the goal is defined badly, if it does not measure what it should or reflect the system's real welfare, the system cannot produce a desirable result.

Systems, like the three wishes in the fairy tale, have a terrible tendency to produce exactly and only what you ask. If national security is defined as military spending, the system produces spending, not necessarily security. If good education is measured by money spent per student or by standardized test scores, the system produces those figures.
card.rule: Be careful what you ask a system to produce: it will produce exactly that.
card.limits: Meadows asks whether a measure correlates with the real aim; a good measure can be a fine goal.
card.example: A hospital that gets paid per patient seen may rush visits, because that is what the target pays for.

concepts.title: Confusing effort with result
concepts.question: What is the common mistake of confusing effort with result?

paragraphs: Meadows says her examples confuse effort with result, one of the most common mistakes in designing systems around the wrong goal. Counting money spent per student measures effort, not learning. Counting implants measures effort, not health.

Her advice at the end of the trap: specify indicators and goals that reflect the real welfare of the system, and take special care not to confuse effort with result, or you will end up with a system producing effort, not result.
card.rule: Measure what you want achieved, not how much was done to try.
card.limits: Effort measures can be useful as inputs; the error is treating them as the outcome.
card.example: A charity that reports meals handed out rather than hunger reduced is measuring effort.

concepts.title: GNP as the wrong goal
concepts.question: What is wrong with GNP as a measure of national success?

paragraphs: Meadows calls adopting GNP, the money value of the final goods and services an economy produces, perhaps the worst mistake of this kind. It lumps goods and bads: more car accidents and repairs raise it. It counts only marketed goods: hiring child minders raises it. It ignores distribution: a rich family's costly second home raises it more than a poor family's basic home.

It measures effort rather than achievement, and production rather than efficiency: light bulbs giving the same light for one-eighth the electricity and lasting ten times longer would make GNP go down.
card.rule: GNP counts activity, good or bad, and not welfare.
card.limits: Meadows says there is every reason to want a thriving economy but none in particular to want GNP to rise.
card.example: A storm that destroys homes can raise GNP through rebuilding spending.

concepts.title: Throughput versus capital stocks, and better goals
concepts.question: What distinction does Meadows draw between throughput and stocks, and what goals could replace GNP?

paragraphs: GNP, Meadows says, measures throughput, the flows of stuff made and bought in a year, rather than capital stocks, the houses, cars and computers that are the source of real wealth and pleasure. She suggests the best society might be one that keeps capital stocks usable with the lowest possible throughput, not the highest.

If you define a society's goal as GNP, it will produce GNP, but not welfare, equity, justice or efficiency unless you define and regularly report those. The world would differ if nations competed on the highest per-capita stocks with the lowest throughput rather than on per-capita GNP.
card.rule: Define and measure the outcome you want, such as stocks, health or equity, or you will get flows.
card.limits: This is the author's opinion about better goals, not a tested result.
card.example: A firm rewarded for how much it produces rather than how long its products last invites waste.

concepts.title: Wrong goal versus rule beating
concepts.question: How does seeking the wrong goal differ from rule beating?

paragraphs: Meadows calls seeking the wrong goal almost the opposite of rule beating. In rule beating the system evades an unpopular or badly designed rule while seeming to obey it. In seeking the wrong goal the system obediently follows the rule and produces exactly the specified result, which is not what anyone wants.
Both problems can be present at once with the same rule.
card.rule: Obedient to a bad rule means wrong goal; clever around a rule means rule beating.
card.limits: Both problems can occur at once around the same rule.
card.example: A call center told to hang up after five minutes: staff who follow it obey a wrong goal, and staff who hang up early to hit targets beat the rule.

concepts.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
concepts.title: Sailboats optimized for the rules
concepts.question: What happened to sailboat design when rules defined how races are won?

paragraphs: Meadows tells a story. People once raced sailboats for fun, using boats built for fishing, hauling or weekend sailing. To make races more interesting between boats of similar speed, rules evolved that defined classes by length, sail area and other parameters.

Soon boats were designed to win within the rules, not for normal sailing: strange-looking, strange-handling boats that squeezed out speed. Today racing sailboats are fast, responsive and nearly unseaworthy, need expert athletic crews, and are so optimized around the present rules that they have lost resilience; a rule change would make them useless.
card.rule: A goal defined by narrow rules can reshape the system to serve the rules and lose its original purpose and resilience.
card.limits: Our reading: the story is an illustration, and Meadows does not claim all rule systems end this way.
card.example: A school curriculum built around one exam may teach only what the exam rewards.

concepts.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
concepts.title: Telling the eight traps apart
concepts.question: How can you tell which of the eight traps a situation shows, and what does each one call for?

paragraphs: Meadows names eight system traps in this chapter. Policy resistance: several actors pull one stock apart. Tragedy of the commons: users share the cost of damage to a resource. Drift to low performance: the goal slides with perceived results. Escalation: each actor's goal chases a rival's state.

Success to the successful: winners gain the means to win again. Shifting the burden: an intervenor's fix weakens the system's own capacity. Rule beating: people meet the letter of a rule and defeat its purpose. Seeking the wrong goal: the system faithfully produces what the indicator measures.

Each trap has its own way out: let go and align goals, restore feedback, anchor standards, refuse or negotiate, level the field, strengthen the system and withdraw, redesign rules, choose better indicators.
card.rule: Name the structure first, then use the way out that fits it.
card.limits: Real situations can combine traps, and Meadows says a wrong goal and rule beating can operate at once on the same rule.
card.example: A hospital where waiting lists stay long under every manager, staff hit targets by reclassifying patients, and each ward copies the busiest ward's staffing shows several structures at the same time.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
concepts.title: What a leverage point is
concepts.question: What makes a place in a system a leverage point?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A leverage point is a place in a system where a small change can lead to a large shift in behavior.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author borrows the idea from Jay Forrester and notes it is also an old legend: the silver bullet, the trimtab, the magic password. People want to know where such points are, because leverage points are points of power.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Rather than pushing hard on a problem everywhere, you ask which part of the system's structure, if nudged slightly, would redirect the whole pattern of behavior. (Our reading)

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Changing the structure of systems so they produce more of what we want and less of what is undesirable.

card.rule: Look for the small change in structure that shifts behavior a lot, not for the place where the most effort is already spent.
card.limits: The author has no quick or easy formula for finding leverage points in complex systems, and calls her own list a work in progress.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
concepts.title: Intuition that pushes the wrong way
concepts.question: Why do people who know a system well often push on the right lever in the wrong direction?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Leverage points are often counterintuitive, so people involved in a system tend to push them the wrong way.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Forrester observed that people deep in a system often sense where the leverage is, but more often than not they push the change in the wrong direction. Complex systems, in his word, are counterintuitive.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Before pushing a lever, test the direction of the push as well as the location. (Our reading)

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Making changes that improve a system instead of systematically worsening the problem.

card.rule: Check the direction of a push, not only the place, because intuition often has it backward.
card.limits: She says leverage points are frequently, not invariably, unintuitive; and where intuition is right, we too often use them backward.
card.example: In Forrester's World model, growth was the leverage point, yet world leaders push to speed it up. He found much slower growth was needed. His urban study found that less subsidized low-income housing leaves a city better off, even its poorer residents.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
concepts.title: The twelve places, ranked
concepts.question: In what order does the author rank the twelve places to intervene, and what does the ranking mean?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The author lists twelve places to intervene in a system, counted down from 12, the weakest, to 1, the strongest.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: She proposed the list during a frustrating meeting on global trade regimes, distilling decades of analysis by many people. She calls it a work in progress, an invitation to think more broadly, not a recipe.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: 12 numbers, 11 buffers, 10 stock-and-flow structures, 9 delays, 8 balancing loops, 7 reinforcing loops, 6 information flows, 5 rules, 4 self-organization, 3 goals, 2 paradigms, 1 transcending paradigms.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Thinking more broadly about system change than adjusting numbers.

card.rule: Read the list upward from 12 to 1: the smaller the number, the more leverage.
card.limits: The author calls the list tentative and its order slithery, with exceptions to every item that can move it up or down.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
concepts.title: Numbers: adjusting the faucets
concepts.question: What does the author mean by numbers, and why are they the most popular intervention point?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Numbers are the constants and parameters of a system: the sizes of its flows, such as taxes, subsidies and standards.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: In a bathtub picture, parameters are how wide the faucets and drain are open. Many can be varied, so they are popular intervention points, and because they touch voters they are politically charged.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Examples she gives: the minimum wage, air-quality standards, allowed annual timber cuts, the deficit's tax and spending flows, a bank's service charge, how much goes to conservation each year.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Adjusting a system's flows to move a stock toward what we want.

card.rule: A parameter is a setting on a flow; it changes how fast stocks fill or drain.
card.limits: Some parameters are physically locked in and cannot be changed at all.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
concepts.title: Why numbers carry little leverage
concepts.question: Why are numbers dead last in the list even though so much attention goes to them?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Numbers rank last because changing them rarely changes how a system behaves.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author says perhaps 90, 95 or 99 percent of our attention goes to parameters, yet they hold little leverage: if the economy is stagnant, wildly variable or growing out of control, tweaking them rarely kick-starts, stabilizes or slows it.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Examples: campaign contribution caps have not cleaned up politics, strict smog standards left Los Angeles air less dirty but not clean.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spending attention on interventions that can change behavior, not on details.

card.rule: Treat a number adjustment as detail work: important to the people in the flow, rarely a change of system behavior.
card.limits: Parameters matter in the short term and to the individual standing directly in the flow.
card.example: She calls it arranging the deck chairs on the Titanic.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
concepts.title: When a number does matter
concepts.question: When do parameters become leverage points after all?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A parameter becomes a leverage point when it moves into a range that triggers something higher on the list.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Interest rates and birth rates, for example, control the gain around reinforcing feedback loops. System goals are also parameters that can make big differences. Such critical numbers are rarer than people think, since most systems are built or evolved to stay far from them.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Before investing effort in a number, ask whether it sits near a threshold that would set off a loop or change a goal; if not, the effort is probably wasted. (Our reading)

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Spending effort on the few numbers that matter, not the many that do not.

card.rule: Fight over a number only if it can push the system into a range that triggers a higher leverage point.
card.limits: Mostly, the numbers are not worth the sweat put into them, says the author.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
concepts.title: Changing the players
concepts.question: Why does replacing the people in a system usually change little?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Putting different people on the controls changes little if the system, goals and rules stay the same.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Firing people and hiring new ones, including electing different politicians, is also a parameter adjustment. The faucets are the same old faucets, plumbed into the same system and turned using the same information, goals and rules.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Electing a different president changed less than people expected, the author says, because every president is plugged into the same political system. Changing how money flows in that system would make more difference. (Her example, my gloss.)

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Putting effort where it changes the system, not only who operates it.

card.rule: Swapping players is a low-level move unless it also changes the information, goals or rules they work under.
card.limits: People do matter when their arrival also changes the information, goals or rules they work under. (Our reading)

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
concepts.title: Buffers steady a system
concepts.question: Why are big stocks more stable than small ones with the same flows?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A buffer is a large stabilizing stock, big relative to its flows, and it makes a system steadier.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: A lake and a river differ in just this: a huge bathtub with slow flows against a small one with fast flows. Floods are more catastrophic in rivers because a stock that is big relative to its flows absorbs fluctuation.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Money kept in the bank rather than living from the flow of change through your pocket; a store holding inventory instead of reordering as customers carry stock out the door.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keeping important stocks stable when flows fluctuate.

card.rule: Raising a buffer's size, relative to its flows, usually stabilizes the system.
card.limits: A buffer that is too big makes a system inflexible and slow to react.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
concepts.title: Why buffers rank low
concepts.question: Why does the author keep buffers low on the list even though they help?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Buffers are costly and hard to change, so changing their size is rarely a practical leverage point.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: There is sometimes magical leverage in buffer size, but buffers are usually physical, such as a dam cast in concrete or the acid-absorbing capacity of soils. Too big a buffer also makes a system inflexible and slow to react.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: You can often stabilize a system by increasing a buffer's capacity, but weigh the cost of building and maintaining it against what it buys.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Balancing stability against flexibility and cost.
