card.rule: Enlarge a buffer when stability is worth its cost, remembering it is physical and hard to change.
card.limits: She says a buffer can be too big, making the system inflexible.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
concepts.title: Physical structure shapes behavior
concepts.question: How much can the physical layout of stocks and flows decide how a system behaves?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The physical plumbing of a system, its stocks, flows and where they meet, can have an enormous effect on how it operates.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: A badly laid out structure fixes behavior in place, and add-on controls cannot repair it. The only way to fix a poorly laid out system is to rebuild it, if you can.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Hungary's road system sent all cross-country traffic through central Budapest, which set its pollution and commuting delays. Amory Lovins's team gained large energy savings just by straightening bent pipes and enlarging pipes that were too small.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Getting the layout right so the system works without constant correction.

card.rule: When behavior is built into the physical layout, only changing the layout fixes it.
card.limits: Rebuilding is often the slowest and most expensive change, and some structures cannot be changed.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
concepts.title: Why structure ranks low
concepts.question: Why is physical structure rarely a leverage point even though it matters?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Physical structure is crucial but rarely a leverage point, because changing it is rarely quick or simple.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Rebuilding is often the slowest and most expensive kind of change, and some structures cannot change at all. People age at a fixed pace, so the baby-boom swell moved on through schools, jobs and retirement whatever anyone did.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The leverage lies in proper design in the first place. Once built, it lies in knowing the structure's limits and bottlenecks, using it efficiently, and avoiding fluctuations or expansions that strain its capacity.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Designing well up front and operating within a structure's limits afterward.

card.rule: Design structures carefully at the start, then work within their limits instead of hoping to rebuild.
card.limits: She notes some structures are unchangeable, not just costly.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
concepts.title: Delays cause oscillation
concepts.question: How do delays in a feedback loop cause a system to overshoot and undershoot?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Delays in feedback loops are critical determinants of behavior and a common cause of oscillations.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: If you adjust a stock toward a goal using late information about its state, or if the information is timely but your response is slow, you overshoot and undershoot. The same goes when action takes long, as with power plants that take years to build.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Electricity industries worldwide swing between overcapacity and undercapacity even with immense forecasting effort. A system cannot respond to short-term changes when it has long-term delays.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Matching the rate of response to the rate of change.

card.rule: Late information or slow response makes a system overshoot and undershoot its goal.
card.limits: The effect depends on the delay relative to the rate of change of the stock.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
concepts.title: Too short, too long
concepts.question: What goes wrong when a delay is too short, and what goes wrong when it is too long?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A delay matters relative to how fast the stock being controlled changes: too short causes overreaction, too long causes oscillation or collapse.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Delays that are too short cause overreaction, chasing your tail, with oscillations amplified by a jumpy response. Delays that are too long cause damped, sustained or exploding oscillations, depending on how much too long.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Where a system has a threshold, a danger point beyond which irreversible damage can occur, an overlong delay produces overshoot and collapse.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keeping responses in step with the speed of change.

card.rule: Judge a delay against the rate of change of the stock it controls, not by its length alone.
card.limits: A delay is only too long or too short relative to the stock's rate of change.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
concepts.title: Slow the change, not the delay
concepts.question: Why does the author prefer slowing growth to shortening delays?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Because delays are hard to shorten, it is usually easier to slow the rate of change so that inevitable delays cause less trouble.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Things take as long as they take: the construction time of a major plant, a child's maturation, a forest's growth. That is why growth rates sit higher on the list than delay times. Factories and prices cannot adjust instantly.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: In Forrester's World model, slowing economic growth gave more leverage than faster technology or freer market prices, which try to speed up adjustment. There is more leverage in slowing the system so technologies and prices can keep up.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Letting adjustments catch up with change.

card.rule: Slow the change rather than wishing delays away.
card.limits: A delay that can be changed does matter, but the author warns to be sure to change it in the right direction.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
concepts.title: What a balancing loop needs
concepts.question: What parts must a balancing feedback loop have, and why keep loops that are rarely used?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A balancing loop keeps a stock near a goal, and needs a goal, a way to detect deviation and a way to respond.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The thermostat is the classic case: the setting is the goal, the thermostat detects deviation, and the furnace or cooler responds. Complex systems hold many such loops so they can self-correct under different conditions, though some stay idle most of the time.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Idle loops, like a nuclear plant's emergency cooling or your ability to sweat and shiver, matter for long-term welfare. Stripping them out because they look costly narrows the range of conditions the system survives,.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A system that can self-correct under many conditions.

card.rule: Keep each loop complete, goal, monitor and response, and keep the rarely used ones.
card.limits: Short-term, removing an idle loop shows no effect, so the cost appears only later.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
concepts.title: Keeping price and voting signals true
concepts.question: Why does the author say the real leverage in markets and democracy is keeping their feedback signals undistorted?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A market works as a balancing loop only while its price signals are clear, unambiguous, timely and truthful.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Price is the central piece of information for producers and consumers. Prices that reflect full costs tell consumers what they can afford and reward efficient producers. Subsidies, taxes and other confusion twist the signal.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Her remedies: antitrust and truth-in-advertising laws, pollution fees that internalize costs, removing perverse subsidies, leveling the playing field. The real leverage is stopping the distortion.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Self-correcting markets that reward efficient producers.

card.rule: Protect the accuracy of the signals a balancing loop runs on.
card.limits: Markets are marvels of self-correction only as long as the signals stay undistorted.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
concepts.title: Democracy as a feedback loop
concepts.question: Why does the author count democracy as a balancing loop, and what threatens it?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Democracy is a balancing loop that puts self-correcting feedback between the people and their government, and it depends on honest information.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Informed voters respond to what their representatives do by voting them in or out. The loop needs a free, full, unbiased flow of information back and forth between electorate and leaders.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Billions are spent to limit, bias and dominate that flow. Let those who distort price signals influence leaders, let the distributors of information be self-interested partners, and no necessary balancing feedback works well: market and democracy both erode.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Governments that stay answerable to the people.

card.rule: Guard the flow of unbiased information that lets voters correct their government.
card.limits: Her claim is about information flow; she does not say any one reform restores it.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
concepts.title: Strength relative to impact
concepts.question: When must a balancing loop be strengthened, and how?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A balancing loop's strength matters relative to the impact it is meant to correct, so if the impact grows the feedback must grow too.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: A thermostat copes on a cold day but is no match for open windows. Big industry needs big government to check it, and a global economy needs global regulation.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Strengthening a loop includes preventive medicine and good nutrition, integrated pest management, the Freedom of Information Act, environmental monitoring, whistleblower protection, and impact fees and pollution taxes.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Giving a system the ability to correct itself in proportion to the threats it faces.

card.rule: Scale the corrective loop to the size of the impact it must correct.
card.limits: The strength of a loop depends on accuracy and speed of monitoring, power of response and directness of corrective flows.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
concepts.title: Reinforcing loops drive growth and collapse
concepts.question: What does a reinforcing loop do, and why are unchecked ones rare?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A reinforcing feedback loop is self-reinforcing: the more it works, the more power it gains to work some more.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The more people catch the flu, the more they infect; the more money in the bank, the more interest. Such loops are sources of growth, explosion, erosion and collapse. An unchecked one would destroy its system, which is why there are so few: a balancing loop usually kicks in.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Epidemics run out of infectible people or people avoid infection; the soil erodes to bedrock or people plant trees and build check dams. The first outcome is the loop running its course, the second is an intervention that reduces its power.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Recognizing which loops are driving a system's growth or collapse.

card.rule: Find where more of something produces the capacity for still more.
card.limits: Unchecked reinforcing loops are rare because balancing loops eventually act.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
concepts.title: Reduce the gain
concepts.question: Why does slowing a reinforcing loop beat strengthening the balancing loops against it?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Reducing the gain around a reinforcing loop, slowing the growth, is usually more powerful than strengthening balancing loops.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Slowing growth gives the many balancing loops time to function. The author compares it to slowing the car when you are driving too fast, instead of calling for more responsive brakes or steering.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: In the World model, population and economic growth rates are leverage points. Look at birth rates, interest rates, erosion rates and any place where the more you have the more you can have.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Letting the system's own balancing processes keep up.

card.rule: Weaken the driving loop instead of piling brakes on top of it.
card.limits: It is far preferable to letting the loop run, but the author gives no formula for how much to slow.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
concepts.title: Success to the successful
concepts.question: How does a winner-takes-more loop work, and where does the author place the leverage?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: In a success-to-the-successful loop, winners gain the resources to win even bigger next time.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Rich people collect interest while poor people pay it; they can pay accountants and lean on politicians to cut taxes; they pass on inheritances and good educations. Antipoverty programs are weak balancing loops against these strong reinforcing ones.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: It would be more effective to weaken the reinforcing loops, which is what progressive income tax, inheritance tax and high-quality public education are meant to do. If the wealthy weaken those measures, government itself becomes a reinforcing structure.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keeping competition and opportunity open.

card.rule: Weaken the loop that feeds winners instead of patching its effects.
card.limits: She calls this a trap; her claim about taxes and schooling is her argument, not neutral fact.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
concepts.title: Adding a missing feedback loop
concepts.question: Why can adding information to a system be a high leverage point?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Adding or restoring a missing information flow is a powerful intervention: it creates a new loop delivering feedback to a place it never reached.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: In a Dutch housing development, electricity use was 30 percent lower in houses with the meter in the visible front hall than in houses with it in the basement, with no other differences. This is not a parameter change or a stronger loop but a new loop.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Missing information flows are among the most common causes of system malfunction.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Letting people see the results of their decisions so the system can correct itself.

card.rule: Where behavior goes uncorrected, check whether the feedback is missing and add it.
card.limits: The feedback must reach the right place in a form that compels; the author says merely informing may not be enough.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
concepts.title: Right place, compelling form
concepts.question: Why is it not enough just to supply information?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Missing feedback must be restored to the right place and in compelling form.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Fish prices rise as fish get scarce, so the last fish become more profitable to catch, a perverse reinforcing loop. Price is the wrong information; population information is what is needed. Telling aquifer users the water level is falling could start a race to the bottom.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: More effective: set the cost of water to rise steeply as pumping begins to exceed recharge.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Feedback people cannot ignore.

card.rule: Deliver the right signal to the decision-maker, in a form that forces a response.
card.limits: Compelling feedback of this sort is the author's proposal, not tested in the chapter.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
concepts.title: Why feedback is missing
concepts.question: Why are feedback loops so often missing, and who resists adding them?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: People systematically tend to avoid accountability for their own decisions, which is why so many feedback loops are missing.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Because decision-makers escape the consequences, feedback is cut off from them. Adding it threatens those used to that protection.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Such leverage points are popular with the masses, unpopular with the powers that be, and effective if you can get those powers to permit them or go around them.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Closing the gap between decisions and their consequences.

card.rule: Expect resistance from those who benefit from missing feedback, and plan to work around it.
card.limits: The author says effective, not guaranteed: it depends on getting permission or going around the powers.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.title: Rules set the boundaries
concepts.question: How do rules shape a system, and how strong are they?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The rules of a system define its scope, boundaries and degrees of freedom, and they are a high leverage point.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Rules range from constitutions and absolute physical laws down through laws, punishments, incentives and informal agreements. Gorbachev opened information flows and changed the economic rules, and the Soviet Union saw tremendous change.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Imagine a college where students grade teachers, there are no degrees, tenure follows solving real problems, or classes are graded as a group. Picturing the new behavior shows how powerful rules are.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Understanding why people behave as they do in a system.

card.rule: To see why a system behaves as it does, start from its rules.
card.limits: Informal agreements are among the weakest rules, and a rule's strength depends on its type.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.title: Power over the rules is power
concepts.question: Why does the author say whoever controls the rules holds real power?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Power over the rules is real power, so to understand a system's deepest malfunctions, look at the rules and at who controls them.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Lobbyists gather when Congress writes laws because the rules decide behavior. The author says the world trade system she was shown has rules designed by corporations, run by corporations, for corporations, and excludes almost any feedback from other sectors.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Most of its meetings are closed even to the press, so there is no information flow and no feedback.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Seeing who writes the rules and whether feedback can reach them.

card.rule: Ask who writes the rules and what feedback reaches them.
card.limits: The trade-system charge is her judgment, offered with the caveat that the list is tentative.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
concepts.title: Self-organization
concepts.question: What is self-organization, and why is it the strongest form of resilience?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Self-organization is a system's power to add, change or evolve its own structure; the author calls it the strongest form of resilience.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: In biology it is evolution, in human economies technical advance or social revolution. It means changing anything lower on the list: new physical structures such as brains, wings or computers, new loops, or new rules. A system that can evolve can survive almost any change by changing itself.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The immune system develops new responses to insults it has never met; the brain takes in new information and produces completely new thoughts.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Systems that survive change by changing themselves.

card.rule: A system that can restructure itself can survive changes that would break a fixed one.
card.limits: The author warns that this power is easy to treat as magic, which hides how it works.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
concepts.title: What self-organization needs
concepts.question: What does self-organization need to work, and what can simple rules produce?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Self-organization needs raw material, a highly variable stock of information, and a means of experimenting by selecting and testing new patterns.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: For biological evolution the raw material is DNA, variety comes from mutation, and testing comes from an environment in which some individuals do not survive. For technology, the raw material is science's accumulated understanding and selection is whatever the market rewards or funders pay for.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Clever rules governing how, where and what a system can add or subtract can yield complex patterns from quite simple rules.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Understanding where innovation comes from.

card.rule: Keep the raw material of variety and the means of testing it alive.
card.limits: The author suggests self-organization needs only quite simple rules, not miracles.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
concepts.title: Protect variety
concepts.question: Why does the author call wiping out diversity a systems crime?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Because variety is the raw material of evolution, eliminating it destroys a system's capacity to adapt.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The stock of DNA built up over billions of years is the source of evolutionary potential, like science libraries and training for technology. Cultures store behavioral repertoires from hundreds of thousands of years.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Allowing species to go extinct is a systems crime, as would be randomly eliminating science journals. Insisting on a single culture shuts down learning and cuts resilience.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Resilience through experimentation and diversity.

card.rule: Encourage variability, experimentation and diversity, even though it means losing control.
card.limits: The author calls this lever obvious but unpopular, since diversity means losing control.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
concepts.title: Goals outrank self-organization
concepts.question: Why is a system's goal a stronger leverage point than its ability to self-organize?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The goal of a system is a leverage point superior to its self-organizing ability, because the goal bends everything below it.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: If the goal is to bring more and more of the world under one central planning system, then physical stocks and flows, loops, information flows and even self-organizing behavior will be twisted to conform.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: She says a technology such as genetic engineering is neither good nor bad in itself: it depends on who wields it and with what goal.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Aiming the whole system.

card.rule: Check the goal first; everything lower on the list bends toward it.
card.limits: The diversity-destroying drive for control shows how a goal can undo self-organization.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
concepts.title: Loop goals and whole-system goals
concepts.question: How do a loop's goal and the goal of a whole system differ?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Every balancing loop has its own goal, but the larger, less obvious goal of the whole system is the higher leverage point.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: If you want a warmer room you know to change the thermostat setting, and most people see that. Even people inside a system rarely recognize the goal their whole system serves. Profit is only a rule, a condition for staying in the game.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The point of the corporate game is to grow and bring customers, suppliers and regulators under its control, shielding itself from uncertainty. The goal of keeping a market competitive must trump each firm's goal of eliminating rivals, as balance and evolution trump each population's urge to reproduce without limit.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Naming the real purpose a system serves.

card.rule: Ask what the whole system is for, not only what each loop aims at.
card.limits: A goal is dangerous when no higher-level balancing feedback holds it in check.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
concepts.title: A leader who changes the goal
concepts.question: When can changing a person change a whole system?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Changing players is a low-level move, except at the top, where a single player can have the power to change the system's goal.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Only very occasionally, a new leader of an organization states a new goal and swings thousands or millions of intelligent people off in a new direction. The author names Dartmouth College and Nazi Germany as examples.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Reagan said over and over that the aim was to get government off our backs. Public discourse changed thoroughly afterward.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Understanding the high leverage of articulating a goal.

card.rule: A new goal, stated, repeated and insisted upon, can redirect a system.
card.limits: The author argues larger changes and corporate power let Reagan succeed, so the leader is not the whole story.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
concepts.title: Paradigms
concepts.question: What is a paradigm, and why do societies leave it unstated?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A paradigm is a society's shared idea of how the world works, the great unstated assumptions beneath its systems.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: These beliefs are unstated because everyone already knows them. Forrester's saying: whatever a tax law says, payments will push up against the society's idea of what is fair.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Examples she gives of our culture's assumptions: money measures real worth, so those paid less are worth less; growth is good; nature is a stock of resources; one can own land.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Seeing the beliefs a system rests on.

card.rule: Ask which unstated shared assumptions a system rests on.
card.limits: She says these assumptions seem obvious only from inside the culture.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
concepts.title: Paradigms as the source of systems
concepts.question: Why are paradigms the source of everything else about a system?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Paradigms are the sources of systems: goals, information flows, feedbacks, stocks and flows all come from shared agreements about the nature of reality.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Emerson put it that every nation surrounds itself with a material apparatus corresponding to its state of thought, so the least enlargement of ideas would cause the most striking changes of external things.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The Egyptians built pyramids because they believed in an afterlife; we build skyscrapers because we believe downtown space is valuable. Copernicus and Kepler, Einstein, and Adam Smith each intervened at the paradigm level.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Changing a system at its root.

card.rule: Trace a system's goals and structures back to the beliefs that produced them.
card.limits: Our reading: the claim is that beliefs shape systems, not that every feature of a system can be traced to one belief.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
concepts.title: How paradigms change
concepts.question: Is changing a paradigm hard, and how is it done?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A paradigm can shift in a single mind in a millisecond, but whole societies resist challenges to their paradigms harder than anything else.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Nothing physical, expensive or slow is involved in the change itself: all it takes is a click in the mind, a falling of scales from the eyes. Resistance comes from the society around it.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Following Kuhn: keep pointing at the anomalies and failures of the old paradigm; speak and act loudly and confidently from the new one; put people with the new paradigm in visible, powerful places; skip reactionaries and work with active change agents and the open-minded middle.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Shifting how a society sees the world.

card.rule: Point to anomalies, act from the new view, place its holders in visible positions, and work with the open-minded.
card.limits: The steps are Kuhn's account as the author relays it; she warns that whole societies resist hardest.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.title: Staying unattached to paradigms
concepts.question: What does it mean to transcend paradigms, and why does the author rank it above changing them?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The highest leverage point is to stay unattached in the arena of paradigms, realizing that no paradigm is true and that even this realization is a paradigm.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Every paradigm, including the one that shapes your own worldview, is a tremendously limited understanding of an immense universe. The author describes this as letting go into not-knowing, what Buddhists call enlightenment.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: A person who holds paradigms loosely can pick whichever helps achieve a purpose, rather than defending a worldview as if it were reality. (Our reading)

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Freedom to choose the view that serves your purpose.

card.rule: Hold your worldview loosely, since no paradigm is the truth.
card.limits: The author calls this a gut-level realization, not a technique with steps.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.title: Where mastery leads
concepts.question: What does the author say becomes possible once paradigms lose their grip?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Everyone who has entertained the idea that no worldview is certain has found it a basis for radical empowerment.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: If no paradigm is right, you can choose whatever one helps your purpose.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: She says it is in this space of mastery that people throw off addictions, live in constant joy, bring down empires, get locked up, burned or shot, and have impacts lasting millennia.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Power through humility, not through certainty.

card.rule: Let go of certainty to gain the freedom to choose and to act.
card.limits: Her claims here are personal testimony and assertion, not evidence from the models in the chapter.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.title: Each level shapes those below
concepts.question: How are the higher points on the list related to the lower ones?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Higher points shape lower ones: paradigms give rise to goals, structure, rules, delays and parameters, and goals bend what lies below them.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author writes that a paradigm is the mind-set out of which the system, its goals, structure, rules, delays and parameters, arises, and that a system goal twists everything further down the list toward it. Self-organization can change anything lower on the list.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Because lower points sit inside higher ones, tuning a number changes less than changing the rules or the goal that set the number, and changing a goal changes more than changing a rule. (Our reading)

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Choosing the level of intervention that matches the problem.

card.rule: Move up the list when lower-level fixes keep failing.
card.limits: Our reading: the order is a guide to relative power, not a strict ladder in which each step always outranks the one below.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.title: Higher leverage, more resistance
concepts.question: Why does resistance grow as leverage grows?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The higher the leverage point, the more the system will resist changing it.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Societies often rub out truly enlightened beings for this reason. The author notes that the magical leverage points are not easily accessible even if we know where they are and which direction to push.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Expect hard push-back when you target goals or paradigms, and expect your own paradigms to resist too.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Realistic expectations about hard changes.

card.rule: Plan for resistance in proportion to the leverage you seek.
card.limits: She gives no figure for resistance; the link is stated, not measured.

concepts.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
concepts.title: Mastery as dancing with the system
concepts.question: What does the author conclude mastery of systems really involves?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Mastery has less to do with pushing leverage points than with strategically, profoundly, madly letting go and dancing with the system.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: There are no cheap tickets to mastery. You have to work hard, whether that means rigorously analyzing a system or rigorously casting off your own paradigms and throwing yourself into the humility of not-knowing.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Combine rigor in analysis with willingness to let go of fixed views, and treat the list as an invitation to think, not as a recipe. (Our reading on combining them)

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Working with a system instead of trying to control it.

card.rule: Work hard at understanding, then let go and dance with the system.
card.limits: She offers this as her conclusion, not a procedure.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Get the Beat of the System
concepts.title: The mistake of expecting prediction and control
concepts.question: Why does the author call it a terrible mistake to see systems thinking as the key to prediction and control?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Do not treat systems thinking as the key to prediction and control. The author says people raised in the industrial world are likely to make exactly this mistake when they first get enthused.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The industrial mind-set assumes such a key exists, so the new lens seems to confirm it. The author and fellow MIT students shared the hope and, enchanted by what they saw, exaggerated their findings. Like explorers who sought a passage to India and reached another hemisphere, they found something real, but not what they thought.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Our reading: when a new method excites you, state what you hope it will deliver and check the claims you make for it against that hope, since the author says the exaggeration came from expectation.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A truer account of what the lens is worth: the author says systems thinking proved to have greater worth than expected, but in a different way.

card.rule: Value systems thinking for what it reveals, not as a promise of prediction and control.
card.limits: The warning is not that the lens is weak. The author says it turned out to be worth more than the group had thought; it simply was not a tool for control.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Get the Beat of the System
concepts.title: Knowing how to fix a system is not fixing it
concepts.question: Why did understanding systems not make the author's group follow their own advice?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Understanding how to fix a system is one thing; wading in and fixing it is quite another.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author says social systems are the external form of cultural thinking patterns and of deep human needs, emotions, strengths and weaknesses. Changing them is not as easy as saying now all change, nor can we trust that he who knows the good will do the good.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The group lectured on the structure of addiction and could not give up coffee. They knew the dynamics of eroding goals and let their own jogging programs erode. They warned against escalation and shifting the burden, then created them in their own marriages.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Realism about change, starting with oneself.

card.rule: Insight into how a system works does not by itself change behaviour inside it, including your own.
card.limits: The author does not say insight is useless. It helped the group understand much; it is not enough on its own to change anything.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Get the Beat of the System
concepts.title: Insights that raise questions about people
concepts.question: What kinds of questions did the author's systems insights open up about people?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A systems insight can raise more questions than it answers, and many lie in the human mind, heart and soul.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Like other lenses humanity has built, this one revealed wondrous new things, many of them wondrous new mysteries. The author says what was unique was not the answers or even the questions, which whole disciplines already pursued, but that a tool born of engineering and mathematics leads its users to confront deeply human mysteries.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The author's examples: decision makers who resist the information a better loop would give them; the wish to key loops to real values that cannot be measured; a harmful system nobody dares sweep away; people convinced they are powerless.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Humility about method: the author concludes that getting along in a world of complex systems needs more than technocracy.

card.rule: When a systems fix stalls, look for the human question beneath it: how people screen information, what they value, what they fear, and what they believe is possible.
card.limits: The author does not say systems thinkers were first or alone in asking these questions. Other disciplines have asked and partly answered them.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Get the Beat of the System
concepts.title: Giving up the role of omniscient conqueror
concepts.question: What does the author say complex systems rule out, and what role must we give up?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Self-organizing, nonlinear feedback systems are inherently unpredictable and not controllable, so we must give up the role of omniscient conqueror.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: They can be understood only in the most general way. Foreseeing the future exactly and preparing for it perfectly is unrealizable, and making a complex system do what you want works only temporarily at best. For any but the most trivial objective we cannot optimize, and do not even know what to optimize.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Seek a general understanding of how the system behaves rather than an exact forecast, and treat any success at control as temporary.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A sustainable relationship to nature, to each other and to the institutions we create.

card.rule: Do not aim at exact prediction, lasting control or optimization of a complex system; aim at general understanding.
card.limits: The author says such systems are understandable in the most general way, so the lesson is not to stop understanding, only to stop expecting exact foresight and control.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Get the Beat of the System
concepts.title: Dancing with systems instead of controlling them
concepts.question: If systems cannot be controlled, what does the author say there is still to do?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: We cannot control systems or figure them out, but we can dance with them. Illusions of control hide a different sort of doing.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The future cannot be predicted but can be envisioned and brought lovingly into being. Systems cannot be controlled but can be designed and redesigned. We can expect surprises, learn from them and even profit from them, and listen to what a system tells us to find how its properties and our values can work together.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The author learned dancing with great powers from whitewater kayaking, gardening, music and skiing. Each demands that you stay wide awake, pay close attention, take part flat out and respond to feedback.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Results better than our will alone could ever produce.

card.rule: Replace control with attentive participation: envision, design and redesign, expect surprises and listen.
card.limits: Dancing is not passivity. The author calls it a different sort of doing, one that asks you to participate flat out.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Get the Beat of the System
concepts.title: The guidelines as a whole
concepts.question: What are the guidelines for, and how does the author want them read?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The guidelines are take-home practices that follow from a worldview built on feedback, nonlinearity and systems responsible for their own behavior.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: They come from the author's years of modelling complex systems and spending time with modelers, and they are the concepts and practices that penetrate the discipline so deeply that one begins to practise them, however imperfectly.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The author calls the list a start-off dancing lesson: practices colleagues adopt, consciously or not, on meeting new systems. It runs from watching a system's behaviour, through information, language, feedback policies, responsibility and humility, to wider time, disciplines and caring.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Learning to dance with systems.

card.rule: Read the guidelines as practices that grow out of a systems worldview, not as a finished rulebook.
card.limits: The author says the list is probably not complete and is not unique to systems thinking, since there are many ways to learn to dance.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Get the Beat of the System
concepts.title: Get the beat of the system
concepts.question: Why does the author say to watch a system's behaviour before disturbing it?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Before you disturb the system in any way, watch how it behaves, and study its beat.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Starting with behaviour forces you to focus on facts, not theories. It keeps you from falling too fast into your own beliefs or misconceptions, or those of others, and the author says it saves you many wrong turns.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Learn the system's history. Ask people who have been around a long time what has happened. If possible, find or make a time graph of actual data, since memories are not always reliable about timing.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Action based on what the system really does, not on what people say it does.

card.rule: Watch and record how a system actually behaves over time before you try to change it.
card.limits: Our reading: the guideline presumes a system you can observe for a time. For a brand-new system with no history the first step is still to watch what it does as early as possible.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Get the Beat of the System
concepts.title: Starting with behaviour changes the questions
concepts.question: How does starting with a system's behaviour change the questions asked about it?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Starting with behaviour turns thinking toward dynamic, not static, analysis, and away from defining a problem by the lack of a favorite solution.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Dynamic questions ask how we got here, what other behavior modes are possible and where we will end up if we do not change direction. A history of several variables plotted together begins to suggest which elements are in the system and how they might connect.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Listen to a family talk, a committee meeting or media pundits. People leap to solutions in predict, control or impose-your-will mode. Examples: the problem is we need to find more oil; the problem is we don't have enough salesmen.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Problems defined by what the system does, not by the solution we prefer.

card.rule: Define the problem by the system's behaviour over time, and ask how it got there and where it is heading.
card.limits: Our reading: a proposed solution is not worthless; it comes after the system's behaviour is understood rather than being used to define the problem.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Expose Your Mental Models to the Light of Day
concepts.title: Expose your mental models
concepts.question: Why does the author want mental models put where others can see and challenge them?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Expose your mental models to the light of day, and remember that everything anyone knows is only a model.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Drawing structural diagrams and writing equations forces assumptions into view, and models must be complete, add up and be consistent. Mental models are slippery: assumptions slide around, one thing for one discussion and something contradictory for the next.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Diagrams and equations are not required. Words, lists, pictures or arrows will do. Invite others to challenge your assumptions and add their own, and collect as many explanations as possible instead of championing one.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Clearer thinking, faster admission of uncertainty and correction of mistakes, and mental flexibility.

card.rule: Put your model into any visible form, invite challenge, and keep several explanations alive until evidence rules some out.
card.limits: The author says you need not use diagrams and equations, though he calls them a good practice. Exposing a model helps only if you are willing to revise it when the evidence says so.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.title: Honor, respect and distribute information
concepts.question: Why does the author say to honor information, and what does he say about the power of those who control it?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Do not distort, delay or withhold information. Give a system timely, accurate and complete information.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Information holds systems together. Decision makers cannot respond to information they lack, to information that is inaccurate, or in good time to information that is late. The author guesses most of what goes wrong in systems comes from biased, late or missing information.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The author would add an eleventh commandment to the first ten: Thou shalt not distort, delay, or withhold information. You can drive a system crazy by muddying its information streams, and make it work better with surprising ease by improving them.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Feedback loops that work.

card.rule: Keep information timely, accurate and complete, and share it with those who must act on it.
card.limits: Our reading: the guideline is about the quality and flow of information, not about drowning decision makers in everything. The author says what matters is that it be timely, accurate and complete.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
concepts.title: Use language with care
concepts.question: Why does the author say honoring information begins with the cleanest possible use of language?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Keep language as concrete, meaningful and truthful as possible, and avoid language pollution.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Our information streams are composed mostly of language, and our mental models are mostly verbal. Unclean language therefore pollutes both the streams and the models.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The author warns of what Wendell Berry calls tyrannese: language that refers to nothing in particular. His examples include a Peacekeeper missile, collateral damage and ethnic cleansing.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Clear information streams.

card.rule: Say what you mean in concrete, meaningful, truthful words so that information and mental models stay clean.
card.limits: The guideline concerns language that is meaningless or destructive of meaning. Our reading: technical terms with a clear meaning are not tyrannese; the author asks for more precise language, not less.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
concepts.title: Enrich language with systems concepts
concepts.question: Why must a society enlarge its language to fit its growing understanding of systems?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: The second step of respecting language is to enlarge it to be consistent with our enlarged understanding of systems.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author says industrial society is only beginning to pay attention to and use complexity, so it is only beginning to have words for systems. A society cannot easily use what it has no words for.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Old words such as carrying capacity, structure, diversity and system are coming to have richer and more precise meanings, and new words are having to be invented.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: The ability to talk about complexity.

card.rule: Learn and use words for systems concepts so that you can talk, and therefore think, about complexity.
card.limits: Our reading: new vocabulary helps only when its words are used with a clear meaning; the first step, concrete and truthful language, still applies to the new words.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Pay Attention to What Is Important, Not Just What Is Quantifiable
concepts.title: Pay attention to quality, not just quantity
concepts.question: Why should we pay attention to what is important even when it cannot be quantified?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Pay attention to what is important, not just what is quantifiable. Be a quality detector.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Our culture, obsessed with numbers, holds that what we can measure matters more than what we cannot. If quantity forms the goals of our loops, our attention, language and institutions, then quantity will be the result. Pretending something does not exist because it is hard to quantify leads to faulty models.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: If something is ugly, tacky, out of proportion, unsustainable or humanly demeaning, say so. Refuse the ploy that if you cannot define and measure it, you need not pay attention. No one can define or measure justice, democracy, security, freedom, truth or love.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Keeping unmeasured values alive: without people to speak for them and systems designed to produce them, they cease to exist.

card.rule: Name and defend qualities that cannot be measured, and do not set goals only around what is easy to count.
card.limits: The author does not reject numbers. Modelers in his own field had to put numbers on qualities such as prejudice; the point is to include what matters, not to drop measurement.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
concepts.title: Make feedback policies for feedback systems
concepts.question: Why should policies for self-adjusting systems change with the state of the system?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Make policies that change depending on the state of the system, since a dynamic, self-adjusting feedback system cannot be governed by a static, unbending policy.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author says it is easier, more effective and usually much cheaper to design policies that respond to the system's state. Where uncertainty is great, the best policies contain feedback loops and meta-feedback loops: loops that alter, correct and expand loops, designing learning into management.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The author's example is President Carter's proposal for a gasoline tax proportional to the fraction of oil consumption that had to be imported. If imports rose, the tax would rise; if imports fell to zero, the tax would fall to zero.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Policies that adjust themselves and learn as conditions change.

card.rule: Tie a policy to the state of the system it governs, and build in loops that let the policy itself be corrected.
card.limits: The author says feedback policies need great care where uncertainty is great, and that they can be hard to explain to people who do not think in feedback terms.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
concepts.title: Policy structured for learning
concepts.question: What made the Montreal Protocol an example of a policy designed for learning?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Build learning into a policy: set targets, require monitoring, and provide for changing the targets when the facts differ from expectations.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: In 1987 there was no certainty about the danger to the ozone layer, its rate of degradation or the effect of different chemicals. The author says that under such uncertainty a policy with a meta-feedback loop is best.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: The protocol set targets for phasing down the most damaging chemicals. It also required monitoring and reconvening an international congress to change the schedule if damage proved more or less than expected.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Acting under uncertainty without locking in a wrong schedule.

card.rule: When facts are uncertain, set targets and provide for monitoring and revision of the targets.
card.limits: The author does not claim it succeeded. He says only that it was a feedback policy structured for learning, and hopes it worked in time.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Go for the Good of the Whole
concepts.title: Go for the good of the whole
concepts.question: Why should we serve the whole system rather than maximize one of its parts?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Go for the good of the whole: remember that hierarchies exist to serve the bottom layers, not the top, and do not maximize parts of systems while ignoring the whole.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author’s stated ground is the purpose of a hierarchy: it exists to serve the bottom layers, so a part, or the top, that gains while the whole loses defeats that purpose. He gives the guideline briefly, with little argument.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Aim to enhance total-system properties such as growth, stability, diversity, resilience and sustainability.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A system that works as a whole for those at its base.

card.rule: Judge changes by their effect on the whole system's properties, not by how well one part does.
card.limits: The author states this guideline briefly and does not set out its limits. Our reading: parts still need care; the guideline asks only that no part be maximized at the whole’s expense.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Listen to the Wisdom of the System
concepts.title: Listen to the wisdom of the system
concepts.question: Why should we pay attention to what a system already does before we charge in to improve it?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Aid and encourage the forces and structures that help the system run itself. Do not be an unthinking intervenor who destroys its self-maintenance capacities.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author notes that many of these forces and structures lie at the bottom of the hierarchy, where outsiders seldom look. What already exists has value that is easy to overlook.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Before you charge in to make things better, pay attention to the value of what is already there. Our reading: ask the people inside the system what stands in the way of what they are already doing.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Interventions that build on a system's own strengths.

card.rule: Find and support what already keeps a system running before you replace or add to it.
card.limits: Our reading: this does not rule out outside help. The author's own example ends with outside help of a specific kind: small loans and classes for existing traders.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.title: Locate responsibility in the system
concepts.question: Why should we look for the ways a system creates its own behavior, not only for outside causes?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Locate responsibility in the system: look for the ways it creates its own behavior.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Triggering events, the outside influences that bring forth one behavior rather than another, deserve attention. Yet blaming or trying to control the outside influence can blind one to the easier task of increasing responsibility within the system.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Check the triggers, and ask what in the system's own structure makes it respond to them in the way it does.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Problems solved at the structure that produces them.

card.rule: Pay attention to outside triggers, but look first for the system's own part in its behaviour.
card.limits: The author says some outside events can and should be controlled. The guideline does not say outside influences never matter.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.title: Intrinsic responsibility
concepts.question: What does the author mean by intrinsic responsibility, and how can a system be designed for it?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: A system has intrinsic responsibility when it sends feedback about the consequences of decisions directly, quickly and compellingly to the decision makers.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author's example is a plane's pilot, who rides in the front and so feels the results of every decision at once.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Design systems so that the people who decide are the ones who experience the results.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Decisions made with their consequences in view.

card.rule: Design systems so that the people who decide also feel the consequences soon and strongly.
card.limits: The author gives a short list of examples and says they are enough to start thinking; he does not claim a complete method.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.title: Stay humble, stay a learner
concepts.question: What should you do when you do not know how a system will respond?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: When you do not know, do not bluff and do not freeze. Learn, by experiment: trial and error.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: Working with systems constantly reminds the author how incomplete his mental models are, how complex the world is and how much he does not know. Pretending you are in control is a recipe for mistakes and for not learning from them.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Take small steps, monitor constantly and be willing to change course as you learn where the path leads. In a world of complex systems it is not appropriate to charge ahead with rigid, undeviating directives.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Learning as the system shows what it does.

card.rule: When uncertain, take small steps, watch the results and change course as you learn.
card.limits: The author says Stay the course is only a good idea if you are sure you are on course. Our reading: small steps suit uncertain ground, and a clear, tested course can be held.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.title: Embrace your errors
concepts.question: Why does the author call error-embracing the condition for learning?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Error-embracing, the author's term from Don Michael, means seeking, using and sharing information about what went wrong with what you expected.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: It is the condition for learning: you cannot learn from a mistake you hide.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Admit mistakes openly and use them. The author says this is hard, because it means making mistakes and, worse, admitting them, and it takes a lot of courage.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Learning, for people and for institutions.

card.rule: Seek, use and share information about what went wrong against what you expected.
card.limits: Our reading: error-embracing is a stance toward information about mistakes. It does not say that mistakes are good in themselves.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.title: Celebrate complexity
concepts.question: Why does the author want us to celebrate a messy, nonlinear world rather than resist it?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Celebrate complexity: the universe is messy, nonlinear, turbulent and dynamic, and that is what makes it interesting, beautiful and workable.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The world spends its time in transient behaviour on its way somewhere else, not in neat equilibria. It self-organizes and evolves, creating diversity and uniformity.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Resist the pull of the mind toward straight lines, whole numbers, uniformity and certainty. We can celebrate and encourage self-organization, disorder, variety and diversity.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A way of living that welcomes the world as it is.

card.rule: Welcome self-organization, variety and disorder as the working character of a living world.
card.limits: The author admits part of the human mind is drawn to straight lines and certainty. The guideline does not call tidiness wrong; it asks us not to demand it of the world.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.title: Expand time horizons
concepts.question: Why does the author want time horizons expanded, and why does he say short and long term are not separate?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Expand time horizons, and watch both the short term and the long term, which are nested within each other.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The interest rate, with payback periods and discount rates, gives a rational, quantitative excuse for ignoring the long term. The official horizon of industrial society reaches only to the next election or the payback period of current investments. The author says the longer the operant time horizon, the better the chances for survival.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Do not keep your head down looking at the next step on a tricky path, nor peer far ahead and miss what is underfoot. Watch both the short and the long term: the whole system.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Survival and sound decisions over time.

card.rule: Look at both the immediate and the long-range effects of a decision, since time scales are nested.
card.limits: The author says that in a strict systems sense there is no long-term and short-term distinction. The guideline is not a rule to prefer the long term over the short.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.title: Defy the disciplines
concepts.question: Why must someone studying a system be ready to cross the boundaries of academic disciplines?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Follow a system wherever it leads, whatever you majored in or whatever the textbooks say.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: A system will lead across traditional disciplinary lines. To understand it you must learn from economists, chemists, psychologists and theologians without being limited by them.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Penetrate their jargons, integrate what they tell you, recognize what they honestly see through their lenses and discard the distortions that come from narrowness. They will not make it easy.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Seeing systems whole.

card.rule: Follow the system across disciplines, and take from each field what it honestly sees.
card.limits: The author says seeing systems whole needs more than usual interdisciplinary work, which is often people from different disciplines talking past each other.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.title: Expand the boundary of caring
concepts.question: Why does systems thinking give practical reasons for caring about people and parts outside our own interest?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Expand the horizons of caring, not only of time and of thought.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: There are moral reasons for it, and systems thinking adds practical ones: the real system is interconnected, and no part of the human race is separate from other humans or from the global ecosystem.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Your heart cannot succeed if your lungs fail, your company if your workers fail, the rich in Los Angeles if the poor fail, Europe if Africa fails, or the global economy if the global environment fails.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: Making moral and practical rules coincide.

card.rule: Count more people and parts as your own concern, because in an interconnected system their failure becomes yours.
card.limits: The author says the moral reasons stand on their own; the practical reasons are added for those who are not persuaded by moral arguments.

concepts.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
concepts.section: Don’t Erode the Goal of Goodness
concepts.title: Do not erode the goal of goodness
concepts.question: How does the drift-to-low-performance trap erode morality, and what does the author say to do about it?

blocks.label: Principle
blocks.text: Do not erode the goal of goodness. Do not weigh the bad news more heavily than the good, and keep standards absolute.

blocks.label: Why it holds
blocks.text: The author says modern industrial culture has eroded the goal of morality through the system archetype of drift to low performance. Bad behaviour is held up as typical, goodness is barely noticed, expectations fall, the gap between desired and actual behaviour narrows, and fewer actions are taken to affirm ideals.

blocks.label: What it looks like
blocks.text: Notice and affirm examples of goodness, and hold standards at their level rather than adjusting them to actual behaviour.

blocks.label: End it serves
blocks.text: A culture that keeps morality as a goal.

card.rule: Keep standards absolute and give good news its due weight so the goal of goodness is not worn away.
card.limits: The author says systems thinking can only tell us what to do here; it cannot do it. The rest depends on people.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: One claim, three parts
concepts.question: What single claim does the whole book build on, and how do its three parts develop it?

paragraphs: Meadows opens with a claim: a system's own structure produces its pattern of behavior over time. The same outside push, given to a different system, is likely to produce a different result. Her Slinky and box show it. The Introduction states this claim, and Part One (Chapters One and Two) supplies the vocabulary of structure: stocks, flows and feedback loops, then zoo examples whose behavior follows from them.

Part Two, Systems and Us (Chapters Three to Five), turns from how systems are built to how we meet them: why they work so well, why they surprise us and how some structures trap us. Part Three, Creating Change (Chapters Six and Seven), asks what to do: where to intervene in a system, and how to live in a world of systems we cannot fully control.

Our reading: one question runs through all three parts. If structure causes behavior, how do we understand it, how does it catch us out, and what do we change? Meadows announces the order of topics, but she does not give the book a one-line thesis of this kind.
card.rule: State the book as one claim, that structure produces behavior, and place each part as an answer to what follows from it.
card.limits: Our reading: the guiding question is a summary we built, not the author's own sentence. Compressing a book to one claim leaves out most of its examples and many of its smaller arguments.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: The same building blocks, chapter after chapter
concepts.title: Stocks, flows, delays and loops return
concepts.question: Where do stocks, flows, delays and feedback loops return after Chapter Two, and what work do they do there?

paragraphs: Chapter One defines the pieces. A stock is an accumulation, flows change it, and a feedback loop is a stock whose level changes the flow that changes it. A balancing loop pulls the stock toward a goal; a reinforcing loop amplifies what is already happening. Because stocks change slowly, they act as delays, buffers and momentum.

The same pieces keep working. In Chapter Two, a delay inside a balancing loop makes a dealership's inventory oscillate. Chapter Four lists delays among the reasons systems surprise us, and says they shape behavior. In Chapter Six, delays are item 9 on the list of places to intervene, and buffers are item 11. Reinforcing and balancing loops are items 7 and 8.

Our reading: the book is easiest to outline by following these pieces. Whenever a later chapter explains a puzzling behavior, ask which stock is rising or falling, which flows drive it, which delay slows the response and which loop does the correcting or the amplifying.
card.rule: When a later chapter names a behavior, trace it back to a stock, its flows, a delay or a loop from Chapter One.
card.limits: Our reading: not everything is built from these four pieces. Goals, rules and paradigms, the top of Chapter Six's list, concern purpose and belief, which the author ranks above the loops.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.section: Why systems work, and what they rest on
concepts.title: Loops that restore, rebuild and nest
concepts.question: How do resilience, self-organization and hierarchy build on the feedback loops of Part One?

paragraphs: Chapter Three names three properties of systems that work well: resilience, self-organization and hierarchy. Resilience, Meadows says, comes from a rich structure of many feedback loops that work in different ways to restore a system after a large shock. One balancing loop returns a stock to its goal. Resilience means several loops, with different mechanisms, different time scales and backups.

She then climbs a ladder. A set of loops that can restore or rebuild other loops is meta-resilience. Loops that can learn, create, design and evolve ever more complex restorative structures give a still higher level, and systems that can do this are self-organizing. In other words, self-organization is the loop idea turned on the structure itself.

Hierarchy adds layers: subsystems manage themselves while the larger system coordinates them. Hierarchies grow from the bottom up, and the upper layers exist to serve the lower ones. Chapter Four's warning is that we mistreat, misdesign or misread systems if we do not respect all three properties.
card.rule: To explain why a system works well, look for layered loops that restore it, structure that can rebuild itself, and a hierarchy that serves its parts.
card.limits: Meadows adds that systems pushed too far may fall apart or show unseen behavior. Our reading: hierarchy is described through subsystems and information, not as loops, so the link to Part One is looser there.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Every reason for surprise is a gap between model and world
concepts.question: What do the reasons for surprise in Chapter Four have in common, and what does Meadows say about being surprised anyway?

paragraphs: Chapter Four opens with three truths. Everything we think we know about the world is a model. Our models usually match the world well, which is why we succeed as a species. But they fall far short of representing it fully, so we make mistakes and are surprised. The book, Meadows says, is poised on a duality: we know a great deal, but not nearly enough.

The rest of the chapter is what she calls a warning list of ways our models miss real complexity. We watch events instead of behavior over time and structure. We draw false boundaries, assume more rationality than people have, and overlook limiting factors, nonlinearities and delays. Our reading: each item is a place where the map leaves out part of the territory.
Her verdict: even if you understand all these characteristics, you may be surprised less often, but you will still be surprised. The list reduces surprise; it does not end it.
card.rule: Treat each reason for surprise as a gap between model and world, learn the list to be surprised less often, and expect some surprise anyway.
card.limits: Meadows presents the chapter as a warning list, not a cure. Our reading: the common thread, a model falling short, is ours; she lists the items separately.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: From surprising to perverse
concepts.question: How do the traps of Chapter Five differ from the ordinary surprises of Chapter Four?

paragraphs: Chapter Five starts by saying that delays, nonlinearities and fuzzy boundaries appear in just about any system and generally should not be changed. But some systems are more than surprising. They are perverse: structured to produce truly problematic behavior. Meadows calls the common structures archetypes, or traps.

Our reading of how the traps use the earlier pieces: policy resistance rests on balancing loops held by actors with different goals, as Chapter Two led us to expect. Escalation and success to the successful are reinforcing loops. The tragedy of the commons is missing feedback from a resource to its users. Drift and seeking the wrong goal are about goals that slide or are set badly.

Meadows's point is that blaming, disciplining, firing, twisting policy levers harder or hoping for better events will not fix structural problems. Traps can be escaped by recognizing them early or by changing the structure: new goals, altered feedback loops or added ones. That is why she calls them opportunities as well.
card.rule: When a bad pattern keeps recurring, name the archetype and change the structure rather than blaming the actors.
