card.limits: The archetypes are not a complete list: Meadows says there are many forms of systems trouble, some unique and many strikingly common. Escaping a trap is possible, not guaranteed.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: The list from numbers to paradigms
concepts.question: What principle orders Meadows's twelve places to intervene, and how sure is she of that order?

paragraphs: Chapter Six begins from Jay Forrester's observation that people inside a system often sense where its leverage points are, but push in the wrong direction. Meadows offers a list of twelve places to intervene, numbered from 12, Numbers, up to 1, Transcending Paradigms. The smaller the number, the greater the leverage.

The list climbs from details to the sources of a system: numbers, buffers, stock-and-flow structure, delays, balancing loops, reinforcing loops, information flows, rules, self-organization, goals, paradigms, and the freedom to hold paradigms loosely. Each step up shapes what lies below it. Paradigms, for example, are the mind-set from which goals, structure, rules, delays and parameters arise. The higher the point, the more the system resists change there.

Meadows is cautious about her own order. She calls it a work in progress and an invitation to think more broadly about system change, not a recipe. She adds that exceptions can move any item up or down the list.
card.rule: When fixes at a low level keep failing, look higher up the list, expect more resistance as you climb, and treat the order as a guide.
card.limits: The list is the author's own tentative ordering. High leverage does not mean easy: the higher the point, the more the system resists.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: Which lever answers which trap
concepts.question: Which leverage points of Chapter Six does Meadows herself tie to traps of Chapter Five, and which links are ours?

paragraphs: The book never prints one table of traps against leverage points, but Chapter Six names several itself. Under reinforcing loops (item 7), she describes the success-to-the-successful trap and says it is more effective to weaken the loops that feed winners than to add weak balancing programs. Under information flows (item 6), she uses the commons: fisheries collapse because little feedback runs from the fish population to investment decisions.

Under rules (item 5), she describes a trade system whose rules shut out feedback from most of society and push nations into reinforcing races to the bottom, and she says power over the rules is real power. Under goals (item 3), she says if a goal is to gather more under one central control, everything lower on the list bends to it.

Our reading: the remaining traps fit the same ladder. Policy resistance, where actors pull apart, points toward larger shared goals. Seeking the wrong goal points to goals as a lever. Chapter Five's ways out, new goals, new loops, new feedback, are the changes Chapter Six ranks.
card.rule: Match a trap to the lever that changes its structure, and say plainly which links the author makes and which are inference.
card.limits: The mapping is not one trap to one lever: a trap can be addressed at several levels. Meadows warns that the list is tentative and has exceptions.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: From control to dancing
concepts.question: How does Chapter Seven turn the book's findings into a way of living, and why does it give up on control?

paragraphs: Chapter Seven opens by correcting an expectation: that systems thinking is the key to prediction and control. Meadows says self-organizing, nonlinear, feedback systems are inherently unpredictable and not controllable, and understandable only in the most general way. So she replaces the conqueror with the dancer: we cannot control systems or figure them out, but we can dance with them.

The chapter ends with practices she calls systems wisdoms: behavioral consequences of a worldview built on feedback, nonlinearity and systems responsible for their own behavior. Several echo earlier chapters in her own words. Our reading of some pairs: expose your mental models echoes Chapter Four's every-map-is-a-model; honor information echoes the missing feedback of Chapters Five and Six; celebrate complexity echoes self-organization in Chapter Three.

She does not offer the list as a finished rulebook. She says it is probably incomplete and not unique to systems thinking, and that she is still a student. Her own group, she admits, lectured on addiction yet could not give up coffee.
card.rule: Replace the aim of control with attentive practices that fit an unpredictable, interconnected world, and trace each to the finding it rests on.
card.limits: Most of the links to earlier chapters are our reading. The author says the list is incomplete and that many other ways to learn to dance exist.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: The limits the author states herself
concepts.question: Where does Meadows say herself that her models, lists or systems thinking fall short?

paragraphs: Meadows states limits at several points. The zoo of Part One is too neat: it separates the animals from each other and from their concealing environment. Models are not the real world, and the book rests on a duality of much knowledge and more ignorance. The twelve leverage points are a tentative list with a slithery order, and she insists they are not a recipe.

Chapter Seven adds more. Her own early group understood how to fix a system but did not follow its own advice, and their insights raised at least as many questions as they answered, especially about the human mind and heart. Complex systems cannot be predicted or controlled, and exact foresight is unrealizable.

Her closing admission: systems thinking by itself cannot bridge the gap between understanding and implementation, but it can lead us to the edge of what analysis can do and point beyond, to what the human spirit must do.
card.rule: Read each of the author's claims together with the limit she places on it.
card.limits: Our reading: the limits are her own, and they tighten the argument rather than withdraw it, since they follow from the same view that systems are partly unpredictable.

concepts.unit: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
concepts.title: A complementary lens, and what lies beyond it
concepts.question: What does Meadows conclude about the value of systems thinking, and what does she say lies beyond it?

paragraphs: Her conclusion has three strands. First, the systems lens is complementary, not superior. She does not think the systems way of seeing is better than the reductionist way; each lens, the eye, the microscope, the telescope and systems theory, shows things that are really there, so the more ways of seeing the better.

Second, what the lens offers: it helps us reclaim intuition about whole systems, understand parts, see interconnections, ask what-if questions about future behavior and be creative and courageous about redesign. Chapter Six sums up mastery as letting go and dancing with the system.

Third, its edge. Systems thinking can tell us what to do, for example not to weigh bad news more heavily than good, but it cannot do it. It leads to the edge of what analysis can do and points to what the human spirit must do. Our reading: this returns to the Introduction's hope that insights can make a difference in ourselves and in our world.
card.rule: Sum up the book as a complementary lens that deepens understanding and redesign but cannot replace human action.
card.limits: This is the author's own closing, not a verdict on every field. Our reading: other lenses are judged by what they reveal, so the complement claim is a modest one.

questions.q: Meadows holds a Slinky and then its box in the same way and pulls away her lower hand. What happens?
options: Both drop and bounce, because the same hand movement acts on each of them equally
Both hang still, because a hand pulled away gently cannot start any movement at all
The Slinky drops and bounces up and down, while the box hangs there
The box drops quickly and the Slinky hangs still
optionExplain: Tempting if you think the hand is the only cause, but the box does not move.
Tempting if you think a gentle release does nothing, but the Slinky bounces.
Right: the same movement gives a bounce for the spring and nothing for the box.
A guess based on weight; Meadows reports that the box simply hangs.
questions.explain: The Slinky bounces and the box does not. The card next shows why this matters.
questions.rule: Same action, different result.

questions.q: Meadows says the hands that manipulate the Slinky suppress or release a behavior that is ____ in its structure.
questions.explain: Latent means stored in the structure of the spring and not yet showing. The hands only suppress or release it.
questions.rule: The behavior is already in the structure.

questions.q: One bakery fails after a flour shortage, while a neighboring bakery facing the same shortage keeps trading. What does the Slinky lesson suggest?
options: The shortage released behavior latent in the first bakery's own setup, which the second bakery's setup lacked
The shortage alone caused the failure, and the second bakery must have faced a milder version of the shortage
Nothing can be learned from the pair, because two separate cases never show what any structure does when it is pushed
The first owner pulled the wrong lever, so one person's decision accounts for the whole difference in outcomes
optionExplain: Right: like the Slinky and the box, the same push meets two different structures.
This keeps the cause outside and ignores the Slinky and box contrast.
The pair is exactly like the Slinky and box: same push, different result, which is informative.
Personal blame is another outside-the-structure explanation; the lesson points to the structure.
questions.explain: The same shortage met two different structures and gave two results, as the same hand movement did with the Slinky and the box.
questions.rule: Same push, different structure, different result.

questions.q: True or false: If a wooden ruler were held and released like the Slinky, what it did would depend mainly on the ruler's own structure.
questions.explain: The box and the Slinky differ only in structure, and they behave differently. By the same reasoning the ruler's own structure decides what the release does.
questions.rule: Structure decides what a release does.

questions.q: Four students summarize the demonstration. Which summary goes beyond what Meadows says?
options: The hand releases a behavior that the structure of the spring already holds ready to appear
The box shows that the same hand movement does not always produce a bounce
The answer lies within the Slinky itself and not in the hand alone
The hand is irrelevant, because the Slinky would bounce by itself with no one touching it
optionExplain: Accurate: the behavior is latent in the structure and the hand releases it.
Accurate: the box hangs still under the same movement.
Accurate: she says the answer lies within the Slinky.
This overstates: Meadows says the hands suppress or release behavior, so the hand is the trigger.
questions.explain: Meadows gives the hands a role as the trigger that suppresses or releases the behavior. What she denies is that the hand is the whole explanation.
questions.rule: Triggers matter; they are not the whole cause.

questions.q: A town is flooded and its council blames the river. Using the Slinky lesson, which question should the council ask next?
options: Which upstream authority is responsible for the water that reached the town?
How did the town's own layout and policies shape its response to the flood?
How can the river's flow be controlled so such a push never comes again?
Which council member failed to give a warning before the flood arrived?
optionExplain: This looks for another outside party, the same move as blaming the river.
Right: it looks for the behavior latent in the town's own structure.
Controlling the push is the habit of acting on the world; the lesson asks about the structure that responds.
This looks for an individual to blame instead of the structure.
questions.explain: The flood is the hand and the town is the Slinky, so the lesson sends the council to the town's structure. Meadows warns that this is easy to accept for Slinkies but can be heretical for cities.
questions.rule: Ask what in the structure made it respond this way.
questions.teaches: Meadows says the idea is easy to understand for Slinkies but can be heretical when applied to individuals, companies, cities, or economies.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows argues that the ups and downs of a market economy are inherent in its structure.
questions.explain: She says political leaders do not cause recessions or booms, because the ups and downs come from the structure of the market economy. The card next sets out the reasoning.
questions.rule: Look to the structure for the pattern.

questions.q: In Meadows' definition, a system is a set of things ____ in such a way that they produce their own pattern of behavior over time.
questions.explain: Interconnection is the core of her definition: the things are linked so that together they produce a characteristic pattern of behavior.
questions.rule: Interconnected things produce their own pattern.

questions.q: A chain of cafes loses customers after a rival opens nearby. Which analysis follows Meadows' argument?
options: Blame the rival entirely, since its opening is the only event that changed in the neighborhood
Examine the chain's own pricing, staffing and quality policies, which shaped its response
Replace the regional manager
Wait for the rival to fail, since the arrival of a competitor is outside the chain's control
optionExplain: This assigns the whole cause to the outside event, which Meadows rejects.
Right: the chain creates its losses at least in part through its own policies.
This finds a culprit; the argument points to the structure, not to one person.
This treats the event as the only cause; the chain's own policies are within its control.
questions.explain: Meadows says companies create their losses at least in part through their own business policies, so the cafes' own structure is the first place to look.
questions.rule: Look first at your own policies.

questions.q: Two farms face the same drought. One grows a single rain-fed crop; the other grows several crops and irrigates. What does Meadows' reasoning predict?
options: Both will suffer equally, because the same drought is the cause of whatever result follows
Both will do equally well, because a system responds only to what it controls inside itself
Only the single-crop farm will be affected
Results will probably differ, because each farm's own structure shapes its response
optionExplain: This contradicts the claim that the same event gives different results in different systems.
Outside events can still trigger behavior; the claim is that the response is characteristic of the system.
This overstates: a diverse farm may cope better, but nothing in the claim says outside events cease to matter.
Right: the same event applied to different systems is likely to give different results.
questions.explain: The drought is the same, but the two farms are different systems, so Meadows expects different responses.
questions.rule: Same event, different system, different result.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says competitors play no part at all when a company loses market share.
questions.explain: She says competitors rarely cause the loss and may be there to scoop up the advantage, while the company creates its losses at least in part through its own policies. The role is reduced, not removed.
questions.rule: Hedged claims are not absolute claims.

questions.q: A hospital blames one nurse for repeated medication delays. How would Meadows' view reframe the problem?
options: Study the ward's schedules, staffing and handover rules, which may produce delays for anyone
Accept the nurse as the cause, since a person is the only part of a ward that acts and decides
Look for a passing outside event, such as a flu wave, and treat the ward itself as irrelevant
Treat the delays as random, since no study of the ward could explain them at all
optionExplain: Right: the ward is a system, and its structure may produce the pattern.
This is the individual-blame view that Meadows argues against.
An outside event may trigger delays, but the claim is that the system's own structure shapes the response.
Meadows says a system's response is characteristic of itself, which can be studied.
questions.explain: The delays are a pattern, and a pattern is a system behavior. Meadows applies the same logic to illness and addiction.
questions.rule: Study the structure behind a repeated pattern.
questions.teaches: Meadows applies the claim to illness and addiction: the flu virus does not attack you, since you set up the conditions for it to flourish, and addiction is not the failing of an individual.

questions.q: Meadows finds her claims both unsettling and common sense. What does she say explains the double reaction?
options: Two schools of economics that disagree about whether outside events or internal structure matter more
Two generations of readers, one trained before computers and one trained after they became common
Two familiar experiences: training in analysis, and a lifetime of dealing with complex systems
Two kinds of evidence, studies of nations and studies of individuals, that point in opposite directions
optionExplain: She does not mention rival schools of economics here.
She does not split readers by generation.
Right: she traces resistance and recognition to two experiences everyone has had.
She does not cite two bodies of evidence; she speaks of kinds of experience.
questions.explain: She links resistance to analytical training and recognition to everyday dealings with complex systems. The card next tells both.
questions.rule: Two experiences, two reactions.

questions.q: Match each item to the description Meadows gives.
pairs: Tracing direct paths from cause to effect
Practical understanding built up without analysis, often without words
Naming presidents, competitors or viruses as the causes of problems
questions.explain: Analytical training traces direct causes and so encourages naming single culprits. Lived experience gives a practical, often wordless feel for how connected things behave.
questions.rule: Analysis traces causes; experience senses wholes.

questions.q: After a failed product launch, a manager's first move is to find who made the mistake. Which source does Meadows' account give for that move?
options: A lack of intelligence, which keeps people from seeing how the parts of a project connect
Modern computers, which make people treat every event as a number to be assigned to someone
Training that teaches us to trace a direct path from an effect back to a single cause
A distrust of authority, which makes people reject any explanation offered from above
optionExplain: Meadows credits ordinary people with a practical understanding of systems, not a lack of intelligence.
She says systems theory is tied to computers, but not that they cause blame-finding.
Right: she says analytical training leads us to see particular causes of our problems.
Nothing in the passage mentions distrust of authority as a source of blame-finding.
questions.explain: The manager is using the habit of tracing a path from an effect to one cause, which Meadows ties to training in analysis.
questions.rule: Analytical habit looks for the single cause.

questions.q: Which statement misreports what Meadows says about analytical training?
options: It is a mistaken habit that should be dropped in favor of intuition alone
It is a source of much personal and societal power in our lives
It leads us to see presidents and competitors as the causes of our problems
It teaches us to look at things in small, understandable pieces
optionExplain: This misreports her: she credits the training with much power and does not ask us to drop it.
Accurate: she says the training is the source of much personal and societal power.
Accurate: she says it leads us to name such causes.
Accurate: she lists looking at small pieces as part of the training.
questions.explain: Meadows calls analytical training a source of much power. Her point is that it is one of two experiences, and the other, lived experience of systems, should be reclaimed too.
questions.rule: Credit what analysis gives; add what it misses.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows would expect a gardener who has not studied systems to have no practical understanding of how her garden responds.
questions.explain: She says we built up a practical understanding of how complex systems work, intuitively and often without words. A gardener is likely to have it even without systems vocabulary.
questions.rule: Practical understanding can exist without words for it.

questions.q: A council trained in budget analysis plans to cut one bus line, but residents who use it warn of knock-on effects. Which pairing fits Meadows' account?
options: Residents show training in analysis, while the council shows lived experience of complex systems
Both groups use the same analysis and differ only in which figures they choose to count
The council shows systems thinking, while residents show the habit of blaming a single cause
Analysis traces one cause and effect, while residents' lived experience senses the whole
optionExplain: This swaps the two experiences.
Residents' warning about knock-on effects is not an analysis of figures; it comes from living in the system.
The council is acting on one part; residents are the ones sensing connections.
Right: this pairs analytic cause-and-effect with the intuitive sense of connection.
questions.explain: The council reasons from a single cause and effect, a product of analytic training. Residents draw on lived dealings with a connected system. Meadows adds that we are ourselves such systems.
questions.rule: Both pulls show up in one decision.
questions.teaches: Meadows counts every person, organization, animal, garden, tree and forest we meet as a complex system, and our own bodies as magnificent examples of integrated, self-maintaining complexity.

questions.q: Meadows says systems theory, for all its equations, can often be translated into what?
options: Plain statistics that any reader can check with a calculator in a few minutes
Traditional wisdom that people already hold at some level
Rules of thumb written by managers for use inside a single firm
Legal principles that courts have applied to disputes about shared resources
optionExplain: She does not claim systems ideas reduce to statistics.
Right: she says systems theory deals in truths known at some level by everyone.
She does not tie the translation to managers' rules of thumb.
Legal principles are not mentioned in the passage.
questions.explain: She says the jargon can be translated directly into traditional wisdom. The card next gives three pairs.
questions.rule: Old sayings often name systems truths.

questions.q: Match each systems principle to the saying Meadows pairs it with.
pairs: Feedback delays make a problem hard to solve once it shows
A stitch in time saves nine
A reinforcing loop rewards winners with the means to win more
The rich get richer and the poor get poorer
A diverse system is more stable than a uniform one
Do not put all your eggs in one basket
questions.explain: Each pair translates a technical principle into everyday words: delays, reinforcement and diversity.
questions.rule: Each principle has an everyday twin.

questions.q: A farmer plants one wheat variety across every field, and one blight ruins the harvest. Which saying and principle fit?
options: A stitch in time: a delay in feedback let the blight grow before anyone noticed it
Eggs in one basket: a uniform system with little diversity is vulnerable to shock
The rich get richer: the wheat variety kept winning and squeezed out every rival crop
Many hands make light work: spreading the labor over more workers would have saved the crop
optionExplain: A delay could matter, but the facts given point to the uniformity of the crop.
Right: one variety everywhere is a uniform system, exposed to a single shock.
No competition or reinforcing loop is described; the case is about one uniform crop, not a rival crop winning.
This saying is not one Meadows pairs with a systems principle and does not fit the facts.
questions.explain: Planting one variety everywhere is the uniform, low-diversity case that Meadows says is more vulnerable to external shock.
questions.rule: Uniform systems are fragile.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows pairs the idea that a diverse system with many pathways is more stable with the saying that the rich get richer.
questions.explain: She pairs diversity with putting eggs in one basket. The rich get richer is her saying for a reinforcing loop in which winners gain the means to win again.
questions.rule: Match principle to the right saying.

questions.q: Two online marketplaces compete. The one with more sellers draws more buyers, which draws still more sellers. What outcome does the reinforcing loop point to?
options: Both marketplaces settle at equal size, since each one's gain is offset by the other's loss
The smaller marketplace is protected, since a diverse market is more stable than a uniform one
Early trouble goes unseen, so the problem is hard to fix once it becomes apparent to anyone
Winning supplies the means to win further, so in the end all but a few competitors drop out
optionExplain: That describes balance, not the snowballing of a reinforcing loop.
This mixes up the diversity principle with the reinforcing loop.
This is the delay principle, which the scenario does not describe.
Right: winners gain the means to win again and rivals drop out.
questions.explain: Each win feeds the next, which is the rich-get-richer pattern. Meadows states it as the competitive exclusion principle.
questions.rule: Reinforcing winners crowd out rivals.
questions.teaches: Meadows states this as the competitive exclusion principle: if a reinforcing feedback loop rewards the winner with the means to win further competitions, all but a few competitors are eliminated. She also cites Mark 4:25 for it.

questions.q: According to Meadows, why do hunger, poverty and war persist despite great analytical effort?
options: They are systems problems, behaviors characteristic of the structures that produce them
Too little money and technical talent has been directed at them over the centuries
Powerful groups deliberately keep them going because they profit from the disorder
Their causes are external agents that are too distant or too large for ordinary people to control
optionExplain: Right: she calls them systems problems that yield only to restructuring.
She says brilliance and analytical ability have been directed at them.
She says no one deliberately creates them or wants them to persist.
She locates the cause in internal structure, not in distant external agents.
questions.explain: She argues the problems are produced by system structure. The card next explains why that defeats technical fixes.
questions.rule: Structural problems resist outside fixes.

questions.q: Meadows says hunger, poverty and war are intrinsically ____ problems, undesirable behaviors characteristic of the structures that produce them.
questions.explain: She calls them systems problems: no one deliberately creates them or wants them to persist, yet the structures produce them.
questions.rule: Persistence needs no villain, only a structure.

questions.q: A city keeps widening a congested highway, and the congestion keeps returning. Which response matches Meadows' advice?
options: Hire better engineers, since a persistent problem means the technical work so far was weak
Find the group of drivers responsible and target them
Ask what in the city's structure keeps producing congestion, not what fix to try next
Accept the congestion as a fact of nature, since problems that persist cannot be changed
optionExplain: Meadows says technical brilliance has been applied to such problems without success.
This is the casting of blame she says we must stop.
Right: repeated fixes that fail point to the structure behind the problem.
She says such problems yield when we restructure the system.
questions.explain: The widening is a technical fix on one part. A problem that keeps returning is a sign of structure, which is where Meadows says to look.
questions.rule: Repeated failure of fixes points at structure.

questions.q: Which summary overstates Meadows' view?
options: Some serious problems, such as smallpox, were solved by focusing on external agents
Some of the problems that persist are rooted in the internal structure of complex systems
Looking for external causes has solved no serious problem, so it should be dropped
We would rather think that a problem's cause is out there than in here, in ourselves
optionExplain: Accurate: she names smallpox among the successes.
Accurate: those are the real messes she describes.
This overstates: she names smallpox and food production as successes of looking outward.
Accurate: she says this is our psychological and political preference.
questions.explain: Meadows credits the outward-looking approach with real successes. Her point is that it fails for problems rooted in internal structure.
questions.rule: Know where an approach stops working.

questions.q: True or false: If a society removes a villain it blames for a structurally rooted problem, Meadows' view predicts the problem is likely to remain.
questions.explain: If the structure produces the behavior, removing a person leaves the structure in place, so the pattern can return.
questions.rule: Removing the culprit leaves the structure.

questions.q: A grower sprays a field to kill a pest, then finds fewer pollinators and a worse harvest. Which idea from Meadows helps explain this?
options: A solution aimed at one external agent can create new problems because the field sits inside a larger system
A solution fails when the person applying it does not use enough of the chemical to reach every pest
A solution that works on one pest once proves the pest was the whole cause of the earlier harm to the field
A solution works better on a system that has first been taken apart into small pieces and studied one at a time
optionExplain: Right: the fix acted on one part of a connected system.
More chemical is the same outside-in fix, only stronger.
A single success does not show the pest was the whole story, and the worse harvest suggests it was not.
Breaking things into pieces is the reductionist habit that overlooks the connections.
questions.explain: Because the field is part of a larger system, acting on one part can disturb others. Meadows notes that this has happened with solutions in many fields.
questions.rule: Fixes act on connected parts.
questions.teaches: Meadows says that because they are embedded in larger systems, some of our solutions have created further problems.

questions.q: Which benefit does Meadows promise from systems thinking in a complex, fast-changing world?
options: Exact forecasts of future events
A set of technical fixes that remove problems without anyone having to change how they think
Proof that outside forces are not the real source of any difficulty people face
The freedom to identify root causes of problems and to see new opportunities
optionExplain: She speaks of asking what-if questions about possible futures, not exact forecasts.
She says the way of thinking has to change, and offers no technical fix.
She says outside events can unleash behavior; she does not claim to prove them irrelevant.
Right: root causes and new opportunities are the benefits she names.
questions.explain: She promises freedom to see root causes and opportunities. The card next lists what the lens helps us do.
questions.rule: Systems thinking widens choices.

questions.q: Which three of these abilities does Meadows say the systems lens helps us hone?
options: Understanding parts
Forecasting exact future events
Seeing interconnections
Replacing intuition with equations
Asking what-if questions about possible future behaviors
Avoiding any study of the parts
optionExplain: Right: she lists honing our abilities to understand parts.
She speaks of what-if questions, not exact forecasts.
Right: seeing interconnections is on her list.
She wants us to reclaim intuition, not replace it.
Right: what-if questions about possible future behaviors are on her list.
She keeps understanding parts on her list.
questions.explain: Her list has four items: understand parts, see interconnections, ask what-if questions and be creative and courageous about redesign.
questions.rule: The lens adds abilities; it does not remove old ones.

questions.q: A library director sees falling visits. Which step uses the ability to ask what-if questions about possible future behaviors?
options: Survey a hundred patrons about authors they dislike and remove those authors from the shelves
Sketch how changing opening hours and layout might alter future visit patterns
Hire a consultant to forecast next year's visits to the exact number before any decisions
Compare each branch's visit count with last year's to find the single worst branch
optionExplain: This responds to current complaints and does not explore how the system might behave.
Right: it explores possible futures under different changes.
Meadows speaks of what-if questions, not exact forecasting.
Ranking branches looks at past parts and does not ask what might happen if something changed.
questions.explain: A what-if question varies something and asks how behavior over time might change, which the sketch of hours and layout does.
questions.rule: Vary something and ask what follows.

questions.q: Meadows says three things follow once we see how structure relates to behavior. Put them in her order.
items: See the relationship between structure and behavior
Understand how systems work and what makes them produce poor results
Learn how to shift them into better behavior patterns
questions.explain: Seeing the link comes first, then understanding how systems work and fail, then shifting them toward better patterns.
questions.rule: See first, understand next, then redesign.
questions.teaches: Meadows says that once we see the relationship between structure and behavior, we can understand how systems work, what makes them produce poor results, and how to shift them into better behavior patterns.
questions.hint: Seeing something comes before understanding it, and understanding comes before changing it.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the systems lens works by replacing our intuition about whole systems with mathematical analysis.
questions.explain: She says it lets us reclaim our intuition about whole systems, and she keeps the discussion nontechnical.
questions.rule: The lens revives intuition.

questions.q: A team member says: if the trouble lies in our own setup, we can change it, but we can no longer point at an outsider. Which reaction of Meadows' does this capture?
options: Frightening, since it means a problem rooted in structure can never be solved by anyone who tries
Comforting, since solutions are in our hands, and disturbing, since we must think differently
Reassuring only, since seeing a problem in a new way removes any need to act differently afterwards
Irrelevant to her view
optionExplain: She says the solutions are in our hands.
Right: this is her pair of reactions.
She says we must do or see or think things differently.
She says to stop casting blame.
questions.explain: The team member feels both the comfort of having power over the cause and the discomfort of giving up an outside culprit.
questions.rule: The idea comforts and disturbs.
questions.teaches: Meadows calls the systems idea comforting, since the solutions are in our hands, and disturbing, since we must do, see or think about things in a different way.

questions.section: Purpose and method of the book
questions.q: Who does Meadows say her book is intended for?
options: Professional systems analysts who want to move from field work into computer models and simulations
Engineering students who must learn the equations of feedback before they can use any diagrams
Managers who need ready-made rules for fixing the problems that arise in their companies
People wary of the word systems, who may have done systems thinking all their lives
optionExplain: She says the book is nontechnical, so it is not aimed at analysts building models.
She says she shows how far one can go without mathematics.
She offers a way of seeing and thinking, not ready-made rules.
Right: she writes for the wary, who may already think in systems.
questions.explain: She writes for readers who are wary of the field but already think in systems. The card next adds how she writes.
questions.rule: Know the intended reader.

questions.section: Purpose and method of the book
questions.q: Meadows uses diagrams because words come ____ at a time, while systems happen all at once.
questions.explain: Words and sentences come one at a time in linear order, but systems are connected in many directions at once.
questions.rule: Pictures show everything at once.

questions.section: Purpose and method of the book
questions.q: An engineer shows visitors a subway network with a map instead of reading out a list of stations. Which reasoning of Meadows' matches?
options: A picture shows all the parts and their connections at once, which one-at-a-time words cannot
A picture is easier to memorize, so visitors remember the stations after a single viewing of it
A picture hides the equations, so visitors are not frightened by the mathematics of the network
A picture is a more modern medium than text, so it suits an up-to-date subject like transit
optionExplain: Right: this is her reason for using diagrams.
Memorability is not the reason she gives.
Avoiding mathematics is a separate point, about keeping the book nontechnical.
She does not appeal to fashion.
questions.explain: She says pictures work better than words for this language because you can see all the parts of a picture at once.
questions.rule: Use a picture when everything is connected at once.

questions.section: Purpose and method of the book
questions.q: True or false: According to Meadows, a reader with no mathematics or computing background can still make real progress toward understanding systems from this book.
questions.explain: She keeps the discussion nontechnical to show how far you can go without mathematics or computers.
questions.rule: The book needs no math.

questions.section: Purpose and method of the book
questions.q: A teacher must introduce a complicated wiring diagram to nervous trainees. Which approach matches Meadows' plan for her pictures?
options: Show the full finished diagram first, so trainees see how large the whole is
Skip the diagram and read the connections out one at a time in order
Build the diagram up gradually, beginning with very simple pictures
Begin with the mathematics behind each wire, so the picture has a firm basis
optionExplain: This starts with the most complicated picture, the opposite of her plan.
This returns to one-at-a-time words, which she says cannot show connections at once.
Right: she builds her systems pictures up gradually from simple ones.
She keeps the discussion nontechnical.
questions.explain: Meadows starts with very simple pictures and adds to them, and she expects readers to find the graphical language easy to understand.
questions.rule: Build pictures from simple to complex.
questions.teaches: Meadows says she will build up systems pictures gradually, starting with very simple ones, and expects readers to understand this graphical language easily.

questions.q: Where does Meadows begin her tour of systems?
options: With a systems zoo of common types, before any definition of the parts involved in them
With leverage points for change
With the definition of a system and its parts, then the feedback loop built from them
With archetypes called system traps, because they are the most common problems people meet
optionExplain: The zoo comes after the basics.
Leverage points come late in the book.
Right: she starts with the basics and builds up to the feedback loop.
Archetypes come after the zoo and the discussion of why systems work and surprise us.
questions.explain: She begins with the definition and dissection of parts. The card next lays out the whole route.
questions.rule: Basics before examples.

questions.q: Put the stages of Meadows' road map in the order she plans to present them.
items: The basics: a system, its parts and the feedback loop
The systems zoo of common system types
Why systems work so well and why they surprise us
Archetypes: system traps and opportunities
Leverage points for restructuring systems
The largest lessons from systems thinkers' wisdom
questions.explain: She moves from basics to examples, then to why systems work and surprise us, then to archetypes, leverage points and finally the lessons.
questions.rule: Basics, zoo, why, traps, leverage, lessons.

questions.q: A reader wants a glossary and the model equations behind Part One. Where does Meadows point them?
options: The Appendix, which also holds a bibliography and a list of systems principles
The systems zoo, where each animal is given with its governing equations
The closing chapter on lessons, which gathers the technical material in one place
The chapter on leverage points, which restates every model as a set of equations
optionExplain: Right: the Appendix holds the glossary, bibliography, principles and equations.
The zoo introduces types of systems; the equations are in the Appendix.
The closing lessons are about wisdom, not technical material.
Leverage points are about where to intervene, not about restating the models.
questions.explain: Meadows says the Appendix offers ways to dig deeper, including a glossary and equations for the models of Part One.
questions.rule: Look in the Appendix for the technical material.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly separates the feedback loop from the systems zoo?
options: The loop is a collection of common system types, and the zoo is the basic operating unit of a system
The loop is a common problem structure, and the zoo explains why systems so often surprise us
The loop is a set of leverage points for change, and the zoo is the list of the closing lessons
The loop is the basic operating unit built from the parts; the zoo is a collection of common types
optionExplain: This swaps the two terms: the loop is the basic unit, the zoo the collection of types.
Common problem structures are the archetypes, and the zoo only supplies examples.
Leverage points and lessons come near the end and are different things.
Right: the loop is the unit and the zoo is a collection of types.
questions.explain: The feedback loop is where the parts come together, and the zoo gathers examples of systems built from such units.
questions.rule: Unit first, then collection.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows uses a few zoo examples as a foundation before she steps back to ask why systems work well and surprise us.
questions.explain: She says that with a few zoo animals as a foundation she will step back to discuss how and why systems work and why they surprise us.
questions.rule: Examples come before the general discussion.

questions.q: Two neighboring schools draw on one limited budget and each overspends, leaving too little for both. Which archetype and setting from Meadows' list fit?
options: Eroding goals, seen in the business rules and incentives that shape new technologies and their development
Tragedy of the commons, seen in shared water among communities or money among schools
Policy resistance, seen in decision-making power and relationships within a family, community or nation
Addiction, seen in dependence on many more agents than caffeine, alcohol, nicotine or narcotics
optionExplain: Her eroding goals example concerns rules and incentives for technology.
Right: she places the commons in shared water or financial allocation.
Her policy resistance example concerns decision-making power and relationships.
Addiction is about dependence, not a shared budget.
questions.explain: Shared, limited resources drawn on by several parties match her tragedy of the commons example. The other three archetypes she names are matched with different settings.
questions.rule: Match the archetype to the structure.
questions.teaches: Meadows names four archetypes in the introduction: tragedy of the commons, eroding goals, policy resistance and addiction, each tied to a setting. She first called archetypes system traps, then added and opportunities.

questions.q: How does Meadows compare the systems way of seeing with the reductionist way of thinking?
options: As superior: it replaces reductionism wherever the two disagree about a problem
As complementary: each reveals real things that the other leaves unseen
As equivalent: both reveal exactly the same facts by different routes of reasoning
As contradictory: only one can be true, so readers must choose between them
optionExplain: She says she does not think it is better.
Right: she calls them complementary and therefore revealing.
Her lens image says each shows different things.
She says everything seen through each lens is actually there.
questions.explain: She says complementary, not better. The card next explains with the lens comparison.
questions.rule: Different lenses, different views.

questions.q: Meadows says the systems way of seeing is ____ to the reductionist way of thinking, and therefore revealing.
questions.explain: Complementary means each adds something the other lacks.
questions.rule: Complementary, not superior.

questions.q: A planner tests soil at one site and also models how traffic, housing and jobs interact across the region. Which view fits Meadows?
options: The regional model is better, so the soil test adds nothing that matters for the planning
The soil test is better, because only measurable parts are really there to be studied
The two approaches conflict, so the planner should pick whichever one is more modern
Each approach shows real features of the place, and neither makes the other unnecessary
optionExplain: She does not rank the systems view above analysis.
She says everything seen through each lens is actually there.
She sees the lenses as complementary, not in conflict.
Right: this is the complementary view.
questions.explain: The soil test looks at a part, and the model looks at interconnections; both show things that are really there.
questions.rule: Use more than one lens.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says that what a microscope shows is less real than what systems theory shows.
questions.explain: She says everything seen through each kind of lens is actually there.
questions.rule: Every lens shows real things.

questions.q: Meadows argues that more ways of seeing are better when the world is messier. Which change would weaken that argument?
options: A world that grew less crowded, less connected and slower to change
A world in which more people adopted the reductionist way of thinking
A world in which computers became faster at solving analytic problems
A world in which people trusted their intuition more than before
optionExplain: Right: her argument rests on the world being messy, crowded, interconnected and fast-changing.
More reductionism does not change how messy the world is.
Faster computing does not change how messy the world is.
Greater trust in intuition does not change how messy the world is.
questions.explain: Her case for more lenses depends on the world's growing messiness. If those conditions eased, the case would be weaker.
questions.rule: Check the condition an argument depends on.

questions.q: A physicist sits in on an ecology seminar and remarks: you ask different kinds of questions here. What explanation does Meadows' lens account offer?
options: One group is better trained, so its questions come closer to the truth
The groups study different objects, so their questions can have nothing in common
A different lens shows different things, each of them actually there
The ecologists hold looser standards, so they avoid the hard questions of analysis
optionExplain: Meadows does not rank the lenses.
She says all the lenses show real things of one world.
Right: different lenses lead to different questions and views.
She does not suggest systems thinkers avoid analysis.
questions.explain: A lens determines what you notice and ask. Meadows recounts that a Dartmouth colleague said something very like this to her group.
questions.rule: Questions follow from the lens.
questions.teaches: A Dartmouth engineering professor told Meadows' research group that they ask different questions and see things he does not; she hopes the book, especially its conclusion, shows how and why.

questions.section: Interlude • The Blind Men and the Matter of the Elephant
questions.q: What lesson does Meadows say the story of the blind men and the elephant teaches?
options: Blind people can learn about large objects only by working together as a group of explorers
A person who holds a firm opinion should defer to the one with the most experience of the matter
A system's behavior cannot be known from the elements it is made of alone
Large things should be studied by dividing them into smaller parts to begin with, then adding up
optionExplain: The story does not say people must pool their findings, and the lesson she names is different.
The story does not concern deference to experience.
Right: this is the lesson she draws.
Dividing into parts is the very approach the story warns about when taken alone.
questions.explain: She says knowing the elements is not enough to know the system's behavior. The card next retells the story.
questions.rule: Parts do not reveal the whole.

questions.section: Interlude • The Blind Men and the Matter of the Elephant
questions.q: According to Meadows, the behavior of a system cannot be known from the ____ of which it is made alone.
questions.explain: The lesson is that knowing the elements alone does not reveal the behavior of the system.
questions.rule: Elements alone do not give behavior.

questions.section: Interlude • The Blind Men and the Matter of the Elephant
questions.q: A new manager reads each department's budget on its own and judges the company healthy. Which mistake does the story point to?
options: Assuming that knowing each part separately shows how the connected whole will behave
Relying on figures supplied by the departments, who have an interest in looking healthy
Reading the budgets in the wrong order, so the total came out distorted by timing
Giving too much weight to the one department that has the largest budget
optionExplain: Right: the manager is feeling parts and calling it the whole.
Biased figures could be a problem, but the story is about parts versus whole.
Order is not the issue the story raises.
Weighting is a separate error; the story is about missing the whole.
questions.explain: Each budget is one part, like an ear or a leg. The company's behavior depends on how the parts interact.
questions.rule: Parts do not add up to behavior.

questions.section: Interlude • The Blind Men and the Matter of the Elephant
questions.q: True or false: By the story's lesson, a perfect inventory of a system's elements would still not reveal how the system behaves.
questions.explain: The lesson says the behavior of a system cannot be known just by knowing its elements, however completely they are listed.
questions.rule: A list of parts is not an account of behavior.

questions.section: Interlude • The Blind Men and the Matter of the Elephant
questions.q: Which reading of the story goes beyond what Meadows says?
options: Each man felt only one part of the elephant out of the many parts that it has
Each man perceived the elephant wrongly on the basis of the one part he felt
The lesson is simple, yet it is one that we often ignore in everyday life
Touch is unreliable, so the men erred because they relied on it
optionExplain: Accurate: the story says each had felt one part out of many.
Accurate: the story says each perceived it wrongly.
Accurate: Meadows says the lesson is simple but often ignored.
This goes beyond the text: the error was taking a part for the whole, not the sense used.
questions.explain: Each man's feeling was of a real part. The mistake was to take a part for the whole, not a failure of touch.
questions.rule: The error was partial, not false, perception.

questions.section: Interlude • The Blind Men and the Matter of the Elephant
questions.q: Three analysts each study one product line of a firm and each confidently reports on the firm's prospects. What does the story add?
options: Confidence shows an analyst has understood the whole, since the parts reveal it in time
Confidence can come from feeling one part, which is not knowing how the whole behaves
Disagreement among the analysts proves that none of the reports is based on facts
Each analyst should study a smaller part, until the reports no longer conflict
optionExplain: The lesson is the opposite: parts alone do not reveal the whole.
Right: this is what the story shows about a confident partial view.
Each report may be based on facts about its part; the problem is the leap to the whole.
Narrowing further repeats the error.
questions.explain: In the story each man spoke with confidence from the part he could feel. The analysts share that position.
questions.rule: Confidence from a part is not knowledge of the whole.
questions.teaches: In the story each man thought he knew something because he could feel a part, and one said he had the real facts about the elephant.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: What makes a football team more than a crowd of people wearing the same kit?
options: It has far more people in it than a crowd usually has at one time
Its members are all physically fit and are trained for years
Its members are linked by rules and serve a purpose together
It owns a field, a ball and the equipment used in play
optionExplain: Size alone does not organize anyone; a bigger crowd is still a crowd.
Fitness is an attribute of the players, not of how they are connected.
Right: connections and a shared purpose are what turn a set of parts into a whole.
Equipment is a set of elements; without links and purpose it is only a pile of things.
questions.explain: Parts become a system through their links and what the whole does. The card next shows how Meadows names these.
questions.rule: Parts plus links plus purpose make a system.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: Meadows says a system must consist of elements, interconnections, and a function or ____.
questions.explain: Her definition names three kinds of ingredient: elements, interconnections, and a function or purpose.
questions.rule: Every system has elements, interconnections and a purpose.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: In a hospital ward, which item is an interconnection rather than an element?
options: The nurses who staff the ward on the night shift each week of the year
The beds and monitoring equipment installed along the ward
The patients admitted to the ward during the current month
Handover notes that pass patient information between nursing shifts
optionExplain: Nurses are elements: the things being connected.
Equipment is an element, a tangible part.
Patients are elements too; they are linked by care routines, not themselves the link.
Right: the notes are a relationship, a flow of information that links parts.
questions.explain: Interconnections are the relationships and flows that join elements; people and equipment are the elements.
questions.hint: Which item joins other things together?
questions.rule: A system is elements plus interconnections plus a function or purpose, organized so that together they achieve something.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: A clock factory keeps all its machines and workers but they no longer interact or share any output. What do Meadows’ three ingredients suggest?
options: It would remain a full system, because every one of its elements is still present
A collection of parts, not a system, since links and purpose would be missing
It would become a larger system, because there is more independence
It would be a system with no purpose, which Meadows allows
optionExplain: Elements alone do not make a system; this ignores the other two ingredients.
Right: without interconnections and a purpose, elements are only a collection.
Independence removes links, which makes it less of a system, not more.
Meadows names a function or purpose as one of three required kinds of thing.
questions.explain: Removing interconnections and purpose leaves elements without the organization that defines a system.
questions.rule: Remove the links and the purpose, and the system is gone.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: True or false: According to Meadows, a complete list of a system’s parts fully describes the system.
questions.explain: A list gives only the elements. The interconnections and the function or purpose are also needed, and they are harder to see.
questions.rule: A parts list is not a system description.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: A football club’s owner says its purpose is to win trophies, while fans say it is to have fun. Which reading fits Meadows’ team example?
options: Several purposes at once: winning, fun, exercise or money, or all of them
Only the owner’s answer counts, because the owner has the most control over it
Only one answer can be true, so the team needs a single purpose
Neither answer counts, since a purpose cannot be about enjoyment
optionExplain: Right: she lists winning, fun, exercise and making millions, “or all of the above”.
Meadows does not rank purposes by who holds power.
She allows a system to serve more than one purpose.
Fun appears in her own list of purposes for the team.
questions.explain: A system can serve several purposes together.
questions.teaches: The purpose of a football team, in Meadows’ example, can be to win games, have fun, get exercise, make millions of dollars, or all of the above.
questions.rule: A system is elements plus interconnections plus a function or purpose, organized so that together they achieve something.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: What is the main difference between a heap of sand on a road and a digestive system?
options: The digestive system is made of many more separate parts than the pile of sand is
The sand has no shape, whereas the digestive system has a fixed shape
The digestive system sits inside a body, and sand sits outdoors
A system’s parts affect one another and together serve a function; sand grains do not
optionExplain: Number of parts is not the test; sand has far more grains than the gut has organs.
Shape is not Meadows’ criterion.
Location is irrelevant to whether something is a system.
Right: interaction and a shared function separate a system from a heap.
questions.explain: What separates them is relationships and function, not size or place. The card next gives Meadows’ four tests.
questions.rule: Interaction and function separate systems from heaps.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: True or false: Sand scattered on a road by happenstance is a system, because it is made of many grains.
questions.explain: Many parts alone do not make a system. Add or remove sand and you still have sand on the road, since there are no interconnections or function.
questions.rule: Many parts do not make a system.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: Sort each item into system or not a system, going by Meadows’ questions.

items.t: A beehive
A heap of gravel on a building site
A football team
Sand scattered on a road by happenstance
A digestive system
A box of loose, unconnected screws

questions.explain: The system items have parts that affect each other and together do something none does alone. The heaps are only collections.
questions.rule: Parts that interact and act together make a system.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: You add or remove random pieces from a sand pile and from a football team’s roster. Which one changes what you have?
options: Both equally, because any change to parts changes the whole
Neither, because the identity of any collection depends only on the container holding it
Mostly the roster: random changes soon leave a different system, while sand stays sand
Mostly the sand, because it has fewer connections to hold it together
optionExplain: Meadows contrasts them: sand stays sand after additions or removals.
Containers do not define identity in her account.
Right: the team depends on specific parts and links, the sand does not.
Reverse: sand has none, so changes leave it unchanged in kind.
questions.explain: A system is sensitive to arbitrary changes in its parts; a heap is not.
questions.rule: Heaps tolerate random change; systems do not.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: True or false: Meadows presents all four of her questions as equally required conditions for being a system.
questions.explain: The first three are asked together, and the fourth is added only with the word perhaps. It checks whether the behavior persists in a variety of circumstances.
questions.rule: The persistence question is an extra check.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: Residents of a new apartment block are strangers. On the view Meadows reports, when does it become a social system?
options: As soon as every flat is let and the building is full
Once new relationships arise among the residents and a system forms
When the building has stood for a few decades without any repairs being made
Never, because only a neighborhood of houses can be a system
optionExplain: Filling the flats adds parts but no links.
Right: relationships are what create a system.
Age by itself creates no relationships.
Her point is that relationships, not building type, matter.
questions.explain: The view treats an old neighborhood where people know each other as a system, and a block of strangers as not one until relationships arise.
questions.teaches: Some people say an old city neighborhood where people know each other and communicate regularly is a social system, while a new apartment block full of strangers is not until new relationships arise.
questions.rule: To test for a system, ask whether there are identifiable parts, whether they affect each other, and whether together they do something none does alone.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: A thermostat-run building holds its temperature as the weather changes. Which description fits best?
options: Each part individually decides to keep the temperature steady for the whole building
The behavior is chance, since nonliving parts cannot respond
The building only adds up the effects of its separate parts
The whole acts in a goal-seeking way that no single part does alone
optionExplain: Parts do not each decide; they take part in a mechanism.
The regulation is not chance; nonliving parts can form a mechanism that responds to the weather.
Behavior that is only a sum would show no goal-seeking.
Right: the regulation belongs to the whole arrangement.
questions.explain: Goal-seeking is a property of the whole. The card next lists the lifelike behaviors Meadows names.
questions.rule: The whole can show behavior the parts lack.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: A system is more than the ____ of its parts.
questions.explain: Meadows says a system has a wholeness, with mechanisms to maintain it, that the parts alone do not have.
questions.rule: The whole is more than the sum of its parts.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: A coral reef regrows branches broken in a storm. Which trait named by Meadows does this show?
options: Proof that reefs are not systems, since only animals recover
A random event that has nothing to do with the reef’s structure
Self-repair over some range of disruptions, a sign of resilience
Evidence that the reef is a heap of independent, unconnected corals
optionExplain: She says systems of nonliving or living parts can repair themselves.
Mechanisms, not chance, produce the recovery.
Right: repair after disruption fits her description.
Independent corals could not coordinate repair.
questions.explain: Mending injuries is one of the lifelike behaviors she lists.
questions.rule: Mending injury marks a resilient system.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: True or false: A system that contains or consists of nonliving things cannot show lifelike behavior.
questions.explain: Meadows says systems act in lifelike ways although they may contain or consist of nonliving things.
questions.rule: Lifelike behavior needs organization, not life.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: A student writes: systems are self-repairing, so they survive any disruption. What does Meadows say that corrects this?
options: Self-repair belongs only to living systems and never to social or mechanical ones
Systems repair themselves only when someone outside directs it
Self-repair holds over at least some range of disruptions, not every kind
Self-repair is rare and appears only in very large systems
optionExplain: She includes systems with nonliving parts and social systems.
Self-organizing systems repair without outside direction.
Right: her wording is bounded; self-repair holds over at least some range of disruptions.
She says systems often repair themselves, not rarely.
questions.explain: Meadows says self-repair works over a range of disruptions; beyond that range the system can still fail.
questions.rule: Resilience has a limit.

questions.section: More Than the Sum of Its Parts
questions.q: A research lab spins out a start-up with a product nobody had pictured. Which remark of Meadows fits?
options: Out of one system, completely new and unimagined systems can arise
New systems can only be built from plans that were made before they exist at all
Nested systems never give rise to anything not already inside
A system keeps its parts fixed, so nothing new can come from it
optionExplain: Right: this is her statement about evolutionary systems.
She says systems can evolve into what was never imagined.
Nesting does not forbid novelty.
Systems change; they are not frozen.
questions.explain: Some systems are evolutionary, and new systems can arise out of old ones.
questions.teaches: Out of one system other completely new, never-before-imagined systems can arise.
questions.rule: Expect a system to maintain its wholeness, responding, adapting and repairing itself, because the whole does things the parts alone do not.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: When describing a school as a system, which of these counts as an element?
options: Only the classrooms, books and people, since elements must always be physical things
Only the rules and timetable, since elements are always rules
Only the goal of the school, since elements are purposes
Both the classrooms and an intangible such as its reputation for good teaching
optionExplain: Physical things are elements, but not the only ones.
Rules are interconnections, not all elements.
Purpose is a separate ingredient.
Right: elements can be visible or intangible.
questions.explain: Elements include intangibles. The card next explains where to stop listing.
questions.rule: Elements can be intangible.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Meadows says elements do not have to be physical things; school pride in a university is an example of an ____ element.
questions.explain: Intangibles such as school pride and academic prowess are elements too.
questions.rule: Intangibles are elements.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: You list the elements of a hospital. Which is an intangible element?
options: The operating theatres on the third floor of the main building
The trust that patients place in the staff
The drugs held in the central pharmacy at any given time
The beds counted on each ward during a night shift
optionExplain: Operating theatres are tangible rooms, so they are physical elements, not intangible ones.
Right: trust cannot be touched but shapes the system.
Drugs held in a pharmacy are physical things, so they are tangible elements.
Beds can be counted and touched, so they are tangible elements.
questions.explain: Intangibles are real elements of the system.
questions.hint: Which element could you not touch or count?
questions.rule: List the elements, physical and intangible, but stop before you lose the system and turn to the relationships between them.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: An analyst keeps dividing a city into sub-elements and sub-sub-elements. What does Meadows predict?
options: She loses sight of the system, unable to see the forest for the trees
She finds the purpose of the city becomes clearer with each further division
She discovers that each sub-element behaves exactly like the city
She ends with a complete explanation of how the city behaves
optionExplain: Right: endless dissection loses the whole.
The purpose is the least obvious part, and listing does not reveal it.
Sub-elements do not mirror the whole.
Listing elements does not explain behavior.
questions.explain: After a point, more detail hides the system.
questions.rule: Stop dissecting; look at connections.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: True or false: In Meadows’ account, only visible, tangible things can be elements of a system.
questions.explain: She names intangibles such as school pride and academic prowess as elements.
questions.rule: Elements need not be physical.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Researchers have catalogued every part of a rainforest but cannot say how the parts influence each other. What does Meadows’ remark suggest?
options: It means the catalogue must be wrong, since knowing the parts always reveals the links
It shows interconnections do not exist in rainforests
It shows that elements are harder to learn than links
That is typical: elements are easier to learn about than interconnections
optionExplain: Parts do not automatically reveal links.
Rainforests are systems and have links.
Her claim is the reverse: she says elements are easier to learn about than interconnections.
Right: she says elements are easier to learn about.
questions.explain: Knowledge of elements runs ahead of knowledge of interconnections.
questions.teaches: It is easier to learn about a system’s elements than about its interconnections.
questions.rule: List the elements, physical and intangible, but stop before you lose the system and turn to the relationships between them.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: What links the roots and leaves of a tree into a working whole?
options: The fact that both parts are made of exactly the same kinds of living cells
Signals and flows that let each part respond to what the other is doing
The total number of leaves and roots the tree grows
The age of the tree, which sets how the parts behave
optionExplain: Shared material does not create response.
Right: relationships between parts, not their sameness.
A count of leaves and roots describes the parts but does not link them to each other.
Age describes how long the tree has lived; it is not a relationship between its parts.
questions.explain: Responsive signals link the parts. The card next gives Meadows’ tree example.
questions.rule: Signals and flows link parts.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: In Meadows’ tree example, what happens when the roots meet dry soil?
options: The trunk thickens to store more water against the drought
The leaves open wider so that rain is collected as soon as it falls
The loss of water pressure signals the leaves to close their pores
The roots send a signal that makes the leaves drop at once
optionExplain: Tree trunks do not thicken in response to dry soil in her account; she describes a pressure signal instead.
Opening wider would lose more water.
Right: this is her example of a signal between parts.
Leaf fall is tied to shorter days, not dry soil.
questions.explain: In her tree example, the loss of water pressure in the roots signals the leaves to close their pores, so pressure changes act as signals.
questions.rule: Signals let parts respond to one another.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Which is an interconnection of a restaurant system?
options: The chefs employed in the kitchen during evening service
Order tickets passing from the waiters to the kitchen
The tables and chairs set out in the dining room
The sign above the door showing the restaurant’s name
optionExplain: Chefs are elements: the people who are connected by the tickets, not the connection itself.
Right: the tickets are a flow that links parts.
Furniture is made of elements; it is part of the restaurant, not a link between parts.
A sign is a physical element of the restaurant, not a relationship between its parts.
questions.explain: Interconnections are relationships; people and objects are elements.
questions.rule: To understand a system, look for the signals, flows and rules that link its elements.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Match each system to one of its interconnections as Meadows describes them.
pairs: Pressure signals between roots and leaves
questions.explain: Each pairing uses an example from the chapter.
questions.rule: Each system has its own links.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A university cancels exams and grades but keeps its buildings, students and professors. Which part of the system has changed?
options: Only its elements, because no person has been replaced and the buildings remain
Only its purpose, because teaching has been dropped
Nothing, since a system is defined by its buildings
Its interconnections, since exams and grades are relationships between people
optionExplain: The same people remain; the link was removed.
Purpose was not mentioned in the scenario; only exams and grades were removed.
Buildings are elements, and they were not changed in this scenario.
Right: grades are among her university interconnections.
questions.explain: Cutting a link changes the interconnections.
questions.rule: To understand a system, look for the signals, flows and rules that link its elements.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says no one understands all the relationships that allow a tree to do what it does.
questions.explain: Many tree relationships remain poorly understood, which illustrates that interconnections are harder to learn than elements.
questions.rule: Interconnections are often poorly known.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: As autumn days shorten, a deciduous tree sheds its leaves. Which interconnection does Meadows describe?
options: Chemical messages move nutrients into the trunk and roots and weaken the stems
Roots signal the trunk to grow a fresh set of new leaves for the long winter ahead
Wind pressure on the branches forces the stems to break
Leaves absorb extra sunlight until their stems give way
optionExplain: Right: this is her example of a seasonal signal.
Leaves are shed in autumn, not grown, and the signals Meadows describes cause the shedding.
Meadows describes chemical messages.
Her account is about shorter days, not extra sunlight.
questions.explain: As days shorten, chemical messages move nutrients into the trunk and roots and weaken the stems, so seasonal signals link the tree's parts.
questions.teaches: As days shorten in temperate zones, a deciduous tree sends chemical messages that make nutrients move out of the leaves into trunk and roots and weaken the stems so the leaves fall.
questions.rule: To understand a system, look for the signals, flows and rules that link its elements.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A shopper decides whether to buy a coat. Which things feed that decision as information?
options: Prices, her income and savings, and what the shops have in stock
Only the color and fabric of the coat that is hanging on the shop rack
Only the number of coats the factory made last season
Only the shopper’s age and the town where she was born
optionExplain: Right: a decision draws on several signals about money and availability.
Features of the coat describe the item but say nothing about whether she can or should buy it.
Factory output is not a signal the shopper receives when deciding.
Age and birthplace do not tell her about prices, funds or supply.
questions.explain: Decisions run on several signals. The card next shows how Meadows treats them.
questions.rule: Look for the signals that reach decision points; they are often the hidden connections that explain what a system does.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Many interconnections in systems operate through the flow of ____.
questions.explain: Information holds systems together and plays a great role in determining how they operate.
questions.rule: Information is a major kind of interconnection.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A delivery firm reroutes its vans after live traffic reports. What kind of interconnection is the report?
options: A physical flow, because the report travels along the same roads
An element, because a report is a visible object the firm owns
A flow of information that reaches a decision point
A purpose, because the firm wants to avoid delays in delivery
optionExplain: The vans move physically, but the report itself is information, not material.
Elements are the parts being linked; the report is the link carrying a signal.
Right: the report is a signal that changes what a decision maker does.
Avoiding delay may be the aim, but the report is the means of linking road and routing.
questions.explain: Reports and prices act as signals, which makes them interconnections.
questions.hint: Does the report move material or tell someone something?
questions.rule: Look for the signals that reach decision points; they are often the hidden connections that explain what a system does.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A shop manager stops receiving sales figures. What does Meadows’ view imply about her shop as a system?
