options: Her decisions lose the signals that tie them to the shop, cutting a link
Nothing changes, since decisions never really depend on information at all
The shop becomes a heap at once, since its parts all disappear
Its purpose changes, since information is what defines purposes
optionExplain: Right: information is part of what holds the system together.
Meadows says information holds systems together and shapes how they operate.
The parts stay; it is a link that was removed, which does not turn a system to a heap.
Purpose is a separate ingredient and not defined by information flow.
questions.explain: Cutting a flow of information cuts an interconnection.
questions.rule: Cut the signal and you cut the link.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says information interconnections are often harder to see than physical flows.
questions.explain: Information links are signals to decision points; she says the system reveals them to those who look.
questions.rule: Information links hide more easily.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A town knows its river is polluted yet nothing changes. What else does Meadows say is needed to trigger action?
options: Nothing more, since knowing about a problem always triggers action
A larger number of people who can name the town’s river
A rule that any information must be written down first
Information about resources, incentives and consequences too
optionExplain: She says information about a problem is necessary but not sufficient for action.
Knowing the river’s name adds nothing about means or motives to act.
Writing information down does not supply resources, incentives or consequences.
Right: awareness is necessary but not sufficient.
questions.explain: Knowing about pollution is not enough; she says the system also needs information that links to resources, incentives and consequences.
questions.teaches: Information about the existence of a problem may be necessary but not sufficient to trigger action; information about resources, incentives and consequences is necessary too.
questions.rule: Look for the signals that reach decision points; they are often the hidden connections that explain what a system does.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A company says it values customers, yet cuts support staff every year and ignores complaints. Where does its real purpose show?
options: In its mission statement, since that is the official wording of its aims
In what it consistently does with its money and effort
In what the newest employee thinks after the first week
In what its competitors claim about the market this year
optionExplain: Statements are stated goals, which can differ sharply from actions.
Right: behavior is the evidence.
A new employee sees only a small slice of what the company does.
Rivals see little of its internal choices, so they cannot show its aim.
questions.explain: Actions show purpose. The card next gives Meadows’ frog example.
questions.rule: Judge a system’s purpose by what it consistently does, not by what it says.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Meadows says purposes are deduced from ____, not from rhetoric or stated goals.
questions.explain: She says the best way to deduce a purpose is to watch how a system behaves for a while.
questions.rule: Deduce purpose from behavior.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A school announces a focus on reading, yet puts nearly all its time and money into sports. What does Meadows’ method conclude?
options: Reading is not its real purpose, whatever the announcement says
Reading is its real purpose, since the school itself says so
The school has no purpose at all, because its words and actions clash
The school’s purpose is whatever its head teacher declares
optionExplain: Right: her government example makes the same point.
Proclaiming a goal is rhetoric; she says rhetoric does not set the purpose.
Behavior still shows a purpose; the clash just tells you the stated one is not it.
Her method rejects the declared goal as evidence in favor of observed conduct.
questions.explain: When words and actions clash, trust the actions.
questions.rule: Judge a system’s purpose by what it consistently does, not by what it says.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: True or false: In Meadows’ frog example, the frog’s purpose has to do with catching flies, not with turning in any direction.
questions.explain: The frog catches flies whether it turns right, left or backward, so its purpose is the flies.
questions.rule: Read purpose from what the behavior achieves.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Which observation is better evidence of a hospital’s purpose?
options: The wording on the banner that hangs in its main lobby
Where it actually spends its budget and staff time over several years
What the chief executive says in the speech at the annual dinner each year
The goals printed in the glossy brochure it gives to visitors
optionExplain: A banner is a stated goal, which is the rhetoric Meadows says to look past.
Right: sustained behavior shows what the system is for.
A speech is also stated goals, not conduct.
A brochure is also stated goals; it describes aims rather than showing them.
questions.explain: Spending and effort over time are the evidence.
questions.rule: Judge a system’s purpose by what it consistently does, not by what it says.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A foundation set up to fight a disease keeps operating long after a cure is found. Which remark of Meadows helps explain this?
options: Systems always dissolve once the goal they were created for is met
Only nonhuman systems ever have functions that persist over time
Almost every system works to ensure its own perpetuation
A system’s purpose is whatever its founders originally wrote down
optionExplain: The foundation shows the opposite: it kept going after its goal was met.
She says function and purpose are not sharply divided between human and nonhuman systems.
Right: systems tend to keep themselves going.
Purpose is deduced from behavior, not read from founding documents.
questions.explain: Systems often work to keep themselves going.
questions.teaches: An important function of almost every system is to ensure its own perpetuation.
questions.rule: Judge a system’s purpose by what it consistently does, not by what it says.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Each driver on a motorway wants to get home sooner, and a jam forms that nobody wanted. What best explains it?
options: One careless driver caused it deliberately in order to slow all the others down
Sensible individual aims combined into a pattern no single driver intended
Jams arise only when a road has been badly built from the start
The drivers secretly agreed to bunch up in one place together
optionExplain: No single driver has to want the jam; ordinary individual aims are enough to produce it.
Right: combined aims can produce an unwanted whole.
Road design can matter, but the jam here comes from how the drivers act together.
No agreement is needed; many separate, sensible choices combine into the jam.
questions.explain: The whole can behave in a way no part wants. The card next gives Meadows’ example.
questions.rule: To explain a stubborn result, look at how all the actors’ separate purposes combine, rather than for one villain’s intent.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Meadows says the purposes of subunits may add up to an overall ____ that no one wants.
questions.explain: Each actor can pursue a reasonable aim while the combined result is something nobody intended.
questions.rule: Combined purposes can produce unwanted behavior.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Several fishing crews each try to maximize their catch, and the fish stock collapses. Which of Meadows’ points does this show?
options: Separate, reasonable purposes can add up to an outcome nobody intended
One crew wanted the collapse and planned it with great care
The stock collapsed because the fish have no purposes of their own to protect it
The outcome proves the crews are not part of the system
optionExplain: Right: each crew’s aim was reasonable, yet the total result was not wanted.
Her point is that no one needs to intend the outcome.
The fishes’ purposes are not her point; the human actors’ combined aims are.
The crews are actors inside the system, as the drug example’s actors are.
questions.explain: Same pattern as the drug example, in a fresh setting.
questions.rule: To explain a stubborn result, look at how all the actors’ separate purposes combine, rather than for one villain’s intent.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Police arrest one dealer. Reading Meadows’ account, what is the likely effect on the drug-and-crime system?
options: The whole system collapses, since one actor held it together
The system turns into a mere heap, because one part of it has been removed
Little, since many actors’ combined purposes still produce the pattern
Addiction and crime end, since the single cause is gone
optionExplain: She says the system is extremely difficult to eradicate, not fragile.
Losing one element rarely turns a system into a heap.
Right: our reading of her argument is that the structure survives losing one actor.
Single causes are the view her account moves away from.
questions.explain: Persistence follows from many combined purposes.
questions.rule: To explain a stubborn result, look at how all the actors’ separate purposes combine, rather than for one villain’s intent.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says a system’s purpose must be one that some single actor within it intends.
questions.explain: She says system purposes are not necessarily those intended by any single actor.
questions.rule: A whole can have a purpose nobody chose.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: In Meadows’ drug-and-crime example, where do governments and police stand in relation to the system?
options: Outside the system, acting on it from above without ever being a part of it
They are the single cause of the whole problem
They are actors inside it, and their actions help make up its behavior
They are irrelevant to the pattern that results
optionExplain: She lists governments that outlaw substances and use police among the actors.
She names many actors, so no single one is the cause.
Right: she lists them among the actors.
Their actions are part of the combined purposes that make the pattern.
questions.explain: Remedies can be part of the system they try to fix.
questions.teaches: In Meadows’ example, governments that make harmful substances illegal and use police power to interdict them are among the actors whose combined actions make up the system.
questions.rule: To explain a stubborn result, look at how all the actors’ separate purposes combine, rather than for one villain’s intent.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A hospital department head cuts nurse hours to meet a budget, and patient care suffers. What is going on?
options: A sub-purpose, balancing the budget, works against the overall purpose
The hospital has no purpose, so nothing in it can conflict
Budgets and patient care are never related to each other
The department head has become an element of a different system altogether
optionExplain: Right: a part’s aim can pull against the whole’s aim.
A hospital has the purpose of caring for patients, so conflict is possible.
Budgets and care are linked here: the cut harms the care.
The head remains inside the hospital system, pursuing a narrower aim.
questions.explain: Sub-purposes and overall purposes can pull apart. The card next gives Meadows’ university example.
questions.rule: Check whether the sub-purposes of the parts serve or undermine the purpose of the whole.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Match each university role to its purpose in Meadows’ example.
pairs: Discover, preserve and pass on knowledge
questions.explain: These are the purposes at each level of the nested system.
questions.rule: Check whether the sub-purposes of the parts serve or undermine the purpose of the whole.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A sales team is paid per deal and promises features nobody can build, which harms the firm. Which idea does this show?
options: A system with no purposes inside it that could ever come into conflict
A conflict that can only occur inside a university
A perfect match between sub-purpose and overall purpose
A sub-purpose in conflict with the purpose of the whole firm
optionExplain: The sales team clearly has a purpose, which is to close deals.
Meadows uses universities as an example, not as the only place conflict arises.
A match would mean no harm to the firm, but harm occurs here.
Right: the team pursues its own aim at the firm’s expense.
questions.explain: As in the university example, a sub-purpose (deals closed) can conflict with the purpose of the whole firm.
questions.rule: Check whether the sub-purposes of the parts serve or undermine the purpose of the whole.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: If every sub-purpose in a school stayed in harmony with its overall purpose, what would Meadows expect?
options: A failing system, since harmony removes all competition from the organization
A more successful system, since keeping them in harmony is essential
No change, since sub-purposes never really affect the whole system at all
A system with no purpose, since harmony cancels all aims
optionExplain: She says harmony is essential, not harmful.
Right: harmony is an essential function of successful systems.
Sub-purposes can affect the whole, which is why conflicts matter.
Harmony aligns aims; it does not erase them.
questions.explain: Harmony between levels is what success requires.
questions.rule: Keep sub-purposes in harmony with the whole.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: True or false: Sub-purposes inside a system automatically match the system’s overall purpose.
questions.explain: Meadows warns they can conflict, and says keeping them in harmony is an essential function.
questions.rule: Check whether the sub-purposes of the parts serve or undermine the purpose of the whole.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A firm cuts its research staff to hit this quarter’s budget target. Which of Meadows’ university examples does it most resemble?
options: The administrator who balances the budget by firing professors
The student who cheats in order to get good grades in his courses
The professor who wins tenure by teaching well
The graduate who donates money to the library
optionExplain: Right: budget aims damaging the core work.
Cheating is a different example of conflict, aimed at grades rather than budgets.
Winning tenure by teaching well is not a conflict with the university’s purpose.
A donation is not in her account and does not harm the purpose.
questions.explain: Budget goals can damage the work they exist to serve.
questions.teaches: In Meadows’ examples, a professor could ignore students in order to publish papers, and an administrator could balance the budget by firing professors.
questions.rule: Check whether the sub-purposes of the parts serve or undermine the purpose of the whole.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A town replaces every one of its shopkeepers over twenty years, yet keeps its market days and customs. What is true of its market?
options: It is a different market, since none of the original people remain
It has become a heap, since the new parts no longer match the old
It has no identity at all, because identity belongs only to individuals
It is probably the same market, because its rules and purpose carry on
optionExplain: People are elements, and Meadows says swapping elements usually has the least effect.
A heap lacks links, but the market’s rules and customs still link its parts.
Identity can live in the pattern of links and purpose, as with a university.
Right: structure and aim outlast the people in them.
questions.explain: Identity rides on links and purpose. The card next explains the ranking Meadows gives.
questions.rule: Swapping elements rarely changes what a system is, provided the links and purpose survive.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: True or false: Replacing every player on a football team usually leaves it recognizably a football team.
questions.explain: Meadows says changing elements usually has the least effect, although the team may play much better or much worse.
questions.rule: Element swaps rarely change what a system is.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A shop replaces all its staff over five years but keeps its rules, layout and goals. What does Meadows expect of the shop?
options: It becomes a new shop, since a system is nothing more than the people in it
It stays essentially the same system, since links and purposes are intact
It dissolves, since every one of its parts has now changed
It changes its purpose, because new staff always bring new aims
optionExplain: People are elements, and Meadows says systems outlast complete substitution of elements.
Right: elements come and go; links and purpose hold the system.
Systems such as the university survive constant turnover of members.
The goals were kept in this scenario, so nothing here changes the purpose.
questions.explain: The system persists while its links and purpose persist.
questions.rule: Swapping elements rarely changes what a system is, provided the links and purpose survive.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Now suppose the replacement staff arrive with a new rule book and a new aim. What does Meadows’ reasoning say?
options: Nothing much, since the building and its shelves stay exactly the same as before
The shop will certainly become identical to what it was
The change reaches links and purpose, so the system may be greatly altered
The system will end, since any change at all destroys systems
optionExplain: Shelves and buildings are elements, the least important part.
Nothing guarantees a return to the old shop once rules and aims have changed.
Right: now more than elements have changed.
Systems can change dramatically without ceasing to exist.
questions.explain: Change the condition and the verdict changes with it.
questions.rule: Element swaps matter little; link and purpose changes matter a lot.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Meadows says particular elements can matter: swapping players may make a team play much ____ or much worse.
questions.explain: Elements usually have the least effect, but not no effect.
questions.rule: Least effect does not mean no effect.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A national parliament replaces every member after an election yet remains the same institution. Which of Meadows’ examples does this match?
options: A river whose water is replaced while its banks stay the same
A tree that loses all its leaves every autumn but changes nothing else
A bathtub that fills while its drain is left plugged up
The U.S. Congress, which keeps its identity as its members change
optionExplain: The river is not one of her examples of identity through member turnover.
Her tree example is about cells and leaves, not institutional members.
The bathtub appears later, as a model of stocks and flows.
Right: she cites General Motors and the U.S. Congress.
questions.explain: Institutions persist through changes of members.
questions.teaches: General Motors and the U.S. Congress somehow maintain their identities even though all their members change.
questions.rule: Swapping elements rarely changes what a system is, provided the links and purpose survive.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A basketball team and a football team could in principle draw on the same athletes. What would make the two games differ?
options: The rules and relationships among the players, not who they are
The athletes’ hair color and height would decide the matter completely
The name of the stadium would decide the matter
The size of the crowd would decide the matter
optionExplain: Right: the rules shape the game.
Individual traits are properties of elements, which matter least.
A stadium’s name is a label and changes no relationships.
A crowd watches the game; it does not define how it is played.
questions.explain: Rules are interconnections. The card next uses this example.
questions.rule: Changing relationships usually changes system behavior, sometimes dramatically.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Change the rules from football to basketball, Meadows says, and you have a whole new ____ game.
questions.explain: Changing the rules, which are interconnections, can turn the same players into a different game.
questions.rule: New rules can make a whole new game.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A company keeps all its staff but switches from managers deciding to staff voting on everything. What does Meadows suggest?
options: Nothing changes, since the very same people remain in all of their usual roles
Only the elements changed, so the system is exactly the same
Behavior may change a lot, because the relationships changed, not the people
The company ceases to exist, since voting is not allowed
optionExplain: The people are the same, but how they decide changed, and links matter.
Decision rules are interconnections, not elements.
Right: changing relationships usually changes system behavior.
Nothing in her account says that such a change ends the company.
questions.explain: Same players under new rules can behave very differently.
questions.rule: Changing relationships usually changes system behavior, sometimes dramatically.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: True or false: If the same players and the same purpose remain, changing the rules cannot alter a system much.
questions.explain: Meadows says changing interconnections can change a system dramatically even when the players stay the same.
questions.rule: New rules can mean a new game.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Replace all teachers with equally qualified ones, or replace teachers' grades with classmates' votes: which change does Meadows expect to alter a school more?
options: The classmate votes, since they change interconnections, not elements
Replacing the teachers, since people are always what matter most in a school
Both equally, since every change counts the same in a system
Neither, since a school is unchanged by any reform at all
optionExplain: Right: links usually matter more than elements.
Meadows says elements usually have the least effect.
She distinguishes the effects of changing elements, links and purpose.
Changing relationships usually changes system behavior.
questions.explain: Changing the links, here who judges whom, alters the system more than swapping equally good elements for others.
questions.rule: Changing relationships usually changes system behavior, sometimes dramatically.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Meadows imagines a tree whose gas exchange runs in reverse of the usual. What does she say it would be?
options: A larger tree that grows much faster
A tree that has lost all of its leaves
A fungus living in the soil nearby
An animal rather than a tree
optionExplain: Reversing the exchange changes the kind of system, not its growth.
Leaf loss is a different change of elements.
Fungi are not mentioned in her example.
Right: she says it would be an animal.
questions.explain: Reversing a basic link changes what kind of system it is.
questions.teaches: If a tree took in oxygen and gave off carbon dioxide instead of the reverse, Meadows says it would no longer be a tree but an animal.
questions.rule: Changing relationships usually changes system behavior, sometimes dramatically.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Two hospitals have identical staff, buildings and rules. One aims at healing and the other at maximum profit per bed. What follows?
options: They will behave identically, since everything else about them is the same
They will probably behave very differently because their purposes differ
They will differ only in the color of their signs and uniforms
They will differ only if their staff are all replaced first
optionExplain: Meadows says a change in purpose can change a system profoundly even if all else stays.
Right: purpose drives behavior, so two hospitals with different aims behave differently.
Surface features are not the point; behavior is what changes.
Replacing staff changes elements, the least important part.
questions.explain: A purpose shapes what a system does. The card next explains.
questions.rule: When behavior needs explaining, ask first what the system is for.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: The least obvious part of a system, its function or ____, is often the most crucial determinant of its behavior.
questions.explain: Meadows says purpose is hard to see yet often decides what a system does.
questions.rule: Ask what the system is for.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A board shifts a hospital’s aim from healing to profit but keeps its staff, wards and rules. What does Meadows expect?
options: Nothing changes, since the staff and the rules are exactly the same as before
Only its signs change, since the wards stay as they are
It stops being a system, since an aim is not a part
Its behavior changes profoundly, since a change of purpose can do that
optionExplain: She says a change in purpose changes a system profoundly with elements and links unchanged.
Behavior, not just signage, would change.
A purpose is one of the three ingredients, so changing it keeps a system with a new aim.
Right: purpose changes behavior.
questions.explain: When the board changes the aim from healing to profit, the same staff, wards and rules produce very different behavior.
questions.rule: When behavior needs explaining, ask first what the system is for.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A sports team keeps its players and rules but now aims to lose. What does her reasoning predict about how it plays?
options: It would play exactly as it did before, since all of the players are unchanged
It would play very differently, even with every element and rule unchanged
It would stop being a team at that very moment
It would play better than before, since purpose has no effect
optionExplain: Her example says changing the purpose from winning to losing changes the system.
Right: purpose changes behavior.
It remains a team, but a team with a different aim.
If purpose had no effect, her claim that it is often crucial would fail.
questions.explain: What if the aim changes? Behavior changes.
questions.rule: Same parts and rules, new aim, new behavior.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: True or false: If every element and interconnection stays the same, a system’s behavior must stay the same.
questions.explain: Meadows says a change in purpose changes a system profoundly even if every element and interconnection stays the same.
questions.rule: When behavior needs explaining, ask first what the system is for.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A university is run chiefly to bring in money and win football games. Which remark of Meadows does that illustrate?
options: Universities can have only one possible purpose
A university’s purpose can never be changed
People have imagined many purposes besides disseminating knowledge
Football games are the only purposes that a university can ever have
optionExplain: She lists several imagined purposes, so there is more than one.
She says a change in purpose is possible and drastic.
Right: she lists making money, indoctrinating people and winning football games.
Football is one of several purposes she mentions, not the only one.
questions.explain: Different purposes make different universities.
questions.teaches: People have imagined many purposes for a university besides disseminating knowledge, such as making money, indoctrinating people, or winning football games.
questions.rule: When behavior needs explaining, ask first what the system is for.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A founder says only people matter in a company, while processes and goals do not. How would Meadows likely respond?
options: The founder is fully right, because elements decide everything in a company
All three, people, links and purposes, are essential and interact
The founder is wrong, because only purposes matter at all
The founder is wrong, because only processes matter at all
optionExplain: She says elements are often least important in defining a system.
Right: she calls the ranking question unsystemic.
Purpose is often most crucial, but she says all three are essential.
Interconnections are critically important but not the only thing.
questions.explain: Ranking one ingredient alone misses the system. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Ask how elements, links and purpose work together; do not rank them in isolation.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: True or false: Meadows regards asking which of elements, interconnections or purposes is most important as an unsystemic question.
questions.explain: She says all are essential, all interact and all have their roles.
questions.rule: Do not rank the ingredients in isolation.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A manager claims that processes alone explain why a team succeeds. What does Meadows’ view suggest?
options: The claim is right, since processes are the interconnections of the team
The claim is right, because elements never matter at all
The claim is wrong, because interconnections never matter
It leaves out elements and purposes, which also play essential roles
optionExplain: Interconnections are critical but not the whole story.
Elements can matter, as a team playing better or worse shows.
Meadows says changing relationships usually changes behavior.
Right: all three ingredients interact, so explaining success by processes alone leaves out elements and purposes.
questions.explain: Meadows says elements, interconnections and purposes are all essential and all interact, so none explains a team alone.
questions.rule: Ask how elements, links and purpose work together; do not rank them in isolation.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A new chief executive changes the reporting rules and the company’s aim. May the company change direction?
options: Yes, since a leader can set new rules or a new purpose
No, since a company’s people alone decide its direction, not its leader
No, since leaders never matter in any system
Only if all of the staff are replaced first
optionExplain: Right: this is her Brezhnev-to-Gorbachev point.
Her point is that the same people can play a different game under new rules.
She says a leader may or may not turn a nation, so leaders can matter.
Replacing staff is not needed when rules or purpose change.
questions.explain: A leader can change the rules or the aim, and either change can send the whole company in a new direction.
questions.rule: Ask how elements, links and purpose work together; do not rank them in isolation.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: Meadows calls the question of which of elements, interconnections or purposes matters most an ____ question.
questions.explain: All three are essential and interact, so ranking them in isolation misses the system.
questions.rule: Do not rank the ingredients in isolation.

questions.section: Look Beyond the Players to the Rules of the Game
questions.q: A new national leader wants a rapid change of direction. What limit does Meadows note?
options: There is no limit at all, since leaders turn nations whichever way they will
Leaders cannot change anything about the rules or purposes of a nation at all
Slow-changing land, factories and people limit how fast direction can turn
Only the wealth of a nation limits what a leader is able to do with it
optionExplain: She says there is a limit to the rate at which any leader can turn a nation.
She says a leader can set new rules or a new purpose.
Right: slow physical elements limit the rate of change.
The limit she names is slow-changing physical elements, not wealth.
questions.explain: Slow elements cap how fast direction can change.
questions.teaches: Because land, factories and people are long-lived, slowly changing physical elements, there is a limit to the rate at which any leader can turn the direction of a nation.
questions.rule: Ask how elements, links and purpose work together; do not rank them in isolation.

questions.q: Which of these is a stock in Meadows’ sense?
options: The interest paid into the account during one year
The deposits the holder makes each month
The fees the bank charges when it processes a transfer
The money sitting in a savings account today
optionExplain: Interest paid over a year is an amount moving in, which makes it a flow rather than a store.
Deposits are amounts added over time, so they are flows into the stock.
Fees leave the account over time; they are another flow, not the balance itself.
Right: the money present now is an accumulation, a stock.
questions.explain: A stock is what has built up; flows are what change it. The card next defines both.
questions.rule: A stock is an accumulation at one moment, and it records everything its flows have done so far.

questions.q: A stock is the present ____ of the history of changing flows within the system.
questions.explain: Meadows describes a stock as the present memory of the history of its changing flows: what has built up is the record of past filling and draining.
questions.rule: A stock remembers its flows.

questions.q: A bookstore holds 4,000 books and sells 300 a week. Which pairing names a stock and a flow correctly?
options: Stock: the 300 books sold each week; flow: the 4,000 books on the shelves
Stock: the 4,000 books on the shelves; flow: the 300 books sold each week
Both are stocks, because both are counts of books
Both are flows, because both involve books moving at some time
optionExplain: This reverses the roles; weekly sales change the shelf count, not the other way around.
Right: the shelves hold an accumulation, and sales are the rate at which it changes.
A count of books sold per week is a rate of change, not a store of books.
The shelf total is what is present at one moment, which makes it a stock.
questions.explain: Count what is there for a stock; count what moves per unit of time for a flow.
questions.hint: Which number could you read off in a photograph of the shelves?
questions.rule: A stock is an accumulation at one moment, and it records everything its flows have done so far.

questions.q: Ignoring migration, a town’s births and deaths stop for a while. What does its population, as a stock, show?
options: It stays at the level its past flows built up, still recording them
It drops to zero because nothing is flowing any longer
It rises steadily because the flows have stopped acting on it at all
It resets to its starting value because the flows are gone
optionExplain: Right: the stock stays where earlier flows left it.
A stock does not vanish when flows pause; it keeps what accumulated.
Without inflow or outflow nothing pushes it upward.
A stock does not reset; it holds the net result of its history.
questions.explain: Flows change a stock; without flows it simply stays.
questions.rule: No flow, no change in the stock.

questions.q: True or false: In Meadows’ account, a stock can be intangible, such as self-confidence or hope.
questions.explain: She names self-confidence, good will and hope as stocks. A stock is an accumulation of material or information.
questions.rule: Stocks can be intangible.

questions.q: A team’s confidence grows after wins and shrinks after losses. Which part is the flow in Meadows’ terms?
options: The confidence itself, which is the rate of change in the team’s spirits
The coach, who is the flow between games
The size of the stadium, which sets the stock
The wins and losses, which add to or drain the stock of confidence
optionExplain: Confidence is what accumulates, so it is the stock.
A coach is a person, not a flow of the confidence stock.
Stadium size is not what changes confidence.
Right: successes and failures are flows that change the stock.
questions.explain: Flows include nonphysical events such as successes and failures.
questions.teaches: Flows include growth and decay and successes and failures, so a flow need not be a physical flow.
questions.rule: A stock is an accumulation at one moment, and it records everything its flows have done so far.

questions.q: In a diagram of a bathtub system, which part would be drawn as a box?
options: The faucet pouring water in
The water in the tub
The drain carrying water out
The speed at which water leaves
optionExplain: The faucet controls an inflow, which is a pipe rather than a box.
Right: the water level is the stock.
The drain carries an outflow, again a pipe.
A speed is a rate, belonging to a flow.
questions.explain: The stock is the box; the pipes are flows. The card next gives the full convention.
questions.rule: Read a stock as a box, a flow as a pipe with a tap, and ask what each tap controls.

questions.q: In Meadows’ diagrams, what does the small T on a pipe stand for?
options: A tank that stores the flow for later release into the box
A cloud that marks where the flow begins
A faucet that can turn the flow higher, lower, on or off
A sensor that reports the size of the stock
optionExplain: Storage is a stock, drawn as a box.
Clouds are drawn separately, as sources and sinks.
Right: the T is a control on the flow.
Information links appear later in the chapter, as thin curved arrows.
questions.explain: In her diagrams the small T on a pipe is a faucet: the flow it controls can be turned higher or lower, on or off.
questions.rule: Read a stock as a box, a flow as a pipe with a tap, and ask what each tap controls.

questions.q: Order these parts of the bathtub system along the path water takes in a stock-and-flow diagram.
items: Faucet on the inflow pipe
Inflow pipe
Box for the water in the tub
Outflow pipe
Drain tap
questions.explain: The path runs from the inflow tap through the inflow pipe to the box, then out through the outflow pipe and its tap.
questions.rule: Read a stock as a box, a flow as a pipe with a tap, and ask what each tap controls.

questions.q: You turn the faucet on one pipe to zero in a diagram. What does that show?
options: The stock vanishes because its box is cut off
That flow is shut off, so only the other flows can change the stock
The cloud fills up because the water must go somewhere
The other pipes also stop, since all of the flows share one single tap
optionExplain: A closed pipe leaves the stock at its level; it does not delete it.
Right: a closed faucet means no flow through that pipe.
Clouds mark ignored sources and sinks; they are not filled by blocked flows.
Each pipe has its own faucet; closing one affects only that flow.
questions.explain: Each tap controls its own flow; with one pipe at zero, that flow is off and only the other flows can change the stock.
questions.rule: Read a stock as a box, a flow as a pipe with a tap, and ask what each tap controls.

questions.q: True or false: A diagram with one box and two pipes shows exactly what a real tub does, with nothing left out.
questions.explain: Any diagram is a simplified version of the real world. The drawer decides what to show, such as leaving out evaporation.
questions.rule: Every diagram leaves things out.

questions.q: Meadows’ diagrams use small clouds at the ends of some pipes. What do the clouds stand for?
options: Stocks whose levels are too large to draw as boxes
Weather that affects the speed of the flows
Information links that direct the action of the people at the faucets
Wherever the flows come from or go to, which the diagram ignores
optionExplain: Stocks are boxes, whatever their size.
Clouds are not about weather; they mark sources and sinks that the diagram ignores.
Information links are shown as curved arrows, a separate symbol.
Right: clouds are sources and sinks.
questions.explain: The small clouds mark sources and sinks that the diagram ignores, meaning what is left out of view.
questions.teaches: The clouds in a stock-and-flow diagram stand for wherever the flows come from and go to: the sources and sinks being ignored for the purposes of the present discussion.
questions.rule: Read a stock as a box, a flow as a pipe with a tap, and ask what each tap controls.

questions.q: A reservoir behind a dam has water entering and leaving. Which is an outflow?
options: Evaporation from the surface of the reservoir
Rain falling onto the reservoir
River water running into it from the upstream catchment
The volume of water held behind the dam
optionExplain: Right: evaporation removes water from the stock.
Rain adds water, so it is an inflow.
River water entering is also an inflow.
The volume held is the stock itself.
questions.explain: Identify what adds to and removes from the stock. The card next shows Meadows’ examples.
questions.rule: For any system, name the stock first, then list what flows into it and what flows out.

questions.q: Why does Meadows draw the mineral deposit with no inflow?
options: Minerals can never be added to a deposit under any conditions at all
Mining is the only flow that systems thinkers study
New ore forms so slowly that its inflow is minute short of eons
A deposit has an inflow, but it equals the flow of ore mined
optionExplain: The inflow exists; it is simply minute.
Mining is one flow among many in her other examples.
Right: the inflow is negligible over the time period of interest.
Equal flows would keep the stock steady, which mining does not.
questions.explain: Ignore a flow only when it is negligible for the time you study.
questions.rule: For any system, name the stock first, then list what flows into it and what flows out.

questions.q: Sort each item into inflow to the reservoir or outflow from it.

items.t: Rain falling on the lake
River water arriving from upstream
Evaporation from the surface
Water discharged through the dam

questions.explain: Rain and rivers add water. Evaporation and discharge remove it.
questions.rule: For any system, name the stock first, then list what flows into it and what flows out.

questions.q: A drought halves the river water arriving at a reservoir, while discharge and evaporation stay as before. What follows for the stock?
options: It rises, since the river is the main outflow
It stays level, since the dam always balances the flows
It falls, since the outflows now exceed the inflows
It falls to zero in the same instant
optionExplain: The river is an inflow, so a smaller river flow cuts the filling, not the draining.
Nothing in a dam forces the flows to balance; a halved inflow with unchanged outflows lowers the stock.
Right: with the outflows now larger than the inflows, the stock falls.
Stocks change over time, not instantly.
questions.explain: When outflows exceed inflows the stock falls, so a drought that halves the river water leaves the reservoir losing water.
questions.rule: For any system, name the stock first, then list what flows into it and what flows out.

questions.q: True or false: Leaving the mineral deposit’s inflow out of the picture means Meadows believes no inflow exists.
questions.explain: She says it is minute over periods shorter than eons, so she simplifies. The omission depends on the time period.
questions.rule: Omission is a choice of time scale.

questions.q: Wood in living trees is a stock, and loggers’ harvest feeds a lumber inventory at a mill. What does this show about flows?
options: One flow can drain one stock and fill another, linking the two
A flow can only ever belong to one single stock at any given time
Linking two stocks means they are the same stock
Harvest is a stock, because wood is physical
optionExplain: Right: the harvest drains the forest and fills the inventory.
Her chain shows a flow serving two stocks at once.
The stocks stay separate, joined by the flow.
Harvest is a flow of wood, not a store.
questions.explain: The harvest flow drains the stock of trees and fills the mill's lumber inventory, so one flow can link two stocks.
questions.teaches: The logging harvest is an outflow from the stock of trees and flows into another stock, an inventory of lumber at a mill, from which lumber is sold to customers.
questions.rule: For any system, name the stock first, then list what flows into it and what flows out.

questions.q: You are shown a line graph of a lake’s water level over ten years. What should you notice first?
options: The overall pattern of the line and where it changes direction
Only the exact value of the single highest point found on the line
The color and thickness of the line that has been plotted
The number of gridlines that have been drawn behind the plot
optionExplain: Right: shape and turning points tell the story.
One peak is an individual event, and Meadows favors trends over events.
Styling of the line says nothing about the system’s behavior.
Gridlines are decoration and do not describe behavior over time.
questions.explain: Pattern comes first. The card next explains how Meadows reads such graphs.
questions.rule: Read the shape and the turning points of a line first, and the exact numbers afterward.

questions.q: On a behavior-over-time graph, the shape of the line usually matters more than the precise ____ on the axes.
questions.explain: Pattern and turning points come first; exact numbers are often less important.
questions.rule: Read shape and turning points first.

questions.q: A graph shows a company’s cash climbing steadily and then flattening at a level. What does Meadows’ way of reading ask you to notice?
options: Only the single highest month, which tells the whole story all by itself
The line is approaching a limit or goal, and the bend marks the change
Nothing in particular, since graphs of cash never carry meaning
Only the number printed at the top of the vertical axis
optionExplain: Meadows prefers trends to individual events like one high month.
Right: the flattening shows approach to a level.
She uses graphs precisely to read trends and approaches to goals or limits.
The exact axis numbers are often less important than the pattern.
questions.explain: Meadows asks you to look at the shape of the line and where it bends; a flattening line suggests a limit or goal.
questions.rule: Read the shape and the turning points of a line first, and the exact numbers afterward.

questions.q: True or false: The variable on a behavior-over-time graph may be either a stock or a flow.
questions.explain: Meadows says the variable may be a stock or a flow.
questions.rule: Read the shape and the turning points of a line first, and the exact numbers afterward.

questions.q: One reader says sales hit a peak in March. Another says sales are leveling off. Which reading follows Meadows’ advice?
options: The second, since she favors trends over individual events
The first, since single events describe behavior best of all
Neither, since a graph cannot support either kind of claim
Both equally, since events and trends are the same thing
optionExplain: Right: trends are what the graphs are for.
She says systems thinkers look at trends rather than individual events.
Graphs are used to read trends and approach to a goal or limit.
Events and trends differ, and she prefers the trend.
questions.explain: Meadows says systems thinkers use graphs to understand trends over time rather than focusing on individual events.
questions.rule: Read the shape and the turning points of a line first, and the exact numbers afterward.

questions.q: The horizontal axis of a behavior graph is time. What does Meadows say it lets you do?
options: Predict the exact future value of a variable from the line alone, with certainty
Ignore the vertical axis, since time alone explains everything
Prove which single event caused the whole trend
Ask what came before and what may come next, over a sensible horizon
optionExplain: She says you can ask questions, not that you can compute exact futures.
Both axes matter; the point is the pattern over time.
A graph of time invites questions but does not by itself prove causes.
Right: before, next and horizon.
questions.explain: The time axis frames the questions you ask.
questions.teaches: The horizontal axis of time lets you ask what came before and what might happen next, and helps you focus on the time horizon appropriate to the question or problem you are investigating.
questions.rule: Read the shape and the turning points of a line first, and the exact numbers afterward.

questions.q: A tub is draining. You turn on the tap until inflow exactly equals outflow. What does the water level do?
options: It keeps falling, since the drain is still open and running
It stays where it was when the two flows became equal
It rises until the tub is full again, because the tap is on
It jumps back to the level it had before the draining began
optionExplain: The drain is still open, but the tap now exactly offsets it.
Right: matched flows hold the level.
Equal flows add no net water, so the level does not rise.
The stock has no memory of an earlier level to return to.
questions.explain: Equal flows hold the level. The card next names this state.
questions.rule: A stock rises when inflows exceed outflows, falls when outflows exceed inflows, and holds when they match.

questions.q: When inflows equal outflows, Meadows says the stock is held in dynamic ____ at whatever level it had.
questions.explain: Dynamic equilibrium means the level is steady even though water keeps flowing through.
questions.rule: Equal flows, steady stock.

questions.q: A warehouse receives 200 units a day and ships out 260. What happens to its inventory?
options: It rises, because 200 units arrive in the warehouse every day
It stays constant, because both flows are large in size
It falls, because the outflow exceeds the inflow
Nothing can be said without knowing the starting level first
optionExplain: Arrivals are only one side; shipments are larger.
Large flows do not guarantee a balance; only equal flows do.
Right: net outflow of 60 units a day.
The direction depends on the flows, though the exact level depends on the start.
questions.explain: Compare the sums of inflows and outflows.
questions.rule: A stock rises when inflows exceed outflows, falls when outflows exceed inflows, and holds when they match.

questions.q: The warehouse then ships only 200 units a day, matching arrivals. Now what happens to its inventory?
options: It rises back to the level it had before the shipments grew
It stops falling and stays at whatever level it reached
It falls faster than before, since shipping has now slowed down
It drops to zero at once, since shipments are still going on
optionExplain: Equal flows do not refill the stock; they only stop its decline.
Right: matched flows give dynamic equilibrium.
Net flow is now zero, so the fall stops.
Stocks do not empty instantly, and with equal flows they do not empty at all.
questions.explain: When outflow equals inflow the stock stops changing and holds whatever level it has reached.
questions.rule: A stock rises when inflows exceed outflows, falls when outflows exceed inflows, and holds when they match.

questions.q: True or false: In dynamic equilibrium, water keeps flowing through the tub even though the level stays constant.
questions.explain: Inflow equals outflow, so the level holds while water continues to flow through.
questions.rule: Equilibrium is balance, not rest.

questions.q: A reservoir stood at 60 percent when its inflow and outflow became equal. At what level will it hold?
options: A full reservoir, since equilibrium means the maximum level
Half full, since equilibrium always means the middle level
Empty, since equilibrium means zero net water in the stock
Sixty percent, the level it had when the flows matched
optionExplain: Equilibrium has no preferred level; it holds the one present.
The middle is not special either.
Zero net flow does not mean zero water.
Right: equilibrium holds whatever level existed.
questions.explain: A stock holds steady at whatever level it has when inflow equals outflow, so any level can be an equilibrium.
questions.teaches: The stock is held in dynamic equilibrium at whatever level it happened to be when the two sets of flows became equal, not at a fixed target.
questions.rule: A stock rises when inflows exceed outflows, falls when outflows exceed inflows, and holds when they match.

questions.q: A town wants more water in its reservoir. Besides bringing in more water, what else could raise the level?
options: Nothing else, since only a larger inflow can add to a stock
Draw the level down first so the reservoir has room to refill completely later
Reduce the water that leaves, for example by repairing leaks in the pipes
Measure the water more carefully at the dam each morning
optionExplain: Net change is inflow minus outflow, so shrinking the outflow also lifts the level.
Drawing down lowers the stock, which is the opposite of the goal.
Right: a smaller outflow has the same net effect on the level as a larger inflow.
Better measurement describes the stock but does not change it.
questions.explain: Cutting an outflow also raises a stock. The card next generalizes this.
questions.rule: To raise a stock, consider lowering its outflows as well as raising its inflows.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the human mind tends to notice inflows more easily than outflows.
questions.explain: She says we focus more easily on stocks than flows, and among flows on inflows rather than outflows.
questions.rule: People overlook outflows.

questions.q: A firm is short of staff. Besides hiring more people, which option follows Meadows’ logic?
options: Reduce the rates of quitting and firing, so fewer people leave
Count the existing staff more often so that gaps show sooner
Rename the vacant positions so that they sound more attractive to applicants
Raise the price of the firm’s products to cover recruiting
optionExplain: Right: lowering the outflow of staff builds the workforce just as hiring does.
Counting shows the stock but does not change it.
Titles may help recruiting but do not touch either flow directly.
Pricing might fund hiring later, but it changes neither the hiring nor the leaving rate.
questions.explain: A workforce can be built up by raising hiring or by lowering quitting and firing.
questions.hint: Think of the staff as water in a tub with a drain.
questions.rule: To raise a stock, consider lowering its outflows as well as raising its inflows.

questions.q: An oil-based economy gets a breakthrough in energy efficiency. What is its effect on the stock of available oil, per Meadows?
options: None, because efficiency does nothing to oil that is still underground
Worse than a discovery, because less oil is used and sold
The opposite of a discovery, since it lowers the inflow
The same as discovering a new oil field, though others profit
optionExplain: It reduces how fast the stock is used, so it does affect how long the oil lasts.
Using less oil preserves the stock, so it is not worse.
It lowers an outflow, not the inflow, and the effect on the stock is positive.
Right: burning less oil shrinks the outflow, which equals adding to the stock.
questions.explain: Efficiency acts on the outflow side of the same bathtub.
questions.rule: To raise a stock, consider lowering its outflows as well as raising its inflows.

questions.q: A stock can be increased by decreasing its ____ rate as well as by increasing its inflow rate.
questions.explain: Both routes change the net flow into the stock.
questions.rule: Cut the outflow or raise the inflow.

questions.q: A nation wants a larger stock of factories and machines. Which route does Meadows say is often cheaper than building more?
options: Slowing the rate at which factories and machines wear out or are discarded
Raising the rate of investment in new buildings and plant equipment each year
Counting its machines more carefully each year
Selling its older machines to other nations
optionExplain: Right: she says cutting the wear-out rate can often boost wealth more cheaply.
Investment is the inflow route, which she says is often costlier.
Counting does not change the stock.
Selling would add an outflow and shrink the stock.
questions.explain: The cheaper route may be on the outflow side.
questions.teaches: A nation’s wealth can be boosted by investment in more factories and machines, or often more cheaply by decreasing the rate at which they wear out, break down or are discarded.
questions.rule: To raise a stock, consider lowering its outflows as well as raising its inflows.

questions.q: A model of a tub ignores evaporation. When is that reasonable?
options: Whenever a model needs to be easy to draw on paper
Only when the model has been checked against every single flow in the real world
Never, since a model must include every real flow
When the time period is short enough that the flow is too small to matter
optionExplain: Ease of drawing is not the criterion; relevance to the question is.
A model cannot contain every flow, so full checking is impossible.
A model that included everything would no longer be a model.
Right: ignoring a tiny flow is a judgment about time scale.
questions.explain: Models drop what is negligible. The card next gives Meadows’ reasoning.
questions.rule: Decide which flows matter over your time period, include those, and remember the model leaves the rest out.

questions.q: Meadows says all models, whether mental or mathematical, are ____ of the real world.
questions.explain: Models leave things out on purpose, such as evaporation from the tub.
questions.rule: Every model simplifies.

questions.q: A city planner models a lake for a two-day boat race and ignores slow groundwater seepage. What does Meadows’ reasoning say?
options: The model is invalid, because every flow must be included
The model is sound only if seepage is larger than the rainfall on the lake
The choice is sound if the seepage is insignificant over those two days
The model is sound because seepage never matters
optionExplain: No model can include every flow, so requiring all of them would make any model invalid.
Size relative to rainfall is not the test; size over the period is.
Right: relevance to the time period decides.
Seepage can matter on longer time scales.
questions.explain: Judge a dropped flow by the period studied.
questions.rule: Decide which flows matter over your time period, include those, and remember the model leaves the rest out.

questions.q: The same planner now models the lake over twenty years for water supply. What happens to the earlier choice?
options: It still holds, because flows never change in importance as time goes by
It may not hold: a flow small over two days can add up over twenty years
It holds, because older models are always more accurate
It no longer matters, because lakes are not systems
optionExplain: Importance depends on how long the flow acts.
Right: the time horizon changes what counts as negligible.
Age of a model does not improve accuracy.
Lakes with stocks and flows are systems.
questions.explain: A longer horizon can promote a small flow into a large one.
questions.rule: Re-check dropped flows when the time scale changes.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows treats leaving evaporation out of the bathtub as a mistake she is hiding from the reader.
questions.explain: She states the assumption openly, saying evaporation is insignificant over the time period of interest. Dropping it is a deliberate simplification.
questions.rule: Decide which flows matter over your time period, include those, and remember the model leaves the rest out.

questions.q: Meadows draws one coffee drinker’s diagram with an extra stock for stored body energy rather than a simple cloud. What does she say this shows?
options: A diagram must always show every stock in the body
Clouds are forbidden in her diagrams from then on
Complex diagrams are always more accurate than simple ones for any purpose
We each choose how much complexity to look at; diagrams simplify
optionExplain: She chose to add one stock, not all stocks.
She says she could have drawn a cloud.
She does not say complexity equals accuracy.
Right: the detail level is a choice.
questions.explain: The modeller chooses the level of detail.
questions.teaches: All system diagrams are simplifications of the real world, and each of us chooses how much complexity to look at.
questions.rule: Decide which flows matter over your time period, include those, and remember the model leaves the rest out.

questions.q: A city suddenly doubles the water flow into its reservoir. What happens to the level at that moment?
options: It begins to rise gradually, since the extra water takes time to build up
It doubles at once, because the flow into it has doubled
It stays unchanged for a year before it begins to move
It falls first, because stocks respond in the opposite direction to flows
optionExplain: Right: the stock lags behind the flow, so it begins to rise gradually rather than jumping.
A flow changes the rate of filling, not the level itself.
It begins to rise immediately, just slowly.
A stock rises when its inflow exceeds its outflow; nothing makes it move opposite to its inflow.
questions.explain: The flow changes at once; the stock does not. The card next names this momentum.
questions.rule: Flows can change suddenly but stocks change gradually, so stocks act as delays, buffers and momentum.

questions.q: A stock takes time to change because ____ take time to flow.
questions.explain: Water cannot run out or in instantly, so the level changes only gradually.
questions.rule: Stocks lag their flows.

questions.q: An economy depends on oil-burning furnaces and engines, and the price of oil changes suddenly. What does Meadows expect?
options: It switches at once, since prices direct every decision made
It switches at once, since furnaces are always cheap to replace in an economy
It cannot switch fast, since its stock of equipment changes slowly
It does not switch at all, since prices never matter to it
optionExplain: Prices change at once, but the stock of equipment does not.
Replacing a large stock of furnaces and engines takes years.
Right: the equipment stock has momentum.
Prices can matter over longer periods as the stock turns over.
questions.explain: An economy built on oil-burning equipment cannot switch fast, because the stock of equipment turns over slowly.
questions.rule: Flows can change suddenly but stocks change gradually, so stocks act as delays, buffers and momentum.

questions.q: The drain of a full tub is opened all the way. What does Meadows say happens to the water level?
options: It falls steadily, but not instantly, since water cannot leave at once
It drops to zero at the very moment that the drain has been opened wide
It stays full until the faucet has been turned off
It rises at first because of pressure behind the drain
optionExplain: Right: she says water cannot run out instantly.
A level does not vanish instantly; the water needs time to leave.
The faucet is not involved in this case.
Nothing in her account has the level rising when the drain opens.
questions.explain: Even a wide-open drain takes time to empty a tub, so the level falls steadily rather than instantly.
questions.rule: Flows can change suddenly but stocks change gradually, so stocks act as delays, buffers and momentum.

questions.q: True or false: Because flows can change abruptly, Meadows concludes that stocks also change abruptly.
questions.explain: Stocks generally change slowly, even when the flows into or out of them change suddenly.
questions.rule: Flows can change suddenly but stocks change gradually, so stocks act as delays, buffers and momentum.

questions.q: Stratospheric pollutants took decades to accumulate. What does Meadows say about their removal?
options: It will happen quickly once the emissions have stopped altogether for good
It is impossible because a stock never decreases
It depends only on the price of the pollutants
It will also take decades, because the stock drains only gradually
optionExplain: Stopping an inflow does not empty a stock; it only stops its growth.
Stocks decrease when outflows exceed inflows.
Price is not the constraint on how fast the stock drains.
Right: the stock accumulated slowly and so drains only gradually, taking decades to clear.
questions.explain: Stocks drain as slowly as they filled, so pollutants that took decades to accumulate will take decades to leave.
questions.teaches: It took decades to accumulate the stratospheric pollutants that destroy the earth’s ozone layer, and it will take decades for those pollutants to be removed.
questions.rule: Flows can change suddenly but stocks change gradually, so stocks act as delays, buffers and momentum.

questions.q: A city adopts a new recycling policy and sees little change after one month. What would a systems thinker conclude?
options: The policy has failed and should be dropped immediately
It is too soon to judge, since the relevant stocks change slowly
The policy works perfectly because nothing at all got any worse in the month
Policies cannot affect stocks at all, so this is expected
optionExplain: Giving up too soon is the error Meadows warns against.
Right: slow stocks mean slow results.
No visible change in a month is not evidence of success; slow stocks simply have not moved yet.
Policies act on flows, and flows change stocks over time.
questions.explain: Know the pace of the stock. The card next shows both sides of lag.
questions.rule: Know how fast your stocks can change: it keeps you from expecting miracles, from giving up early, and from wasting the room that lags give you.

questions.q: Knowing the rates of change of stocks lets you use a system’s ____ much as a judo expert uses an opponent’s.
questions.explain: Meadows says you can use the opportunities presented by a system’s momentum to guide it toward a good outcome.
questions.rule: Work with a system’s momentum.

questions.q: A farmer notes that the soil on the hillside took centuries to build. Which statement fits Meadows’ view of lag?
options: The soil will vanish in a single season, whatever is done to protect it
Large stocks give no time at all to react to problems
Soil is not a stock, because it is a physical thing
It rarely erodes all at once, leaving time to correct bad practice
optionExplain: Her example says soil that built up over centuries rarely erodes all at once.
She says lags allow room to maneuver and revise policies.
Physical things such as wood and water are her standard examples of stocks.
Right: lag as a source of stability.
questions.explain: A stock built up over centuries rarely erodes all at once, and that lag gives room to correct bad practice before the damage is complete.
questions.rule: Know how fast your stocks can change: it keeps you from expecting miracles, from giving up early, and from wasting the room that lags give you.

questions.q: A government decrees rapid industrialization by next year. What does Meadows’ reasoning predict?
options: It can be achieved at once by decree alone
It is limited by how fast factories are built and workers educated
It will be faster if no one is educated
It depends on nothing except the amount of money that the state has available
optionExplain: A decree can change flows but not the stocks of factories and trained people.
Right: stocks set the pace of system dynamics.
Education is part of what limits the pace.
Money alone cannot instantly build factories or train workers.
questions.explain: Stocks set the pace of system dynamics: industrialization cannot go faster than factories can be built and workers educated.
questions.rule: You cannot build a stock faster than flows allow.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says time lags from stocks can be sources of stability as well as sources of problems.
questions.explain: Lags can cause problems but also give room to maneuver, to experiment and to revise policies.
questions.rule: Lags cut both ways.

questions.q: Groundwater is pumped faster than it recharges. What does Meadows say about the lag in this case?
options: The aquifer is damaged the same day that pumping begins, whatever the rate
Pumping faster than recharge never harms an aquifer
For a long time, before the aquifer is drawn down enough to be damaged
Groundwater is not a stock, so no lag exists
optionExplain: Her point is that damage takes a long time to appear.
Overpumping eventually draws the aquifer down far enough to harm it.
Right: the lag delays visible damage.
Groundwater is a stock; its recharge is an inflow.
questions.explain: The lag lets you pump groundwater faster than it recharges for a long time before damage shows, which is why it can hide a problem.
questions.teaches: You can pump groundwater faster than it recharges for a long time before the aquifer is drawn down far enough to be damaged.
questions.rule: Know how fast your stocks can change: it keeps you from expecting miracles, from giving up early, and from wasting the room that lags give you.

questions.q: Why do shops keep a stock of goods in a back room?
options: So that no further delivery is ever needed again from any supplier of goods
So that sales and deliveries can differ from day to day without trouble
So that sales can never exceed what is delivered that day
So that goods never actually have to move through the shop
optionExplain: A stock still needs refilling or it runs out.
Right: the stock absorbs differences between inflow and outflow.
Sales can exceed deliveries for a while, which is the whole point.
Goods still flow into and out of the stock.
questions.explain: Stocks decouple flows. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A stock lets flows differ for a while, and people watch stocks and adjust flows to keep levels acceptable.

questions.q: Stocks allow inflows and outflows to be independent of each other and temporarily out of ____.
questions.explain: The stock absorbs the difference between the two flows.
questions.rule: Stocks let flows differ for a while.

questions.q: A farm sells wheat all year but harvests only once. Which stock makes this possible?
options: The grain stored in silos between harvests
The seed packets stacked on the shelves of the shop
The rain falling on the fields during the growing months
The price list posted in the market on selling days
optionExplain: Right: stored grain lets output and sales differ.
Seeds are an input, not what lets sales continue after the harvest.
Rain feeds growth but cannot supply the sales after harvest.
A price list carries information, not goods.
questions.explain: Stored goods decouple harvest from sales.
questions.rule: A stock lets flows differ for a while, and people watch stocks and adjust flows to keep levels acceptable.

questions.q: Inventory in a retail chain climbs too high. What does Meadows say people typically do?
options: Stop all sales to protect the stock of goods held in the shops
Order even more goods to balance the level
Cut prices or raise advertising so that sales go up
Ignore the stock, since it is only a number
optionExplain: Stopping sales would raise inventories further.
Ordering more adds to the inflow, worsening the excess.
Right: they act on flows to bring the stock back into range.
Meadows says people monitor stocks constantly and act on them.
questions.explain: Decisions regulate stocks by adjusting flows.
questions.rule: A stock lets flows differ for a while, and people watch stocks and adjust flows to keep levels acceptable.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says a forest must be harvested at exactly the rate the trees grow.
questions.explain: She says harvesting at exactly that rate is not feasible; the standing wood is a stock that lets the flows differ.
questions.rule: A stock lets flows differ for a while, and people watch stocks and adjust flows to keep levels acceptable.

questions.q: Goods pass from distributors to wholesalers to retailers. What do inventories along that chain allow, per Meadows?
options: Demand and production to be forced into exact equality at every stage
The chain to run without any decisions being made
Production to run smoothly while demand varies, and the reverse
Prices to stay fixed whatever events occur
optionExplain: Inventories allow the two to differ, not to be equal.
Decisions still regulate the stock levels.
Right: inventories decouple production from demand.
Nothing in her account fixes prices; the inventories are about smoothing production against demand.
questions.explain: Inventories along a chain act as buffers, letting production run smoothly while demand varies, and the reverse.
questions.teaches: Inventories of products along a chain from distributors to wholesalers to retailers allow production to proceed smoothly although customer demand varies, and allow demand to be filled even though production rates vary.
questions.rule: A stock lets flows differ for a while, and people watch stocks and adjust flows to keep levels acceptable.

questions.q: The temperature of a greenhouse stays near 22 degrees through hot days and cold nights. What does that most suggest?
options: Some mechanism is acting on it to keep it within a range
Pure luck, since temperatures drift at random from hour to hour
That the greenhouse has no connection to the outside weather
That the walls alone determine the temperature inside
optionExplain: Right: persistent behavior points to a control mechanism.
Random drift would not hold a steady range over many days.
The weather acts on the greenhouse; something offsets its effect.
Walls alone cannot hold a range against changing weather.
questions.explain: Steady behavior suggests a mechanism. The card next names it.
questions.rule: Treat a persistent pattern in a stock as a clue to look for the loop that produces it.

questions.q: A behavior that persists over time is probably produced by a ____ that operates through a feedback loop.
questions.explain: A persistent pattern suggests a mechanism at work, and that mechanism operates through a feedback loop.
questions.rule: A persistent pattern points to a loop.

questions.q: A town’s population stays between 9,000 and 10,000 for fifty years despite many births, deaths and moves. What should a systems thinker suspect?
options: That the town is not a system at all, only a place on the map of the region
Mechanisms, such as housing or jobs, that hold the stock in a range
That its births and deaths are exactly zero
That randomness alone explains the stability
optionExplain: A persistent pattern suggests a system.
Right: look for the loop behind the pattern.
Flows exist; they are held in balance by mechanisms.
Randomness would not hold a narrow range for fifty years.
questions.explain: Persistent behavior points to a mechanism.
questions.rule: Treat a persistent pattern in a stock as a clue to look for the loop that produces it.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says that a stock which declines swiftly in every circumstance may also be under a feedback mechanism.
questions.explain: She includes stocks that grow by leaps and bounds or decline swiftly as well as stocks held within a range.
questions.rule: Treat a persistent pattern in a stock as a clue to look for the loop that produces it.

questions.q: A student says feedback loops explain only steady stocks, not ones that grow or fall. What does Meadows say?
options: Loops can lie behind stocks that grow, decline or hold in a range
The student is right, since only steady stocks ever have feedback loops
Loops explain only growth and no decline
Loops explain only declines, not steady levels
optionExplain: Right: her examples include all three patterns.
She lists growth, decline and holding steady as patterns a loop can produce.
Decline is included in her list, not excluded.
Steady levels are included in her list too.
questions.explain: A loop can drive any of the three patterns.
questions.rule: Treat a persistent pattern in a stock as a clue to look for the loop that produces it.

questions.q: A reader says a stock’s steady behavior proves that a specific loop exists. What caution fits Meadows’ wording?
options: No caution is needed, since a steady pattern is final proof of a loop
The pattern shows that no loop can exist
Steady behavior has no connection to loops
It is only a hint, so the loop still has to be found and checked
optionExplain: Her wording is first hint, a prompt to investigate rather than final proof of a loop.
Persistent patterns point toward loops, not away.
Steady behavior is exactly the kind of pattern she links to loops.
Right: a persistent pattern is a first hint, so the loop still has to be identified and checked.
questions.explain: A hint prompts the search for the mechanism.
questions.teaches: Meadows describes the consistent behavior pattern over a long period as only the first hint of a feedback loop, which is why you must still look for the mechanism.
questions.rule: Treat a persistent pattern in a stock as a clue to look for the loop that produces it.

questions.q: Which situation contains a feedback loop?
options: A tank drained at a fixed rate whatever the water level in it
A person who works more hours when her balance falls and fewer when it grows
A rain gauge that collects whatever rain happens to fall on it
A warehouse that receives exactly the same delivery every week whatever its stock
optionExplain: A fixed drain rate ignores the level, so nothing feeds back.
Right: the balance changes her earning, which changes the balance.
The gauge level has no effect on how much rain falls.
Fixed deliveries do not respond to the stock level.
questions.explain: A loop needs the stock to affect its own flow. The card next defines it.
questions.rule: Look for a stock whose level changes the flow that changes it.

questions.q: A feedback loop is formed when changes in a stock affect the flows into or out of that ____ stock.
