questions.explain: The loop closes because the stock’s own level changes the flow that changes it.
questions.rule: The stock acts on its own flows.

questions.q: A savings account pays 4 percent a year. Why is the yearly interest not a fixed amount?
options: The bank changes the interest rate at random every year
The account holder decides how much interest is paid out each month by choice
The bank’s percentage rule applies to the balance, so interest varies with it
Interest is a stock itself, and stocks cannot be held fixed
optionExplain: The rate is a fixed rule here; what varies is the balance it applies to.
The holder does not set the interest; the bank’s rule does.
Right: the stock size drives the inflow.
Interest is a flow into the balance, not a stock.
questions.explain: Interest depends on the balance, which is what closes the loop.
questions.rule: Look for a stock whose level changes the flow that changes it.

questions.q: You work more hours when your cash is low and fewer when it is high. Your cash grows large. What does the loop do?
options: You work more hours, because larger cash needs more work to look after it
You cut your hours, lowering the inflow and keeping cash in range
Nothing changes, because loops only act on low stocks
The loop breaks, because the stock got too large
optionExplain: Larger cash weakens the reason to work more.
Right: the loop adjusts the inflow to the level.
Meadows says you feel free to work less when cash is large.
A loop keeps operating at any level of the stock; it responds in both directions.
questions.explain: A balancing loop responds in both directions: when cash is large you cut hours, lowering the inflow and keeping cash in range.
questions.rule: Look for a stock whose level changes the flow that changes it.

questions.q: True or false: A fixed monthly salary paid regardless of the account balance is not part of a feedback loop.
questions.explain: Nothing in the salary responds to the stock level, so the chain stays open.
questions.rule: No response to the stock means no loop.

questions.q: A household cuts its spending whenever its savings dip. Meadows says an account can also have a loop that adjusts spending. What does this show?
options: A loop can adjust outflow, inflow, or both, in response to the stock
Loops can adjust only inflows and never outflows, whatever stock is involved
Loops need two separate stocks to operate
Spending is a stock, so it cannot be adjusted
optionExplain: Right: the monitor may change inflow, outflow or both.
She imagines an outflow-adjusting loop for spending.
One stock is enough for a loop, as the checking account example shows.
Spending is a flow out of the stock, so it can be adjusted like any other flow.
questions.explain: Loops can act on either side of the stock.
questions.teaches: Whoever or whatever monitors the stock’s level starts a corrective process that adjusts the rates of inflow or outflow, or both.
questions.rule: Look for a stock whose level changes the flow that changes it.

questions.q: A river fills a lake at its own pace and a canal drains it at a fixed rate. Does the lake have a feedback loop?
options: Yes: any lake that is filled and drained must contain a loop
Yes: the river reacts to how high the lake has become
No: the lake level affects neither flow, so the chain is open
Yes: the canal carries information about the lake back upstream
optionExplain: Having an inflow and an outflow does not make a loop.
Nothing says the river responds to the lake level, so it adds no feedback.
Right: a loop needs the stock level to influence a flow.
A fixed canal carries water, not information about the level.
questions.explain: A loop needs a response to the stock level. The card next gives the parts.
questions.rule: To test for a loop, ask whether the stock’s level reaches a decision that changes a flow back into the same stock.

questions.q: Put the steps of a feedback loop in order, starting from the stock.
items: The stock’s level is observed
A decision or rule responds to that level
The decision changes a flow into or out of the stock
The changed flow alters the stock’s level
questions.explain: The chain runs from the stock through a level-dependent decision to a flow, and back to the stock.
questions.rule: To test for a loop, ask whether the stock’s level reaches a decision that changes a flow back into the same stock.

questions.q: Which of these describes a closed feedback loop?
options: A furnace that runs on a timer whatever the temperature in the room happens to be
A furnace whose fuel is delivered every Monday by a supplier
A furnace that switches on when the room temperature falls below a set level
A furnace that a visitor paints a new color each year
optionExplain: A timer ignores the stock level, so the chain stays open.
Weekly delivery does not respond to the room’s temperature.
Right: the stock (room warmth) decides the flow of heat.
Painting does not connect the stock to any flow.
questions.explain: Level-dependent action closes the chain.
questions.rule: To test for a loop, ask whether the stock’s level reaches a decision that changes a flow back into the same stock.

questions.q: The sensor that reports room temperature to a furnace is disconnected, and the furnace keeps running. What is the system now?
options: An open chain: the level no longer affects the flow, so there is no feedback
Still a loop, because the furnace and the room are still part of the same building
A bigger loop, because more heat is being produced
A loop with no stock, because the room has no temperature
optionExplain: Right: cutting the information link opens the chain.
Without the link, the level cannot guide the furnace.
More heat does not mean more feedback.
The room still has a temperature; it simply no longer guides the flow.
questions.explain: With the information link cut, the stock’s level can no longer influence the flow, so the chain is open and there is no feedback.
questions.rule: To test for a loop, ask whether the stock’s level reaches a decision that changes a flow back into the same stock.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says every system contains at least one feedback loop.
questions.explain: She says not all systems have loops; some are open-ended chains in which stock levels do not affect flows.
questions.rule: To test for a loop, ask whether the stock’s level reaches a decision that changes a flow back into the same stock.

questions.q: A manager wants a bigger inventory. Meadows stresses that action in a stock-and-flow diagram runs through flows. What does she do?
options: She changes the stock level directly, by deciding what it ought to be
She changes the information link into the stock
She waits, because stocks cannot be influenced
She adjusts a flow such as orders in, because stocks change only via flows
optionExplain: A stock cannot be set directly; it only accumulates flows.
The link only carries information to the decision.
Flows can be adjusted, which does change stocks.
Right: change happens by adjusting flows.
questions.explain: A stock changes only through its flows, so a manager who wants a bigger inventory must adjust a flow such as orders in.
questions.teaches: A diagram of a loop emphasizes that action or change always proceeds through adjusting flows.
questions.rule: To test for a loop, ask whether the stock’s level reaches a decision that changes a flow back into the same stock.

questions.q: You feel drowsy and drink coffee. Later you feel jittery and skip the next cup. What pattern is this?
options: Snowballing: each cup makes you want another one even more than before
Self-correcting: your actions push your energy toward a level you want
Random: your behavior has no link to your energy
One-way: coffee only ever raises your energy level
optionExplain: Skipping a cup after being jittery shows the opposite of snowballing.
Right: your actions respond to the gap in both directions.
The pattern follows the energy level, so it is not random.
You also reduced coffee when energy was high.
questions.explain: Opposing the change is the mark of a balancing loop. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A balancing loop compares the stock with a goal and acts on the gap to push the stock back toward it.

questions.q: The gap between the actual level of a stock and its ____ level drives the corrective action of a balancing loop.
questions.explain: The discrepancy between actual and desired levels drives the decision to adjust.
questions.rule: Act on the gap between actual and goal.

questions.q: A manager wants 500 units in a warehouse, and it holds 800. Which action fits a balancing loop?
options: Order more units, since the stock already looks quite large to her
Do nothing, since a gap of 300 is not a signal
Raise the goal to 800 every time stock passes it
Cut orders or promote sales so the stock falls toward 500
optionExplain: Ordering more would widen the gap between 800 and 500 instead of closing it.
The gap is exactly what drives action.
Raising the goal removes the gap rather than acting on it.
Right: the loop acts to shrink the gap.
questions.explain: A balancing loop acts to shrink the gap, so with stock above the goal the manager should cut inflow or raise outflow.
questions.rule: A balancing loop compares the stock with a goal and acts on the gap to push the stock back toward it.

questions.q: Someone shoves the stock far above the goal. What does a balancing loop do?
options: It amplifies the rise so the stock climbs even further
It acts to pull the stock back down toward the goal
It freezes the stock where it was pushed
It switches off because the goal has been missed
optionExplain: Amplifying a rise is what a reinforcing loop does.
Right: a balancing loop opposes whatever direction of change is imposed, pulling a high stock down.
A balancing loop does not freeze stocks; it opposes the push.
A missed goal is the reason it acts, so it switches on rather than off.
questions.explain: A balancing loop opposes imposed change: push the stock up and it pulls it down.
questions.rule: A balancing loop compares the stock with a goal and acts on the gap to push the stock back toward it.

questions.q: True or false: A balancing loop keeps its stock at exactly one fixed value.
questions.explain: The level may not stay completely fixed. It stays within an acceptable range.
questions.rule: A balancing loop compares the stock with a goal and acts on the gap to push the stock back toward it.

questions.q: Why does Meadows label a loop diagram stored energy in body rather than low energy level?
options: Because low energy is the only state that a feedback loop can ever fix here
Because labels are chosen by the reader afterward
Loops correct in both directions, so labels avoid assuming a direction
Because stored energy never rises above the goal
optionExplain: The same loop reduces coffee when energy is high.
Her labels are chosen by the author for the diagram.
Right: labels are direction-free because the loop corrects too much as well as too little.
Energy can run too high, as the jittery drinker shows.
questions.explain: Neutral labels fit a loop that works both ways.
questions.teaches: Meadows’ diagram labels are direction-free, because a feedback loop can correct an oversupply as well as an undersupply: too much coffee and extra energy make the drinker lay off caffeine.
questions.rule: A balancing loop compares the stock with a goal and acts on the gap to push the stock back toward it.

questions.q: A cup of coffee at 90 degrees stands in a 20 degree room. When does its temperature fall fastest?
options: Near the end, when it is almost at room temperature
At the start, when the gap to room temperature is greatest
At a constant speed all the way down
Only after an hour, once the cup has warmed the table beneath it
optionExplain: Near the end the gap is small, so cooling is slow.
Right: a bigger gap means a faster change.
A constant speed would ignore the shrinking gap.
The cooling starts at once and is fastest then.
questions.explain: The gap sets the speed. The card next explains.
questions.rule: When correction is proportional to the gap, a stock closes in on its goal quickly at first and ever more slowly near the end.

questions.q: True or false: The rate of cooling depends on the difference between the temperature of the coffee and the temperature of the room.
questions.explain: The greater the difference, the faster the coffee cools.
questions.rule: Bigger gap, faster change.

questions.q: You make iced coffee on a hot day and leave it out. What does the loop do?
options: It stays cold, because cold drinks resist warming
It warms at a steady rate and then overshoots the temperature of the room
It cools further, because the gap points the other way
It warms toward room temperature, fast at first and then slower
optionExplain: The loop works in both directions, so it warms.
Steady warming and overshoot would ignore the shrinking gap.
The gap points upward here, so the change does too.
Right: the same loop works from below the goal.
questions.explain: The loop is the same from either side of the goal.
questions.rule: When correction is proportional to the gap, a stock closes in on its goal quickly at first and ever more slowly near the end.

questions.q: Two cups sit in a 20 degree room, one at 80 degrees and one at 40. Which one starts changing temperature faster?
options: The 80 degree cup, because its gap to the room is larger
The 40 degree cup, because cooler drinks settle faster than hot ones
Both equally, because they are in the same room
Neither, because rate depends only on the cup’s size
optionExplain: Right: the rate of change follows the size of the gap, and the 80 degree cup has the bigger gap.
Rate depends on the gap, which is smaller for the cooler cup.
The room is the same but the gaps differ, and the gap sets the rate.
Meadows says the rate depends on the temperature difference.
questions.explain: Cooling speed depends on the difference from the room, so the cup with the larger difference changes faster.
questions.rule: When correction is proportional to the gap, a stock closes in on its goal quickly at first and ever more slowly near the end.

questions.q: As the gap between a stock and its goal shrinks, a balancing loop changes the stock more ____.
questions.explain: The change is fast at first and slower as the discrepancy decreases.
questions.rule: Closer to the goal means slower change.

questions.q: Which of these does Meadows cite as showing the same gradual approach to a goal as cooling coffee?
options: A snowball growing larger as it rolls downhill
A savings account compounding at a fixed percentage every single year
A radioactive element decaying and a missile finding its target
A rabbit population doubling in each season
optionExplain: Growth that feeds on itself is a reinforcing pattern.
Compounding interest is her example of a reinforcing loop.
Right: these are among her goal-seeking examples.
Her rabbits illustrate reinforcing growth.
questions.explain: Many natural processes home in on a goal.
questions.teaches: The same gradual approach to a system-defined goal appears when a radioactive element decays, a missile finds its target, an asset depreciates, a reservoir is brought to its desired level, the body adjusts blood sugar, or a car is pulled to a stop at a stoplight.
questions.rule: When correction is proportional to the gap, a stock closes in on its goal quickly at first and ever more slowly near the end.

questions.q: True or false: Having a balancing loop is enough to guarantee that a stock reaches the loop’s goal.
questions.explain: A loop can fail for many reasons. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: A loop is not a guarantee.

questions.q: Which are ways feedback can fail, according to Meadows? Select all that apply.
options: Information arrives too late or at the wrong place
Information is unclear, incomplete or hard to interpret
The action triggered is too weak, delayed or ineffective
The stock has more than one inflow
The goal has been written down in advance
optionExplain: Right: lateness and misplacement are named failures.
Right: unclear or incomplete signals are named failures.
Right: weak or delayed action is a named failure.
Several inflows are common and do not by themselves make a loop fail.
Writing a goal down does not make feedback fail, and it may help.
questions.explain: Meadows names late or misplaced information, unclear information, and weak or delayed action.
questions.rule: When a goal is missed, check the loop’s information and action for lateness, weakness or confusion.

questions.q: A city’s flood sirens sound after the river has already overtopped its banks. Which failure is this?
options: Information arrives too late for the corrective action to work
The goal of the loop is unclear to the residents
The action triggered is too strong for the situation it was meant to fix
The stock being watched is not a physical thing
optionExplain: Right: the signal comes too late for the corrective action to work, which is a named failure.
The goal here, safety from flooding, is clear; the timing is the problem.
Nothing in the case says the siren is too strong; the trouble is that it sounds too late.
Whether the stock is physical has nothing to do with the failure.
questions.explain: A signal that comes after the river has overtopped is information that arrives too late for corrective action, a classic failure.
questions.rule: When a goal is missed, check the loop’s information and action for lateness, weakness or confusion.

questions.q: True or false: A feedback loop too weak to bring its stock to the goal still counts as a feedback loop.
questions.explain: Meadows says the mechanism may not be strong enough; its presence does not mean it works well.
questions.rule: A loop can exist and still fall short.

questions.q: A student says that because a feedback loop exists, it must be working well. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing is wrong, since feedback loops always work as intended
The presence of a mechanism does not mean it works well
Loops work only if they are large
Loops never exist in real systems
optionExplain: She warns that a mechanism may not work well, so the student is wrong that existence implies success.
Right: she says the presence of a mechanism does not necessarily mean the mechanism works well.
Size is not her criterion; weakness, delay or poor information are the failures she lists.
Loops are common in real systems, as she says directly, so this misreads her.
questions.explain: The existence of a feedback mechanism does not mean it works well; loops can fail in several named ways.
questions.rule: When a goal is missed, check the loop’s information and action for lateness, weakness or confusion.

questions.q: Why can a balancing loop frustrate a reform that tries to move a stock far from its goal?
options: Balancing loops resist change as well as providing stability
They never respond to changes imposed on the stock in any way
They amplify whatever change is imposed
They only matter when the stock is physical
optionExplain: Right: the same pull toward the goal resists reform.
They respond by opposing the change, which is why they resist reforms.
Amplifying is what reinforcing loops do.
Stocks need not be physical, and that has nothing to do with resistance.
questions.explain: The same balancing loop that gives stability also resists change, so it can frustrate a reform that moves a stock far from its goal.
questions.teaches: Balancing feedback loops are equilibrating or goal-seeking structures in systems and are both sources of stability and sources of resistance to change.
questions.rule: When a goal is missed, check the loop’s information and action for lateness, weakness or confusion.

questions.q: The more rabbits there are, the more baby rabbits are born, and they grow up to have babies too. What is this?
options: A balancing circle in which more rabbits somehow bring fewer new rabbits
No loop at all, since births are independent of parents
A fixed cycle in which the number of rabbits never changes
A self-multiplying circle in which the stock boosts its own inflow
optionExplain: More rabbits bring more births here, the opposite of balancing.
Births depend on how many parents exist.
The number grows as the rabbits breed, so it is not a fixed cycle.
Right: the stock feeds its own growth.
questions.explain: The stock amplifies itself. The card next names this loop.
questions.rule: A reinforcing loop makes more of whatever is already happening to a stock, upward or downward.

questions.q: True or false: A reinforcing loop enhances whatever direction of change is imposed on it.
questions.explain: It generates more input the more there already is, and less when there is less, so it amplifies change either way.
questions.rule: A reinforcing loop makes more of whatever is already happening to a stock, upward or downward.

questions.q: The more soil erodes, the fewer plants grow, so fewer roots hold the soil. What kind of loop is this?
options: Balancing, since erosion keeps the soil within a range
Reinforcing, a runaway collapse in which loss of soil causes more loss
Neither, since soil is not a stock
Reinforcing, but a growth loop, since the soil keeps increasing over time
optionExplain: Erosion here speeds up with more erosion, which a balancing loop would oppose.
Right: a destructive reinforcing loop.
Soil is an accumulation, so it is a stock.
The soil decreases, so the loop drives decline, not growth.
questions.explain: Reinforcing loops can run downward as well as upward.
questions.rule: A reinforcing loop makes more of whatever is already happening to a stock, upward or downward.

questions.q: A reinforcing loop is knocked so that its stock falls a little. What happens next?
options: It pulls the stock back up to where it was before the dip
It holds the stock at the lower level
It generates less input, so the stock falls further
It reverses direction at random
optionExplain: Pulling back is a balancing loop’s job.
A reinforcing loop does not hold levels steady.
Right: the dip is amplified, because less in the stock generates less input.
Nothing in a reinforcing loop is random; it follows the stock level.
questions.explain: A reinforcing loop amplifies: a stock that falls generates less input, so it falls further, turning a small dip into a bigger one.
questions.rule: A reinforcing loop makes more of whatever is already happening to a stock, upward or downward.

questions.q: Sort each pattern into balancing or reinforcing.

items.t: A jittery drinker skips coffee
Hot coffee cooling toward the room
Rabbits breeding more rabbits
Interest earning more interest
Erosion thinning the roots that hold soil
A thermostat switching a furnace off

questions.explain: Balancing loops oppose change and seek a goal. Reinforcing loops amplify change.
questions.rule: A reinforcing loop makes more of whatever is already happening to a stock, upward or downward.

questions.q: Which kind of stock is most likely to sit in a reinforcing loop?
options: One that is physical in nature and therefore cannot be counted at all
One that can reproduce itself or grow as a fraction of itself
One that only ever flows out and never in
One that is held at a fixed target level
optionExplain: Being physical or uncountable does not create self-reinforcement.
Right: reproducing stocks feed on themselves.
A stock with no inflow has nothing to amplify.
A target level suggests balancing, not reinforcing.
questions.explain: Self-reproducing stocks form reinforcing loops.
questions.teaches: Reinforcing loops are found wherever a system element has the ability to reproduce itself or to grow as a constant fraction of itself, such as populations and economies.
questions.rule: A reinforcing loop makes more of whatever is already happening to a stock, upward or downward.

questions.q: $100 earns 5 percent a year with no deposits. How do the dollars added each year behave?
options: They stay the same, five dollars every year
They shrink each year, because the balance is gradually used up over time
They alternate between large and small amounts
They grow each year, because interest is earned on a larger balance
optionExplain: A flat five dollars would be linear growth, which ignores earlier interest.
Nothing uses the balance up; interest adds to it, so the yearly additions rise.
Nothing in the interest rule alternates; each year adds a percent of the balance.
Right: each year’s interest is a percent of a bigger stock.
questions.explain: Interest is earned on interest. The card next names the pattern.
questions.rule: Where a stock feeds its own growth, the amount added each period grows too, so growth is exponential, not linear.

questions.q: Growth that goes faster and faster because the more there is, the more is added, is called ____ growth.
questions.explain: That is exponential growth, the typical output of a reinforcing loop.
questions.rule: Where a stock feeds its own growth, the amount added each period grows too, so growth is exponential, not linear.

questions.q: A pest population in a cornfield doubles each week. Why is this “bad news” exponential growth?
options: The loop makes the pests multiply ever faster, and the growth is harmful
Pests multiply at a steady, slow and predictable rate through the season
Exponential growth is always bad news whatever grows
The loop is balancing, so the pests will soon fade away
optionExplain: Right: exponential growth is good or bad depending on what grows.
Doubling each week means the numbers added keep getting bigger.
Meadows says it is good or bad news depending on what grows.
A doubling pest population shows reinforcement, not balance.
questions.explain: The same mechanism can be welcome or harmful.
questions.rule: Where a stock feeds its own growth, the amount added each period grows too, so growth is exponential, not linear.

questions.q: The $100 account earns 8 percent a year instead of 4 over twelve years. How does the total interest compare?
options: It exactly doubles, since the rate itself has doubled from four to eight percent
It is less than doubled, since time is fixed
It more than doubles, because higher rates compound on larger balances
It is the same, since both run twelve years
optionExplain: Compounding makes the effect larger than the rate ratio suggests.
The faster feedback adds more than proportional growth.
Right: about $152 of interest at 8 percent against about $60 at 4 percent.
Time is equal but rates differ, which changes the interest.
questions.explain: Higher rates strengthen the loop: 8 percent over twelve years gives more than twice the interest of 4 percent (our arithmetic).
questions.rule: Where a stock feeds its own growth, the amount added each period grows too, so growth is exponential, not linear.

questions.q: True or false: In exponential growth, the amount added each period grows because it depends on the stock already there.
questions.explain: The more is there, the more is added, which is why growth goes faster and faster.
questions.rule: Linear adds a constant; exponential adds a constant fraction.

questions.q: At a low interest rate, a savings graph looks like a straight line for the first few years. What would a careful reader conclude?
options: It is still exponential; the speeding up is hard to see early on
It is linear, since lines that look straight over several years must be linear
The reinforcing loop is not operating at low rates
Growth only becomes exponential after twelve years
optionExplain: Right: the acceleration is present but small.
Looking straight early on does not prove it is linear.
A reinforcing loop operates at any positive rate.
The growth is exponential from the start.
questions.explain: Early on, exponential growth can look linear.
questions.teaches: The growth of a bank account at lower interest rates may look linear in the first few years, but in fact growth goes faster and faster.
questions.rule: Where a stock feeds its own growth, the amount added each period grows too, so growth is exponential, not linear.

questions.q: Which growth rate makes a stock double fastest?
options: 2 percent a year
5 percent a year
7 percent a year
10 percent a year
optionExplain: A low rate gives a long doubling time.
Five percent doubles more slowly than ten percent does.
Seven percent doubles more slowly than ten percent does.
Right: the higher the rate, the sooner the doubling.
questions.explain: Higher rates double sooner. The card next gives a shortcut for how soon.
questions.rule: Doubling time is about 70 divided by the percentage growth rate.

questions.q: Doubling time is approximately ____ divided by the growth rate, expressed as a percentage.
questions.explain: This is Meadows’ shortcut for exponential growth.
questions.rule: Doubling time is about 70 over the rate.

questions.q: A town’s population grows exponentially at 2 percent a year. About how long until it doubles?
options: About 14 years
About 35 years
About 20 years
About 70 years
optionExplain: That is the doubling time for 5 percent.
Right: 70 divided by 2 is 35 years.
That does not follow from dividing 70 by 2.
70 years would be the answer for 1 percent.
questions.explain: Divide 70 by the percentage rate: 70 divided by 2 gives about 35 years.
questions.rule: Doubling time is about 70 divided by the percentage growth rate.

questions.q: An economy grows 3.5 percent a year. After about 20 years, what has happened to its output?
options: It has roughly doubled
It has grown by about 3.5 times
It has grown by exactly 70 percent
It has barely changed
optionExplain: Right: 70 divided by 3.5 is 20, so output doubles in about twenty years.
That would apply to a much higher rate.
Adding 3.5 percent twenty times gives 70 percent only if growth were linear.
At 3.5 percent compounding, twenty years is large.
questions.explain: At 3.5 percent the doubling time is about 70 divided by 3.5, which is 20 years.
questions.rule: Doubling time is about 70 divided by the percentage growth rate.

questions.q: True or false: At 10 percent growth a year, Meadows’ rule gives a doubling time of about 7 years.
questions.explain: 70 divided by 10 is 7. Using 100 instead of 70 would wrongly give 10.
questions.rule: Use 70 over the percentage rate.

questions.q: Meadows says $100 at 7 percent doubles in 10 years. How does money at 5 percent compare?
options: It takes about 7 years to double, which is shorter
It takes about 14 years to double, which is longer
It takes about 10 years, the same as 7 percent
It never doubles at that rate
optionExplain: A lower rate gives a longer doubling time, not a shorter one.
Right: 70 divided by 5 is 14 years.
The rate changed, so the time changes too.
It does double, just more slowly, in about 14 years.
questions.explain: Our arithmetic from the 70 rule: 70 divided by 5 is 14 years, against 10 years at 7 percent. A lower growth rate gives a longer doubling time.
questions.teaches: Under the 70 rule, a lower growth rate gives a longer doubling time.
questions.rule: Doubling time is about 70 divided by the percentage growth rate.

questions.q: A bakery uses profits to buy more ovens, which bake more bread and make more profit. What drives its growth?
options: A balancing loop that holds the bakery’s output at a fixed target
An outside event that has nothing to do with the bakery
A reinforcing loop in which output funds more capacity, which raises output
A fixed supply of ovens that limits the bread baked
optionExplain: A balancing loop would oppose growth, but profits are growing the ovens.
The growth comes from within the bakery’s own loop.
Right: the more it makes, the more it can build.
The ovens are not fixed; profits keep adding them.
questions.explain: Output funds capacity. The card next shows the same loop for an economy.
questions.rule: When output is reinvested to raise capacity, the capital stock feeds its own growth.

questions.q: Order the steps of Meadows’ reinvestment loop.
items: More machines and factories (capital)
More goods and services (output)
More investment in new machines and factories
Still more capital
questions.explain: Capital produces output, output is invested, and investment adds to capital.
questions.rule: When output is reinvested to raise capacity, the capital stock feeds its own growth.

questions.q: A software firm reinvests its earnings in hiring engineers, who build products that earn more. Which loop does this resemble?
options: A balancing loop in which earnings fall as staff rise
The reinvestment loop in which output funds more capacity
A chain with no feedback, since earnings are separate from hiring
A loop in which the staff are the only flow
optionExplain: The earnings grow with staff here, which is not balancing.
Right: output feeds back into capacity.
The earnings feed back into hiring, so there is feedback.
Hiring is a flow into a stock of staff, with earnings as another link.
questions.explain: Earnings are reinvested in capacity that raises output, the same reinforcing structure as machines and factories in an economy.
questions.rule: When output is reinvested to raise capacity, the capital stock feeds its own growth.

questions.q: An economy stops investing any output in new capital. What happens to the loop?
options: It speeds up, since more of the output stays available to be consumed instead
It continues unchanged, since capital makes itself
It reverses into a balancing loop immediately
It is broken: capital gets no inflow, so growth from reinvestment stops
optionExplain: Output stays available, but nothing converts it into capital.
Capital does not grow without investment.
Stopping investment removes the link, not the type of loop.
Right: no investment, no growth in capital.
questions.explain: If capital gets no new investment inflow, the reinforcing loop is cut and growth from reinvestment stops.
questions.rule: When output is reinvested to raise capacity, the capital stock feeds its own growth.

questions.q: True or false: In the reinvestment loop, capital is the stock and investment is the inflow that adds to it.
questions.explain: Machines and factories accumulate in the capital stock, and new investment flows into it.
questions.rule: Name the stock before the flows.

questions.q: An analyst asks which single loop is the central engine of growth in an economy. What does Meadows name?
options: The balancing loop in which prices adjust to demand in each market
The loop in which births are balanced by deaths
The reinforcing loop from capital to output to investment
A chain of stocks with no feedback at all
optionExplain: Price adjustment is a balancing example, not her growth engine.
A birth and death balance is not described as the engine.
Right: she calls this the central engine of growth.
An open chain has no loop to produce growth.
questions.explain: Meadows names the reinforcing loop from capital to output to investment as the engine of growth in an economy.
questions.teaches: The reinvestment loop of capital and output is the central engine of growth in an economy.
questions.rule: When output is reinvested to raise capacity, the capital stock feeds its own growth.

questions.q: A report says poverty causes high birth rates. What question would a systems thinker add?
options: Who is to blame for the report’s conclusion about poverty?
Why are birth rates and poverty unrelated?
How might high birth rates in turn deepen poverty?
How can the report’s data be made larger?
optionExplain: Blame is what a systems thinker stops seeking.
The report links them; the question is about the reverse link.
Right: ask whether the effect acts back on the cause.
Data size does not address whether the effect acts back on the cause.
questions.explain: Ask whether the effect acts back on the cause. The card next gives Meadows’ habit.
questions.rule: Ask what B does back to A, and replace the hunt for blame with the question of what the system is.

questions.q: A systems thinker asks: if A causes B, can B also ____ A?
questions.explain: Feedback thinking looks for the influence running back from effect to cause.
questions.rule: Look for the arrow back.

questions.q: A manager blames a salesperson for falling sales. Using Meadows’ habit, what should the manager ask next?
options: Which other salesperson can be blamed instead of this one?
Why do salespeople never seem to try hard enough to meet their targets?
How soon can the salesperson be replaced?
What loops among sales, pricing and staffing might produce this?
optionExplain: Shifting blame is the habit she asks you to drop.
This assumes a cause and ignores the system.
Replacing the person looks only at an element.
Right: the manager asks what the system is rather than who is to blame.
questions.explain: Meadows says you stop looking for who is to blame and start asking what the system is.
questions.rule: Ask what B does back to A, and replace the hunt for blame with the question of what the system is.

questions.q: You begin to look for loops instead of culprits. What happens to your search for blame?
options: It becomes the main purpose of the whole analysis of the problem
It gives way to asking what the system is behind the behavior
It stays exactly as before
It is replaced by ignoring the problem
optionExplain: She says you stop looking for who is to blame.
Right: this is the shift she describes.
Her habit changes the search from blame toward structure.
The system question is a way of studying the problem.
questions.explain: Seeing the loop shifts attention from blaming someone to asking what system produces the behavior.
questions.rule: Ask what B does back to A, and replace the hunt for blame with the question of what the system is.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows states that falling in love is certainly a decision made with no feedback involved.
questions.explain: Students suggest it as a non-feedback decision, but she leaves it to the reader to decide whether it really involves no feedback.
questions.rule: Ask what B does back to A, and replace the hunt for blame with the question of what the system is.

questions.q: A news item says the central bank acted to slow the economy. What additional view does Meadows suggest?
options: The economy must also have done something to affect the bank
The economy cannot affect the bank at all
The bank is the only real actor in the whole system we are examining
The news item is certainly false
optionExplain: Right: look for the reverse influence.
Her point is that influence runs both ways.
She says A and B may influence each other.
She does not judge the news item false.
questions.explain: Influence may run both ways, so if the bank acts on the economy, the economy has also acted on the bank.
questions.teaches: When you hear that the Federal Reserve Bank has done something to control the economy, you will also see that the economy must have done something to affect the Federal Reserve Bank.
questions.rule: Ask what B does back to A, and replace the hunt for blame with the question of what the system is.

questions.q: A stock sits in both a reinforcing loop and a balancing loop. What decides what it does?
options: Only the older loop, whichever one happened to begin first in the system
Only the reinforcing loop, since it is always stronger
Only the balancing loop, since it always wins in the end
The relative strengths of the loops pulling it in different directions
optionExplain: Age of a loop does not decide its strength.
Reinforcing loops are not always stronger.
Balancing loops do not always win; the stronger loop prevails.
Right: loops of differing strengths pull against each other.
questions.explain: Strength decides. The card next explains.
questions.rule: When loops compete, predict the stock’s behavior from their relative strengths, not from any one loop.

questions.q: True or false: In real systems, feedback loops rarely come singly.
questions.explain: They are linked together in complex patterns, with several loops acting on one stock.
questions.rule: When loops compete, predict the stock’s behavior from their relative strengths, not from any one loop.

questions.q: Sort each force on a growing company into a reinforcing or a balancing loop.

items.t: Profits reinvested to raise output
Word of mouth that brings in more customers, who bring in more
Competitors cutting prices as the firm grows
A manager cutting orders when the warehouse is full

questions.explain: Reinforcing loops amplify growth. Balancing loops oppose it and pull a stock toward a range.
questions.rule: Reinforcing amplifies; balancing opposes.

questions.q: The reinforcing loop on a stock strengthens while the balancing loop stays the same. What is likely?
options: The stock settles at its goal faster than before the change
Both loops cancel exactly
The reinforcing pull gains ground over the balancing one
The balancing loop speeds up automatically
optionExplain: A weaker balancing loop would settle it less firmly.
Cancelling needs equal strength, which no longer holds.
Right: the stronger loop gains influence.
Nothing makes the balancing loop speed up on its own; the stronger reinforcing loop simply gains ground.
questions.explain: A loop that gains strength shifts the balance of pulls, so the stock follows the stronger loop.
questions.rule: When loops compete, predict the stock’s behavior from their relative strengths, not from any one loop.

questions.q: A student says a stock with both kinds of loops must either explode or settle at a goal. What does Meadows add?
options: Nothing is wrong: those two are the only possible outcomes for such a stock
Complex systems do much more than stay steady, explode or approach goals
Stocks with both kinds of loops always remain constant over the years
Complex systems always collapse into chaos
optionExplain: She says complex systems do more than that.
Right: complex systems do much more than stay steady, explode exponentially or approach goals smoothly.
Constant levels are only one possible behavior.
She does not say they always collapse.
questions.explain: Meadows adds that complex systems do much more than stay steady, explode or approach goals; there are more patterns than those two.
questions.rule: When loops compete, predict the stock’s behavior from their relative strengths, not from any one loop.

questions.q: A company’s cash flow is adjusted by the levels of its cash, inventory and staff. What does this show about flows?
options: A flow can respond to only one stock at a time, the one it enters
A flow can never fill and drain at once
Flows ignore all the other stocks except the single one they enter
A single flow may be adjusted by the contents of several stocks
optionExplain: She says a flow may depend on three or five or twenty stocks.
A flow can fill one stock while draining another.
Flows can respond to many stocks, not just the one they enter.
Right: this is the pattern she describes.
questions.explain: A single flow can be adjusted by the contents of several stocks at once, so flows are shared among stocks.
questions.teaches: A single flow may be adjusted by the contents of three or five or twenty stocks, and it may fill one stock while it drains another and feed into decisions that alter yet another.
questions.rule: When loops compete, predict the stock’s behavior from their relative strengths, not from any one loop.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A teacher wants students to grasp how complex systems behave. Which route does Meadows favour in this chapter?
options: Begin with simple, familiar systems and draw general principles from them
Begin with abstract general theory and add examples only at the very end of the course
Begin with the most complex real systems so no detail is hidden
Avoid examples, because they distort the general principles
optionExplain: Right: she says specific examples teach better than abstractions.
Plausible for a textbook, but she names examples as the better way in.
Complete realism sounds honest, but she picks simple systems so behavior is visible.
She treats examples as the route to the principles, not a distortion of them.
questions.explain: She argues that examples teach better than generalities, and that simple systems make the behavior visible. The card next explains the zoo comparison.
questions.rule: Study systems one at a time to see their characteristic behavior, and remember that real systems are mixed together.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: True or false: In the zoo comparison, the systems are grouped by family, such as single-stock systems and two-stock systems.
questions.explain: The author groups her examples by family so that you can compare characteristic behaviors, as monkeys differ from bears.
questions.rule: The zoo groups systems by family.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A magazine explains a city's traffic by drawing it as a self-contained loop, apart from housing and jobs. Which zoo caution applies?
options: Traffic is too simple a system to belong in any zoo
Separating the traffic system makes it visible but hides its links to other systems
A neat diagram proves the traffic system has no outside links
Grouping systems by family makes comparison impossible
optionExplain: The author chooses simple systems on purpose, so simplicity is not the fault.
Right: the neatness that helps you see it also removes the surrounding connections.
Separation is the diagram's choice; it says nothing about whether links exist.
Grouping by family is what lets the zoo show characteristic behavior.
questions.explain: The zoo makes animals understandable by separating them from each other and from their concealing environment. The cost is that real systems connect and interact.
questions.rule: Isolation shows behavior and hides connections.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Meadows says her zoo is far from a ____ representation of the variety of systems.
questions.explain: She admits the collection gives an idea of the variety but does not represent all of it.
questions.rule: The zoo is a sample, not the whole list.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Which summary of the zoo comparison misreads the author?
options: The zoo gives an idea of variety but is far from a complete representation of systems
The zoo is too neat because it separates systems from each other
The zoo shows systems exactly as they occur in nature, mixed with their surroundings
The zoo groups single-stock systems apart from two-stock systems
optionExplain: This matches her statement, so it is not the misreading.
This matches her warning that the collection is too neat.
Right: this is the misreading; she says the zoo separates the animals from their normal environment.
This matches how the chapter is organised, so it is accurate.
questions.explain: Real systems are mixed in ecosystems; the zoo deliberately pulls them apart so the behavior is visible.
questions.rule: Tidy models are not the untidy world.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A student asks why the chapter does not show these systems interacting. What does the author say about the plan?
options: Interactions between systems are too weak to matter in practice
Interacting systems cannot be understood, so the book omits them
The single-stock examples already include every interaction
Ecosystems of interacting systems come later; for now she shows one system at a time
optionExplain: She says real systems do connect and interact; she defers them, not dismisses them.
She promises to return to ecosystems, so they are not omitted.
She says they are separated from each other, so they do not include interactions.
Right: she defers interactions and looks at one animal at a time.
questions.explain: After describing the zoo's neatness she writes that ecosystems come later and that for the moment she will look at one animal at a time.
questions.rule: Look at one system at a time first; interactions come later.
questions.teaches: The author defers ecosystems of interacting systems to later in the book and first looks at one system at a time.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A room has a thermostat-controlled furnace, and heat also leaks outdoors. How many goals is the room temperature pulled toward?
options: Two: the thermostat setting and the outside temperature
One: the thermostat setting, because the leak is not a feedback loop
One: the outside temperature, because the furnace only adds heat
None: a stock holds quantities and cannot have a goal
optionExplain: Right: each balancing loop pulls toward its own goal.
The leak is a loop too: the bigger the gap with the outside, the faster the loss.
The furnace is governed by a loop aimed at the setting, so it is a goal of its own.
The stock is the thing being pulled; the loops around it carry the goals.
questions.explain: Two balancing loops act on the same stock, each with its own goal. The card next describes them.
questions.rule: A stock with two balancing loops is pulled toward two goals at once: the thermostat setting and the outside temperature.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: True or false: With only the leak loop and no furnace, a warm room would cool slowly toward the outside temperature.
questions.explain: The leak loop alone acts like a cooling coffee cup; the book shows a warm room cooling very slowly toward 10°C.
questions.rule: The leak loop alone drags the room toward the outside temperature.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A freezer sits in a warm kitchen. Its thermostat switches the cooling, and heat seeps in through the walls. Which description fits?
options: Only one loop acts, aimed at the kitchen temperature
One balancing loop pulls toward the freezer setting; another pulls toward the kitchen temperature
Two reinforcing loops push the temperature up and down
Neither loop has a goal, because the freezer is a machine
optionExplain: The cooling loop is aimed at the freezer setting, so there are two loops.
Right: same structure as the thermostat, with the signs of heat flow reversed.
Both loops here are goal-seeking, which makes them balancing, not reinforcing.
A thermostat setting is exactly the goal of the cooling loop.
questions.explain: The freezer has a stock-maintaining loop aimed at its setting and a leak loop aimed at the surroundings, like the room.
questions.rule: Look for the maintaining loop and the leak loop.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: The better the insulation, the ____ a warm room cools toward the outside temperature when the furnace is off.
questions.explain: Insulation weakens the leak loop, so the temperature drop is slower.
questions.rule: Better insulation weakens the leak loop.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A student says: the furnace loop and the leak loop are one loop running in two directions. What is the correction?
options: They are the same loop, but the furnace loop is reinforcing
Only the furnace loop is a feedback loop; the leak is a fixed flow
They are two separate balancing loops with different goals: the setting and the outside temperature
The leak loop is not part of the model, since it hurts the goal
optionExplain: Both are balancing; neither amplifies its own change.
The leak grows with the gap to the outside, so it is a loop.
Right: each has its own goal and its own flow.
The model includes it deliberately, as the book's Figure 15 shows.
questions.explain: One loop adds heat to reach the setting; the other lets heat escape toward the outside. They share only the stock.
questions.rule: Two loops, two goals, one stock.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A thermostat is wired to an air conditioner in a hot climate. Which statement fits the two-loop structure?
options: The thermostat loop stops working, because it cannot cool a room
Only one balancing loop remains, because heat stops moving
Both loops now pull the room toward the same goal
The thermostat loop removes heat toward the setting; the leak loop brings heat in from outside
optionExplain: The author notes the same mechanism can cool when connected to an air conditioner.
Heat still moves between the room and the outside, so the second loop remains.
The loops still have different goals, the setting and the outside temperature.
Right: the roles reverse but the structure stays the same.
questions.explain: Meadows notes the thermostat may heat or cool, depending on whether it is attached to a furnace or an air conditioner. The structure of two competing balancing loops is unchanged.
questions.rule: Same structure, reversed directions.
questions.teaches: A thermostat can regulate cooling as well as heating when it is connected to an air conditioner instead of a furnace.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A thermostat is set to 18°C in a house that loses heat outdoors. Where will the room temperature most likely settle?
options: Slightly below 18°C
Exactly 18°C, because the thermostat switches the furnace off at 18°C
Above 18°C, because the furnace overshoots when it switches off
At the outside temperature, because the leak always wins
optionExplain: Right: the leak means the furnace never fully catches up.
It would hold exactly there only if nothing leaked.
Overshoot would need a delay in the loop; here the shortfall comes from the leak.
The heating loop dominates when insulation and furnace size are adequate.
questions.explain: The leak drains heat even as the furnace restores it, so the room stays a little under the setting. The card next explains the mechanism.
questions.rule: When a leak runs alongside a maintaining loop, the stock levels off a little short of the goal.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: True or false: In the book's simulation the room temperature levels off slightly below the 18°C thermostat setting.
questions.explain: The book states that the room levels off slightly below 18°C because of the leak.
questions.rule: A leak keeps the stock slightly under the goal.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A tank is topped up from a pipe whenever the level falls below a mark, but a small hole drains it. What level results?
options: Exactly at the mark, because the refill pipe is controlled by the level
Slightly under the mark
Above the mark, because the pipe can deliver faster than the hole drains
The tank empties, because a hole beats any refill pipe
optionExplain: The refill responds to a shortfall, so some shortfall must exist for it to act.
Right: the same bucket-with-a-hole logic applies.
A faster pipe lets the level approach the mark but the loop stops refilling at the mark.
Only if the hole outpaces the pipe; the card assumes the refill is adequate.
questions.explain: A refill that reacts to a shortfall acts only after the level has dropped, so the leak keeps the level a little low.
questions.rule: Maintaining loops respond to a shortfall, so a leak leaves a small one.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: With the same thermostat setting, a better-insulated house settles ____ to the setting, because the leak is slower.
questions.explain: A slower leak leaves a smaller shortfall. The book says a well-insulated house is more comfortable than a poorly insulated one, even one with a big furnace.
questions.rule: Weaker leak, smaller shortfall.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: Which explanation of the room settling below 18°C is mistaken?
options: The leak drains heat even while the furnace restores it
The outflow rises as the room gets warmer than the outside
The thermostat is broken, because a working one would hold exactly 18°C
It takes time for the furnace to correct for the heat that has already been lost
optionExplain: This is the book's explanation, so it is accurate.
This is stated in the book and is accurate.
Right: this is the mistake; a working system with a leak settles slightly below.
The book says this and it is accurate.
questions.explain: The shortfall is a normal consequence of two competing balancing loops, not a fault.
questions.rule: Falling short is the normal behavior of competing loops.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A kettle with a thermostat holds water at a set temperature in a cold garage. Why does the water settle a little under the setting?
options: The element heats only after the water has already passed the setting
Cold air has no effect once the thermostat is working
A kettle is not a feedback system, so no pattern applies
Heat loss to the cold air continues while the element is restoring it
optionExplain: That would give overshoot, not a steady shortfall.
The book's point is that the leak keeps acting while the thermostat works.
A thermostat-controlled kettle has the same competing-loop structure.
Right: same leak-versus-maintaining-loop logic as the room.
questions.explain: In the book's model the room warms nearly to the target and then levels off slightly below. Meadows adds that the outflow rate is higher on cold days than on warm days, so the shortfall varies with the weather.
questions.rule: Leak size changes the shortfall.
questions.teaches: The outflow rate is higher on cold days than on warm days, so the right thermostat setting is hard to calculate exactly.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: You owe 2,000 on a credit card that adds interest each month. What must a repayment do to clear the debt?
options: Exceed the interest and charges added each month, or the balance will not fall
Equal the balance divided by the months you plan to take
Match the interest added each month, then wait for it to fall
Be as small as possible, since the interest charged shrinks as time passes and the debt ages
optionExplain: Right: repayments must outrun the charges that keep refilling the debt.
This ignores the charges added while you pay, so the target slips away.
Matching the charges only holds the balance steady, it does not reduce it.
Waiting lets charges accumulate; the debt falls only if you outpace them.
questions.explain: The balance is a stock with a draining repayment and a refilling charge. The next card names the principle.
questions.rule: Set a stock-maintaining loop's goal to allow for the drains and inflows acting on the stock, or it will fall short of or exceed the target.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: To hold a room at a desired temperature against a leak, set the thermostat a little ____ the desired temperature.
questions.explain: The setting compensates for the heat leaking out while the furnace works.
questions.rule: Aim the setting above the target to offset the leak.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A pond owner wants the water at 1.5 metres while evaporation lowers it daily. A float valve refills below the mark. What helps?
options: Nothing, because a float valve always holds the level exactly at the mark
Allow for evaporation when setting the mark
Lower the mark, because less water means less evaporation
Remove the valve, since refilling disturbs the natural level
optionExplain: The valve acts on a shortfall, so evaporation leaves the level a little low.
Right: the goal must anticipate the daily drain, like the thermostat set above the target.
A lower mark moves the target away from what the owner wants.
Without refilling the level would fall steadily and miss the aim entirely.
questions.explain: Whatever drains or fills the stock while the loop corrects must be built into the goal or the compensation.
questions.rule: Include the drain in the plan.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: True or false: A card-holder who ignores monthly interest and repays a flat amount will still clear the balance on schedule.
questions.explain: Ignoring the charges incurred while paying means the plan will miss its target, falling short or taking longer.
questions.rule: An ignored flow shows up as a missed target.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A manager says: set the target at the level we want, and the control loop will deliver it. What does Meadows' principle say is wrong?
options: The loop cannot reach any target, because every loop has a delay
A target should never be set, only a rate of change
It overlooks flows that drain or fill the stock, which make the loop miss the target
The loop delivers the target, but only after the stock has stopped moving
optionExplain: The point concerns other flows, not that no target is reachable.
The principle adjusts the goal for flows; it does not ban targets.
Right: the target alone is not enough when other flows act on the stock.
The stock never stops moving while drains and fills continue.
questions.explain: A mental model without all the important flows leads to surprise. The goal must be set with the drains and fills in view.
questions.rule: Model every important flow.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A firm wants to raise its work force to a higher level. According to the author, what must its hiring do?
options: Match the target headcount in a single round of hires
Slow down as the headcount nears the target, to avoid overshooting the goal
Ignore departures, which are outside the firm's control
Be fast enough to make up for those who quit while it is hiring
optionExplain: The target alone ignores the quitters leaving during the hiring.
The author's point concerns flows that drain the stock, not overshoot.
Departures are a draining flow the mental model must include.
Right: workers leaving drain the stock as new ones are added.
questions.explain: Gearing up a work force is another stock-maintaining loop: hires fill the stock, quitting drains it, and the hiring rate must allow for the drain.
questions.rule: Hire faster than people leave.
questions.teaches: When gearing up a work force, you have to hire fast enough to correct for those who quit while you are hiring.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A thermostat reads 16°C and switches the furnace on. What can this feedback act on?
options: Only the room's later temperature
The 16°C reading itself, by warming the room backwards in time
Nothing, because a furnace cannot affect a measured temperature
The thermostat setting, which changes to match the reading
optionExplain: Right: the signal arrives after the behavior that caused it.
A signal about a past state cannot alter that state.
The furnace does affect future temperatures; it cannot undo the past one.
The setting is the goal, which the loop does not rewrite.
questions.explain: A reading describes what has already happened, so the response can influence only what happens next. The card next states the principle.
questions.rule: Feedback can change only future behavior: a flow responds to a stock after a delay, never instantly to another flow.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: True or false: According to Meadows, even nonphysical information takes time to feed back into a system.
questions.explain: She says the information delivered by a feedback loop, even nonphysical, cannot deliver a signal fast enough to correct the behavior that drove the current feedback.
questions.rule: Feedback always arrives after the behavior that caused it.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A café manager reads Monday's sales report on Tuesday and changes Wednesday's order. Which behavior can the order affect?
options: Monday's sales, since the report triggered the decision to place the order
Later days' stock and sales, not the Monday sales already reported
Tuesday's report, which the order will then correct
All sales so far, because the order revises the totals
optionExplain: The report describes Monday after it ended; nothing can change it.
Right: the decision influences only future behavior.
The report is already written; the order cannot rewrite it.
Orders add stock for the future; they do not rewrite recorded sales.
questions.explain: Information about what happened comes after the fact, so the response acts on what follows.
questions.rule: A decision cannot undo what produced the signal.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A flow can react only to a change in a ____, and only after a slight delay to register the information.
questions.explain: Meadows says a flow cannot react instantly to a flow; it reacts to a stock after a delay.
questions.rule: Flows respond to stocks, with a delay.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A planner argues that because feedback is only information, it arrives instantly, so responses need no delay. Which reply fits the author?
options: Information is instant, but physical goods are what cause the delays
Feedback loops contain delays only when a person is involved
Even nonphysical information takes time to register, so there will always be delays in responding
The planner is right for stocks but not for flows
optionExplain: She says nonphysical information also needs time to feed back.
Delay is a general property, not one that depends on who responds.
Right: the author states this directly.
A flow reacting to a flow is the case she says is impossible instantly.
questions.explain: The principle covers physical and nonphysical feedback alike: a response comes only after the signal is registered.
questions.rule: No signal is instant.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: An economist builds a model in which production changes the instant a price changes. What does Meadows say about such models?
options: They are sound, since prices are only information, and information is received instantly by all
They are sound if consumption responds but production does not
They fail because prices never influence production
They err by assuming immediate response, a reason real economies do not behave like them
optionExplain: She argues against exactly this assumption.
She names both consumption and production as responding with delay.
Her complaint is about speed of response, not about prices lacking influence.
Right: she gives this as an example of the delay being ignored.
questions.explain: She says many economic models wrongly assume consumption or production can respond immediately to a change in price, which is one reason real economies do not behave like the models.
questions.rule: Models that skip response delays mislead.
questions.teaches: Many economic models wrongly assume consumption or production respond immediately to a price change, which is one reason real economies do not behave like them.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A shop holds 100 units, orders take a week, and 20 units sell weekly. What goes wrong if it orders only the visible shortfall?
options: It falls short, because sales keep draining stock while the order is on its way
It overshoots, because orders arrive faster than sales
It hits 100 exactly, since the order equals the shortfall
Nothing, because stock stays still until an order arrives
optionExplain: Right: the shortfall grows during the wait.
Orders do not arrive faster than sales in the setup; the stock falls because 20 units sell every week while the order is on its way.
The shortfall it saw is not the shortfall that exists when stock arrives.
The stock changes every day as customers buy.
questions.explain: The stock goes on changing during the wait, which the next card names.
questions.rule: Where a stock keeps changing while you correct it, plan for what will drain or fill it during the correction.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the thermostat's control problem is serious because you cannot find a workable setting.
questions.explain: She says that for thermostats the control problem is not serious; the trouble is greater in other systems with the same structure.
questions.rule: The thermostat is the forgiving case.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A chemist wants a steady concentration in a reactor with continuous flow through it. Which mistake matches the book's warning?
options: Measuring the concentration more than once during the run
Adding the visible shortfall without allowing for what flows out meanwhile
Setting a target concentration at all, since targets tend to cause some drift over time
Using a reactor with any flow, since flow is always harmful
optionExplain: Measuring is not the problem; ignoring the flow is.
Right: the stock keeps changing while the correction is made.
The structure of the loops, not the existence of a target, creates the trap.
The trap comes from ignoring the flow, not from its presence.
questions.explain: Meadows lists a continuously flowing chemical reaction among the systems fooled in the same way as the store.
questions.rule: Allow for flows during the correction.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: If a store ignores the goods sold during its order wait and the wait grows longer, the shortfall will ____.
questions.explain: A longer wait lets more sales drain the stock before the order arrives.
questions.rule: Longer waits, larger shortfalls.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: Which reasoning about inventory is mistaken?
options: The store cannot order instantly to fill an apparent shortfall
Goods sold while an order is on its way can leave stock too low
We can order instantly to make up any shortfall we see, so waiting sales do not matter
Inventory, like a thermostat room, has a draining loop and a refilling loop
optionExplain: This is the book's point: the store cannot order instantly to fill an apparent shortfall.
This is the book's point: goods sold while an order is on its way can leave stock too low.
Right: this ignores the goods sold while the order is on its way.
This matches the structure the book describes.
questions.explain: Instant ordering is exactly what the store cannot do.
questions.rule: Orders do not arrive when placed.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A treasurer keeps a bank balance at a set level. Which other stocks can fool a controller the same way?
options: The age of a building and the number of its tenants
The price of a share and the interest on a loan
The speed of a car and the height of a hill
The level of water in a reservoir and a chemical concentration in a flowing reaction
optionExplain: These are not stocks held at a level by competing loops in the text.
The author's list contains stocks you try to hold at a level, not prices or rates.
The list concerns controlled stocks, not these quantities.
Right: the author lists cash balances, reservoirs and chemical concentrations.
questions.explain: The book says you can be fooled in the same way when maintaining a cash balance, the level of water in a reservoir, or the concentration of a chemical in a continuously flowing reaction system.
questions.rule: Cash, water and chemicals share the trap.
questions.teaches: The same trap catches anyone holding a cash balance, a reservoir water level or a chemical concentration in a flowing reaction at a set level.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A furnace holds a house steady through normal winters. Which change could make it fail to hold the setting?
options: A colder spell combined with larger leaks, draining heat faster than the furnace adds it
A thermostat that switches the furnace on more often
A room that is warmer than the setting
Better insulation along the walls
optionExplain: Right: when the drain outpaces the furnace, the setting cannot be held.
A responsive switch helps the furnace, it does not weaken it.
A warm room reduces demand on the furnace.
Better insulation slows the leak, giving the furnace an easier job.
questions.explain: The furnace can hold the setting only while it can add heat faster than heat leaks out. The card next names this limit.
questions.rule: A balancing loop holds its goal only while it is stronger than the forces pulling the stock away.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: Every balancing feedback loop has its ____ point, where other loops pull the stock away from its goal more strongly than it can pull back.
questions.explain: That is the author's term for the limit of a balancing loop.
questions.rule: Breakdown is where the opposing loops win.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A café's air conditioner coped last summer. This summer a heatwave arrives and a door seal fails. What has changed in loop terms?
options: The thermostat loop has become reinforcing and amplifies heat
The loop letting heat in has strengthened, so the cooling loop may reach its breakdown point
The cooling loop has no breakdown point, since it has a goal
Only the weather matters, so the loops are unaffected
optionExplain: The thermostat loop stays balancing; what has changed is the strength of the loop pulling heat in.
Right: a stronger opposing loop can overwhelm the maintaining loop.
The author says every balancing loop has one.
The seal failure also strengthens the heat loop, and the weather acts through the loops.
questions.explain: The opposing loop has been strengthened by outside heat and a bigger leak.
questions.rule: Strengthen the opposing loop and the breakdown point nears.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: Which changes would push the thermostat system toward its breakdown point? Select all that apply.
options: Thicker insulation
A smaller furnace
Colder outside air
A more powerful furnace
Larger leaks in the walls
optionExplain: Thicker insulation weakens the cooling loop, moving away from breakdown.
Right: a smaller furnace weakens the heating loop.
Right: colder air strengthens the cooling loop.
A more powerful furnace strengthens the heating loop, moving away from breakdown.
Right: leaks strengthen the cooling loop.
questions.explain: A weaker heating loop or a stronger cooling loop makes breakdown more likely.
questions.rule: Weaken the maintaining loop or strengthen the drain and breakdown comes closer.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A student says the cold spell showed the thermostat loop stopped existing. What is the correction?
options: The loop is gone because it cannot work below freezing
The loop became reinforcing once the outside temperature fell below freezing
The thermostat setting changed itself to match the outside
The loop still operates, but the opposing loop is stronger for a while
optionExplain: The furnace was still running at full output.
Its structure is unchanged; only the relative strength changed.
The setting stays what it was; the room cannot reach it.
Right: dominance shifted; the heating loop did not disappear.
questions.explain: Breakdown is a matter of relative strength between loops, not of a loop vanishing.
questions.rule: Outweighed is not absent.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: In the book's well-functioning 24-hour run, the outside dips below freezing. What does the furnace's heat inflow do?
options: It tracks the outflow to the outside, and the room temperature barely varies
It lags the outflow, so the room swings widely through the day
It stays fixed at a set level while the outflow changes, so the room follows the weather
It stops entirely below freezing to avoid damage
optionExplain: Right: inside its limits, the loop keeps pace and the stock hardly varies.
That describes the leaky-house run, not the well-functioning one.
The furnace inflow responds to the shortfall rather than staying fixed.
Nothing in the model switches the furnace off below freezing; its inflow tracks the heat draining out.
questions.explain: Meadows describes the furnace inflow as nicely tracking the outflow of heat, with temperature varying hardly at all once the room has warmed up. Failure occurs when the drain exceeds the furnace's capacity.
questions.rule: Within limits the loop tracks the drain.
questions.teaches: In the well-functioning run, the furnace's heat inflow tracks the outflow to the outside and the room temperature varies hardly at all once warmed up.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A furnace is running at full output, yet the room is cooling. Under what condition is this possible?
