options: The thermostat has been set above the room temperature
Heat leaking out is greater than the furnace's output
The furnace is adding heat to the outside air
The room has stopped following the bathtub logic
optionExplain: A higher setting calls for more heat, it does not explain cooling at full output.
Right: the stock falls whenever outflow exceeds inflow.
Heat added to the room goes into the room stock; the question is about net change.
Stocks follow net flow in every case, including this one.
questions.explain: Whenever outflow exceeds inflow the stock falls, even if the inflow is at its maximum. The card applies this to the book's graph.
questions.rule: To explain behavior over time, ask at each moment whether the inflow is ahead of or behind the outflow.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: True or false: Whenever the furnace is putting in more heat than is leaking out, the room temperature rises.
questions.explain: This is the bathtub rule applied to the room's heat.
questions.rule: Inflow above outflow means the stock rises.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A savings account earns 100 a month in interest and is charged 120 a month in fees. What does the balance do?
options: It rises by 100, since interest is the only flow that matters
It stays fixed, since both flows are small compared with the balance
It falls by 20 each month, since the outflow is ahead of the inflow
It rises by 20 a month, since flows are added
optionExplain: The 120 outflow is also acting on the stock.
The stock changes with any nonzero net flow.
Right: the net flow is negative.
Outflow subtracts, giving a net of 20 less per month, not more.
questions.explain: Net flow decides the direction. Here the outflow exceeds the inflow, so the stock falls.
questions.rule: Direction of change comes from net flow.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: Put the leaky-house run in the order it unfolds.
items: Both temperatures are cool, the furnace inflow beats the leak, and the room warms
The outside is mild and the furnace replaces most of the lost heat, so the room stays near the desired temperature
The outside falls, the leak grows, the furnace cannot keep up, and the room cools
The outside warms, the leak slows, the furnace pulls ahead and the room warms again
questions.explain: The sequence follows the shifting balance between the furnace's inflow and the leak's outflow.
questions.rule: Follow the order of inflow versus outflow.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A student says the room began warming again at the end because the furnace's output rose. What is the correction?
options: Output rose because the thermostat setting was raised
Warming resumed because the room became better insulated
Warming resumed because the furnace was replaced by a larger one during the cold spell
The furnace was already at full output; the leak slowed enough for it to pull ahead
optionExplain: The run does not change the thermostat setting; the furnace output was already at full tilt.
The insulation is unchanged; the outside temperature changed.
The same furnace is described as running at full tilt.
Right: the furnace was operating at full tilt throughout.
questions.explain: Warming resumed because the leak shrank, not because the furnace did more.
questions.rule: A stock can turn because the other flow changed.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: A student studies the leaky-house graph beside the loop diagram. What does Meadows say this reveals?
options: How the two loops and shifts in their relative strength produce the behavior over time
That the thermostat setting varies with the time of day
That only the furnace loop shapes the behavior over time, because it is the stronger one
That the behavior is random and cannot be linked to structure
optionExplain: Right: structure and shifting strength explain the unfolding behavior.
The setting is fixed; the graph shows other variables moving.
Dominance shifts between the loops, so neither alone shapes the whole run.
She says relating graph to diagram gives a sense of how structure leads to behavior.
questions.explain: She says that studying the changes on the graph and relating them to the feedback-loop diagram gives a good sense of how the structural interconnections, the two loops and how their strengths shift, lead to behavior over time.
questions.rule: Behavior comes from structure plus shifting strength.
questions.teaches: Relating the graph to the loop diagram shows how the structure, two feedback loops whose strengths shift relative to each other, leads to the unfolding behavior over time.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A population has constant birth and death rates, and the birth rate is the higher one. What pattern follows?
options: Steady growth by the same number each year, since the rates are constant over time
Exponential growth, because the births loop is stronger than the deaths loop
A levelling off, because deaths always catch up with births
Decline, because a balancing loop always wins in the long run
optionExplain: Constant rates give a constant percentage, which compounds, not a constant number.
Right: the reinforcing loop dominates.
Deaths catch up only if the two loops come to equal strength.
Neither loop wins by nature; the stronger one at the time decides.
questions.explain: A reinforcing loop that is stronger than the balancing loop produces exponential growth. The card next explains.
questions.rule: With constant fertility and mortality, the stronger loop decides: births ahead means exponential growth, deaths ahead means decline.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: True or false: In the population model the births loop is reinforcing and the deaths loop is balancing.
questions.explain: Births add to the population in proportion to its size, which reinforces; deaths pull it down, which balances.
questions.rule: Births reinforce; deaths balance.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A herd has 6 births and 8 deaths per 100 animals each year, constant. What does Meadows' structure predict?
options: It grows exponentially, because births are a reinforcing loop that outpaces everything else
It stays constant, because both rates are constant
It declines, because the balancing death loop is stronger than the births loop
It oscillates, because the two loops compete
optionExplain: The births loop is reinforcing but weaker here, so it does not decide.
Constant rates do not mean constant numbers; the gap decides.
Right: deaths exceed births, so the herd dies off.
Two loops of this kind give growth, decline or levelling, not oscillation.
questions.explain: With the death loop stronger, the stock falls.
questions.rule: Compare the two loops.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: If constant mortality is higher than constant fertility, the population will gradually ____.
questions.explain: Deaths exceed births every year, so the stock falls.
questions.rule: Stronger deaths loop, falling stock.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Someone claims that any stock with a reinforcing loop must grow. What is the flaw?
options: Reinforcing loops produce decline, not growth
The stock grows only if the balancing loop is absent
The claim is correct, since reinforcing loops dominate by definition
A stronger balancing loop can outweigh it, so the stock can decline
optionExplain: Reinforcing loops amplify; they grow or shrink a stock by compounding.
Both loops can be present, and growth still wins if reinforcing is stronger.
A reinforcing loop does not win by definition; the stock follows whichever loop is stronger.
Right: growth depends on which loop is stronger.
questions.explain: The balance of strengths decides, not the type of loop alone.
questions.rule: Strength matters, not type alone.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A student says the births-and-deaths structure applies only to living creatures. What does the author say it describes?
options: Every living population and every economy
Only populations of people, since economies lack births
Only simple organisms, because complex ones have more loops
Only closed systems with no exchange with the outside
optionExplain: Right: the book says it describes every living population and every economy.
She applies the structure to economies as well.
She calls it one of the most common structures, including for people.
The text says nothing limiting it to closed systems.
questions.explain: Meadows says this structure describes every living population and every economy, which is why she follows it with the capital example.
questions.rule: Population and economy share the structure.
questions.teaches: The reinforcing-plus-balancing pair describes every living population and every economy.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A country has 18 births and 10 deaths per 1,000 people a year. If these rates hold, what happens to its population?
options: It shrinks, because deaths are counted first
It grows, because births exceed deaths by 8 per 1,000 a year
It stays stable, because both rates are small
It grows by 18 per 1,000, because deaths are not included in the count
optionExplain: Order of counting is irrelevant; only the net flow matters.
Right: the net flow is positive.
Small rates still produce a net change if they differ.
Deaths are an outflow and must be subtracted.
questions.explain: The net flow is births minus deaths. The card next works through the 2007 numbers.
questions.rule: Compare the two flows: whichever is larger decides whether the stock grows or falls.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: With fertility of 21 and mortality of 9 per 1,000, the ____ loop dominates the system.
questions.explain: Fertility exceeds mortality, so the births loop (reinforcing) dominates.
questions.rule: Larger flow, dominant loop.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A town has 14 births and 16 deaths per 1,000 people a year. What does the structure predict if rates hold?
options: A slow rise, since births are close to deaths
Dynamic equilibrium, since the rates are nearly equal and the gap is small
A slow decline, since the death loop is slightly stronger
Rapid growth, since both rates are high
optionExplain: Closeness does not matter; the sign of the net flow does.
Equilibrium needs equal flows, not nearly equal ones.
Right: net flow is minus 2 per 1,000.
The rates are not high enough to offset each other, and the net is negative.
questions.explain: Deaths exceed births, so the population falls slowly.
questions.rule: Net flow decides.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: If fertility drops from 21 to 12 per 1,000 and mortality stays at 9, how does growth change?
options: It turns to decline, since fertility has fallen
It stops at once, since the rates are closer
It speeds up, since smaller families live longer
It continues but more slowly
optionExplain: Fertility has fallen but remains above mortality.
Growth stops only when the flows are equal.
Growth does not speed up; the setup leaves mortality at 9, and the net flow shrinks.
Right: the net flow shrinks from 12 to 3 per 1,000.
questions.explain: A smaller gap means slower growth, not decline.
questions.rule: Smaller gap, slower change.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.rule: Use net flow.
questions.q: True or false: With 21 births and 9 deaths per 1,000, 21 people per 1,000 are added to the population each year.
questions.explain: Deaths remove 9 of them, so the net gain is 12 per 1,000.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A terrible disease raises mortality to 30 per 1,000 while fertility stays at 21. What does the author say happens?
options: The population keeps growing, since fertility is unchanged from before
The death loop dominates and the population gradually decreases
The population levels off at once, since the loops cancel
The population collapses within a year, since 30 is high
optionExplain: Births are lower than deaths now, so growth ends.
Right: more die than are born each year.
They do not cancel; deaths exceed births.
The text says it would gradually decrease.
questions.explain: In the book's Figure 23 scenario, more people die each year than are born and the population decreases gradually.
questions.rule: Death loop wins, decline follows.
questions.teaches: If a terrible disease raised mortality to 30 per 1,000 with fertility at 21, the death loop would dominate and the population would gradually decrease.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Births per year fall until they equal deaths per year, and then both stay constant. What does the population do?
options: It keeps growing, since it has more people than before
It declines, since the fall in births continues
It levels off, with births exactly balancing deaths
It oscillates around the starting level
optionExplain: Size alone does not matter; only the net flow does.
Births stopped falling once they equalled deaths.
Right: equal flows leave the stock steady.
Nothing in the setup introduces oscillation; equal constant flows hold the stock level.
questions.explain: Equal flows hold the stock at one level. The card next names this state.
questions.rule: When the flows change, the stock's line bends; if inflow comes to equal outflow, the stock levels off in dynamic equilibrium.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: When births exactly balance deaths, the population is in dynamic ____.
questions.explain: Dynamic equilibrium means the flows are equal, so the stock stays steady even though people are still being born and dying.
questions.rule: Equal flows give dynamic equilibrium.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A country's births fall from 25 to 10 per 1,000 over thirty years while deaths hold at 10. What does the population do?
options: It grows at a steady rate for the whole period
It starts falling in the first year
It levels off at once, since both rates will eventually equal 10 per 1,000
It grows at a slowing rate, then levels off once births equal deaths
optionExplain: The gap shrinks, so the rate of growth shrinks too.
Births start above deaths, so it begins by growing.
It levels only when the rates are equal, at the end.
Right: the line bends as the gap closes.
questions.explain: As the gap between births and deaths closes, growth slows, then stops.
questions.rule: Closing gap, bending line.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: True or false: If fertility drops below mortality and stays there, the population levels off immediately.
questions.explain: Below-mortality fertility makes the population decline; it levels off only if fertility equals mortality.
questions.rule: Equal flows level a stock; unequal flows move it.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Which statement about changing flows is mistaken?
options: A stock's graph cannot bend
Changing fertility and mortality bends the population line
The UN assumes fertility declines as countries develop
Equal fertility and mortality give a level population
optionExplain: Right: changing flows are exactly what bend the stock's line.
Meadows says changing flows create a change in the behavior of the stock.
This is the UN assumption described in the text.
Equal fertility and mortality give a level population, which is dynamic equilibrium, so this is accurate.
questions.explain: A stock accumulates its flows; when the flows change, the accumulation bends.
questions.rule: Flows shape the stock's line.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Why does the UN now assume that the rise in life expectancy will slow in some regions over the next fifty years?
options: Because fertility is expected to rise in those regions
Because of the HIV/AIDS epidemic in those regions
Because mortality is already high and cannot fall faster
Because developed countries have stopped medical research
optionExplain: Fertility assumptions are separate from the life expectancy change.
Right: the book names the epidemic as the reason.
The text says mortality is already low in most parts of the world.
The book gives no such reason.
questions.explain: The author explains that, because of HIV/AIDS, the UN assumes increasing life expectancy will slow in affected regions. Assumptions about flows are themselves open to change.
questions.rule: Flow assumptions change with events.
questions.teaches: Because of HIV/AIDS, the UN assumes the trend of rising life expectancy over the next fifty years will slow in affected regions.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A stock is acted on by two competing loops. What decides how it behaves at a given time?
options: The loop that was added to the system first
The average of the strengths of the two loops, which comes out at zero
The loop that has the stronger effect on the stock at that time
The loop with the largest number of parts
optionExplain: Order of addition has no effect on strength.
Averaging would hide the actual strength each loop has.
Right: the dominant loop sets the behavior.
The number of parts does not decide strength.
questions.explain: Whichever loop has the stronger impact decides. The card next names this dominance.
questions.rule: Complex behaviors often arise as the relative strengths of feedback loops shift, so that first one loop and then another dominates.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: When one loop has a stronger impact on behavior than another, it is said to ____ the system.
questions.explain: Dominance is the term for a loop whose impact on behavior is stronger.
questions.rule: The stronger loop dominates.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A start-up grows through word of mouth, then rivals take customers away until growth stops. What happened to the loops?
options: The reinforcing loop was removed from the system entirely
A new reinforcing loop replaced the old one
The balancing loop dominated from the beginning
Dominance shifted from the growth loop to a balancing loop, ending at equal strength
optionExplain: Loops can weaken without disappearing.
Nothing in the story adds another reinforcing loop; the balancing loop of rivals' competition gained strength.
The early growth shows the reinforcing loop dominated first.
Right: the reinforcing loop weakened relative to the balancing loop.
questions.explain: Growth first, then a balance, shows a shift of dominance between loops.
questions.rule: Watch which loop is ahead as strengths change.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.rule: Equal loops, level stock.
questions.q: True or false: When neither loop dominates, the stock keeps growing.
questions.explain: With equal strength the stock stays level, in dynamic equilibrium.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A student says that a dominated loop has stopped operating. What is the correction?
options: It operates only when the dominant loop is switched off
It still operates, but its effect on behavior is weaker than the dominant loop's
It has been replaced by the dominant loop
It is operating at full strength but hidden
optionExplain: Both loops operate at the same time.
Right: dominance is about relative strength.
Loops are not replaced; their relative strengths change.
Its strength is lower, not hidden.
questions.explain: Dominance describes which loop has more impact, not which loop exists.
questions.rule: Weaker is not absent.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Which event in the thermostat example does Meadows give as shifting dominance?
options: The thermostat setting was raised well above the outside temperature on a cold day
The furnace cycled off and on near the setting
The outside temperature fell and heat leaking out overwhelmed the furnace
The room reached the setting exactly at the end
optionExplain: Raising the setting is a choice, not a shift in the loops' relative strength.
This is normal operation with the heating loop dominating.
Right: dominance shifted from the heating loop to the cooling loop.
The room levels off slightly below the setting.
questions.explain: Meadows recalls the thermostat to illustrate shifting dominance: when the outside temperature fell, the leak overwhelmed the furnace and dominance moved from the heating loop to the cooling loop.
questions.rule: Dominance can shift with conditions.
questions.teaches: The thermostat showed shifting dominance when falling outside temperatures let the leak overwhelm the furnace, moving dominance from the heating loop to the cooling loop.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A stock has one reinforcing loop and one balancing loop. Which list names every behavior it can show?
options: Growth only, since the reinforcing loop always wins
Growth and decline only, since a stock cannot hold steady
Growth, decline and endless oscillation
Growth, decline, levelling off, or a sequence of these
optionExplain: The balancing loop can win or tie.
Equal strength gives levelling off.
Oscillation does not arise from this two-loop structure.
Right: these are the outcomes the author lists.
questions.explain: The stock grows, declines or levels depending on which loop is stronger, and may pass through them in sequence. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: A reinforcing loop plus a balancing loop on one stock gives growth, decline, levelling off, or a sequence of these.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Match each loop situation to the behavior it produces.
questions.explain: Each pairing follows the author's list of possible behaviors.
questions.rule: The dominant loop sets the behavior.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A subscription service gains members through referrals and loses them through cancellations. Cancellations rise above referrals. What follows?
options: Decline, because the balancing loop has come to dominate
Continued growth, since referrals reinforce themselves whatever else happens
Levelling off, since both loops operate
A sequence only, since two loops are present
optionExplain: Right: the stronger loop sets the behavior.
Referrals reinforce, but the balancing loop is now stronger.
Levelling needs equal strength, not both operating.
A sequence needs strengths to change; here one loop outweighs the other.
questions.explain: When the balancing loop outweighs the reinforcing loop, the stock falls.
questions.rule: Stronger balancing loop, decline.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A stock grows exponentially and then levels off. At the levelling point the two loops are ____ in strength.
questions.explain: Levelling off marks the moment the growth loop has weakened to match the balancing loop.
questions.rule: Plateau means equal strength.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A student says one reinforcing and one balancing loop can give endless oscillation. What does the author say?
options: The claim is right, since two loops can produce any pattern
For this simple structure, the listed behaviors are the only ones possible
The claim is right if the stock is large enough
The claim is wrong because stocks never change direction
optionExplain: She limits the behaviors for this structure.
Right: she states these are the only ones possible for it.
Size does not change the possible patterns.
Stocks can change direction; the sequence behavior shows it.
questions.explain: Meadows says these are the only behaviors possible for a simple system of one reinforcing and one balancing loop.
questions.rule: Know the whole repertoire.
questions.teaches: Growth, decline, levelling off and sequences of these are the only behaviors possible for a simple system of one reinforcing and one balancing loop.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A climate scenario assumes emissions fall 3% a year. Can anyone settle today whether that assumption is right?
options: Yes, by checking the model's equations for errors
Yes, by averaging expert opinions
No, because it is a guess about the future, which cannot be proved until it arrives
No, because scenarios are never useful
optionExplain: Equations check the model, not the future.
Opinions can differ, but averaging them is still a guess about the future.
Right: the future is inherently uncertain.
Scenarios are useful; the point is that the input cannot be proved.
questions.explain: Whatever the driving factors will do is uncertain, so the card next says how to use scenarios.
questions.rule: Treat the future of the driving factors as an uncertain guess, test several scenarios, and judge for yourself which deserve to be taken seriously.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Meadows' first question for testing a model asks whether the ____ factors are likely to unfold this way.
questions.explain: Driving factors are the variables, such as fertility and mortality, that move the stock.
questions.rule: The first question is about the drivers.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A budget assumes sales will rise 10% every year. According to the author, how should a reader treat this?
options: As a fact, because a budget is written by experts
As worthless, because the future cannot be known
As correct if the arithmetic is right
As a guess to test against other growth paths, then judge which deserves belief
optionExplain: The future cannot be established as fact by authority.
Scenarios are still useful for exploring what would happen.
Correct arithmetic does not make the assumption true.
Right: test several scenarios and decide which to take seriously.
questions.explain: Run several paths and judge which one might really be possible.
questions.rule: Test several scenarios, then judge.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.rule: Scenarios explore; they do not prove.
questions.q: True or false: Running the model with three different birth-rate paths shows which path will actually occur.
questions.explain: Scenario runs show what would happen under each path; they cannot say which path will occur.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A reader says that because the first question cannot be answered factually, the scenario is worthless. What is wrong with this?
options: The reader is right, since unprovable claims cannot be used in any analysis
Scenarios still show what would happen under different driver paths
The question can be answered factually after all
Only the second question matters, so the first is dropped
optionExplain: The author uses the scenarios to explore consequences.
Right: exploring possibilities is a purpose of systems analysis.
She says it cannot until the future happens.
All three questions are part of testing a model.
questions.explain: The uncertain future does not stop the analysis from testing a range of paths.
questions.rule: Uncertain inputs still support exploration.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A modeller says her model predicts the 2050 population. What does the author say dynamic systems studies are usually designed to do?
options: Predict exactly what will happen to the stock
Prove the driving factors will remain constant
Explore what would happen if driving factors unfold in a range of ways
Replace judgement with calculation
optionExplain: She says they are usually not designed to predict.
The factors are not assumed constant; they are varied.
Right: the studies explore rather than predict.
She says you must be the judge of the scenarios.
questions.explain: Meadows says dynamic systems studies usually are not designed to predict what will happen, but to explore what would happen if a number of driving factors unfold in a range of different ways.
questions.rule: Use models to explore, not to predict.
questions.teaches: Dynamic systems studies usually are not designed to predict what will happen; they explore what would happen if a number of driving factors unfold in different ways.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: What should decide whether a model of a population is useful, according to the author?
options: Whether the birth and death rates it uses turn out to be correct
Whether it predicts next year's exact population
Whether it uses as many variables as possible
Whether it responds to changes in birth and death rates with a realistic pattern of behavior
optionExplain: Nobody can know the future rates, so this cannot be the test.
She says such studies usually do not aim to predict.
Complexity is not the test of utility.
Right: the pattern of response is the test.
questions.explain: A model is useful if its reactions have the right pattern. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Judge a model by whether it responds to its inputs with a realistic pattern of behavior, not by whether the scenarios come true.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says model utility depends mainly on whether its driving scenarios are realistic.
questions.explain: She says utility depends not on whether the driving scenarios are realistic, since no one can know that, but on whether the model responds with a realistic pattern of behavior.
questions.rule: Pattern of response, not scenario realism.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A flu model grows when infections beat recoveries and shrinks otherwise, with counts 30% off. How does the author's test rate it?
options: Useful, because the pattern of behavior is realistic even though the numbers are off
Useless, because its numbers are wrong
Useful only if the counts are corrected first
Useless, because flu cannot be modelled by loops
optionExplain: Right: the pattern is what matters.
The author accepts numbers being off if the pattern is right.
The test concerns pattern, not corrected counts.
The reasoning applies to any system whose loops are captured.
questions.explain: The population model has the same property: wrong numbers, realistic behavior.
questions.rule: Pattern first, numbers second.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: The second question asks how good the ____ is: does it capture the inherent dynamics of the system?
questions.explain: It is the question about the model, as distinct from the scenario.
questions.rule: The second question tests the model itself.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A critic says the model is worthless because its numbers are off. What does the author's reasoning say about this?
options: The critic is right, since numbers define a model
Off numbers do not matter if the basic behavior pattern is realistic
The numbers matter, but only for populations
Numbers are irrelevant, so any model is acceptable as long as it looks plausible
optionExplain: She treats the pattern as the test.
Right: she says the numbers are off but the behavior is realistic.
Nothing limits the test to populations; the test is whether the pattern of behavior is realistic.
The pattern of behavior must still be realistic.
questions.explain: The model passes on pattern even where the figures are inexact.
questions.rule: Pattern of behavior is the test.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: What does the author say a more detailed population model would add to her simple one?
options: Exact future birth rates
A removal of the balancing loop
Separate age groups
A guarantee that its numbers are correct
optionExplain: Future rates cannot be known, so no model can add them.
The balancing loop is part of any population structure.
Right: she says a more detailed model would distinguish age groups.
She does not claim a more detailed model guarantees numbers.
questions.explain: She calls the population model very simple and says a more detailed one would distinguish age groups, while the basic pattern would stay realistic.
questions.rule: Detail refines the model; the pattern is what tests it.
questions.teaches: A more detailed population model would distinguish age groups.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A population model treats the birth rate as an outside input. Which question exposes a possible weakness?
options: Is the model written in a clear style?
Are the numbers in the model printed to enough decimal places?
Does the model start at the present year?
Does population size feed back to influence the birth rate?
optionExplain: Style does not test whether the input is independent.
Precision does not test the boundary.
The start year does not address what drives the birth rate.
Right: if it does, the birth rate is inside the system.
questions.explain: If population influences the birth rate, the rate is not independent. The card next states the question.
questions.rule: Ask what drives the model's driving factors, and check whether they are really outside the system or part of it.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: The third question about a model is a question about system ____.
questions.explain: It asks whether the driving factors are outside the system or embedded in it.
questions.rule: The third question is about boundaries.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A traffic model treats the number of cars as an outside input. Which check follows the author's third question?
options: Whether congestion itself changes how many people choose to drive
Whether cars are painted in different colors
Whether the model has more than two variables
Whether the input is typed into the model as a round number or a decimal
optionExplain: Right: if so, the input is driven from inside the system.
This has nothing to do with the boundary.
The count of variables does not test independence.
Typing format does not test independence.
questions.explain: The check is whether the driving factor is also pushed around by the system's own behavior.
questions.rule: Look for feedback onto the drivers.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.rule: Fixed drivers can hide loops.
questions.q: True or false: A model that fixes a birth rate which really falls as population grows leaves out a balancing feedback loop.
questions.explain: A rate that responds to population size is part of a balancing loop, which a fixed input leaves out.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Which claim about fertility and mortality does the author reject?
options: They are influenced by economics, the environment and social trends
They are affected at least in part by the size of the population
They are independent of everything else in the system
They are driven by feedback loops of their own
optionExplain: She lists these as influences.
She says some of their loops are affected by population size.
Right: she says they are governed by feedback loops too.
She says fertility and mortality are driven by feedback loops of their own, so this claim is hers.
questions.explain: Treating them as independent ignores loops that connect them to the rest of the system.
questions.rule: Drivers are usually inside a larger system.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Which part of the larger system does Meadows say is an important influence on population?
options: The weather, which has the same structure
The thermostat, which regulates population
The inventory of cars, which has the same structure
The economy, which has the same kind of reinforcing-plus-balancing structure
optionExplain: She does not name the weather.
The thermostat is a separate example.
Inventory is a later example and not the piece she names here.
Right: she introduces the economy as the piece that affects population.
questions.explain: She names the economy as one important piece of the larger system that affects population, and says it has the same structure as population.
questions.rule: Look to the economy as a driver.
questions.teaches: One important piece of the larger system that affects population is the economy, which is itself a reinforcing-loop-plus-balancing-loop system.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: In the capital system, which population quantity corresponds to the share of output a society invests?
options: Fertility
Mortality
Population size
Life expectancy
optionExplain: Right: investment fraction is the counterpart of fertility.
Mortality corresponds to the rate at which capital is retired.
Size corresponds to the capital stock, not to a rate.
Life expectancy relates to capital lifetime, not to the investment share.
questions.explain: Investment is capital's way of reproducing. The card next sets out the full match.
questions.rule: Capital has a reinforcing loop of investing output, like births, and a balancing loop of depreciation, like deaths.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Match each part of the population system to its counterpart in the capital system.
pairs: Fraction retired each year, set by average lifetime
questions.explain: Capital has the same reinforcing-plus-balancing structure as population.
questions.rule: Births match investment; deaths match depreciation.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A bike-share company buys new bikes from fare income while bikes wear out. Which parts match births and deaths?
options: Fares are the deaths loop, since income leaves customers
Buying bikes from income is the births loop; bikes wearing out is the deaths loop
Wearing out is the births loop, since bikes are replaced
Neither applies, since bikes are not people
optionExplain: Fare income feeds the investment, so it supports the births loop.
Right: the same two-loop structure applies.
Wearing out removes capital, so it matches deaths.
The author says the match is in structure, not appearance.
questions.explain: Output invested in new capital is reinforcing; depreciation is balancing.
questions.rule: Invest to grow; depreciate to shrink.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.rule: Invest more, grow faster.
questions.q: True or false: A society that invests a larger fraction of its output strengthens the loop that grows its capital.
questions.explain: The greater the fraction invested, the faster the capital stock grows.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A student says depreciation is a reinforcing loop because capital keeps declining. What is the error?
options: Depreciation is reinforcing but limited by the amount of investment
Depreciation is not a loop, only a fixed outflow
Declining always means reinforcing
Depreciation is balancing: more capital means more wearing out, which pulls capital down
optionExplain: It is balancing; investment is the reinforcing loop.
It depends on the amount of capital, so it is a loop.
Type depends on how the loop acts on itself, not on direction alone.
Right: more stock leads to more loss, a balancing relationship.
questions.explain: Depreciation scales with the capital stock, which makes it a balancing loop like deaths.
questions.rule: More stock, more loss: balancing.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Which historical pattern does Meadows say world capital has followed, like world population?
options: Dominance by its reinforcing loop, with exponential growth
Dominance by its balancing loop, with steady decline
Equilibrium, with births balancing deaths
Oscillation, with long cycles of boom and bust
optionExplain: Right: she says over recent history world capital has been growing exponentially.
She says capital has been growing, not declining.
She describes growth, not equilibrium.
She does not describe world capital as oscillating here.
questions.explain: She states that over recent history world capital, like world population, has been dominated by its reinforcing loop and has been growing exponentially.
questions.rule: Both stocks have been dominated by growth loops.
questions.teaches: Over recent history world capital, like world population, has been dominated by its reinforcing loop and has been growing exponentially.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Two economies invest the same share of output with the same efficiency, but one has longer-lived machines. Which grows faster?
options: The one with shorter-lived machines, since it replaces machines more often
The one with longer-lived machines
Neither, because only investment affects growth
They grow equally, since the investment shares are equal
optionExplain: Replacement is a cost; it drains the stock.
Right: a longer lifetime means a smaller fraction retired.
Depreciation also affects growth.
Their depreciation differs, so growth differs.
questions.explain: A longer lifetime lowers depreciation, so capital grows faster. The card next explains.
questions.rule: With investment fraction and efficiency fixed, capital declines, holds or grows as its lifetime is shorter than, equal to or longer than the break-even lifetime.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: If capital's lifetime is too short for investment to keep up with depreciation, the economy slowly ____.
questions.explain: Capital wears out faster than it is replaced.
questions.rule: Short lifetime, decline.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Investment adds a tenth of capital each year (output one quarter of capital, 40 percent invested). Lifetime is 8 years. What follows?
options: Capital grows, since 8 is a short lifetime
Capital holds steady, since 8 is close to 10
Capital declines, since an eighth is retired each year but only a tenth is added
Capital grows, since 40 percent is a large share
optionExplain: A short lifetime means faster retirement, which reduces growth.
Only equality of a tenth and the retired fraction would hold it steady.
Right: depreciation outruns investment.
The large share is already counted in the tenth added.
questions.explain: An eighth retired is more than a tenth added, so the stock falls. This is our arithmetic using the book's logic.
questions.rule: Compare the fraction added with the fraction retired.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.rule: Longer lifetime, bigger net gain.
questions.q: True or false: With a tenth of capital added each year, a 20-year lifetime lets capital grow.
questions.explain: A twentieth is retired while a tenth is added, so the net gain is positive. This is our arithmetic using the book's logic.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A student says longer-lived capital wears out more, so the economy declines. What is the correction?
options: Longer lifetime means a smaller fraction must be retired each year, so growth is faster
Longer lifetime raises output, which then falls
Capital with a long lifetime cannot be replaced
The student is right if the investment share is high enough to matter
optionExplain: Right: lifetime and depreciation rate move in opposite directions.
Output is not what changes here; the retired fraction is.
Replacement is a smaller burden, not an impossible one.
The effect of lifetime does not reverse with the share.
questions.explain: A long lifetime lowers the retirement fraction, which favors growth.
questions.rule: Longer life, less retired.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A firm wants its stock of skilled staff to grow without raising hiring. Which approach fits the principle in the book?
options: Raise the target headcount instead
Reduce the rate at which staff leave
Ask each leaver to stay a week longer
Stop counting departures in the model
optionExplain: A higher target does not change either flow.
Right: you can grow a stock by decreasing its outflow as well as increasing its inflow.
Lengthening notice delays exit but does not change the rate afterwards.
Hiding a flow does not change it.
questions.explain: Meadows notes that this is a principle already met earlier: you can make a stock grow by decreasing its outflow rate as well as by increasing its inflow rate.
questions.rule: Cut outflow to grow a stock.
questions.teaches: You can make a stock grow by decreasing its outflow rate as well as by increasing its inflow rate.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: According to the author, what effect does a richer economy usually have on a population's death and birth rates?
options: It raises both, since there is more to live on
It lowers deaths and raises births
It lowers both, through better health care and other changes
It has no effect, since populations follow their own loops of births and deaths
optionExplain: The author says the usual effects are lower rates.
She says birth rates are usually lower too.
Right: richer economies usually have lower death and birth rates.
She states output feeds back to population in several ways.
questions.explain: Output feeds back to population in many ways. The card next links the two structures.
questions.rule: A long-term economic model should link population and capital, because each feeds back on the other.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: True or false: Population affects the economy only by supplying labor.
questions.explain: Population also increases demands on consumption, which lowers the investment fraction.
questions.rule: Population works through labor and through consumption.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A national model keeps population fixed while capital grows. Which link does the author's reasoning say is missing?
options: Feedback from the thermostat to capital
A link from capital lifetime to the weather
A link from the interest rate to itself
Feedback from output to population, and from population to investment and labor
optionExplain: The thermostat is not part of this system.
Nothing in the text connects capital lifetime to the weather; the missing links are between population and capital.
The missing links are between population and capital.
Right: the two structures affect each other in both directions.
questions.explain: A model with only one direction misses loops that connect the stocks.
questions.rule: Link both ways.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.rule: Consumption crowds out investment.
questions.q: If a larger population raises demands for consumption, the investment fraction ____.
questions.explain: More output is consumed, leaving less to invest.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A student says richer economies have higher birth rates, so output feeds population growth. What is wrong?
options: Richer economies have higher death rates, which offsets the birth effect
The author says a richer economy usually has a lower birth rate
Output does not feed back to population at all
The student is right, since births rise with wealth
optionExplain: She says richer economies usually have lower death rates.
Right: she states the reverse.
She lists several ways it does.
This contradicts the text: she says a richer economy usually has a lower birth rate.
questions.explain: The usual effect of a richer economy is a lower birth rate.
questions.rule: Check the direction of each link.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: What does the author call the central question of economic development?
options: How to make population stop growing altogether
How to lengthen capital lifetime to infinity
How to keep capital accumulation from growing more slowly than population, so people get richer
How to measure output in a single number
optionExplain: The question concerns the relative growth of the two loops.
Lifetime is one factor, not the central question.
Right: capital must outgrow population for people to get richer.
Measurement is not the question she names.
questions.explain: She says the central question is how to keep the reinforcing loop of capital accumulation from growing more slowly than the reinforcing loop of population growth, so that people get richer instead of poorer.
questions.rule: Capital must outgrow population.
questions.teaches: The central question of economic development is how to keep capital accumulation from growing more slowly than population growth, so people get richer instead of poorer.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: What do a population and an industrial economy share, despite looking very different?
options: The same people and the same buildings
The same outside environment and inputs
The same numerical rates of growth
A stock governed by a reinforcing growth loop and a balancing loop
optionExplain: They are different entities; what they share is structure.
Their environments differ; what a population and an industrial economy share is feedback structure.
The numbers differ; the structure is what matches.
Right: they share feedback structure.
questions.explain: They share feedback structure. The card next states the general point.
questions.rule: Systems with similar feedback structures produce similar behavior, however different they look.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Systems with similar feedback structures produce similar dynamic ____.
questions.explain: This is the insight that lets one zoo animal teach about another.
questions.rule: Same structure, similar behavior.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A hot pizza cools on a counter. Which other process in the chapter shares its feedback structure?
options: A warmed room cooling, since each declines through a balancing loop
A population growing exponentially, since both change over a long period of time
A furnace running at full output, since both involve heat
A fishing fleet expanding, since both involve profit
optionExplain: Right: the author groups cooling things with decaying and aging things.
Growth comes from a reinforcing loop, not a balancing one.
Heat is not the shared feature; the loop type is.
This is a growth structure, unlike cooling.
questions.explain: Cooling, decay and dying-off all follow a balancing loop pulling a stock toward a lower level.
questions.rule: Match by loop, not by material.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Sort each process by the loop that drives it.

items.t: A coffee cup cooling
A radioactive substance decaying
Steel mills wearing out
Births raising a population
Reinvested output building more capital
A warmed room cooling

questions.explain: Cooling, decay and wearing out are balancing declines; births and reinvestment are reinforcing growth.
questions.rule: Classify by loop.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: A student says populations and factories look so different that they must behave differently. What is the author's reply?
options: The student is right, since structure has no role in deciding how systems behave
Looks do not matter; similar feedback structures produce similar behavior
They behave alike only because both involve people
They behave alike only if their numbers are equal
optionExplain: She says structure is the central insight.
Right: appearance is not what decides behavior.
Factories do not involve people in the way populations do.
Numbers need not match for patterns to match.
questions.explain: Outward appearance is irrelevant to the pattern; structure is what counts.
questions.rule: Structure beats appearance.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: What does Meadows say a population and an industrial economy have in common that lets both grow exponentially?
options: Both are limited by their environment from the start
Both are driven by the same outside planner
Both can reproduce themselves out of themselves
Both have a fixed number of members
optionExplain: Limits come later in the chapter and are not what makes them grow.
The text offers no such planner.
Right: self-reproduction drives the reinforcing loop.
Their stocks grow, so numbers are not fixed.
questions.explain: She says a population is nothing like an industrial economy, except that both can reproduce themselves out of themselves and thus grow exponentially, and both age and die.
questions.rule: Self-reproduction drives growth.
questions.teaches: A population and an industrial economy are alike in that both can reproduce themselves out of themselves and thus grow exponentially.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A dealer keeps enough stock for ten days of sales. Sales rise. What happens to her desired inventory?
options: It stays the same, because ten days is a fixed target for the dealer
It falls, because faster sales empty the lot sooner
It rises only after sales have stopped rising
It rises, because ten days of coverage now means more cars
optionExplain: The target is days of coverage, so the number of cars moves with sales.
Faster sales raise the cars needed for ten days, not lower them.
Desired inventory follows perceived sales as they rise.
Right: coverage is tied to the sales rate.
questions.explain: Desired inventory is defined as ten days of sales, so it moves with the sales rate. The card next shows the loops.
questions.rule: Inventory is held by two competing balancing loops: sales drain it and orders for deliveries refill it.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: True or false: The dealership model has two competing balancing loops, one through sales and one through deliveries.
questions.explain: Sales drain the stock and orders refill it, like the thermostat.
questions.rule: Drain loop plus resupply loop.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A bakery holds flour for four days of baking and orders when stock falls short. Which loops match the dealership's?
options: Baking drains the flour, and orders for deliveries resupply it, two competing balancing loops
Baking is reinforcing because more bread needs more flour
Only one loop acts, because orders are not feedback
Two reinforcing loops push the flour up and down
optionExplain: Right: a drain loop and a resupply loop.
More use drains stock; it does not reinforce the stock.
Orders respond to the gap, so they form a loop.
Both loops are goal-seeking, so they are balancing.
questions.explain: The structure is the thermostat's: use drains the stock and ordering refills it.
questions.rule: Look for drain and resupply.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: If perceived sales rise, the dealer's desired inventory will ____.
questions.explain: Ten days of coverage at a higher sales rate means more cars.
questions.rule: Higher sales, higher desired inventory.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Which description of the dealer's model is wrong?
options: Higher sales raise perceived sales and the gap to desired inventory
Higher sales lead directly to lower orders, which refill the lot
Higher orders bring more deliveries and raise inventory
The model is a version of the thermostat structure
optionExplain: This follows the model: higher sales raise perceived sales and widen the gap to desired inventory.
Right: higher sales lead to higher perceived sales and higher orders.
This follows the model: higher orders bring more deliveries and raise inventory.
She describes the dealer's model as a version of the thermostat structure, so this is accurate.
questions.explain: Orders rise when the gap to desired inventory widens after sales rise.
questions.rule: Higher sales, higher orders.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Why does the dealer need to hold inventory at all, according to the author?
options: Cars lose value if delivered too quickly
Customers prefer to see a large display lot
Daily purchases are unpredictable, and deliveries from suppliers may be delayed
Factories cannot produce fewer cars than are sold
optionExplain: The author gives no such reason.
The reasons given concern timing, not display.
Right: both reasons call for a buffer.
The text does not say factories cannot produce fewer cars; the reason she gives is unpredictable purchases and delayed deliveries.
questions.explain: She needs inventory because deliveries and purchases do not match perfectly each day, customers are unpredictable, and she wants a buffer in case deliveries are delayed.
questions.rule: A buffer absorbs mismatch in timing.
questions.teaches: The dealer holds inventory because daily purchases are unpredictable and because deliveries from suppliers may be delayed occasionally.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A shop orders stock based on the average of the last five days of sales. What is that averaging?
options: A delivery delay in the goods arriving
A response delay in how much is ordered
A storage delay in how long goods sit
A perception delay in the information reaching the decision
optionExplain: Delivery is about the time goods take to arrive.
Response concerns how much of the gap is closed at once.
Storage is not one of the three delays.
Right: the decision uses past sales rather than the latest.
questions.explain: Averaging over past days slows the information. The card next names all three delays.
questions.rule: Name each delay in a loop: how long it takes to perceive a change, to respond to it and to deliver the result.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Match each delay to what it means for the dealer.
pairs: Averaging sales over the past five days
Making up one third of a shortfall with each order
Five days from order to arrival at the dealership
questions.explain: Each delay sits at a different point in the loop: information, decision, goods.
questions.rule: Perception, response, delivery.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A restaurant owner waits a week of low bookings before cutting staff, then cuts a few shifts at a time. Which delays are these?
options: A perception delay, then a response delay
Two delivery delays, since staff are delivered
A response delay, then a perception delay
Neither, because the owner is not a dealer
optionExplain: Right: waiting for a trend is perception; partial cuts are response.
Delivery concerns goods arriving after an order.
The order is reversed: waiting for a trend is perception.
The delays apply to any decision loop.
questions.explain: Waiting to be sure of a trend is perception; adjusting in small steps is response.
questions.rule: Information first, then action.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Making up the whole shortfall in a single order instead of a third at a time would ____ the response delay.
questions.explain: Closing the gap at once leaves almost no delay in the response.
questions.rule: Bigger steps, shorter response delay.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A student says the delivery delay is the time the dealer takes to decide. What is the correction?
options: It is the time the dealer takes to average the past sales over several days
It is the time for the factory to receive, process and deliver an order
It is the time the dealer takes to order a third
It is the time customers take to buy
optionExplain: Averaging past sales over several days is the perception delay, not the delivery delay.
Right: it is the supplier's time, not the dealer's.
Taking time to order a third of the shortfall is the response delay, not the delivery delay.
Nothing in the text describes customer purchase time as one of the three delays.
questions.explain: The delivery delay is in the physical process outside the dealer's decisions.
questions.rule: Delivery belongs to the supplier.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Why does the dealer average sales over five days instead of reacting to each day's figure?
options: Because she cannot see daily sales
Because the factory requires five days' notice before any order is processed
To sort real trends from temporary dips and spikes
Because averages are always more accurate
optionExplain: The text says the delay is intentional, not forced.
The factory's notice period would be a delivery delay; the five-day average is the dealer's perception delay.
Right: the perception delay is intentional.
The reason is to separate trends from blips.
questions.explain: The perception delay is intentional: the dealer does not react to every blip in sales and averages to sort real trends from temporary dips and spikes.
questions.rule: Averaging trades speed for steadiness.
questions.teaches: The dealer's perception delay is intentional: she averages sales to sort real trends from temporary dips and spikes.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A balancing loop acts on its stock only after a long delay. What pattern is most likely?
options: A smooth approach to the goal, as with no delay
Permanent growth away from the goal
A flat line, because the delay freezes the stock
Oscillation around the goal, as corrections overshoot and then reverse
optionExplain: A smooth approach is the pattern without delays.
Balancing loops pull toward the goal; delay makes them swing, not run away.
The stock keeps changing during a delay.
Right: delays cause corrections to arrive late and overshoot.
questions.explain: Late corrections overshoot and swing back. The card next shows it with the dealer.
questions.rule: A delay in a balancing feedback loop makes a system likely to oscillate.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: True or false: According to Meadows, the dealer's inventory oscillates because she is careless in her ordering.
questions.explain: She says it is not because the dealer is stupid but because she lacks timely information and faces physical delays.
questions.rule: Structure, not carelessness, causes the swings.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A bath mixer changes temperature only after a long wait, and the bather retunes the tap each time it feels wrong. What follows?
options: Hot and cold swings, as each correction arrives too late
A steady temperature, since the bather corrects constantly
Ever hotter water, since the bather keeps turning up
No change, since the mixer is the cause
optionExplain: Right: delayed feedback causes oscillation.
Constant correction on late information produces swings.
Corrections go both ways, so swings reverse.
The mixer's delay is exactly what creates the swings.
questions.explain: Corrections made on late information overshoot, then reverse.
questions.rule: Late feedback, swinging response.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Put the dealer's oscillation in the order it unfolds after a step up in sales.
items: Sales step up and inventory drops
The dealer, sure the rise will last, orders more cars
The large volume of orders arrives and inventory more than recovers
The dealer cuts back orders but earlier high orders still arrive
She orders too little and inventory gets too low again
questions.explain: The cycle comes from acting on delayed information with delayed results.
questions.rule: Each correction overshoots because of delay.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Which conclusion from the oscillation is mistaken?
options: She lacks timely information about what customers will do
The dealer is irrational
Physical delays stop her orders from acting at once
A delay in a balancing loop makes oscillation likely
optionExplain: The author gives lack of timely information as a cause of the oscillation, so this conclusion is sound.
Right: the oscillation comes from delays, not from foolish choices.
The author gives physical delays as a cause, so this conclusion is sound.
This is the author's rule: a delay in a balancing loop makes oscillation likely.
questions.explain: She is struggling in a system in which timely information is not available.
questions.rule: Look at structure before blaming people.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Which everyday experience does Meadows use to show oscillation caused by a long response delay?
options: A kettle that switches itself off at a set temperature once the water boils
A car idling at a traffic light
A shower with a long pipe between the mixer and the showerhead
A balloon slowly losing its air
optionExplain: A kettle has no long delay between action and result.
A car idling at a light is not her example of oscillation from a long response delay.
Right: the pipe delays the effect of each adjustment.
A slow leak is a draining flow, not an oscillation, and is not her example.
questions.explain: She suggests taking a shower where a very long pipe lies between the hot and cold mixer and the showerhead, and experiencing hot and cold oscillations because of a long response delay.
questions.rule: Long pipes give swinging showers.
questions.teaches: A shower with a very long pipe between the mixer and the showerhead gives hot and cold oscillations because of a long response delay.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A dealer's inventory swings badly. She makes her reaction to shortfalls faster. What is the most likely result?
options: The swings disappear, since she reacts sooner
Nothing changes, since delays are unaffected
The swings shrink a little, as with perception time
The swings get much worse
optionExplain: Reacting sooner on delayed information increases overshoot.
Her reaction time is one of the delays.
Perception change did little, and reaction change did much more harm.
Right: faster reaction overshoots more.
questions.explain: Faster reaction worsened the oscillation in the book's run. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A lever with a strong effect can worsen a system if you pull it the wrong way, so check the direction before acting.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Shortening the dealer's reaction time from three days to two made the oscillations much ____.
questions.explain: Acting faster made the oscillations worse, because the quick response pushed a strong lever in the wrong direction.
questions.rule: Faster reaction, worse swings.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A warehouse manager fixes stock swings by counting hourly instead of daily and correcting at once. What risk does the book's example warn of?
options: A strong lever pulled the wrong way can worsen the swings
None, since more information always lowers swings
The counts will be wrong, since hourly counts are noisy and incomplete
The warehouse will run out of space
optionExplain: Right: fast correction can intensify oscillation.
The dealer's faster response made things worse.
Noise is not the book's point; it is the direction of the lever.
Nothing in the example concerns warehouse space; the warning is about pulling a strong lever the wrong way.
questions.explain: Strong levers pulled in the wrong direction produce perverse results.
questions.rule: Check which way the lever should go.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.rule: Different delays, different effects.
questions.q: True or false: Shortening the perception delay from five days to two eliminated the oscillations.
questions.explain: Not much happened; if anything the oscillations were a bit worse.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A manager says high leverage means pulling the lever improves the system. What is the flaw?
options: High-leverage levers have no effect on systems
Wrong direction is impossible once a lever with strong effect has been chosen
A lever with strong effect can do harm if pulled in the wrong direction
Leverage only matters for physical levers
optionExplain: High-leverage levers have a strong effect on systems, so saying they have none is wrong.
The book shows a strong lever pulled the wrong way making things worse, so wrong direction is possible.
Right: leverage is strength of effect, not direction of benefit.
The author applies it to policies.
questions.explain: The dealer picked a lever that does matter and pulled it the wrong way.
questions.rule: Strong effects cut both ways.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A cafe owner cannot change how long her bakery takes to deliver. Which choices does the dealer's case suggest she examines?
options: Only the delivery delay, as it is the one that matters most in the system
No delays, as delays cannot be changed
Only the weather, as it affects deliveries
The delays she controls herself, such as how fast she reacts
optionExplain: The dealer could not change the factory delay and worked on her own.
The dealer could change her own perception and reaction times.
The weather is not in the case.
Right: the dealer also cannot change the factory's delay and works on her own.
questions.explain: The dealer says there is not much she can do about the factory's delivery delay, so she works on her own side: how fast she reacts.
questions.rule: Work on the delays you control.
questions.teaches: The dealer cannot do much about the delivery delay from the factory, so she changes the delays on her own side, such as how quickly she reacts.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A dealer's orders overshoot after every change in sales. Which adjustment is most likely to calm the swings?
options: Making up smaller parts of the shortfall over a longer time
Making up the whole shortfall in the next order
Averaging sales over fewer days
Doing nothing, as oscillation cannot be changed by the dealer's own choices
optionExplain: Right: a slower response damps the overshoot.
A bigger, faster correction raises overshoot.
The book shows this does little and may worsen swings.
The dealer damps it by changing a delay.
questions.explain: Slowing an overreaction calms the swings. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Slowing a response that overreacts can damp oscillations, so check the delays before speeding anything up.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: True or false: In the book, lengthening the dealer's response delay from three days to six greatly damped the oscillations.
questions.explain: She finds the new equilibrium fairly efficiently.
questions.rule: Longer response delay damped the swings.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A manager swings between too many and too few staff because she re-plans fully each week. Following the dealer's lesson, what might help?
