options: Closing the whole staffing gap every day of the week
Closing only part of the staffing gap each week
Dropping the target headcount
Ignoring the gap
optionExplain: This shortens the response and risks worse swings.
Right: smaller partial adjustments lengthen the response and damp swings.
The problem is the speed of adjustment, not the target.
Ignoring the gap means no balancing loop at all.
questions.explain: A slower response avoids overreacting to delayed information.
questions.rule: Adjust in smaller steps.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.rule: Slower response, calmer swings.
questions.q: With a six-day response delay, the oscillations in inventory are greatly ____.
questions.explain: A longer response delay damps the overshoot, and the system finds its new equilibrium fairly efficiently.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A reader concludes that lengthening any delay damps oscillations in every system. What does the author say instead?
options: Longer delays always increase oscillations
Delays have no effect on behavior
Only delivery delays matter
The effect depends on the type of delay and on the other delays in the system
optionExplain: The six-day response damped them.
She says they are strong determinants.
She names several delays as important.
Right: changing a delay may or may not change the behavior much.
questions.explain: Changing a delay may or may not make a large change.
questions.rule: No delay rule is universal.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Which delay does the author call the most important in the dealer's system, even though she cannot control it?
options: The delivery delay from the factory
The perception delay in averaging sales
The response delay in making up shortfalls
A delay in customers deciding to buy
optionExplain: Right: she says it is the most important, but even without control the dealer can learn to manage inventory well.
The perception delay is under the dealer's control, so it is not the delay she cannot control.
The response delay is under the dealer's control, so it is not the one she cannot control.
A customer-side delay in deciding to buy is not one of the three delays she names.
questions.explain: Meadows says the most important delay is the one not under the dealer's direct control, the delivery delay from the factory, yet she can still learn to manage inventory quite well.
questions.rule: Manage what you cannot change.
questions.teaches: The most important delay in the dealer's system is the delivery delay from the factory, which she does not control, but she can still manage inventory quite well.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Which explanation of business cycles does Meadows favour?
options: The decisions of presidents and governments
Linked industries with delayed feedback, amplified by reinforcing loops
Random shocks with no structure behind them
Consumers changing tastes at fixed intervals
optionExplain: She says the cycles do not come from presidents.
Right: structure with delays is the cause she names.
She attributes them to system structure.
She does not offer such a cause.
questions.explain: She traces the cycles to structure. The card next explains it.
questions.rule: Business cycles arise mainly from delayed balancing loops, amplified by reinforcing loops, across linked industries, not from leaders.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says business cycles come mainly from presidents.
questions.explain: She says they do not come from presidents, although presidents can ease or intensify them.
questions.rule: Cycles come from structure.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A factory cuts output, so it hires fewer workers, who then buy fewer cars, so the factory cuts output again. Which loop type is this?
options: A balancing loop that restores production after each cut in output
A delay with no loop
A reinforcing loop, working in the downward direction
A thermostat loop
optionExplain: It pushes production further from its starting level.
The chain feeds back to production, so it is a loop.
Right: less production, fewer jobs, fewer sales, less production.
A thermostat loop returns to a goal; this one moves away.
questions.explain: The jobs-and-sales link reinforces in both directions.
questions.rule: Reinforcing loops work both ways.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.rule: Speculators amplify.
questions.q: Speculators who trade auto shares on recent performance add another ____ loop to the system.
questions.explain: A production upsurge lifts share prices and vice versa, which adds to the swings.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Which view contradicts the author on business cycles?
options: A president's policies are the primary cause of every cycle
Presidents can ease or intensify the optimism of upturns
Interconnected industries respond to each other through delays
Multipliers and speculators amplify the swings
optionExplain: Right: she says cycles do not come from presidents.
She says presidents can ease or intensify the mood of upturns, so this does not contradict her.
Interconnected industries responding to each other through delays is her account of cycles.
Multipliers and speculators amplifying swings is part of her account of cycles.
questions.explain: The structure is the primary cause; leaders affect only mood and degree.
questions.rule: Structure first, leaders second.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: How does the author describe economies in general?
options: Simple systems with a single stock and no delays
Extremely complex systems full of balancing loops with delays, and inherently oscillatory
Stable systems that oscillate only after outside shocks
Systems with reinforcing loops only
optionExplain: She calls them extremely complex.
Right: delays in balancing loops make them oscillate.
She calls them inherently oscillatory.
She says they are full of balancing loops with delays.
questions.explain: She concludes that economies are extremely complex systems, full of balancing feedback loops with delays, and inherently oscillatory.
questions.rule: Economies oscillate by structure.
questions.teaches: Economies are extremely complex systems full of balancing feedback loops with delays, and they are inherently oscillatory.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A new product's sales have grown fast for years. What does the limits-to-growth view say about its future?
options: Sales will keep growing at the same pace for as long as customer demand stays high enough
Sales will stop only if the company decides to stop growing
A balancing loop exists, such as market saturation, even if it does not yet dominate
No limit exists until sales actually begin to fall
optionExplain: Sustained growth in a finite environment cannot continue.
The constraint is part of the system, not a company choice.
Right: no physical system grows forever.
A limit can exist before it dominates.
questions.explain: A finite environment means a constraint is present before it shows. The card next explains.
questions.rule: In a physical, exponentially growing system there must be at least one reinforcing loop driving growth and at least one balancing loop constraining it.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: True or false: According to Meadows, a physical system can grow exponentially forever if it has a strong enough reinforcing loop.
questions.explain: No physical system can grow forever in a finite environment, so there must be a constraining balancing loop.
questions.rule: Growth needs a limit loop to be present.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A rumor spreads as each person who hears it tells others. What does the limits-to-growth view predict will eventually constrain it?
options: The reinforcing loop of telling others
The speed at which people can talk
Nothing, since a rumor is not a physical thing and cannot be limited
Running out of people who have not yet heard it
optionExplain: This is the growth driver, not the constraint.
Speed matters, but the eventual constraint is the pool of listeners.
The book lists a rumor among the growing entities with limits.
Right: a rumor, like a virus, runs out of susceptible people.
questions.explain: A growing rumor depletes its pool of people who have not heard it.
questions.rule: Find the pool being used up.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: A virus spreading through a population will eventually run out of ____ people to infect.
questions.explain: The pool of susceptible people limits the epidemic.
questions.rule: Growth uses up what it feeds on.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Which statement misreads the limits-to-growth idea?
options: A system has a constraint only once its growth has visibly slowed
A growing entity needs a reinforcing loop to drive its growth in the first place
A finite environment sets a limit to growth
A hot product will eventually saturate its market
optionExplain: Right: the constraining loop exists even before it dominates.
A growing entity needs a reinforcing loop to drive its growth, so this reading is accurate.
A finite environment sets a limit to growth, so this reading is accurate.
A hot product saturating its market is the book's example, so this reading is accurate.
questions.explain: The balancing loop is there from the start; dominance comes later.
questions.rule: A hidden limit is still a limit.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Meadows says the limits on a growing system may be temporary or permanent. What must eventually happen?
options: The system eventually finds a way to escape every limit for good, with no accommodation at all
Some accommodation: the system adjusts to the constraint, the constraint to the system, or both
The limit disappears once the system is large enough
The system stops existing
optionExplain: She says it may get around limits for a while, not forever.
Right: growth cannot continue unconstrained.
Size does not remove the limit.
Accommodation is not the same as disappearance.
questions.explain: She writes that the system may get around limits for a short or a long while, but eventually there must be an accommodation in which the system adjusts to the constraint, the constraint to the system, or both to each other.
questions.rule: Limits force an accommodation.
questions.teaches: Limits on growth may be temporary or permanent, but eventually the system adjusts to the constraint, the constraint to the system, or both to each other.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: An oil company's equipment lasts 20 years. What share of its capital stock is retired each year?
options: One tenth, or 10 percent
Twenty percent, since the lifetime is 20
One twentieth, or 5 percent
Nothing, since oil equipment does not wear out
optionExplain: 10 percent would match a 10-year lifetime.
The lifetime is a number of years, not a percentage.
Right: a 20-year lifetime retires 1/20 each year.
Depreciation applies to all capital.
questions.explain: A lifetime of L years retires one L-th of the stock each year. The card next sets out the company.
questions.rule: The oil company is a capital system: reinvested profit is the reinforcing loop, depreciation the balancing loop, and profit is income minus cost.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A 20-year capital lifetime means ____ percent of the capital stock is retired each year.
questions.explain: One twentieth of the stock wears out each year, which is 5 percent (our arithmetic from the 20-year lifetime).
questions.rule: Retirement fraction is one over lifetime.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A refinery's equipment lasts 25 years. What share of its stock is retired each year?
options: Five percent, as with the oil example
Twenty-five percent
Two and a half percent
Four percent
optionExplain: 5 percent matches a 20-year lifetime.
This reads the lifetime as a percentage.
This would need a 40-year lifetime.
Right: one twenty-fifth is 4 percent.
questions.explain: One twenty-fifth is 4 percent. This is our arithmetic using the book's rule.
questions.rule: Retirement is one over lifetime.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.rule: Profit limits investment.
questions.q: True or false: If profit is too small to fund 5 percent growth, the company invests whatever profit it can.
questions.explain: The goal is a limit on growth, and investment is capped by profit.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A student says the company invests exactly 5 percent whatever its profit. What is the error?
options: 5 percent is the depreciation rate, not a goal
5 percent is a goal; if profit is too small, it invests only what profit allows
The company invests more than the goal when profit is high
The company never invests, since oil is nonrenewable
optionExplain: It is both the depreciation share and the growth goal; the goal is limited by profit.
Right: the goal is limited by profit.
The text gives no rule that the company invests more than its goal when profit is high.
It invests profits to build capital.
questions.explain: The 5 percent is the growth goal, but investment is limited by profit: if profit is too small, the company invests only what profit allows.
questions.rule: Goals are capped by profit.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A company sells 1,000 barrels at 50 each, with 100 units of capital costing 20 each to operate. What is profit by the book's definitions?
options: 50,000, income alone
52,000, income plus cost
48,000, which is 50,000 income minus 2,000 cost
2,000, cost alone
optionExplain: Profit subtracts cost, so income alone of 50,000 overstates it.
Cost is subtracted from income, not added, so 52,000 is wrong.
Right: income is price times amount; cost is capital times operating cost per unit.
2,000 is the cost alone; profit is income minus cost.
questions.explain: The book defines income as price times amount extracted, and cost as capital times operating cost per unit of capital; profit is income minus cost. The figures here are ours.
questions.rule: Profit = price x amount minus capital x unit cost.
questions.teaches: Income is the price of oil times the amount extracted, and cost is capital times the operating cost per unit of capital.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: An oil field is being drained with no new oil entering. What happens to the effort needed per barrel as extraction continues?
options: It falls, since equipment becomes more experienced
It stays the same, since oil is oil
It falls, since the company has paid off its equipment
It rises, since the remaining oil is deeper, more dilute or under less pressure
optionExplain: The book says yield per unit of capital falls.
Remaining oil is harder to reach.
Depreciation is a separate matter from yield.
Right: the next barrel is harder to get.
questions.explain: With no input, depletion makes each barrel costlier. The card next shows the loop.
questions.rule: In a nonrenewable resource system, more capital speeds extraction, which depletes the stock and lowers yield per unit of capital, so profit and investment fall.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: Put the links of the depletion loop in order, starting with capital.
items: More capital
A higher extraction rate
A lower resource stock
A lower yield per unit of capital
Lower profit and investment, so slower capital growth
questions.explain: Each link follows from the previous one and closes the balancing loop on capital.
questions.rule: Capital depletes the resource that feeds its profit.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A gold mine's ore grade falls as the richest seams are mined. What happens to the profit per unit of equipment?
options: It falls, since each unit of equipment yields less gold
It rises, since less ore is left to handle
It stays the same, since the price of gold is fixed and so is the mine
It rises, since the mine is better known
optionExplain: Right: yield per unit of capital declines as the resource is depleted.
Handling is not the issue; yield per unit of capital falls.
With constant price, lower yield still lowers income.
Knowledge does not restore ore grade.
questions.explain: Lower yield with constant price and cost means lower income per unit of capital.
questions.rule: Depletion cuts yield.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: The lower the resource stock, the ____ the yield of resource per unit of capital.
questions.explain: Depletion makes the remaining resource harder to get.
questions.rule: Less resource, lower yield.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: Which description of the nonrenewable resource stock is wrong?
options: It has no input feeding it
It has an inflow that slows as extraction speeds up
Its next barrel is harder to get as more of the resource is extracted
Its depletion lowers the yield per unit of capital
optionExplain: The book says a nonrenewable stock has no input feeding it, so this description is accurate.
Right: a nonrenewable stock has no input.
This is the book's description.
The book's loop is that depletion lowers the yield per unit of capital, so this description is accurate.
questions.explain: The stock only drains; nothing refills it.
questions.rule: Nonrenewable means no inflow.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: Besides lowering capital efficiency, what else does the author say depletion feeds back into in the real world?
options: The price of oil only, with a different pattern of behavior as a result
The depreciation lifetime only
Operating cost, and the ensuing behavior is the same
Nothing else, since only yield matters
optionExplain: She says the pattern is the same.
Lifetime is not the channel she names.
Right: in the real world depletion acts through both, with the same pattern.
She says depletion feeds back through operating cost as well.
questions.explain: Meadows says she could assume depletion feeds back through operating cost as well as capital efficiency, and that in the real world it does both; either way the behavior pattern is the classic dynamics of depletion.
questions.rule: Different channels, same depletion pattern.
questions.teaches: In the real world depletion feeds back through operating cost as well as capital efficiency, and the behavior pattern is the same classic dynamics of depletion.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A deposit could supply a company's starting scale of operation for 200 years. When does extraction peak if capital grows exponentially?
options: At about 200 years, when the deposit is gone
At about 100 years, halfway through the supply
Never, since the deposit is so large
Far sooner, at about 40 years
optionExplain: Extraction rises faster than the starting scale, so it peaks sooner.
Exponential growth makes it earlier than the halfway mark.
The depletion loop eventually halts growth.
Right: exponential growth shortens the time.
questions.explain: A growing scale of operation uses the stock far faster than the starting scale suggests. The card next gives the numbers.
questions.rule: Exponential growth in extraction uses up a large deposit far sooner than its size suggests: a 200-year supply peaks near year 40, and by year 50 costs overwhelm income and the operation shuts down quickly.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: At 5 percent growth a year, capital and extraction double in about ____ years.
questions.explain: The book says capital and extraction double in the first 14 years.
questions.rule: 5 percent a year doubles in about 14 years.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A mine's extraction grows 5 percent a year from today's level. About how long until it doubles?
options: About 14 years
About 5 years
About 20 years
About 40 years, the time to the peak
optionExplain: Right: the book gives 14 years for 5 percent growth.
5 is the growth rate, not the doubling time.
20 is the equipment lifetime, not the doubling time.
40 is the time to the extraction peak.
questions.explain: Doubling at 5 percent a year takes about 14 years.
questions.rule: 5 percent doubles in about 14 years.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: By year 50 in the book's run, what has happened to the operation?
options: It is still growing, since 150 years of oil remain
Maintenance cost has overwhelmed income, so it shuts down and leaves the costly last oil in the ground
It continues at a steady level for 150 more years
It has exhausted the oil completely
optionExplain: The depletion loop has ended the growth.
Right: profits no longer keep investment ahead of depreciation.
The operation shuts down quickly.
The last, most expensive resource stays in the ground.
questions.explain: Cost outgrows income, profit fails to cover depreciation, and capital falls.
questions.rule: Costs end the boom before the oil does.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.rule: Growing use shortens a supply.
questions.q: True or false: With a 200-year supply, extraction keeps rising for about 200 years.
questions.explain: Exponential growth in extraction makes it peak near year 40.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: In the book's run, what is the state of capital and extraction after 28 years?
options: Capital has halved and extraction is rising
Capital and extraction have both quadrupled
Capital is unchanged and extraction has peaked
Capital has quadrupled but extraction is starting to lag because yield per unit of capital is falling
optionExplain: Capital has not halved: after two doublings it has quadrupled.
Extraction lags while capital quadruples.
Capital has quadrupled; the peak is near year 40.
Right: depletion begins to bite before the peak.
questions.explain: After 28 years, two doublings, capital has quadrupled while extraction is starting to lag because yield per unit of capital falls.
questions.rule: Capital outpaces extraction as yield falls.
questions.teaches: After 28 years the capital stock has quadrupled, but extraction is starting to lag because of falling yield per unit of capital.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A deposit turns out to be four times larger than thought, and extraction grows 5 percent a year. About how much later is the peak?
options: About 28 years, two doublings of 14 years each
About 400 years, four times as long
About 14 years, since only the size changed
About 100 years, since four times the oil would last far longer
optionExplain: Right: four times is two doublings.
Time to the peak does not scale with the size.
Each doubling adds about 14 years, and four times is two doublings.
The peak moves by only a few decades.
questions.explain: Each doubling of the resource adds one doubling time of the growth. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Each doubling of a nonrenewable resource delays the peak of exponentially growing extraction by only about one doubling time of the growth, here 14 years.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: Each doubling of the resource makes a difference of only about ____ years in the timing of the peak.
questions.explain: This equals the doubling time at 5 percent growth.
questions.rule: Each doubling adds about 14 years.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A city's water demand grows 5 percent a year, and a survey finds twice as much aquifer water. About how much longer before use peaks?
options: About twice as long, since there is twice as much water
About 14 years more
About 5 years more, matching the growth rate
No time at all, since demand is unchanged
optionExplain: Exponential growth makes the extra time much smaller.
Right: one doubling of the resource adds about one doubling time.
The doubling time, not the growth rate, sets the added time.
Extra water does delay the peak, by about 14 years.
questions.explain: The reasoning is the book's, applied to a new case; the numbers are ours.
questions.rule: One doubling of the stock adds one doubling time.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.rule: Count the doublings.
questions.q: True or false: Under the same growth, a resource eight times larger delays the peak by about 42 years.
questions.explain: Eight is three doublings, and each adds about 14 years. This is our arithmetic using the book's rule.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A planner says a resource twice as large will double the time before the peak. What is the error?
options: The peak moves by half as much, 7 years
The peak does not move at all
The planner is right if the deposit is deep
Exponential growth means the peak moves only about 14 years, not twice as far
optionExplain: The book gives 14 years per doubling.
The peak does move, by about 14 years per doubling of the resource.
Depth plays no role in this reasoning.
Right: growth swallows the extra stock quickly.
questions.explain: Doubling the stock buys one extra doubling time of growth, not double the lifetime.
questions.rule: Exponents shrink the gain.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: Whose lifetime does the author say is affected by the 14-year shift in the peak, besides profits?
options: Jobs and communities that depend on the extraction industry
Only the lifetime of the machinery
Only the lifetime of shareholders' investments in the oil company
Only the lifetime of the oil field's licence
optionExplain: Right: the shift matters for jobs and communities.
Machinery has a separate 20-year lifetime.
The author names jobs and communities.
No licence is mentioned; the lifetimes affected are those of jobs and communities.
questions.explain: She says each doubling shifts the peak by about 14 years, and likewise the lifetime of any jobs or communities dependent on the extraction industry.
questions.rule: Peak timing sets the lifetime of dependent communities.
questions.teaches: The 14-year shift in the peak also sets the lifetime of any jobs or communities dependent on the extraction industry.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A town depends on an oil field for jobs. Which two numbers does the author say matter most to its workers?
options: The price of oil and the size of the workforce
The size of the resource and the desired growth rate of capital
The age of the equipment and the number of owners of the company
The size of the resource alone
optionExplain: The author names resource size and capital growth rate.
Right: both together set the lifetime of jobs.
These are not the two numbers she names.
That is the key number only for someone seeking maximum rate of money.
questions.explain: A job's lifetime depends on how big the resource is and how fast capital grows. The card next explains.
questions.rule: How long a nonrenewable resource lasts depends on its size and on the growth rate of the capital extracting it: faster growth gives an earlier peak.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: True or false: In the book's graph, a 7 percent desired growth rate makes a 200-year supply peak within 40 years.
questions.explain: A higher reinvestment rate brings the peak sooner.
questions.rule: Faster growth, earlier peak.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A council wants a company's oil field to provide jobs for many decades. Which lever does the model point to?
options: Raise the reinvestment of profits
Lower the capital lifetime
Slow the company's desired growth rate of capital
Expect jobs to last as long as the deposit does, whatever the growth rate
optionExplain: Raising reinvestment of profits brings the peak sooner, not later.
The book does not say this stretches the peak.
Right: slower growth stretches out the peak.
Fast growth makes the deposit last far less than its nominal supply.
questions.explain: A lower growth goal trades speed for duration.
questions.rule: Slower capital growth, longer job lifetime.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.rule: More reinvestment, earlier peak.
questions.q: If a company raises the share of profits it reinvests, the peak of extraction comes ____.
questions.explain: More reinvestment means faster capital growth and an earlier peak.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A manager says the size of the resource is the only important number for everyone. What does the author say?
options: Size alone matters only if you want to extract at the maximum rate; workers also need the growth rate
Size does not matter at all
The growth rate alone matters for everyone
No number matters, since extraction is random
optionExplain: Right: workers care about the lifetime of their jobs.
Size is the key number for the maximum-rate view.
The growth rate alone is not what matters for everyone; size matters for those who want the maximum rate.
The author treats both numbers as important.
questions.explain: Which numbers matter depends on what you care about.
questions.rule: Goals decide which numbers matter.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: Beyond company profits, what does the author say the choice of growth rate affects?
options: Only the company's share price
The social and natural environments of the region
Only the price of oil worldwide and the profits of competing companies
Nothing outside the company
optionExplain: She names regional environments as well.
Right: she asks the reader to imagine these effects.
She says the effects are on the region.
She asks the reader to imagine wider effects.
questions.explain: After the graph she asks the reader to imagine the effects of a fast-growth choice not only on the profits of the company but on the social and natural environments of the region.
questions.rule: Growth choices have regional effects.
questions.teaches: A fast growth rate in extraction affects not only company profits but the social and natural environments of the region.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: Oil becomes scarce and its price rises steeply while demand holds firm. How does this affect the capital stock in the model?
options: It collapses sooner, since high prices reduce demand
It stops growing, since the resource is scarcer
It builds higher before it collapses
It stays the same, since price does not affect capital
optionExplain: Demand is assumed firm in the short term.
Higher profit keeps investment going.
Right: higher profits fund more investment.
Price changes profit, which funds capital.
questions.explain: Higher profits fund more investment, so capital grows larger. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Rising prices or falling costs let capital grow larger before it collapses, and the resource then runs out even faster.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: True or false: In the book, a rising oil price lets the capital stock grow higher before it collapses.
questions.explain: A higher price raises profit, which supports more investment, so the capital stock grows higher before it collapses.
questions.rule: Higher price, higher capital peak.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: Cyanide leaching lets a mine profit from old tailings by cutting operating cost. Which price scenario does this resemble?
options: A falling price, since both reduce the need for capital
A constant price, since the price did not change
No scenario, since technology is outside the model
A rising price, since both raise profit and let capital reach more costly resources
optionExplain: A falling price lowers profit; cheaper operation raises profit, like a rising price.
The effect on profit is the same as a rising price.
The author says technology acts like a price rise.
Right: lower costs and higher prices have the same effect.
questions.explain: Either route increases the profit per unit of capital.
questions.rule: Raise price or cut cost: same effect.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.rule: Taller peak, steeper fall.
questions.q: With a rising price, the resource is depleted ____ at the end than under a constant price.
questions.explain: A larger capital stock draws the resource down faster before it collapses.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: A commentator says rising prices save a depleting resource by slowing extraction. What is the error?
options: Higher prices cut demand to zero
Higher prices raise profit and investment, so extraction rises and depletion speeds up
Higher prices lower profit
The commentator is right if prices rise enough
optionExplain: The book assumes demand holds firm in the short term.
Right: higher price speeds the draw-down.
Higher prices raise profit, not lower it.
More profit pays for more capital, not less extraction.
questions.explain: A price rise funds more capital and faster extraction.
questions.rule: Price rises can hasten depletion.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: What do resource companies do, according to the author, well before depletion makes capital less efficient in one place?
options: Stop investing altogether to save capital
Lower the price to extend the deposit's life
Shift investment to discovery and development of another deposit
Wait until the deposit is completely gone before moving to another site
optionExplain: The book says they shift investment.
Lowering the price to stretch the deposit's life is not a step she describes.
Right: companies understand the dynamic and move elsewhere.
She says they move well before depletion bites.
questions.explain: She notes that resource companies understand this dynamic and shift investment to finding and developing another deposit elsewhere. The question of whether there are global limits follows.
questions.rule: Local limits can be dodged by moving.
questions.teaches: Resource companies understand the dynamic of depletion and, well before it makes capital less efficient in one place, shift investment to discovering and developing another deposit elsewhere.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Which resource is refilled by a steady input whatever its current state?
options: A school of fish
A stand of trees
A pasture of grass
Water in a river
optionExplain: Fish regenerate through their own reproduction.
Trees regenerate from themselves.
Grass regenerates from itself.
Right: nonliving renewable resources are refilled by a steady input.
questions.explain: Nonliving renewable resources are refilled by an input independent of their state. The card next sorts them.
questions.rule: A renewable resource has an input that refills its stock: living resources regenerate through a reinforcing loop, nonliving ones through a steady input.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Sort each renewable resource by how it regenerates.

items.t: Fish
Trees
Grass
Sunlight
Wind
Water in a river

questions.explain: Living resources reproduce themselves; nonliving ones are refilled from outside.
questions.rule: Living resources reinforce; nonliving ones are refilled.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A magazine sells to people who need a new issue every month, so potential buyers keep returning. What kind of structure is this?
options: A renewable resource system
A nonrenewable system, since each sale uses up a customer
A reinforcing loop with no stock
A thermostat system with a furnace
optionExplain: Right: the author gives regularly bought products as an example.
Regular buyers return, so the stock is regenerated.
A stock of customers exists and is replenished.
A magazine's customers are not a heating system; the structure is a regenerating stock of buyers.
questions.explain: Customers who must buy again are a regenerated stock.
questions.rule: Regular buyers renew the stock.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A cold virus spares its victims, who can catch another cold, so the stock of susceptible people is ____.
questions.explain: The stock of potential victims keeps being refilled.
questions.rule: Spared victims refill the stock.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A student says wind is regenerated through a reinforcing loop like fish. What is the correction?
options: Wind is a nonrenewable stock
Wind is refilled by a steady input, not by reproducing itself
Fish are refilled by a steady input too
The student is right, since both fish and wind are renewable resources
optionExplain: The book lists wind as a nonliving renewable resource.
Right: only living resources use the reinforcing loop.
Fish reproduce from themselves.
Both are renewable but regenerate differently.
questions.explain: The way a resource regenerates differs for living and nonliving ones.
questions.rule: Same label, different refill.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Which insect case does the author give as a renewable resource system?
options: An infestation that destroys the whole plant so that it cannot regenerate
A swarm that never feeds
An infestation that destroys part but not all of a plant, which regenerates
A hive that produces honey
optionExplain: The example needs the plant to regenerate.
The example involves feeding on the plant.
Right: the plant can regenerate and the insect can eat more.
A hive producing honey is not her example of a renewable resource system with an insect.
questions.explain: She lists an insect infestation that destroys part but not all of a plant; the plant regenerates and the insect can eat more.
questions.rule: Partial damage keeps the stock renewing.
questions.teaches: An insect infestation that destroys part but not all of a plant has the renewable-resource structure: the plant regenerates and the insect can eat more.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A fish population is at its densest, limited by food and habitat. How fast does it reproduce?
options: At its maximum, since there are most fish to breed
At a fast and rising rate
At a steady rate unaffected by density
Near zero
optionExplain: Reproduction peaks at a middle density.
At the densest level, rates are low, not fast and rising, because crowding limits reproduction.
Regeneration depends on density.
Right: crowding limits reproduction.
questions.explain: Crowded fish are limited by food and space. The card next gives the full shape.
questions.rule: Regeneration of a living resource is nonlinear: near zero when crowded, fastest at a middle density, and slowing again when depleted.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: True or false: In the model, a fish population that is depleted far below its natural level breeds faster and faster.
questions.explain: Past the maximum reproduction point, depletion makes it breed slower and slower.
questions.rule: Too few fish breed slowly.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A crowded forest has little regrowth. Following the fish pattern, what happens to regrowth if foresters thin it moderately?
options: It speeds up, since space and nutrients are freed
It slows, since fewer trees can seed
It stays the same, since density does not matter for trees or fish
It stops, since thinning kills the forest
optionExplain: Right: moderate thinning raises regeneration, as a modest fish decline does.
Moderate thinning frees resources; very heavy cutting would slow regrowth.
Density matters for regeneration.
Moderate thinning does not stop regrowth; only very heavy cutting would slow it.
questions.explain: Reproduction rises as density falls from a crowded level, up to a maximum. The forest case is our application.
questions.rule: Moderate depletion can speed regrowth.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.rule: Past the peak, depletion slows regrowth.
questions.q: Beyond the point of maximum reproduction, a smaller fish population regenerates ____.
questions.explain: Fish that cannot find each other, or whose niche is taken, breed slower and slower.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Which statement about fish regeneration is mistaken?
options: Very dense fish reproduce near zero
A modest fall in population speeds regeneration
More fish always means a faster breeding rate
Depleted fish may fail to find each other
optionExplain: The book says very dense fish reproduce near zero, so this statement is accurate.
The book says a modest fall in population speeds regeneration, so this statement is accurate.
Right: crowded fish reproduce near zero.
The book gives this as a reason depleted fish reproduce slowly, so this statement is accurate.
questions.explain: Regeneration rises and then falls as density drops.
questions.rule: Density and breeding are not proportional.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Which three nonlinear relationships does the author say the simplified fishery model contains?
options: Price, depreciation and wages
Regeneration, capital lifetime and the interest rate on loans
Yield, tax and population
Price, regeneration rate and yield per unit of capital
optionExplain: Depreciation and wages are not among the three.
Lifetime and interest are not among them.
Tax and population are not among them.
Right: these are the three she names.
questions.explain: She names three nonlinear relationships: price (scarcer fish cost more), regeneration rate (scarce fish do not breed much, nor do crowded fish) and yield per unit of capital (efficiency of fishing technology and practice).
questions.rule: Three nonlinear links drive the fishery.
questions.teaches: The simplified fishery model has three nonlinear relationships: price (scarcer fish cost more), regeneration rate, and yield per unit of capital.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Sonar helps boats find scarce fish. What does the model suggest happens to a stable fishery?
options: It can become unstable, with oscillations in harvest, capital and fish
It becomes more stable, since catches are higher
It stays exactly the same, since fish regenerate
It improves with no downside, since boats are more efficient
optionExplain: Right: better efficiency weakens the balancing feedback.
Higher efficiency weakens the signal that depletion sends.
The balancing loop through yield changes.
The model shows instability and collapse.
questions.explain: Better efficiency keeps boats profitable longer as fish decline. The card next gives the runs.
questions.rule: A slight increase in yield per unit of capital can turn a stable fishery into an oscillating one, and a larger one into collapse.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: True or false: In the first run, the fishing fleet comes into equilibrium with the fish and the harvest stays high and steady.
questions.explain: Falling profits stop capital growth in time, so the fleet and the fish stabilize.
questions.rule: In the stable run the balancing loop acts in time.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A logging firm gets a machine that finds scattered trees profitably even when forest density is low. What does the fishery model suggest?
options: Greater safety, since more trees are found
Greater risk of overshoot and collapse
No change, since forests regenerate
Slower logging, since trees are harder to find
optionExplain: Finding trees at low density removes the warning.
Right: better yield at low density weakens the balancing signal.
Regeneration can be overwhelmed.
The machine makes finding them easier.
questions.explain: Technology that preserves yield at low density keeps the fleet growing past safe levels.
questions.rule: Efficiency can weaken the brake.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.rule: More efficiency, worse outcome here.
questions.q: With even better fishing technology, the fishery ends in overshoot and ____ of fish, capital and harvest.
questions.explain: Boats stay profitable at very low fish density, so the resource and the industry collapse.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A manager says that because technology raises yield per boat, it can only help a fishery. What is the error?
options: Higher yield lowers fish stocks directly, not through capital
Higher yield has no effect on the loops
The manager is right, because yield is always good
Higher yield weakens the loop that restrains capital, which can cause oscillation or collapse
optionExplain: The effect runs through the balancing loop on capital.
It changes the strength of the balancing loop.
The model shows that higher yield can cause harm by disabling the loop that warns of depletion.
Right: high leverage in the wrong direction.
questions.explain: A tweak that improves efficiency can disable the feedback that warns of depletion.
questions.rule: Check what a boost does to the brake.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: What does the author call the result of the largest efficiency gain, in which fish become nonrenewable in practice?
options: The marine equivalent of desertification
A dynamic equilibrium
A shifting dominance
A buffer against depletion that protects the fleet and the fish
optionExplain: Right: a near-wipeout of fish and industry.
Dynamic equilibrium is a stable outcome, not the wipeout she describes.
This describes loops trading strength, not the wipeout.
This is the opposite of the outcome.
questions.explain: She says the nearly complete wipeout of fish and fishing industry is the marine equivalent of desertification, and the fish have been turned, for all practical purposes, into a nonrenewable resource.
questions.rule: Overharvest can turn renewable into nonrenewable.
questions.teaches: A nearly complete wipeout of the fish and the fishing industry is the marine equivalent of desertification, turning fish for all practical purposes into a nonrenewable resource.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A fishing fleet stops growing well before the fish stock drops below its critical threshold. What does the system do?
options: It oscillates around the equilibrium
It comes smoothly into equilibrium
It collapses, since all fishing depletes fish
It grows forever, since fish regenerate
optionExplain: Oscillation needs slower feedback.
Right: fast feedback leads to a smooth equilibrium.
Stopping in time avoids collapse.
No physical system grows forever; the fleet stops growing in time and comes smoothly into equilibrium.
questions.explain: Stopping before the threshold keeps regeneration intact. The card next states the rule.
questions.rule: The outcome depends on the resource's critical threshold and on how fast and how well the balancing loop stops capital growth.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Match each strength of the balancing loop to the outcome.
pairs: Fast and effective, stopping capital before the threshold
Very weak, capital grows past the threshold
questions.explain: The speed and strength of the balancing loop decides the outcome.
questions.rule: Faster feedback, safer outcome.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A herder adds cows quickly and notices pasture decline only after the grass is badly damaged. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Smooth equilibrium, since grass regenerates
Steady growth, since grass is renewable
Collapse, since feedback arrives after the regeneration threshold is crossed
No change, since cows eat little
optionExplain: Smooth equilibrium needs fast feedback.
Growth cannot continue once the threshold is crossed.
Right: weak, late feedback allows overshoot past the threshold.
The scenario describes damaging overgrazing.
questions.explain: The balancing feedback is too slow to stop capital growth in time.
questions.rule: Late brakes cause collapse.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: If the balancing feedback is slower and less effective, the system will ____ rather than settle smoothly.
questions.explain: Slower feedback means overshoot, then a swing back.
questions.rule: Slow brakes cause swings.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A student says the outcome depends only on the size of the fish stock. What is missing?
options: The price of boats and the cost of fuel
The number of fishing nations
Nothing; stock size decides everything
The critical threshold and the speed and strength of the balancing loop
optionExplain: These are not the two determinants named.
The number of fishing nations is not named as a determinant.
The book names two other determinants.
Right: these are the two determinants.
questions.explain: The threshold and the balancing loop together decide.
questions.rule: Two determinants, not one.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Which New England industry does the author cite as an example of very long cycles of growth, overcutting, collapse and regeneration?
options: Logging, now in its third cycle
Whaling, now in its fifth cycle
Textile mills, now in their third cycle
Fishing, now in its first cycle
optionExplain: Right: the resource regenerated each time.
Whaling is not named as her example of very long cycles.
Textile mills are not named in this context; her example is logging.
Fishing in its first cycle is not her example; New England logging is in its third cycle.
questions.explain: She says very long-term cycles have been observed, for example in New England logging, now in its third cycle of growth, overcutting, collapse and regeneration. This is not true for all resource populations, and technology can drive some to extinction.
questions.rule: Some renewable systems cycle; others do not recover.
questions.teaches: Very long renewable-resource cycles of growth, overcutting, collapse and regeneration have been observed in New England logging, now in its third cycle, but this is not true for all resource populations.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Which kind of resource can support harvest indefinitely, but only up to a limited rate?
options: A nonrenewable resource, limited by the size of its stock
A renewable resource, limited by its regeneration rate
Both kinds, at any rate
Neither, because all resources run out
optionExplain: A nonrenewable resource is exhausted, not sustained.
Right: renewable resources are flow-limited.
The rate is limited for renewables.
Renewables can last indefinitely at a limited rate.
questions.explain: The limit for renewables is the rate; for nonrenewables it is the total. The card next states this.
questions.rule: Nonrenewable resources limit the total that can be taken (stock-limited); renewable ones limit the rate (flow-limited).

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Match each resource kind to its type of limit.
pairs: The rate of extraction from oil
The rate of harvest from fish
questions.explain: Nonrenewable resources are limited by the stock; renewable ones by the flow.
questions.rule: Stock versus flow limits.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A forest regrows 2 percent a year. A firm cuts 5 percent a year for decades. Which statement fits the flow-limit idea?
options: The forest is safe, since it is renewable
The forest is stock-limited, so it lasts forever
The cut exceeds the regeneration rate, so the forest may be pushed below its critical threshold
The forest regrows faster as it is cut
optionExplain: Renewable only supports harvest at the regeneration rate.
A renewable resource is flow-limited.
Right: harvest above the regeneration rate is unsustainable.
Regrowth has a finite maximum rate.
questions.explain: Harvest above the regeneration rate risks driving the stock past its threshold. The figures are ours.
questions.rule: Harvest within the regeneration rate.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.rule: Faster extraction, shorter life.
questions.q: True or false: A nonrenewable resource that is extracted faster has a shorter lifetime.
questions.explain: The stock is not renewed, so a faster draw-down empties it sooner.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: A student says renewable resources can be harvested at any rate forever. What is the correction?
options: They can be harvested indefinitely only at a rate equal to their regeneration rate
They can be harvested at any rate for a limited time
They cannot be harvested at all
They are stock-limited like oil
optionExplain: Right: flow-limited, not unlimited.
The corrected claim is about the rate that is sustainable.
They can be harvested at a limited rate.
Renewable resources are flow-limited.
questions.explain: A harvest faster than regeneration can drive the resource below its threshold.
questions.rule: The limit is a rate.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Does the author say renewable limits, unlike nonrenewable ones, allow a physical stock to grow forever?
options: Yes; renewable limits allow endless growth of capital
No; neither allows it, but the constraints are dynamically quite different
No; and they impose the same constraint
Yes; only nonrenewable limits matter
optionExplain: Neither kind allows endless growth.
Right: both limit growth, in different ways, because of stocks and flows.
She says the constraints are dynamically different.
Both renewable and nonrenewable limits matter, and neither allows endless growth.
questions.explain: She concludes that neither renewable nor nonrenewable limits to growth allow a physical stock to grow forever, but the constraints are dynamically quite different because of the difference between stocks and flows.
questions.rule: Different limits, same impossibility of endless growth.
questions.teaches: Neither renewable nor nonrenewable limits allow a physical stock to grow forever, but the constraints are dynamically different because of the difference between stocks and flows.

questions.q: What answer does Meadows give to the question of why systems work so well?
options: Well-run systems are shielded from every outside shock by strong managers who plan each response ahead of time
Systems stay in balance because their stocks are fixed in size and never change over the years
Highly functional systems tend to show three characteristics: resilience, self-organization and hierarchy
Systems work well only when engineers have designed each part in advance and tested it alone
optionExplain: Plausible, since control sounds protective, but she describes systems that recover and adapt, not systems shielded from shocks.
Plausible because balance is a theme of Chapter Two, but nothing in the chapter says stocks are fixed in size.
Right: these are the three characteristics she names.
Plausible for machines, but she includes communities and ecosystems that no engineer designed.
questions.explain: She names resilience, self-organization and hierarchy. The card next shows what each one means.
questions.rule: When a system works well, look for resilience, self-organization and hierarchy.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says that systems pushed too far can fall apart or behave in ways not seen before.
questions.explain: She grants this at the start of the chapter, and then adds that systems by and large manage quite well.
questions.rule: Systems can fail when pushed too far.

questions.q: A hospital is praised as a well-functioning system. Which question follows Meadows' way of explaining why?
options: Does it show resilience, self-organization and hierarchy?
Which single manager holds the most direct control over every ward?
How many written rules has it adopted to remove all variation?
How much does it spend per patient compared with other hospitals?
optionExplain: Right: she explains good function through these three properties.
Control is tempting, but she does not explain good function by one controlling manager.
Rules feel like order, but she values systems that adapt, not systems stripped of variation.
Cost is a fair question in general, but it is not her explanation for how systems work well.
questions.explain: Her approach is to ask which of the three properties the system shows.
questions.hint: Look at the three characteristics she names.
questions.rule: When a system works well, look for resilience, self-organization and hierarchy.

questions.q: A town has coped well with every flood so far. A flood far larger than any before arrives. What does Meadows' opening suggest?
options: The town will cope again, because a system that has worked well in every earlier flood is certain to continue
The town will gain strength, because each flood it meets adds to the harmony it already has
The town will be unaffected, because the flood is only a larger version of an event it has met
The town may fall apart or behave in ways nobody has seen, because pushing a system too far has limits
optionExplain: Past success is persuasive, but she warns that pushing too far can break a system.
Strengthening is possible for some systems, but she does not say a larger shock adds strength.
Size looks like the only difference, but she says extreme pressure can change how a system behaves.
Right: she says a system pushed too far may fall apart or show unobserved behavior.
questions.explain: A new, much larger shock is the case where the usual recovery may not hold.
questions.rule: Success so far does not remove the limits.

questions.q: Chapter Two’s simple systems create their own behavior from their ____.
questions.explain: Meadows says behavior comes from structure, which is why the next three properties are described as features of structure.
questions.rule: Behavior comes from structure.

questions.q: Leopold's epigraph says only a fool discards seemingly useless parts of a good system. What does he advise a forester who finds a useless-looking species?
options: Remove it, since a part with no known use only adds clutter to an otherwise well-working system of parts
Keep it, since a system we like but do not understand may depend on parts whose use we cannot yet see
Study it for a season and discard it if no use appears, because every part must justify itself to the whole
Replace it with a species whose use is known, since understanding comes before preservation
optionExplain: Tidying up is tempting, but Leopold calls discarding such parts foolish.
Right: Leopold calls keeping every cog and wheel the first precaution of intelligent tinkering.
A trial period sounds careful, but his point is that not understanding a part is no reason to discard it.
Replacing sounds responsible, but it still discards a part we do not understand.
questions.explain: Leopold's epigraph argues for caution: a good system we do not understand may depend on parts whose use we cannot yet see.
questions.teaches: Leopold’s opening advice: when nature has built something good that we do not understand, discarding seemingly useless parts is foolish; keep every cog and wheel.
questions.rule: When a system works well, look for resilience, self-organization and hierarchy.

questions.q: In everyday language, which kind of system would you call resilient?
options: One that stays exactly the same whatever happens in the world around it, however large the change
One that springs back to working order after it has been pressed or stretched
One that grows as large and as quickly as its resources will allow
One that has the fewest parts and therefore the fewest ways to fail
optionExplain: Staying unchanged sounds strong, but a rigid system breaks instead of recovering.
Right: bouncing back is the core of the word.
Growth is a kind of success, but it says nothing about recovering from knocks.
Fewer parts can help, but resilience is about recovery, not part count.
questions.explain: Bouncing back after a knock is the core of the word. The card next gives Meadows’ sense.
questions.rule: Resilience means recovering.

questions.q: Meadows names ____ or rigidity as the opposite of resilience.
questions.explain: A brittle system breaks instead of springing back.
questions.rule: The opposite of resilience is brittleness.

questions.q: A dry twig snaps when bent far, while a green sapling bends and then straightens. Which statement fits Meadows’ sense of the word?
options: The twig is more resilient, because it keeps its shape until the moment it breaks
Both are equally resilient, because neither changes shape when left alone
Neither is resilient, because the word applies only to living systems such as bodies
The sapling is the resilient one, and the twig is brittle
optionExplain: Holding shape looks like strength, but it ends in breaking, which is brittleness.
Looking only at rest hides the difference that appears under stress.
Her examples include machines and communities as well as living bodies.
Right: the sapling springs back, the twig breaks.
questions.explain: Resilience shows when the thing is pressed or stretched.
questions.hint: Which one springs back?
questions.rule: Resilience is the ability to bounce back and persist in a changing environment; brittleness is its opposite.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows uses the ordinary dictionary meaning of resilience instead of a definition specific to one field.
questions.explain: She notes that definitions differ by field and picks the plain dictionary sense.
questions.rule: She uses the plain dictionary sense.

questions.q: A supply contract works only if nothing in its environment ever varies. What does the definition suggest once conditions start to vary a lot?
options: It is exposed as brittle, since resilience is about persisting within a variable environment
It becomes more resilient, since variation tests the contract and so strengthens it from one change to the next
It stays resilient, since a contract that has worked so far is proven to persist
It becomes irrelevant, since resilience concerns only physical things that can be stretched
optionExplain: Right: needing constancy is the opposite of persisting in a variable environment.
Testing may strengthen some systems, but one that needs constancy has nothing to bounce back with.
Past performance in constant conditions says nothing about varying ones.
Meadows applies the idea to systems of many kinds, not just physical objects.
questions.explain: Persisting in a variable environment is the test.
questions.rule: Resilience is tested by variation.

questions.q: Meadows’ dictionary sense covers more than shape. Which recovery also counts as resilience?
options: A person who feels no effect from the setback at any time, because nothing ever reaches them
A person who slowly forgets the setback over many years
A person quickly recovering their good humor after a setback
A team that avoids all risk, so that no setback has the chance to occur in the first place
optionExplain: Feeling nothing is not recovery; there was nothing to recover from.
Slowly fading is not quick recovery of strength or spirits.
Right: the dictionary meaning includes quickly recovering spirits or good humor.
Avoiding risk is the opposite of persisting through variation.
questions.explain: The dictionary sense includes recovering strength, spirits, good humor or any other aspect quickly.
questions.teaches: Meadows’ dictionary definition also covers quickly recovering strength, spirits, good humor or any other aspect, not only bouncing back in shape.
questions.rule: Resilience is the ability to bounce back and persist in a changing environment; brittleness is its opposite.

questions.q: A home has one thermostat and one heater. Which change would Meadows expect to make the home more resilient?
options: Fit a more precise thermostat but keep the single heater as the only source of warmth
Remove the thermostat so the room does not react to small changes in temperature
Fit a stronger heater so the single loop acts faster and harder when it is needed
Add a fireplace and better insulation that each restore warmth in a different way
optionExplain: Precision improves one loop, but if that heater fails nothing else restores warmth.
Removing feedback removes restoring power altogether.
A stronger single loop is still one loop; its failure leaves nothing behind it.
Right: different mechanisms give backup if one fails.
questions.explain: Several loops that work in different ways give backup. The card next explains this.
questions.rule: Several loops beat one.

questions.q: Resilience comes from several balancing loops working through different mechanisms, at different time scales, and with ____.
questions.explain: Redundancy means one loop can take over when another fails.
questions.rule: Redundant loops back each other up.

questions.q: A small farm survives a drought because it has a well, stored feed and a second crop that tolerates dry weather. What does this show?
options: One balancing loop tuned precisely to a single target, which is all that resilience needs
Several loops working through different mechanisms, with backup if one fails
Meta-meta-resilience, because the farm has stored some feed ahead of time
Static stability, because the farm’s output is the same in every single year
optionExplain: The farm has several mechanisms, not one tuned loop, so this reading does not fit the case.
Right: well, feed and drought-tolerant crop are separate restoring mechanisms.
Meta-meta-resilience means loops that learn and design new structures, which storing feed does not show.
Nothing says output is constant; the farm's point is its backup mechanisms, not steady yields.
questions.explain: Different ways to restore a system, in parallel, are what Meadows describes.
questions.hint: Count the separate ways the farm can recover.
questions.rule: Look for several balancing loops with different mechanisms, time scales and backup, not one loop.

questions.q: Put these in order from the simplest to the highest level of resilience.
items: A single balancing loop returns a stock to its desired state
Several loops with different mechanisms and redundancy restore the system
Loops that restore or rebuild other loops (meta-resilience)
Loops that learn, create, design and evolve restorative structures (meta-meta-resilience)
questions.explain: Meadows climbs from one loop, to many loops, to loops that rebuild loops, to loops that learn and evolve new structures.
questions.rule: Resilience has levels.

questions.q: A manager says: Our hospital is resilient because its one backup generator has not failed yet. What does Meadows’ account say is missing?
options: A faster generator, since resilience means no more than how quickly power returns
A rule against change, since resilience requires every part to stay constant
Backup through several different mechanisms and time scales, so one failure does not remove all restoring power
A larger hospital, since resilience grows with the number of departments
optionExplain: Speed helps one loop but does not add different mechanisms.
Resilience can be dynamic; rules against change do not add loops.
Right: one loop, even a reliable one, is not a rich structure of loops.
Size is not the measure; the variety of restoring loops is.
questions.explain: One reliable loop is still one loop; Meadows wants several mechanisms on different time scales so one failure does not end restoration.
questions.rule: Reliability of one loop is not redundancy.

questions.q: Meadows says even rich resilient systems have limits. Which case in the chapter shows this?
options: A human body with a learning intelligence still cannot keep itself from eventually dying
A body that stops repairing rips after its intelligence has learned to transplant its own organs
An ecosystem that loses its feedback loops once its species begin to move around in space and time
A single balancing loop that fails to bring a stock back to its desired state
optionExplain: Right: Meadows says no body-plus-intelligence has yet been resilient enough to avoid death.
Transplants are part of the resilience she praises, not a sign of its end.
Moving species are one of the ways she says ecosystems stay resilient.
A single loop failing is her example of weak resilience, not of a limit to a rich structure.
questions.explain: Even the most resilient systems she describes have limits.
questions.teaches: Even a rich resilient system has limits: the human body with a self-organizing intelligence has not been resilient enough to keep itself from eventually dying.
questions.rule: Look for several balancing loops with different mechanisms, time scales and backup, not one loop.

questions.q: True or false: A system whose condition barely varies from year to year must be resilient.
questions.explain: Constant systems can be fragile. The card next shows why constancy and resilience are different.
questions.rule: Judge resilience by the ability to recover, not by how little a system varies.

questions.q: Meadows says static stability is something you can see, while resilience is often hard to ____.
questions.explain: Static stability shows up as small variation, but resilience may only become visible when its limits are exceeded.
questions.rule: Stability is visible; resilience may not be.

questions.q: Forest X has looked the same for fifty years. Forest Y has regular pest outbreaks followed by recovery. What can be said under Meadows’ view?
options: Y may be the resilient one, since recurring outbreaks can be normal and resilience acts to restore them
X must be the more resilient one, because a system that varies less from year to year will recover better after a knock
Neither can be judged, because outbreaks of any kind signal that a system is failing
Y is brittle, because an outbreak shows that its balancing loops have stopped working
optionExplain: Right: dynamic cycles can be what resilience maintains.
Less variation looks like strength, but she says constant systems can be unresilient.
Her text says periodic outbreaks may be the normal condition, not a sign of failure.
An outbreak followed by recovery shows the loops working.
questions.explain: Cycles with recovery are compatible with resilience.
questions.hint: Does the forest come back after each outbreak?
questions.rule: Judge resilience by the ability to recover, not by how little a system varies.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says resilience may be hard to see unless a system’s limits are exceeded and its structure breaks down.
questions.explain: Static stability shows as small variation, but resilience may only become visible when its balancing loops are overwhelmed.
questions.rule: Do not read resilience off variation.

questions.q: A firm smooths its yearly output by cutting every spare buffer. What does Meadows’ reasoning predict?
options: Both stability and resilience improve, since removing buffers strengthens every property that a system can have
Both fall, since stability and resilience are the same property under two different names in her account
Visible stability and output may look better while the less visible resilience has been sacrificed
Neither changes, since a buffer is not part of any feedback loop in the system and so cannot matter
optionExplain: Buffers often provide the backup that gives resilience.

Plausible because the two words sound alike, but Meadows separates them: stability is visible variation, resilience is the hidden ability to recover. Output smoothness can rise while recovery power falls.
Right: people trade the hard-to-see property for the visible one.
Buffers can be part of restoring loops; removing them matters.
questions.explain: Visible gains can hide invisible losses.
questions.rule: Ask what hidden resilience a visible gain costs.

questions.q: According to the ecologist C. S. Holling, what can holding a system rigidly constant cause to evolve?
options: More resilience, because the loops stop being tested by changes
Fragility
Greater productivity, while the resilience is left untouched
Faster self-organization, because the system becomes more orderly
optionExplain: Untested loops do not become stronger; he says the opposite.
Right: his epigraph says a straitjacket of constancy can cause fragility to evolve.
He is warning against constancy as a cost to resilience, not claiming it leaves it untouched.
Self-organization needs freedom and some disorder, not tight order.
questions.explain: Holling’s epigraph supports the point that constancy can breed fragility.
questions.teaches: The ecologist C. S. Holling warned that placing a system in a straitjacket of constancy can cause fragility to evolve.
questions.rule: Judge resilience by the ability to recover, not by how little a system varies.

questions.q: A factory removes all spare stock to save money. Which risk would Meadows point out?
options: It becomes immune to disruption, since waste was the only weakness the factory had
It loses output at once, since stock is the thing that produces goods
It gains resilience, since fewer moving parts leave fewer things that can fail
It becomes more exposed to disruptions in fuel, traffic or computers
