questions.explain: The release is a single event, the oscillation is the pattern over time, and the coil's mechanics are the structure that produces it.
questions.rule: Event, behavior, structure.

questions.q: A hospital board explains a rise in infections by a week of short staffing. At which level is this explanation?
options: Behavior level: it shows a pattern over a period of time
Structure level: it names the stocks, flows and loops involved
None, because it gives a cause
Event level: one happening used to explain another
optionExplain: One week is a point, not a pattern.
No stocks, flows or loops are traced, so this is not a structure-level explanation.
Giving a cause does not make it structural.
A one-week gap is an event, like those in market reports.
questions.explain: Staffing last week causing infections this week is event-event analysis.
questions.rule: One-week causes are events.

questions.q: From event-event explanations of the market, what can you do, according to Meadows?
options: Predict tomorrow's moves but not change how the market behaves
Neither predict tomorrow nor change the market
Change how the market behaves but not predict tomorrow's moves
Both predict and change, with practice
optionExplain: She says they give no ability to predict.
She says such explanations give no ability to predict or to change behavior.
They give no power to change it either.
She says event-event explanations give neither the power to predict nor the power to change behavior.
questions.explain: Event-event analysis offers no predictive or changing power.
questions.rule: Events alone cannot guide action.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says much analysis in the world goes no deeper than events.
questions.explain: She says much analysis in the world goes no deeper than events, which is why the Slinky's levels are worth showing.
questions.rule: Do not assume analysis is deep.

questions.q: A coach blames a losing run on bad luck, then on an injury, then on weather. What does Meadows say about this style?
options: It reveals the structure beneath through its many repeated causes
It predicts the next result better than patterns over time can
It gives no ability to change the behavior of the system
It is sound because every cause that is named is a real cause
optionExplain: Repeated events are still events.
She says it has no predictive value.
She says event-event explanations leave us unable to alter the system, for instance to make the market less volatile.
The causes may be real; the level is shallow.
questions.explain: Meadows adds that such explanations also cannot make the stock market less volatile or a better guide to company health.
questions.rule: Event chains do not give leverage.
questions.teaches: Event-level explanations give no ability to change a system's behavior, for example to make the stock market less volatile or a better vehicle for investment.

questions.q: Economic news reports GNP, a flow. What does Meadows say is neglected?
options: The stock of factories, farms and businesses that produce it
The past trend in income over the same years, which models study
The opinions of consumers about the future state of the economy
The central bank's interest rate decisions over the same years
optionExplain: Right: flows are followed, stocks neglected.
Trends are what these models study.
Her point is about stocks and flows.
These are inputs the models already use.
questions.explain: The neglected item is the physical capital stock. The card next explains why that matters.
questions.rule: Do not forget the stock.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says flows respond to stocks, so there is no reason to expect a stable link between flows.
questions.explain: She says flows respond to stocks, not to other flows, so there is no reason to expect a stable relation between them.
questions.rule: Flows follow stocks.

questions.q: An analyst finds a hospital's admissions and discharges moved together for ten years. Following Meadows, why might they have done so?
options: Admissions directly cause discharges according to a stable law
Discharges are the more important of the two flows in a hospital
Both respond to the same stock, such as patients in beds
The data are too short to show any link
optionExplain: She says no flow is expected to bear a stable link to another.
She does not rank flows; the joint movement is explained by a shared stock, not by a more important flow.
Flows governed by the same stock vary together under ordinary conditions.
Her argument is not about length of data.
questions.explain: A shared stock can make flows move together without one driving the other.
questions.rule: Common stock, common movement.

questions.q: Meadows says flows rise and fall in response to stocks, not to other ____.
questions.explain: That is her reason for doubting stable flow-to-flow equations.
questions.rule: Stocks drive flows.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a criticism Meadows makes of behavior-based models?
options: They ignore past data altogether
They overemphasize flows and underemphasize stocks
They look for stable links between flows that do not exist
They cannot show how stocks affect flows through feedback
optionExplain: They use past trends heavily; that is their method.
This is her first criticism: behavior-based models overemphasize flows and underemphasize stocks.
This is her second, more serious criticism.
This is part of her first criticism.
questions.explain: These models rely on past data. Their fault is where they look in it.
questions.rule: Past data is not the fault.

questions.q: A fisheries analyst tracks only monthly catches, not the fish population. Why might analysts do this, per Meadows?
options: Stocks cannot affect flows in a fishery, which has no feedback
Catches are easier to model with feedback loops
Catch data are more accurate than stock data in a fishery
Flows show interesting variation and rapid change
optionExplain: Stocks drive flows in her account.
Her point is the opposite: feedback from stocks is missed.
She says nothing about accuracy.
She says economists follow flows for exactly this reason.
questions.explain: Flows are where the action seems to be, which is why they get the attention, and why the stock is missed.
questions.rule: Fast change draws the eye to flows.
questions.teaches: Economists follow flows because that is where the interesting variations and most rapid changes in systems show up.

questions.q: You hold heat-flow data for a room but know nothing about thermostats. When would your fitted equation stop working?
options: When a different day of the week arrives with a different pattern
When the system's structure changes, such as an opened window
When the data are more than a year old
Never, if the data were recorded accurately and kept up to date
optionExplain: The weekday is not in her account; the equation breaks when the structure changes.
Right: the equation holds only while the structure holds.
Age of the data is not her point; the equation fails when the structure changes, however recent the data.
Accuracy does not protect against a change in structure.
questions.explain: The fit holds only while the structure is unchanged. The card next sets out why.
questions.rule: Equations ride on structure.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says a behavior-level equation alone helps you cut the fuel bill while keeping the same room temperature.
questions.explain: She says you must dig into the system's structure for that.
questions.rule: To change a system, study its structure.

questions.q: A shop's sales equation worked for five years, then failed when a rival opened next door. Which Meadows point fits?
options: Flows always follow other flows in the long run, so the equation should hold
The equation holds only until the system's structure changes
The equation was an event-level explanation of single happenings
Five years is too short a period of data for any equation to hold
optionExplain: She says flows respond to stocks.
The new rival changed the structure the equation rested on.
It used patterns over time, which is behavior level.
Her point is structure change, not data length.
questions.explain: Fitted equations carry the old structure inside them.
questions.rule: A changed structure voids the fit.

questions.q: Behavior-based models are fair near-term, poor longer-term and terrible at telling how to ____ the economy's performance.
questions.explain: Meadows says these models cannot tell one how to improve performance.
questions.rule: Forecasting is not improving.

questions.q: Which conclusion from a well-fitting equation goes beyond what Meadows allows?
options: It may predict tomorrow's temperature while nothing in the system changes
It fits because both flows share one governing stock, the room temperature
It could break if the insulation is improved
It will tell us what to change if the room temperature plummets
optionExplain: She allows this: the fit can forecast while the structure is unchanged.
She gives this as the reason both flows move together: they share one governing stock.
She names this as a breaking change.
She says a behavior-level analysis would not help with a plunge.
questions.explain: The fit can forecast under stable structure; it cannot guide repair.
questions.rule: Fit is not a repair manual.

questions.q: A firm blames repeated quality problems on whichever event came last, without studying their history or process. Which of Meadows' diagnoses of surprise fits?
options: Fascination with events, too little attention to history, and too little skill at reading structure from it
Misdrawn boundaries, ignored limits and long delays in feedback
Nonlinear responses, shifting limits and bounded rationality in decisions
Models that are too large to understand, and diagrams that connect everything
optionExplain: These are her three reasons systems of all kinds surprise us.
Misdrawn boundaries, ignored limits and delays are other sources of surprise she covers, not these three failings.
Nonlinearity, shifting limits and bounded rationality are other sources of surprise, not the three failings here.
This is a different trap, covered under boundaries.
questions.explain: Meadows closes the section by naming three failings: too much fascination with events, too little attention to history, and too little skill at reading structure from history.
questions.rule: Look at the history for clues to structure.
questions.teaches: Meadows' diagnosis: we are too fascinated by events, pay too little attention to history, and lack skill at seeing in history the clues to structure.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: What does it mean for a relationship to be linear, according to Meadows?
options: The effect is always larger than the cause that produced it
The effect repeats in a regular wave over a period of time
It can be drawn as a straight line, with constant proportions
Each effect feeds back to change the cause that produced it
optionExplain: Size of effect is not the test; proportion is.
Waves describe behavior over time, not linearity.
Right: the effect grows in step with the cause.
That describes feedback, which can be linear or not.
questions.explain: A straight line means constant proportions. The card next adds the nonlinear case.
questions.rule: Linear means constant proportions.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says nonlinear systems can generally be taken apart and added together like linear ones.
questions.explain: She says nonlinear systems generally cannot be solved or added together, unlike linear systems whose pieces add up.
questions.rule: Linear pieces add up; nonlinear pieces do not.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: Which one of these relationships is nonlinear?
options: A taxi charges a set fee per kilometre, so 10 km costs double 5 km
A plant given 2 units of water grows 4 cm, 4 units gives 8 cm
A worker paid by the hour earns twice as much for 20 hours as for 10
A little salt improves a soup, but triple the salt ruins it
optionExplain: A set fee per kilometre keeps a constant proportion, so it is linear.
Constant proportion across the range: linear.
Pay per hour keeps a constant proportion, so it is linear.
Here more of the cause reverses the effect, so the line bends.
questions.explain: Only the salt case lacks a constant proportion.
questions.rule: Straight line means linear; a bend means nonlinear.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: If 10 pounds of fertilizer adds 2 bushels and 20 pounds adds 4, a linear relationship predicts that 30 pounds adds ____ bushels.
questions.explain: In a linear case each extra 10 pounds adds another 2 bushels, so 30 pounds adds 6.
questions.rule: Linear: same step each time.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says linear equations are solvable, which makes them suitable for textbooks.
questions.explain: She says linear equations are solvable, which makes them suitable for textbooks.
questions.rule: Solvable, so used in textbooks.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: A gardener doubles the dose of plant food hoping to double the growth. What might Meadows' fertilizer case suggest?
options: Exactly twice the growth, as the first dose showed
No extra growth, or even harm, from too much of a good thing
The same growth as before the extra dose, in every plant
A larger gain than doubling, as plants respond more over time
optionExplain: She uses the case to show this fails.
In her case 100 pounds added 10 bushels, 200 added none and 300 lowered the yield.
She says the yield even went down at 300.
Her case shows the reverse: more fertilizer gave no gain and then a loss.
questions.explain: In her example 100 pounds raised yield by 10 bushels, 200 pounds by nothing, and 300 pounds lowered it, because the soil was damaged.
questions.rule: More is not always more.
questions.teaches: In the fertilizer case 100 pounds added 10 bushels, 200 pounds added nothing and 300 pounds lowered yield, because too much of a good thing damaged the soil.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: A small push gave a small response. What may twice the push give in a nonlinear system?
options: Exactly twice the response, as small pushes reveal the rule
Half the response, since effects always fade
A far smaller, far larger or no response at all
The same response, because systems resist change
optionExplain: Doubling the response is the linear case, which a nonlinear system need not follow.
Fading is one possibility among others, not the rule.
Right: nothing guarantees twice the response.
Resistance to change is not her point; without proportion, the response can be anything.
questions.explain: Without proportion, any outcome is possible. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Do not assume proportion.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says car speed on a highway drops in proportion to traffic density across the whole range.
questions.explain: Speed is affected only slightly over a large range, then drops off quickly, and at a certain point traffic jams and speed falls to zero.
questions.rule: Traffic slows slowly, then suddenly.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: A manager sees one free coffee day lift morale a little, so offers perks every day. Which mistake does Meadows' warning describe?
options: Expecting a lot of a cure to do a lot of good because a little did some
Ignoring how long it takes for morale to change after the perks
Drawing the boundary of the office too narrowly around the staff
Explaining morale by single events instead of patterns over time
optionExplain: This is the reasonable expectation that nonlinearity foils.
That is a delay, not a nonlinearity.
Drawing the office boundary too narrowly is a boundary error, not a nonlinearity mistake.
Explaining morale by single events is an event-level error, not the nonlinearity trap.
questions.explain: A little may help while a lot may bring no gain or harm.
questions.rule: A little good does not mean a lot is better.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: Soil erosion can go on for a long time with little effect on yield, until topsoil wears down to the depth of the ____ zone.
questions.explain: After that point, a little further erosion can make yields plummet.
questions.rule: Thresholds hide behind long calm.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: An engineer says: three more cars a minute slowed traffic slightly, so thirty more will slow it ten times as much. What is the flaw?
options: It forgets that cars on a highway have any effect on speed
It treats the highway as a system with no stocks or flows
It assumes a proportional response in a relationship that is nonlinear
It counts cars when it should count the drivers instead
optionExplain: Cars do affect speed, just not in proportion.
The flaw is proportion, not missing stocks.
Speed barely changes over a wide range, then drops sharply.
Her point does not turn on the unit.
questions.explain: Extrapolating from a gentle range misses the knee in the curve.
questions.rule: Mind the knee in the curve.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: A charity sends one thoughtful reminder email and donors respond, so it emails daily. Which Meadows example warns of the likely result?
options: Advertising: a little tasteful promotion awakens interest, a lot causes disgust
Fertilizer: more food always gives more growth, whatever the dose
The thermostat: the room temperature depends on past heat flows
The Slinky: oscillation follows the release
optionExplain: The response can reverse as the amount rises.
Her fertilizer case shows the opposite.
That example is about flows and stocks, not dose.
That example is about events and structure.
questions.explain: Meadows notes that a little tasteful advertising can awaken interest while a lot of blatant advertising can cause disgust.
questions.rule: More of the same can reverse the effect.
questions.teaches: More of the same can reverse the response: a little tasteful advertising awakens interest in a product, while a lot of blatant advertising causes disgust for it.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: Besides confounding our expectations, what else do nonlinearities do, according to Meadows?
options: Make every feedback loop weaker as the system ages over time
Keep a system close to equilibrium
Remove all delays from the feedback loops of the system
Change the relative strengths of loops and flip a system's mode
optionExplain: She says strengths change, not that all weaken.
Her point is the possibility of flipping.
Delays are a separate feature of loops, not something nonlinearity removes.
Right: they cause shifting dominance of loops.
questions.explain: Nonlinearity can hand control from one loop to another. The card next explains how.
questions.rule: Nonlinearity shifts dominance.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says nonlinearities can flip a system from one mode of behavior to another.
questions.explain: They change the relative strengths of feedback loops and can flip the mode.
questions.rule: Strengths shift, modes flip.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: A viral app grows fast, then stalls abruptly when server limits bite. Which Meadows idea fits?
options: Growth was a simple event with no loop of any kind behind it
A reinforcing loop was overtaken by a balancing loop as a limit tightened
The app's boundary was drawn too widely
A delay made the growth look faster than it really was
optionExplain: Growth like this has a loop behind it.
This is the swing from exponential growth to a dominant balancing loop.
The stall comes from loop strengths, not boundaries.
Delays are not the main point.
questions.explain: Exponential growth under a reinforcing loop gives way when a balancing loop suddenly dominates.
questions.rule: Reinforcing, then balancing.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: In a system, a nonlinearity sharply weakens a reinforcing loop past some stock level. What may follow?
options: Growth accelerates, as the loop is no longer held back by anything
A balancing loop becomes dominant, so growth gives way to levelling
Nothing changes, as loops are fixed in strength by the system's structure
The system leaves its structure behind
optionExplain: The loop is the one being weakened.
This is the sudden swing she describes.
She says nonlinearities change loop strengths.
The structure remains; dominance shifts.
questions.explain: When one loop weakens past a threshold the other can take over.
questions.rule: Dominance can pass between loops.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: Meadows calls nonlinearities the chief cause of the shifting ____ seen in several systems of the zoo.
questions.explain: Shifting dominance is the sudden swing from one dominant loop to another.
questions.rule: Shifting dominance.

questions.section: Linear Minds in a Nonlinear World
questions.q: In a board game, reaching ten points changes the rules for everyone. Which part of Gleick's remark in the chapter does this illustrate?
options: Linear systems can be taken apart and then put together again
Nonlinear systems always add up like their separate pieces do
Solvable equations make the best cases for use in textbooks
Nonlinearity means playing the game changes the rules
optionExplain: This describes linear systems, not rule changes.
He says they cannot be added together.
He says linear equations suit textbooks.
This is his wording, quoted by Meadows.
questions.explain: Gleick says that twisted changeability makes nonlinearity hard to calculate, but it also creates rich kinds of behavior that never occur in linear systems.
questions.rule: Rules that change as you play.
questions.teaches: Gleick adds that this changeability makes nonlinearity hard to calculate but creates rich kinds of behavior that never occur in linear systems.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: Why did the budworm become a serious pest only recently, in Meadows' account?
options: The lumber industry turned to spruce and fir when the pine was gone
Budworm outbreaks began only in the twentieth century, with the first sprays
DDT caused the first outbreaks, after farmers began to use it widely
Spruce and fir suddenly became more fragile and easier to kill
optionExplain: Right: the value of the trees changed, not the budworm.
Tree rings show at least 400 years of outbreaks.
The outbreaks predate DDT by centuries.
Her account is about changing value, not fragility.
questions.explain: The pest was old; the concern was new. The card next tells the spraying story.
questions.rule: Concern follows economic value.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: True or false: Despite the annual sprays, the budworm resurged every year.
questions.explain: Annual sprays continued through the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s and the budworm still resurged each year.
questions.rule: Spraying did not end the outbreaks.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: A city sprays against mosquitoes each summer, and they return every year. Which part of Meadows' story does this parallel?
options: A pest noticed only after its host tree became commercially valuable
A pest controlled entirely by its natural enemies in a stable way
Insecticides renewed year after year while the problem recurs
A computer model finding the budworm barely detectable in most years
optionExplain: That is the change in tree value, not the spraying.
That was the system before the sprays.
The budworm came back each year despite annual sprays.
That is the Holling and Baskerville finding.
questions.explain: The mosquito case echoes recurring resurgence under repeated spraying.
questions.rule: Repeated fixes, repeated returns.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: With a decade of annual spraying and annual resurgence, Meadows reports that by 1980 the spraying costs were ____.
questions.explain: Costs had become unmanageable; New Brunswick spent $12.5 million that year.
questions.rule: Costs climbed while the problem stayed.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: True or false: When DDT was banned, other insecticides replaced it and the spraying of the forests continued.
questions.explain: Other insecticides, such as fenitrothion, acephate, Sevin and methoxychlor, replaced DDT and spraying went on.
questions.rule: The policy outlived its tool.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: A farmers' cooperative protects a crop with a stopgap until harvest, knowing the pest will return. Which view in Meadows' account is this?
options: Holling's claim that outbreaks cannot be controlled by anyone at all
The citizens' view that poisons should drench the landscape every year
The model's finding that predators are unnecessary to the forest
The forester's view that spraying buys time until the mill is ready
optionExplain: That is not the forester's view.
The citizens objected to drenching the landscape.
The model found the predators matter, so it did not find them unnecessary.
This is the modest aim the forester stated for spraying.
questions.explain: A forester said insecticides buy time; that is all the manager wants, to preserve trees until the mill is ready for them.
questions.rule: A fix may only buy time.
questions.teaches: One forester said insecticides buy time, which is all a forest manager wants: to preserve the trees until the mill is ready for them.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: In Holling and Baskerville's account, what kept the budworm barely detectable in most years before spraying?
options: Hard winters that killed most of the larvae each year
Natural predators, including birds, a spider, a wasp and diseases
Regular forest fires that cleared the fir away every few years
Foresters who picked the larvae off the trees by hand each year
optionExplain: Cold winters are not mentioned.
Right: a set of natural enemies held it in check.
Fires are not part of her account.
Hand removal of larvae is not described; natural enemies kept the budworm down.
questions.explain: Predators kept it low. The card next explains the cycle in full.
questions.rule: Predators held it in check.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says that without budworm outbreaks balsam fir would crowd out spruce and birch.
questions.explain: Fir is the most competitive tree and, left to itself, would make the forest a monoculture of fir.
questions.rule: Outbreaks cut back the dominant tree.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: A long record shows the fir share falling sharply while spruce and birch rise. By the budworm cycle, what most likely happened?
options: Fir became less competitive for some reason unrelated to the budworm
Predators multiplied and the budworm vanished from the forest
An outbreak cut back the fir, opening space for others
Foresters sprayed the forest with DDT to protect the fir
optionExplain: The cycle explains the shift without another cause.
Predators hold it low; the fir loss follows an outbreak.
This is how an outbreak reopens the forest.
Spraying came later in the story; it does not explain the long-run shift from fir to spruce and birch.
questions.explain: Outbreaks hit the fir and let spruce and birch in.
questions.rule: Outbreak, then space for others.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: Put one turn of the natural cycle in order, starting with fir building up.
items: Fir builds up in the forest
The budworm explodes in an outbreak
The outbreak cuts the fir back
Spruce and birch move into the gaps
questions.explain: As fir builds up an outbreak becomes likely; the outbreak cuts the fir back; spruce and birch fill the gaps, until fir moves back in.
questions.rule: A repeating cycle.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: Which statement misdescribes the system before spraying?
options: Outbreaks came every year, so the forest was never stable
The budworm was barely detectable in most years
Predators held the budworm in check between outbreaks
Fir returned after each outbreak
optionExplain: Outbreaks came every few decades and lasted six to ten years.
The model's finding is that the budworm was barely detectable in most years, so this is accurate.
Predators held the budworm in check between outbreaks, so this is accurate.
Fir returned after each outbreak in the cycle, so this is accurate.
questions.explain: Outbreaks were infrequent. Between them predators kept the budworm very low.
questions.rule: Rare outbreaks, long calm.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: An ecologist records an eight-year outbreak, then thirty quiet years. Does this fit the budworm cycle?
options: No: outbreaks should come every single year in the forest
No: outbreaks should last less than a year each time
Yes: six to ten years, every few decades
Yes, but only if spraying had been used in the forest
optionExplain: The record she gives is every few decades.
Her outbreaks lasted six to ten years.
The pattern matches her description.
Her cycle is the pre-spraying one.
questions.explain: Meadows says every few decades there was an outbreak lasting six to ten years.
questions.rule: Match records to the cycle.
questions.teaches: Outbreaks recurred every few decades and each lasted six to ten years.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: What does event-level analysis blame for a budworm outburst, per Meadows?
options: The warm, dry springs in the weeks before it
The shortage of birds that year in the forest
The age of the surviving pines in the forest
The timing of the spraying schedule that year
optionExplain: Right: the visible final trigger.
Predators are part of the structural story.
Pines are not part of the cycle.
Spraying is part of the later story.
questions.explain: The springs are the event-level explanation. The card next shows the structure behind it.
questions.rule: Events point at triggers.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: True or false: Over a wide range predators multiply faster when budworms are more numerous, but beyond some point they cannot multiply faster.
questions.explain: A reinforcing relationship turns into a nonrelationship, and the budworm takes off.
questions.rule: Predators saturate.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: A call centre adds staff in step with rising calls until trained staff run out, then queues explode. Which part of the budworm story matches?
options: The warm, dry spring that triggers the outbreak in the forest
The fir monoculture crowding out spruce and birch
The budworm starving after it has killed the fir
Predators' response ends, so the pest takes off
optionExplain: That is the final trigger, not the saturating response.
That concerns tree competition.
That is the crash, not the takeoff.
The balancing response stops growing, leaving the reinforcing growth free.
questions.explain: The call centre's staffing response saturates just as predator multiplication does.
questions.rule: Controls can saturate.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: When the budworm finally kills off much of the fir, the reinforcing loop of reproduction yields dominance to the balancing loop of ____.
questions.explain: Only the budworm's own food shortage stops an outbreak, and the crash is nonlinear.
questions.rule: Starvation ends the outbreak.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: True or false: Because warm, dry springs trigger outbreaks, studying fir density loses nothing.
questions.explain: The probability of an outbreak rises nonlinearly as fir builds up; the springs are only the final trigger.
questions.rule: Triggers are not causes.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: Yeast in a vat is given more sugar and reproduces faster than in proportion to the extra food. Which budworm feature does this match?
options: Predators multiplying faster as the pest grows more numerous in the forest
Reproductive potential rising faster than the food supply
The crash when the food supply is cut
Warm, dry springs aiding the survival of larvae in the forest
optionExplain: This concerns the predators' growth, not the pest's own response to food.
This is how the budworm responds to more fir.
That concerns the end of the outbreak.
Warm, dry springs are the weather trigger, not the response to extra food.
questions.explain: Meadows says the budworm's reproductive potential increases more than proportionately to the availability of its favorite food.
questions.rule: Growth that outpaces food.
questions.teaches: The budworm's reproductive potential rises more than proportionately to the supply of its favorite food, balsam fir.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: Meadows calls the budworm system ecologically stable. What does she mean?
options: It shows no change at all from one year to the next year
It oscillates over decades but stays within bounds
It keeps the same trees on the land for a very long time
It yields a steady supply of timber
optionExplain: She describes decades-long oscillation.
Right: stable within bounds.
Tree species change through the cycle.
That is the economic view, which she says is unstable.
questions.explain: Stability here means a bounded cycle that can continue. The card next sets this against the economy.
questions.rule: Stable within bounds.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the budworm cycle is ecologically stable within bounds and could go on forever.
questions.explain: It oscillates over decades but is stable within bounds.
questions.rule: Cycles can be stable.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: A river floods meadows every few years, feeding wetlands but wrecking farms on the floodplain. Which lesson from the budworm fits?
options: Floods and outbreaks are random events with no pattern to them
An ecosystem that cycles must eventually collapse under the cycle
Only the economic view of stability counts
What is stable for the ecosystem can be unstable for the economy
optionExplain: Both floods and outbreaks follow cycles, so they are not patternless random events.
She says the budworm system can go on forever.
She sets two views side by side.
The wetlands thrive while the farms depend on steady conditions.
questions.explain: The same cycle looks stable or unstable depending on whose supply it affects.
questions.rule: Stability depends on the viewpoint.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: If the logging economy depends on a steady supply of fir and spruce, the natural budworm cycle is economically ____.
questions.explain: A cycle that cuts the fir periodically cannot give a steady supply.
questions.rule: Steady supply needs steady trees.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: True or false: A cycle that cuts the fir back periodically must be ecologically unsustainable and cannot go on forever.
questions.explain: Meadows says the system can go on forever; it is the economy that is unstable.
questions.rule: Do not mix ecological and economic stability.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: In a pond, a snail eats the dominant algae that would otherwise smother other plants. Which budworm role does the snail resemble?
options: The budworm, which lets other tree species persist
The pesticide, which removes the pest and its natural enemies
The logging industry, which needs a steady supply of the trees
The warm spring, which triggers an outbreak
optionExplain: This is how Meadows describes the budworm's main effect.
The snail is not described as removing an enemy.
The snail does not depend on a supply.
The spring is a trigger, not a role.
questions.explain: Meadows says the main effect of the budworm is to allow tree species other than fir to persist.
questions.rule: A check on the dominant species keeps diversity.
questions.teaches: The main effect of the budworm is to allow tree species other than fir to persist.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: Why does spraying make the budworm system more fragile, according to Meadows?
options: It makes the budworm resistant to the spray within a single season
It stops spruce and birch from growing back in the forest at all
It kills the pest's enemies too and keeps fir density high
It raises the temperature in warm, dry springs in the forest
optionExplain: Resistance is not her argument.
Her account concerns fir density and predators.
Right: weaker control loop, richer food.
Weather is not affected by spraying in her story.
questions.explain: Spraying removes a natural check and keeps the budworm's food high. The card next spells this out.
questions.rule: Spraying cuts the natural check.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: True or false: Spraying kills the pest's natural enemies too, weakening the loop that keeps the budworm in check.
questions.explain: It kills the natural enemies too, weakening the loop that keeps the budworm in check.
questions.rule: Insecticides do not choose.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: A farm sprays a crop pest and kills the beetles that ate it. Pest numbers spike whenever spraying lapses. Which budworm lesson fits?
options: A warm, dry spring was the true cause of each spike in pests
Pesticides never work on any crop pests in any circumstances
The farm's boundary was drawn too widely around the crop
Weakening the enemies' loop leaves the system dependent on the policy
optionExplain: Blaming a weather event is event-level thinking, not the structural lesson of the budworm.
Her point is about the system, not an absolute.
The trouble is a boundary drawn too narrowly, not widely.
The farm is now locked into spraying.
questions.explain: Removing the enemies removed the natural brake, so only the spray holds the pest back.
questions.rule: Policy replaces a natural loop.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: Holling warns that if the spraying policy fails there will be an outbreak more intense than any ____ before.
questions.explain: The managers have an incipient volcano: failure would bring an outbreak never seen before.
questions.rule: Failure releases the pent-up risk.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: True or false: Spraying lowers fir density, which moves the budworm away from the edge of explosion.
questions.explain: Spraying keeps fir density high, which moves the budworm up its nonlinear reproduction curve.
questions.rule: Spraying keeps the food high.

questions.section: Interlude • Spruce Budworms, Firs, and Pesticides
questions.q: A resort extends pest spraying to more land each year to hold pests down. What does Holling's phrase for the budworm case suggest?
options: A permanent end to outbreaks in the sprayed area for good
Persistent semi-outbreak conditions over ever larger areas
A return to the natural cycle in the sprayed area soon after
An even supply of timber across all areas
optionExplain: Holling describes a standing risk, not an end.
This is how Holling describes what forest practice set up.
The practice displaces the natural cycle.
That is the economic hope, not Holling's finding.
questions.explain: Holling says forest management set up persistent semi-outbreak conditions over larger and larger areas.
questions.rule: Control can spread the risk.
questions.teaches: Holling calls the result persistent semi-outbreak conditions, spreading over larger and larger areas.

questions.q: On a system diagram, what does a cloud stand for?
options: A feedback loop too complicated to draw on a single page
A region of the system where nothing happens at all
A stock at the start or end of a flow, ignored for now
A delay in the information passing around the system
optionExplain: Clouds mark stocks at the ends of flows, not complicated loops.
Clouds stand for stocks, which do exist.
Right: sources and sinks outside the boundary.
Delays are a different feature.
questions.explain: Clouds are ignored stocks at the edge of the diagram. The card next says why they matter.
questions.rule: A cloud hides a stock.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says clouds on a diagram usually mark a real boundary of the system.
questions.explain: She says they rarely mark a real boundary, because systems rarely have real boundaries.
questions.rule: Clouds are chosen, not found.

questions.q: A hospital flowchart shows patients arriving from a cloud. How should Meadows' warning be applied?
options: Ask what lies behind the cloud, such as referrals and illness
Accept it, since every cloud in a diagram is a true boundary
Remove it, as diagrams should show only closed loops of flows
Replace it with a single number for the arrivals each day
optionExplain: The cloud hides a stock that may shape arrivals.
She says most clouds are not real boundaries.
Clouds are acceptable simplifications.
A number would hide the stock again.
questions.explain: Treat a cloud as a question: what source is being ignored?
questions.rule: Ask what lies behind it.

questions.q: Meadows says that beyond the clouds of a diagram, the only boundaries are those of word, thought, perception and social ____.
questions.explain: These boundaries are artificial, mental-model boundaries.
questions.rule: Boundaries are agreed, not found.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says there is no firmly determinable boundary between the sea and the land.
questions.explain: She says there is no firmly determinable boundary between the sea and the land.
questions.rule: Nature draws no clean borders.

questions.q: A marsh where reeds meet dune grass shelters more species than either habitat alone. Which Meadows observation does this fit?
options: Boundaries are always the place where one system ends
Fewer species live where two habitats meet and mix
Complexities arise at boundaries, and mixed borders breed diversity
Edges of systems are the simplest part of them to model
optionExplain: She says systems rarely have real ends.
She says the reverse: borders and edges breed diversity.
She gives forest edges and the Czech-German border as examples.
She says the greatest complexities arise at boundaries, so edges are not the simplest part.
questions.explain: Meadows says the greatest complexities arise at boundaries, and disorderly, mixed-up borders are sources of diversity and creativity.
questions.rule: Edges breed complexity.
questions.teaches: The greatest complexities arise exactly at boundaries, and disorderly, mixed-up borders are sources of diversity and creativity.

questions.q: A model shows a dealer's cars arriving from a cloud. When is that acceptable?
options: When the stocks behind it are unlikely to matter over the period
When the diagram would otherwise get crowded with arrows
When the dealer has no control over how the supply arrives
When the cloud comes at the start of the flow, not the end
optionExplain: Right: the test is influence over the period.
Crowding alone is not the test.
Control over the supply is not her test; the test is whether the hidden stock would influence behavior.
The position of the cloud is not the test.
questions.explain: The test is whether the hidden stocks matter for the question. The card next gives the case.
questions.rule: Does the hidden stock matter?

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says cars really do come from a cloud into the dealer's inventory.
questions.explain: Cars come from the transformation of raw materials with capital, labor, energy, technology and management.
questions.rule: Every flow has a source.

questions.q: A bakery model draws flour as arriving from a cloud. When would that mislead?
options: If the bakery sells every loaf it bakes each day
If flour is guaranteed to be abundant throughout the study
If the model only covers a single week of baking
If a flour shortage is possible in the period studied
optionExplain: Strong demand supports the cloud.
Guaranteed abundance supports the cloud.
A short period can make clouds safer, not riskier.
A possible shortage makes the hidden stock matter.
questions.explain: A cloud misleads when a stock behind it could run short or glut.
questions.rule: Possible shortage means open the cloud.

questions.q: If raw materials are guaranteed to be abundant and consumers keep demanding the products, Meadows says that ____ will do.
questions.explain: In that case the stocks behind the flows will not change behavior.
questions.rule: Safe clouds, if supply and demand are secure.

questions.q: Which test for using a cloud is NOT Meadows'?
options: Whether the stock is likely to influence behavior significantly
A cloud is acceptable whenever the diagram would otherwise be too complex to read
The time period of interest
Whether a shortage or a glut is possible
optionExplain: This is her test: whether the stock is likely to influence behavior significantly.
Her test is influence on behavior, not complexity.
The time period of interest is part of her test, so this is hers.
She includes whether a shortage or a glut is possible, so this is hers.
questions.explain: Her test concerns influence over the period, not tidiness.
questions.rule: Influence, not convenience.

questions.q: A model draws a town's births and deaths as flows from and to clouds. Which new fact would make that boundary unserviceable?
options: A rise in the number of births each year in the town
Large migration, or a shortage of cemetery space
A change in the town's name or its local government
A longer life expectancy for the residents of the town
optionExplain: More births alone do not remove the cloud.
Meadows says cradle-to-grave boundaries fail in these cases.
A name has no effect on the flows.
This changes numbers, not the cloud.
questions.explain: Meadows says the cradle-to-grave boundaries would be unserviceable if the population had significant migration or if cemetery space was limited.
questions.rule: A cloud fails when the hidden flow matters.
questions.teaches: Even the cradle-to-grave boundary for a population fails if there is significant in- or out-migration, or if the problem is limited cemetery space.

questions.q: Which statement about boundaries around a system best matches Meadows?
options: A true boundary exists for each system and analysts must find it, not invent it
Any boundary is fine, since all choices lead to the same answer
A model should follow every link until it covers the whole planet
There is no single legitimate boundary; purpose decides
optionExplain: She says there are no separate systems.
She says narrow boundaries produce surprise.
She rejects following every link around the planet; models need boundaries.
Right: boundaries are invented for the question at hand.
questions.explain: Boundaries are chosen for a purpose. The card next explains how to choose.
questions.rule: Purpose picks the boundary.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says there is no single legitimate boundary to draw around any system.
questions.explain: She says there is no single, legitimate boundary; the world is a continuum.
questions.rule: No single true boundary.

questions.q: Two groups study the same river: one drinking water, the other shipping. What does Meadows' lesson allow?
options: Each may rightly draw its own boundary
Only one group is right, and the other must switch to its boundary
Both must model the whole planet to be valid in any way
Neither should draw any boundary, since all lines are artificial
optionExplain: Boundaries depend on the purpose of the discussion.
There is no single legitimate boundary.
She does not require modeling the whole planet; boundaries are needed to understand anything.
She says we must make boundaries to understand anything.
questions.explain: The right boundary depends on the questions asked.
questions.rule: Different questions, different boundaries.

questions.q: Where to draw a boundary around a system depends on the ____ of the discussion.
questions.explain: The questions we want to ask decide the boundary.
questions.rule: Ask the question first.

questions.q: True or false: Since boundaries are artificial, Meadows concludes a model should have none.
questions.explain: She says that to understand anything we have to simplify, which means making boundaries.
questions.rule: We still need boundaries.

questions.q: A town assumes its landfill will last indefinitely. Which point of Meadows' about long-term thinking does this ignore?
options: Dumps are always the best boundary to draw for waste problems
Garbage disappears into a cloud when it has been buried
As the footprint expands, the long term becomes the short term
Geological cycles will refill the landfill within a year or so
optionExplain: She says the full flow can matter.
She says people's models picture garbage going away; that is the mistake.
Landfills fill up, and mines run out, with surprising suddenness.
Geological cycles act over eons.
questions.explain: Meadows says whether the full flow from mine to dump matters depends on who wants to know, for what purpose, over how long, and the long term is increasingly the short term.
questions.rule: The long term can arrive suddenly.
questions.teaches: As the physical economy grows and society's ecological footprint expands, the long term is increasingly becoming the short term, so landfills fill, and mines run out, with surprising suddenness.

questions.q: What does Hardin say the popular term side-effects roughly means?
options: Effects that are small compared with the principal effect
Effects that appear outside the target area
Effects caused by chance rather than action
Effects I had not foreseen or do not want to think about
optionExplain: Hardin says they deserve no lesser rank.
The term is about our attention, not geography.
He does not say they are chance.
Right: it protects us from thinking in systems.
questions.explain: Hardin treats the term as an excuse. The card next gives the boundary lesson.
questions.rule: Side effects are effects.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says drawing boundaries too narrowly can lead the system to surprise you.
questions.explain: Her example is highways that attract housing and refill with cars.
questions.rule: Narrow boundary, surprise.

questions.q: A council widens a road to ease congestion; homes spread along it and congestion returns. What was the error?
options: The boundary included too many separate systems at once
The boundary left out the settlement patterns
The road was an event, not a part of any system
Cars should have been counted as a flow, not as a stock of vehicles
optionExplain: Her error is leaving the pattern out.
Highways attract housing along their length, as in her example.
The road is part of the system.
The error is the boundary, not the type of variable.
questions.explain: The road changed where people live, and that fed back onto the road.
questions.rule: Include what responds to your action.

questions.q: A park is managed only inside its fence. Which of these may cross the fence and surprise the managers?
options: The park's official perimeter line itself
Migrating wildlife
The park's entry fee schedule
Acid rain
Water flowing into, out of or under the park
optionExplain: The line does not move.
She lists migrating wildlife.
Not among the crossing effects.
She lists acid rain.
She lists these waters.
questions.explain: She lists nomadic peoples, migrating wildlife, waters, effects of development at the edges, acid rain and climate change.
questions.rule: Fences do not stop flows.

questions.q: True or false: Hardin holds that effects called side-effects deserve a lower rank than the principal effect.
questions.explain: He says side-effects no more deserve the adjective side than the principal effect does.
questions.rule: No effect is merely a side effect.

questions.q: A town dumps sewage in a river and downstream towns object. How far should the sewage boundary extend, per Meadows?
options: The whole river and perhaps its groundwater, not the next watershed
The town's own limits only, since the sewage began there
The whole planet's water cycle, since all water is connected
Only the river itself, never the soil or the groundwater
optionExplain: This is her reading of the case.
That is the narrow boundary that caused the problem.
She says this is probably not needed.
She suggests groundwater might also be included.
questions.explain: Meadows says the boundary must include the whole river, perhaps also the soil and groundwater, and probably not the next watershed or the planetary hydrological cycle.
questions.rule: Extend to what feeds back; stop where it ceases to matter.
questions.teaches: For the sewage case Meadows says the boundary must cover the whole river, might cover the soil and groundwater, and probably need not cover the next watershed or the planetary hydrological cycle.

questions.q: What trap does Meadows say systems analysts often fall into with boundaries?
options: Making boundaries too narrow, so that they miss the feedback
Refusing to draw any boundary at all around a system
Making boundaries too large, so the answer is obscured
Letting politicians choose the boundary
optionExplain: That is the first trap, which she says is common.
She says analysts do draw them.
Right: the opposite trap to narrow boundaries.
The trap she names is the analysts' own.
questions.explain: Analysts overshoot in the other direction. The card next gives the example.
questions.rule: Too big is also wrong.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says large, everything-connected diagrams can obscure the answers to the questions at hand.
questions.explain: They produce piles of information that may only serve to obscure the answers.
questions.rule: More is not clearer.

questions.q: A planner needs to cut a city's traffic emissions, and her team models the entire regional economy. What would Meadows say?
options: The model may bury the answer; fit its reach to the question
The broader the model, the better the advice it can give
The model is fine since it includes the traffic in the city
The team should drop all but one variable from the model
optionExplain: Too large a boundary can obscure the answer.
She rejects the bigger-model game.
Including traffic does not make the rest useful.
That would be the narrow trap.
questions.explain: A model should be only as wide as the question needs.
questions.rule: Fit the model to the question.

questions.q: If you drew a model of the whole climate to cut one country's CO2 emissions, Meadows says the detail may not be ____.
questions.explain: Full climate detail is interesting but may not be necessary for that question.
questions.rule: Detail has a cost.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows names the attitude that anything less than everything is academically illegitimate as a trap.
questions.explain: She describes the attitude that anything less is academically illegitimate, as the trap.
questions.rule: Do not confuse size with rigor.

questions.q: A consultant rejects a colleague's compact model because it leaves things out, calling it unscholarly. Which Meadows phrase fits?
options: Clouds are a necessary part of models of flows
The right boundary rarely follows a political border or a river
Everything physical goes somewhere
If you have considered less, you are academically illegitimate
optionExplain: This is about simplifying, not the attitude.
This is about borders, not model size.
Everything physical goes somewhere is about material flows, not about the attitude toward model size.
This is the attitude she mocks.
questions.explain: Meadows presents the bigger-is-better attitude as a game and a trap.
questions.rule: Bigger models are not truer.
questions.teaches: Analysts who draw boundaries too large treat anything less as academically illegitimate, in a my-model-is-bigger-than-yours game.

questions.q: Why, according to Meadows, are rivers poor borders for managing water?
options: They rarely flow between countries, so they are seldom used
They make handy borders but the worst for managing water
They are too small to have an effect on the water supply
They change course too slowly to be mapped as borders
optionExplain: She says they are used as borders.
Right: a river is one system split by a border.
Size is not her point; rivers make poor borders because they split a single water system.
The speed of river course changes is not her point; rivers join a water system across a border.
questions.explain: A river splits a single water system between countries. The card next gives more examples.
questions.rule: Borders cut water systems.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the right boundary for a problem rarely matches an academic discipline or a political boundary.
questions.explain: She says it rarely coincides with either.
questions.rule: Problems ignore borders.

questions.q: Two neighboring countries share a river and each manages only its own bank. What would Meadows predict?
options: Better outcomes, since each country controls its own part of it
Trouble managing the water, as the right boundary is the river
No difference, since boundaries are only words in people's minds
A fairer share, since both sides act rationally for themselves
optionExplain: A border down the river splits one water system, so owning one bank does not give better control.
Rivers are handy borders but the worst for managing water.
Boundaries of word still have real effects.
Her point is about boundary, not fairness.
questions.explain: A river is one water system, so each country managing only its own bank splits the system; a shared river needs a shared view.
questions.rule: Manage the whole system.

questions.q: Meadows says that for ozone depletion, greenhouse gases and ocean dumping, national boundaries mean ____.
questions.explain: Air crosses borders even more freely than water.
questions.rule: Air ignores borders.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says we are usually flexible enough to find the right boundary for each new problem.
questions.explain: She says ideally we would, but we are rarely that flexible and get attached to accustomed boundaries.
questions.rule: We cling to old borders.

questions.q: A diagram shows people entering a prison from a cloud. What should such a cloud prompt, per Meadows?
options: Stopping the analysis there, since the flow begins outside the system
Replacing the cloud with a smaller cloud covering fewer sources
Counting only the people already inside the prison at the time
Thinking beyond the border, such as what supplies the people
optionExplain: This treats the cloud as a wall, which is her warning.
A smaller cloud still hides the source.
Counting only people already inside ignores the inflow, which is the question the cloud raises.
She says a cloud should start thinking beyond the borders, not stop it.
questions.explain: Her examples of clouds that should start thinking, not stop it: what drives the supply of people given new sentences, where fuel rods go after replacement, and what happens to an unemployed person whose registration lapses.
questions.rule: A cloud is a prompt to look further.
questions.teaches: Her examples of clouds that should start thinking, not stop it: what drives the supply of people given new sentences, where fuel rods go after replacement, and what happens to an unemployed person whose registration lapses.

questions.q: Why do systems surprise us, in this part of Meadows' chapter?
options: Our minds like single causes and avoid limits
The world has too few causes for any of us to track at once
Limits are rare, and we exaggerate the few that exist
Our plans never involve limits of any kind in the real world
optionExplain: Right: she links surprise to simple thinking and neglect of limits.
She says many causes act at once.
She says virtually all inputs are limited.
She says we dislike thinking about limits in our plans.
questions.explain: We prefer one cause and one effect, and we avoid limits. The card next lists what real processes need.
questions.rule: Many causes, many limits.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says that multiple inputs produce multiple outputs and virtually all are limited.
questions.explain: This is her description of the real world.
questions.rule: Everything is limited.

questions.q: A cafe owner counts only customers and chefs as what the cafe needs. Which gap does Meadows' list point to?
options: Nothing is missing; customers and chefs are all that matter to it
Only land, since all the other inputs can be bought
Energy, water, supplies, insurance and other inputs also matter
Only the owner's plans, which set the limits for the cafe
optionExplain: Her point is that more than a few things matter.
She does not rank inputs this way.
Her lists show many inputs behind any process.
The limits are in the world, not the plan.
questions.explain: A real process rests on many inputs, each of which can run short.
questions.rule: Look beyond the obvious inputs.

questions.q: A patch of growing grain needs many nutrients; Meadows lists nitrogen, phosphorus and ____ among them.
questions.explain: She lists nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and dozens of minor nutrients.
questions.rule: Grain has many inputs.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says our minds like to think about limits, especially when our plans are involved.
questions.explain: She says we do not like thinking about limits when our own plans and desires are involved.
questions.rule: We avoid limits.

questions.q: A startup lists capital, labor and technology as its inputs. Which further input from Meadows' manufacturing list does it overlook?
options: A competitor's price list for the same sort of work
The founder's reputation among investors and customers
A better office address in a busier part of the city
Functioning families that raise producers and consumers
optionExplain: A competitor's price list is not on her list of manufacturing inputs.
A founder's reputation is not on her list of inputs.
An address in a busier part of the city is not on her list of inputs.
This is on her list, with infrastructure and a healthy ecosystem.
questions.explain: Her industrial list also includes public infrastructure and services, functioning families, and a healthy ecosystem to supply inputs and absorb wastes.
questions.rule: Inputs include the social and natural base.
questions.teaches: An industrial process also depends on public-funded infrastructure and services, functioning families raising producers and consumers, and a healthy ecosystem that supplies inputs and absorbs wastes.

questions.q: Grain has plenty of nitrogen but is short of phosphorus. What does Liebig's law say about adding more nitrogen?
options: It will help a little, as every nutrient adds some growth
It will not help, as phosphorus is the limiting input
It will harm the grain, as any excess of nitrogen does
It will help only if potassium is also added to the soil
optionExplain: The law says the shortest input sets the limit.
Right: the shortest input limits.
Harm from excess nitrogen is not the law's point; the law says the shortest input sets the limit.
Potassium is not the missing input.
questions.explain: More of an abundant input does not help. The card next generalizes.
questions.rule: The scarcest input sets the limit.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the input most important to a system at any time is the one that is most limiting.
questions.explain: She states the concept this way: the input most important to a system at any time is the one that is most limiting.
questions.rule: Most limiting means most important.

questions.q: A clinic has many doctors but too few sterile instruments. Where does Meadows' reasoning say to put effort?
options: On hiring more doctors, since they are the main resource
On advertising to bring in more patients
On sterile instruments, the most limiting input
On equally raising every input
optionExplain: More of a plentiful input does not help.
Demand is not the limit here; the clinic's output is held back by instruments.
Adding doctors does not raise output while instruments are short.
Equal effort wastes effort on abundant inputs.
questions.explain: The scarcest needed input sets the output.
questions.rule: Fix the bottleneck.

questions.q: Meadows says bread will not rise without yeast, no matter how much ____ it has.
questions.explain: The missing yeast limits the bread however much flour is present.
questions.rule: The missing input rules.

questions.q: Which advice gets Liebig's law wrong?
options: Add more of whichever nutrient the plant has most of
Check whether phosphorus is short before adding nitrogen to it
Find which input is most limiting right now
Do not add potassium if the real shortage is something else
optionExplain: Adding a plentiful input does not help.
Checking for a phosphorus shortage before adding nitrogen follows the law.
Finding the most limiting input follows the law.
Not adding potassium when something else is short follows the law.
questions.explain: The law directs effort to the shortest input.
questions.rule: Do not feed the abundant.

questions.q: Agronomists assume they know what belongs in artificial fertilizer. How does Meadows question that assumption?
options: She argues that fertilizers are harmless to the life in soil because they feed the grain
She says that every needed nutrient is already identified by science
They may have missed nutrients or harmed soil microbes
She argues that nitrogen alone is enough for all growing grain
optionExplain: She asks whether they interfere with soil functions.
She asks whether some are missing.
She asks these questions about agronomists' assumptions.
She does not say nitrogen alone is enough; she lists several nutrients agronomists might have missed.
questions.explain: Meadows asks whether essential nutrients remain unidentified, how fertilizers affect soil microbes, and what limits fertilizer production.
questions.rule: Even experts may not know the limiting factor.
questions.teaches: Meadows asks whether there are essential nutrients agronomists have not identified, how artificial fertilizer affects soil microbes, and what limits the production of fertilizer.

questions.q: Why did economics come to track mostly capital and labor?
options: They were the most common limits when economics evolved
They are the only inputs that can be measured in money
They are the only inputs that cost money to a producer
Economists were forbidden to study the environment in those days
optionExplain: Right: the theory matched the limits of its time.
Measurement is not her reason.
Cost to a producer is not her reason; the theory matched the limits of its era.
She gives no such reason; economics tracked capital and labor because they were the common limits.
questions.explain: The theory fitted its era. The card next explains what changed.
questions.rule: Theory follows past limits.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says most economic production functions track labor and capital, and sometimes technology.
questions.explain: She describes economic production functions as tracking labor and capital, and sometimes technology.
questions.rule: Two or three tracked factors.

questions.q: A farm region's model tracks only capital and labor, but its wells begin to run low. What does Meadows' view suggest?
options: The model is still complete, as capital and labor are what matter
Labor must be the problem after all, since output has fallen
Capital should be raised until the water supply returns again
The model misses the new limit, water
optionExplain: It leaves out the factor now limiting.
Labor is still not the limit in this case.
Capital does not create water.
Limiting factors shift to clean water and similar inputs.
questions.explain: When the limit moves, the tracked factors stop explaining output.
questions.rule: Re-check the limit.

questions.q: As the economy grows relative to the ecosystem, limits shift to clean water, clean air, dump space and acceptable forms of energy and raw ____.
questions.explain: She names clean water, clean air, dump space and acceptable energy and raw materials as the factors that become limiting.
questions.rule: Limits shift to the environment.

questions.q: Which statement misreads the section?
options: Economics evolved when labor and capital were common limits
Capital and labor have never been limiting factors
Focus on only two factors becomes unhelpful as the economy grows
The limiting factors can shift over time
optionExplain: She says economics evolved when labor and capital were common limits, so this is accurate.
She says they were the most common limits in economics' early days.
She says a focus on two factors becomes unhelpful as the economy grows, so this is accurate.
She says limiting factors can shift over time, so this is accurate.
questions.explain: She says capital and labor were once the most common limits.
questions.rule: Limits change over time.

questions.q: Rich countries send capital and technology to a poor country and its economy still fails to grow. What explanation does Meadows suggest?
options: Capital and technology never help any economy, in any place
Capital and technology may not be the limits there
The poor country refuses to make use of the capital it receives
The economy cannot grow in any case, whatever it is given
optionExplain: She does not say capital and technology never help; she says they may simply not be the most limiting factors.
She says donors never think of this.
Refusing the capital is not her explanation; the donors overlook that other factors may be the limits.
She does not say the economy cannot grow; she says capital and technology may not be what limits it.
questions.explain: Meadows says rich countries wonder why economies do not develop, never thinking that capital or technology may not be the most limiting factors.
questions.rule: Supply the missing input, not the familiar one.
questions.teaches: Rich countries transfer capital or technology to poor ones and wonder why economies still do not develop, never thinking that these may not be the most limiting factors.

questions.q: What does Forrester's company model show about limits as a company grows?
options: The limit stays at the same factor throughout the growth
Limits vanish once the company is large enough to ignore them
Only outside events, such as the market, change the limits
The limits shift as the company grows
optionExplain: The model shows the limit moving from one factor to another as the company grows.
Limits remain; the factor changes.
The company's own growth changes them.
Right: shifting limits.
questions.explain: The limit moves as the company grows. The card next gives the sequence.
questions.rule: Limits move with growth.

questions.q: Order the limits that Forrester's growing company meets, from first to last.
items: Production capacity falls behind orders
Labor skill is too thin after hurried hiring
Order-fulfillment and record-keeping systems clog
questions.explain: Delivery delays push expansion of plants; hurried hiring cuts quality; training fixes quality and then the order system clogs.
questions.rule: Each fix reveals the next limit.

questions.q: A shop fixes slow service by hiring staff, then finds the stockroom cannot keep up. Which Meadows idea is this?
options: Growth ended one limit and exposed the next one
A cloud hiding a flow from the people drawing the diagram
A delay in perception between the shop and its customers
A linear response to hiring, with each new hire adding the same
optionExplain: This matches the company story.
A cloud is a boundary issue; the shop's case is about the next bottleneck appearing.
The case concerns the next bottleneck, not a delay.
The point is the shifting limit.
questions.explain: Each fix removes one limit and brings the next into view.
questions.rule: Fixes move the limit.

questions.q: When one factor ceases to be limiting, growth occurs until another factor becomes ____.
questions.explain: Growth changes the relative scarcity of factors.
questions.rule: Growth moves the limit.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says that once a company has solved its present limit, another factor becomes limiting as it grows.
questions.explain: She says growth changes the scarcity of factors until another becomes limiting.
questions.rule: There is always a next limit.

questions.q: A growing plant, a growing epidemic and a growing city all meet limits. What does Meadows say surrounds each of them?
options: Only plants meet limits, as they depend on soil and sun
Epidemics have no limits, since germs can spread anywhere
Each is surrounded by layers of limits
Cities stop growing at the same size, whatever the place
optionExplain: She lists many growing things.
She includes epidemics among growing things surrounded by layers of limits.
She names plants, children, epidemics, products, companies, cities and economies.
She does not say cities stop at the same size; each meets its own layers of limits.
questions.explain: Meadows lists growing plants, children, epidemics, products, technologies, companies, cities, economies and populations as surrounded by layers of limits.
questions.rule: Every growing thing has layers of limits.
questions.teaches: Layers of limits surround every growing plant, child, epidemic, new product, technological advance, company, city, economy and population, not only companies.

questions.q: What does Meadows say about perpetual growth of a physical entity in a finite environment?
options: It is possible if the next limit is watched closely enough
It is possible if technology keeps improving year after year
It is impossible, so growth should never be attempted at all
It is impossible; the choice is which limits to accept
optionExplain: She says watching limits is not a recipe for perpetual growth.
She does not claim technology makes perpetual growth possible; growth in a finite environment cannot go on forever.
She says choose limits, not stop growing.
Right: limits are certain, only their source is a choice.
questions.explain: Growth cannot go on forever. The card next says who sets the limits.
questions.rule: Limits are certain.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says limits to growth can be self-imposed, and if they are not they will be system-imposed.
questions.explain: If people do not set their own limits, the environment will.
questions.rule: Self-imposed or system-imposed.

questions.q: A fishing town votes a catch quota before stocks collapse. Which Meadows idea does this show?
options: A cloud hiding the source of the fish from the town
Choosing and enforcing its own limit early
A delay in the information passed to the fishers of the town
Event-level analysis of each catch landed at the harbor
optionExplain: This is about limits, not boundaries.
This matches her self-imposed limits.
The quota is a chosen limit, not a delay.
The quota acts on the structure of the fishery, not on single catches as events.
questions.explain: A limit set by people avoids one set by collapse.
questions.rule: Set the limit yourself.

questions.q: If managers and governments do not choose their own limits, Meadows says the ____ will choose and enforce them.
questions.explain: System-imposed limits come from the supporting environment.
questions.rule: The environment will choose.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says that if a firm makes a perfect product at an affordable price, its growth can continue indefinitely.
questions.explain: It will be swamped with orders until some limit reduces the perfection or raises the price.
questions.rule: Success meets limits.

questions.q: A city meets its residents' needs better than any other and people flock to it. What does Meadows expect?
options: The city grows without end, since people keep arriving to it
The flow of newcomers stops at once when the city is full
Some limit eventually brings down the city's ability to satisfy needs
The city shrinks to its original size within a few years
optionExplain: She says growth cannot continue forever.
She expects them to flock until a limit bites.
This is her example of a successful city.
She does not say the city shrinks back in a few years; she says some limit eventually brings down its ability to satisfy needs.
questions.explain: Meadows says people will flock to the city until some limit brings down its ability to satisfy their needs.
questions.rule: Success invites limits.
questions.teaches: If a city meets its inhabitants' needs better than any other, people will flock there until some limit brings down the city's ability to satisfy them.

questions.q: What correction did Jay Forrester tell modelers to apply to estimated delays?
options: Ask everyone, guess, and multiply by three
Halve the longest estimate given by anyone in the system
Use the shortest estimate given by anyone in the system
Add one year to every estimate that anyone in the system gives
optionExplain: Right: delays are underestimated.
He did not suggest shortening.
Estimates are too short already.
He gave a multiplier, not a fixed addition.
questions.explain: Delays take longer than we expect. The card next explains why they matter.
questions.rule: Multiply by three.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says every stock is a delay.
questions.explain: Every stock takes time to fill or drain, so it works as a delay.
questions.rule: Stocks are delays.

questions.q: A project team guesses its approval process will take two weeks. What would Forrester's correction suggest to plan for?
options: About one week
About two weeks
About six weeks
About three weeks
optionExplain: That shortens instead of lengthening.
Planning for two weeks ignores the correction that people guess delays too short.
Two weeks multiplied by three.
That adds one, not multiplies by three.
questions.explain: People guess too short; the multiplier corrects it.
questions.rule: Triple the guess.

questions.q: Forrester's rule: ask everyone how long they think a delay is, make your best guess, and multiply by ____.
questions.explain: Forrester's correction is to ask everyone, make your best guess, and multiply by three, since people guess delays too short.
questions.rule: Multiply by three.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says delays are ubiquitous: every stock is a delay and most flows have them.
questions.explain: She says delays are ubiquitous; every stock is a delay and most flows have them.
questions.rule: Delays are everywhere.
