questions.q: Pig prices rise and fall in about four-year waves, and cocoa prices in about eleven-year waves. What does Meadows attribute these cycles to?
options: Gestation and maturation delays in breeding populations
Seasonal weather alone, which sets the same cycle each year
Changes in the advertising of the product to consumers
Variations in the money supply from one year to the next
optionExplain: She names 4-year cycles for pigs, 7 for cows, 11 for cocoa trees.
She names delays, not weather.
She does not name advertising.
She does not name the money supply.
questions.explain: Meadows says the delay in building up breeding populations causes the characteristic oscillations in commodity prices: 4 years for pigs, 7 for cows and 11 for cocoa trees.
questions.rule: Biology sets the delay.
questions.teaches: Gestation and maturation delays in building up breeding populations cause commodity price cycles of about 4 years for pigs, 7 years for cows and 11 years for cocoa trees.

questions.q: If you worry about oscillations that take weeks, which delays does Meadows say you can probably ignore?
options: Those that last weeks, since they are the same as the cycle
Those that last days only, since they are within the weeks
No delays can be ignored; all must be included in the model
Those lasting minutes, or years
optionExplain: Those are the ones that matter.
The weeks-long scale includes days.
She says what matters depends on the question.
Right: they sit at other frequencies.
questions.explain: Delays at very different time scales can be ignored. The card next explains the principle.
questions.rule: Match the time scale.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the important delays in a model depend on the purpose of the discussion.
questions.explain: She says the delays that matter depend on the purpose of the discussion, just as the appropriate boundaries do.
questions.rule: Purpose picks the delays.

questions.q: A study of how a region's economy develops over decades includes hourly traffic jams. What does Meadows' view suggest?
options: They must be included, as every delay in the system matters
Those short oscillations can usually be ignored
They are the main driver of development in the region
They cannot exist without cars on the roads of the region
optionExplain: What matters depends on the frequencies studied.
Decades-long development usually allows ignoring oscillations of weeks.
She does not say hourly jams drive regional development; they are too fast to matter for decades.
The point is time scale, not cars.
questions.explain: For a study over decades, oscillations of hours or weeks can usually be ignored because the delays that matter depend on the time scale.
questions.rule: Choose the time scale.

questions.q: The world peeps, squawks, bangs and thunders at many ____ all at once.
questions.explain: Her image for the many time scales at which things happen.
questions.rule: Many frequencies.

questions.q: Which statement misreads Meadows on delays?
options: Which delays matter depends on the question being asked
A model should include every delay in the system
Minute-long delays may be ignored in a study lasting weeks
Years-long delays may be ignored in a study lasting weeks
optionExplain: She says which delays matter depends on the question asked, so this is accurate.
She says significance depends on the frequencies of interest.
She says minute-long delays may be ignored in a study lasting weeks, so this is accurate.
She says years-long delays may be ignored in a study lasting weeks, so this is accurate.
questions.explain: She asks the modeler to pick delays by time scale.
questions.rule: Not every delay matters.

questions.q: A hospital manager studies how patients queue within a single shift. Which of Meadows' parallels applies?
options: Delays are all equally important to every study of a hospital
Only delays longer than a year matter to a hospital study
Only delays shorter than a minute matter to a hospital study
As with boundaries, delays depend on purpose and time scale
optionExplain: She says delays differ in importance depending on the frequencies studied.
Delays longer than a year are not the only ones that matter; relevance depends on the frequencies being studied.
Delays shorter than a minute are not the only ones that matter; relevance depends on the time scale studied.
She compares delays and boundaries.
questions.explain: Meadows writes that just as appropriate boundaries depend on purpose, so do the important delays.
questions.rule: Same purpose rule as boundaries.
questions.teaches: Just as the appropriate boundaries depend on the purpose of the discussion, so do the important delays.

questions.q: What does Meadows say can happen when a decision maker responds to delayed information?
options: Actions are too much or too little, missing the goal
Actions are exactly on target, since delays force care
Actions become faster, as pressure builds
Actions no longer matter to the system
optionExplain: Right: decisions are off target.
Delays push decisions off target.
Her point is accuracy, not speed.
She says they matter and may overshoot.
questions.explain: Delays lead to overshoot or undershoot. The card next gives the full list.
questions.rule: Delayed information, off-target action.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says acting too fast can nervously amplify short-term variation and create unnecessary instability.
questions.explain: Quick reactions to short-term swings can make things worse.
questions.rule: Fast is not always better.

questions.q: A shower controller reacts to the water temperature only after a long lag, and the water swings hot then cold. What does Meadows' view say?
options: The swings come from random changes in the pipes
The controller should react faster at once to each change
The delay in the feedback loop causes the swings
The swings are an event, with no cause in the structure
optionExplain: Her account blames the delay in the feedback loop, not random changes in the pipes.
Fast action may amplify variation.
Oscillations come from delays.
They come from structure and delay.
questions.explain: A lag in the loop makes the correction arrive late and overshoot.
questions.rule: Late correction overshoots.

questions.q: Meadows says delays are often sensitive leverage ____ for policy, if they can be made shorter or longer.
questions.explain: Changing a delay may utterly change behavior.
questions.rule: Delays are leverage points.

questions.q: Which claim does Meadows NOT make?
options: Delays determine how timely the information is
Delays affect how accurately a system hits its targets
Overshoots, oscillations and collapses come from delays
Longer delays always make a system more stable
optionExplain: She says delays determine how timely the information is, so she does make this claim.
She says delays affect how accurately a system hits its targets, so she does make this claim.
She says overshoots, oscillations and collapses come from delays, so she does make this claim.
She says changing the delay may utterly change behavior, not that longer is steadier.
questions.explain: She does not give a direction for the effect of a longer delay.
questions.rule: Delay length changes behavior.

questions.q: The electric industry builds plants slowly, and so swings between overcapacity and undercapacity. Which cause does Meadows name?
options: A fixed price of electricity set by the regulators
Long delays in building new power plants across the industry
Customers' refusal to use power in the evening hours
A lack of any feedback in the industry about demand
optionExplain: She does not name a regulated price; the cause she names is the long delay in building plants.
She says this causes cycles of overcapacity then brownouts.
Evening usage habits are not her cause; the cause is the delay in building power plants.
The feedback exists; the delay is the issue.
questions.explain: Meadows says long delays in building power plants plague the electricity industry with cycles of overcapacity and then undercapacity leading to brownouts.
questions.rule: Slow supply gives cycles.
questions.teaches: Because of long delays in building new power plants, the electricity industry is plagued with cycles of overcapacity and then undercapacity leading to brownouts.

questions.q: What does Meadows say is essential when feedback loops contain long delays?
options: Faster reaction to each new problem
Waiting until the problem is obvious
Some sort of foresight
Removing the feedback altogether
optionExplain: Speed alone may amplify variation.
She says this misses the chance.
Right: waiting until a problem is obvious is too late.
She does not suggest removing the feedback; she says foresight is essential with long delays.
questions.explain: Foresight is her answer to long delays. The card next gives her examples.
questions.rule: Look ahead.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says Gorbachev could change the Soviet physical economy almost overnight.
questions.explain: He could transform its information system virtually overnight, but not the physical economy, which takes decades.
questions.rule: Information is fast; the economy is slow.

questions.q: A city waits until its reservoirs are visibly low before building new ones, which takes years. What does Meadows' view imply?
options: It is acting too late, since long delays call for foresight
It is acting wisely, as it responds to real evidence of need
It should act faster at once on each small change in the level
It should ignore the delay in construction when it plans
optionExplain: To act only when a problem is obvious misses a chance.
She says waiting for evidence misses the chance.
Fast action may add instability.
The construction delay is the point: it means the city has to plan ahead.
questions.explain: A long delay means the response must start before the problem is obvious.
questions.rule: Start before it shows.

questions.q: Meadows says human fossil-fuel emissions have already induced changes in climate that will not be fully revealed for a generation or ____.
questions.explain: The oceans respond over decades to warmer temperatures.
questions.rule: Climate responds slowly.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says acting only once a problem becomes obvious is the best way to solve it when delays are long.
questions.explain: She says to act only then is to miss an important opportunity to solve the problem.
questions.rule: Obvious means late.

questions.q: Reunification brought more hardship, over a longer time, than politicians foresaw. Which cause does Meadows give?
options: The bad intentions of the planners towards the east
A lack of money in West Germany for the changes needed
Long delays that the politicians did not allow for
The speed of the information system of the Soviet Union
optionExplain: She does not blame the planners' intentions; she points to delays they did not allow for.
A lack of money is not her explanation; delays are.
She uses the East German case to illustrate delays.
Her contrast is between information and the physical economy.
questions.explain: Meadows says delays help us see why the absorption of East Germany produced more hardship over a longer time than politicians foresaw.
questions.rule: Physical change is slow.
questions.teaches: Delays help explain why the absorption of East Germany by West Germany produced more hardship over a longer time than the politicians foresaw.

questions.q: What does Meadows say about the invisible hand?
options: It would be nice, but rational choices often add up to results nobody likes
It always works, as selfish choices are good for all in the end
It never works, and markets have no value for anyone
It works only in fishing, where choices are hidden from others
optionExplain: Right: she sets Smith's hope against evidence.
She rejects the claim that selfish choices always work out well for all.
She does not say markets have no value; she says rational choices often add up to results nobody wants.
Fishing is one of her counterexamples where the invisible hand fails, not the only place it works.
questions.explain: Her evidence runs against the invisible hand. The card next gives the cases.
questions.rule: Rational parts, poor whole.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says tourists who flock to a place can end up complaining that it has been ruined by tourists.
questions.explain: She gives Waikiki and Zermatt as examples of rational choices adding up to an unwanted result.
questions.rule: Individually rational, collectively poor.

questions.q: Every farmer in a district plants more wheat to earn more, and prices collapse. Which Meadows example does this match?
options: Tourists flocking to Waikiki and complaining of the crowds
Fishermen overfishing a stock until their own catch falls
Corporations timing a business cycle by their joint investments
Farmers producing surplus wheat, butter or cheese, so prices fall
optionExplain: Crowding at Waikiki is her tourism example, not the wheat surplus case.
Overfishing is her fishery example, not the farmers' surplus.
Joint investment timing is her business cycle example, not the wheat price collapse.
This is one of her listed cases.
questions.explain: Each farmer acts rationally, yet together they cause the collapse.
questions.rule: Aggregate result, not individual intent.

questions.q: Herman Daly calls the failure of the invisible hand the invisible ____.
questions.explain: Daly's name for it is the invisible foot.
questions.rule: Invisible hand, invisible foot.

questions.q: Which reading of Meadows is wrong?
options: Rational short-term choices can add up to unwanted results
People acting in their own interest reliably promote society's good
The invisible hand would make economic analysis much easier
Fishermen who overfish destroy their own livelihood
optionExplain: She says rational short-term choices can add up to unwanted results, so this reading is right.
She says this does not hold.
She says the invisible hand would make analysis easier, so this reading is right.
She says overfishers destroy their own livelihood, so this reading is right.
questions.explain: She argues the invisible hand does not reliably work.
questions.rule: Do not trust the hand.

questions.q: Companies each expand when times are good, and a downturn follows. Which Meadows example fits?
options: Poor people having more babies than they can support at all
Corporations collectively making investment decisions that cause downturns
Tourists ruining a resort by crowding into it every summer
Farmers producing surplus butter that sends its price lower
optionExplain: Poor people having more babies is another example on her list, not the investment downturn.
This is on her list.
Crowded resorts are another example on her list, not the investment downturn.
Surplus butter is another example on her list, not the investment downturn.
questions.explain: Meadows lists corporations whose collective investment decisions cause downturns, along with overcrowded resorts, surpluses, overfishing and poverty.
questions.rule: Individual choices, shared downturn.
questions.teaches: Meadows lists corporations making investment decisions that collectively cause business-cycle downturns, and poor people having more babies than they can support, among rational choices with results nobody likes.

questions.q: What does bounded rationality mean, according to Meadows?
options: People make irrational decisions because they are careless or lazy
People have perfect information but they have poor judgment
Only experts can decide rationally, and others guess at random
People make reasonable decisions on incomplete information
optionExplain: The decisions are reasonable for the information.
Their information is imperfect.
She makes no claim that only experts decide rationally; everyone has bounded rationality.
Right: reason works within limited information.
questions.explain: Reasonable decisions, limited information. The card next gives examples.
questions.rule: Rational within limits.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says fishermen know how many fish there are and how many other fishermen will catch that day.
questions.explain: She says fishermen know neither how many fish there are nor how many other fishermen will fish that day.
questions.rule: Information is partial.

questions.q: A shop manager orders stock without knowing what rivals plan or how big the market is. Which Meadows idea applies?
options: Delayed information leads to systematic over- or underinvestment
The manager is irrational and careless about the order
The manager has perfect information about the market and rivals
The manager should ignore delays when placing stock orders
optionExplain: This matches her businessmen example.
The decision is reasonable given the information.
The manager lacks market information, so perfect information is the opposite of the case.
Delays are part of the problem.
questions.explain: A reasonable decision on partial information can still go wrong.
questions.rule: Partial view, systematic error.

questions.q: Because their information and responses are delayed, businessmen systematically under- and ____.
questions.explain: Meadows says they systematically under- and overinvest.
questions.rule: Error is systematic.

questions.q: Which statement misreads bounded rationality?
options: Information about distant parts of the system is especially lacking
Decisions rest on the information people have
It means individuals decide irrationally given what they know
Responses to information are themselves delayed
optionExplain: She says information about distant parts of the system is especially lacking, so this is accurate.
She says decisions rest on the information people have, so this is accurate.
Decisions are reasonable given the information.
She says responses to information are themselves delayed, so this is accurate.
questions.explain: Rationality is bounded, not absent: people decide reasonably on the information they have.
questions.rule: Reasonable but limited.

questions.q: A fisherman has a boat mortgage and does not know the fish population. What does Meadows expect him to do?
options: Fish less than needed to repay the mortgage
Wait for full information first
Stop fishing to protect the stock
Overfish
optionExplain: Her example is of overfishing.
Waiting is not what she predicts.
Pressures and imperfect knowledge push the other way.
This is her stated example.
questions.explain: Meadows says that a fisherman with a mortgage, a family to support and imperfect knowledge of the fish population will overfish.
questions.rule: Pressure plus partial knowledge gives overfishing.
questions.teaches: A fisherman with a mortgage on his boat, a family to support and imperfect knowledge of the fish population will overfish.

questions.q: What does Simon call people who try to meet their needs well enough before moving on?
options: Optimizers
Satisficers
Maximizers of the whole
Free riders
optionExplain: Optimizers seek the best, which he says we do not.
Right: from satisfy and sufficient.
He denies we aim at the whole system's good.
'Free riders' is not Simon's term; he calls them satisficers.
questions.explain: Satisficing means good enough for now. The card next sets this against the optimizer.
questions.rule: Good enough, then move on.

questions.q: True or false: Simon says people are omniscient, rational optimizers.
questions.explain: Simon says we are blundering satisficers, not omniscient, rational optimizers.
questions.rule: Not optimizers.

questions.q: A driver takes the first parking space that is close enough instead of scanning for the best one. Which idea does this show?
options: Optimizing across every available space in the car park
Seeing the full range of possibilities before choosing a space
Satisficing: meeting the need well enough, then moving on
Having perfect information about every other driver nearby
optionExplain: The driver did not search all options.
The driver stopped looking early.
Good enough, then on to the next decision.
The driver knew nothing of others' plans.
questions.explain: Simon's satisficers stop once the need is met well enough.
questions.rule: Good enough, then move on.

questions.q: Meadows says we do not know what others are planning to do until they ____.
questions.explain: Others' plans only become known when carried out.
questions.rule: Plans are hidden until acted on.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says that people find a long-term optimum within their limited view.
questions.explain: Within our limited view we find a choice we can live with for now, not a long-term optimum.
questions.rule: No long-term optimum.

questions.q: A firm keeps a failing product line for years, and drops it only when a regulator forces the change. Which satisficer trait is this?
options: Sticking to a choice it can live with, changing when forced
Seeking the long-term optimum for the whole system of products
Foreseeing the effects of its actions on the whole system
Learning what rivals plan well before they act on it
optionExplain: This is how Meadows describes satisficers.
Satisficers do not seek the long-term optimum for the whole system of products.
Satisficers often fail to foresee these.
We do not know what others plan until they act.
questions.explain: Meadows says we find a choice we can live with for now, stick to it, and change our behavior only when forced.
questions.rule: Satisficers change when forced.
questions.teaches: Satisficers stick to a choice they can live with for now and change their behavior only when forced.

questions.q: What does Meadows say about the two assumptions of Smith-based economics?
options: Both are confirmed by the evidence of the past two centuries
The first holds, but the second fails when many people act
Neither stands up long against the evidence
The second holds, but the first fails when information is poor
optionExplain: She says the evidence runs against both assumptions, not for them.
She says neither assumption stands up, so 'the first holds' is wrong.
Right: both fail.
She says neither assumption stands up, so 'the second holds' is wrong.
questions.explain: She rejects both. The card next states them.
questions.rule: Both fail.

questions.q: True or false: According to Meadows, the controversy over bounded rationality and Smith-based economics is over.
questions.explain: She says the controversy over bounded rationality and Smith-based economics is far from over.
questions.rule: Still a live dispute.

questions.q: A textbook assumes buyers know all prices and that their purchases automatically produce the best outcome for society. Which of Meadows' points does this assume?
options: Both assumptions she says fail: perfect information and harmony
Neither of them, since it is a purely descriptive textbook
Only bounded rationality, as the textbook describes real buyers
Only the tragedy of the commons, which the textbook explains
optionExplain: The textbook assumes both.
The textbook assumes both perfect information and automatic harmony, so 'neither' is wrong.
The textbook assumes the opposite of bounded rationality: perfect information and optimizing buyers.
That is an outcome, not an assumption.
questions.explain: Perfect optimality plus summed harmony is the textbook picture she questions.
questions.rule: Spot the assumptions.

questions.q: Meadows says the next chapter describes structures that cause bounded rationality to lead to ____.
questions.explain: She names addiction, policy resistance, arms races, drift to low performance and the tragedy of the commons.
questions.rule: Structures can turn bounds into disaster.

questions.q: Which is NOT among the structures Meadows says she will describe next?
options: Arms races
Drift to low performance
The tragedy of the commons
Monopoly pricing
optionExplain: She names arms races among the structures to come, so it is not the odd one out.
She names drift to low performance among the structures to come, so it is not the odd one out.
She names the tragedy of the commons among the structures to come, so it is not the odd one out.
She names addiction, policy resistance, arms races, drift to low performance and the tragedy of the commons.
questions.explain: She names addiction, policy resistance, arms races, drift to low performance and the tragedy of the commons; monopoly pricing is not among them.
questions.rule: Check the list.

questions.q: An adviser says markets will manage fish stocks since each fisher pursues gain. Why has Smith's model appealed for two hundred years, per Meadows?
options: It has been confirmed by every test made of it in 200 years
It removes the need to think about others' good or feedback
It was first shown to hold for fisheries and farm markets
It treats information as incomplete and delayed for all actors
optionExplain: She says the assumptions do not stand up.
This is her explanation of its appeal.
She gives fishing as a counterexample.
That is bounded rationality, the rival view.
questions.explain: Meadows says that if the invisible hand worked, there would be no need to think about the good of other people or about the operations of complex feedback systems.
questions.rule: An appealing idea can still be false.
questions.teaches: Smith's model has had strong appeal for two hundred years because, if it held, there would be no need to think about the good of other people or about the operations of complex feedback systems.

questions.q: Which of these does Meadows say behavioral scientists find about how we read information?
options: We weigh all signals equally, whatever their source or strength
We pay too much attention to recent events, too little to the past
We give the future too much weight in our daily decisions
We welcome all news, whatever its content and our own views
optionExplain: She says we do not weigh them correctly.
Right: an exaggerated present.
She says we discount the future too much.
She says we keep out news we dislike.
questions.explain: We misjudge even the information we hold. The card next lists the biases.
questions.rule: Biases cloud judgment.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says we give too little attention to recent experience and too much to the long past.
questions.explain: She says the reverse: we live in an exaggerated present, paying too much attention to recent experience and too little to the past.
questions.rule: Recency over history.

questions.q: After one bad winter, a town pays for expensive flood walls and ignores decades of records showing calm. Which tendency is this?
options: Discounting the future at a rate that makes no sense
Misperceiving risk in general, thinking some things safe or dangerous
Perfect optimizing of the town's choices over all years
Living in an exaggerated present
optionExplain: The case overweights the near past, not the future.
The error here is about timing and recency, not the level of risk.
The town ignored the long record, so it was not optimizing over all the years.
Too much attention to recent experience.
questions.explain: Recent events outweigh long-term behavior.
questions.rule: Recency over history.

questions.q: Meadows says we discount the future at rates that make no economic or ____ sense.
questions.explain: She says the rates make no economic or ecological sense.
questions.rule: Future costs are undervalued.

questions.q: Which statement is NOT among the biases Meadows lists?
options: We overvalue the distant past
We misperceive risk, thinking some things more dangerous than they are
We discount the future at rates that make no economic sense
We live in an exaggerated present, with too much attention to recent events
optionExplain: She says we do the opposite: too much present, too little past.
She lists misperceiving risk among the biases, so it is among them.
She lists discounting the future at nonsensical rates among the biases, so it is among them.
She lists living in an exaggerated present among the biases, so it is among them.
questions.explain: Our bias is toward the present, not the past.
questions.rule: Present, not past.

questions.q: A manager refuses to read a report that contradicts the company's long-held view. Which tendency from Meadows is this?
options: Misperceiving the risk in the report as higher than it is
Discounting the future too heavily when weighing the report
Not letting in information that clashes with our models
An exaggerated present, where only recent events count for much
optionExplain: The case is about rejecting the report.
The case is about refusing the report's content, not about discounting the future.
This is her stated tendency.
The case is about fit with a model.
questions.explain: Meadows says we do not let in at all the news we do not like, or information that does not fit our mental models.
questions.rule: Models filter what we see.
questions.teaches: We do not give all incoming signals their appropriate weights, and we do not let in at all news we dislike or information that does not fit our mental models.

questions.q: If you moved into the role of someone whose behavior you have not understood, what does Meadows say would probably happen?
options: You would keep your own view and then change the system around you
You would judge the other person more harshly than before
You would refuse the role because it clashes with your views
You would face the role's information and pressures and act like them
optionExplain: She says this is distinctly unlikely.
She says you would come to understand them.
The question assumes you are in it.
Right: the role shapes behavior.
questions.explain: The role shapes the behavior more than the person does. The card next gives her cases.
questions.rule: Role over person.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says that in her simulation games, students playing fishermen tend to overfish.
questions.explain: In her simulation games, students playing fishermen tend to overfish, because the role pushes them that way.
questions.rule: The game recreates the pressures.

questions.q: A union organizer is promoted to plant manager and soon talks about labor costs. Which Meadows point is this?
options: The organizer was insincere from the start about worker interests
Being in a position brings its information and pressures, and its view
The organizer lacks any bounded rationality of the kind described
Organizers should never be promoted into management at all
optionExplain: She says the role explains the change.
A manager probably stops seeing labor as a deserving partner.
Every actor has bounded rationality; the case shows the role changing what the person sees.
She does not argue against promoting organizers; her point is that roles shape views.
questions.explain: The new role changes what the person sees and must answer for.
questions.rule: Roles shape views.

questions.q: If you become a financier, Meadows says you will probably overinvest during booms and ____ during busts.
questions.explain: Financiers as a group overinvest in booms and underinvest in busts, which she uses to show that roles shape behavior.
questions.rule: Roles repeat patterns.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says replacing one individual with another in the same position is likely to make a large difference.
questions.explain: She says it is not likely to make much difference.
questions.rule: The role stays the same.

questions.q: In Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment, what did the players do, according to Meadows?
options: They refused to take on any role during the experiment
They all behaved in the same way, whatever role they had
They took on the attitudes of guards and prisoners quickly
They took years to adopt the roles of guards and prisoners
optionExplain: She says the opposite: the players quickly took on the attitudes of their roles.
Guards and prisoners acted differently.
This is her description.
She says it was an amazingly short time.
questions.explain: Meadows says the players, in an amazingly short time, took on the attitudes and behaviors of prison guards and prisoners.
questions.rule: Roles take hold quickly.
questions.teaches: In Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment, players took on the attitudes and behaviors of prison guards and prisoners in an amazingly short time.

questions.q: What does Meadows say about blaming individuals for bad outcomes?
options: It rarely helps produce a better outcome
It is the quickest fix for most system problems
It is needed so that people learn to act better
It is irrelevant because no person ever acts wrongly
optionExplain: Right: the behavior comes from the position.
She says blaming individuals rarely helps, so it is not the quickest fix.
She does not argue that blame teaches people to act better; blame rarely produces a better outcome.
She says understanding is not an excuse.
questions.explain: Blame rarely works. The card next says what does.
questions.rule: Blame rarely helps.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says understanding why behavior is rational within its bounds excuses narrow-minded behavior.
questions.explain: It provides an understanding, not an excuse.
questions.rule: Understand, do not excuse.

questions.q: A water board's engineer is blamed for repeated shortages, and a new engineer takes over under the same rules. What does Meadows expect?
options: Large improvement, since a new person brings new ideas to it
A complete fix, since blame has been placed on someone
Little change, since the position stays the same
Worse shortages, since the new staff lack the needed skills
optionExplain: She says replacing an individual in the same position makes little difference, so a large improvement is unlikely.
Blame rarely helps, so a complete fix is not what she expects.
Replacing an individual in the same position makes little difference.
She does not say worse shortages follow; she says little changes when the position stays the same.
questions.explain: The structure around the person produces the behavior.
questions.rule: Change the position, not just the person.

questions.q: Meadows says change comes first from stepping outside the limited information of one place and getting an ____.
questions.explain: A wider view lets goals and incentives be restructured.
questions.rule: Wider view first.

questions.q: Which conclusion goes beyond what Meadows says?
options: Since behavior is rational, no one is ever responsible
Behavior arises from what a person in the position can see
Replacing an individual makes little difference in a position
Restructuring information and incentives can change the results
optionExplain: She says understanding is not an excuse.
She says behavior arises from what a person in the position can see, so this is within her account.
She says replacing an individual makes little difference, so this is within her account.
She says restructuring information and incentives can change results, so this is within her account.
questions.explain: She explains behavior without excusing it.
questions.rule: Explain, do not excuse.

questions.q: A company gives each driver real-time data on fleet-wide delays, and driver behavior improves within weeks. Which Meadows point does this illustrate?
options: Drivers are inherently careless unless they are watched closely
Delays always produce collapse in any system that has them
Behavior is fixed and cannot change once a habit is formed
Even slight enlargement of bounded rationality changes behavior quickly
optionExplain: The data fixed it without a change of drivers.
The case is about information.
Her point is that it changes quickly.
This is her observation about how quickly behavior can change.
questions.explain: Meadows says it is amazing how quickly and easily behavior can change with even slight enlargement of bounded rationality.
questions.rule: Better information changes behavior.
questions.teaches: Behavior can change quickly and easily with even slight enlargement of bounded rationality, by providing better, more complete, timelier information.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: Houses in a Dutch suburb used very different amounts of electricity, at the same price. What explained the gap?
options: The size of the families living in each of the houses
The meter's position
The age of the buildings and of their electric wiring
The price paid per unit of electricity in each house
optionExplain: The families were similar, so family size does not explain the gap.
Right: seen often or rarely.
They were built at the same time.
All were charged the same price.
questions.explain: The meter's position made the difference. The card next gives the details.
questions.rule: Visible feedback.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: True or false: In the Dutch houses, the families with the highest use had the meter in the front hall.
questions.explain: The high users had it in the basement, where it was rarely seen.
questions.rule: Hidden meter, higher use.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: A firm moves the office water meter to the entrance. What would Meadows' meter story predict?
options: No change, since staff do not pay the bill
Staff see the usage and likely use less
Higher use, since the meter reminds them of water
Lower use only if prices rise
optionExplain: The story shows seeing alone changed use.
Seeing the figure often changes behavior.
The story points the other way.
Price did not differ in the story.
questions.explain: Making a flow visible gives the actor information they lacked.
questions.rule: Visible usage.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: Some Dutch houses used one-third less ____ than others with the same price and similar families.
questions.explain: The houses with the meter in the front hall used one-third less.
questions.rule: One-third less.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the lower use in the Dutch houses was explained by cheaper electricity.
questions.explain: All houses were charged the same price for electricity.
questions.rule: Price was equal.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: A smart plug shows a household's live power use on a phone. Which feature of the Dutch meter does this share?
options: It lowers the price of power at peak times of the day
It forces households to use less when they use too much
It delays the bill until the end of the month each time
It shows use as it happens, like the faster wheel
optionExplain: The Dutch houses all paid the same price.
The meter only informed; it forced nothing.
The meter showed use continuously.
This is how the meter gave the household information.
questions.explain: In the old meters the wheel turned faster as the household used more electricity, and a dial added up the kilowatt-hours.
questions.rule: Show use as it happens.
questions.teaches: In these meters the wheel turned faster as the household used more electricity, and a dial added up the accumulated kilowatt-hours.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: What do Meadows' examples of the liver, undisturbed ecosystems and traditional cultures have in common?
options: The right feedback reaches the right place at the right time
They are all managed by government agencies and their policies
They have perfect information about every part of the world
They are all free markets of the kind Smith described
optionExplain: Right: structure supplies the information.
She says we do not need agencies for them.
They work despite bounded rationality.
The market is a separate case.
questions.explain: Good structure supplies the right feedback. The card next applies this to the market.
questions.rule: Structure supplies information.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the free market lets producers and consumers make locally rational decisions with the best information about their own choices.
questions.explain: She says the free market does this in some ways: producers and consumers decide locally, with good information about their own choices.
questions.rule: A real strength of markets.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: A factory sells goods freely, but its smoke harms neighbors who are not its customers. Which market tendency of Meadows' does this show?
options: Creating a monopoly, with one seller controlling the market
Discriminating against the poor in the prices of its goods
Creating undesirable side effects, or externalities, left uncorrected
Overshooting its sustainable carrying capacity over time
optionExplain: No single seller has taken over the market in the case; the harm falls on neighbors outside it.
The harm falls on neighbors, not on a class of buyers.
Buyers and sellers decide locally; the neighbors' harm falls outside.
That concerns total scale, not harm to bystanders.
questions.explain: Local, informed decisions leave the damage to bystanders uncorrected.
questions.rule: Locally rational, globally flawed.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: Besides monopolies and externalities, Meadows says a free market tends to discriminate against the ____.
questions.explain: She also names overshooting its sustainable carrying capacity.
questions.rule: Four tendencies.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: Which statement misreads Meadows?
options: Some systems regulate themselves despite bounded rationality
The liver gets exactly the information it needs
The market lets informed actors decide freely
The free market is entirely self-regulating
optionExplain: She says some systems regulate themselves despite bounded rationality, so this reading is right.
She says the liver gets exactly the information it needs, so this reading is right.
She says the market lets informed actors decide freely, so this reading is right.
She says it is only partly so.
questions.explain: She says the market works in some ways and not in others.
questions.rule: Partly self-regulating.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: An undisturbed pond keeps itself in balance without any manager. Which Meadows idea is this?
options: A system that overshoots its carrying capacity and then collapses
A self-regulating system whose parts stabilize the whole
A system needing many government policies to keep it in balance
A cloud hiding a flow from those who draw the diagram
optionExplain: That describes the market tendency.
She gives undisturbed ecosystems as examples.
She says such systems need none.
A cloud is a boundary feature of diagrams, unrelated to a pond balancing itself.
questions.explain: Meadows says in undisturbed ecosystems and traditional cultures the average individual, species or population behaves in ways that serve and stabilize the whole.
questions.rule: Some systems manage themselves.
questions.teaches: We have no government agencies or dozens of failed policies about self-regulating systems such as the liver, undisturbed ecosystems and traditional cultures.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: If actors' bounded rationality does not serve the whole, what does Meadows say makes a difference?
options: Replacing the actors with better people who know more
Warning the actors about the harm that they cause to others
Redesigning the information and incentives the actors face
Removing all rules so that the actors are free to act
optionExplain: New actors in the same system do not improve it.
Warning does not change their information or incentives.
Right: change the system.
Free action in a badly structured system is the problem.
questions.explain: Redesign beats replacement. The card next sets out her prayer.
questions.rule: Redesign, do not replace.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says putting new actors into the same badly structured system will improve its performance.
questions.explain: She says putting new actors into the same badly structured system will not improve its performance.
questions.rule: Same structure, same outcomes.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: A hospital's nurses keep missing handover details, and the manager replaces them. Months later the errors continue. What would Meadows suggest?
options: Redesign the information and incentives for handover
Replace the new nurses with others, who may do better
Blame the earlier nurses, who started the habit
Leave it alone, since errors are a rational result
optionExplain: Fix the structure the nurses work within.
Replacement does not alter the system.
Blaming the earlier nurses is blame, which she says rarely helps.
She asks us to restructure systems that fail.
questions.explain: Replacing the nurses does not change the system around them; she suggests redesigning information, incentives and the rest of what shapes their decisions.
questions.rule: Fix the structure.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: Meadows' paraphrased prayer asks for the courage to ____ the systems that are not structured appropriately.
questions.explain: The other parts ask for serenity and wisdom to know the difference.
questions.rule: Serenity, courage, wisdom.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: Which reading of the prayer is wrong?
options: Leave well-structured systems to run freely
Restructure systems that are not well structured
Every system should be restructured, whatever its state
Wisdom lies in knowing which is which
optionExplain: Leaving well-structured systems to run freely is the first part of the prayer.
Restructuring poorly structured systems is the second part of the prayer.
The prayer also counsels exercising bounded rationality freely in well-structured systems.
Knowing which is which is the third part of the prayer.
questions.explain: The prayer asks for judgment about which systems need change.
questions.rule: Judge before restructuring.

questions.section: Interlude • Electric Meters in Dutch Houses
questions.q: A bank's loan officers all over-lend in booms. Which factors does Meadows say to adjust?
options: Their information, incentives, goals, stresses and constraints
Only the officers' personal integrity and their sense of duty
Only the interest rate that the bank charges to its borrowers
Only the number of officers the bank has on its staff
optionExplain: These define each actor's bounded rationality.
She says person-level change makes little difference.
The interest rate alone is a narrow set; she names information, incentives, goals, stresses and constraints.
Staffing numbers alone are a narrow set; she names a broader range of factors.
questions.explain: Meadows lists information, incentives, disincentives, goals, stresses and constraints as what determine an actor's bounded rationality.
questions.rule: Adjust what the actor faces.
questions.teaches: An actor's bounded rationality is determined by the information, incentives, disincentives, goals, stresses and constraints impinging on that actor.

questions.q: A company's service quality keeps slipping, whoever runs it. What cause does Meadows treat as the likelier one?
options: The way the system is structured, which would shape any manager's results
A run of weak managers who each lack the skills the job needs
A string of unlucky outside events with no pattern linking them
Too little pressure on the policy levers so far, so far more force is needed
optionExplain: Right: Meadows traces recurring patterns to structure, which would shape any manager's results.
It is a natural guess, but replacing people is one of the responses she says leaves structure intact.
Bad luck can matter, yet hoping for a better run of events is listed among responses that do not fix structure.
Pushing levers harder is one of the standard responses she says will not fix a structural problem.
questions.explain: Meadows blames recurring problems on system structure, not on particular actors. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: When bad behavior keeps recurring, look for the system structure behind it and change that, instead of blaming people or pushing harder.

questions.q: In this chapter, what does the word archetype mean?
options: A typical person whose role in a system is easy to recognize, such as a regulator or a customer
A single dramatic event that sets off trouble in several other parts of a system
A system whose behavior surprises us
A system structure that produces a common pattern of problematic behavior
optionExplain: The word sounds like a character type, but here it names a structure, not a person.
Events are what tend to get blamed; the archetype is the structure beneath them.
Those properties produce surprise; archetypes are the structures that are perverse, not just surprising.
Right: Meadows defines archetypes as the structures behind common patterns of problematic behavior.
questions.explain: An archetype is a recurring structure behind problematic behavior.
questions.rule: Archetype means structure, not person and not event.

questions.q: A city bans a pollutant, fines the offending firm, then sees the same pollution from the next firm. Which reading fits Meadows?
options: The fine was too small
The structure rewards polluting, so removing one actor leaves the pattern in place
The second firm is a worse operator than the first
The pattern will fade by itself if the city waits for a more favorable run of conditions
optionExplain: This is the push-harder response, which she says does not fix structure.
Right: When the same behavior returns with a new actor, the structure is the likelier cause.
This blames an actor; the same behavior from a new actor points elsewhere.
Hoping for a favorable sequence of events is another response she lists as ineffective.
questions.explain: When the behavior reappears with new actors, the structure is the more likely cause.
questions.rule: When bad behavior keeps recurring, look for the system structure behind it and change that, instead of blaming people or pushing harder.
questions.hint: Ask what stayed the same when the actor changed.

questions.q: Which responses does Meadows say will not fix a structural problem? Select all that apply.
options: Blaming the people involved
Twisting the policy levers harder
Adding a new feedback loop
Reformulating the system's goals
Hoping for a more favorable sequence of events
optionExplain: Right: blaming is on her list.
Right: more force on the same structure is on her list.
This is one of her ways out, because it alters the structure.
This is one of her ways out, since goals are part of structure.
Right: waiting for luck leaves the structure untouched.
questions.explain: Blaming, firing, harder lever-twisting, hoping for luck and tinkering at the margins leave structure alone; changing goals or loops does not.
questions.rule: When bad behavior keeps recurring, look for the system structure behind it and change that, instead of blaming people or pushing harder.

questions.q: If a school changes its principal but leaves its incentives and goals as they are, Meadows expects the same behavior to ____.
questions.explain: Because the behavior comes from structure, a new actor in the same structure tends to produce the same pattern.
questions.rule: When bad behavior keeps recurring, look for the system structure behind it and change that, instead of blaming people or pushing harder.

questions.q: True or false: The author argues that nonlinearity and fuzzy boundaries are flaws that should be removed so systems become easier to manage.
questions.explain: She says these properties generally cannot or should not be changed, and that the better course is to expect, appreciate and use the world's complexity. Our reading: only the perverse structures are targets for change.
questions.rule: Learn to live with complexity; change only the perverse structures.

questions.q: A reader calls the eight traps rare textbook curiosities. What does the author's own experience suggest?
options: They are rare, which is why she had to search many years of reports to find cases
They are common: one week of one newspaper gave her examples of every archetype
They appear only in economics, so newspapers can report very few of them
They are common in the news but cannot occur inside firms, hospitals or schools
optionExplain: The text says the opposite: examples were easy to find in a single week.
Right: Meadows says she had no trouble finding examples of every archetype in one week of one newspaper.
Her examples come from news on many subjects, not economics alone.
Nothing in the chapter limits them to news; companies, hospitals and schools all appear as cases.
questions.explain: Meadows says she found enough examples of each archetype in one week of the International Herald Tribune.
questions.rule: When bad behavior keeps recurring, look for the system structure behind it and change that, instead of blaming people or pushing harder.
questions.teaches: Meadows found examples of every archetype in a single week of one newspaper, which shows how prevalent they are.

questions.q: A government has tried a new anti-crime program every few years, and crime is about the same. What is a fair guess about the cause?
options: Each program was carried out with too little determination, so more resolve will do it
Crime is a reinforcing loop, so it must keep rising each year
Programs aimed at social problems fail in every case, whatever structure surrounds them
Some balancing structure in the system is holding crime near its usual level
optionExplain: Possible, but effort followed by no change across many programs points to structure first.
Rising would be a different pattern; here the level stays about the same.
An absolute claim the chapter does not make; later cases such as Sweden show partial success.
Right: A stabilizing loop can hold an unwanted state in place; the card shows how.
questions.explain: A persistent unwanted state despite repeated effort suggests a stabilizing structure. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: If effort year after year produces no change, suspect a balancing structure that holds the unwanted state in place.

questions.q: What is the primary symptom of a balancing feedback loop structure, as the chapter recalls it?
options: Not much changes despite outside forces pushing the system
Behavior grows exponentially until it runs into a limit that stops it
The system swings wildly up and down
The system collapses as soon as it reaches the goal that its loop was set up to seek
optionExplain: Right: A balancing loop stabilizes, so behavior persists against outside pushes.
That is the symptom of a reinforcing loop, which Chapter Two contrasts with balancing loops.
Delays can cause oscillation, but that is not the primary symptom named here.
Reaching a goal leads a balancing loop to settle, not to collapse.
questions.explain: Balancing loops hold behavior steady against outside pushes.
questions.rule: If effort year after year produces no change, suspect a balancing structure that holds the unwanted state in place.

questions.q: Which situation is the best example of fixes that fail?
options: A fishery that collapses after a large new fleet arrives and takes the catch faster than it regrows
A cup of coffee that cools to room temperature and then stays at that temperature
Decades of job-creation programs that leave unemployment no lower
A savings account that grows steadily from compound interest over many decades
optionExplain: This is overuse of a shared resource, another trap, not effort met by unchanged results.
A balancing process, but no policy effort is being resisted and no bad state persists.
Right: The trap appears as long, energetic policy effort that yields stubborn non-results.
This is reinforcing growth, a different structure.
questions.explain: The trap shows up as energetic effort that produces non-results.
questions.rule: If effort year after year produces no change, suspect a balancing structure that holds the unwanted state in place.

questions.q: A thermostat set at 18 C is in a room whose window is opened wide in winter. What does the balancing loop do?
options: It gives up and lets the room drift to the outdoor temperature once the window is open
It turns into a reinforcing loop that cools the room faster and faster each minute
It ignores the open window
It keeps working to hold the room near 18 C, using more heat
optionExplain: A working balancing loop resists the disturbance, even if it loses some ground.
A balancing loop does not turn itself into a reinforcing one.
The loop responds to the gap between goal and actual state, whatever its cause.
Right: A balancing loop acts on the gap, so it pushes back against the disturbance.
questions.explain: The loop acts on the discrepancy, which is why outside pushes meet counteraction.
questions.rule: A balancing loop pushes back against disturbances.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says persistent behavior produced by a balancing loop is a problem only when the behavior is one people do not want.
questions.explain: She contrasts body temperature, where persistence is wanted, with persistent patterns that are undesirable. Our reading: the trap is defined by the unwanted state, not by persistence itself.
questions.rule: If effort year after year produces no change, suspect a balancing structure that holds the unwanted state in place.

questions.q: A system held in an unwanted state by a balancing loop shows the trap of fixes that ____, also called policy resistance.
questions.explain: Meadows names the trap fixes that fail, or policy resistance.
questions.rule: If effort year after year produces no change, suspect a balancing structure that holds the unwanted state in place.

questions.q: A town builds more car lanes each decade to end congestion, yet delays stay. Which diagnosis follows the chapter's logic best?
options: Many drivers adjust their choices to the new capacity, so the old state returns
The town should build lanes faster, so that supply finally outruns demand for road space
Congestion is a law of nature, so no policy could ever change it in any town
The lanes were built with poor materials, so they fail to carry as much traffic
optionExplain: Right: Other actors adjust to the new capacity, so the old state comes back.
This is the push-harder response the chapter says leaves the trap in place.
The chapter offers ways out, so it does not call every such state fixed.
An engineering fault would not explain the same result after every new expansion.
questions.explain: Meadows says resistance comes from other actors adjusting to a policy; the next idea explains why. Meadows adds that no single policy has yet brought down health care costs in the United States, which is another area of policy resistance.
questions.rule: If effort year after year produces no change, suspect a balancing structure that holds the unwanted state in place.
questions.teaches: Meadows adds that no single policy has yet brought down health care costs in the United States, another area of policy resistance.

questions.q: Why might a policy meet resistance even when everyone is acting sensibly by their own lights?
options: Most people dislike any new policy on principle, however sensible it is
Sensible actors would never resist a sensible policy
Each actor has its own goal and corrects any gap from it
The policy contains a hidden flaw that its designers failed to see in advance
optionExplain: Resistance in the chapter comes from goals and gaps, not general dislike.
The chapter's point is that sensible actors with different goals do collide.
Right: Each actor has its own goal and corrects any gap, so goals can collide.
Resistance can meet a well-made policy; the issue is how actors respond.
questions.explain: Resistance can arise from rational actors with different goals. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Look for each actor's own goal and its own corrective response to find the source of resistance.

questions.q: Meadows says policy resistance comes from the bounded ____ of the actors in a system.
questions.explain: She traces resistance to the bounded rationalities of actors, each with its own goal.
questions.rule: Look for each actor's own goal and its own corrective response to find the source of resistance.

questions.q: Farmers want high crop prices, consumers want low ones, and the state wants a stable supply. Which description fits Meadows?
options: All three share one goal and disagree only about the methods to reach it
Each watches prices and acts on the gap between price and its own goal
Only the state acts on the price
Their actions cancel each other only in the case where their goals happen to be equal
optionExplain: They have different goals, which is the source of the conflict.
Right: Each actor compares the monitored variable with its own goal and acts on the gap.
In the chapter every actor monitors the variable and acts to correct a gap.
Actions oppose each other because the goals differ, not because they match.
questions.explain: Different goals around one variable mean opposing corrective actions.
questions.rule: Look for each actor's own goal and its own corrective response to find the source of resistance.

questions.q: In this structure, what happens to an actor's effort as the gap between its goal and the actual state widens?
options: It usually becomes more emphatic
It usually weakens, since the goal looks out of reach
It stays constant, whatever the gap
It switches to another variable
optionExplain: Right: Meadows says usually the greater the discrepancy, the more emphatic the action.
The chapter says the opposite for ordinary actors; weakening describes goal-lowering in a different trap.
The response scales with the gap, not fixed.
The actor keeps working on the same variable and pushes harder; the chapter does not describe switching variables.
questions.explain: Meadows says usually the greater the discrepancy, the more emphatic the action. Corrective action grows with the discrepancy.
questions.rule: Bigger gaps bring harder corrective action.

questions.q: Which pair names two variables that Meadows lists as ones actors monitor?
options: Rainfall and altitude
Voltage and pressure
Humidity and noise
Income and housing
optionExplain: Rainfall and altitude are not variables she lists; her actors watch things like income, prices and housing.
Voltage and pressure are physical quantities, not among the variables she names for actors.
Humidity and noise are not on her list; she names income, prices, housing, drugs and investment.
Right: she lists income, prices, housing, drugs and investment.
questions.explain: Her list is income, prices, housing, drugs or investment.
questions.rule: Look for each actor's own goal and its own corrective response to find the source of resistance.

questions.q: True or false: In Meadows's account, an actor's corrective effort usually grows more emphatic as the gap from its goal widens.
questions.explain: Usually the greater the discrepancy, the more emphatic the action.
questions.rule: Look for each actor's own goal and its own corrective response to find the source of resistance.

questions.q: A university tries to cut late assignments; students, teachers and the registrar each have different aims. Why might a stricter deadline policy meet resistance?
options: Students dislike rules in general
Each group corrects its own gap, so a stricter rule pulls against the others' goals
The registrar controls the outcome alone, so the other groups cannot affect the policy
A stricter rule makes the gap vanish for every group at once, so resistance is impossible
optionExplain: Resistance in the card comes from goals and gaps, not from dislike.
Right: A stricter rule favoring one group's goal widens the others' gaps and triggers their responses.
The chapter pictures several actors, none in sole control.
A gap closing for one actor widens it for others.
questions.explain: In Meadows's picture, advancing one actor's goal widens other actors' gaps and triggers their responses. Meadows notes that an actor can be an institution as well as a person, each with its own goal.
questions.rule: Look for each actor's own goal and its own corrective response to find the source of resistance.
questions.teaches: Actors in a policy-resistance system can be institutions as well as individuals: Meadows writes his, her or its own goals.

questions.q: If one group wins a gain against a problem and the others respond, what is the likely net result on the shared stock?
options: A lasting win for the group that made the gain
A faster move in the winning direction
Little change, with everyone spending more effort
An end to all effort, since the problem is settled
optionExplain: The chapter says the gain triggers responses that pull the stock back.
Other actors' responses slow it down.
Right: countermoves tend to produce a standoff. The card next explains it.
Effort continues, because the standoff persists.
questions.explain: A gain by one actor draws counter-efforts. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: In a standoff, everyone works hard to hold the system where no one wants it, and each escalation draws a response.

questions.q: In Meadows's drug-supply picture, what do pushers want the supply to do?
options: Stay as high as possible
Stay as low as possible
Stay in the middle, so prices are neither too high nor too low
Fall to zero, ending the market and the risk that comes with it entirely
optionExplain: Addicts are the group she says wants the stock high.
Enforcement agencies want it low.
Right: Meadows says pushers want the supply in the middle so prices stay steady.
No actor in her list wants this except possibly enforcement; pushers want a middle level.
questions.explain: Meadows says pushers want the supply in the middle so prices stay steady. Pushers want the stock in the middle.
questions.rule: In a standoff, everyone works hard to hold the system where no one wants it, and each escalation draws a response.

questions.q: Which passage best shows the ratchet mode?
options: Each side's increase in effort leads the others to increase theirs, and nobody wants to be first to ease off
One side wins a clear victory and the other sides quit trying after that
All sides agree on a new shared goal and put their efforts into it together
Effort falls on every side after a gain, because all of them can afford to relax
optionExplain: Right: In a ratchet, each side's rise in effort provokes the rest, and easing off is hard.
The ratchet is about mutual intensification, not quitting.
That is the way out of resistance, not the ratchet.
The ratchet runs the other way: effort rises, and falling is hard.
questions.explain: A ratchet makes intensifying easy and reducing difficult.
questions.rule: In a standoff, everyone works hard to hold the system where no one wants it, and each escalation draws a response.

questions.q: If enforcement cuts drug imports at the border, what does Meadows describe as happening to street prices and crime?
options: Prices fall and crime falls
Prices rise and crime falls
Prices stay flat while crime falls
Prices rise and addicts commit more crimes to pay for drugs
optionExplain: Falling prices would not produce the pull-back she describes.
She says addicts need more money, so crime rises.
Her chain begins with a price rise, and the others do react.
Right: Cutting imports raises prices, which pushes addicts to commit more crimes.
questions.explain: The cut raises prices, and that sets off further actions.
questions.rule: In a standoff, everyone works hard to hold the system where no one wants it, and each escalation draws a response.

questions.q: True or false: According to Meadows, if one actor in a standoff lets up, the others drag the system closer to their own goals.
questions.explain: She says that if any single actor lets up, the others drag the system closer to their goals and farther from the goal of the one who let go.
questions.rule: In a standoff, everyone works hard to hold the system where no one wants it, and each escalation draws a response.

questions.q: Meadows says this structure can operate in a ____ mode, where intensifying anyone's effort leads to intensifying everyone else's.
questions.explain: In ratchet mode, effort rises on every side and is hard to reduce.
questions.rule: In a standoff, everyone works hard to hold the system where no one wants it, and each escalation draws a response.

questions.q: Two neighboring firms each keep a large security staff because the other does. What does the ratchet idea suggest about cutting back?
options: It is easy, since each firm gains an edge by cutting its own staff first
It needs mutual trust, since the first to cut appears to lose ground
It is impossible under any circumstances
It happens on its own as costs rise, so neither firm needs to do anything about it
optionExplain: She says reducing intensification is hard, not easy.
Right: Meadows says backing off together takes mutual trust, as the first to cut seems to lose ground.
She names mutual trust as what makes it possible.
Rising costs do not release the ratchet by themselves; she says backing off together takes mutual trust.
questions.explain: Mutual trust is the condition she names for backing off together. If one firm cuts alone, the other drags the situation toward its own goal, which is why backing off takes trust.
questions.rule: In a standoff, everyone works hard to hold the system where no one wants it, and each escalation draws a response.
questions.teaches: In a policy-resistance system, if any single actor lets up, the others drag the system closer to their goals and farther from the goal of the one who let go.

questions.q: A government bans a widely used practice to raise a national statistic. What might happen after a short rise?
options: The statistic keeps rising once people understand the ban and learn to accept it
People find costly ways around the ban, pulling the statistic back
Public cooperation with the ban grows with time as people see its purpose
The ban becomes unnecessary
optionExplain: The chapter's case shows a rise followed by a return.
Right: Resistance can undo a short-lived gain, as the card shows for Romania.
Resistance, not cooperation, set in.
The rise did not hold in the Romanian case.
questions.explain: Resistance can undo a short-lived gain. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A policy that goes against the goals people hold may win briefly and then be undone by their response, at great human cost.

questions.q: What happened to the birth rate shortly after Romania banned abortions in 1967?
options: It halved
It stayed unchanged
It doubled and held at that level
It tripled
optionExplain: The text says it tripled. Here, the first effect was a tripling.
It tripled at first. Here, the first effect was a tripling.
It tripled, and later fell back. Here, the first effect was a tripling.
Right: the birth rate tripled shortly after the ban.
questions.explain: the birth rate tripled shortly after the ban. The first effect was a tripling.
questions.rule: A policy that goes against the goals people hold may win briefly and then be undone by their response, at great human cost.

questions.q: Which was a cost of Romania's policy, according to Meadows?
options: Dangerous illegal abortions that tripled maternal mortality
A collapse of the national currency brought on by the sudden rise in births
A shortage of teachers once the larger generation of children reached school
A fall in the life expectancy of the elderly
optionExplain: Right: Meadows says dangerous illegal abortions tripled the maternal mortality rate.
No currency collapse is described; the cost she names is a rise in dangerous illegal abortions and maternal deaths.
No teacher shortage is given as a cost of the policy in her account.
She does not report a fall in the elderly's life expectancy; the cost she names is maternal mortality.
questions.explain: Maternal mortality tripled through dangerous illegal abortions.
questions.rule: A policy that goes against the goals people hold may win briefly and then be undone by their response, at great human cost.

questions.q: Why did the birth rate return nearly to its previous level?
options: Contraceptives and abortions were made legal again soon after the ban took effect
The government lowered its target once it saw how costly the policy had become
Families too poor to raise many children resisted the government's pull
Population fell because of a famine that struck the country in the following years
optionExplain: They remained illegal during the period described.
The text says the dictator tried long to overpower the resistance.
Right: Families too poor to raise many children resisted the government's pull.
No famine is described; the rate returned because families resisted, not because of a national catastrophe.
questions.explain: The population's own goals, not a policy change, pulled the rate back.
questions.rule: A policy that goes against the goals people hold may win briefly and then be undone by their response, at great human cost.

questions.q: True or false: In Meadows's account, Romania's rise in births lasted, and policy resistance appeared only after the dictator fell.
questions.explain: Resistance set in after the early rise and the rate came back down while the ban stood; the ban was repealed once the government fell.
questions.rule: A policy that goes against the goals people hold may win briefly and then be undone by their response, at great human cost.

questions.q: After Romania's abortion ban, the birth rate first tripled and then slowly came back ____ nearly to its previous level.
questions.explain: The population's resistance pulled the rate back down.
questions.rule: A policy that goes against the goals people hold may win briefly and then be undone by their response, at great human cost.

questions.q: A city taxes a popular product heavily. Sales drop, then recover through informal channels. Which part of the Romanian pattern does this match?
options: An unbroken decline in sales of the product after the tax was introduced
A move to an overarching shared goal that all the groups could pull toward
A tax that the public welcomed and treated as a reasonable public measure
An early gain, then the population's workaround pulls the state back
optionExplain: Sales recovered here, so a pull-back occurred.
No shared overarching goal appears in the tax case; the groups keep pulling against each other.
The population resisted, as in Romania.
Right: An early gain followed by a workaround that pulls the state back is the Romanian pattern.
questions.explain: As in Romania, the early gain is followed by a pull-back as the population finds a way around the policy.
questions.rule: A policy that goes against the goals people hold may win briefly and then be undone by their response, at great human cost.
questions.teaches: Ceausescu, who tried to overpower the resistance, was executed with his family when his government fell, and the new government's first act was to repeal the ban.

questions.q: A rule is met with fierce, widespread workarounds. Which response does the author consider the effective alternative to more force?
options: Give up the ineffective rule and redirect the energy
Enforce the rule harder and longer
Wait quietly for the resistance to tire itself out over the next few years
Keep the rule but hide it from the public so that fewer people have cause to resist
optionExplain: Right: Letting go is her counterintuitive alternative to overpowering.
Overpowering can work, but with heavy costs she describes.
Waiting passively is not the alternative she offers; she says to let go of the failing policy and redirect the effort.
Hiding the rule is not an option she discusses; her alternative is to give up the ineffective rule itself.
questions.explain: Letting go is her alternative to overpowering. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: When a policy is met by equal resistance, consider letting go, because much of the trouble is a reaction to the policy itself.

questions.q: What does Meadows say can happen when overpowering stops working or the power is let up?
options: A smooth return to agreement
A gradual fading of resentment
Explosive consequences
Prompt cooperation from all actors
optionExplain: The risk is the opposite. Here, overpowering stores up resentment that can burst out.
She says overpowering builds monumental resentment.
Right: she warns of explosive consequences if the power is let up.
A tempting pick, but it does not fit the chapter. Overpowering stores up resentment that can burst out.
questions.explain: Overpowering stores up resentment that can burst out.
questions.rule: When a policy is met by equal resistance, consider letting go, because much of the trouble is a reaction to the policy itself.

questions.q: Which is an example of the 'let go' response?
options: A city doubles the penalty for breaking an unenforceable ban to deter the evaders
A city repeals an unenforceable ban and spends the saved effort on other measures
A city postpones the ban for one year while keeping it on the books
A city adds a second, related ban to close the gaps that people are using
optionExplain: Doubling the penalty is overpowering: more force against the same resistance, not a release.
Right: Letting go means ending the ineffective policy and redeploying the energy.
This delays the policy rather than giving it up.
This extends control rather than releasing it.
questions.explain: Letting go means ending the policy and redeploying the effort.
questions.rule: When a policy is met by equal resistance, consider letting go, because much of the trouble is a reaction to the policy itself.

questions.q: After a policy is dropped, what does Meadows expect from those who were pulling against it?
options: They calm down too, since much of their action responded to the policy
They push harder, sensing weakness in the other side and wanting to gain ground
They turn on one another, since the common enemy is no longer there
They keep resisting out of habit for as long as the old policy is remembered
optionExplain: Right: Much of the opposing action was a response to your own action, so it eases when you ease.
The chapter expects the opposite.
Nothing in her account has the resisters turning on one another; she says they ease when you ease.
She links their calming to yours.
questions.explain: Much of the opposing action was a response to your own action.
questions.rule: When a policy is met by equal resistance, consider letting go, because much of the trouble is a reaction to the policy itself.

questions.q: True or false: Letting go means the original policy aim is achieved by other means at once.
questions.explain: Meadows says you will not get your way; letting go calms the system and opens the chance to find better means.
questions.rule: When a policy is met by equal resistance, consider letting go, because much of the trouble is a reaction to the policy itself.

questions.q: Meadows says the alternative to overpowering policy resistance is so counterintuitive that it is usually unthinkable: let ____.
questions.explain: Letting go means giving up ineffective policies.
