questions.rule: When a policy is met by equal resistance, consider letting go, because much of the trouble is a reaction to the policy itself.

questions.q: A parent forbids a hobby; the teenager hides it, and tension grows. Which step best follows the chapter's reasoning about what letting go makes possible?
options: Increase supervision of the teenager until the hobby is dropped for good
Treat the hobby itself as the sole cause of the tension between parent and teenager
Announce the rule again, more firmly
Use the calm to learn the teenager's goals and look for a shared aim
optionExplain: More supervision is overpowering, the very response she says feeds the resistance.
The chapter points to structure and goals, not one cause.
This is more of the same effort.
Right: Calming down gives the chance to study the feedbacks and look for aligned goals.
questions.explain: Meadows says calming down gives a chance to understand the bounded rationality behind feedbacks.
questions.rule: When a policy is met by equal resistance, consider letting go, because much of the trouble is a reaction to the policy itself.
questions.teaches: Calming down creates the chance to study the system's feedbacks and the bounded rationality behind them, and to find a way to meet everyone's goals.

questions.q: A nation wants more births. Which first step does Meadows's approach favor?
options: Ban the practices that limit births
Find out why families have few children
Tell citizens that large families are good
Wait to see whether the rate recovers
optionExplain: This is Romania's route, which went badly.
Right: a nation might discover it is not because they dislike children.
Persuasion is not the step she describes.
She describes active inquiry. Here, ask why, then design to meet the real obstacles.
questions.explain: Ask why, then design to meet the real obstacles. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Before applying force, ask why people behave as they do, and use the answer to shape the policy.

questions.q: What obstacle to larger families did the Hungarian government find?
options: High taxes on children
A shortage of doctors
Cramped housing
Religious objections
optionExplain: High taxes on children are not what Hungary found; the obstacle she names is cramped housing.
A doctor shortage is not mentioned; Hungary's government found cramped housing was a reason for small families.
Right: it found that cramped housing was one reason.
Religious objections are not named; the obstacle she reports is cramped housing.
questions.explain: it found that cramped housing was one reason. Cramped housing was one reason.
questions.rule: Before applying force, ask why people behave as they do, and use the answer to shape the policy.

questions.q: Which action follows the Hungarian approach?
options: Penalize adults who remain childless
Make contraceptives illegal so that more families have children by default
Reward larger families with more living space
Offer a one-time cash bonus for every child born in the coming year
optionExplain: Penalizing the childless is a push against people's goals, not the approach of finding their obstacles she describes.
Making contraceptives illegal is Romania's approach, the policy that triggered resistance.
Right: Hungary's policy addressed an obstacle the families themselves faced.
A one-time cash bonus is not the Hungarian policy she describes, which tackled housing space.
questions.explain: Hungary tackled a cause the families themselves faced.
questions.rule: Before applying force, ask why people behave as they do, and use the answer to shape the policy.

questions.q: Meadows says the Hungarian policy was only partially successful. Why?
options: Housing was not the only problem
Families wanted no children at all and so ignored the policy altogether
Romania's policy next door interfered with the effect of Hungary's housing reward
The reward of living space was too small for any family to notice or respond to
optionExplain: Right: Housing was not the only obstacle, so more than one thing held family size down.
She says the issue was not that families dislike children.
Romania's policy is not offered as a cause; the stated reason is that housing was not the only obstacle.
She does not say the reward was too small to notice; she says other obstacles remained.
questions.explain: Housing was not the only obstacle, so more than one thing held family size down. More than one obstacle was in play.
questions.rule: Before applying force, ask why people behave as they do, and use the answer to shape the policy.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the Hungarian policy was far more successful than Romania's and avoided its disastrous results.
questions.explain: She says it was far more successful than Romania's and avoided its disastrous results.
questions.rule: Before applying force, ask why people behave as they do, and use the answer to shape the policy.

questions.q: Hungary's government found that ____ housing was one reason for small family size.
questions.explain: Cramped housing was one obstacle Hungary found by asking why.
questions.rule: Before applying force, ask why people behave as they do, and use the answer to shape the policy.

questions.q: A city wants more cyclists. Which first step mirrors Hungary?
options: Fine drivers on the cycling routes
Print posters praising the health benefits of cycling and display them in every district
Close the busiest road to cars for good, so that cyclists have it entirely to themselves
Survey residents about why they do not cycle, then address those reasons
optionExplain: This punishes rather than asks why cycling is low.
This is exhortation without inquiry into the obstacles.
This imposes a change without learning the cause.
Right: Asking why people do not cycle and acting on the answers mirrors Hungary.
questions.explain: Learn the obstacles, then design around them. Meadows says a nation may find that families lack the resources, living space, time or security to have more children, not that they dislike children.
questions.rule: Before applying force, ask why people behave as they do, and use the answer to shape the policy.
questions.teaches: A nation that wants a higher birth rate may find that families lack resources, living space, time or security, and not that they dislike children.

questions.q: Several groups pull a shared system in different directions. What does the author call the most effective way out?
options: Let the strongest group decide the matter and have the others accept the result
Find a larger goal they can all work toward
Remove the groups' ability to act on the system until they have all calmed down
Split the shared system into private pieces and give each group its own piece
optionExplain: This is overpowering, not alignment.
Right: Aligning goals through a larger shared goal is the most effective way out.
Disabling the groups is not a remedy she offers; the most effective way out is a larger goal they share.
She uses privatization for commons, not for this trap.
questions.explain: Aligning goals is the key. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Where actors pull apart, search for a larger goal they can all pull toward and let go of the narrower goals.

questions.q: In Meadows's account, what agreed goal did Sweden find?
options: A fixed national birth rate that every household would be asked to help reach
The quality of child care, not the size of the family
Maximum economic growth
Lower government spending
optionExplain: Sweden did not set a birth-rate number; its agreed goal was the quality of child care.
Right: Sweden found agreement on the quality of child care, not the size of families.
Maximum economic growth is not the goal she reports for Sweden.
The policy increased investment.
questions.explain: Sweden found agreement on the quality of child care, not the size of families. Sweden aligned on quality of child care.
questions.rule: Where actors pull apart, search for a larger goal they can all pull toward and let go of the narrower goals.

questions.q: Which is an example of an overarching goal that harmonizes actors?
options: Two firms cutting prices in turn to beat each other in the same market
A city fining polluters whose waste harms everyone downstream of the plant
A school publishing a ranking of its pupils so that each tries to come out on top
A wartime economy in which firms, workers and the state all serve victory
optionExplain: Cutting prices in turn to beat each other is escalation, not a goal everyone shares.
That is enforcement, not alignment of goals.
Competition is not a shared goal.
Right: A wartime economy has every feedback loop serving one shared goal.
questions.explain: A wartime economy has every feedback loop serving one shared goal. One goal served by every feedback loop.
questions.rule: Where actors pull apart, search for a larger goal they can all pull toward and let go of the narrower goals.

questions.q: With Sweden's policy in place, what did the birth rate do over time?
options: It went up and down several times without causing panic
It rose steadily and never fell again once the new policy took effect
It fell sharply and stayed low for the rest of the century
It was held at a constant level by law
optionExplain: Right: The rate went up and down several times without panic, since the goal was not the number.
The text says it went up and down.
It did not stay low; the rate went up and down several times, without panic.
Sweden set no legal target level; the goal was child care quality, so no number was held constant.
questions.explain: Because the goal was not the number of births, swings were calm.
questions.rule: Where actors pull apart, search for a larger goal they can all pull toward and let go of the narrower goals.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says harmonizing goals can fail in some systems, but is still worth looking for.
questions.explain: She says it is not always possible, but is worth looking for.
questions.rule: Where actors pull apart, search for a larger goal they can all pull toward and let go of the narrower goals.

questions.q: Sweden's government and people agreed on the quality of ____, not on the size of the family.
questions.explain: Their shared goal was the quality of child care.
questions.rule: Where actors pull apart, search for a larger goal they can all pull toward and let go of the narrower goals.

questions.q: A town council, shopkeepers and residents disagree over a pedestrian zone. Which step best follows the Swedish example?
options: Take a vote and let the majority decide, then move on to the next issue
Ask each side to restate its demands more firmly so the council hears them
Look for a shared aim, such as a lively safe town center, and design around it
Delay a decision until feelings have cooled and see whether the matter resolves
optionExplain: A majority vote leaves the minority's goal unmet; it settles the issue without aligning goals.
This entrenches narrower goals.
Right: Looking for a shared aim all sides accept follows the Swedish example.
Waiting for feelings to cool does not look for a shared aim, which is what the Swedish example does.
questions.explain: Seek the goal on which the parties agree. Sweden's policy looked odd in a time of low births because it included free contraceptives and abortion, following the principle that every child should be wanted.
questions.rule: Where actors pull apart, search for a larger goal they can all pull toward and let go of the narrower goals.
questions.teaches: Sweden's policy looked odd in a time of low births because it included free contraceptives and abortion, following the principle that every child should be wanted.

questions.q: Several actors pull one stock toward different goals. What does an effective new policy tend to produce?
questions.explain: Effective policies provoke resistance. The card next gives the trap and the way out.
questions.rule: Policy resistance: many actors pulling one stock; the way out is to let go and seek shared or larger goals.
options: Agreement from all the actors
More resistance from actors whose goals it moves the stock away from
A lasting gain that needs little extra effort to hold
A fall in effort by all actors
optionExplain: Working for one actor does not satisfy the others, who respond.
Right: An effective policy pulls the stock away from other actors' goals and provokes them.
The others' counter-effort undoes much of the gain.
Effort tends to rise as each side responds.

questions.q: According to the trap statement, what is the result for the actors?
options: A result that one actor likes and the others accept as the price of peace
A result that satisfies every actor's goal at the same time
A result that changes quickly as each new policy takes effect on the system
A result no one likes but everyone works to maintain
optionExplain: The point is that no one is satisfied.
The goals conflict, so they cannot all be met.
The stock hardly moves in the trap, so the result does not change quickly with each new policy.
Right: The trap statement says the result is one no one likes but everyone works to maintain.
questions.explain: The trap statement says the result is one no one likes but everyone works to maintain. A standoff nobody wants.
questions.rule: Policy resistance: many actors pulling one stock; the way out is to let go and seek shared or larger goals.

questions.q: Which plan matches the way out?
options: Bring all parties together to redefine a larger shared goal
Pick a winner among the parties and have the others adapt to that party's goal
Increase enforcement until the resistance ends and compliance is complete
Remove the parties' ability to see the stock
optionExplain: Right: The way out brings in all the actors to seek a larger goal they share.
Choosing a winner leaves the other actors' goals unmet, so their resistance continues.
More enforcement is overpowering, which she says leaves heavy costs and keeps the standoff alive.
Hiding the stock from the actors is not a remedy she suggests; the way out is a shared goal.
questions.explain: The way out brings in all the actors to seek a larger goal they share. Bring in all actors.
questions.rule: Policy resistance: many actors pulling one stock; the way out is to let go and seek shared or larger goals.

questions.q: Put these steps of the way out in order.
items: Let go of the ineffective policy
Bring all the actors together
Redirect the energy once spent on resistance
Seek goals everyone can pull toward
questions.explain: The card gives this sequence. Our reading: it follows the order of her statement.
questions.rule: Policy resistance: many actors pulling one stock; the way out is to let go and seek shared or larger goals.

questions.q: True or false: The way out of policy resistance is to let go of overpowering and bring in all the actors.
questions.explain: She says to let go and bring in all the actors.
questions.rule: Policy resistance: many actors pulling one stock; the way out is to let go and seek shared or larger goals.

questions.q: Which case is a policy-resistance trap rather than a different archetype?
options: Two firms keep raising their bids to outdo each other in an auction
A shared pasture becomes overgrazed as each herdsman adds animals
Rival groups each respond to a new rule by pulling the shared stock back toward their own goal
A rich family uses its wealth to gain more wealth than any competitor
optionExplain: Two firms raising bids against each other is escalation, a different archetype.
A shared pasture overgrazed by each herdsman is the tragedy of the commons, a different archetype.
Right: Opposed corrective efforts on one stock mark policy resistance.
That is success to the successful.
questions.explain: Resistance is about opposed corrective efforts on one stock. Meadows adds that when all feedback loops serve one goal, as in wartime mobilization or recovery after a disaster, the results can be amazing.
questions.rule: Policy resistance: many actors pulling one stock; the way out is to let go and seek shared or larger goals.
questions.teaches: Meadows names wartime mobilization and recovery after war or natural disaster as the most familiar examples of harmonized goals.

questions.q: Each person on a shared pasture gets the full benefit of an extra animal but only a share of the damage. What is a fair guess?
options: Each holds back, since all will suffer
Each adds animals, and the pasture is ruined for all
The herd sizes settle at a balanced level
The weakest herdsmen leave first and the rest are safe
optionExplain: Holding back costs the individual and helps everyone; the logic pushes the other way.
Right: the card next shows why this is rational for each.
Nothing in the commons logic produces a balanced stopping point; each herdsman's incentive is to add more.
The ruin falls on all users. Here, individual gain with shared cost drives overuse.
questions.explain: Each herdsman gets the full gain from an extra animal and shares the cost, so each adds animals and the pasture is ruined; the card shows why.
questions.rule: When one user keeps the whole gain and shares the cost, each user's best move is to take more, and all are ruined together.

questions.q: In Hardin's example, what is the herdsman's gain from one more animal compared with his share of the cost?
options: The gain is nearly +1; his share of the cost is only a fraction of -1
The gain and the cost are both shared equally among all the herdsmen
The gain is a fraction of +1 while the cost is the full -1 of the overgrazing
Both the gain and the cost fall on him alone, so he weighs them fully
optionExplain: Right: The herdsman gets the whole proceeds, but the damage is shared across all users.
He receives the whole gain from his animal, not an equal share of it; only the cost is shared.
This reverses Hardin's accounting.
The cost is spread over all users, not borne by him alone.
questions.explain: The herdsman gets the whole proceeds, but the damage is shared across all users. Whole gain, fractional cost.
questions.rule: When one user keeps the whole gain and shares the cost, each user's best move is to take more, and all are ruined together.

questions.q: Forty households each pump water from one aquifer. Which reasoning mirrors the herdsman's?
options: Each thinks: pumping more will cost me the whole shortage, so I should pump less
Each thinks: my own pumping will decide the fate of the entire aquifer
Each thinks: the others will pump less if I pump more, so the aquifer will be fine
Each thinks: pumping more gives me all the water, and the shortage is spread over everyone
optionExplain: The cost is shared, not borne alone.
Each user's share is too small for that thought.
Expecting others to pump less is not the herdsman's reasoning; each assumes the shortage will be shared.
Right: Each household keeps the full benefit of pumping while the shortage is spread over all.
questions.explain: Each household keeps the full benefit of pumping while the shortage is spread over all. The same asymmetry: private gain, shared cost.
questions.rule: When one user keeps the whole gain and shares the cost, each user's best move is to take more, and all are ruined together.

questions.q: If one herdsman alone showed restraint while the rest kept adding animals, what does the logic predict?
options: The pasture recovers because his restraint sets an example the others then follow
The pasture is still overused, and he gives up a gain others take
He is rewarded with better grass on the part of the pasture that he leaves alone
The others follow his lead
optionExplain: Restraint by one does not change the rest's incentives.
Right: His restraint does not change the others' incentives, so the pasture is still overused.
The common grass is shared; no reward goes to him.
Their calculation is unchanged by his choice.
questions.explain: Individual restraint does not change the incentive structure.
questions.rule: When one user keeps the whole gain and shares the cost, each user's best move is to take more, and all are ruined together.

questions.q: True or false: According to Meadows, the tragedy occurs even though each herdsman acts rationally in his own interest.
questions.explain: Hardin's herdsmen are called rational; each follows his own best interest. The tragedy comes from the structure around that rationality.
questions.rule: When one user keeps the whole gain and shares the cost, each user's best move is to take more, and all are ruined together.

questions.q: In Hardin's account the herdsman's share of the cost of overgrazing is only a ____ of -1.
questions.explain: The harm is shared by all, so each bears a fraction of it.
questions.rule: When one user keeps the whole gain and shares the cost, each user's best move is to take more, and all are ruined together.

questions.q: What example caused Hardin to write his article, according to Meadows?
options: Overfishing of the oceans by fleets that share the same open stocks of fish
Pollution of rivers by factories that dump waste into the same stretch of water
Families having any number of children while society bears the costs
Crowded national parks whose natural beauty is ruined by uncontrolled visitors
optionExplain: Overfishing is a commons example, but not the one Meadows says prompted Hardin's article.
River pollution is a commons example, but not the source of Hardin's article.
Right: Meadows says Hardin wrote about families having any number of children while society bears the costs.
She lists parks as an example, but not as the cause of his article.
questions.explain: Meadows says population growth was the example behind Hardin's article. Hardin wrote about a commons of social support: families may have any number of children while society bears the costs of education, health care and environmental protection.
questions.rule: When one user keeps the whole gain and shares the cost, each user's best move is to take more, and all are ruined together.
questions.teaches: Hardin wrote his article about a commons of social support: if every family can have any number of children but society pays for their education, health care and environmental protection, births can exceed what society can support.

questions.q: What makes overgrazing worse than a smaller harvest alone?
options: Cows prefer thin grass and eat it faster than they would eat thick grass
Herdsmen forget to rotate their herds between the parts of the pasture
Past a threshold the damaged resource regenerates less
The pasture grows too fast and crowds out the plants the cows would like
optionExplain: Grass preferences of cows are not part of the logic; the point is that damage lowers regeneration.
Rotation of herds is not in the account; the worsening comes from the erosion loop.
Right: Erosion feeds on itself: past a threshold the damaged resource regenerates less.
The opposite holds: it regenerates less.
questions.explain: Erosion is a reinforcing loop. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A commons fails when overuse pushes the resource past a threshold where it loses the ability to renew itself.

questions.q: What does erodable mean for the commons in Meadows's account?
options: Beyond a threshold, less resource means less ability to regenerate
It can never recover once any of it has been used by anyone
It is shared by a large group of users, rather than owned by any one of them
Its price is rising because it has become scarcer to the people who rely on it
optionExplain: Right: Erodable means beyond a threshold, less resource means less ability to regenerate.
She says regeneration weakens beyond a threshold, not at once.
That is what makes it a commons, not what makes it erodable.
Price is not the meaning of the term here.
questions.explain: Erodable means beyond a threshold, less resource means less ability to regenerate. Erosion means weakened regeneration.
questions.rule: A commons fails when overuse pushes the resource past a threshold where it loses the ability to renew itself.

questions.q: Which resource best fits a commons that is limited and erodable?
options: A beam of sunlight falling on a city street through the morning hours
A traffic rule that every driver in the city follows without being asked
A river's steady water supply in a rainy region where it never runs short
A hillside pasture whose soil washes away when the grass is eaten down
optionExplain: Sunlight is not eroded by use, so it is not a limited erodable commons.
It is not a physical resource that erodes.
It is not limited in the same sense.
Right: A hillside pasture loses soil as the grass is eaten down, so it regenerates less.
questions.explain: Erosion loop needs a resource that degrades with use.
questions.rule: A commons fails when overuse pushes the resource past a threshold where it loses the ability to renew itself.

questions.q: As grass cover thins and soil washes away, the grass grows ____ poorly.
questions.explain: Meadows describes a reinforcing loop in which less soil gives worse grass.
questions.rule: A commons fails when overuse pushes the resource past a threshold where it loses the ability to renew itself.

questions.q: True or false: The erosion loop in a commons is another reinforcing feedback loop, running downhill.
questions.explain: She calls it another reinforcing feedback loop running downhill.
questions.rule: A commons fails when overuse pushes the resource past a threshold where it loses the ability to renew itself.

questions.q: A forest is logged faster than it grows back. Which sign would indicate the erosion loop has begun?
options: Timber prices rise as supply tightens and buyers compete for what is left
Soil loss that makes regrowth poorer, so each year's harvest regrows less
More owners buy forest land, hoping to profit from the rising prices
Heavier rainfall arrives, which helps the trees but not the soil
optionExplain: A price signal is not the erosion loop.
Right: Soil loss makes regrowth poorer, so each harvest regrows less than the last.
Ownership changes are not the loop.
Rainfall is not described as the sign.
questions.explain: Damage reduces the ability to regenerate. Meadows says such cases are overexploitation of renewable resources, a structure already met in the systems zoo.
questions.rule: A commons fails when overuse pushes the resource past a threshold where it loses the ability to renew itself.
questions.teaches: A commons failing through overuse of a renewable resource is the same structure as overexploitation of renewable resources in the systems zoo.

questions.q: What feature of a shared resource most helps overuse continue?
options: The resource is very large
Users' decisions do not respond to the condition of the resource
Users dislike one another
Users are poorly informed about prices
optionExplain: Size is not the key; a huge resource still gets overused if users get no signal from its condition.
Right: Weak feedback from the resource to its users lets overuse continue.
Dislike is not required for the trap.
Prices are not the central link.
questions.explain: Weak feedback is the heart of the structure. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A commons fails when the state of the resource does not feed back into the decisions of its users, or does so too late.

questions.q: Meadows says the tragedy arises from missing or too long ____ feedback from the resource to the growth of users.
questions.explain: She describes missing or too long delayed feedback.
questions.rule: A commons fails when the state of the resource does not feed back into the decisions of its users, or does so too late.

questions.q: Which change would restore the missing feedback in a shared fishery?
options: Let boats enter freely and place no demands on them
Raise the price of fish so that every catch is worth more to each boat
Advertise the fishery to more boats so that the cost of the damage is spread further
Make each boat's catch depend on the visible state of the stock
optionExplain: This leaves the feedback weak.
A price rise does not connect to the stock's condition.
This adds users and spreads the cost even thinner.
Right: Tying each boat's catch to the stock's visible state links resource condition to user decisions.
questions.explain: Tying each boat's catch to the stock's visible state links resource condition to user decisions. Strengthen the link from resource to users.
questions.rule: A commons fails when the state of the resource does not feed back into the decisions of its users, or does so too late.

questions.q: In the immigrant example, what effect does news that laws may be tightened have on a hopeful immigrant?
options: It gives more reason to hurry
It discourages him from coming
It has no effect
It makes him support the tightening
optionExplain: Right: Meadows says so explicitly.
She says the opposite. Here, rush to get in before the door closes.
She says it adds urgency. Here, rush to get in before the door closes.
A tempting pick, but it does not fit the chapter. Rush to get in before the door closes.
questions.explain: Meadows says so explicitly. Rush to get in before the door closes.
questions.rule: A commons fails when the state of the resource does not feed back into the decisions of its users, or does so too late.

questions.q: True or false: In a commons, the more users there are, the less resource each user has.
questions.explain: She says the more users, the more resource is used and the less there is per user.
questions.rule: A commons fails when the state of the resource does not feed back into the decisions of its users, or does so too late.

questions.q: A town park has free entry, a growing visitor count and trampled lawns. Which statement best describes the missing feedback?
options: Visitors dislike each other, so they trample the lawns out of spite
The park is too big for any visitor to notice the damage anywhere in it
Visitors feel no cost from damage, so more keep coming
The lawns are unpopular, so visitors see no reason to look after them
optionExplain: Dislike is not the missing link.
The park's size is not the missing link; the missing link is that visitors feel no cost from the damage.
Right: Visitors bear none of the damage, so more keep coming.
Popularity of the lawns is not the link; visitors bear none of the damage, so nothing makes them hold back.
questions.explain: Users are unaffected by the condition of the resource until it is lost. With no feedback to users, the harvest rate eventually exceeds the resource's capacity, the erosion loop kicks in and all the users are ruined.
questions.rule: A commons fails when the state of the resource does not feed back into the decisions of its users, or does so too late.
questions.teaches: With no feedback to users, the harvest rate eventually exceeds the resource's capacity, the erosion loop kicks in and all the users are ruined.

questions.q: A factory saves money by dumping waste into a river used by many towns. What kind of structure is this?
options: A balancing loop that protects the river by punishing the factory's dumping
A policy-resistance standoff in which several actors pull the river's state apart
A purely private cost that falls only on the factory that does the dumping
A shared sink, where gains are private and harm is shared
optionExplain: Nothing in the case punishes dumping or protects the river, so it is not a balancing loop.
The towns do not pull against the factory on one stock in the case; the harm simply falls on them.
The harm falls on the towns, not the factory.
Right: The river is a shared sink: the factory keeps the savings and the towns share the harm.
questions.explain: The river is a shared sink: the factory keeps the savings and the towns share the harm. Sinks are commons. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Whether a commons is a source or a sink, it fails when users gain in full and bear only a fraction of the damage.

questions.q: Which of these does Meadows treat as a common sink?
options: A shared place where pollution is dumped
A national park that attracts crowds whose numbers are not controlled
A shared pasture where several herdsmen graze their cattle together
A fishery in which many boats take fish from the same stock
optionExplain: Right: A common sink is a shared place where pollution is dumped.
A park is a resource, not a sink.
A pasture is a resource, not a sink.
A fishery is a resource, not a sink.
questions.explain: A common sink is a shared place where pollution is dumped. A sink is where waste goes.
questions.rule: Whether a commons is a source or a sink, it fails when users gain in full and bear only a fraction of the damage.

questions.q: Which is a commons problem according to the chapter?
options: A business that charges fair prices and earns an ordinary profit
A person who saves money in a private account for the future
A nation emitting carbon dioxide by burning fossil fuels
Two firms competing in advertising, each trying to be louder than the other
optionExplain: A fair-priced ordinary business involves no shared resource or shared harm.
Private savings are owned by one person, so cost and benefit stay together; no commons.
Right: Burning fossil fuels loads a shared sink with carbon dioxide, which is on her list.
That is escalation, not a commons.
questions.explain: Climate change from fossil fuel use is on her list.
questions.rule: Whether a commons is a source or a sink, it fails when users gain in full and bear only a fraction of the damage.

questions.q: If a polluter can dump downstream or downwind, what does Meadows expect about its motive to stop?
options: It will stop soon, since pollution comes back
It has no rational reason to desist
It will stop only when fined
It will stop when others pollute
optionExplain: Downwind pollution may never return to it.
Right: No feedback reaches the polluter.
Her point is about weak feedback. Here, no feedback reaches the polluter.
A tempting pick, but it does not fit the chapter. No feedback reaches the polluter.
questions.explain: A polluter who dumps downstream or downwind feels no feedback from the damage, so it has no rational reason to stop.
questions.rule: Whether a commons is a source or a sink, it fails when users gain in full and bear only a fraction of the damage.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says a polluter reaps a large gain and lives with only a fraction of the pollution.
questions.explain: She says it reaps a large gain and lives with only a fraction (or none) of the pollution.
questions.rule: Whether a commons is a source or a sink, it fails when users gain in full and bear only a fraction of the damage.

questions.q: Shared places where pollution can be dumped are called common ____.
questions.explain: Meadows extends the commons to sinks as well as sources.
questions.rule: Whether a commons is a source or a sink, it fails when users gain in full and bear only a fraction of the damage.

questions.q: Meadows asks how willing you are to carpool to cut air pollution. What is she showing?
options: That the commons logic is easy to understand from one's own behavior
That carpooling is useless
That air is private property
That regulation is unneeded
optionExplain: Right: She is showing that the commons logic is easy to see in our own behavior.
Her question does not call carpooling useless; it shows how reluctant we are when the benefit is shared.
Air is a shared sink, a commons, not private property.
She argues the structure favors selfish behavior, so regulation matters.
questions.explain: Selfish behavior is more convenient and profitable than responsible behavior in a commons. Meadows says the structure of a commons makes selfish behavior much more convenient and profitable than behavior responsible to the community and the future.
questions.rule: Whether a commons is a source or a sink, it fails when users gain in full and bear only a fraction of the damage.
questions.teaches: Meadows says the structure of a commons makes selfish behavior much more convenient and profitable than behavior responsible to the whole community and the future.

questions.q: Which remedy for a shared resource gives each user a direct link to the consequences of their own use?
questions.explain: Privatizing makes the link direct. The card sets out all three remedies.
questions.rule: Match the remedy to the feedback it supplies: moral pressure, direct feedback through ownership, or indirect feedback through regulators.
options: Appealing to users' sense of morality
Hiring regulators to monitor and penalize use
Dividing it so each person bears the results of their own actions
Teaching users how overuse damages the resource
optionExplain: Moral appeal is tempting, but it relies on persuasion rather than a link between use and consequence.
Regulators do supply a link, but an indirect one that runs through them.
Right: Dividing the resource puts gains and losses on the same decision maker, which is a direct feedback link.
Education informs users, yet they still bear only a fraction of the cost of their own use.

questions.q: What does privatization do for feedback?
options: It links the resource to users indirectly, through regulators who monitor it
It replaces feedback with moral pressure on each user to hold back
It removes feedback altogether
It links the resource's condition directly to those who use it
optionExplain: Linking the resource to users through regulators is regulation, not privatization.
Moral pressure on each user is exhortation, not privatization.
The opposite: gains and losses land on the same owner.
Right: Privatization makes a direct link from the resource's condition to its users.
questions.explain: Privatization makes a direct link from the resource's condition to its users. Privatization creates direct feedback.
questions.rule: Match the remedy to the feedback it supplies: moral pressure, direct feedback through ownership, or indirect feedback through regulators.

questions.q: A town limits boat licenses and inspects catches. Which remedy is this?
options: Exhortation
Regulation
Privatization
Education
optionExplain: Exhortation relies on appeals to conscience; limiting licenses and inspecting catches is enforced by regulators.
Right: Mutual coercion via regulators and penalties.
Privatization would give each user a separate share; a town limiting licenses keeps the resource shared.
Education tries to inform users; licenses and inspections are mutual coercion through regulators.
questions.explain: Mutual coercion via regulators and penalties.
questions.rule: Match the remedy to the feedback it supplies: moral pressure, direct feedback through ownership, or indirect feedback through regulators.

questions.q: If a regulatory body is uninformed or weak, what does Meadows expect?
options: Users will behave well anyway
Privatization becomes the only remedy left, since regulation has failed
The indirect feedback will not work
Exhortation becomes more effective, because users will seek out guidance themselves
optionExplain: She says regulators must be capable and honest for rules to work.
Many resources cannot be privatized, and she does not say regulation's failure makes it the only remedy.
Right: If regulators are uninformed or weak, the indirect feedback fails.
She does not say weak regulation improves exhortation; the indirect feedback simply fails.
questions.explain: Regulators must have expertise, deterrence and concern for the community.
questions.rule: Match the remedy to the feedback it supplies: moral pressure, direct feedback through ownership, or indirect feedback through regulators.

questions.q: True or false: Hardin's phrase mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon, describes regulation.
questions.explain: Mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon, is Hardin's phrase for regulation, not for privatization.
questions.rule: Match the remedy to the feedback it supplies: moral pressure, direct feedback through ownership, or indirect feedback through regulators.

questions.q: Hardin's blunt name for the third option, regulation, is mutual ____, mutually agreed upon.
questions.explain: The phrase is mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon.
questions.rule: Match the remedy to the feedback it supplies: moral pressure, direct feedback through ownership, or indirect feedback through regulators.

questions.q: A village shares a well. Which remedy gives each household a direct stake in the well's condition?
options: A sign asking people to take care of the well and to take no more than they need
A guard paid by the council to watch the well and report anyone who takes too much
Dividing the water rights so each household owns a measured share
A speech by the mayor about the value of wells and how they can run dry
optionExplain: A sign asking for restraint is exhortation, an appeal with no direct stake.
A paid guard is regulation, an indirect link through an outside monitor.
Right: Dividing the water rights into measured shares ties gains and losses together.
A speech about the value of wells is education, which gives no household a direct stake.
questions.explain: Ownership ties gains and losses together. Even an owner may still abuse the resource, but now it takes ignorance or irrationality to do so.
questions.rule: Match the remedy to the feedback it supplies: moral pressure, direct feedback through ownership, or indirect feedback through regulators.
questions.teaches: An owner of a privatized resource may still abuse it, but doing so now takes ignorance or irrationality.

questions.q: What weakness does Hardin see in protecting a commons by tradition alone?
options: It can attract people who do not respect the tradition
It collapses within a single generation in every culture that has tried it
It costs too much to keep up
It is too strict, so people give up on it rather than follow its rules
optionExplain: Right: An honor system can attract people who do not respect the tradition.
Contradicted: some cultures managed it for generations.
Cost is not the weakness Hardin names; his concern is that tradition fails when newcomers do not honor it.
Strictness is not his point; the problem is that people who do not respect the tradition can join.
questions.explain: Honor systems depend on honor. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: An honor system works only as long as everyone honors it, so exhortation alone is a fragile defense.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says some cultures have managed common resources effectively for generations through education and exhortation.
questions.explain: Yes, she says so, while noting Hardin's doubt.
questions.rule: An honor system works only as long as everyone honors it, so exhortation alone is a fragile defense.

questions.q: Which situation shows the weakness Hardin names?
options: A town fines polluters and the pollution stops within the same year
A farmer owns his land and conserves it because he bears the cost of ruin
A village shares a well and every household complies with the old customs
A shared lake's custom of modest fishing is broken by a newcomer who ignores it
optionExplain: This shows regulation working.
This shows privatization working.
A village whose households all comply with custom shows tradition working, not the weakness.
Right: A newcomer who ignores a shared custom shows that tradition has no hold on outsiders.
questions.explain: A tradition has no force against those outside it.
questions.rule: An honor system works only as long as everyone honors it, so exhortation alone is a fragile defense.

questions.q: If more outsiders arrive in a community that relies on tradition, what does Hardin's view predict?
options: The tradition grows stronger as it is explained to the new arrivals
More people who may not honor the tradition, so protection weakens
No change, since a tradition keeps working however many people come
An automatic move to privatization
optionExplain: Explaining the tradition does not make newcomers honor it; his view is that protection weakens as outsiders arrive.
Right: More outsiders mean more people who may not honor the tradition, so protection weakens.
His view is that it can be undermined.
Nothing says outsiders choose privatization; the prediction is only that tradition weakens.
questions.explain: More outsiders mean more people who may not honor the tradition, so protection weakens. Honor systems rely on honor.
questions.rule: An honor system works only as long as everyone honors it, so exhortation alone is a fragile defense.

questions.q: True or false: Hardin concludes that exhortation cannot work in any culture.
questions.explain: Meadows says some cultures have managed this way; Hardin only doubts it is dependable.
questions.rule: An honor system works only as long as everyone honors it, so exhortation alone is a fragile defense.

questions.q: Common resources protected only by tradition or an honor system may attract those who have no ____.
questions.explain: An honor system depends on everyone having honor.
questions.rule: An honor system works only as long as everyone honors it, so exhortation alone is a fragile defense.

questions.q: A neighborhood garden runs on an honor system. A few take produce without helping. What does this show?
options: Gardens cannot be shared at all
The honor system relies on everyone sharing it
Honor systems are wrong in every case and should be replaced by a guard
Education is useless, since a few people will ignore whatever they are taught
optionExplain: An overreach; the lesson is about reliance on honor.
Right: The honor system relies on everyone honoring it.
An overreach; Hardin says only that it is undependable.
An overreach; the chapter keeps education as one remedy.
questions.explain: Our reading: the local case matches Hardin's concern. Meadows says privatization works more reliably than exhortation, if society will let some individuals learn the hard way.
questions.rule: An honor system works only as long as everyone honors it, so exhortation alone is a fragile defense.
questions.teaches: Privatization works more reliably than exhortation, if society is willing to let some individuals learn the hard way.

questions.q: A team's results vary. Managers recall the poor weeks most strongly. What is the likely effect on their view of performance?
options: They judge it more accurately, since bad weeks teach most
They judge it as better, since they react to bad weeks
Their view is unaffected by memory
They judge it as worse than it really is
optionExplain: Vivid memory is not the same as accuracy.
Reacting does not lift the perceived level.
Perception depends on what is remembered.
Right: the card shows this negative bias.
questions.explain: The actor tends to believe bad news more than good. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Check whether the actor's perception of performance is biased toward bad news before trusting the gap it reacts to.

questions.q: In drift to low performance, what are the best results treated as?
options: Aberrations
Targets to meet again
Proof of a trend
Measurement errors only in the worst months
optionExplain: Right: The best are dismissed; the worst stay in memory.
That would be the way out. Here, the best are dismissed; the worst stay in memory.
The actor dismisses them. Here, the best are dismissed; the worst stay in memory.
The dismissal applies to the best results.
questions.explain: The best are dismissed; the worst stay in memory.
questions.rule: Check whether the actor's perception of performance is biased toward bad news before trusting the gap it reacts to.

questions.q: A hospital director focuses on three complaints and ignores a year of rising satisfaction scores. Which part of the archetype is this?
options: The goal is rising along with performance
A competitor is escalating
The perceived state is more negative than the actual state
An intervenor is doing the hospital's work
optionExplain: The case shows a gloomy view of the facts, not a rising goal.
No rival is involved in the case; the director's own view of the data is the issue.
Right: The director's perceived state is more negative than the actual state.
No outside helper does the hospital's work; the archetype here is a biased perception of the state.
questions.explain: The director's perceived state is more negative than the actual state. Bad news weighs more than good.
questions.rule: Check whether the actor's perception of performance is biased toward bad news before trusting the gap it reacts to.

questions.q: A manager starts weighing good and bad results equally. Which part of the archetype has she removed?
options: The goal's dependence on perceived performance
The negative bias in perceived performance
The comparison of goal with perceived state
The corrective action taken when a gap appears
optionExplain: This is a separate element of the archetype and would remain in place.
Right: weighing good and bad results equally removes the bias that makes things look worse than they are.
The comparison is the balancing loop itself, which the manager still performs.
Corrective action still follows any gap, so it is not what she changed.
questions.explain: The archetype has two twists: a negative bias in perceiving results, and a goal that follows perceived results. Weighing results equally removes the first.
questions.rule: Check whether the actor's perception of performance is biased toward bad news before trusting the gap it reacts to.

questions.q: In drift to low performance, the actor tends to believe ____ news more than good news.
questions.explain: Best results get dismissed and worst results stay in memory.
questions.rule: Check whether the actor's perception of performance is biased toward bad news before trusting the gap it reacts to.

questions.q: True or false: In drift to low performance, the actor sees performance as worse than it really is.
questions.explain: The actor tends to believe bad news more than good, so things look worse than they are.
questions.rule: Check whether the actor's perception of performance is biased toward bad news before trusting the gap it reacts to.

questions.q: Which of Meadows's examples shows a person drifting without any institution involved?
options: Her jogging program, which faded away
Falling market share, as a firm slowly loses ground to its rivals
The state of America's public schools over the last several decades
Eroding quality of service at a hospital that once had high standards
optionExplain: Right: Meadows lists her own jogging program, which faded away, as a case of drift.
A firm losing market share is an institutional example; her case without any institution is the personal jogging program.
The state of America's public schools involves an institution, the school system.
A hospital's eroding service is an institutional example, not a person drifting alone.
questions.explain: She includes her own jogging program. Meadows also lists weight gained despite periodic diets and the state of America's public schools among her examples.
questions.rule: Check whether the actor's perception of performance is biased toward bad news before trusting the gap it reacts to.
questions.teaches: Increased fat in spite of periodic diets and the state of America's public schools are further examples of drift to low performance.

questions.q: Why might performance fall steadily even though a team compares itself with a goal each period?
options: The team never measures anything
The goal is set far too high
The goal itself keeps being lowered to match results
Results improve too fast
optionExplain: The loop includes a comparison.
A high fixed goal would trigger correction.
Right: Goals that follow results shrink the gap that would prompt action.
Results are falling in this case.
questions.explain: Sliding goals shrink the gap. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: If the standard falls whenever performance falls, the gap never gets large enough to trigger correction.

questions.q: Put the downhill loop in order, starting with the perceived state.
items: Perceived performance drops
The desired state is lowered
The gap shrinks
Less corrective action is taken
Actual performance falls
questions.explain: Each step feeds the next, and the loop closes back to the perceived state.
questions.rule: If the standard falls whenever performance falls, the gap never gets large enough to trigger correction.

questions.q: Which remark signals eroding goals?
options: We must return to the level we reached in our best year
Well, we are not doing much worse than last year
We will check the figures again next month
We need to find who is to blame
optionExplain: Returning to the best year's level keeps a high standard, the opposite of an eroding goal.
Right: the standard follows past results.
Checking the figures again says nothing about the standard sliding with past results.
Hunting for blame is not a sign of a falling goal; eroding goals show up as acceptance of a lower standard.
questions.explain: the standard follows past results. The standard slips with the record.
questions.rule: If the standard falls whenever performance falls, the gap never gets large enough to trigger correction.

questions.q: What happens to corrective action as the desired state falls toward the actual state?
options: It weakens, since the gap gets smaller
It strengthens, since the situation is worse
It stays the same
It shifts to another actor
optionExplain: Right: Smaller gap, less action.
The gap matters, not the level. Here, smaller gap, less action.
It depends on the gap. Here, smaller gap, less action.
A tempting pick, but it does not fit the chapter. Smaller gap, less action.
questions.explain: Corrective action follows the gap between desired and actual state; when the goal falls toward performance, the gap and the action both shrink.
questions.rule: If the standard falls whenever performance falls, the gap never gets large enough to trigger correction.

questions.q: True or false: In this archetype the standard falls along with the perceived performance.
questions.explain: The standard falls with the perceived state; that is the trap.
questions.rule: If the standard falls whenever performance falls, the gap never gets large enough to trigger correction.

questions.q: A runner lowers her weekly target each time she misses it. Which statement fits?
options: She is escalating against a rival whose weekly target she is trying to beat
She is shifting a burden to a coach who takes over the work of training
She is beating a rule by meeting its letter while defeating its purpose
The target is tied to results, so the gap needed to prompt effort never opens
optionExplain: No rival's target is involved; the runner's target follows her own results.
No coach takes over her training, so this is not a shifted burden.
No rule is being evaded; the runner's own target is sliding with her results.
Right: When the target follows the results, the gap that would prompt effort never opens.
questions.explain: Eroding goals fit individual habits. The trap is also known as eroding goals, because the goal itself erodes as performance does.
questions.rule: If the standard falls whenever performance falls, the gap never gets large enough to trigger correction.
questions.teaches: The trap is also known as eroding goals, because the goal itself erodes as performance does.

questions.q: Why do people often fail to respond to a decline that happens slowly?
options: Slow changes cannot be measured, so there is no way to notice them
They adjust their expectations as the decline proceeds
Slow changes do not matter
Slow declines are reversed by the system itself before they do any harm
optionExplain: They can be measured; people lose the memory of earlier standards.
Right: They adjust their expectations as the decline proceeds.
They can do as much damage as a sudden fall.
Nothing makes a slow decline reverse itself; unnoticed, it keeps lowering expectations.
questions.explain: Gradual change erodes expectations. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Slow declines escape correction because the memory of better times fades along with the performance.

questions.q: What does Meadows say about the truth of the boiled-frog story?
options: She says the story is a proven fact of animal behavior and cites a study
She says the story is false and offers it only as an example of folk error
She does not know whether it is true
She does not mention the story and instead uses the name eroding goals alone
optionExplain: She expresses doubt, not certainty.
She says she does not know, not that it is false.
Right: She says she does not know whether the story is true; it serves as an illustration.
She does mention the story and gives it as another name for the trap.
questions.explain: She says she does not know whether the story is true; it serves as an illustration. It is an illustration.
questions.rule: Slow declines escape correction because the memory of better times fades along with the performance.

questions.q: A sudden drop in quality would likely cause what, according to Meadows?
options: Lowered expectations that spread quietly through the whole organization over time
No response at all
An agitated corrective process
A new and lower goal that people would adopt almost overnight to restore calm
optionExplain: That comes with slow drift, not a sudden plunge.
Slow drift draws no response; a plunge does.
Right: A sudden plunge would trigger an agitated corrective process.
The goal slides only when the decline is gradual.
questions.explain: A sudden plunge would trigger an agitated corrective process. Plunge triggers correction.
questions.rule: Slow declines escape correction because the memory of better times fades along with the performance.

questions.q: If a firm's quality drops 1 percent each month, what does the archetype predict about staff concern?
options: It stays low, since each step is small
Concern rises a little more each month, as the cumulative loss becomes obvious
Concern stays low for most months and then jumps sharply once the total is large
Concern is unaffected by the drop
optionExplain: Right: Concern stays low, since each monthly step is too small to alarm anyone.
Gradual change erases the contrast that would raise concern.
The archetype describes continued lulling, not a late alarm.
Concern is lulled by small steps, not absent by nature.
questions.explain: Concern stays low, since each monthly step is too small to alarm anyone. Gradual drift lulls everyone.
questions.rule: Slow declines escape correction because the memory of better times fades along with the performance.

questions.q: True or false: Drift to low performance is usually a gradual process, not a sudden collapse.
questions.explain: She describes drift as a gradual process that lulls everyone into lower expectations, not a sudden collapse.
questions.rule: Slow declines escape correction because the memory of better times fades along with the performance.

questions.q: Another name for drift to low performance is eroding ____.
questions.explain: Drift to low performance is also called eroding goals, because the goal erodes along with performance.
questions.rule: Slow declines escape correction because the memory of better times fades along with the performance.

questions.q: A town's streetlights fail one by one over years. Which statement fits best?
options: A sudden event caused the decline
Neighbors are escalating against one another by letting their own lights fail
An outside helper is hiding the problem by repairing the lights in secret
The slow pace lets residents get used to the dark
optionExplain: The case describes a gradual change over years.
No rivalry is described; the lights fail slowly and residents adapt.
No outside helper is described covering up the problem; the slow pace itself dulls notice.
Right: A slow decline lets residents get used to the dark.
questions.explain: Gradual decline lulls. A slow decline lulls everyone into lower and lower expectations, lower effort and lower performance.
questions.rule: Slow declines escape correction because the memory of better times fades along with the performance.
questions.teaches: A slow decline lulls everyone into lower and lower expectations, lower effort and lower performance.

questions.q: A club's standards sag after every poor season. Which change would stop the sag?
options: Tie the standard to the latest season
Tie the standard to its best seasons rather than its worst
Drop standards altogether
Ignore all results and rely on the club's reputation to hold its level
optionExplain: That keeps the standard following results, as in eroding goals.
Right: Tying the standard to its best seasons turns the downhill loop into an uphill one.
Without a standard there is no gap to prompt action.
Relying on reputation drops the gap between standard and result; both of her antidotes keep a standard in play.
questions.explain: Best-based goals lift performance. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Fix the standard, or anchor it to the best results, so the same loop pulls performance up instead of down.

questions.q: One antidote to eroding goals is to keep standards ____, regardless of performance.
questions.explain: One way to break the slide is to hold standards absolute, so they do not follow performance down.
questions.rule: Fix the standard, or anchor it to the best results, so the same loop pulls performance up instead of down.

questions.q: Which policy applies the second antidote?
options: Set the target from last year's average, so that it reflects typical results
Set this year's target from the best year on record
Set the target from the worst year on record
Set no target for the year, so that no one is discouraged by missing it
optionExplain: Averages are pulled down by the worst results.
Right: Setting the target from the best year on record anchors it to the best performance.
That anchors the goal to the worst, the trap itself.
Without a target no gap exists to prompt effort.
questions.explain: Setting the target from the best year on record anchors it to the best performance. Use the best results.
questions.rule: Fix the standard, or anchor it to the best results, so the same loop pulls performance up instead of down.

questions.q: If perception has an upbeat bias, how are the worst results treated?
options: As the new normal
As aberrations to be ignored forever
As the standard
As temporary setbacks
optionExplain: Treating the worst as the new normal is the downbeat bias; the upbeat bias treats the worst as temporary.
Upbeat bias does not ignore the worst forever; it treats the worst results as temporary setbacks.
The standard is the best results under the upbeat bias; the worst are not the standard.
Right: Best is the standard; worst is temporary.
questions.explain: Best is the standard; worst is temporary.
questions.rule: Fix the standard, or anchor it to the best results, so the same loop pulls performance up instead of down.

questions.q: Which statement misreads the antidote?
options: It requires removing the feedback loop that sets goals from performance
It reuses the same structure with an upward bias in how performance is perceived
It turns the reinforcing loop from a downhill one into an uphill one
It treats the worst results as temporary setbacks and the best as the standard
optionExplain: Right: The antidote keeps the same structure; it does not remove the loop that links goals to performance.
This describes the antidote correctly: the same structure with an upward bias in perception.
This describes the antidote correctly: the downhill reinforcing loop becomes an uphill one.
This describes the antidote correctly: the worst are temporary setbacks and the best the standard.
questions.explain: The antidote keeps the same structure; it does not remove the loop that links goals to performance. Meadows says use the same structure.
questions.rule: Fix the standard, or anchor it to the best results, so the same loop pulls performance up instead of down.

questions.q: True or false: One antidote to eroding goals is to make goals follow the best performances of the past.
questions.explain: The antidote is to follow the best performances, or keep standards absolute.
questions.rule: Fix the standard, or anchor it to the best results, so the same loop pulls performance up instead of down.

questions.q: Meadows applies the antidote to her own faded jogging program. What does she say would be true now?
options: She would have given up sooner
She would still be failing
She would be running marathons by now if she had applied it
She would have found a coach to take over the training and so improved
optionExplain: The lesson points toward higher performance, not quitting.
She says the same structure would pull her upward.
Right: She says she would be running marathons by now if she had applied the lesson.
No coach appears in her remark; the lesson is about the standard she set herself.
questions.explain: Upbeat bias would have lifted her. Meadows says she would be running marathons by now if she had applied the lesson to her jogging, which shows the same structure can pull performance up.
questions.rule: Fix the standard, or anchor it to the best results, so the same loop pulls performance up instead of down.
questions.teaches: Meadows says that if she had applied this lesson to her jogging, she would be running marathons by now, showing the same structure can drive performance upward.

questions.q: A system's results worsen year after year while its targets are lowered. Which archetype is that?
options: Policy resistance, in which several actors hold a stock at a state nobody wants
Escalation, in which two rivals raise their goals to stay ahead of each other
Rule beating, in which people meet the letter of a rule and defeat its spirit
Drift to low performance
optionExplain: Resistance holds the state steady rather than letting it worsen.
Here targets are lowered, not raised against a rival.
Nobody is evading a rule; the case is about targets sliding as results worsen.
Right: Worsening results with lowered targets are the signs of drift to low performance.
questions.explain: Worsening plus slipping goals. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Persistent bad is resistance; steadily worsening with a slipping goal is drift.

questions.q: Which phrase describes the drift trap's cause in Meadows's statement?
options: Standards influenced by past performance, with negative bias
Competing actors pulling one stock toward their own different goals
A shared resource used up
An outside helper taking over a job and weakening the original system
optionExplain: Right: Standards influenced by past performance, with a negative bias, cause the drift.
That is the cause of policy resistance.
That is the cause of the commons trap.
That is the cause of shifting the burden.
questions.explain: Standards influenced by past performance, with a negative bias, cause the drift. Eroding goals.
questions.rule: Persistent bad is resistance; steadily worsening with a slipping goal is drift.

questions.q: A town's roads stay as poor as ever under four administrations that each pulled different levers. Which archetype?
options: Drift to low performance
Escalation
Policy resistance
Success to the successful
optionExplain: Roads don't worsen here. Here, stuck, not worsening.
Escalation needs rivals raising their goals against each other; the roads have no such rivals.
Right: Stuck, not worsening.
Success to the successful needs winners gaining resources to win more; the roads show none of that.
questions.explain: Roads that stay as poor as ever show a stuck state held by opposed pulls, which is policy resistance; drift would show worsening roads.
questions.rule: Persistent bad is resistance; steadily worsening with a slipping goal is drift.

questions.q: If standards were fixed at an absolute level, what would you expect in a drift system?
options: The downhill loop gets worse
The eroding-goal loop is cut, and gaps trigger corrective action
Nothing changes, because the actor's perception stays as biased as before
Escalation begins, as the actor starts to compare itself with other actors
optionExplain: A fixed standard removes the slide rather than worsening it.
Right: Absolute standards cut the eroding-goal loop, so gaps prompt corrective action.
Perception stays biased, but the standard no longer follows it down.
Nothing in the drift structure creates a rival, so escalation does not begin.
questions.explain: Absolute standards cut the eroding-goal loop, so gaps prompt corrective action. Absolute standards break the loop.
questions.rule: Persistent bad is resistance; steadily worsening with a slipping goal is drift.

questions.q: True or false: Drift to low performance is a form of policy resistance in which several actors pull a stock in opposite directions.
questions.explain: Drift involves one actor's slipping goal; resistance involves several actors with opposed goals.
questions.rule: Persistent bad is resistance; steadily worsening with a slipping goal is drift.

questions.q: In drift to low performance, the actor's goal ____ as perceived performance falls.
questions.explain: The desired state is influenced by the perceived state.
questions.rule: Persistent bad is resistance; steadily worsening with a slipping goal is drift.

questions.q: Which pairing is right?
options: Fixes that fail: stuck state; drift: worsening state
Fixes that fail: a worsening state; drift: a state that stays stuck
Both traps: a state that improves steadily
Both traps: a state that moves at random with no pattern to explain it
optionExplain: Right: Resistance leaves a bad state stuck, while drift lets it keep getting worse.
This reverses the two patterns.
Both are traps that produce poor results.
Both are structures that produce characteristic patterns.
questions.explain: Resistance holds the state; drift lets it sink. In drift, the balancing loop that should hold performance up is overwhelmed by a reinforcing loop heading downhill.
questions.rule: Persistent bad is resistance; steadily worsening with a slipping goal is drift.
questions.teaches: In drift to low performance, the balancing loop that should keep the system state acceptable is overwhelmed by a reinforcing loop heading downhill.

questions.q: Two rivals each try to end up slightly ahead of the other. What is the likely pattern?
options: They settle at an equal level once each has matched the other's position
The weaker one drops out immediately and the contest is over at once
The pattern swings back and forth between them without any overall growth
Both push further and further, in a reinforcing spiral
optionExplain: Nothing holds the rivals at equality; each aims to be a little ahead, so the level keeps rising.
Collapse comes later, after a build-up.
Each step raises the level; the loop is reinforcing.
Right: Each actor sets its goal above the other's, so both push further in a reinforcing spiral.
questions.explain: Chasing a rival reinforces. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: In escalation each actor sets its goal by the rival's state and adds a little more, so the loop reinforces.

questions.q: The decision rule that leads to escalation is: I'll ____ you one.
questions.explain: Meadows names the rule I'll raise you one.
questions.rule: In escalation each actor sets its goal by the rival's state and adds a little more, so the loop reinforces.

questions.q: Which setting is escalation, not a thermostat-style loop?
options: A room heater that aims for 18 degrees whatever the weather outside
Each firm sets its price a little below the other's
A bank that sets a fixed interest rate and keeps it for the whole year
A farm that aims for a set yield from its land every year in turn
optionExplain: Its goal is absolute, like the thermostat the card contrasts.
Right: In escalation the goal depends on the other actor's state, as with undercutting a rival's price.
A fixed rate does not depend on a rival's state.
A fixed target is absolute, not tied to another actor.
questions.explain: In escalation the goal depends on the other actor's state, as with undercutting a rival's price. The goal depends on the other actor's state.
questions.rule: In escalation each actor sets its goal by the rival's state and adds a little more, so the loop reinforces.

questions.q: If one rival's state suddenly rises, what happens to the other's goal?
options: It stays fixed, because its goal does not depend on the first actor
It falls to match the first actor's lower position from before
It rises above the first's new level
It becomes absolute, like a thermostat setting that no longer responds
optionExplain: In escalation the goal is tied to the other's state.
The goal is raised above, not lowered to match.
Right: The other actor's goal rises above the first's new level: it ups it.
The thermostat contrast is the opposite of escalation.
questions.explain: The other actor's goal rises above the first's new level: it ups it. Each ups the other.
questions.rule: In escalation each actor sets its goal by the rival's state and adds a little more, so the loop reinforces.

questions.q: True or false: According to Meadows, escalation is not necessarily a bad thing.
questions.explain: She says escalation is not necessarily a bad thing: competition over a desirable goal can hasten progress.
questions.rule: In escalation each actor sets its goal by the rival's state and adds a little more, so the loop reinforces.

questions.q: Two universities compete to build better laboratories. Under Meadows's view, when is that still a trap?
options: Never, since a goal as desirable as a better laboratory cannot cause a trap
Only if one of the two universities eventually wins the contest outright
When the contest has no stopping point and costs soar
Only when the competition turns violent
optionExplain: She says escalating in a good direction can be a problem.
Winning is not her test; the lack of a stopping point is.
Right: Even good escalation becomes a problem when it has no stopping point and the costs soar.
Violence is not required; costs alone can make it a problem.
questions.explain: Even good escalation can be hard to stop. Hospitals each trying to outdo the others in costly diagnostic machines can push health care costs out of sight.
questions.rule: In escalation each actor sets its goal by the rival's state and adds a little more, so the loop reinforces.
questions.teaches: Meadows notes that even escalating in a good direction can be a problem because it isn't easy to stop; hospitals racing to buy costly diagnostic machines push health costs out of sight.

questions.q: Two candidates keep escalating attacks on each other. What do voters end up knowing?
options: Little about either candidate's positive features
More about each candidate's policies
Which candidate is the more honest
Nothing new, since the campaign remains the same as it was at the start
optionExplain: Right: Smears crowd out the positive information voters would need.
She says voters lose sight of positive features.
Smears do not reveal honesty; they crowd out the positive information voters need.
The campaign changes as each side smears back.
questions.explain: Negative campaigns erode information. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Look for two actors who each set their level by the other's, and find the reinforcing loop.

questions.q: In a price war, what is the typical end?
options: Prices settle at a fair level once both firms see the cost of cutting
Prices rise for good once the weaker firm has left the market
The competitors merge by common choice before either runs out of money
Both sides lose money, and one may go bankrupt
optionExplain: The spiral continues until someone breaks.
Meadows ends the case with losses and possible bankruptcy.
No merger is described; the price war ends in losses and possibly a bankruptcy.
Right: In a price war both sides lose money, and one may go bankrupt.
questions.explain: In a price war both sides lose money, and one may go bankrupt. Both lose.
questions.rule: Look for two actors who each set their level by the other's, and find the reinforcing loop.

questions.q: Which is escalation?
options: A baker who keeps prices steady through the year whatever the others do
Billboards getting bigger as each firm tries to be noticed
A shop that cuts its prices once after a poor season and then holds them
A town that builds a new library
optionExplain: A baker holding prices steady is not responding to a rival's state, so there is no spiral.
Right: Advertisers escalate by doing something louder and bigger than the competitor.
A single cut is not a spiral against a rival.
A library built because residents asked involves no rival, so it is not escalation.
questions.explain: Advertisers escalate by doing something louder and bigger than the competitor. Louder, bigger, brasher.
questions.rule: Look for two actors who each set their level by the other's, and find the reinforcing loop.

questions.q: If one side in an arms race increases its weapons, what does Meadows expect from the other?
options: An immediate reduction
A scramble to surpass it
No change
A request for talks as the first step
optionExplain: An immediate reduction is the reverse of escalation; each increase drives a further increase.
Right: Each increase drives the other.
No change would stop the spiral, but Meadows says each increase drives the other side's.
A request for talks is a way out, not what each side's increase provokes.
questions.explain: In an arms race each side's increase drives the other side's, so the other scrambles to surpass it.
questions.rule: Look for two actors who each set their level by the other's, and find the reinforcing loop.

questions.q: Which description is wrong?
options: The race cost trillions of dollars and weakened both economies
Each side exaggerated reports of the other's arms to justify its own
Two economies were degraded as the weapons grew more destructive
Each side in the arms race blamed only itself
optionExplain: The text states that the race cost trillions and weakened both economies, so this is not the false one.
The text says each side exaggerated reports of the other's arms, so this is not the false one.
The text says both economies were degraded as the weapons grew more destructive, so this is true.
Right: The statement is wrong: each side blamed the other, though Meadows says each was escalating itself.
questions.explain: The statement is wrong: each side blamed the other, though Meadows says each was escalating itself. Systematically, each side escalated itself.
questions.rule: Look for two actors who each set their level by the other's, and find the reinforcing loop.

questions.q: Price wars can end with the ____ of one of the competitors.
questions.explain: Meadows says this kind of escalation can end in bankruptcy.
questions.rule: Look for two actors who each set their level by the other's, and find the reinforcing loop.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says each side in the arms race was, in systems terms, escalating itself.
questions.explain: Each side's weapons development started a process sure to require more weapons development later.
questions.rule: Look for two actors who each set their level by the other's, and find the reinforcing loop.

questions.q: Cocktail party voices get louder as people raise theirs to be heard. Which is the closest archetype?
options: Escalation
Policy resistance
Commons
Drift
optionExplain: Right: Meadows lists increasing loudness among escalation cases. Meadows says escalation also produces ever-louder conversation at cocktail parties, ever-longer limousines and ever-raunchier rock bands.
