Policy resistance has opposed actors pulling one stock apart; loud voices rising together is a race.
A commons is a shared resource overused with delayed feedback; speaking louder is a race, not a commons.
Drift is an eroding goal; here each voice raises its level against the others.
questions.explain: Meadows lists increasing loudness among escalation cases. Meadows says escalation also produces ever-louder conversation at cocktail parties, ever-longer limousines and ever-raunchier rock bands.
questions.rule: Look for two actors who each set their level by the other's, and find the reinforcing loop.
questions.teaches: Meadows says escalation also produces the increasing loudness of conversation at cocktail parties, the lengthening of limousines and the raunchiness of rock bands.

questions.q: If nothing interrupts an escalating rivalry, how does it usually end?
options: It levels off at a comfortable point
It fades when interest wanes
One or both competitors break down
The rivals merge
optionExplain: A reinforcing loop does not level off by itself; exponential growth cannot go on forever.
Interest does not fade in her account; the spiral ends when someone breaks down.
Right: Exponential growth cannot go on forever. The card next shows why.
Merging is not her ending; escalation ends in someone's collapse or a negotiated exit.
questions.explain: Exponential growth cannot go on forever. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A reinforcing race does not level off by itself; it ends when someone breaks.

questions.q: Because escalation is a reinforcing feedback loop, it builds ____.
questions.explain: Because escalation is a reinforcing feedback loop, it builds exponentially, which is why it reaches extremes so fast.
questions.rule: A reinforcing race does not level off by itself; it ends when someone breaks.

questions.q: In a price war each side's discount doubles every round: 1, 2, 4, 8 percent. What does this pattern show?
options: A linear trend, because each round adds a steady amount to the cut
A balancing loop, because the rivals are responding to each other's moves
A steady state, because the same kind of move is repeated in every round
An exponential build-up
optionExplain: Doubling steps add more each round, so they are not linear.
The response reinforces rather than stabilizes.
The size of the move grows each round.
Right: Doubling again and again is exponential build-up.
questions.explain: Doubling again and again is exponential build-up. Doubling signals exponential growth.
questions.rule: A reinforcing race does not level off by itself; it ends when someone breaks.

questions.q: If the rivals keep the loop running, what is the likely outcome?
options: Extremes reached faster than expected, then collapse
A slow and safe approach to a balance, with time to react along the way
A final stable level, reached when both rivals tire of the contest
A stronger relationship between the rivals after they have tested each other
optionExplain: Right: A reinforcing race reaches extremes faster than expected and ends in someone's collapse.
Reinforcing loops do not level off by themselves.
Nothing in the structure produces a stable level; the loop keeps feeding itself.
A stronger relationship is not suggested; the usual end is breakdown.
questions.explain: A reinforcing race reaches extremes faster than expected and ends in someone's collapse. Exponential then collapse.
questions.rule: A reinforcing race does not level off by itself; it ends when someone breaks.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says escalation can carry a competition to extremes faster than anyone would believe.
questions.explain: She says it can carry a competition to extremes faster than anyone would believe.
questions.rule: A reinforcing race does not level off by itself; it ends when someone breaks.

questions.q: A small company is outbid in an advertising race and goes under. Which detail from the chapter does this echo?
options: The race ends by a negotiated disarmament that the two firms sign
The race ends because one firm chooses unilateral disarmament
The spiral stops through one competitor's collapse
A new balancing loop appears and brings the advertising race under control
optionExplain: That is a way out, not what happened to the small company.
The small company did not choose to withdraw.
Right: The spiral stops when one competitor collapses.
Nothing in the case adds a balancing loop; the spiral ends when one competitor collapses.
questions.explain: Collapse is the default ending. Meadows says exponential growth cannot go on forever, so an escalating spiral is stopped by someone's collapse.
questions.rule: A reinforcing race does not level off by itself; it ends when someone breaks.
questions.teaches: Exponential growth cannot go on forever, so an escalating spiral is stopped by someone's collapse.

questions.q: Two firms are locked in a spiral of ever-bigger giveaways. Which exit does Meadows describe?
options: Give away more than the rival does in order to win the contest
Either one backs off, or both agree to new limits
Wait until the rival tires of the contest and drops out on its own
Ignore the rival completely
optionExplain: That feeds the loop rather than interrupting it.
Right: Either side can refuse to compete, or both can negotiate new limits.
Meadows does not offer waiting as an exit.
Unilateral disarmament has the cost of the rival's short-term advantage.
questions.explain: Two exits: refuse to compete or negotiate. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Interrupt the reinforcing loop, either by backing off yourself or by negotiating new balancing controls.

questions.q: What is unilateral disarmament in this context?
options: Deliberately reducing your own state to induce reductions in the rival's
Forcing the rival to reduce its own state by threatening it with penalties
Negotiating a joint agreement under which both sides reduce together
Hiding your own state from the rival so it cannot try to surpass it
optionExplain: Right: Unilateral disarmament means deliberately reducing your own state to induce reductions in the rival's.
That is coercion, not a voluntary reduction by you.
A joint agreement for both sides to reduce is negotiated, not unilateral, disarmament.
Concealment is not what the term means.
questions.explain: Unilateral disarmament means deliberately reducing your own state to induce reductions in the rival's. One-sided reduction.
questions.rule: Interrupt the reinforcing loop, either by backing off yourself or by negotiating new balancing controls.

questions.q: Which is an example of negotiated disarmament?
options: A firm cutting its own advertising budget in the hope that rivals will follow
A new and louder campaign meant to win back the attention of consumers
A merger of two rival firms that ends the competition between them
Regulations limiting the size and placement of advertisements
optionExplain: That is unilateral, not negotiated.
A louder campaign is the escalation itself, not a negotiated limit.
A merger that ends competition is not the negotiated limit on a race she describes.
Right: Rules on the size and placement of advertisements are negotiated limits that add balancing loops.
questions.explain: Rules on the size and placement of advertisements are negotiated limits that add balancing loops. New balancing loops set limits.
questions.rule: Interrupt the reinforcing loop, either by backing off yourself or by negotiating new balancing controls.

questions.q: What must a party to unilateral disarmament be able to do?
options: Hide its plans so that the rival cannot see what the party intends to do
Survive the rival's short-term advantage
Predict the rival's reply exactly
Raise its prices so that it can pay for the cost of backing off
optionExplain: Hiding plans is not a condition she names; the party must be able to survive the rival's short-term advantage.
Right: The party must survive the rival's short-term advantage.
Predicting the rival's reply exactly is not a condition she names for backing off.
Raising prices is not a condition she names for unilateral disarmament.
questions.explain: The party must survive the rival's short-term advantage. Meadows says so.
questions.rule: Interrupt the reinforcing loop, either by backing off yourself or by negotiating new balancing controls.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says unilateral disarmament is a natural move within the logic of an escalation system.
questions.explain: She says that within the logic of the system this option is almost unthinkable, yet it can work if done with determination and if one survives the rival's short-term advantage.
questions.rule: Interrupt the reinforcing loop, either by backing off yourself or by negotiating new balancing controls.

questions.q: Deliberately reducing your own state to induce reductions in a rival's is called ____ disarmament.
questions.explain: Unilateral disarmament interrupts the reinforcing loop.
questions.rule: Interrupt the reinforcing loop, either by backing off yourself or by negotiating new balancing controls.

questions.q: Neighbors keep raising fences higher. Which step would be a new balancing loop?
options: One neighbor building a fence even higher than the others as a warning
Each neighbor blaming the other for starting the contest of fences
A local rule capping fence height
Planting trees along the fences
optionExplain: A taller fence as a warning feeds the race rather than putting a limit on it.
Blame adds no control; a balancing loop needs a limit on fence height.
Right: A local rule capping fence height is a negotiated balancing loop.
This does not limit the competition.
questions.explain: Negotiated limits add balancing loops. Meadows adds that such agreements are not usually easy to get and never very pleasing to the parties, but are much better than staying in the race.
questions.rule: Interrupt the reinforcing loop, either by backing off yourself or by negotiating new balancing controls.
questions.teaches: Disarmament agreements in escalation systems are not usually easy to get and are never very pleasing to the parties, but they are much better than staying in the race.

questions.q: A shared woodlot is divided into family-owned plots. How does this change each family's incentive?
options: Families now have no reason to cut at all
All families now share all costs
Over-cutting now costs the family that does it
Families will cut more, as ownership removes limits
optionExplain: They may still cut; the point is that they bear the cost.
That is the commons arrangement, not privatization.
Right: gains and losses land on one decision maker.
Ownership brings the cost home, which discourages abuse.
questions.explain: Privatizing moves consequences onto the decider. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Privatize where a resource can be divided, so users feel the cost of their own overuse.

questions.q: Why does privatization restore feedback?
options: Gains and losses fall on the same decision maker
Regulators monitor each owner and penalize any who overuse the resource
Owners are persuaded by moral appeal to be moderate in what they take
The resource becomes unlimited, so overuse can no longer harm anyone
optionExplain: Right: Gains and losses fall on the same decision maker, so the owner feels the loss.
Regulators monitoring each owner is regulation, not what makes privatization restore feedback.
Moral appeal is exhortation, not the mechanism of privatization.
Privatizing leaves the resource limited.
questions.explain: Gains and losses fall on the same decision maker, so the owner feels the loss. The owner feels the loss.
questions.rule: Privatize where a resource can be divided, so users feel the cost of their own overuse.

questions.q: Which resource could be privatized, as Meadows's logic allows?
options: The atmosphere, which Meadows says cannot be divided among private owners
Fish across the open sea
The radio spectrum, which she treats under permits and regulation
A grazing pasture split into fenced plots
optionExplain: She names it as something that cannot be privatized.
She names the fish of the sea as unprivatizable.
She treats broadcast frequencies as a regulated commons.
Right: A pasture can be divided into fenced plots, so it can be privatized.
questions.explain: A pasture can be divided into fenced plots, so it can be privatized. Only divisible resources can be privatized.
questions.rule: Privatize where a resource can be divided, so users feel the cost of their own overuse.

questions.q: An owner of a private plot lacks the self-control to stay under its carrying capacity. Who is harmed, on Meadows's account?
options: Every user of the whole commons
Mainly that owner, not others
Only the regulators
No one, as ownership prevents harm
optionExplain: The plot is private, so harm stays with the owner.
Right: Private abuse hurts the abuser.
No regulators are involved on a private plot, so only the owner bears the harm.
Ownership does not prevent abuse, only makes the owner bear the harm; owners may still be ignorant or irrational.
questions.explain: On a private plot the harm from abuse falls mainly on the owner, since gains and losses fall on the same decision maker.
questions.rule: Privatize where a resource can be divided, so users feel the cost of their own overuse.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says privatization works better than exhortation provided society lets some individuals learn the hard way.
questions.explain: She says it works more reliably than exhortation under that condition.
questions.rule: Privatize where a resource can be divided, so users feel the cost of their own overuse.

questions.q: Meadows says many resources, such as the atmosphere and the fish of the sea, cannot be ____.
questions.explain: Where privatization is impossible, regulation remains.
questions.rule: Privatize where a resource can be divided, so users feel the cost of their own overuse.

questions.q: A town wants to protect ocean fish stocks by dividing the sea into private plots. What does the chapter suggest?
options: It will work as it does for pastures
It will not work, because fish cannot be privatized
It is the only way to protect any commons
It makes exhortation unnecessary
optionExplain: She says the sea's fish cannot be privatized.
Right: The chapter says fish of the sea cannot be privatized, so that plan will not work.
She also describes exhortation and regulation.
This does not address why the plan fails.
questions.explain: Where privatization is impossible, regulation remains. Where a resource cannot be privatized, only the option of mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon, is left.
questions.rule: Privatize where a resource can be divided, so users feel the cost of their own overuse.
questions.teaches: Meadows says that when a resource such as the atmosphere or the fish of the sea cannot be privatized, that leaves only the option of mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon.

questions.q: A quota on a shared resource is set by an agency. What does it need to work?
options: Users who all agree in advance to follow the quota without any penalty
A very large fine
Public silence, so that regulators can act without having to explain the rule
Informed, capable and honest regulators with means to enforce it
optionExplain: Agreement helps, but she says enforcement by policing and penalties is needed.
Deterrence is one of three conditions, not the only one.
Rules work best when mutually agreed and understood.
Right: Regulators need expertise, deterrence and concern for the whole community.
questions.explain: Regulation depends on regulators. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Regulation works only if regulators can read the resource, deter abuse, and serve the whole community.

questions.q: What does Hardin call regulation?
options: Mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon
Mutual aid, mutually earned
Forced sharing, in which the state takes and redistributes the resource
Collective ownership, in which the whole community holds the resource as one
optionExplain: Right: Hardin calls it mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon.
'Mutual aid, mutually earned' is not Hardin's phrase; his is mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon.
Forced sharing with state redistribution is not Hardin's description of regulation.
Collective ownership is not his phrase for regulation, which is mutual coercion.
questions.explain: Hardin calls it mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon. His blunt phrase.
questions.rule: Regulation works only if regulators can read the resource, deter abuse, and serve the whole community.
questions.hint: Four words after mutual coercion.

questions.q: Which regulator would fail the chapter's test?
options: An agency with skilled monitors who can read the state of the commons
An agency with real penalties that can deter those who ignore the rules
An agency staffed by weak or corrupt officials
An agency devoted to the good of the whole community rather than to itself
optionExplain: Skilled monitors satisfy the chapter's test that regulators be informed.
Real penalties satisfy the test that regulators can deter violators.
Right: Regulators cannot be uninformed, weak or corrupt.
An agency devoted to the community satisfies the test that regulators care for the whole.
questions.explain: Regulators cannot be uninformed, weak or corrupt. Cannot be uninformed, weak or corrupt.
questions.rule: Regulation works only if regulators can read the resource, deter abuse, and serve the whole community.

questions.q: If regulators cannot correctly monitor the commons, what happens to the feedback?
options: It becomes direct, as users learn to read the commons for themselves
It improves, since users are free to act on their own judgment
It is unaffected, since the penalties alone will keep users in line
It breaks down, and users get the wrong signals
optionExplain: Regulation is indirect by nature.
Her condition is that regulators interpret correctly.
The link depends on correct monitoring.
Right: The indirect feedback breaks down because users receive wrong signals.
questions.explain: The indirect feedback breaks down because users receive wrong signals. Regulators must interpret correctly.
questions.rule: Regulation works only if regulators can read the resource, deter abuse, and serve the whole community.

questions.q: Which forms can regulation take, per Meadows? Select all that apply.
options: Outright bans
Quotas and permits
Taxes and incentives
Moral appeals
Dividing the resource
optionExplain: Right: on her list.
Right: on her list.
Right: on her list.
This is exhortation.
This is privatization.
questions.explain: Regulation includes bans, quotas, permits, taxes and incentives, enforced by police and penalties.
questions.rule: Regulation works only if regulators can read the resource, deter abuse, and serve the whole community.

questions.q: Regulators need the expertise to monitor the commons, effective means of ____, and the good of the whole community at heart.
questions.explain: These are the three conditions Meadows gives.
questions.rule: Regulation works only if regulators can read the resource, deter abuse, and serve the whole community.

questions.q: Why does Meadows say all regulatory systems need police power even when most people comply?
options: Because of the occasional noncooperator
Because most people never comply with a rule unless they are watched
Because regulation exists to punish people rather than to protect the commons
Because compliance is irrelevant once a rule has been written into law
optionExplain: Right: Even where most people comply, there is the occasional noncooperator.
She says most people comply most of the time.
Her purpose for regulation is to protect the commons.
Compliance matters; she says purpose and agreement help it.
questions.explain: Most comply with agreed rules, but not all. Meadows adds that most people comply most of the time when rules are mutually agreed and understood, but the occasional noncooperator makes police power necessary.
questions.rule: Regulation works only if regulators can read the resource, deter abuse, and serve the whole community.
questions.teaches: Most people comply with regulatory systems most of the time, as long as they are mutually agreed upon and their purpose is understood.

questions.q: A town charges households for garbage by the amount they put out. What does this change?
questions.explain: The fee restores feedback. The card next shows other forms of the same idea.
questions.rule: Good regulation limits the freedom to abuse while keeping the freedom to use.
options: Each household now feels the cost of its own use
Households lose the right to dispose of any waste they produce
The cost of garbage disposal is shared equally among all households
Only wealthy households can afford disposal
optionExplain: Right: Each household now feels the cost of its own use.
The fee limits abuse but keeps the freedom to use the service.
That is the commons arrangement that the fee replaces.
The card does not suggest this; the fee tracks use, not wealth.

questions.q: Which arrangement directly restores the missing feedback by making each household feel its own use?
options: A traffic light, which rations the intersection by taking turns
A broadcast permit, which a government agency issues to each applicant
A garbage fee based on the amount thrown away
A bank safe, which keeps outsiders from helping themselves to the money
optionExplain: A traffic light rations the intersection by turns but does not tie any cost to how much each user takes.
A broadcast permit rations access but does not make each user feel the cost of its own use.
Right: A fee based on the amount thrown away makes each household feel its own use.
It protects against theft, not overuse.
questions.explain: A fee based on the amount thrown away makes each household feel its own use. Pay by use restores feedback.
questions.rule: Good regulation limits the freedom to abuse while keeping the freedom to use.

questions.q: A library limits each borrower to five books at a time. Which mutual-coercion example is closest?
options: The bank safe, which prevents outsiders from taking the bank's money
The parking meter, which limits use of a shared resource
The broadcast permit, which gives a license to those who apply
The traffic light, which gives each driver a turn at the intersection
optionExplain: It is about protection from theft, not limits on shared use.
Right: Both meters and library limits cap how much of a shared supply each person uses.
It rations through licensing rather than limits on quantity.
It rations by turns, whereas the library limits quantity.
questions.explain: Both meters and library limits cap how much of a shared supply each person uses. Limits on use of a shared supply.
questions.rule: Good regulation limits the freedom to abuse while keeping the freedom to use.

questions.q: Without traffic lights at a busy junction, what does Meadows expect?
options: A less safe free-for-all
Faster traffic for all drivers
No change in safety
Fewer drivers on the road
optionExplain: Right: Without lights the junction would be a free-for-all that is less safe.
She says lights make passing safer than an unregulated junction.
She says the lights let you pass more safely.
Nothing in the text says lights change how many people drive.
questions.explain: Without lights the junction would be a free-for-all that is less safe. Regulation lets you pass more safely.
questions.rule: Good regulation limits the freedom to abuse while keeping the freedom to use.

questions.q: True or false: Mutual-coercion arrangements limit the freedom to abuse a commons while preserving the freedom to use it.
questions.explain: They limit the freedom to abuse it while preserving the freedom to use it.
questions.rule: Good regulation limits the freedom to abuse while keeping the freedom to use.

questions.q: Garbage fees based on the amount thrown away restore the missing ____ to each household.
questions.explain: Each household feels the economic impact of its own use.
questions.rule: Good regulation limits the freedom to abuse while keeping the freedom to use.

questions.q: Why do you accept being unable to help yourself to the money in a bank, per Meadows?
options: Because the bank owns its customers and may restrict their access
Because banks are forgiving and rarely punish those who help themselves
Because money is worth little once it has been placed inside a bank
Because the same arrangement protects your own money
optionExplain: Nothing says the bank owns its customers; the arrangement protects customers' money.
She says police and jails reinforce the safes.
Your money is protected, not devalued.
Right: The same arrangement that restrains you also protects your own money.
questions.explain: The rule that limits you protects you too. Safes and police stop you from treating a bank as a commons, and in return your own money in the bank is protected.
questions.rule: Good regulation limits the freedom to abuse while keeping the freedom to use.
questions.teaches: Meadows notes that strongboxes and safes, reinforced by police and jails, prevent you from treating a bank as a commons, and in return your own money in the bank is protected.

questions.q: A contest rewards each winner with money that buys better tools for the next contest. What should happen over the rounds?
options: Winners and losers drift toward equality
The same winners pull steadily ahead
The winners rotate each round
Contest interest rises
optionExplain: The reward widens the gap. Here, rewards that feed the next round compound.
Right: the card names this loop.
The reward favors repeat winners. Here, rewards that feed the next round compound.
A tempting pick, but it does not fit the chapter. Rewards that feed the next round compound.
questions.explain: Rewards that feed the next round compound. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: When a win brings the means to win again, the gap between winners and losers widens.

questions.q: What kind of feedback loop is success to the successful?
options: Balancing
Delayed only
Reinforcing
Absent
optionExplain: Balancing loops hold a state. Here, winners get more means to win.
Delay isn't the type. Here, winners get more means to win.
Right: Winners get more means to win.
A tempting pick, but it does not fit the chapter. Winners get more means to win.
questions.explain: Success to the successful is a reinforcing loop: winners gain the means to win more, so the gap keeps widening.
questions.rule: When a win brings the means to win again, the gap between winners and losers widens.

questions.q: Which situation shows the archetype?
options: Two stores that keep matching each other's discounts week after week
A shared well that runs dry because every household draws on it
A store chain uses its profits to undercut and buy out smaller rivals
A rule that people evade by following its wording but not its purpose
optionExplain: Matching discounts week after week is escalation between rivals, not winners gaining means to win more.
A well draining because everyone draws on it is the commons trap.
Right: A chain using profit to undercut and buy out smaller rivals shows winning bringing the means to win more.
Meeting a rule's wording but defeating its purpose is rule beating.
questions.explain: A chain using profit to undercut and buy out smaller rivals shows winning bringing the means to win more. Winning gives the means to win more.
questions.rule: When a win brings the means to win again, the gap between winners and losers widens.

questions.q: In the Monopoly game, how does the game end, unless players quit earlier?
options: One player has bought up everything
The players tie in wealth after the rents cancel out over many turns
The rents balance out, because each hotel owner pays as much as it earns
The bank runs out of hotels first
optionExplain: Right: The game ends with one player owning everything.
The loop widens the gap rather than closing it.
The leader collects more than it pays.
Meadows does not describe this ending.
questions.explain: The game ends with one player owning everything. The winner takes all.
questions.rule: When a win brings the means to win again, the gap between winners and losers widens.

questions.q: True or false: In the neighborhood Christmas-lights contest, the contest was suspended because losers complained of unfair judging.
questions.explain: It was suspended after one family had won three years running with ever more elaborate displays.
questions.rule: When a win brings the means to win again, the gap between winners and losers widens.

questions.q: The winners of a competition receive, as part of the reward, the ____ to compete even better in the future.
questions.explain: That reward is what closes the reinforcing loop.
questions.rule: When a win brings the means to win again, the gap between winners and losers widens.

questions.q: Which condition, per Meadows, makes losers bankrupt, forced out or starved?
options: A large and growing environment in which the winner can expand without cost to others
A rule banning competition altogether so that no one wins or loses
A fair referee who enforces the rules of the game equally on every player
A limited environment in which the winner's gains come out of the losers
optionExplain: Then the winner need not take from the losers.
Without competition there are no winners.
A fair referee is not part of her account; the condition is a limited environment.
Right: The winner's gains come out of the losers in a limited environment.
questions.explain: The winner's gains come out of the losers in a limited environment. Limits mean zero-sum extraction.
questions.rule: When a win brings the means to win again, the gap between winners and losers widens.
questions.teaches: If the winning takes place in a limited environment, such that everything the winner wins is extracted from the losers, the losers are gradually bankrupted, forced out or starved.

questions.q: Two species rely on exactly the same resource in the same place. What outcome does ecology expect?
options: The two species share the resource evenly and both prosper for good
One drives the other out
The two species merge into a single new species that uses both resources
Both thrive because the resource is shared out among them by chance
optionExplain: The principle says two species cannot do that in the same niche.
Right: One species drives the other to extinction, as competitive exclusion says.
Merging into one species is not what the principle describes; one species drives the other out.
Differences give one an edge that compounds.
questions.explain: One species drives the other to extinction, as competitive exclusion says. Competitive exclusion. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Two competitors for the same resource cannot coexist if one's advantage compounds.

questions.q: How does the winning species usually eliminate the loser?
options: By fighting the weaker species directly until it is eliminated
By appropriating all the resource, rather than by direct confrontation
By poisoning the weaker species with chemicals it produces in its niche
By out-breeding the weaker species in one season and then stopping
optionExplain: She says usually not by direct confrontation.
Right: The winner takes all the resource, leaving none for the weaker species.
Poisoning by chemicals is not mentioned; the winner simply takes all the resource.
Her account is of a continuing advantage, not a single season.
questions.explain: The winner takes all the resource, leaving none for the weaker species. It takes the resource.
questions.rule: Two competitors for the same resource cannot coexist if one's advantage compounds.

questions.q: Which market development matches competitive exclusion in Meadows's account?
options: More newspapers in most cities
More farms, smaller in size
Many equal small firms persisting
Many car makers reduced to three
optionExplain: She says only one is left in most cities.
Farms decline while size grows. Here, markets concentrate.
A tempting pick, but it does not fit the chapter. Markets concentrate.
Right: Markets concentrate.
questions.explain: Meadows says the many U.S. car makers were reduced to three, not one, because of antitrust laws.
questions.rule: Two competitors for the same resource cannot coexist if one's advantage compounds.

questions.q: With a finite market and no antitrust law, what does Meadows expect of two competing firms?
options: One takes over everything, as long as it keeps reinvesting
They split the market equally and stay equal over the years
They stop competing and cooperate to share the finite market
Prices fall forever as the two firms undercut each other in turn
optionExplain: Right: One firm takes over everything, provided it keeps reinvesting and expanding.
Compounding advantage prevents that.
Nothing in her account has the firms cooperating; the winner keeps reinvesting and takes over.
That is escalation, not this structure.
questions.explain: One firm takes over everything, provided it keeps reinvesting and expanding. Capital accumulation compounds.
questions.rule: Two competitors for the same resource cannot coexist if one's advantage compounds.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says Marx's analysis that competition eliminates competition is demonstrated wherever a competitive market exists.
questions.explain: She says that particular analysis is demonstrated wherever there is or was a competitive market.
questions.rule: Two competitors for the same resource cannot coexist if one's advantage compounds.

questions.q: In ecology, success to the successful is called the competitive ____ principle.
questions.explain: The principle says one species drives the other out of a shared niche.
questions.rule: Two competitors for the same resource cannot coexist if one's advantage compounds.

questions.q: Why did U.S. car makers drop to three and not one, per Meadows?
options: Customer loyalty
Import tariffs
Antitrust laws
Government ownership
optionExplain: Customer loyalty is not her explanation; antitrust laws prevented the last step.
Import tariffs are not what she names; antitrust laws stopped the consolidation at three.
Right: Laws prevented the last step. The automobile companies in the United States fell to three, not one, because of antitrust laws.
Government ownership is not what stopped it; she credits antitrust laws.
questions.explain: Laws prevented the last step. The automobile companies in the United States fell to three, not one, because of antitrust laws.
questions.rule: Two competitors for the same resource cannot coexist if one's advantage compounds.
questions.teaches: Meadows says the automobile companies in the United States fell to three, not one, because of antitrust laws, while most major cities have only one newspaper left.

questions.q: Why might a poor family struggle to escape poverty through a bank loan?
options: They cannot find a bank that is open at hours they are able to visit
They have no need to invest
Interest rates are lower for them
Most banks will not lend to people with low income and few assets
optionExplain: Opening hours are not her point.
She says they cannot invest in improvements.
She says they pay exorbitant rates, if they can borrow at all.
Right: Most banks will not lend to people with low income and few assets.
questions.explain: Most banks will not lend to people with low income and few assets. Credit favors the rich. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Look for a link where having more makes getting more easier and having less makes it harder.

questions.q: In the landowner example, what does the landowner do with the tenants' payments?
options: Buys more land
Gives them back
Invests in the tenants' schools
Reduces their rent
optionExplain: Right: The loop continues.
Giving the payments back would end the loop; the landowner keeps the payments and buys more land.
Investing in tenants' schools is not in the example; the loop is the landowner's gain buying more land.
Reducing rent would weaken the loop; the example has the landowner using the payments to expand.
questions.explain: The landowner uses the income from tenants to buy more land, so the loop of gain continues.
questions.rule: Look for a link where having more makes getting more easier and having less makes it harder.

questions.q: Which is an example of the rich getting richer, per Meadows?
options: The poor receive new technology first
The rich pay the highest prices because they buy in large quantities
Wealthy people have more ways to avoid taxation
The poor get a larger share of government spending than their numbers warrant
optionExplain: She says ideas and technologies come to the poor last.
She says the poor pay the highest prices.
Right: The wealthy have more ways to avoid taxation than the poor.
She says a disproportionately small part goes to their needs.
questions.explain: The wealthy have more ways to avoid taxation than the poor. Advantages compound.
questions.rule: Look for a link where having more makes getting more easier and having less makes it harder.

questions.q: If poor farmers can borrow only from local moneylenders at exorbitant rates, what happens to their investment?
options: It rises, because high rates push farmers to invest more to repay the loan
It is held back, which keeps them poor
It is unaffected, since farmers invest the same amount whatever the rate
It shifts to the rich, who take over the farmers' land at the first default
optionExplain: Exorbitant rates discourage investment.
Right: Investment is held back, which keeps the farmers poor.
The cost of credit does affect what can be invested.
Not her account here; she describes landowners buying more land.
questions.explain: Investment is held back, which keeps the farmers poor. No access to credit blocks improvement.
questions.rule: Look for a link where having more makes getting more easier and having less makes it harder.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the poor pay the lowest prices because they buy in small quantities.
questions.explain: She says they pay the highest prices because they buy small quantities.
questions.rule: Look for a link where having more makes getting more easier and having less makes it harder.

questions.q: Tenant farmers pay part of their crops to the landowner, who uses the income to buy more ____.
questions.explain: The landowner's gain feeds further gains.
questions.rule: Look for a link where having more makes getting more easier and having less makes it harder.

questions.q: Which pairing shows who meets disease and pollution first and who gets ideas and technology first?
options: The poor meet disease first; ideas come to the rich first
The rich meet disease and pollution first
The poor get technology first
Both groups meet disease and technology at the same time and in equal measure
optionExplain: Right: Disease and pollution reach the poor first, while ideas and technologies reach them last.
She says the poor meet disease and pollution first.
She says ideas and technologies come to them last.
She describes an asymmetry: the poor meet disease and pollution first and ideas last, so equal timing is wrong.
questions.explain: Meadows lists this asymmetry. Meadows adds that the poor are often unorganized and inarticulate, so a disproportionately small part of government spending goes to their needs.
questions.rule: Look for a link where having more makes getting more easier and having less makes it harder.
questions.teaches: Meadows adds that the poor are often unorganized and inarticulate, so a disproportionately small part of government expenditure goes to their needs.

questions.q: A small firm cannot beat a giant at its own game. Which escape does Meadows mention?
options: Copy the giant exactly
Wait for the giant to fail on its own
Merge with the giant, which ends the competition by absorbing the small firm
Move into a different product or niche
optionExplain: That stays in the same competition.
Waiting for the giant to fail is not an escape she offers; the small firm gets out of the contested game itself.
She does not offer merging as an escape.
Right: Moving into a different product or niche takes the firm out of the contested game.
questions.explain: Moving into a different product or niche takes the firm out of the contested game. Diversify. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Losers can leave the contested game and start another, if the winner cannot crush the new one.

questions.q: What does diversification allow losers to do?
options: Win the original competition by finding a better way of doing the same thing
Leave that competition and start another
Reduce the winners' wealth by taxing their gains from the competition
Remove the competition altogether
optionExplain: It sidesteps the original game rather than winning it.
Right: Diversification lets losers leave that competition and start another.
That is a leveling policy, not diversification.
It does not remove the competition; it leaves it.
questions.explain: Diversification lets losers leave that competition and start another. Get out of the game.
questions.rule: Losers can leave the contested game and start another, if the winner cannot crush the new one.

questions.q: Which is an example of diversification by a company?
options: Cutting prices further than the dominant firm in the same market
Lobbying for weak antitrust enforcement so that the firm can grow
Creating a service that does not compete directly with existing ones
Merging with a rival to form a larger firm in the same line of business
optionExplain: That stays in the same contest.
That helps the winner, not the loser.
Right: Creating a service that does not directly compete with existing ones is diversification.
That is consolidation, not a new niche.
questions.explain: Creating a service that does not directly compete with existing ones is diversification. New niche.
questions.rule: Losers can leave the contested game and start another, if the winner cannot crush the new one.

questions.q: What may happen later to a successful offshoot market?
options: It stays free of competition for ever
It disappears at once, because the dominant firm always crushes new rivals
It may attract competitors and move toward exclusion again
It becomes a commons, because every firm then draws on its customers
optionExplain: She says new markets attract competitors in time.
She says power to crush offshoots is not guaranteed.
Right: A successful offshoot may attract competitors and move toward exclusion again.
Nothing makes the offshoot market a commons; its success draws competitors and the exclusion cycle can restart.
questions.explain: A successful offshoot may attract competitors and move toward exclusion again. The cycle can restart.
questions.rule: Losers can leave the contested game and start another, if the winner cannot crush the new one.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says diversification works equally well as a strategy for the poor.
questions.explain: She says it doesn't work as a strategy for the poor.
questions.rule: Losers can leave the contested game and start another, if the winner cannot crush the new one.

questions.q: Species and companies sometimes escape competitive exclusion by ____.
questions.explain: Diversifying lets losers leave the contested game.
questions.rule: Losers can leave the contested game and start another, if the winner cannot crush the new one.

questions.q: A dominant firm buys every promising start-up in its field. What does this do to diversification as an escape?
options: It blocks the escape
It assists it
It leaves it unaffected
It guarantees it
optionExplain: Right: Power to crush or buy offshoots.
A tempting pick, but it does not fit the chapter. Power to crush or buy offshoots.
The power to buy up offshoots blocks it.
Diversification is not guaranteed. Here, power to crush or buy offshoots.
questions.explain: Diversification is an escape only if the dominant firm cannot crush or buy the offshoot; a firm buying every start-up blocks it (Our reading).
questions.rule: Losers can leave the contested game and start another, if the winner cannot crush the new one.
questions.teaches: Diversification is not guaranteed, especially if the monopolizing firm or species has the power to crush all offshoots, buy them up, or deprive them of the resources they need.

questions.q: A game lets the leader buy extra moves every round. Which design change would best keep the game fair?
options: Let the leader keep everything
Remove all the rules, so players are free to compete however they wish
Penalize the losers, so that they try harder in the following round
Give weaker players a handicap or restart on equal terms
optionExplain: That leaves the reinforcing loop untouched.
That would help the leader further.
Penalizing the losers widens the gap and feeds the reinforcing loop further.
Right: A handicap or an equal restart is a way of leveling the playing field.
questions.explain: Equalizers keep games alive. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Cap the winners' share, level the field, or reward success without biasing the next round.

questions.q: What is a potlatch?
options: A tax on land charged to the largest landowners in a society
A ritual in which those with the most give away many possessions to those with the least
A contest in which families compete to build the finest houses
A market where traditional societies trade goods for other goods
optionExplain: It is a ritual of giving, not a tax.
Right: A potlatch is a ritual in which those with the most give away goods to those with the least.
It is a ritual of giving, not a building contest.
It is a ritual of giving, not a market.
questions.explain: A potlatch is a ritual in which those with the most give away goods to those with the least. A traditional equalizer.
questions.rule: Cap the winners' share, level the field, or reward success without biasing the next round.

questions.q: Which measure restarts the game with each new generation, per Meadows?
options: Charity, which helps people in need but does not start a new round
Taxation on inheritance
Labor unions, which raise the bargaining power of workers during a round
Antitrust law, which caps the share of the market any one firm can hold
optionExplain: She lists it as an equalizer, but not as a restart.
Right: Taxation on inheritance restarts the game with each new generation.
They shift advantage during the game, not at its start.
It limits winners within a round, not between generations.
questions.explain: Taxation on inheritance restarts the game with each new generation. Inheritance tax.
questions.rule: Cap the winners' share, level the field, or reward success without biasing the next round.

questions.q: If the biggest firms win the power to weaken antitrust administration, what happens to the loop?
options: It is capped more tightly
It becomes a balancing loop
It stops
It runs more freely
optionExplain: Winners weaken the controls, so the loop is capped less tightly, not more.
The loop stays reinforcing; winners weaken the antitrust balancing loop that restrained it.
The loop does not stop; with weakened antitrust it runs more freely.
Right: Winners weaken the controls.
questions.explain: Antitrust laws are the control on the loop; if the biggest firms win the power to weaken them, the loop runs more freely.
questions.rule: Cap the winners' share, level the field, or reward success without biasing the next round.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says equalizing mechanisms come only from simple morality.
questions.explain: She says they may come from morality or from the practical understanding that frustrated losers could destroy the playing field.
questions.rule: Cap the winners' share, level the field, or reward success without biasing the next round.

questions.q: Meadows calls the most obvious way out periodically leveling the ____ field.
questions.explain: Games and traditional societies build in equalizers.
questions.rule: Cap the winners' share, level the field, or reward success without biasing the next round.

questions.q: A league adds a salary cap to stop rich clubs buying all the best players. Which category is this?
options: A feedback control that limits the winners' advantage
Diversification, because the clubs move into different kinds of sport
Escalation, because the rich clubs now outspend each other for the players
Exhortation, because the league asks rich clubs to show restraint
optionExplain: Right: A salary cap limits the winners' advantage by feedback control, as antitrust laws do.
Clubs stay in the same competition.
A cap restrains spending rather than driving it up.
A cap is a rule, not an appeal to morality.
questions.explain: Equalizers keep everyone in the game. Meadows says that losers with no hope of winning could grow frustrated enough to destroy the playing field, which is a practical reason to equalize.
questions.rule: Cap the winners' share, level the field, or reward success without biasing the next round.
questions.teaches: Meadows says losers who cannot escape the game and have no hope of winning could grow frustrated enough to destroy the playing field, a practical reason to equalize.

questions.q: What feature of a contest makes winners pull steadily away from losers?
questions.explain: The reward feeding the next round is the cause. The card next states the trap and its exits.
questions.rule: Break the loop by diversifying, capping shares, leveling the field, or unbiased rewards.
options: Losers are less able than winners
Winners receive public attention
Contests are held too often
Winners are rewarded with the means to win again
optionExplain: Skill may differ at the start, but the loop, not the gap in skill, makes the divide grow.
Attention may follow, but it is not the means to win again.
Frequency speeds the loop up but does not cause it.
Right: A reward that helps in the next round makes a reinforcing loop, so the gap widens.

questions.q: What is the cause of the trap in Meadows's statement?
options: Winners cheat, using methods that the losers are unable to match
Competitors collude, so that the market is shared out between them
Winners are systematically rewarded with the means to win again
Losers give up, which hands the contest to the winners by default
optionExplain: The trap needs no cheating; the cause is the reward that feeds the next round.
Collusion is not her cause; winners are rewarded with the means to win again.
Right: The cause is a reward that feeds the next round of competition.
Losers are eliminated by the loop, not by choice.
questions.explain: The cause is a reward that feeds the next round of competition. The reward feeds the next round.
questions.rule: Break the loop by diversifying, capping shares, leveling the field, or unbiased rewards.

questions.q: A city gives the winner of an annual contest a prize it cannot reinvest in the contest. Which way out is this?
options: Diversification, which lets losers leave and start another game
An antitrust limit, which caps the share any winner may hold
Leveling the field, which reduces the strongest players' advantage
A reward that does not bias the next round
optionExplain: Diversification lets losers leave for another game; here the prize itself is unbiased.
An antitrust limit caps the share a winner may hold; here the prize cannot be reinvested.
Leveling the field reduces the strong players' advantage; here the reward is unbiased.
Right: A reward that cannot be reinvested does not bias the next round.
questions.explain: A reward that cannot be reinvested does not bias the next round. Rewards without bias.
questions.rule: Break the loop by diversifying, capping shares, leveling the field, or unbiased rewards.

questions.q: If the loop runs uninhibited, what is the end state?
options: The winners take all and the losers are eliminated
Everyone ends up with equal shares as the reinforcing loop slows
A new balance is reached at which the winners stop gaining ground
The leader changes from round to round
optionExplain: Right: The winners take all and the losers are eliminated.
The loop widens the gap between winners and losers; it does not equalize shares.
Nothing in the loop produces a new balance; left uninhibited, the winners take all.
The loop keeps the same winners ahead.
questions.explain: The winners take all and the losers are eliminated. Eventually winners take all.
questions.rule: Break the loop by diversifying, capping shares, leveling the field, or unbiased rewards.

questions.q: True or false: Success to the successful is a balancing loop.
questions.explain: Success to the successful is a reinforcing loop, because winners gain the means to win again.
questions.rule: Break the loop by diversifying, capping shares, leveling the field, or unbiased rewards.

questions.q: Strict limits on the fraction of the pie any one winner may win are what ____ laws do.
questions.explain: Antitrust laws are the example she gives.
questions.rule: Break the loop by diversifying, capping shares, leveling the field, or unbiased rewards.

questions.q: Which pair of archetypes both involve reinforcing loops between competitors, yet differ in who is chasing whom?
options: Escalation and commons
Drift and resistance
Escalation, where each chases the other, and success to the successful, where winners gain means
Rule beating and wrong goal
optionExplain: The commons involves shared overuse with missing feedback, not a chase between competitors.
Drift and resistance are not both reinforcing contests between competitors.
Right: Both are reinforcing. Success to the successful is called the competitive exclusion principle in ecology, while escalation ties each actor's goal to the other's state.
Rule beating and wrong goal are not reinforcing loops between competitors.
questions.explain: Both are reinforcing. Success to the successful is called the competitive exclusion principle in ecology, while escalation ties each actor's goal to the other's state.
questions.rule: Break the loop by diversifying, capping shares, leveling the field, or unbiased rewards.
questions.teaches: Success to the successful is the ecologists' competitive exclusion principle, while escalation is a contest where each actor's goal is tied to the other's state.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: A farm needs more fertilizer each year to harvest the same crop. What is the closest everyday label for this pattern?
options: A fair price for inputs that the farm buys each season to grow crops
Dependence on an outside fix
A healthy investment that builds the farm's capacity for the long term
A random fluctuation in yields that has no pattern from one year to next
optionExplain: A fair price does not explain a growing need.
Right: Needing ever more fertilizer is a dependence on an outside fix.
An investment would build capacity, not dependence.
The need grows steadily, which is a pattern.
questions.explain: Addiction extends beyond drugs. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Addiction is a pattern, not just a chemical: any actor can come to depend on an outside fix.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Which is NOT among Meadows's examples of addiction in larger systems?
options: A company's reliance on its own research staff
Industry's dependence on government subsidy
Western economies' dependence on cheap oil, which she lists as an example
Weapons makers' dependence on government contracts, which she lists as an example
optionExplain: Right: A company's reliance on its own research staff is not on her list of addictions.
Industry's dependence on subsidy is on her list, so it is not the odd one out.
Western economies' dependence on cheap oil is on her list, so it is not the odd one out.
Weapons makers' dependence on government contracts is on her list, so it is not the odd one out.
questions.explain: Her list is subsidies, fertilizer, oil and contracts.
questions.rule: Addiction is a pattern, not just a chemical: any actor can come to depend on an outside fix.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Which stock is metaphysical rather than physical in her structure?
options: A corn crop, which she gives as an example of a physical stock
Barrels of oil held in storage by a country or company
A pile of grain in a warehouse awaiting sale to buyers
A person's sense of well-being
optionExplain: Corn is a physical stock, not a metaphysical one.
Stored oil is a physical stock, not a metaphysical one.
Stored grain is a physical stock, not a metaphysical one.
Right: A person's sense of well-being is her example of a metaphysical stock.
questions.explain: She says stocks can be metaphysical, such as self-worth.
questions.rule: Addiction is a pattern, not just a chemical: any actor can come to depend on an outside fix.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: In this structure, what does the actor compare to decide what action to take?
options: The goal against another actor's goal, to see who is further ahead
The goal against a perception of the actual state
The past against the future, to decide how fast to change
The intervenor's effort against its cost
optionExplain: Comparing goals with another actor's goal is escalation, not the addiction structure.
Right: The actor compares the goal with a perception of the actual state of the stock.
Comparing past with future is not how she describes the actor's decision.
Weighing effort against cost is not how she describes the actor's comparison.
questions.explain: The actor compares the goal with a perception of the actual state of the stock. A standard balancing loop.
questions.rule: Addiction is a pattern, not just a chemical: any actor can come to depend on an outside fix.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: True or false: Meadows applies the term addiction to industries, farmers and economies as well as to individuals.
questions.explain: She applies the term to industries, farmers, economies and manufacturers as well.
questions.rule: Addiction is a pattern, not just a chemical: any actor can come to depend on an outside fix.

questions.q: Shifting the burden to the intervenor is also called addiction or ____.
questions.explain: She lists addiction, dependence, shifting the burden.
questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.rule: Addiction is a pattern, not just a chemical: any actor can come to depend on an outside fix.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: A country depends on imports of one fuel and cannot cope when supplies stop. Which of Meadows's examples is this closest to?
options: Farmers who rely on fertilizer to harvest crops from tired land
Weapons makers who rely on government contracts for their orders
Western economies addicted to cheap oil
Pushers who set prices to keep the drug supply in the middle
optionExplain: Fertilizer on tired land is a different dependence, not an import of one fuel.
Government contracts for weapons are a different dependence from a fuel import.
Right: Dependence on one cheap fuel is the pattern she describes as Western economies' addiction to cheap oil.
Pushers setting prices belong to the resistance example, not to dependence on a fuel.
questions.explain: Dependence on a cheap input. Most people understand addictions such as alcohol, nicotine, caffeine, sugar and heroin, but not everyone recognizes the same structure in larger systems.
questions.rule: Addiction is a pattern, not just a chemical: any actor can come to depend on an outside fix.
questions.teaches: Most people understand the addictive properties of alcohol, nicotine, caffeine, sugar and heroin, but not everyone recognizes addiction in larger systems.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: A farmer adds fertilizer to exhausted soil and gets a bumper crop. What is the likely long-run picture?
options: The soil is restored by the fertilizer
The next crop will be larger without more fertilizer
The soil is no better, and the fertilizer wears off
The fertilizer improves the soil's capacity
optionExplain: Fertilizer feeds the crop, not the soil's own fertility.
The effect is not lasting. Here, the state created by the intervention does not last.
Right: the card explains the pattern.
Meadows says soil fertility is unchanged.
questions.explain: The state created by the intervention does not last. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A fix that hides the symptom leaves the cause untouched, and the symptom returns when the fix wears off.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: What do drugs change for the boy in Meadows's example?
options: His perception of his state, not his real situation
His real situation, which improves as his mood lifts and his energy returns
His goal, which shifts from well-being to getting through the day
The famine around him
optionExplain: Right: The drugs change his perception of his state, not his real situation.
She says they do nothing to improve his real situation.
His goal stays well-being; the drugs only change how he perceives his state.
The drugs leave the famine as it was.
questions.explain: The drugs change his perception of his state, not his real situation. Perception, not reality.
questions.rule: A fix that hides the symptom leaves the cause untouched, and the symptom returns when the fix wears off.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Which action matches the pattern of masking a symptom?
options: A hospital that hires more nurses to cut the waiting time
A hospital that studies why waits arise and fixes the bottleneck
A hospital that adds clinics so that patients are seen elsewhere
A hospital hides long waits by moving patients between rooms
optionExplain: Hiring nurses to cut waiting time tackles a cause of the wait.
Studying why waits arise and fixing the bottleneck addresses the cause.
Adding clinics changes where patients are seen and adds capacity, a real response.
Right: Hiding long waits by shuffling patients changes appearances, not the cause.
questions.explain: Hiding long waits by shuffling patients changes appearances, not the cause. Changing appearances, not the cause.
questions.rule: A fix that hides the symptom leaves the cause untouched, and the symptom returns when the fix wears off.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: When the subsidy given to an ineffective company is spent, what returns?
options: Profits, which continue because the company is now healthy again
The original difficulties
Respect in society, which follows the company whatever its results
Efficiency, which the subsidy had improved while it lasted
optionExplain: The subsidy was propping them up.
Right: When the subsidy is spent, the original difficulties return.
It depended on profits that the subsidy sustained.
The subsidy did nothing for efficiency.
questions.explain: When the subsidy is spent, the original difficulties return. The intervention doesn't last.
questions.rule: A fix that hides the symptom leaves the cause untouched, and the symptom returns when the fix wears off.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the states created by interventions like drugs, subsidies or fertilizer last indefinitely.
questions.explain: She says they do not last; the intoxication wears off.
questions.rule: A fix that hides the symptom leaves the cause untouched, and the symptom returns when the fix wears off.

questions.q: The states created by interventions do not last: the intoxication wears off, the subsidy is spent, the fertilizer is ____.
questions.explain: The fertilizer is consumed or washed away.
questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.rule: A fix that hides the symptom leaves the cause untouched, and the symptom returns when the fix wears off.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: A manager hides falling sales by changing how they are reported. Which part of the pattern is this?
options: An addiction to alcohol, which dulls a person's view of their state
An intervention that alters the perceived state, not the real one
A commons, in which users share the harm that each one causes
A rule that is evaded, with staff meeting the wording but not the purpose
optionExplain: Alcohol is not involved in the case.
Right: Changing how sales are reported alters the perceived state, not the real one.
No shared resource is overused here; the manager is altering the report of the state.
Closer to rule beating, but here the report itself is altered.
questions.explain: Change perception only. Meadows defines addiction as a quick and dirty solution to the symptom, which distracts from the harder task of solving the real problem.
questions.rule: A fix that hides the symptom leaves the cause untouched, and the symptom returns when the fix wears off.
questions.teaches: Addiction is finding a quick and dirty solution to the symptom of a problem, which distracts from the harder, longer-term task of solving the real problem.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Someone helps a struggling system by doing its job for it. What may happen to the system's own ability?
options: It grows stronger through watching how the intervenor does the work
It stays unchanged, since the intervenor only adds to what exists
It passes to the intervenor, who now keeps it for as long as it is needed
It may weaken, so more help is needed
optionExplain: In the trap, capacity weakens.
The trap depends on a decline in capacity.
Capacity does not transfer; it atrophies.
Right: The system's own ability may weaken, so more help is needed.
questions.explain: Help can undermine capacity. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: If help weakens the capacity it replaces, the need for help grows in a reinforcing loop.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Order the steps of the trap.
items: The system's own correction is weak
The intervenor takes some load
The problem reappears at the root
More of the solution is applied
The system's own capacity atrophies further
questions.explain: Each round, the system depends more on the intervenor.
questions.rule: If help weakens the capacity it replaces, the need for help grows in a reinforcing loop.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: A city keeps trucking water to a village instead of repairing its failing wells. What loop is forming?
options: Dependence, as the village's own water capacity declines
Escalation, in which the city and village raise their efforts against each other
Competitive exclusion, in which one party wins the means to win again
Rule beating, in which the village meets the wording of a rule only
optionExplain: Right: Trucked water lets the village's own water capacity decline, producing dependence.
No rival raises its effort against the city; the village simply loses capacity.
No contest is described, so there is no winner gaining means to win again.
No rule is being evaded; the village's own capacity declines.
questions.explain: Trucked water lets the village's own water capacity decline, producing dependence. Intervention weakens the original system.
questions.rule: If help weakens the capacity it replaces, the need for help grows in a reinforcing loop.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: If the intervention does not undermine the system's capacity, what does the trap lack?
options: An intervenor, since someone must still step in to take the load
A balancing loop, since the system still tries to correct its state
The reinforcing loop of growing dependence
A problem, since there must be something that needs correcting
optionExplain: The trap still has an intervenor.
The system still has its own balancing loop.
Right: Without atrophy there is no reinforcing loop of growing dependence.
A problem is still present; what is missing without atrophy is the reinforcing loop of dependence.
questions.explain: Without atrophy there is no reinforcing loop of growing dependence. Atrophy closes the loop.
questions.rule: If help weakens the capacity it replaces, the need for help grows in a reinforcing loop.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the system's capacity can be undermined by active destruction or by simple neglect.
questions.explain: She says the undermining can be by active destruction or by simple neglect.
questions.rule: If help weakens the capacity it replaces, the need for help grows in a reinforcing loop.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Meadows says the intervenor often earns congratulations early on. Who gives them?
options: The system that has been helped, which thanks its helper warmly
Outside critics, who admire the speed with which the system recovered
The regulators, who approve of the help as a step toward a solution
Mostly the intervenor to itself
optionExplain: She says the praise comes from the intervenor.
She does not mention outside critics; the congratulations come mostly from the intervenor.
She does not mention regulators.
Right: Mostly the intervenor congratulates itself.
questions.explain: Mostly the intervenor congratulates itself. Self-congratulation.
questions.rule: If help weakens the capacity it replaces, the need for help grows in a reinforcing loop.
questions.teaches: The early success draws congratulations, usually self-congratulations by the intervenor to the intervenor, before the original problem reappears.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Is handing a burden to an outside helper a mistake in every case?
options: No, it can be sensible and even necessary
Yes, helpers always weaken systems
Yes, unless the helper is a government
No, because systems never recover on their own
optionExplain: Right: the card gives the test.
Meadows says it can be good. Here, judge by effect on capacity.
The identity of the helper does not settle it; the test is the effect on the system's capacity.
Systems do recover on their own in many cases; the point is that help is not always a mistake.
questions.explain: Judge by effect on capacity. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Shifting a burden is fine when it works and lasts; it is a trap when it erodes the system's own capacity.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Which does Meadows give as an example where shifting the burden can be better?
options: Calculators for children
Social Security, which she lists among shifts that left families less able
Smallpox vaccination compared with natural partial immunity
Cheap oil for Western economies
optionExplain: She lists this among burden shifts that cost a capacity.
She lists it as a burden shift, not as a clearly better case.
Right: Full protection from vaccination beats partial natural immunity.
She names it as a dependence, not a better case.
questions.explain: Full protection from vaccination beats partial natural immunity. Vaccines give full protection.
questions.rule: Shifting a burden is fine when it works and lasts; it is a trap when it erodes the system's own capacity.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Which scenario is a trap rather than a sound intervention?
options: Vaccination that gives full protection against a serious disease
A tutoring service that leaves students unable to study alone
A fire department that puts out fires in a town's buildings
A hospital that treats acute illness that people cannot treat alone
optionExplain: This is an example of sound help.
Right: A tutoring service that leaves students unable to study alone erodes their own capacity.
A fire department meets a need the system cannot meet itself, so it is sound help.
Treating acute illness people cannot treat alone is sound help, not a trap.
questions.explain: A tutoring service that leaves students unable to study alone erodes their own capacity. The test is atrophy.
questions.rule: Shifting a burden is fine when it works and lasts; it is a trap when it erodes the system's own capacity.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: If a vaccine's protection lasts, what does Meadows expect compared to partial natural immunity?
options: A better outcome
A worse outcome, since natural immunity is always stronger
No difference, since both protect people from the disease in the end
A hidden harm that appears later and offsets the gain from vaccination
optionExplain: Right: A vaccine that lasts gives a better outcome than partial natural immunity.
She says 100 percent protection is preferable.
She says full protection beats partial.
She does not mention any such harm.
questions.explain: A vaccine that lasts gives a better outcome than partial natural immunity. 100 percent beats partial.
questions.rule: Shifting a burden is fine when it works and lasts; it is a trap when it erodes the system's own capacity.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says transferring responsibility to an outside helper can be good, but becomes a trap when it undermines capacity.
questions.explain: She says it can be a good thing, but becomes a trap when it undermines the system's capacity.
questions.rule: Shifting a burden is fine when it works and lasts; it is a trap when it erodes the system's own capacity.

questions.q: A burden shift becomes a trap when the intervention weakens the system's own ____ to maintain itself.
questions.explain: The test is what happens to the system's own capacity.
questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.rule: Shifting a burden is fine when it works and lasts; it is a trap when it erodes the system's own capacity.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Which question helps tell a sound intervention from a trap?
options: Is the helper well funded and able to keep up the help over many years?
Does the helper work quickly enough to bring relief to the system?
Is the help popular with the public who see it being delivered?
Does it strengthen or erode the system's own capacity to cope?
optionExplain: Funding is not the test of whether capacity erodes.
Speed is not the test; fast relief is part of the trap.
Popularity is not the test; the question is whether capacity is strengthened or eroded.
Right: The test is whether the help strengthens or erodes the system's own capacity.
questions.explain: Our reading, from her description of the trap. Meadows lists elder care as an example: families once cared for the aged, and after Social Security and nursing homes most lack the space, time, skills or willingness.
questions.rule: Shifting a burden is fine when it works and lasts; it is a trap when it erodes the system's own capacity.
questions.teaches: Families used to care for the aged until Social Security and nursing homes took over, and now most no longer have the space, time, skills or willingness.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Why might a well-meaning helper start a cycle of dependence?
options: Wanting to make a profit from the dependence that the help creates
Not foreseeing that small help can lead to growing dependency
Intending harm to the system by making it weak and reliant on the helper
Following a law that requires the helper to take over the system's tasks
optionExplain: She calls the intervenor well-meaning, so profit from dependence is not the reason.
Right: A helper may not foresee that small help can grow into dependency.
She calls the intervenor well-meaning; harm is not intended.
A legal requirement is not one of her two reasons, which are failures of foresight.
questions.explain: A helper may not foresee that small help can grow into dependency. A failure of foresight. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Both sides can fail to foresee the dependency that begins with small help.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Which system does Meadows say is feeling the strains of the intervention sequence?
options: The Swedish education system
The Romanian economy, which she discusses in the resistance case
The American health-care system
The Somali food market
optionExplain: The Swedish education system is not what she names as strained by the intervention sequence.
Romania's economy belongs to her resistance case, not to the strained system here.
Right: She names the American health-care system.
The Somali food market is not named here; she names the American health-care system.
questions.explain: She names the American health-care system. Her named example.
questions.rule: Both sides can fail to foresee the dependency that begins with small help.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: A community accepts free food aid year after year and abandons its own farming. Which reason applies?
options: The helper wanted a profit from the community's continued need
The aid was too small to change what the community was doing
The helped did not think through its long-term loss of control
The farmland was too large for the community to manage by itself
optionExplain: Nothing in the case suggests the aid giver wanted profit; the helped community overlooked its loss of control.
The point is the dependence, not the size.
Right: The helped community overlooked the long-term loss of control that comes with the shift.
The size of the farmland is not the reason; the community shifted the burden without thinking through the cost.
questions.explain: The helped community overlooked the long-term loss of control that comes with the shift. The helped side overlooks vulnerability.
questions.rule: Both sides can fail to foresee the dependency that begins with small help.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: As dependency grows, what happens to the intervenor?
options: Its capacity may be strained
It gains more freedom
It is relieved of the burden as the system learns to cope alone
It leaves the system once its first efforts have been completed
optionExplain: Right: Its capacity may be strained as dependency grows.
Dependency tightens the intervenor's load rather than giving it freedom.
The dependence is increasing, so the intervenor is not relieved.
The intervenor is drawn deeper.
questions.explain: Its capacity may be strained as dependency grows. Ever-increasing dependency strains the helper.
questions.rule: Both sides can fail to foresee the dependency that begins with small help.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the helped party fully understands the long-term loss of control.
questions.explain: She says the helped may not think through that loss.
questions.rule: Both sides can fail to foresee the dependency that begins with small help.

questions.q: The intervenor may not foresee that a small urge to help can lead to ever-increasing ____.
