questions.explain: Dependency eventually strains the intervenor.
questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.rule: Both sides can fail to foresee the dependency that begins with small help.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: In the AA definition Meadows cites, what is addiction?
options: Seeking help from others when a person cannot cope on their own
Avoiding all helpers so that no one has any hold over you
Refusing to change habits that are known to be harmful to health
Repeating the same behavior and expecting different results
optionExplain: Seeking help when you cannot cope is not the AA definition she cites.
Avoiding all helpers is not the definition she cites.
Close in spirit, but not the quoted definition.
Right: The AA definition is repeating the same behavior and expecting different results.
questions.explain: Her quote of AA. Meadows cites the Alcoholics Anonymous definition: repeating the same stupid behavior over and over and expecting different results.
questions.rule: Both sides can fail to foresee the dependency that begins with small help.
questions.teaches: Meadows cites the definition used in Alcoholics Anonymous: repeating the same stupid behavior over and over and expecting different results.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Insect pests appear in a monoculture. What response does Meadows warn against?
options: Planting varied crops so that pests do not find a single food source
Spraying pesticide again and again
Rotating crops through the seasons so that pests do not build up
Allowing natural predators to return so that they eat the pests
optionExplain: She suggests polyculture as a nonaddictive policy.
Right: Spraying pesticide again and again is the quick fix she warns against.
She suggests rotation as a nonaddictive policy.
She lists restoring natural controls as the proper remedy.
questions.explain: Spraying pesticide again and again is the quick fix she warns against. Pesticide addiction. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A policy that hides the symptom is easy to adopt and makes the cause worse.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: What does Meadows say about the appeal of addictive policies?
options: They are expensive to explain
They are easy to sell and simple to fall for
They are unpopular with voters, who see through them at once
They are rarely adopted
optionExplain: She says the opposite: addictive policies are easy to sell, not costly to explain.
Right: Addictive policies are easy to sell and simple to fall for.
She says they are easy to sell.
She says they are insidious because they are adopted.
questions.explain: Addictive policies are easy to sell and simple to fall for. Insidious because easy.
questions.rule: A policy that hides the symptom is easy to adopt and makes the cause worse.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: The 1970s response of the Soviet Union and the United States to oil price shocks, per Meadows, was to do what?
options: Ration the demand
Raise taxes sharply
Ban all oil use
Fix the price
optionExplain: Rationing demand would have shown the shortage; she says price fixing hid the depletion.
Raising taxes sharply is not the response she names; both countries fixed the price.
Banning all oil use is not what either country did; they fixed the price.
Right: Price fixing hid the depletion.
questions.explain: Fixing the price hid the depletion, so people could pretend nothing was happening and go on burning oil.
questions.rule: A policy that hides the symptom is easy to adopt and makes the cause worse.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: After the pesticide kills the bugs, what does Meadows expect?
options: Pests return in greater outbursts, needing more pesticide
A permanent solution, since the pesticide removes the cause of the pests
Fewer pests each year
Healthier ecosystems, as the farmland is cleared of harmful insects
optionExplain: Right: Pests return in greater outbursts and need more pesticide.
The cause, monoculture, is untouched.
She says outbursts get bigger.
She says the ecosystem controls are destroyed.
questions.explain: Pests return in greater outbursts and need more pesticide. The loop deepens.
questions.rule: A policy that hides the symptom is easy to adopt and makes the cause worse.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says price-fixing in the 1970s encouraged acknowledging that oil is a nonrenewable resource.
questions.explain: It let people pretend that nothing was happening and go on burning oil.
questions.rule: A policy that hides the symptom is easy to adopt and makes the cause worse.

questions.q: Addictive policies are insidious because they are so easy to ____.
questions.explain: They are easy to sell and simple to fall for.
questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.rule: A policy that hides the symptom is easy to adopt and makes the cause worse.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Which comparison does Meadows use for the search for more oil?
options: A gambler doubling his bet in the hope of winning back his losses
A hunter tracking a rare animal across the last wild country
A drunk ransacking the house for one more bottle
A sailor chasing the horizon in the hope of finding new land
optionExplain: A gambler doubling his bet is not her image for the search for more oil.
A hunter tracking a rare animal is not her comparison; hers is a drunk searching for one more bottle.
Right: She compares the search to a drunk ransacking the house for one more bottle.
A sailor chasing the horizon is not her comparison for the oil search.
questions.explain: Her image. Meadows compares the hunt for one more oil deposit to a drunk ransacking the house for one more bottle.
questions.rule: A policy that hides the symptom is easy to adopt and makes the cause worse.
questions.teaches: Meadows compares the hunt for one more oil deposit to a drunk ransacking the house in hopes of finding one more bottle, polluting beaches and invading the last wilderness areas.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: A country wants to cut its oil dependence. What is the cost it faces?
options: No cost at all
Only a short delay in oil supply that businesses can plan around
The complete loss of the economy as the country goes without
The pain of confronting the real state and higher prices
optionExplain: She says withdrawal is painful.
She describes real economic pain.
Losing the whole economy overstates her claim; the cost is the pain of facing the real state and paying more.
Right: The cost is the pain of facing the real state and paying higher prices.
questions.explain: The cost is the pain of facing the real state and paying higher prices. Withdrawal hurts. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Withdrawal means facing the real state; a replacement policy can ease the pain.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: What does withdrawal mean in Meadows's account?
options: Facing the real, deteriorated state and taking postponed actions
Walking away from the problem so that it no longer demands attention
Doubling the intervention to be sure that the problem is controlled
Hiding the symptoms better so that the pain is felt less
optionExplain: Right: Withdrawal means facing the real, deteriorated state and taking the actions the addiction let you put off.
Walking away is avoidance; withdrawal means facing the deteriorated state and acting.
Doubling the intervention deepens the trap rather than withdrawing from it.
That is what the addiction does.
questions.explain: Withdrawal means facing the real, deteriorated state and taking the actions the addiction let you put off. Confront reality.
questions.rule: Withdrawal means facing the real state; a replacement policy can ease the pain.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Which is a nonaddictive policy for the pest case?
options: More pesticide applied on a wider area of the farm each season
Price fixing to hide the effects of a shortage from the buyers
Crop rotation and polyculture
A subsidy to cover losses caused by pests in the field
optionExplain: More pesticide each season is the addictive policy she warns about.
That is the oil example of an addictive policy.
Right: Crop rotation and polyculture reduce the crop's vulnerability to pests.
That is another form of masking the problem.
questions.explain: Crop rotation and polyculture reduce the crop's vulnerability to pests. Her example.
questions.rule: Withdrawal means facing the real state; a replacement policy can ease the pain.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: The longer you wait to withdraw, what happens to the process?
options: It gets easier
It gets harder
It becomes unnecessary
It stays the same
optionExplain: It does not get easier; the longer the wait, the harder the withdrawal.
Right: The longer the wait, the harder the withdrawal.
It does not become unnecessary; waiting only makes withdrawal harder.
It does not stay the same; the longer you wait, the harder it gets.
questions.explain: The longer the wait, the harder the withdrawal.
questions.rule: Withdrawal means facing the real state; a replacement policy can ease the pain.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says withdrawal cannot be done gradually.
questions.explain: She says sometimes it can be done gradually.
questions.rule: Withdrawal means facing the real state; a replacement policy can ease the pain.

questions.q: Sometimes there is no way out but to go cold ____ and bear the pain.
questions.explain: Meadows lists cold turkey as one possible route.
questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.rule: Withdrawal means facing the real state; a replacement policy can ease the pain.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Which is group support in her list meant to restore?
options: The self-image of the addict
The price of drugs, which would fall if the demand were cut
The supply of fuel
The soil, which is the pest example's concern
optionExplain: Right: Group support is meant to restore the self-image of the addict.
Group support is for the addict's self-image, not drug prices.
Fuel supply belongs to the oil example, not to what group support restores.
Soil belongs to the pest example, not to what group support restores.
questions.explain: Nonaddictive policy first. Group support to restore the addict's self-image is one of Meadows's nonaddictive policies for easing withdrawal.
questions.rule: Withdrawal means facing the real state; a replacement policy can ease the pain.
questions.teaches: Group support to restore the addict's self-image is one of Meadows's examples of a nonaddictive policy that eases withdrawal.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: An agency wants to help a village with failing water supply. Which start does Meadows favor?
options: Take over the supply and run it directly
Buy bottled water for the village so that people have drink now
Wait to be asked before offering any help to the village
Ask why its own water-keeping mechanisms are failing
optionExplain: That is the heroic takeover she warns against.
Buying bottled water relieves the symptom but does not ask why the village's own mechanisms fail.
Waiting to be asked is not what she proposes; she favors asking why the system's own mechanisms fail.
Right: She favors asking why the system's own correcting mechanisms are failing.
questions.explain: She favors asking why the system's own correcting mechanisms are failing. Start with questions. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Help the system help itself, then step back.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Order the intervenor's steps.
items: Ask why the natural correction is failing
Remove obstacles to it
Make its mechanisms more effective
Remove yourself
questions.explain: First understand, then strengthen, then step back.
questions.rule: Help the system help itself, then step back.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: A consultant is brought into a failing team. Which plan follows the way out?
options: Run the team indefinitely
Build the team's own skills, then leave
Hide the team's problems from the rest of the company
Replace the team with a fresh group that has no history of failure
optionExplain: Running the team indefinitely breeds dependence, the trap itself.
Right: Building the team's own skills and then leaving restores its capacity.
Hiding the team's problems denies the signal and leaves the capacity unbuilt.
That abandons the system's own capacity.
questions.explain: Building the team's own skills and then leaving restores its capacity. Restore the system's own capacity.
questions.rule: Help the system help itself, then step back.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: If you are the dependent party, what does Meadows say about timing?
options: Wait until the intervenor leaves so that the move is not disruptive
Delay until the problem eases so that the cost is smaller
Do it right away; delay makes withdrawal harder
Never withdraw, since the dependence has become part of the system
optionExplain: Waiting for the intervenor to leave only makes withdrawal harder.
Delaying until the problem eases makes the withdrawal harder, not smaller.
Right: She says to act right away, because delay makes withdrawal harder.
She advises rebuilding capability and then withdrawing.
questions.explain: She says to act right away, because delay makes withdrawal harder. The longer you wait.
questions.rule: Help the system help itself, then step back.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says helping a system help itself can be much cheaper and easier than taking over its running.
questions.explain: She says it can be much cheaper and easier.
questions.rule: Help the system help itself, then step back.

questions.section: Shifting the Burden to the Intervenor—Addiction
questions.q: Which policy is symptom-relieving or signal-denying?
options: Insulating homes so that less oil is needed in the first place
Rotating crops so that pests cannot build up in one field
Fixing a price so people ignore a shortage
Training local technicians to maintain the equipment themselves
optionExplain: Insulating homes restructures the system to need less oil.
Rotating crops restructures the system so pests cannot build up.
Right: Fixing a price so people ignore a shortage relieves the symptom and denies the signal.
This builds the system's own capacity.
questions.explain: Fixing a price so people ignore a shortage relieves the symptom and denies the signal. Signals hidden.
questions.rule: Help the system help itself, then step back.
questions.teaches: Meadows says the trap arises when a policy reduces or disguises the symptoms yet interferes with the actions that could solve the real problem.

questions.q: Staff meet a rule's wording exactly while defeating its purpose. What is this called?
options: Rule beating
Policy resistance
Escalation
Drift
optionExplain: Right: the card defines it.
That involves actors pulling a shared stock apart.
A rivalry spiral. Here, letter but not spirit.
Standards eroding. Here, letter but not spirit.
questions.explain: the card defines it. Letter but not spirit. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Rule beating is evasion that keeps the letter of a rule and defeats its purpose.

questions.q: When does rule beating become a problem, according to Meadows?
options: Whenever any rule is evaded, however small the departure from it
When the rules are written down rather than passed on by custom
When someone in authority notices that the rule is being evaded
When it leads to large, unnatural distortions of the system
optionExplain: She says it is a problem only when it leads to large distortions.
Written form is not her test; the problem is large, unnatural distortions.
Being noticed is not her test.
Right: It becomes a problem when it leads to large distortions that would make no sense without the rules.
questions.explain: It becomes a problem when it leads to large distortions that would make no sense without the rules. Large distortions.
questions.rule: Rule beating is evasion that keeps the letter of a rule and defeats its purpose.

questions.q: A city caps bus fares and operators respond by cutting routes to the cheapest-to-run stretches. Which is the best description?
options: Drift to low performance
Rule beating that distorts the service
Success to the successful
A commons, in which a shared resource is overused by all of its users
optionExplain: No eroding standard is described; operators comply with the cap in a distorting way.
Right: Cutting routes to the cheapest stretches meets the fare cap but defeats its aim.
No winner-take-all loop is described; operators respond to a fare cap.
No shared resource is overused; the case turns on compliance that defeats the aim.
questions.explain: Cutting routes to the cheapest stretches meets the fare cap but defeats its aim. Complying with the cap while defeating its aim.
questions.rule: Rule beating is evasion that keeps the letter of a rule and defeats its purpose.

questions.q: Would rule beating happen in a system with no rules?
options: Yes, it is a fixed trait of people and appears whatever the rules
No: it exists only in relation to rules
Yes, though milder, since people still look for ways to get around norms
Only in large systems, where rules are too many for people to follow
optionExplain: Rule beating is a response to rules, so it does not appear where there are none.
Right: Rule beating exists only in relation to rules, so none occurs without them.
Without rules there is nothing to evade.
Size is not her condition; rule beating arises wherever rules exist, in large or small systems.
questions.explain: Rule beating exists only in relation to rules, so none occurs without them. Our reading: it responds to rules.
questions.rule: Rule beating is evasion that keeps the letter of a rule and defeats its purpose.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says all rule beating is destructive.
questions.explain: She says it is a problem only when it leads to large distortions; she gives some examples as less serious.
questions.rule: Rule beating is evasion that keeps the letter of a rule and defeats its purpose.

questions.q: Rule beating means abiding by the letter, but not the ____, of the law.
questions.explain: The evasion keeps the wording and defeats the purpose.
questions.rule: Rule beating is evasion that keeps the letter of a rule and defeats its purpose.

questions.q: Which of her examples is lighter in tone?
options: Hunting endangered species to free land
Pointless spending at the end of a fiscal year to avoid budget cuts
Cassava imports that replaced feed grain imports under European rules
Calvin planning twenty good deeds a day to impress Santa
optionExplain: Hunting endangered species to free land is a destructive example, not a light one.
That is a real example of waste.
That is an economic distortion.
Right: Calvin's plan for twenty good deeds a day is a light example from a comic strip.
questions.explain: Calvin's plan for twenty good deeds a day is a light example from a comic strip. Her comic strip.
questions.rule: Rule beating is evasion that keeps the letter of a rule and defeats its purpose.
questions.teaches: Meadows opens with a cartoon in which Calvin plans spontaneous acts of good will to win leniency from Santa, a light example of rule beating.

questions.q: A rule affects lots of ten acres or less. Where would you expect many new lots to appear?
options: Slightly over the ten-acre line
Exactly at ten acres, where the rule applies and approval is complex
Far below the limit, in very small lots that are also covered by the rule
Evenly across all sizes
optionExplain: Right: Lots slightly over ten acres escape the rule and so cluster just past the limit.
Lots of ten acres or less are covered.
Very small lots are covered by the rule, so there is no reason for them to cluster there.
The rule shapes the pattern, so lot sizes are not spread evenly but pile up just past the limit.
questions.explain: Evasion clusters at the edge. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Find the rule's edge, and see what behavior piles up just past it.

questions.q: Why do departments spend pointlessly at year end?
options: Auditors require departments to spend their full budget each year
Prices drop at the end of the year
Unspent budget means a smaller allocation next year
Staff are paid bonuses for the amount they spend before the year ends
optionExplain: Auditors requiring full spending is not stated; the cause is the fear of a smaller budget next year.
Falling prices are not part of her account; the cause is the budget rule.
Right: An unspent budget means a smaller allocation next year, so departments spend.
Bonuses for spending are not stated; the motive is to avoid a smaller allocation.
questions.explain: An unspent budget means a smaller allocation next year, so departments spend. The budget rule drives the behavior.
questions.rule: Find the rule's edge, and see what behavior piles up just past it.

questions.q: Which would be a new case of the same pattern?
options: A baker who makes more bread when demand for it rises
A firm that raises its prices when its costs go up
A team that asks for more time when a project proves harder than planned
Drivers slowing only where speed cameras sit
optionExplain: Making more bread as demand rises is an ordinary market response, not evasion of a rule.
Raising prices when costs go up is an ordinary market response, not evasion of a rule.
This is an ordinary response to difficulty.
Right: Slowing only where speed cameras sit is compliance that depends on being observed.
questions.explain: Slowing only where speed cameras sit is compliance that depends on being observed. Compliance only where observed.
questions.rule: Find the rule's edge, and see what behavior piles up just past it.

questions.q: After the grain import limits, what did Europe import in place of corn?
options: Cassava
Rice
Soybeans
Barley
optionExplain: Right: Cassava was left out.
Rice is not the import she names; cassava replaced the limited grains.
Soybeans are not the import she names; cassava slipped past the grain rules.
Barley is not the import she names; cassava slipped past the rules.
questions.explain: Cassava was left off the restricted list, so cassava imports replaced the limited grains; no one thought of it when the rules were drafted.
questions.rule: Find the rule's edge, and see what behavior piles up just past it.

questions.q: True or false: The cassava substitution arose because the rule writers deliberately excluded cassava.
questions.explain: No one thought of cassava while the restrictions were being drafted.
questions.rule: Find the rule's edge, and see what behavior piles up just past it.

questions.q: Vermont's Act 250 covers lots of ten acres or less, and now Vermont has many lots a little over ____ acres.
questions.explain: Builders cluster just beyond the rule's edge.
questions.rule: Find the rule's edge, and see what behavior piles up just past it.

questions.q: What did some landowners do on finding an endangered species on their land?
options: They reported it to the authorities in order to claim public funds
They sold the land at once to avoid the restrictions on development
Hunted or poisoned it so they could develop
They built around the habitat to leave the species untouched
optionExplain: This is the opposite of what she says.
Selling the land at once is not what she reports; some landowners hunted or poisoned the species.
Right: Some landowners hunt or poison the species so that they can develop the land.
Building around the habitat is not what she reports; some landowners destroyed the species instead.
questions.explain: Meadows says so. The rule is met on paper: development does not proceed where an endangered species is documented as present.
questions.rule: Find the rule's edge, and see what behavior piles up just past it.
questions.teaches: Rule beating produces the appearance of rules being followed: development does not proceed where an endangered species is documented as present.

questions.q: A speed limit is obeyed near police cars only. What does this show?
options: The limit is working as intended
The letter is met near enforcement, the spirit is not
Drivers never exceed the limit anywhere
The limit is set too high
optionExplain: It works only where police are near.
Right: The letter of the limit is met near enforcement while its spirit is not.
Obedience is limited to the vicinity of police.
Nothing says the limit is too high; the point is that people obey only near police.
questions.explain: Appearance of compliance. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Design rules with the system's evasive responses in mind.

questions.q: What does Meadows say rule makers should keep in mind?
options: The system's self-organizing evasive possibilities
The cost of enforcement alone
The popularity of the rule among those who must follow it
The number of rules in force at any time in the organization
optionExplain: Right: She says rule makers should allow for the system's self-organizing evasive possibilities.
Enforcement cost is not her warning; she warns that systems self-organize ways around rules.
Popularity of the rule is not her warning; the issue is the system's evasive possibilities.
The number of rules is not her warning; she asks rule makers to expect evasion.
questions.explain: She says rule makers should allow for the system's self-organizing evasive possibilities. Design with the whole system.
questions.rule: Design rules with the system's evasive responses in mind.

questions.q: A firm rewards call-center staff by calls closed. Staff hang up on hard cases. This is?
options: Policy resistance, with several actors pulling a stock in different directions
Escalation, with each staff member raising goals against a rival
A commons, with a shared resource overused by many users
Rule beating that meets the letter but loses the purpose
optionExplain: No stock is being pulled by opposed actors; staff meet the target and defeat its purpose.
No rival's state sets the staff's target, so it is not escalation.
No shared resource is overused; the issue is a target met in letter only.
Right: Hanging up on hard cases meets the target while defeating the purpose.
questions.explain: Hanging up on hard cases meets the target while defeating the purpose. Letter versus spirit.
questions.rule: Design rules with the system's evasive responses in mind.

questions.q: If a rule is tightened without understanding why it is evaded, what is likely?
options: Better compliance in spirit
More distortion
Less evasion
No change
optionExplain: Better compliance in spirit does not follow; tightening a rule deepens the evasion.
Right: Tightening can deepen distortion (see next idea).
Less evasion does not follow; tightening without understanding invites cleverer evasion.
There is a change: tightening deepens the distortion rather than leaving things as they were.
questions.explain: Tightening can deepen distortion (see next idea).
questions.rule: Design rules with the system's evasive responses in mind.

questions.q: True or false: When rule beating occurs, the letter of the law is broken openly.
questions.explain: In rule beating the letter of the rule is met while its spirit is defeated, so it is not broken openly.
questions.rule: Design rules with the system's evasive responses in mind.

questions.q: Rule beating produces the ____ of rules being followed.
questions.explain: The letter is met while the spirit is not.
questions.rule: Design rules with the system's evasive responses in mind.

questions.q: Which design choice follows from Meadows's warning?
options: Publish the rule widely and wait to see whether anyone evades it
Add penalties first, so that evasion is costly before it starts
Test a draft rule by asking how people might get round it
Ban discussion of the rule
optionExplain: That waits for evasion rather than foreseeing it.
That strengthens enforcement without understanding evasion.
Right: Testing a draft rule by asking how people might get round it foresees evasion.
That suppresses information rather than designing the rule.
questions.explain: Foresee evasion. Meadows adds that rule beating is usually a response of lower levels to overrigid, unworkable or ill-defined rules from above.
questions.rule: Design rules with the system's evasive responses in mind.
questions.teaches: Rule beating is usually a response of the lower levels in a hierarchy to overrigid, deleterious, unworkable or ill-defined rules from above.

questions.q: Staff keep finding workarounds to a rule. What does Meadows advise?
options: Punish the workarounds harder
Ignore them, since they will pass without any action being taken
Treat the workarounds as feedback on the rule
Add more rules to close each gap that staff have found
optionExplain: That is the way further into the trap.
She advises learning from them.
Right: She advises treating the workarounds as feedback on the rule.
Adding rules to close each gap deepens the distortion rather than curing it.
questions.explain: She advises treating the workarounds as feedback on the rule. Listen to the evasion. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Treat evasion as a message about the rule, and redesign the rule to point creativity at its purpose.

questions.q: Meadows says rule beating can be understood as useful ____.
questions.explain: She treats rule beating as useful feedback on the rule: it shows where the rule does not fit.
questions.rule: Treat evasion as a message about the rule, and redesign the rule to point creativity at its purpose.

questions.q: Cyclists ignore a dismount rule on a short bridge. Which response follows Meadows?
options: Ask why, then revise or better explain the rule
Post more guards at the bridge
Fine every cyclist who rides across the bridge without dismounting
Ban cycling on the bridge so that the rule can no longer be broken
optionExplain: Right: Asking why and then revising or better explaining the rule treats evasion as feedback.
More guards are stronger enforcement, the response that deepens evasion.
Fining cyclists is stronger enforcement, not asking why the rule is evaded.
That is overpowering the problem.
questions.explain: Asking why and then revising or better explaining the rule treats evasion as feedback. Revise or explain.
questions.rule: Treat evasion as a message about the rule, and redesign the rule to point creativity at its purpose.

questions.q: What happens if you strengthen enforcement to stamp out evasion?
options: The system returns to normal as the evaders stop their workarounds
Evasion vanishes altogether once the enforcement has been strengthened
Compliance rises at no cost
Usually still greater distortion
optionExplain: She says the way further into the trap.
She expects greater distortion.
She expects a cost in distortion.
Right: Stamping out evasion by force usually produces still greater distortion.
questions.explain: Stamping out evasion by force usually produces still greater distortion. Further into the trap.
questions.rule: Treat evasion as a message about the rule, and redesign the rule to point creativity at its purpose.

questions.q: True or false: Rule beating is usually a response of upper levels to rules from below.
questions.explain: It is usually a response of the lower levels to rules from above.
questions.rule: Treat evasion as a message about the rule, and redesign the rule to point creativity at its purpose.

questions.q: Which rule design best turns self-organization toward the rule's purpose?
options: Rewarding paperwork counts, which invites staff to produce paper
Rewarding teams for actual outcomes
Rewarding speed alone, which invites staff to cut corners
Rewarding silence, which invites staff to avoid reporting problems
optionExplain: Rewarding paperwork points effort at the measure, so staff produce paper, not the purpose.
Right: Rewarding teams for actual outcomes points their creativity at the rule's purpose.
Rewarding speed alone points effort at the measure, so staff cut corners.
Rewarding silence points effort at the measure, so staff hide problems.
questions.explain: Align with purpose. Meadows adds that better design foresees the rules' effects on subsystems, rule beating included.
questions.rule: Treat evasion as a message about the rule, and redesign the rule to point creativity at its purpose.
questions.teaches: Better rule design means foreseeing the rules' effects on subsystems, including any rule beating, and structuring rules so self-organizing capacity turns toward their purpose.

questions.q: A school is judged only by test scores. What will it most reliably produce?
options: Good education, since test scores are a full measure of what is learned
High test scores, which may not equal good education
Lower scores, because the pressure of being tested harms learning
Random results, because the goal does not affect what the school does
optionExplain: Meadows says whether scores correlate with education is open.
Right: A school judged by test scores will reliably produce high test scores, which may not equal good education.
Nothing says scores must fall; the system tends to produce what it is measured on.
The system is directed by its goal.
questions.explain: Systems produce what they measure. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Be careful what you ask a system to produce: it will produce exactly that.

questions.q: What happens if a goal does not reflect the real welfare of the system?
options: It still reaches the desired result by luck
It ignores the goal and follows its own path to a good result
It corrects the goal itself and so avoids the mistake
The system cannot produce a desirable result
optionExplain: She says it cannot produce a desirable result.
Systems obey their goals, so a system does not ignore its goal for a good result.
The system obeys its goal; nothing in the text has it correct the goal on its own.
Right: A goal that does not reflect real welfare means the system cannot produce a desirable result.
questions.explain: A goal that does not reflect real welfare means the system cannot produce a desirable result. Bad goals, bad results.
questions.rule: Be careful what you ask a system to produce: it will produce exactly that.

questions.q: A police force is judged by number of arrests. What is the likeliest effect?
options: More arrests, perhaps of minor offenses, without necessarily less crime
Less crime for certain, because arrests deter the people who commit it
Fewer officers, because the target can be met with fewer arrests
Better trust between police and public, as more people are arrested
optionExplain: Right: A force judged by arrests will produce arrests, perhaps of minor offenses, without necessarily reducing crime.
The measure is effort, not result.
Nothing in the text suggests the force would shrink; it would aim to produce more arrests.
Nothing in the text suggests arrests build trust; the measure is effort, not result.
questions.explain: A force judged by arrests will produce arrests, perhaps of minor offenses, without necessarily reducing crime. Effort measured, not result.
questions.rule: Be careful what you ask a system to produce: it will produce exactly that.

questions.q: If security is defined as military spending and spending drains other parts of the economy, what may happen to security?
options: It must improve
It stays the same
It may be undermined
It becomes irrelevant
optionExplain: Security does not have to improve; spending that drains the economy may undermine it.
Security does not stay the same if spending drains other parts of the economy.
Right: Spending may not equal security.
Security does not become irrelevant; it may be undermined by the very spending meant to secure it.
questions.explain: If security is defined as military spending that drains the economy, the spending may undermine the security it was meant to produce.
questions.rule: Be careful what you ask a system to produce: it will produce exactly that.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says money spent per student is a sure measure of the quality of education.
questions.explain: She says whether such measures correlate with good education is at least worth thinking about.
questions.rule: Be careful what you ask a system to produce: it will produce exactly that.

questions.q: Systems tend to produce exactly and only what you ask them to ____.
questions.explain: Be careful what you ask them to produce.
questions.rule: Be careful what you ask a system to produce: it will produce exactly that.

questions.q: What was the program goal in the early days of family planning in India, per Meadows?
options: The number of births averted each year in the program region
The number of patients counseled about family planning services
The number of years of schooling completed by the women served
The number of IUDs implanted
optionExplain: Births averted is not the goal she reports for early family planning in India; the goal was IUDs implanted.
Counseling numbers are not the goal she names; the program counted IUDs implanted.
Years of schooling are not the program goal she reports.
Right: The goal was the number of IUDs implanted.
questions.explain: The goal was the number of IUDs implanted. Doctors met targets without patient approval.
questions.rule: Be careful what you ask a system to produce: it will produce exactly that.
questions.teaches: Meadows reports that where goals were set as numbers of IUDs implanted, doctors eager to meet targets put loops into women without patient approval.

questions.q: Which indicator measures result, not effort?
options: The share of children reading at their grade level
Hours teachers spend teaching
The number of books bought
The budget per school, which measures resources supplied
optionExplain: Right: The share of children reading at grade level measures an outcome, not an effort.
Hours teachers spend teaching count effort, not result.
The number of books bought counts effort, not what children learn.
Budget per school measures resources supplied, an effort measure.
questions.explain: The share of children reading at grade level measures an outcome, not an effort. Result is the aim. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Measure what you want achieved, not how much was done to try.

questions.q: What does Meadows warn will be produced if effort is confused with result?
options: A system producing nothing
A system producing waste only
A system producing effort, not result
A system producing equity
optionExplain: It produces what the indicator counts.
Her warning is specific: effort instead of result.
Right: A system producing effort, not result, is her warning.
Equity is not what effort measures.
questions.explain: A system producing effort, not result, is her warning. Her final warning.
questions.rule: Measure what you want achieved, not how much was done to try.

questions.q: A road agency counts kilometers of road laid, not journey times saved. This is?
options: A result indicator, because the roads exist at the end of the work
An effort indicator
A welfare indicator, because roads help people to reach places
A balancing goal, because the agency keeps building until it is done
optionExplain: It counts activity, not the benefit people get.
Right: Counting kilometers laid counts effort, not journey times saved.
Roads laid do not measure welfare; they count activity, not the journeys improved.
The label does not describe the kind of indicator.
questions.explain: Counting kilometers laid counts effort, not journey times saved. Counting output of activity.
questions.rule: Measure what you want achieved, not how much was done to try.

questions.q: If a hospital is paid per procedure, what do you expect?
options: More procedures
Better health necessarily
Fewer procedures
Lower costs
optionExplain: Right: The system produces the indicator.
Better health does not follow necessarily; the system produces what the payment counts.
Paying per procedure rewards more procedures, not fewer.
Lower costs are not what the payment rewards; it rewards doing more procedures.
questions.explain: A system produces what its indicator counts, so paying per procedure gives more procedures, not necessarily better health.
questions.rule: Measure what you want achieved, not how much was done to try.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the spending per student and test-score measures are certain to correlate with good education.
questions.explain: She says it is worth thinking about whether they do.
questions.rule: Measure what you want achieved, not how much was done to try.

questions.q: Meadows names confusing effort with ____ as one of the most common mistakes in designing systems around the wrong goal.
questions.explain: Effort measures reward activity, not outcome.
questions.rule: Measure what you want achieved, not how much was done to try.

questions.q: Which fix follows the chapter's advice?
options: Increase the effort measured, since more effort should give more result
Drop all measurement, so that nothing misleads the system
Measure the same thing more often, so that problems are found early
Choose an indicator that reflects the real welfare of the system
optionExplain: Measuring more effort feeds the problem; the fix is a better indicator.
She asks for better indicators, not none.
Measuring more often leaves the indicator unchanged, so it does not fix the goal.
Right: Choosing an indicator that reflects real welfare is her advice.
questions.explain: Fix the indicator. Meadows says the worst such mistake may be adopting GNP as the measure of national economic success, as the next idea explains.
questions.rule: Measure what you want achieved, not how much was done to try.
questions.teaches: Maybe the worst mistake of confusing effort with result has been adopting the GNP as the measure of national economic success.

questions.q: A city has many car crashes and large repair bills. What effect would this have on GNP?
options: GNP falls
GNP rises
GNP stays unchanged
GNP is measured only by good goods
optionExplain: The spending counts. Here, goods and bads together.
Right: the card explains why.
Spending counts. Here, goods and bads together.
It lumps goods and bads. Here, goods and bads together.
questions.explain: the card explains why. Goods and bads together. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: GNP counts activity, good or bad, and not welfare.

questions.q: What does GNP measure, per Meadows?
options: The wealth of citizens, counted as what they own at a given time
The welfare of citizens, counted by their health and happiness
The money value of final goods and services produced
The stock of capital in houses, cars and computers across the nation
optionExplain: It is a flow, not a stock of wealth.
She argues it does not measure welfare.
Right: GNP is the money value of the final goods and services produced.
She says it measures throughput rather than stocks.
questions.explain: GNP is the money value of the final goods and services produced. Production value.
questions.rule: GNP counts activity, good or bad, and not welfare.

questions.q: If parents hired people to raise their children rather than doing it themselves, what happens to GNP?
options: It goes down
It stays the same
It goes up
It becomes undefined
optionExplain: GNP does not fall; paid child care is a marketed service that GNP counts.
GNP does not stay the same; hiring carers adds marketed services.
Right: Only marketed services are counted.
GNP does not become undefined; paid services are simply counted.
questions.explain: GNP counts only marketed services, so paying others to raise children raises GNP even though no child is better cared for.
questions.rule: GNP counts activity, good or bad, and not welfare.

questions.q: New bulbs give the same light with one-eighth the electricity. What happens to GNP?
options: It goes down
It goes up, because the new bulbs are a product that people buy
It does not change, since lighting is the same as before
It doubles, as each household buys a new set of bulbs
optionExplain: Right: Efficiency lowers throughput, so GNP goes down.
Meadows says GNP goes down, because less electricity and fewer bulbs are sold.
Less electricity and fewer bulbs are sold.
She says GNP goes down, not up; households need fewer bulbs and less power.
questions.explain: Efficiency lowers throughput, so GNP goes down. Efficiency lowers throughput.
questions.rule: GNP counts activity, good or bad, and not welfare.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says GNP reflects distributional equity.
questions.explain: GNP says nothing about how wealth is shared; it does not reflect distributional equity.
questions.rule: GNP counts activity, good or bad, and not welfare.

questions.q: GNP stands for gross national ____.
questions.explain: It is the money value of final goods and services produced.
questions.rule: GNP counts activity, good or bad, and not welfare.

questions.q: Governments respond to faltering GNP by pursuing actions that, per Meadows, are often what?
options: Beneficial to long-term welfare, since growth brings lasting gains
Cost-saving for the economy, since they make production cheaper
Neutral in their effect, since they only restore a number to its old level
Wasteful, stimulating inefficient production of things no one particularly wants
optionExplain: She does not call them beneficial to long-term welfare; many are wasteful.
She says they stimulate inefficient production.
She says some threaten the long-term good.
Right: Many of the actions are wasteful, stimulating inefficient production of things nobody particularly wants.
questions.explain: Many of the actions are wasteful, stimulating inefficient production of things nobody particularly wants. Some even threaten the long-term good.
questions.rule: GNP counts activity, good or bad, and not welfare.
questions.teaches: Governments chasing a faltering GNP take many wasteful actions, and some, such as overharvesting forests, threaten the long-term good of the economy, society or environment.

questions.q: A nation wants its people to enjoy good housing. Which indicator targets the real aim?
options: The money spent on building each year
The quality and number of houses standing
The number of builders employed in the industry each year
The price of new homes in the main cities of the country
optionExplain: Money spent on building each year is a flow of spending, that is throughput, not the standing houses.
Right: The quality and number of houses standing is a stock measure of the real aim.
Builders employed measures effort, not the housing people end up with.
The price of new homes does not measure how well housed people are.
questions.explain: The quality and number of houses standing is a stock measure of the real aim. Stocks are real wealth. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Define and measure the outcome you want, such as stocks, health or equity, or you will get flows.

questions.q: In Meadows's usage, what is throughput?
options: The stock of houses and cars that people hold at a given time
The flows of stuff made and purchased in a year
The savings of citizens held in banks and other accounts
The gap in wealth between the richest and poorest citizens
optionExplain: Houses and cars held at a time are capital stocks, the opposite of throughput.
Right: Throughput is the flows of stuff made and purchased in a year.
Savings held in banks are not what she means by throughput.
The wealth gap is not throughput; it is a distribution, not a flow of stuff.
questions.explain: Throughput is the flows of stuff made and purchased in a year. Flows, not stocks.
questions.rule: Define and measure the outcome you want, such as stocks, health or equity, or you will get flows.

questions.q: Which goal would reflect her suggestion of the best society?
options: The highest throughput
The lowest capital stocks
The highest consumption
Keeping capital stocks usable with the lowest throughput
optionExplain: The highest throughput is the opposite of her suggestion, which asks for the lowest throughput.
The lowest capital stocks are the opposite of her suggestion, which keeps stocks usable.
The highest consumption is the opposite of her suggestion of lowest throughput.
Right: The best society keeps capital stocks usable with the lowest possible throughput.
questions.explain: The best society keeps capital stocks usable with the lowest possible throughput. Maintain stocks, minimize flows.
questions.rule: Define and measure the outcome you want, such as stocks, health or equity, or you will get flows.

questions.q: If a society's goal is GNP but nobody reports welfare, what does Meadows expect?
options: The society produces GNP, not welfare or equity
It also produces welfare as a by-product of the extra activity
It produces justice, as rising output makes courts and laws stronger
It produces nothing, because the indicator lacks any real meaning
optionExplain: Right: A society that defines its goal as GNP produces GNP, not welfare or equity.
Welfare does not appear as a by-product; a society produces what it defines and reports as its goal.
Justice does not appear as a by-product of output unless it is defined and reported as a goal.
It produces what the indicator counts.
questions.explain: A society that defines its goal as GNP produces GNP, not welfare or equity. Systems produce what you define.
questions.rule: Define and measure the outcome you want, such as stocks, health or equity, or you will get flows.

questions.q: True or false: Meadows says there is every reason to want GNP to go up.
questions.explain: She says there is every reason to want a thriving economy, but no particular reason to want GNP to go up.
questions.rule: Define and measure the outcome you want, such as stocks, health or equity, or you will get flows.

questions.q: GNP measures throughput, the flows of stuff made and bought, rather than capital ____.
questions.explain: Stocks are the source of real wealth and pleasure.
questions.rule: Define and measure the outcome you want, such as stocks, health or equity, or you will get flows.

questions.q: Which competition would Meadows prefer to nations racing for highest GNP per capita?
options: A race for the highest military budget among the great powers
A race for the biggest population among the nations of the world
A race for the smallest gap between rich and poor
A race for the highest throughput of goods and services each year
optionExplain: A race for military budgets is not among the contests she imagines.
A race for population size is not among her imagined contests.
Right: She lists a race for the smallest gap between rich and poor among better contests.
That is the GNP race she criticizes.
questions.explain: She lists several alternatives. Meadows imagines nations competing on the lowest infant mortality, the greatest political freedom, the cleanest environment or the smallest gap between rich and poor.
questions.rule: Define and measure the outcome you want, such as stocks, health or equity, or you will get flows.
questions.teaches: Meadows imagines nations competing on lowest infant mortality, greatest political freedom, cleanest environment or smallest gap between rich and poor.

questions.q: A hospital follows a rule to discharge patients within two days and sends sick patients home. What problem is this?
options: Rule beating, in which staff evade the rule while seeming to obey it
Policy resistance, in which opposed actors pull one stock apart
Drift to low performance
Seeking the wrong goal
optionExplain: The rule is obeyed here, not evaded.
No opposed actors pull one stock apart; the hospital simply obeys a bad rule.
No eroding standard is described; the rule is fixed, and the hospital follows it faithfully.
Right: Obeying a bad discharge rule and sending sick people home is a wrong-goal problem.
questions.explain: Obeying a bad discharge rule and sending sick people home is a wrong-goal problem. Obedience to a bad goal. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Obedient to a bad rule means wrong goal; clever around a rule means rule beating.

questions.q: What does the system do under seeking the wrong goal?
options: Obediently follows the rule and produces the specified result
It evades the rule while giving the appearance of obeying it
It lowers the rule over time as performance falls
It ignores the goal and follows its own aims instead
optionExplain: Right: The system obediently follows the rule and produces the specified result.
Evading a rule while seeming to obey it is rule beating, not the wrong-goal pattern.
Lowering the rule as performance falls is eroding goals, not the wrong-goal pattern.
The point is that it obeys the goal.
questions.explain: The system obediently follows the rule and produces the specified result. Wrong goal means obedience.
questions.rule: Obedient to a bad rule means wrong goal; clever around a rule means rule beating.

questions.q: Employees shuffle files to appear busy and meet the report. This is?
options: Seeking the wrong goal
Escalation
Rule beating
Success to the successful
optionExplain: They did not obey. Here, way around the rule.
Escalation needs rivals raising goals against each other, not staff faking busyness.
Right: evading the intent while looking compliant.
No winner gains means to win more in the filing case; staff are evading the intent of a report rule.
questions.explain: evading the intent while looking compliant. Way around the rule.
questions.rule: Obedient to a bad rule means wrong goal; clever around a rule means rule beating.

questions.q: If a bad rule is both obeyed by some and evaded by others, what is going on?
options: Only a wrong goal
Both problems at once around the same rule
Only rule beating, since some people are evading the rule
Neither problem, since mixed behavior shows that the rule is workable
optionExplain: Evasion by others is rule beating.
Right: Both problems can be present at once around the same rule.
Obedience by others is the wrong-goal problem.
Mixed behavior shows both problems at once.
questions.explain: Both problems can be present at once around the same rule. Meadows says they can coexist.
questions.rule: Obedient to a bad rule means wrong goal; clever around a rule means rule beating.

questions.q: True or false: Seeking the wrong goal and rule beating are the same problem.
questions.explain: Meadows calls them almost opposite characteristics.
questions.rule: Obedient to a bad rule means wrong goal; clever around a rule means rule beating.

questions.q: In seeking the wrong goal, the system ____ follows the rule and produces its specified result.
questions.explain: Obedience to a badly chosen rule is the mark of this trap.
questions.rule: Obedient to a bad rule means wrong goal; clever around a rule means rule beating.

questions.q: A rule produces a stupid result. Which clue marks a wrong goal rather than rule beating?
options: Staff follow the rule exactly, and the stupid result is what the rule asks for
Staff find a loophole in the rule to avoid doing what it asks, and the result is stupid
The rule is widely ignored, and the result is stupid
The rule is repealed, and the stupid result follows from the absence of any rule
optionExplain: Right: obedience that yields an unwanted result marks a wrong goal.
This is the clue for rule beating, where the way around the rule causes the problem.
Ignoring a rule outright is neither of her two problems.
Without a rule neither problem arises.
questions.explain: In seeking the wrong goal the system obediently produces what the rule specifies. In rule beating the stupid result comes from the way around the rule. Meadows's test: stupid because it is the rule means a wrong goal; stupid because it is the way around the rule means rule beating.
questions.rule: Obedient to a bad rule means wrong goal; clever around a rule means rule beating.
questions.teaches: Meadows's test: stupid things happening because it is the rule point to a wrong goal, while stupid things happening because it is the way around the rule point to rule beating.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: Racing rules reward speed within narrow classes for decades. What do boat designs become?
options: Better all-round boats that sail well in every kind of weather
Cheaper boats that more people can afford to race with
Unchanged boats that are much like the old fishing boats
Highly specialized for the rules, not for normal sailing
optionExplain: The story says the opposite: designs grow narrow and strange, not better all-round.
Nothing in the story says boats became cheaper; they became specialized to the rules.
The story says they became strange.
Right: Designs become specialized for the rules and not for normal sailing.
questions.explain: Design follows the rules. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: A goal defined by narrow rules can reshape the system to serve the rules and lose its original purpose and resilience.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: Why did the racing rules arise?
options: To make boats safer for crews who must sail them in rough seas
To make races more interesting between boats of similar speed
To raise prize money for the winners of the major races
To limit the number of crew that each boat may carry
optionExplain: Crew safety was not the reason given for the rules.
Right: The rules were made to keep races interesting between boats of similar speed.
The races began as sport for fun.
Limiting crew numbers was not the reason given; the rules were to keep races interesting.
questions.explain: The rules were made to keep races interesting between boats of similar speed. Rules defined classes.
questions.rule: A goal defined by narrow rules can reshape the system to serve the rules and lose its original purpose and resilience.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: Which of the following matches the sailboat pattern?
options: A baker improving bread so that customers enjoy it more
A firm lowering its prices to attract more buyers
Cars built to score on a lab emissions test but not on the road
A team losing members because the work has become too hard
optionExplain: Improving bread for customers involves no rule being gamed.
Lowering prices to attract buyers is an ordinary market move, not gaming a rule.
Right: Designing cars for a lab test but not for the road matches designing boats for the racing rules.
Members leaving because work is hard involves no rule being gamed.
questions.explain: Designing cars for a lab test but not for the road matches designing boats for the racing rules. Optimizing around the rule.
questions.rule: A goal defined by narrow rules can reshape the system to serve the rules and lose its original purpose and resilience.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: If the racing rules suddenly changed, what would happen to the current yachts?
options: They would adapt easily
They would improve
They would be useless
They would be unaffected
optionExplain: They would not adapt easily; designs this specialized lost the resilience of normal boats.
They would not improve; boats over-optimized to old rules fit the new ones poorly.
Right: Over-optimized.
They would be affected; yachts shaped for the old rules lose their purpose when the rules change.
questions.explain: Meadows says the boats are so optimized around the present rules that they have lost all resilience, and any change in the rules would render them useless.
questions.rule: A goal defined by narrow rules can reshape the system to serve the rules and lose its original purpose and resilience.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says America's Cup yachts are well suited to fishing and Sunday sails.
questions.explain: She says they are nearly unseaworthy and no one would use them for anything but racing.
questions.rule: A goal defined by narrow rules can reshape the system to serve the rules and lose its original purpose and resilience.

questions.q: Racing sailboats are so optimized around the present rules that they have lost all ____.
questions.explain: Any change in the rules would render them useless.
questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.rule: A goal defined by narrow rules can reshape the system to serve the rules and lose its original purpose and resilience.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: Which archetype does the sailboat story illustrate?
options: Both seeking the wrong goal and rule beating, since boats are designed around the rules
Commons, because the boats share a stretch of water and wear it down
Escalation only, because each designer tries to beat the others
Addiction, because the sailors come to depend on outside support
optionExplain: Right: The boats are built around the rules, which fits both a wrong goal and rule beating (our reading).
No shared resource is overused; the boats are shaped by rules, not by wearing down a commons.
The point is optimization around rules, not just rivalry.
No outside helper breeds dependence among the sailors in the story.
questions.explain: Our reading: it fits goals defined by rules. As races became more serious the rules grew stricter and the designs more bizarre, which deepened the distortion.
questions.rule: A goal defined by narrow rules can reshape the system to serve the rules and lose its original purpose and resilience.
questions.teaches: As the races became more serious, the rules became stricter and the boat designs more bizarre.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: The eight traps in this chapter all share which feature, according to Meadows?
options: A single villain, either a firm or a government, whose bad decisions set the pattern in motion
A sudden outside shock that the system has no time to adjust to before the harm is done
A shortage of money, which explains why none of the traps can be solved by better design
A recurring pattern of poor behavior that comes from system structure and can be escaped by changing it
optionExplain: Meadows says the damage is blamed on actors, but it comes from structure.
The traps are built into ordinary structure, not sudden shocks.
Money is not the shared feature; structure is.
Right: this is how the chapter frames archetypes.
questions.explain: All eight are structures behind recurring bad patterns. The card next lists them.
questions.rule: Name the structure first, then use the way out that fits it.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: Match each trap to the way out that Meadows gives for it.
pairs: Let go and seek goals everyone can share
Keep standards absolute or tied to the best results
Refuse to compete or negotiate controls
Strengthen the system's own capacity, then withdraw
questions.explain: Each way out changes the structure that produces the trap.
questions.rule: Name the structure first, then use the way out that fits it.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: Two rival gyms keep adding free perks to outdo each other, and both now lose money. Which trap is this?
options: Policy resistance, because both gyms pull one shared stock of members toward different goals
Escalation, because each gym sets its offer by the other's and tries to stay slightly ahead
Tragedy of the commons, because the gyms share a pool of customers that is limited
Success to the successful, because the gym with more perks gains the means to win again
optionExplain: Both gyms are chasing each other, not pulling opposite ways on one stock.
Right: the goal is tied to the rival's state, and the loop reinforces.
Nothing erodes a shared resource here; the loop is a contest.
Perks do not return as means to compete; each side is matching the other.
questions.explain: the goal is tied to the rival's state, and the loop reinforces. Goals that chase a rival's state are escalation.
questions.rule: Name the structure first, then use the way out that fits it.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: Sort each situation by the trap it shows.

items.t: A school meets its target of tutoring hours exactly while students learn little
Doctors implant devices to reach a target count without asking patients
A hospital sends patients home on day two because the rule says two days
Landowners poison an endangered species so that their land can be developed
Departments burn leftover budget before year end to avoid a smaller allocation
Importers switch to cassava to avoid limits that name only other feed grains

questions.explain: Obeying a badly chosen rule is a wrong goal; finding the way around a rule is rule beating.
questions.rule: Name the structure first, then use the way out that fits it.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: The trap in which users gain fully but share the cost of damage to a resource is the tragedy of the ____.
questions.explain: Each user keeps the gain and shares the cost, so overuse follows.
questions.rule: Name the structure first, then use the way out that fits it.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says that the way out of every trap is to push the existing policy harder.
questions.explain: Pushing levers harder is among the responses she says leave structure in place; each trap needs a change of structure.
questions.rule: Name the structure first, then use the way out that fits it.

questions.section: Interlude • The Goal of Sailboat Design
questions.q: A firm leans on a subsidy, and two other firms are in a price war. What is Meadows's best way out for each trap?
options: To withdraw slowly from both traps, because quick changes are always worse than slow ones
To avoid getting into the trap in the first place, since escaping later is harder
To raise the intensity of the fix in both, since the traps end only when the rivals give in
To wait for outside events to end both patterns
optionExplain: She says sometimes cold turkey is the only way out of dependence.
Right: she says this for both shifting the burden and escalation.
More of the same effort feeds both traps.
She says the structure can be altered.
questions.explain: For both shifting the burden and escalation, Meadows says the best way out is to avoid getting into the trap.
questions.rule: Name the structure first, then use the way out that fits it.
questions.teaches: For both escalation and shifting the burden, Meadows says the best way out is to avoid getting into the trap.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A sales team keeps missing targets. Which approach fits the idea of a leverage point best?
options: Add equal extra effort to every part of the team's work
Find one spot where a small change shifts results most
Replace members one by one until the numbers improve
Raise every target so people try harder
optionExplain: Plausible because effort feels responsible, but spreading it evenly is not a small change aimed at one spot.
Right: A leverage point is about where you push, not how hard.
Plausible because people drive results, but new hands in the same structure behave much as the old ones did.
Plausible because pressure feels decisive, but a bigger target is a push, not a change of structure.
questions.explain: A leverage point is about where you push, not how hard. The card next defines it.
questions.rule: Look for the small change in structure that shifts behavior a lot, not for the place where the most effort is already spent.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A leverage point is a place in a system where a small ____ can lead to a large shift in behavior.
questions.explain: The definition rests on a small input producing a large shift in behavior.
questions.rule: A small change in the right place can shift behavior a lot.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A café has long queues at noon. Which move is closest to a leverage-point style change?
options: Putting up a sign asking customers for patience during the rush
Asking staff to work faster for a week so the queue clears
Hiring one extra person for every noon shift to add serving capacity
Letting customers order ahead so the queue forms before noon
optionExplain: Plausible, but it tries to change feelings, not the behavior of the queue.
Plausible, but it asks for more effort on the same arrangement and fades.
Plausible, but it adds capacity without changing how demand arrives.
Right: ordering ahead changes when orders enter the system, a small structural change with a wide effect (Our reading).
questions.explain: A leverage-style move changes how the system is arranged, so behavior shifts without extra force.
questions.rule: Look for the small change in structure that shifts behavior a lot, not for the place where the most effort is already spent.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: True or false: A leverage point is any place in a system where a large amount of effort is applied.
questions.explain: The author defines it by the size of the result relative to the change, not by effort. Large effort at the wrong place may do little.
questions.rule: Small change, large shift.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: Two managers spend a month on a failing process: one changes a key structural feature, the other works longer hours. What does the idea predict?
options: Structure may shift behavior far more than hours
Both managers get results in proportion to their hours
The longer hours win, because effort adds up over a month
Neither change can matter, since processes resist all change
optionExplain: Right: Leverage breaks the link between how hard you push and how much changes.
Plausible if results tracked effort, but leverage is exactly where they do not.
Plausible as common sense, but it is the opposite of the leverage idea.
Too strong: the author says changes at leverage points matter a great deal.
questions.explain: Leverage breaks the link between how hard you push and how much changes. (Our reading on the managers.)
questions.rule: Look for the small change in structure that shifts behavior a lot, not for the place where the most effort is already spent.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A household budget is chaotic. Why might finding its leverage point be hard, going by the author's checking-account example?
options: Leverage points exist only in corporations and governments
Households have no stocks or flows, so nothing can be found
Linked stocks and flows get too complicated to figure out
The author says that finances cannot be changed by anyone
optionExplain: She applies the idea to many kinds of systems.
A bank balance is a stock with flows in and out.
Right: One account is simple; a thousand linked accounts and banks make a complex system, which is why leverage points are often not intuitive.
She says only that leverage points are often not intuitive.
questions.explain: One account is simple; a thousand linked accounts and banks make a complex system, which is why leverage points are often not intuitive.
questions.teaches: Plumbing simple stocks and flows together, as in linked bank accounts and banks, can create systems too complex to figure out easily, which is why leverage points are often not intuitive.
questions.rule: Look for the small change in structure that shifts behavior a lot, not for the place where the most effort is already spent.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A city is struggling with poverty and hunger. Which instinctive policy might Forrester's model suggest is pushing the wrong way?
options: Counting the costs of growth alongside its benefits in every decision
Slower or different kinds of growth in some areas, with some negative growth
Faster economic growth as the answer to everything
Looking for the structure that links poverty, hunger and resource depletion
optionExplain: This is what the author asks us to do, not the instinct that pushes wrongly.
This is what the model recommended, not the instinct it contradicted.
Right: leaders fixate on growth as the answer, but the model pointed the other way.
This is the model's own method, not the instinctive policy.
questions.explain: Guess freely: the card shows where Forrester's results ran against instinct.
questions.rule: Check the direction of a push, not only the place, because intuition often has it backward.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: Forrester's word for the behavior of complex systems, which leverage points often share, is ____.
questions.explain: He called complex systems counterintuitive: people involved often sense where leverage is but push the change in the wrong direction.
questions.rule: Leverage points are frequently counterintuitive.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A town's traffic jams worsen. Planners widen the roads, and the jams return worse. Which lesson from this idea applies?
options: A move that feels right may worsen the problem, so test the direction
The planners picked the wrong town, so the lesson does not generalize
Roads are not a leverage point in any city, so none should be built
Traffic jams are caused only by drivers, so planners cannot affect them
optionExplain: Right: the author warns we often use leverage points backward, worsening the problem.
Plausible, but the point concerns direction, not the town chosen.
Too broad: the idea is about testing direction, not banning roads.
Drivers are not the claim; the lesson is about the direction of an intervention in the system's structure (Our reading).
questions.explain: The lesson is to test the direction of a change, since intuitive moves can worsen what they target. (Our reading for the traffic case.)
questions.rule: Check the direction of a push, not only the place, because intuition often has it backward.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, Forrester's World model found that faster economic growth is the answer to most global problems.
questions.explain: The model's leverage point was growth, but it pointed toward much slower, different growth, since growth has costs we usually do not count.
questions.rule: The right lever pushed the wrong way can worsen the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A report says: Forrester found that national policy was right to build massive low-income housing projects. What is wrong with this?
options: He found that only high-income housing affects a city's fortunes
Nothing is wrong; he found that massive projects were the right policy
He found that housing has no effect on the health of a city at all
He found less subsidized low-income housing leaves a city better off
optionExplain: The 1969 study concerned subsidized low-income housing, not high-income housing, and found that less of it left the city better off.
Plausible because policy of the day backed projects, but he was derided for the opposite finding.
Plausible as a cautious reading, but he found a strong effect.
Right: his 1969 study showed the less subsidized low-income housing, the better off the city, even its poorer residents.
questions.explain: Forrester's counterintuitive result is why he was derided at the time.
questions.rule: Check the direction of a push, not only the place, because intuition often has it backward.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A company responds to losing customers by cutting research spending. Using the author's idea, what would she ask first?
options: Whether the cut is large enough to reassure investors
Whether the instinctive push might worsen the problem
Whether competitors have made the same cut this year
Whether staff will believe the plan once announced
optionExplain: Plausible as business sense, but size is not the lesson of this idea.
Right: The author's caution is about direction: well-meant pushes can systematically worsen the problem.
Plausible as context, but copying rivals does not test the direction of a push.
Relevant elsewhere, since she says few believe counterintuitive findings, but it is not the first question.
questions.explain: The author's caution is about direction: well-meant pushes can systematically worsen the problem.
questions.teaches: The author says that when she discovers a system's leverage points, hardly anybody believes her, because they are so counterintuitive.
questions.rule: Check the direction of a push, not only the place, because intuition often has it backward.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A neighbourhood group wants less litter. Which kind of intervention would the author expect to carry the most leverage?
options: Raising the fine for littering by a modest amount each year
Changing what the neighbourhood sees as its shared purpose
Adding one more bin on each street in the neighbourhood
Cleaning the streets slightly more often than before
optionExplain: A small numeric adjustment, the sort she ranks weakest.
Right: a shared purpose sits near the top of her list.
A small physical change, also near the weak end.
