Another adjustment of a flow, ranked at the bottom.
questions.explain: A fair guess: the card next gives the author's ranking.
questions.rule: Read the list upward from 12 to 1: the smaller the number, the more leverage.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: Match each place to its number in the author's count.
questions.explain: She counts down from 12 (numbers) to 1 (transcending paradigms), so smaller numbers are stronger.
questions.rule: Smaller number, stronger lever.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: Order these interventions from the weakest leverage to the strongest on the author's list.
items: Adjusting a tax rate
Adding a feedback signal nobody receives today
Rewriting incentives and penalties
Changing the system's purpose
questions.explain: Numbers (12), information flows (6), rules (5), goals (3).
questions.rule: Weak to strong: numbers, information, rules, goals.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A study note says: she numbers her list so 1 is the least powerful place. What is wrong with this?
options: The list is ordered alphabetically, so numbers carry no meaning
Nothing is wrong, since point 1 is the weakest on her list
The list has no numbers, only a loose set of examples
The count runs from 12 (weakest) to 1 (strongest)
optionExplain: The list is numbered by strength, 12 down to 1; the numbers are her ranking, not an alphabetical order.
Reversed: point 1, transcending paradigms, is the strongest place, and point 12, numbers, is the weakest.
The list is numbered, 12 down to 1, though she calls its order tentative and slithery.
Right: the strongest place, transcending paradigms, is 1; numbers are 12.
questions.explain: Counting down from 12 to 1 means 1 is the strongest.
questions.rule: Read the list upward from 12 to 1: the smaller the number, the more leverage.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: True or false: The author presents her list as a finished recipe for finding leverage points.
questions.explain: She calls it a work in progress and an invitation to think more broadly, and stresses that complex systems are dangerous to generalize about.
questions.rule: The list invites thought; it is not a recipe.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A school wants better student wellbeing. Which proposal sits highest on the author's list?
options: Let students and parents see wellbeing results each term
Lengthen lunch by five minutes to give students more time to eat
Rebuild the playground so that it holds more students safely
Cut the size of one class slightly to help teachers focus
optionExplain: Right: it adds a flow of information, number 6, higher than numbers, buffers or structure.
A longer lunch is a small adjustment to a flow, a number, which is last (12) on her list.
A physical structure, also near the weak end.
A slightly smaller class is another parameter-style tweak, the weakest kind of change on her list.
questions.explain: The author notes the list moves from the physical part of the system to information and control parts, where more leverage can be found.
questions.teaches: After the physical items, the author says the list moves from the physical part of the system into the information and control parts, where more leverage can be found.
questions.rule: Read the list upward from 12 to 1: the smaller the number, the more leverage.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: Which of these is a parameter in the author's sense?
options: A culture's beliefs about what money measures
A law's stated purpose for the whole economy
A national minimum wage
A newly added channel of feedback to citizens
optionExplain: Beliefs about what money measures are a paradigm, number 2 on her list, not a parameter.
The purpose of a whole economy is a goal, number 3 on her list, not a parameter.
Right: a minimum wage is a number setting a flow.
A new channel of feedback adds an information flow, number 6, a higher place than a parameter.
questions.explain: A parameter is a number on a flow. The card next explains.
questions.rule: A parameter is a setting on a flow; it changes how fast stocks fill or drain.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: In the bathtub picture, parameters are adjustments to the ____.
questions.explain: Parameters are like faucet settings: the size of the flows.
questions.rule: Parameters set the size of flows.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: Sort each item: a parameter (a number on a flow) or not?

items.t: The minimum wage
Allowed annual timber cut
The bank's service charge
The system's overall goal
A society's belief that growth is good
A newly added warning signal

questions.explain: Wage levels, cuts and charges are numbers; goals, beliefs and new information channels are higher points.
questions.rule: Numbers are the settings of flows.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: Which statement separates parameters from higher points on the list?
options: Parameters set the purpose and direction of the system
Parameters change the physical shape of the system's pipes
Parameters adjust flow sizes within the existing structure
Parameters decide who gets to see which information
optionExplain: Purpose and direction belong to goals, number 3, far above the parameters at 12.
That describes stock-and-flow structure, number 10 on the list.
Right: Parameters turn faucets; structure and goals are other places.
Who has access to which information is the information-flow point, number 6, not a parameter.
questions.explain: Parameters turn faucets; structure and goals are other places.
questions.rule: A parameter is a setting on a flow; it changes how fast stocks fill or drain.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: True or false: If a drain is blocked so it passes only a small flow, opening it further will not change the flow.
questions.explain: The author notes some parameters are physically locked in; a blocked drain passes little however open it is. (Our reading for opening further.)
questions.rule: Some parameters cannot be varied.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A hospital's flows include admissions and discharges per day. Which is the parameter-style intervention?
options: Changing the target discharge rate per day
Rebuilding the hospital so wards sit nearer the entrance
Giving staff new information on bed availability each morning
Replacing the hospital's mission with a new statement of purpose
optionExplain: Right: a discharge rate is a number setting a flow, a parameter.
Rebuilding wards changes physical structure, number 10 on her list, not a setting on a flow.
New bed-availability information adds an information flow, number 6, a higher place than parameters.
A new statement of purpose changes the goal, number 3, much higher than a parameter.
questions.explain: A discharge rate is a setting on a flow, so it is a parameter; structure, information and goals sit higher on the list.
questions.teaches: The author lists firing people and getting new ones, including politicians, as parameter adjustments too, since new hands on the same faucets rarely change much.
questions.rule: A parameter is a setting on a flow; it changes how fast stocks fill or drain.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A government spends years fighting over a tax rate while the economy stays stagnant. What would the author say?
options: Rates cannot affect anyone in the economy
Cutting the rate will probably restart the stagnant economy
Tax rates are the strongest lever on her list
Parameter changes rarely kick-start a stagnant system
optionExplain: Too strong: she says they matter to people standing in the flow.
Plausible because rates feel powerful, but she says parameter changes rarely kick-start a stagnant system.
She ranks parameters last of the twelve, not first.
Right: she says parameter changes rarely kick-start a stagnant system.
questions.explain: She says changing a parameter rarely kick-starts a stagnant system, however fiercely people fight over the number.
questions.rule: Treat a number adjustment as detail work: important to the people in the flow, rarely a change of system behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: Numbers, the sizes of flows, come ____ on the author's list of powerful interventions.
questions.explain: Number twelve is the weakest place, though most attention goes there.
questions.rule: Numbers are last in leverage but first in attention.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A city has cut its speed limit twice and still has the same crash pattern. What does the idea suggest?
options: Cut it a third time, since the first two cuts moved things in the right direction
Look for higher points than the number itself
Remove the limit, since it plainly does not work
Blame drivers, since the number cannot be the cause
optionExplain: A third cut is more of the same number tweak; she says such changes rarely alter system behavior.
Right: parameters seldom change system behavior, so look higher on the list.
Parameters are weak, not useless: she says they matter in the short term to people standing in the flow.
Blame skips the question; the idea sends you up the list to structure, information, rules and goals.
questions.explain: When repeated tweaks do not move behavior, the leverage is probably elsewhere. (Our reading for the speed-limit case.)
questions.rule: Treat a number adjustment as detail work: important to the people in the flow, rarely a change of system behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A columnist says: the author thinks parameters are unimportant to everyone. Which correction is right?
options: They matter most of all among the twelve places
They matter short term, to those in the flow
They are irrelevant to everyone, even those affected
They are used only by governments, never by firms
optionExplain: She puts numbers last of the twelve, 'dead last' in her words, so they matter least for system change.
Right: Last on the list does not mean unimportant to the people affected.
Too strong: she says people care deeply about taxes and the minimum wage.
Not what she says: corporations adjust wages and prices too.
questions.explain: Last on the list does not mean unimportant to the people affected.
questions.rule: Treat a number adjustment as detail work: important to the people in the flow, rarely a change of system behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: True or false: The author says whatever cap is put on campaign contributions, it does not clean up politics.
questions.explain: She lists contribution caps among parameter changes that leave the system's behavior largely unchanged.
questions.rule: A cap is still a number change within the same system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A company fights a margin decline by shaving price by 2 percent, then 3, then 4. Where does the idea say to look next?
options: Look nowhere, since margins are fixed by the market
Try bigger numerical cuts, since the direction is right
Look only at staff morale, since pricing is settled
Look higher on the list: structure, rules or goals
optionExplain: Too strong: the idea says to look higher, not to give up.
Plausible because the cuts feel directional, but repeating a weak move is what the author warns about.
Plausible but arbitrary; the idea points up the list, not to morale.
Right: Repeated number changes without effect point to a higher place.
questions.explain: Repeated number changes without effect point to a higher place.
questions.teaches: The author notes that the Fed's interest-rate fiddling has not made business cycles go away; we forget upturns end and are shocked by downturns.
questions.rule: Treat a number adjustment as detail work: important to the people in the flow, rarely a change of system behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: When might a change to a single number be a real leverage point?
options: When it enters a range that triggers a higher point
When the number is politically charged and widely argued over
When many people care deeply about its exact value
When it is easy for officials to change quickly
optionExplain: Right: a number matters when its range triggers a higher point, such as the gain of a reinforcing loop.
A charged political fight brings attention, not leverage; she says most attention goes to parameters anyway.
Attention is not leverage; the author says most of it goes to parameters.
Ease of change is not her test; a number matters when it reaches a range that kicks off a higher point.
questions.explain: She says parameters become leverage points when they go into ranges that kick off something higher on the list.
questions.rule: Fight over a number only if it can push the system into a range that triggers a higher leverage point.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: Interest rates and birth rates are parameters that control the gain around ____ feedback loops.
questions.explain: The author gives them as examples of numbers that become leverage points because of what they control.
questions.rule: Numbers matter when they set off a loop.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: Which situation shows a number acting as a leverage point in the author's sense?
options: A city repaints its speed signs a new color
A bank changes its service charge by a few cents
A growth rate near where a runaway loop takes off
A school moves its bell two minutes earlier
optionExplain: Repainting signs is a trivial detail that triggers nothing higher on the list (Our reading).
A small change in a flow, the usual weak case.
Right: A number is a lever when it sets off a feedback behavior higher on the list.
A small adjustment that sets off nothing higher.
questions.explain: A number is a lever when it sets off a feedback behavior higher on the list. (Our reading for the examples.)
questions.rule: Fight over a number only if it can push the system into a range that triggers a higher leverage point.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A friend says: all numbers are equally weak. Which reply fits the author?
options: Numbers are the strongest of the twelve places
Every number is equally weak in every system and range
Weak generally, but critical ones can trigger higher points
Numbers are meaningless in any system
optionExplain: Numbers are number 12, the last and weakest place on her list, not the strongest.
Too absolute: the author makes a caveat for critical ranges.
Right: Weak in general, strong at critical ranges.
She calls numbers weak, not meaningless; people fight over taxes and wages, and critical ranges matter.
questions.explain: Weak in general, strong at critical ranges.
questions.rule: Fight over a number only if it can push the system into a range that triggers a higher leverage point.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: True or false: If a system is built to stay far from its critical parameters, adjusting them will usually shift behavior a lot.
questions.explain: The author says most systems stay far from critical ranges, so such adjustments seldom matter; critical numbers are less common than people think.
questions.rule: Far from the critical range, a number is just detail.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A tenant group argues over whether rent should be 900 or 950. Using the landlord story, what is the best conclusion?
options: Both are likely within a large gray area of fairness
The exact figure decides everything about fairness
One side must be exploited whichever way it falls
Nothing can be decided without a further study
optionExplain: Right: In a gray area, the exact number is not worth much effort.
Plausible if there were a fine line, but the adviser said there is none.
Contradicts the adviser, who said both sides can be getting a fair deal.
Too strong: the adviser told him to stop worrying.
questions.explain: In a gray area, the exact number is not worth much effort.
questions.teaches: The adviser told the landlord there is no fine line at which rent is fair: a large gray area gives both sides a fair deal, so worrying about the exact figure is unnecessary.
questions.rule: Fight over a number only if it can push the system into a range that triggers a higher leverage point.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A manager fires a failing team and hires new people under the same targets and rules. What might the author predict?
options: The rules will rewrite themselves
Everything will change quickly
Performance will fall further
Behavior probably stays similar
optionExplain: The rules stay in force; new people do not rewrite them, and the same rules shape the same behavior.
She says new hands on the same old faucets change the system's behavior little, not quickly or greatly.
She predicts similar behavior, not worse; the system's structure, not the staff, shapes the results.
Right: new people at the same faucets, with the same targets and rules, usually leave behavior much as it was.
questions.explain: New people at the same faucets, with the same targets and rules, usually leave behavior much as it was; the card shows why.
questions.rule: Swapping players is a low-level move unless it also changes the information, goals or rules they work under.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: Changing the players is a parameter change, like putting different hands on the same ____.
questions.explain: The faucets stay plumbed into the same system, turned by the same information, goals and rules.
questions.rule: New hands, same faucets.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A football club replaces its coach every season, but the transfer rules and finances stay as before. What does the idea say?
options: New coaches will transform the club every season
Behavior changes little unless structure or rules change
The club will certainly improve with each new coach
Coaches have no effect on a club at all
optionExplain: Plausible because coaches are visible, but new hands on the same faucets rarely change much.
Right: Different players in the same system behave similarly.
Too certain: the idea predicts little change, not guaranteed gain.
Too strong: the author says changes are small, not zero.
questions.explain: Different players in the same system behave similarly. (Our reading for the club.)
questions.rule: Swapping players is a low-level move unless it also changes the information, goals or rules they work under.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A commentator says: the author claims electing a different president made no difference at all. What is the error?
options: She said the two elections were identical in every respect
She said it was different but not all that different
She said presidents are irrelevant to the system
She said it made the biggest difference of all
optionExplain: She does not say identical; she says electing Clinton was different from electing Bush, but not all that different.
Right: The claim is about limited difference within the same system.
Too strong: she does not call presidents irrelevant.
She does not claim the biggest difference; every president is plugged into the same political system.
questions.explain: The claim is about limited difference within the same system.
questions.rule: Swapping players is a low-level move unless it also changes the information, goals or rules they work under.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: True or false: If the new people are given different goals and rules, the system's behavior may change more than if only the people change.
questions.explain: Goals and rules are higher on the list than who operates the system, so changing them can change behavior more. (Our reading for the comparison.)
questions.rule: Change the system's rules and goals, not only the hands.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 12. Numbers—Constants and parameters such as subsidies, taxes, standards
questions.q: A single new CEO changes a company's stated goal and the whole company turns. How does this fit the idea?
options: It shows that rules are the weakest place
It contradicts the idea that players matter little
It shows that parameters are the strongest place
It is the exception: a top player changing the goal
optionExplain: Rules are number 5, stronger than numbers; the CEO case shows a goal, number 3, at work.
It fits the idea: she says players matter little except at the top, where one player can change the goal.
Parameters are last on her list; a leader changing the goal is a much higher move.
Right: A leader who changes the goal is changing a high point, not just a player.
questions.explain: A leader who changes the goal is changing a high point, not just a player.
questions.teaches: The author notes the exception to this rule is at the top, where a single player can have the power to change the system's goal.
questions.rule: Swapping players is a low-level move unless it also changes the information, goals or rules they work under.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: Why do catastrophic floods happen more often on rivers than on lakes?
options: Rivers hold a small stock relative to fast flows
Rivers are longer, so they collect more water from more places
Lakes have no inflow, so they can never rise at all
Rivers carry more fish, which blocks the channel in a flood
optionExplain: Right: a stock that is small relative to fast flows is less stable.
Her explanation is the size of the stock against its flows, not how long the river is.
Lakes do have flows, just slow ones relative to their stock.
Fish are not in her account; the contrast is stock size relative to flows.
questions.explain: A river holds a small stock relative to its fast flows, a lake a big one relative to slow flows; the card explains buffers.
questions.rule: Raising a buffer's size, relative to its flows, usually stabilizes the system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: In chemistry and other fields, a big stabilizing stock is known as a ____.
questions.explain: The term for a big stock relative to flows is buffer.
questions.rule: A buffer is a big stabilizing stock.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: Sort each case: does it act as a buffer or not?

items.t: Savings kept in the bank
A store's stocked inventory
Calcium in soil that neutralizes acid
A larger breeding population
A faster faucet into the tub
A tighter deadline

questions.explain: Buffers are large stabilizing stocks; flow speeds and deadlines are not.
questions.rule: A buffer is a big stock relative to flows.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: Sort each case: does the stock act as a buffer, or is it small relative to its flows?
questions.explain: She says stocks that are big relative to their flows are more stable: lakes, savings, inventories, and soils with calcium. The pairings with a person's pocket and the store are her examples; the grouping is Our reading.
questions.rule: Raising a buffer's size, relative to its flows, usually stabilizes the system.

items.t: A lake with slow inflow and outflow
A person with savings in the bank
A store that holds inventory on its shelves
A river whose fast flows pass quickly through
Living only from the flow of change through your pocket
Soil with little calcium to neutralize acid rain

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: Which soils would you expect to suffer more from acid rain: ones with a big calcium reserve or ones with a small one?
options: Both equally, since acid rain falls on all soils alike
Ones with a big calcium reserve, because calcium is the acid's source
Ones with a small calcium reserve
Neither, because soils do not react to acid at all
optionExplain: Plausible if buffers were irrelevant, but size matters.
Reversed: the big reserve is the buffer that neutralizes acid.
Right: a small buffer neutralizes less acid, so the soil is more sensitive.
Soils do react: eastern U.S. soils are sensitive to acid rain because they lack big calcium buffers.
questions.explain: Buffer size relative to the load decides stability. Applying the card to soils.
questions.teaches: Soils in the eastern United States are more sensitive to acid rain than those in the west, because they lack big calcium buffers to neutralize acid.
questions.rule: Raising a buffer's size, relative to its flows, usually stabilizes the system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: A conservation group asks how many animals of a rare species to protect. Which answer fits the buffer idea?
options: More than the bare minimum, as a cushion against bad years
Exactly the bare minimum, since any extra animals are wasted
None at all, since populations cannot be buffered
Only the fastest breeders, since they refill quickly
optionExplain: Right: A stock larger than the minimum steadies a population against fluctuation.
Plausible for cost, but it leaves no cushion.
A population is a stock and can be buffered; she says to keep more than the minimum breeding population.
Fast breeders refill quickly but give no cushion; the buffer idea is a stock larger than the bare minimum.
questions.explain: A stock larger than the minimum steadies a population against fluctuation.
questions.teaches: The author says this is why we need to maintain more than the minimum breeding population of an endangered species.
questions.rule: Raising a buffer's size, relative to its flows, usually stabilizes the system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: Why would a business choose to hold small inventories?
options: Small stocks are safer in every circumstance
Customers prefer empty shelves because prices drop
Big buffers are unstable, so careful firms avoid them
Holding stock is costly, and small stocks respond flexibly
optionExplain: Too absolute: she says only that occasional vulnerability can be cheaper.
Customers' taste for empty shelves is not her reason; the reasons are cost and flexible response.
Big stocks are more stable, not less; the reason to avoid them is their cost and their slowness to react.
Right: big stocks cost money to hold, and lean stocks answer shifting demand more flexibly.
questions.explain: Big stocks cost money to hold, and lean stocks answer shifting demand more flexibly; the card sets this against stability.
questions.rule: Enlarge a buffer when stability is worth its cost, remembering it is physical and hard to change.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: Buffers are number ____ on the author's list of leverage points.
questions.explain: Buffers sit near the weak end because they are usually physical and hard to change.
questions.rule: Buffers are real but low in leverage.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: A town wants to raise its flood buffer. Which fact makes this a poor leverage point per the idea?
options: Floods do not occur often enough to matter to planners
Reservoir capacity is cast in concrete and costly to change
Buffers do not stabilize anything, so raising one is pointless
Rivers are too small to need a dam in the first place
optionExplain: How often floods occur is not her point; a dam's capacity is physical and hard to change.
Right: physical buffers like dams are literally cast in concrete and costly to change.
She says buffers do stabilize; they rank low because they are hard to change, not because they are useless.
Whether rivers need a dam is not her argument; the point is that physical buffers are costly to change.
questions.explain: A dam's capacity is literally cast in concrete, so a physical buffer is slow and costly to change; that keeps buffers low on the list.
questions.rule: Enlarge a buffer when stability is worth its cost, remembering it is physical and hard to change.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: A planner says: the bigger the buffer, the better in every case. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong: stability is worth any cost
Big buffers make a system inflexible and cost money
Buffers are never useful, so none should be built
Buffers respond faster than any other part
optionExplain: Stability has a price: she lists the cost of building and maintaining big buffers and the inflexibility they bring.
Right: Buffers have costs and inflexibility.
She says you can often stabilize a system by increasing a buffer, so buffers are useful, just not unlimited.
A too-big buffer reacts slowly, she says, so it is slower, not faster, than the rest of the system.
questions.explain: She says a too-big buffer makes the system inflexible and slow to react, and big buffers cost a lot to build or maintain.
questions.rule: Enlarge a buffer when stability is worth its cost, remembering it is physical and hard to change.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: True or false: The author calls the acid-absorption capacity of eastern U.S. soils a leverage point for easing acid rain damage.
questions.explain: She says it is not one: buffers are usually physical entities that are not easy to change.
questions.rule: Physical buffers are hard to move.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 11. Buffers—The sizes of stabilizing stocks relative to their flows
questions.q: A retailer wonders why rivals run lean stock rooms. Which reason does the buffer trade-off give?
options: Customers dislike choice and avoid large stock rooms
Lean stock rooms are impossible to run profitably
Big stocks stabilize nothing, so lean ones are as safe
Rare vulnerability can cost less than constant inventory
optionExplain: Customers disliking choice is not given as a reason; the trade-off is cost against stability.
She says lean inventories were invented because occasional vulnerability is cheaper, so they can pay.
Big stocks do stabilize; lean rooms accept some vulnerability to save cost and flex with demand.
Right: The trade-off is stability versus cost and flexibility.
questions.explain: The trade-off is stability versus cost and flexibility.
questions.teaches: Businesses invented just-in-time inventories because occasional vulnerability to fluctuations is cheaper for them than certain, constant inventory costs, and small inventories allow more flexible response to shifting demand.
questions.rule: Enlarge a buffer when stability is worth its cost, remembering it is physical and hard to change.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: Traffic from every part of a country must pass through one capital. Which fix is most likely to reach the cause?
options: Change the layout so traffic avoids the center
Fit every car with a new pollution control device
Lower the speed limit in the center
Add more traffic lights in the center
optionExplain: Right: changing the layout reaches the cause, which devices, lights and limits do not.
She names pollution control devices as a poor fix for a layout that funnels all traffic through one city.
She lists speed limits among fixes that do not easily cure a layout problem.
She lists traffic lights among fixes that do not easily cure a layout problem.
questions.explain: Her Budapest example: a layout sending all traffic through one center is not easily fixed by devices, lights or speed limits; the layout is the cause.
questions.rule: When behavior is built into the physical layout, only changing the layout fixes it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: The only way to fix a system that is laid out poorly is to ____ it, if you can.
questions.explain: The author says structure cannot be tuned away; it must be rebuilt.
questions.rule: Bad layout needs rebuilding.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: A hospital's pharmacy is on the far side of the building from every ward. Which remedy fits this idea?
options: Print reminders on the wall about delivery times
Ask nurses to walk faster between ward and pharmacy
Move or add a pharmacy so the layout shortens the journey
Raise the pharmacist's pay to boost output
optionExplain: Reminders leave the layout unchanged, so the long distance and the delay remain (Our reading).
Plausible, but extra effort on the same layout.
Right: Structural problems call for structural fixes.
Plausible, but pay does not shorten distance.
questions.explain: Structural problems call for structural fixes.
questions.rule: When behavior is built into the physical layout, only changing the layout fixes it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: True or false: Pollution control devices on cars would, by themselves, remove the delays that come from a poor road layout.
questions.explain: The author says a layout like the Budapest one is not easily fixed by pollution control devices, traffic lights or speed limits.
questions.rule: Controls cannot undo the layout.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: True or false: According to the author's energy example, straightening bent pipes and enlarging pipes that are too small can bring large energy savings.
questions.explain: Amory Lovins's team did wonders this way.
questions.rule: When behavior is built into the physical layout, only changing the layout fixes it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: A warehouse staff walk miles a day because fast-selling items are stored at the far end. What does the idea predict about retraining staff?
options: Layouts never matter, only the people using them
Retraining will fix everything, since habits drive the walking
Retraining helps little until the layout changes
Staff should walk more slowly to save energy
optionExplain: She says physical structure can have an enormous effect on how a system operates, so layouts do matter.
Retraining leaves the far-end layout in place, so the long walks continue (Our reading).
Right: the layout builds the behavior in, so training alone helps little (Our reading).
Slower walking does not shorten the distance; the layout is the cause (Our reading).
questions.explain: Behavior built into structure is untouched by training alone.
questions.teaches: The author says that if similar energy retrofits were done on all the buildings in the United States, many electric power plants could be shut down.
questions.rule: When behavior is built into the physical layout, only changing the layout fixes it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: A city finds its sewage plant too small, but it is built. According to the author, where does the leverage lie?
options: In knowing its limits and not straining it
In wishing the plant were larger than it is
In rebuilding at once, whatever the cost and delay
In ignoring capacity limits until a failure appears
optionExplain: Right: use it with maximum efficiency and avoid straining it.
Wishing changes nothing; she advises using the structure efficiently and not straining its capacity.
Rebuilding is slow and costly, per the author.
Ignoring limits invites failure; she advises understanding limits and bottlenecks and not straining capacity.
questions.explain: Guess; the card gives the author's advice.
questions.rule: Design structures carefully at the start, then work within their limits instead of hoping to rebuild.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: Physical rebuilding is often the slowest and most ____ kind of change to make in a system.
questions.explain: She calls physical rebuilding often the slowest and most expensive kind of change, which is why structure ranks low.
questions.rule: Rebuilding is slow and costly.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: A planner must choose between designing a rail network carefully now or fixing it later. Which fits the author?
options: Wait for a problem to appear before spending effort
Fixing it later is cheaper than designing it carefully now
Design does not matter once the system runs
Proper design in the first place is the leverage point
optionExplain: Waiting leaves a poor design in place; she puts the leverage in proper design in the first place.
She calls physical rebuilding often the slowest and most expensive change, so fixing later costs more.
Design matters most; structure is crucial and rarely changeable once built.
Right: the leverage is in proper design in the first place.
questions.explain: She puts the leverage in proper design in the first place, since rebuilding afterward is slow and expensive.
questions.rule: Design structures carefully at the start, then work within their limits instead of hoping to rebuild.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: A report says: because physical structure is unimportant, it ranks low. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong: unimportant things rank low
It is crucial; it ranks low because it is hard to change
Structure ranks high on her list, not low
It ranks low because it is easy to change
optionExplain: She calls physical structure crucial; it ranks low because it is hard to change, not unimportant.
Right: Rank reflects changeability, not importance.
Stock-and-flow structure is number 10, low on her list, not high.
The opposite: she says changing it is rarely quick or simple.
questions.explain: Rank reflects changeability, not importance.
questions.rule: Design structures carefully at the start, then work within their limits instead of hoping to rebuild.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: True or false: Because five-year-olds become six-year-olds predictably, a population bulge will move through schools, jobs and retirement whatever policy does.
questions.explain: The author uses the baby-boom swell as a stock-and-flow structure that cannot be changed.
questions.rule: Some stocks move on a fixed schedule.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 10. Stock-and-Flow Structures—Physical systems and their nodes of intersection
questions.q: A car fleet is inefficient. Which prediction fits the structure point?
options: Replacing the fleet overnight is easy once there is a plan
Turnover takes ten to twenty years, so quick fixes are limited
Fleets cannot change at all, so nothing can be done
Efficiency is irrelevant to the structure of a fleet
optionExplain: She says an inefficient car fleet takes ten to twenty years to turn over, so overnight replacement is not easy.
Right: Slow turnover limits how fast structure can change.
She says slow structures limit change, not that nothing can be done; one can use them well and plan ahead.
An inefficient fleet is one of her examples of structure, so efficiency is part of the picture.
questions.explain: Slow turnover limits how fast structure can change.
questions.teaches: The author says an inefficient car fleet takes ten to twenty years to turn over, and that the lifetime of CFC molecules in the ozone layer cannot be hurried either.
questions.rule: Design structures carefully at the start, then work within their limits instead of hoping to rebuild.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: A shopkeeper reorders stock based on last month's sales report. Sales shift weekly. What happens?
options: Prices fall, because stock arrives too late
Stock stays exactly right because the report is accurate
Sales stop, because the shop has no information
Stock swings between too much and too little
optionExplain: Late stock does not lower prices in her account; delayed information produces swings in stock.
The report is accurate but old, and information that is out of date still produces overshoot and undershoot.
The shop has delayed information, not none; sales continue.
Right: late information produces overshoot and undershoot.
questions.explain: Reordering from an old report is a delay in information, so stock overshoots and undershoots; the card explains why delays cause oscillation.
questions.rule: Late information or slow response makes a system overshoot and undershoot its goal.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: Delays in feedback loops are common causes of ____.
questions.explain: Delays make a stock overshoot and undershoot its goal.
questions.rule: Delays cause oscillations.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: A fishery regulator sets quotas from catch data two years old. Which problem does the idea predict?
options: Quotas that overshoot and undershoot the fish population
A perfectly steady fish stock, because the data are official
No fishing at all, since the data are unreliable
Lower prices for fish, since quotas are higher
optionExplain: Right: late information makes the response overshoot and undershoot (Our reading for the fishery).
Official but two-year-old data are still late, so they cannot hold the stock steady.
Old data do not mean no fishing; the idea predicts mis-set quotas, not a ban (Our reading).
Prices are not what the idea predicts; late data make quotas swing around the real stock (Our reading).
questions.explain: Late information leads to mis-set responses.
questions.rule: Late information or slow response makes a system overshoot and undershoot its goal.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: Which two cases both cause oscillations according to the author?
options: Only a slow response, even to information that arrives on time
Only delayed information about the stock
Late information, or slow response to timely information
Neither delay nor slow response
optionExplain: Incomplete: delayed information also does it.
Incomplete: she says a slow response to timely information also causes oscillations.
Right: Either delay type causes oscillation.
She names both causes, late information and slow response, so 'neither' is wrong.
questions.explain: She names both: delayed information about the stock, and a slow response even when the information is timely.
questions.rule: Late information or slow response makes a system overshoot and undershoot its goal.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: True or false: With a power plant taking years to build, forecasting effort alone can make supply match demand exactly.
questions.explain: The author says even with immense effort most electricity industries swing between over- and undercapacity.
questions.rule: Long delays defeat even good forecasts.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: Why does the author say a massive central-planning system functions poorly?
options: It has too much feedback to handle
It has too few trained people to do all the planning
Long delays prevent responding to short-term changes
It is too cheap to run well
optionExplain: Her point is long delay, not an excess of feedback.
Her point is long delay in responding, not a lack of planners.
Right: Delays limit responsiveness.
Cost is not her reason; long delays that block response to short-term change are.
questions.explain: She says a system cannot respond to short-term changes when it has long-term delays, which is why central planning functions poorly.
questions.teaches: The author names the Soviet Union and General Motors as massive central-planning systems that necessarily function poorly because long delays cannot respond to short-term changes.
questions.rule: Late information or slow response makes a system overshoot and undershoot its goal.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: Which problem would you expect from a feedback response that comes far sooner than the situation warrants?
options: Overreaction and chasing your own tail
Perfect stability, since the response is prompt
Slow collapse, since the response is early
No change at all, since the stock is unaffected
optionExplain: Right: too-short delays make responses jumpy.
A prompt response is not steady here: delays that are too short cause overreaction and amplified oscillations.
Slow collapse belongs to overlong delays with a threshold; too-early response gives jumpy overreaction.
The stock is affected; the jumpy response keeps pushing it back and forth.
questions.explain: Delays that are too short cause overreaction and 'chasing your tail', oscillations amplified by a jumpy response; the card follows.
questions.rule: Judge a delay against the rate of change of the stock it controls, not by its length alone.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: Match each delay condition to the behavior the author links to it.
questions.explain: The author ties each condition to a distinct pattern.
questions.rule: Delay length matters relative to the rate of change.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: A thermostat reads temperature once an hour in a drafty room. Which effect fits the idea?
options: No heating at all, because the reading is rare
Overreaction, because an hourly reading is a very short delay
Perfect control, because readings are regular
Overshoot and undershoot, since the delay is long here
optionExplain: A rare reading still gives some heating; the trouble is lateness, which makes the response swing.
An hourly reading is a long delay for a drafty room, and long delays make the response overshoot, not overreact.
Regular readings are still late readings; late information makes the heating swing past the goal and back.
Right: Long delay relative to rate of change causes swings.
questions.explain: Long delay relative to rate of change causes swings.
questions.rule: Judge a delay against the rate of change of the stock it controls, not by its length alone.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: True or false: A one-day delay is long for a system whose stocks change by the hour, but short for one that changes over decades.
questions.explain: The author judges a delay relative to the rates of change in the stock being controlled.
questions.rule: Delays are relative.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: What if a long delay is combined with a danger point beyond which irreversible damage occurs?
options: Gentle damping of the oscillations
Overshoot and collapse
Faster recovery after the shock
No effect on the system
optionExplain: Damping is one outcome of overlong delays in general, but with a danger point she says overshoot and collapse.
Right: overlong delays with a threshold cause overshoot and collapse.
Past a danger point damage can be irreversible, so recovery is harder, not faster.
She calls delays critical determinants of system behavior, so they have a large effect.
questions.explain: Thresholds turn oscillation into collapse.
questions.rule: Judge a delay against the rate of change of the stock it controls, not by its length alone.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: True or false: A driver in fog who brakes late, then hard, then speeds up again shows oscillation from a delayed response (Our reading).
questions.explain: Late response to information makes a system overshoot and undershoot.
questions.teaches: The author lists delays such as the time for a price to adjust to a supply-demand imbalance, and for a new technology to spread through the economy.
questions.rule: Judge a delay against the rate of change of the stock it controls, not by its length alone.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: A river city floods whenever the dam response lags. Which strategy does the author favor in principle?
options: Wish the lag away and hope the response speeds up
Slow the pace of change so responses can keep up
Speed everything up so that the lag matters less
Ignore the lag and trust the dam to cope
optionExplain: Wishing the lag away is what she warns against: things take as long as they take.
Right: slow the change so inevitable delays cause less trouble.
Speeding everything up is the route she calls harder; she prefers to slow the rate of change.
Ignoring the lag lets the oscillations continue; she favors slowing change so delays hurt less.
questions.explain: She prefers slowing the rate of change so inevitable delays cause less trouble, since delays themselves often cannot be changed.
questions.rule: Slow the change rather than wishing delays away.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: Because delays are hard to shorten, it is usually easier to ____ the change rate.
questions.explain: Slowing the change rate lets inevitable delays cause less trouble.
questions.rule: Slow the system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: A start-up grows so fast that hiring and training cannot keep pace. Which move fits the author's logic?
options: Cut training to save time
Hire faster without limit to keep up with the growth
Shorten the time children take to grow
Slow the growth so the organization can adjust
optionExplain: Cutting training leaves the growth loop untouched and weakens the organization's ability to keep pace.
Hiring without limit ignores that people and capital change only so fast.
The growth time of children is her example of a delay that cannot be changed.
Right: Slowing change gives delayed adjustments time.
questions.explain: Slowing change gives delayed adjustments time.
questions.rule: Slow the change rather than wishing delays away.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: A critic says: faster technology and freer prices should be preferred to slower growth. What does the author's World model say?
options: Slowing growth has more leverage than speeding adjustment
Faster technology is the best lever, with freer prices next
Freer prices are best, with faster technology next
All three have equal leverage
optionExplain: Right: The model favored slowing growth.
The model found slowing growth to be a greater lever than faster technology.
Freer prices are an attempt to speed up adjustment, which she ranks below slowing growth.
She ranks them unequally: slowing growth is the greater lever.
questions.explain: In the World model, slowing growth gave more leverage than faster technology or freer prices, which only try to speed up adjustment.
questions.rule: Slow the change rather than wishing delays away.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: True or false: If a delay in your system can be changed, changing it has no big effects.
questions.explain: The author says changing a changeable delay can have big effects, and warns to change it in the right direction.
questions.rule: A changeable delay is real leverage.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 9. Delays—The lengths of time relative to the rates of system changes
questions.q: Financial markets push to cut information and money-transfer delays. What does the author predict?
options: No change, since delays do not matter
Greater calm, since information arrives faster
Wild gyrations
Slower trades, since checks take longer
optionExplain: She says delays matter, and changing them can have big effects, so 'no change' is wrong.
She warns that cutting these delays is asking for wild gyrations, not calm.
Right: the author says the push is asking for wild gyrations.
Slower trades is not her prediction; she predicts wild gyrations.
questions.explain: She says the push to cut information and money-transfer delays in financial markets is asking for wild gyrations; direction matters.
questions.teaches: The author warns that the great push to reduce information and money-transfer delays in financial markets is just asking for wild gyrations.
questions.rule: Slow the change rather than wishing delays away.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: A home heating system has a target temperature. What else does it need to behave as a balancing loop?
options: A larger fuel tank to hold more heating fuel
A second target temperature
A way to detect deviation and to respond
A louder alarm only
optionExplain: More fuel is not part of the loop's logic; a goal, a monitor and a response are.
A second target does not complete the loop; one goal plus detection and response do.
Right: A balancing loop needs a goal, a monitoring device to detect deviation, and a response mechanism.
An alarm alone only signals; the loop also needs a response mechanism.
questions.explain: A balancing loop needs a goal, a monitoring device to detect deviation, and a response mechanism; the card names all three.
questions.rule: Keep each loop complete, goal, monitor and response, and keep the rarely used ones.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: Match each part of the thermostat loop to its role.
questions.explain: Goal, monitor and response are the three parts the author names.
questions.rule: A loop needs goal, monitor and response.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: A dam has a sensor that reports nothing and no spillway. Which part of the loop is missing?
options: A response mechanism, and perhaps the monitor
The goal, since no water level is set
The inflow, since the river fills the dam
Nothing; every part of the loop is present
optionExplain: Right: with no spillway there is no response, and a silent sensor is no monitor either, so check all three parts.
The case does not say the goal is missing; the sensor and the response are the gaps (Our reading).
The inflow is not one of the loop's three parts, which are goal, monitor and response.
A sensor reporting nothing and no spillway mean parts are missing (Our reading).
questions.explain: A balancing loop needs a goal, a monitor and a response; a sensor reporting nothing and no spillway leave the response, and perhaps the monitor, missing (Our reading).
questions.rule: Keep each loop complete, goal, monitor and response, and keep the rarely used ones.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: True or false: Since emergency response loops are rarely used, removing them to save money has no long-term cost.
questions.explain: The author says the short term shows no effect but the long term drastically narrows the conditions the system survives.
questions.rule: Do not strip idle loops.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: If a firm cuts its idle emergency reserves to save cost, what does the author predict?
options: No effect at any time, even when a rare shock arrives
Immediate collapse of the firm
Greater resilience from lower costs
No visible effect at first, then later vulnerability
optionExplain: She says that in the long term, cutting such mechanisms narrows the range of conditions the system survives.
She says there is no effect in the short term, so immediate collapse is not her prediction.
Cutting reserves lowers resilience; she calls it one of the big mistakes.
Right: Costs of removal appear in the long run.
questions.explain: Costs of removal appear in the long run.
questions.rule: Keep each loop complete, goal, monitor and response, and keep the rarely used ones.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: The author calls encroaching on our own time for rest, recreation, socialization and ____ a heartbreaking way of stripping away emergency loops.
questions.explain: Rest is a safeguard that looks unnecessary until stress arrives.
questions.teaches: The author calls encroaching on endangered species' habitats and on our own time for rest, recreation, socialization and meditation heartbreaking ways of stripping away these loops.
questions.rule: Keep each loop complete, goal, monitor and response, and keep the rarely used ones.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: A market is distorted by hidden subsidies. According to the author, what is the real leverage?
options: Raising prices further so that producers earn more
Stopping the distortion so signals stay truthful
Adding more advertising so that buyers know the price
Ending markets altogether and planning supply
optionExplain: Higher prices do not make a signal truthful; she wants prices clear, unambiguous, timely and truthful.
Right: the real leverage is keeping signals from being distorted.
Advertising does not remove a distortion; the real leverage is stopping the distortion itself.
She calls markets marvels of self-correction; she does not call for ending them.
questions.explain: She says the real leverage is keeping the signals from being distorted; the card follows with antitrust and truth-in-advertising laws.
questions.rule: Protect the accuracy of the signals a balancing loop runs on.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: Sort each measure: does it clarify market signals or distort them?

items.t: Full-cost accounting
Pollution fees that internalize costs
Removing perverse subsidies
Antitrust laws
Subsidies that hide true costs
Misleading advertising

questions.explain: Her list of remedies clarifies signals; subsidies and deceptive ads twist them.
questions.rule: Leave signals undistorted.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: A government subsidizes a fuel so its price hides real cost. Which effect does the author's logic predict?
options: Markets work better, because the price is lower
The price signal weakens and consumers misjudge cost
Prices become more truthful, because the state sets them
Supply falls at once, because costs are hidden
optionExplain: A lower subsidized price weakens the market signal rather than helping the market work.
Right: the signal weakens and buyers misjudge the true cost.
Subsidies hide the full cost, so the price becomes less truthful, not more.
Her logic is about misled consumers, not an immediate fall in supply.
questions.explain: A subsidy twists the price signal, so the market's feedback weakens and consumers misjudge what the fuel really costs.
questions.rule: Protect the accuracy of the signals a balancing loop runs on.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: Which measure strengthens a market's price signal rather than distorting it?
options: Ads that overstate a product's quality
Mergers that remove all competitors
A tax break that hides a fuel's real cost
Fees that make polluters pay for their damage
optionExplain: Plausible as marketing, but truth-in-advertising rules exist to stop it.
Plausible as efficiency, but antitrust law exists to prevent it.
Plausible as help to consumers, but it hides cost information.
Right: Truthful prices are the leverage.
questions.explain: Pollution fees internalize costs, so the price tells the truth; she lists them among ways of leveling market playing fields.
questions.rule: Protect the accuracy of the signals a balancing loop runs on.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: True or false: If a price is kept clear, unambiguous, timely and truthful, the author expects markets to operate more smoothly.
questions.explain: She says the clearer and truer the price, the more smoothly markets run.
questions.rule: Clean signals, smooth markets.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: A review site is paid by the products it rates. Using the author's logic, what is at risk?
options: The feedback buyers use to punish poor products
Nothing, since reviews are only opinions
Buyers' wealth only, not their information
Sellers' costs only, not buyers' choices
optionExplain: Right: Corrupted feedback weakens correction.
Paid reviews corrupt the feedback buyers rely on; she says distorted signals weaken the loop that corrects poor products.
Information is exactly what is at risk, not only buyers' wealth.
The risk is to buyers' choices, which depend on the feedback, not only to sellers' costs.
questions.explain: Paid ratings corrupt the feedback buyers use to reward good products and punish poor ones, much like distorted price information.
questions.teaches: The author says companies and governments are fatally attracted to the price leverage point but too often push it in the wrong direction with subsidies, taxes and other forms of confusion.
questions.rule: Protect the accuracy of the signals a balancing loop runs on.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: What keeps voting from correcting a government?
options: Too many elections, which tire voters out
Leaders being too honest about their plans
Voters lacking free, unbiased information on leaders
Voters caring too much about politics
optionExplain: Frequent elections are not her concern; the issue is the flow of information.
Honest leaders would help; her problem is that information is limited and biased.
Right: she says the process depends on the free, full, unbiased flow of information between electorate and leaders.
Caring is not the barrier; the process depends on free, full, unbiased information.
questions.explain: She says the process depends on the free, full, unbiased flow of information between electorate and leaders.
questions.rule: Guard the flow of unbiased information that lets voters correct their government.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: Democracy was invented to put self-correcting ____ between the people and their government.
questions.explain: The author calls it a balancing loop built on feedback.
questions.rule: Democracy is a feedback loop.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: A town's only newspaper is owned by its biggest developer. Which loop is weakened?
options: The thermostat loop in the town hall
The market's price signal only
The voters' feedback to officials
The fishing quota in the harbor
optionExplain: The thermostat is her heating example, unrelated to what a captured newspaper does to voters.
The price signal belongs to the market loop; a captured newspaper bears on what voters learn.
Right: voters' feedback to officials runs on information (Our reading).
A fishing quota is a different loop; the newspaper case concerns voters' information.
questions.explain: A biased newspaper limits the information voters get about officials, which weakens the voters' feedback to them (Our reading).
questions.rule: Guard the flow of unbiased information that lets voters correct their government.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: True or false: The author says democracy erodes when information between electorate and leaders is limited and biased.
questions.explain: That is her condition: the loop needs a free, full, unbiased flow of information, and billions are spent to bias it.
questions.rule: Information quality sustains the loop.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: What if the people who distort price signals gain influence over government leaders?
options: Both market and democracy erode
Markets improve while democracy erodes
Democracy improves while markets erode
Nothing changes in either
optionExplain: Right: the author says both market and democracy erode.
Markets do not improve; she says both market and democracy erode.
Democracy does not improve; she says both erode together.
Something does change: she says neither of the necessary balancing feedbacks works well.
questions.explain: She says that when distorters influence leaders and information is controlled, none of the necessary balancing feedbacks work well.
questions.rule: Guard the flow of unbiased information that lets voters correct their government.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: A club's members vote on the budget but cannot see the accounts. Which prediction fits?
options: The accounts are irrelevant to voting
Members will vote less often
Their voting is a perfect correction anyway
Voting corrects weakly without the information
optionExplain: The accounts are the information voters need; without them votes cannot correct (Our reading).
How often members vote is not the point; the quality of their information is (Our reading).
Voting corrects only when voters are informed; it is not perfect without information.
Right: No information, no correction.
questions.explain: Without the accounts, the members' vote carries no information about results, so its corrective power is weak (Our reading).
questions.teaches: The author says that democracy works better without the brainwashing power of centralized mass communications.
questions.rule: Guard the flow of unbiased information that lets voters correct their government.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: Fishing rules that worked for centuries start failing after sonar appears. What is the likely reason?
options: Fish stopped breeding during the last hundred years
The impact grew while the control stayed the same
Rules never work in the long run
Sonar slows fishing boats down
optionExplain: Her account is about sonar and drift nets, not fish ceasing to breed.
Right: controls were enough until sonar and drift nets let a few actors catch the last fish.
Rules worked for a long time; they failed when technology let a few actors catch the last fish.
Sonar helps spot fish; it does not slow boats.
questions.explain: Controls were enough until sonar and drift nets let a few actors catch the last fish; the impact grew while the control stayed.
questions.rule: Scale the corrective loop to the size of the impact it must correct.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: The strength of a balancing loop is important relative to the ____ it is designed to correct.
questions.explain: If the impact increases, the feedbacks must be strengthened too.
questions.rule: Match the loop to the impact.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: A city's flood defences were built for rainfall that has now doubled. What does the idea call for?
options: Remove the defences to save money
Strengthen the loop to match the larger impact
Do nothing, since defences exist
Wait to see whether rain returns to normal
optionExplain: Removing defences leaves the larger impact uncorrected.
Right: she says that if the impact increases in strength, the feedbacks have to be strengthened too.
Existing defences built for the old rainfall are too weak for double (Our reading).
Waiting is a gamble; when the impact increases, she says the feedbacks have to be strengthened too.
questions.explain: She says that if the impact increases in strength, the feedbacks have to be strengthened too; defences must match the larger load.
questions.rule: Scale the corrective loop to the size of the impact it must correct.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: Sort each item: a way of strengthening balancing loops, or not?

items.t: Preventive medicine
Whistleblower protection
Pollution taxes
Environmental monitoring
Removing the monitoring
Hiding data from the public

questions.explain: The first four add or sharpen corrective feedback; the last two weaken it.
questions.rule: Strengthen the monitoring and response.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: What if the impact on a loop grows but the loop's strength stays the same?
options: Nothing happens to the stock
It strengthens itself in proportion
It works as before, since the loop itself stays unchanged
It loses the ability to keep the stock near its goal
optionExplain: The stock still moves; the loop just cannot keep it near its goal.
Loops do not strengthen themselves in proportion to the impact.
The same strength is weaker relative to a bigger impact, so it does not work as before.
Right: Corrective power must keep pace.
questions.explain: A loop of fixed strength cannot correct a bigger impact; her thermostat with the windows open is no match for the temperature change.
questions.rule: Scale the corrective loop to the size of the impact it must correct.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 8. Balancing Feedback Loops—The strength of the feedbacks relative to the impacts they are trying to correct
questions.q: A software team's incident process is the same as when it had 10 users; it now has 10 million. What does the idea suggest?
options: The corrective loop must grow with the impact
Keep it exactly as it is
Remove it to save time
Hire no new staff until problems appear later on
optionExplain: Right: Loops scale with the impact.
A process built for 10 users is too weak for 10 million (Our reading).
Removing it leaves the larger impact with no corrective loop at all.
