Waiting for problems leaves the loop too weak; the impact has already grown.
questions.explain: As with her fishing and thermostat cases, the corrective loop must grow with the impact it corrects (Our reading for the software case).
questions.teaches: The author says traditional fishing controls were sufficient until sonar, drift nets and other technologies let a few actors catch the last fish.
questions.rule: Scale the corrective loop to the size of the impact it must correct.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: Which statement best describes a reinforcing feedback loop?
options: It keeps a stock near its goal by cancelling out any deviation
It delays a response until information is certain
The more it works, the more power it gains to work some more
It stops flows when a stock reaches its limit
optionExplain: That describes a balancing loop, which cancels deviation.
Waiting for certainty is not what a loop is; a reinforcing loop amplifies itself.
Right: A reinforcing loop is self-reinforcing: the more it works, the more power it gains to work some more.
Stopping flows at a limit is balancing behavior, not reinforcing.
questions.explain: A reinforcing loop is self-reinforcing: the more it works, the more power it gains to work some more.
questions.rule: Find where more of something produces the capacity for still more.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: Sort each case: reinforcing loop or balancing loop?

items.t: More infected people lead to more infections
More money earns more interest
Soil erodes and then supports less vegetation, so erodes more
A thermostat holds a room near its setting
Fever-fighting sweat keeps body heat steady
A store reorders to keep stock at target

questions.explain: Reinforcing loops amplify; balancing loops hold near a goal.
questions.rule: Amplify versus stabilize.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: Sort each case by the kind of feedback loop that drives it.
questions.explain: Reinforcing loops feed on themselves (flu, erosion, and our popularity case); balancing loops pull a stock back toward a goal (thermostat, sweating, prices). The video case is Our reading.
questions.rule: Find where more of something produces the capacity for still more.

items.t: A video is recommended more because it is popular
Flu spreads as more people catch it
Soil erodes, leaving fewer roots, so more soil erodes
A thermostat turns on the furnace when the room is cold
A body sweats or shivers to hold its temperature
A price rises when supply runs short, which cuts demand

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: True or false: A system with an unchecked reinforcing loop will stay stable forever.
questions.explain: The author says it ultimately destroys itself.
questions.rule: Unchecked reinforcing loops end in explosion or collapse.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: What if an epidemic's reinforcing loop runs its course with no intervention?
options: It runs out of infectible people
It lasts forever without limit
It reverses at once without any cause
It stops for no reason at all
optionExplain: Right: the epidemic runs out of infectible people.
She says an unchecked reinforcing loop ultimately destroys itself, so it does not last forever.
It cannot reverse with no cause; the epidemic runs out of infectible people.
It stops for a reason: it runs out of infectible people.
questions.explain: Loops end by exhaustion or intervention.
questions.rule: Find where more of something produces the capacity for still more.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: Nuclear critical mass is a reinforcing loop. What does the author say about the neutrons?
options: The neutrons only decay and add no further neutrons
The neutrons slow the loop down as they multiply
The neutrons balance themselves at a safe stable level
More neutrons make still more, ending in explosion
optionExplain: Neutrons knock into nuclei and generate more neutrons, so they add further neutrons.
They speed up, not slow down: more neutrons knock out still more.
A reinforcing loop does not settle at a safe level; it ends in explosion or meltdown.
Right: A reinforcing loop in physics.
questions.explain: She gives critical mass as a reinforcing loop: more high-energy neutrons generate more, leading to explosion or meltdown.
questions.teaches: The author gives the nuclear case: more high-energy neutrons in a critical mass produce more of them, leading to a nuclear explosion or meltdown.
questions.rule: Find where more of something produces the capacity for still more.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: A runaway cost spiral threatens a project. Which approach does the author favor?
options: Add more brakes to the spiral later, once it is under way
Reduce the spiral's growth rate
Let it run its course, since loops end on their own
Speed up spending to finish sooner
optionExplain: Late brakes are the weaker option; she calls reducing the gain more powerful than strengthening balancing loops.
Right: she calls reducing the gain around a reinforcing loop usually a more powerful lever than strengthening balancing loops.
She calls reducing the gain far more preferable than letting the reinforcing loop run.
Speeding up spending would feed the spiral instead of slowing it.
questions.explain: She calls reducing the gain around a reinforcing loop usually a more powerful lever than strengthening balancing loops.
questions.rule: Weaken the driving loop instead of piling brakes on top of it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: Reducing the ____ around a reinforcing loop is usually a powerful leverage point.
questions.explain: Gain is the strength of a driving loop; reducing it slows the growth, which she calls usually a powerful leverage point.
questions.rule: Reduce the gain.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: A town's population is growing fast and services lag. Which move reflects the author's priority?
options: Building services faster only, without touching growth
Slowing the growth rate to give services time
Doing nothing and waiting for balance
Raising prices on newcomers
optionExplain: Faster services alone leave the growth loop untouched; she favors slowing growth.
Right: slowing growth gives services time (Our reading).
Waiting lets the reinforcing loop run, which she calls far less preferable than intervening.
Raising prices on newcomers is not among her remedies (Our reading).
questions.explain: Slowing the growth rate lets services catch up, as slowing the car beats calling for better brakes (Our reading for the town).
questions.rule: Weaken the driving loop instead of piling brakes on top of it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: Which pair correctly ranks the two interventions per the author?
options: Neither matters on her list
The two are equal in leverage
Strengthening a balancing loop is the stronger lever than reducing the gain
Reducing reinforcing-loop gain beats strengthening a balancing loop
optionExplain: Both are on her list: reinforcing-loop gain is number 7 and balancing loops number 8.
They are unequal: number 7 sits above number 8.
Reversed: she says reducing the gain is usually a more powerful leverage point.
Right: Number 7 beats 8 in leverage.
questions.explain: Reinforcing-loop gain is number 7 and balancing-loop strength number 8, so reducing gain is usually the stronger lever.
questions.rule: Weaken the driving loop instead of piling brakes on top of it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: True or false: Slowing the car when driving too fast is the author's analogy for reducing reinforcing-loop gain.
questions.explain: She contrasts it with calling for brakes or steering advances.
questions.rule: Slow the car.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: Why does the author say slowing growth in the World model gives balancing loops time?
options: Technology and markets have limits and delays
Technology is useless, so time is wasted
Markets cannot adapt at all
Slow growth is free, so it costs nothing
optionExplain: Right: Balancing loops need time.
She does not call technology useless; technology and markets are balancing loops that need time.
Markets can adapt, but she says with limits and delays, which is why time matters.
She does not say slow growth is free; her point is that it gives balancing loops time.
questions.explain: Slowing growth gives the balancing loops, through technology and markets, time to work; she adds they have limits and delays.
questions.teaches: The author says technology and markets are among the many balancing loops in the World model, all with limits and delays.
questions.rule: Weaken the driving loop instead of piling brakes on top of it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: A rich-get-richer pattern persists despite aid programs. Where does the author say effort is better placed?
options: Give more aid, the main answer
Raise interest rates for everyone
Weaken the reinforcing loops that favor winners
Ignore it, since the pattern corrects itself over time
optionExplain: She calls antipoverty programs weak balancing loops set against strong reinforcing ones.
Higher interest rates do not touch the winners' edge; rich people collect interest and poor people pay it.
Right: she says it would be much more effective to weaken the reinforcing loops than to rely on weak balancing aid programs.
She does not say it corrects itself; the wealthy can even weaken the measures that would.
questions.explain: She says it would be much more effective to weaken the reinforcing loops than to rely on weak balancing aid programs.
questions.rule: Weaken the loop that feeds winners instead of patching its effects.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: Sort each measure: weakens the reinforcing loop, or only patches its effects?

items.t: Progressive income tax
Inheritance tax
Universal high-quality public education
A small one-off antipoverty payment
A food bank
A donation drive

questions.explain: The first three act on the loop; the others counter its results.
questions.rule: Weaken the loop.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: A platform's top sellers get featured, so they sell more. Which fix targets the loop?
options: Add a help page for new sellers
Praise small sellers in the newsletter
Cap how far feature placement grows with past sales
Raise fees uniformly for all sellers on the platform
optionExplain: A help page leaves the loop in place; featuring still feeds the top sellers (Our reading).
Praise leaves the placement loop untouched (Our reading).
Right: capping how far placement grows with past sales weakens the loop itself rather than patching its effects (Our reading).
A uniform fee rise leaves the winners' advantage intact (Our reading).
questions.explain: Capping how far placement grows with past sales weakens the loop itself rather than patching its effects (Our reading).
questions.rule: Weaken the loop that feeds winners instead of patching its effects.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: True or false: The author says antipoverty programs are strong balancing loops that easily outweigh the advantages of the rich.
questions.explain: She calls them weak balancing loops against strong reinforcing ones.
questions.rule: Weak patch, strong loop.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: If the wealthy influence government to weaken progressive taxes, what does the author say happens to government?
options: It becomes a structure that reinforces the winners
It becomes more balanced and fairer to everyone in the system
It shrinks in size and power
It keeps working exactly as before
optionExplain: Right: Government can join the loop.
It would be less balanced: she says government shifts from a balancing to a reinforcing structure.
Size and power are not her point; the structure shifts from balancing to reinforcing.
It does change: it joins the loop and reinforces success to the successful.
questions.explain: She says that if the wealthy influence government to weaken such measures, government itself shifts to reinforce success to the successful.
questions.rule: Weaken the loop that feeds winners instead of patching its effects.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 7. Reinforcing Feedback Loops—The strength of the gain of driving loops
questions.q: Which everyday case matches the success-to-the-successful pattern?
options: A savings fund that smooths out irregular income
A delay between ordering stock and its delivery
A thermostat holding a room near its set temperature
High scores bring funding, which raises scores further
optionExplain: A savings fund is a buffer that smooths income, not a loop that favors winners.
A delay between order and delivery is a delay, not a self-feeding loop.
A thermostat is a balancing loop, the opposite of winners getting more.
Right: Winners get the means to win more.
questions.explain: Winners get the means to win more, as with funding that raises scores; this is the pattern, shown in a new setting (Our reading).
questions.teaches: The author warns that the new world trade system, with rules written by corporations, is a recipe for unleashing success-to-the-successful loops until they produce huge accumulations of power and centralized planning systems that destroy themselves.
questions.rule: Weaken the loop that feeds winners instead of patching its effects.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: Two identical houses differ only in where the electricity meter is. What would you expect?
options: More use where the meter is in the visible front hall
Less use where the meter is in the front hall
Identical use in both houses
No relation between meter and use
optionExplain: The visible meter went with lower use, 30 percent lower in the front hall, not higher.
Right: in the Dutch housing case, consumption was 30 percent lower where the meter was in the highly visible front hall.
Use was not identical: it was 30 percent lower where the meter was in the front hall.
The only difference was the meter's location, and use differed, so there was a relation.
questions.explain: In the Dutch housing case, consumption was 30 percent lower where the meter was in the highly visible front hall.
questions.rule: Where behavior goes uncorrected, check whether the feedback is missing and add it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: In the Dutch housing study, electricity use was ____ percent lower with the meter in the front hall.
questions.explain: The visible meter cut use by 30 percent.
questions.rule: Visible feedback changes behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: A small office wants lower printing costs. Which change fits the author's leverage point?
options: Buy bigger printers to print faster
Show each team its printing totals weekly
Cut printing budgets by a fixed share
Ban color printing across the office
optionExplain: Bigger printers add speed, not feedback to the people who decide what to print.
Right: showing teams their totals adds feedback to a place it did not go before, as the meter story did (Our reading for the office).
A fixed budget cut is a number change, the weakest kind of lever.
A ban is a rule, not a new flow of information (Our reading).
questions.explain: Showing teams their totals adds feedback to a place it did not go before, as the meter story did (Our reading for the office).
questions.rule: Where behavior goes uncorrected, check whether the feedback is missing and add it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: The meter story is an example of which intervention?
options: A bigger buffer
A parameter change
A strengthened existing loop
A new feedback loop
optionExplain: A buffer is a stabilizing stock, not a flow of information.
She says the story is not a parameter adjustment.
She says it is not a strengthening of an existing loop; it is a new one.
Right: the author says it is not a parameter change or strengthening.
questions.explain: She calls the meter story a new loop, delivering feedback to a place where it wasn't going before.
questions.rule: Where behavior goes uncorrected, check whether the feedback is missing and add it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: True or false: The author describes the visible-meter effect as a parameter adjustment to an existing loop.
questions.explain: She says it is not a parameter adjustment or a strengthening of an existing loop but a new loop.
questions.rule: A new loop is not a tweak.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: A city compares two ways to cut water waste: rebuilding its pipes or giving households live usage readings. What does the author expect about cost?
options: Information is usually much cheaper than rebuilding
Rebuilding the pipes is cheaper than giving information
The two options cost about the same
Delivering information is impossible at any price
optionExplain: Right: Information is a cheap lever.
She says information is usually much easier and cheaper than rebuilding infrastructure.
She does not call them equal; she calls adding information usually much cheaper.
Delivering information is possible, and she says usually easier and cheaper than rebuilding.
questions.explain: She says adding or restoring information is usually much easier and cheaper than rebuilding physical infrastructure.
questions.teaches: Adding or restoring information is usually a much easier and cheaper intervention than rebuilding physical infrastructure.
questions.rule: Where behavior goes uncorrected, check whether the feedback is missing and add it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: Aquifer users learn the water table is falling. What might happen?
options: Instant recovery of the water table
Calm restraint among all users
A race to the bottom
No change in pumping
optionExplain: She warns the news of a falling water table could start a race to the bottom, not recovery.
Restraint is the hope, but she warns that the news may instead start a race to the bottom.
Right: the author warns of a race to the bottom.
She expects a reaction, a race to the bottom, not no change.
questions.explain: She warns that telling users the groundwater level is dropping could initiate a race to the bottom.
questions.rule: Deliver the right signal to the decision-maker, in a form that forces a response.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: In the author's fisheries example, it is not price information but ____ information that is needed.
questions.explain: Rising price makes catching the last fish more profitable.
questions.rule: Use the right signal.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: A city wants less driving. Which signal fits the author's idea better?
options: A sign saying drive less
A leaflet saying roads are busy
Charges that rise steeply with congestion
A long study report on congestion in the city
optionExplain: A sign tells people to cut driving but gives no compelling signal; she wants feedback in compelling form.
A leaflet about busy roads is information without force (Our reading).
Right: Make feedback compelling.
A report is information in a weak form; she prefers a cost that rises steeply (Our reading).
questions.explain: Like her water-cost example, a charge that rises steeply with the problem is compelling feedback (Our reading for traffic).
questions.rule: Deliver the right signal to the decision-maker, in a form that forces a response.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: A plan says: tell fishers the fish population is falling and the problem will solve itself. What is wrong?
options: Information alone may spark a race; it must compel
Nothing is wrong; information always changes behavior
Population information is useless to fishers
Fishers do not care about the fish stock
optionExplain: Right: information alone can set off a race.
Information does not always change behavior; she warns that aquifer news could start a race to the bottom.
She says population information, not price, is what the fisheries need, so it is not useless.
Fishers' interest is not her point; she says population information is what is needed, in compelling form.
questions.explain: Information alone can set off a race; she wants the feedback in the right place and in compelling form.
questions.rule: Deliver the right signal to the decision-maker, in a form that forces a response.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: True or false: If the price of fish rises as the fish get scarce, catching the last fish becomes less profitable.
questions.explain: The author says it becomes more profitable, producing a reinforcing loop to collapse.
questions.rule: Price is perverse feedback here.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: Which proposal is closest to the author's thought experiments?
options: Mayors hold shorter meetings to save public money
Leaders who sign treaties get a pay increase for each one
Taxpayers are asked to donate to the national debt
Whoever approves a nuclear plant stores its waste at home
optionExplain: Shorter meetings are not among her thought experiments; hers link a decision to its consequence.
Not hers: it rewards rather than links decision and consequence.
Donating to the debt is not hers; her proposals link decisions to consequences.
Right: Tie decisions to consequences.
questions.explain: She suggests that anyone deciding on a nuclear plant would get its waste stored on his or her lawn, linking decision and consequence.
questions.teaches: The author suggests that any town or company putting a water intake in a river should have to place it immediately downstream of its own wastewater outflow.
questions.rule: Deliver the right signal to the decision-maker, in a form that forces a response.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: Why might a proposal to expose officials to the results of their decisions be unpopular with them?
options: It costs too much to carry out
It removes protection from consequences
It is too complex to understand
Nobody wants it, including the public and the press
optionExplain: Cost is not her explanation; she says people avoid accountability for their own decisions.
Right: she says people tend to avoid accountability for their own decisions, so restoring feedback is unpopular with the powers that be.
Complexity is not her point; she says this kind of leverage is unpopular with the powers that be.
She says the masses like such leverage; it is the powers that be who dislike it.
questions.explain: She says people tend to avoid accountability for their own decisions, so restoring feedback is unpopular with the powers that be.
questions.rule: Expect resistance from those who benefit from missing feedback, and plan to work around it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: According to the author, human beings tend systematically to avoid ____ for their own decisions.
questions.explain: That systematic tendency explains why so many feedback loops are missing in the first place.
questions.rule: Missing loops reflect avoided accountability.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: True or false: A company where bonuses are decided without the deciders ever seeing customer complaints is missing a feedback loop (Our reading).
questions.explain: The decision-makers do not feel the consequences of their decisions.
questions.rule: Expect resistance from those who benefit from missing feedback, and plan to work around it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: Who is likely to welcome a proposal to restore missing feedback, per the author?
options: The powers that be
The masses
Both equally
Neither group
optionExplain: She says it is unpopular with the powers that be.
Right: Popular below, unpopular above.
Not equally: she says popular with the masses, unpopular with the powers that be.
She says the masses find this kind of leverage popular.
questions.explain: She says this kind of leverage is popular with the masses and unpopular with the powers that be.
questions.rule: Expect resistance from those who benefit from missing feedback, and plan to work around it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: True or false: If the powers that be refuse a feedback proposal, the author says it cannot be made to happen.
questions.explain: She says you can go around them and make it happen anyway.
questions.rule: Work around resistance.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 6. Information Flows—The structure of who does and does not have access to information
questions.q: Which proposal from the author asks politicians who declare war to share its risk?
options: Shorten their speeches before a declaration
Raise their pay when a war is declared
Give them medals for declaring war
Require them to spend the war on the front lines
optionExplain: Shorter speeches would not put them at risk; her proposal puts them at the front lines.
A pay rise would reward the decision, not tie it to its consequences.
Medals would reward the declaration; her point is to share its risk.
Right: Tie choices to consequences.
questions.explain: She suggests that politicians who declare war should spend that war on the front lines, tying decision to consequence.
questions.teaches: The author suggests, in an old idea, that politicians who declare war should be required to spend that war on the front lines, and that taxpayers might specify which government services their taxes fund.
questions.rule: Expect resistance from those who benefit from missing feedback, and plan to work around it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: The rules of a system define its ____, its boundaries and its degrees of freedom.
questions.explain: Rules mark out what the system can and cannot do.
questions.rule: To see why a system behaves as it does, start from its rules.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Order these rule types from the strongest to the weakest per the author.
items: Constitutions
Laws
Punishments and incentives
Informal social agreements
questions.explain: She says constitutions are the strongest social rules; physical laws are absolute; laws, punishments, incentives and informal agreements are progressively weaker.
questions.rule: Rules vary in strength.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: The author expects that grading a class as a group, instead of as individuals, would change student behavior.
questions.explain: Imagining different rules, such as group grades, is her way of showing how much rules shape behavior.
questions.rule: To see why a system behaves as it does, start from its rules.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: The author calls physical laws such as the second law of thermodynamics absolute rules, whether we like them or not.
questions.explain: She includes them in the ranking of rules.
questions.rule: Physical laws are absolute.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: Changing information flows and economic rules, as Gorbachev did, was followed by tremendous change in the Soviet Union.
questions.explain: The author uses it as a case of changing high-leverage points.
questions.rule: To see why a system behaves as it does, start from its rules.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Gorbachev opened information flows, called glasnost, and changed the economic rules, called ____.
questions.explain: She says Gorbachev opened information flows, called glasnost, and changed the economic rules, perestroika, and the Soviet Union changed.
questions.teaches: The author notes that the Supreme Court, which interprets the Constitution, the rules for writing the rules, has even more power than Congress.
questions.rule: To see why a system behaves as it does, start from its rules.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Why do lobbyists crowd around when a legislature writes a law?
options: Whoever shapes the rules shapes how the system behaves
Laws are cheap to write, so lobbyists stock up
Lobbyists enjoy meetings and travel to the capital
Rules rarely matter, but lobbyists act on habit
optionExplain: Right: she says power over the rules is real power, which is why lobbyists congregate when Congress writes laws.
Cheap writing is not her reason; she says rules are high leverage points.
Travel and meetings are not her explanation; power over the rules is real power.
She says rules matter a great deal: power over the rules is real power, so lobbyists act on purpose, not habit.
questions.explain: She says power over the rules is real power, which is why lobbyists congregate when Congress writes laws.
questions.rule: Ask who writes the rules and what feedback reaches them.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Power over the ____ is real power, says the author.
questions.explain: Rules are number 5 on her list, a high leverage point: whoever writes them shapes how the system behaves.
questions.rule: Rules are power.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: A club's committee writes all rules, meets in private, and takes no feedback from members. Which author's warning applies?
options: Members do not matter to how rules work
Closed meetings are efficient and keep rules safe
Closed rule-making cuts off feedback, concentrating power
Rules do not shape behavior in a club
optionExplain: Members do matter: she wants feedback to reach those who write rules.
Her warning is that closed meetings cut off feedback, as at the world trade talks.
Right: Watch who controls the rules.
She says rules define a system's scope, boundaries and degrees of freedom, so they shape behavior in a club too (Our reading).
questions.explain: She warns of rules written by insiders in closed meetings with no feedback, as in the world trade system (Our reading for the club).
questions.rule: Ask who writes the rules and what feedback reaches them.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Which has more power, per the author?
options: The lobbyists who gather when laws are written
Congress, which writes the laws day to day
The Supreme Court, which interprets the rules for rules
The voters who elect the legislature
optionExplain: Lobbyists seek influence over rules; the comparison she makes is between the Court and Congress, not with lobbyists.
Less, per the author: Congress writes within the Constitution.
Right: Higher-order rules outrank.
She names the Supreme Court as having even more power than Congress; voters are not in that ranking.
questions.explain: She says the Supreme Court, which interprets the Constitution, the rules for writing the rules, has even more power than Congress.
questions.rule: Ask who writes the rules and what feedback reaches them.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: If rule-making excludes feedback from most of society, the author expects the system to stay self-correcting.
questions.explain: She expects racing-to-the-bottom loops and eventual self-destruction.
questions.rule: Cut feedback means no correction.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: The author says the new world trade system forces nations into a race to the bottom on environmental and social safeguards.
questions.explain: She describes reinforcing loops of nations weakening safeguards to attract corporate investment.
questions.teaches: The author says the trade system forces nations into reinforcing loops of racing to the bottom, competing to weaken environmental and social safeguards to attract corporate investment.
questions.rule: Ask who writes the rules and what feedback reaches them.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: Which best describes a system's self-organization?
options: The ability to create new structure and behavior
A bigger buffer that steadies the system's stocks
A system that obeys fixed orders from outside
A thermostat that keeps a room warm
optionExplain: Right: self-organization is the power to add, change or evolve system structure, creating whole new structures and behaviors.
A bigger buffer is the stabilizing stock of point 11, not self-organization.
The opposite: self-organization is a system changing itself, not obeying outside orders.
A thermostat is a balancing loop, not a structure-creating process.
questions.explain: Self-organization is the power to add, change or evolve system structure, creating whole new structures and behaviors.
questions.rule: A system that can restructure itself can survive changes that would break a fixed one.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: In biological systems the power of self-organization is called ____.
questions.explain: In economies it is technical advance or social revolution.
questions.rule: Evolution is self-organization.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: True or false: A company that keeps inventing new products, teams and rules as markets shift is showing self-organization (Our reading).
questions.explain: Adding new structures and rules is what the author means by self-organization.
questions.rule: A system that can restructure itself can survive changes that would break a fixed one.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: Sort each: self-organization, or not?

items.t: Immune system develops a new response
Brain produces a new thought
An economy invents a new technology
Raising a tax rate
Enlarging a reservoir
Moving a meter to the hall

questions.explain: Creating new structure or behavior is self-organization; adjustments within given structure are not.
questions.rule: Evolve vs adjust.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, a system that can evolve can survive almost any change by changing itself.
questions.explain: This is why she calls self-organization the strongest form of resilience.
questions.rule: A system that can restructure itself can survive changes that would break a fixed one.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: How do economists often treat technology, per the author?
options: As a physical stock like a dam or a pipe network
As a costly and slow process that must be funded year by year
As an irrelevant factor that models can safely leave out
As costless magic that adds steady gains
optionExplain: She says economists model technology as magic, coming from nowhere, not as a physical stock like a dam.
She says economists treat technology as costing nothing, not as a costly process funded year by year.
She does not say economists leave it out; she says they model it as magic.
Right: Technology is evolved, not magic.
questions.explain: She says economists often model technology as magic that comes from nowhere and costs nothing; in fact it evolves.
questions.teaches: The author says economists often model technology as magic, coming from nowhere, costing nothing and increasing productivity by some steady percent each year.
questions.rule: A system that can restructure itself can survive changes that would break a fixed one.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: Which two things does an evolving system need?
options: One fixed plan, issued from the center, that everyone obeys exactly
A variable stock of raw material and a way to test new patterns
Large buffers that make the system stable and unchanging
Closed rules and tight control from the center
optionExplain: She says self-organization needs variety and experimentation, not one fixed plan imposed from the center.
Right: self-organization needs an evolutionary raw material, a variable stock of information, and a means of experimenting and selecting.
Large unchanging buffers belong to point 11, not to the raw material and testing evolution needs.
Tight control from the center shuts down evolution; she says the pull toward control destroys diversity.
questions.explain: Self-organization needs an evolutionary raw material, a variable stock of information, and a means of experimenting and selecting.
questions.rule: Keep the raw material of variety and the means of testing it alive.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: Match each part of biological evolution to its role.
questions.explain: The author names these three for evolution.
questions.rule: Raw material, variety, testing.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: In technology, what plays the role of DNA?
options: The prices that the market sets for new products
The body of understanding science has accumulated
The funding that governments give to researchers
The patents that firms file on new devices
optionExplain: Prices act as a selection signal, not the raw material.
Right: Raw material for technology.
Funding is part of the selection mechanism, not the raw material.
Patents are products of the process, not the starting stock.
questions.explain: For technology, she says the raw material is the body of understanding science has accumulated, held in libraries and in people.
questions.rule: Keep the raw material of variety and the means of testing it alive.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: True or false: The author says self-organization requires wildly complicated rules.
questions.explain: She says complex patterns can evolve from quite simple sets of rules.
questions.rule: Simple rules can yield rich patterns.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: What if the testing mechanism disappears (for example nothing is ever tried or selected)?
options: The system gains variety because nothing is eliminated
The system evolves faster because choices are less constrained
Nothing changes since the raw material is still there
The system loses its means of evolving (Our reading)
optionExplain: No testing means nothing is selected, so variety does not turn into adaptation (Our reading).
Without a testing mechanism there is nothing to select with, so evolution slows or stops (Our reading).
Contrary: raw material without testing does not yield adaptation.
Right: Both raw material and testing are needed.
questions.explain: Both raw material and testing are needed.
questions.rule: Keep the raw material of variety and the means of testing it alive.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: The genetic code, with four letters in three-letter words, has been constant for about three ____ years.
questions.explain: Simple, long-lived rules have produced an unimaginable variety of creatures.
questions.teaches: The genetic code contains just four different letters combined into words of three letters, constant for something like three billion years.
questions.rule: Keep the raw material of variety and the means of testing it alive.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: Why would a biologist worship biodiversity?
options: It is the raw material of future evolution
It is the easiest part of nature to measure
It looks pleasant in a landscape
It is cheaper than other resources
optionExplain: Right: diversity, such as the varied stock of DNA, is the source of evolutionary potential, which is why biologists worship it.
Ease of measurement is not her reason; diversity is the raw material of evolutionary potential.
A pleasant look is not her reason; diversity is evolutionary potential.
Cost is not her reason; diversity is the stock evolution draws on.
questions.explain: Diversity, such as the varied stock of DNA, is the source of evolutionary potential, which is why biologists worship it.
questions.rule: Encourage variability, experimentation and diversity, even though it means losing control.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: The author calls allowing species to go extinct a systems ____.
questions.explain: Diversity is the stock of evolutionary raw material.
questions.rule: Extinction destroys potential.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: A company fires everyone who disagrees and enforces one way of working. Which warning applies?
options: The firm gains variety because the survivors are stronger
The firm gains lasting efficiency from having one common method
A single approach shuts down learning and resilience
The firm is unaffected since methods do not shape adaptability
optionExplain: Firing dissenters removes variety rather than adding it; variety is the raw material for adapting.
She says a system that cannot self-evolve, scorning experimentation, is doomed over the long term.
Right: she says insisting on a single culture shuts down learning and cuts back resilience, and the same logic holds in a firm (Our reading).
Methods do shape adaptability: the variety of approaches is the raw material from which a firm learns.
questions.explain: She says insisting on a single culture shuts down learning and cuts back resilience, and the same logic holds in a firm (Our reading).
questions.rule: Encourage variability, experimentation and diversity, even though it means losing control.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: A leader says: let us play safe and wipe out diversity. What does the author say about this?
options: It leaves the lever where it was
It pulls the lever in the right direction
It pushes the lever in the wrong direction
It is the cheapest and surest way to move it
optionExplain: She says wiping out diversity moves the lever, and in the wrong direction.
She says that pushing for control pulls the lever the wrong way, not the right way.
Right: she says wiping out diversity for the sake of control pushes this lever in the wrong direction.
She does not call it cheap; she calls it a mistake that cuts resilience.
questions.explain: She says wiping out diversity for the sake of control pushes this lever in the wrong direction.
questions.rule: Encourage variability, experimentation and diversity, even though it means losing control.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: True or false: A system that scorns experimentation and wipes out the raw material of innovation is doomed in the long term.
questions.explain: She says such a system, when encrusted, is doomed on a variable planet.
questions.rule: Stagnation is fatal.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 4. Self-Organization—The power to add, change, or evolve system structure
questions.q: Why do people undervalue cultural diversity, in the author's view?
options: Almost every culture believes in its own utter superiority
Cultures are almost identical, so none can be lost
Diversity is too costly to maintain in practice
Diversity is invisible and cannot be seen or measured
optionExplain: Right: Culture hides its own value.
Cultures are not nearly identical; they are a store of behavioral repertoires built over hundreds of thousands of years.
Cost is not her explanation; the belief in cultural superiority is.
She does not say diversity is invisible; she says people fail to value it.
questions.explain: She says one aspect of almost every culture is the belief in its own utter superiority, which hides the value of other cultures.
questions.teaches: The author says people appreciate the evolutionary potential of cultures even less than genetic variation, because almost every culture believes in its own utter superiority.
questions.rule: Encourage variability, experimentation and diversity, even though it means losing control.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: If an organization's goal is total control, what happens to its structures and rules?
options: They vanish
They resist it and keep their old form
They stay neutral and unaffected by it
They bend to serve that goal
optionExplain: Structures and rules do not vanish; she says everything lower on the list is twisted to conform.
They do not resist; she says they are twisted to conform to the goal.
They are not neutral toward the goal; she says they are twisted to conform to it.
Right: she says everything lower on the list, including structures, rules and loops, will be twisted to conform to the goal.
questions.explain: She says everything lower on the list, including structures, rules and loops, will be twisted to conform to the goal.
questions.rule: Check the goal first; everything lower on the list bends toward it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: Order these from the weakest to the strongest leverage on the author's list.
items: Rules
Self-organization
Goals
questions.explain: Rules are 5, self-organization 4, goals 3.
questions.rule: Goals outrank self-organization.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: A hospital adopts the goal of earning as much billing revenue as possible. What does the idea predict about its rules and information flows?
options: They will resist and keep their old form
They will be twisted to serve that goal
They will not change at all
They will vanish soon after
optionExplain: She says lower points are twisted to conform, not that they resist and keep their form.
Right: Goals reshape lower points.
She says everything lower is twisted to conform, so they do change.
They are not removed; they are bent to serve the goal.
questions.explain: By her logic a dominant goal bends everything lower, so rules and information flows serve it (Our reading for the hospital).
questions.rule: Check the goal first; everything lower on the list bends toward it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: True or false: The author says genetic engineering is good or bad regardless of who wields it.
questions.explain: She says it depends on who wields it, with what goal.
questions.rule: Judge technology by its goal.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: What if corporations wield genetic engineering to produce marketable products?
options: No real change, since the same genes are being used
A very different goal and selection mechanism
The same direction as natural evolution, only faster
Slower evolution, because products need testing first
optionExplain: She stresses the change of goal and selection mechanism, not the genes, so 'no real change' is wrong.
Right: she says a corporation selling marketable products is a very different goal and selection mechanism than the planet has seen.
Contrary: she says the direction differs from anything the planet has seen.
She does not say slower; she says a very different direction for evolution.
questions.explain: She says a corporation selling marketable products is a very different goal and selection mechanism than the planet has seen.
questions.rule: Check the goal first; everything lower on the list bends toward it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: True or false: The author counts Wal-Mart among systems whose goal is to bring more of the world under one central planning system.
questions.explain: She lists Genghis Khan's empire, the Church, China, Wal-Mart and Disney.
questions.teaches: The author counts the empire of Genghis Khan, the Church, the People's Republic of China, Wal-Mart and Disney as systems whose goal is to bring more of the world under one central planning system.
questions.rule: Check the goal first; everything lower on the list bends toward it.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: A thermostat setting is the goal of a single ____ loop, not of the whole system.
questions.explain: Local loop goals are less powerful than the goal of the whole system.
questions.rule: Ask what the whole system is for, not only what each loop aims at.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: The author says that making profits is only a ____ of the corporate game, not its point.
questions.explain: It is a necessary condition for staying in the game.
questions.rule: Profit is a rule, not the purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: A publisher earns profit but also keeps expanding its share of every market. Which part is the whole-system goal?
options: The fixed office where the company's staff work
The need to pay its bills and cover its costs each month
The activity of printing and selling books to readers
The drive to grow and control its environment
optionExplain: A fixed office is a physical feature, not a goal.
A condition for staying in the game, per the author.
Printing and selling books is the loop activity; the whole-system goal is the drive to grow and control (Our reading).
Right: Look for what the game is for.
questions.explain: Profit is a rule, a necessary condition to stay in the game; the point of the game is to grow and control its environment.
questions.rule: Ask what the whole system is for, not only what each loop aims at.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: Sort each goal: is it a goal of one loop, or a goal of the whole system?
questions.explain: Loop goals matter for pieces of systems, and most people realize that; the larger, less obvious goals are those of the entire system, such as the drive to grow and engulf.
questions.rule: Ask what the whole system is for, not only what each loop aims at.

items.t: Keep enough water behind the dam
Keep the room temperature comfortable
Keep inventories stocked at sufficient levels
Grow and bring the world more under the corporation's control
Engulf everything, as the goal of a cancer or a living population does
Keep the market competitive, ahead of each firm's own goal

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: True or false: An engulfing goal is dangerous only when higher-level balancing feedback does not hold it in check.
questions.explain: She says it is only bad when not balanced by higher-level loops.
questions.rule: Balance the engulfing goal.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: What must trump each corporation's goal of eliminating competitors?
options: Each corporation's goal of raising its profit
Each corporation's goal of building bigger stores
The goal of keeping the market competitive
Each corporation's goal of lowering its prices
optionExplain: Not hers: profit is a rule, a condition for staying in the game.
Bigger stores are not a goal she discusses; the check she names is the goal of keeping the market competitive.
Right: Higher goals check lower ones.
Lowering prices is a competitive move; it does not check the goal to engulf competitors (Our reading).
questions.explain: She says keeping the market competitive has to trump each corporation's wish to eliminate competitors, as balance trumps growth in ecosystems.
questions.teaches: The author says John Kenneth Galbraith recognized long ago the corporate goal of engulfing everything, which she says is also the goal of a cancer and of every living population.
questions.rule: Ask what the whole system is for, not only what each loop aims at.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: When does swapping a person at the top change a system most?
options: When the new person is richer than the last
When the new person is younger than the last
When the new person changes the system's goal
Never, since people do not change systems
optionExplain: A new person's wealth does not change the system; the goal does.
A new person's age does not change the system; the goal does.
Right: changing players is low-level unless a top player changes the system's goal, which she says is the exception.
She says the exception is at the top, where one player can change the goal.
questions.explain: Changing players is low-level unless a top player changes the system's goal, which she says is the exception.
questions.rule: A new goal, stated, repeated and insisted upon, can redirect a system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: Changing players is a low-level move except at the ____, where one player may change the goal.
questions.explain: She says the exception to the rule is at the top, where a single player can have the power to change the system's goal.
questions.rule: Top leaders can change goals.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: A new head teacher announces a new aim for the school and repeats it for years. Which author's idea fits?
options: Articulating a new goal is a high leverage point
Changing a parameter, which is a low leverage point
Lengthening a delay in a feedback loop
Enlarging a buffer that steadies a stock
optionExplain: Right: she credits Reagan's repeating a new goal over and over as showing the high leverage of articulating and insisting on new goals.
A parameter is the weakest lever on her list; announcing a new aim is a goal, number 3.
Lengthening a delay is the number 9 lever, not announcing a goal.
Enlarging a buffer is the number 11 lever, not announcing a goal.
questions.explain: She credits Reagan's repeating a new goal over and over as showing the high leverage of articulating and insisting on new goals.
questions.rule: A new goal, stated, repeated and insisted upon, can redirect a system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: True or false: The author claims Reagan's success shows leaders alone cause system change.
questions.explain: She says larger system changes and corporate power let him get away with it.
questions.rule: Leader plus context.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: What if a leader states a new goal once and then stops mentioning it?
options: The goal spreads on its own without further effort
The goal succeeds fully, as it would with constant repetition
The goal reverses itself because the leader seems unsure
Weaker leverage, since repetition is part of it (Our reading)
optionExplain: She stresses articulating, repeating and insisting, so a goal does not spread on its own.
She stresses repeating and insisting, so a goal stated once would not succeed as fully as a repeated one (Our reading).
Reversal is not her claim; she says the high leverage lies in repeating the goal.
Right: Articulate, repeat, insist.
questions.explain: She stresses articulating, repeating, standing up for and insisting on a goal, so one mention would give weaker leverage (Our reading).
questions.rule: A new goal, stated, repeated and insisted upon, can redirect a system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 3. Goals—The purpose or function of the system
questions.q: True or false: The author says a president could once urge citizens to ask what they could do for the government, and no one laughed.
questions.explain: She contrasts that with Reagan's goal of getting government off our backs.
questions.teaches: The author says a president once could say 'Ask not what government can do for you, ask what you can do for the government' and no one laughed, which shows how far public discourse has since changed.
questions.rule: A new goal, stated, repeated and insisted upon, can redirect a system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: What stops people from questioning a paradigm?
options: It is kept secret by the powerful
It is shared by all, so it goes unstated
Nobody understands what it means
It is illegal to question it
optionExplain: She says paradigms go unstated because everyone already knows them, not because the powerful hide them.
Right: paradigms go unstated because it is unnecessary to state them: everyone already knows them.
Nobody has to fail to understand it; everyone already knows these beliefs.
Illegality is not her explanation; the beliefs are unstated because it is unnecessary to state them.
questions.explain: Paradigms go unstated because it is unnecessary to state them: everyone already knows them.
questions.rule: Ask which unstated shared assumptions a system rests on.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: A society's shared idea of how the world works is its ____.
questions.explain: She calls the shared idea in the minds of society, its great unstated assumptions, the society's paradigm.
questions.rule: A paradigm is a shared mindset.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: True or false: A workplace belief that managers must be obeyed without question is the kind of unstated assumption she calls a paradigm (Our reading).
questions.explain: Shared, unstated beliefs about how things work are paradigms; a pay rate or deadline is not (Our reading for the workplace).
questions.rule: Ask which unstated shared assumptions a system rests on.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: Sort each item: a paradigm assumption or a rule/parameter?

items.t: Growth is good
One can own land
Nature is a stock of resources
The tax rate is 20 percent
Cars drive on the left
The deadline is Friday

questions.explain: Shared beliefs are paradigms; settings and regulations are lower points.
questions.rule: Paradigm = shared belief.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: True or false: Whatever the tax law says, the author, following Forrester, expects payments to push against the society's idea of fairness.
questions.explain: This is Forrester's saying: actual tax payments will push right up against the accepted idea of fairness, whatever the law says.
questions.rule: Law bends to belief.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: Why might another culture be dumbfounded by our assumptions?
options: They share exactly the same assumptions
They did not find them at all obvious
They have no assumptions of their own
They forbid assumptions altogether
optionExplain: Other cultures did not share them; the assumptions dumbfounded other cultures.
Right: Paradigms are not universal.
Other cultures have paradigms of their own; theirs differ.
Forbidding assumptions is not her claim; paradigms are what every society holds.
questions.explain: She says our assumptions utterly dumbfounded other cultures, who thought them not the least bit obvious.
questions.teaches: The author says our culture's assumptions have utterly dumbfounded other cultures, who thought them not the least bit obvious.
questions.rule: Ask which unstated shared assumptions a system rests on.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: Why did Egyptians build pyramids and we build skyscrapers?
options: Pyramids are thousands of years older than skyscrapers
Nobody knows why they were built
Sand is cheaper than steel
Their beliefs about what matters differ
optionExplain: Age is not the reason; the contrast is in what each society believes.
The book gives the beliefs: an afterlife for pyramids, valuable downtown space for skyscrapers.
Costs of materials are not her reason; shared beliefs are.
Right: she says the Egyptians built pyramids for their belief in an afterlife, and we build skyscrapers because we value downtown space.
questions.explain: She says the Egyptians built pyramids for their belief in an afterlife, and we build skyscrapers because we value downtown space.
questions.rule: Trace a system's goals and structures back to the beliefs that produced them.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: Paradigms are the ____ of systems.
questions.explain: Goals, flows, feedbacks and stocks arise from them.
questions.rule: Paradigm first.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: True or false: A city pouring money into highways because its leaders believe the car is freedom shows a paradigm producing a structure (Our reading).
questions.explain: She says systems arise out of shared beliefs about the nature of reality, so a highway-first city shows this (Our reading).
questions.rule: Trace a system's goals and structures back to the beliefs that produced them.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: True or false: The author says Copernicus, Einstein and Adam Smith each intervened at the level of paradigm.
questions.explain: She names Copernicus and Kepler, Einstein and Adam Smith as people who hit a leverage point at the level of paradigm.
questions.rule: Paradigm shifts transform systems.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: According to Emerson, the least enlargement of ideas would cause the most striking changes of external ____.
questions.explain: Ideas clothe themselves in material form.
questions.rule: Trace a system's goals and structures back to the beliefs that produced them.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: Which of Emerson's examples of ideas clothing themselves does the author quote?
options: Societies, houses, cities, language, ceremonies and newspapers
Only laws and taxes, since governments shape the rest
Only the buildings, since timber and brick are physical
Only books and newspapers, since ideas live in print
optionExplain: Right: Ideas take material form.
Too narrow: Emerson lists far more than laws.
Too narrow: he mentions language and ceremonies as well.
Too narrow: he lists societies and cities too.
questions.explain: The quotation says every truth and error 'clothes itself with societies, houses, cities, language, ceremonies, newspapers'.
questions.teaches: Emerson, quoted by the author, said that timber, brick, lime and stone have flown into convenient shape, obedient to the master idea reigning in the minds of many persons.
questions.rule: Trace a system's goals and structures back to the beliefs that produced them.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: Which is harder to change, one person's paradigm or a society's?
options: Both equally
One person's
A society's
Neither can change
optionExplain: Not equally: she says an individual's paradigm can change in a millisecond, while a society's resists hardest.
Reversed: in one person a paradigm shift can happen in a millisecond, in a click of the mind.
Right: she says in one person it can happen in a millisecond, while whole societies resist challenges to their paradigms harder than anything.
Paradigms can change; she describes how, in a person at once and in a society with great resistance.
questions.explain: She says in one person it can happen in a millisecond, while whole societies resist challenges to their paradigms harder than anything.
questions.rule: Point to anomalies, act from the new view, place its holders in visible positions, and work with the open-minded.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: In a single individual, paradigm change can happen in a ____.
questions.explain: She says it takes just a click in the mind.
questions.rule: Fast in a person.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: Which tactic follows the author's account of changing paradigms?
options: Spend most of your effort arguing with the most committed reactionaries
Wait until almost everyone agrees before saying anything about the new view
Keep pointing at the old paradigm's failures while acting from the new one
Stay silent in public and let the evidence persuade people on its own
optionExplain: She advises not wasting time with reactionaries and working with change agents and the open-minded middle.
Waiting is the opposite of her advice to keep speaking and acting from the new paradigm.
Right: Act from the new paradigm.
Silence is the opposite of her advice to speak and act loudly and with assurance from the new view.
questions.explain: Her account: point out the old paradigm's anomalies and failures, and speak and act from the new one with assurance.
questions.rule: Point to anomalies, act from the new view, place its holders in visible positions, and work with the open-minded.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: Sort each tactic: recommended by the author, or not?

items.t: Point to anomalies in the old paradigm
Speak and act from the new one with assurance
Work with the open-minded middle
Put new-paradigm people in visible places
Spend time converting reactionaries
Hide the new view until it is popular

questions.explain: She says not to waste time with reactionaries.
questions.rule: Work with change agents.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: True or false: If a society's paradigm is challenged, it will resist less than any other change.
questions.explain: She says they resist harder than anything else.
questions.rule: Paradigms resist.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.section: 2. Paradigms—The mind-set out of which the system—its goals, structure, rules, delays, parameters—arises
questions.q: How do systems modelers say paradigms change?
options: By building a model that shows the system whole
By passing a law that bans the old way of seeing the world
By offering money to people who accept the new worldview
By holding a vote until most of a society agrees
optionExplain: Right: she says systems modelers change paradigms by building a model, which takes us outside the system and forces us to see it whole.
Plausible because law changes behavior, but the modelers' claim is about seeing, not compelling.
Plausible because incentives work on parameters, but it is not the route modelers describe.
Plausible in politics, but paradigms are not changed by a count of votes in her account.
questions.explain: She says systems modelers change paradigms by building a model, which takes us outside the system and forces us to see it whole.
questions.teaches: Systems modelers say we change paradigms by building a model of the system, which takes us outside it and forces us to see it whole; the author says her own paradigms changed this way.
questions.rule: Point to anomalies, act from the new view, place its holders in visible positions, and work with the open-minded.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: What does it mean to stay unattached in the arena of paradigms?
options: Ignoring evidence that challenges your view
Choosing the best paradigm and defending it
Avoiding every belief of any kind about the world
Seeing that no paradigm is true, even your own
optionExplain: Staying unattached does not mean ignoring evidence; it means holding all worldviews loosely.
Choosing the best paradigm and defending it is clinging, which she says most of us do.
She does not say to avoid all beliefs; she says no paradigm is true.
Right: she says it is to realize that no paradigm is true, including the one that shapes your own worldview.
questions.explain: She says it is to realize that no paradigm is true, including the one that shapes your own worldview.
questions.rule: Hold your worldview loosely, since no paradigm is the truth.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Transcending paradigms is number ____ on the author's list, the strongest leverage point.
questions.explain: Number 1 is above number 2, changing a paradigm, because it means holding every paradigm loosely.
questions.rule: The top of the list.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: A scientist who treats her model as one useful lens and drops it when another serves better is staying unattached (Our reading).
questions.explain: Holding even a favorite model as one lens among many is the non-attachment she describes (Our reading for the scientist).
questions.rule: Hold your worldview loosely, since no paradigm is the truth.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: How does number 1 differ from number 2?
options: Number 2 is a parameter, while number 1 is a rule
Number 2 changes a paradigm; number 1 detaches from all
Number 1 chooses the best paradigm and holds it firmly
Number 1 and number 2 are two names for the same step
optionExplain: Wrong: number 2 is paradigms, number 5 is rules, 12 is numbers.
Right: Number 2 changes a paradigm.
Holding one paradigm firmly is the clinging that number 1 goes beyond.
They are two different steps: changing a paradigm is number 2 and transcending paradigms is number 1.
questions.explain: Number 2 changes a paradigm; number 1 is to stay unattached to all paradigms, seeing none as true.
questions.rule: Hold your worldview loosely, since no paradigm is the truth.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: If no paradigm is right, the author says you may choose whatever one will help achieve your purpose.
questions.explain: She says this is a basis for radical empowerment.
questions.rule: Choose a lens by purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: How do most people react to the idea that no worldview is certain?
options: They welcome it immediately as a source of freedom
They back away, afraid nothing can be relied on
They ignore it and carry on without a thought
They write it down and apply it step by step
