optionExplain: Contrary: she says clingers pedal in the opposite direction.
Right: she says people who cling to paradigms see this possibility and pedal rapidly in the opposite direction.
Not what she says: only those who entertain the idea find it empowering.
Writing it down and applying it step by step misses her point; most people pedal away from the idea.
questions.explain: She says people who cling to paradigms see this possibility and pedal rapidly in the opposite direction.
questions.teaches: The author says people who cling to paradigms, which means nearly all of us, take one look at the possibility that everything they think is nonsense and pedal rapidly in the opposite direction.
questions.rule: Hold your worldview loosely, since no paradigm is the truth.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Why might admitting uncertainty be empowering?
options: It ends all action, because no view can be defended
It proves that nothing matters and no action is worthwhile
It leaves you passive, since every view is equally true
It frees you to choose whichever view serves your purpose
optionExplain: She says admitting uncertainty opens a choice of action, not ends it.
She says it is the basis for radical empowerment, not for despair.
She says that, with no paradigm right, you can choose one that helps your purpose, so you are not passive.
Right: she says that if no paradigm is right, you can choose whatever one will help you achieve your purpose.
questions.explain: She says that if no paradigm is right, you can choose whatever one will help you achieve your purpose.
questions.rule: Let go of certainty to gain the freedom to choose and to act.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: The author says entertaining the idea that no worldview is certain is a basis for radical ____.
questions.explain: She says everyone who has entertained the idea found it the basis for radical empowerment.
questions.rule: Doubt can empower.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: A manager who drops one method and picks whichever suits the task is choosing a paradigm by purpose (Our reading).
questions.explain: If no paradigm is right, you can choose whichever one helps your purpose; the manager does that (Our reading).
questions.rule: Let go of certainty to gain the freedom to choose and to act.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: The author says that no certainty in any worldview leaves no power or reason to act.
questions.explain: She says the reverse: a basis for radical empowerment.
questions.rule: Doubt empowers.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: The author says that entertaining the idea of no certainty in any worldview leaves a person powerless.
questions.explain: She says the opposite: everyone who has entertained it found it a basis for radical empowerment.
questions.rule: Doubt can empower.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Someone freed from their old worldview has no idea what purpose to pursue. What does the author suggest?
options: They may be locked up, burned, crucified or shot
They become rich and are rewarded by their societies
They lose all ideas and become silent
They are crowned as kings by grateful nations
optionExplain: Right: The freedom to choose a view by purpose raises the question of where purpose comes from.
Contrary: she says societies often rub out enlightened beings.
Silence is not her claim; she says you can listen to the universe.
Crowning is not her claim; she says societies often rub out enlightened beings.
questions.explain: The freedom to choose a view by purpose raises the question of where purpose comes from.
questions.teaches: The author says that if you have no idea where to get a purpose, you can listen to the universe.
questions.rule: Let go of certainty to gain the freedom to choose and to act.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: In the author's list, higher points shape what happens at the lower ones.
questions.explain: Paradigms give rise to goals, structure, rules and parameters; goals bend what is below them.
questions.rule: Move up the list when lower-level fixes keep failing.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Match each higher point to what it shapes or can change.
questions.explain: Each higher point shapes those below it: paradigms give rise to goals, goals to structure, rules and information flows.
questions.rule: Higher shapes lower.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: A firm repeatedly fixes pay numbers yet behavior is unchanged. Which move does the idea suggest?
options: Fire everyone and hire a new team
Adjust the numbers again, only more strongly
Look at the rules and goals that set those numbers
Wait for behavior to change by itself
optionExplain: Hiring a new team is a change of players, which she says changes little within the same system.
More of the same number tweak is the weakest lever; the idea says move up the list.
Right: when pay-number fixes fail, the idea says to move up the list to the rules and goals that set the numbers.
Waiting leaves the failing fix in place; the idea says move to a higher point.
questions.explain: When pay-number fixes fail, the idea says to move up the list to the rules and goals that set the numbers.
questions.rule: Move up the list when lower-level fixes keep failing.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Sort each item: part of the lower (physical and parameter) end of the list or the higher (goals and mind-set) end?

items.t: Parameters
Buffers
Stock-and-flow structures
Goals
Paradigms
Transcending paradigms

questions.explain: Numbers, buffers and structures are 12 to 10; goals, paradigms and transcending are 3 to 1.
questions.rule: Low to high.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: If the system's goal changes, the author expects structure, loops and information flows to be twisted to conform.
questions.explain: She says a dominant goal twists everything further down the list, such as flows, loops and information, to conform to it.
questions.rule: Goals bend the rest.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Which is true of the list's order, per the author?
options: It has no order, since all twelve are equally strong
It is fixed, with no exception for any item
It is tentative, with exceptions that move items
It matters only at the top, where all the power sits
optionExplain: She ranks them; numbers are last and paradigms second to transcending.
She calls the list tentative and its order slithery, with exceptions to every item.
Right: Treat the order as a guide.
She says there are leverage points down the list too, for example critical numbers.
questions.explain: She calls the list tentative and its order slithery, with exceptions that can move any item up or down.
questions.teaches: The author calls her list tentative and its order slithery, with exceptions to every item that can move it up or down.
questions.rule: Move up the list when lower-level fixes keep failing.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: The author says that the higher the leverage point, the more the system will resist changing it.
questions.explain: Targeting goals or paradigms meets the strongest resistance.
questions.rule: Plan for resistance in proportion to the leverage you seek.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: The higher the leverage point, the more the system will ____ changing it.
questions.explain: She says the higher the leverage point, the more the system will resist changing it.
questions.rule: Power draws resistance.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: A reformer changing a firm's core purpose should expect stronger resistance than one changing a pay rate (Our reading).
questions.explain: Purpose is a higher leverage point than a number, and she says the higher the point the stronger the resistance (Our reading).
questions.rule: Plan for resistance in proportion to the leverage you seek.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: The author says high leverage points are easy to use once found.
questions.explain: She says they are not easily accessible and the system resists.
questions.rule: High leverage is hard.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: Once you know where a magical leverage point is and which way to push, it is easy to use.
questions.explain: The author says magical leverage points are not easily accessible even when we know where they are and which direction to push.
questions.rule: Plan for resistance in proportion to the leverage you seek.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: What does the author say about the author herself having the list percolating for years?
options: It did not turn her into Superwoman
It was useless and a waste of her time
It made her a master of every system she met
It solved her problems
optionExplain: Right: she says that having the list percolating for years did not make her Superwoman.
She does not call the list useless; she says it did not make her Superwoman.
She does not say it made her a master; she says there are no cheap tickets to mastery.
She does not say it solved her problems; she says it did not make her Superwoman.
questions.explain: She says that having the list percolating for years did not make her Superwoman; knowing is not mastery.
questions.teaches: The author admits that having the list percolating in her subconscious for years has not transformed her into Superwoman.
questions.rule: Plan for resistance in proportion to the leverage you seek.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: The author says mastery has less to do with pushing leverage points than with letting go and ____ with the system.
questions.explain: Her closing image is dancing with the system.
questions.rule: Work hard at understanding, then let go and dance with the system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: The author says there are no cheap ____ to mastery.
questions.explain: She says there are no cheap tickets to mastery; you have to work hard at it.
questions.rule: Mastery takes work.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: A new manager memorizes the twelve points and applies them mechanically. Which author's caution applies?
options: The points are fixed and apply the same way everywhere
The list is a complete formula and its order is exact
Memorizing the twelve places is mastery enough
The list is an invitation to think, not a recipe
optionExplain: She calls the list a work in progress with exceptions, not a fixed rule set.
She says it is not a recipe and that its order is slithery.
She says there are no cheap tickets to mastery; you have to work hard at it, not just memorize.
Right: Do not treat the list as a recipe.
questions.explain: She calls the list an invitation to think more broadly about system change, not a recipe for finding leverage points.
questions.rule: Work hard at understanding, then let go and dance with the system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: The author says there are two routes to mastery: rigorous analysis of a system or rigorously casting off your own paradigms.
questions.explain: She names both: rigorously analyzing a system, or rigorously casting off your own paradigms and accepting not-knowing.
questions.rule: Two kinds of hard work.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: True or false: Seeking to control a system, rather than accepting the humility of not-knowing, leads to the mastery she describes (Our reading).
questions.explain: She links mastery to strategically, profoundly, madly letting go and dancing with the system, not to tighter control (Our reading).
questions.rule: Work hard at understanding, then let go and dance with the system.

questions.unitTitle: Leverage Points—Places to Intervene in a System
questions.q: Why does the author stress that her list is an invitation to think rather than a recipe?
options: She has not studied systems in any depth
Generalizing about complex systems is dangerous
The list contains errors she knows about
Recipes are forbidden in policy work
optionExplain: She draws on decades of analysis; her reason is caution about generalizing, not ignorance.
Right: Treat the list as a guide to thinking.
She does not say it contains known errors; she says it is a work in progress.
She does not forbid recipes; she says complex systems make it dangerous to generalize.
questions.explain: She says complex systems are complex and it is dangerous to generalize about them; the list is a work in progress.
questions.teaches: The author warns that complex systems are complex and it is dangerous to generalize about them, which is why her list is still a work in progress.
questions.rule: Work hard at understanding, then let go and dance with the system.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A student has recently learned to model feedback loops and is thrilled. Which hope is the author most likely to say such a student holds?
options: That the model will show why nothing can ever be understood about complex systems
That the model will finally give a key to prediction and control
That the model will mainly be useful for explaining past events after they occur
That the model will make human values and judgement unnecessary for managers
optionExplain: Enthusiasm runs the other way: new methods raise hopes of mastery, not despair.
Matches the author's own early belief; the card shows why this hope is a mistake.
A cautious aim like this is not the typical error of an enthused beginner.
A related hope, but the author names prediction and control as the mistaken assumption.
questions.explain: The author says enthusiasts tend to assume systems analysis is the key to prediction and control. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Value systems thinking for what it reveals, not as a promise of prediction and control.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, he and the other early MIT systems students first believed that systems thinking would help make systems work.
questions.explain: He says systems thinking was for them more than mind play: it was going to make systems work. That belief is the mistake the chapter opens by correcting.
questions.rule: Early hope: systems thinking would make systems work.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A consultancy says it can forecast traffic five years ahead within one percent once its model is built. Which of the author's points is it?
options: The industrial assumption that a key to prediction and control exists
The consultancy has found the passage to India the author's group was seeking all along
The consultancy is deliberately deceiving the city to win the contract
A feedback model can only be trusted if it is built by people trained at MIT
optionExplain: Right: the promise of exact forecasting is the assumption the author says enthusiasts fall for.
The group's search ended elsewhere; the author says what they found was not what they thought.
The author says his own group's exaggeration was not meant to deceive, so intent is not the issue.
Nothing in the chapter ties the mistake or its remedy to where one trained.
questions.explain: Promising exact forecasts and control from a model repeats the assumption the author warns about. Applying it to traffic is our fresh case.
questions.rule: Beware promises of exact prediction from a model.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Match each part of the author’s explorer comparison to what it stands for in the story of the early systems students.
pairs: The passage to India they were seeking
Systems thinking as the key to prediction and control
The Western Hemisphere they ran into
A lens of greater worth, but not in the way they thought
Their enchantment with the new lens
The reason they exaggerated their findings
questions.explain: The explorers sought one thing and found another; the early students sought control and found a lens of different worth, and their enchantment led them to exaggerate.
questions.rule: A real discovery can differ from the one intended.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: How does the author describe the reason his group exaggerated its findings?
options: It was a calculated move to win research funding for the new discipline
It came from data errors that only showed up after the models were run
It came from their own expectations and hopes, with no intent to deceive
It was forced on them by the sceptical scientific colleagues who surrounded them
optionExplain: The author states there was no intent to deceive, so a funding motive is ruled out.
He puts the cause in expectation and hope, not in faulty data.
Right: they were innocently enchanted by what they could see through the lens.
Colleagues appear later as ridiculing, not as pressing the group to overstate.
questions.explain: The author says the exaggeration was not deceit but the expression of their own expectations and hopes.
questions.rule: Exaggeration can be innocent and still be wrong.
questions.teaches: The author says the early exaggeration was innocent: it expressed the group's own expectations and hopes, not any intent to deceive.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A start-up founder, thrilled by a new analytics method, says it will end guesswork about customers. What check fits the author's account of his group?
options: Trust the claim, because the founder has no intent to deceive anyone and seems sincere
Ask what hope drives the claim and test it against evidence before repeating it
Drop the method, since the author says new lenses never yield anything of worth
Wait for the method to be accepted at a leading university before testing it
optionExplain: The author says innocent intent did not make his group's claims correct.
Right: the author's group exaggerated from hope, so naming the hope is the first guard.
He says the opposite: the lens proved worth more than expected.
The author's lesson is about the user's own hopes, not about institutional approval.
questions.explain: The author's story links exaggeration to hope, so a fresh enthusiast should test claims against evidence. Applying it to a start-up is our reading.
questions.rule: Name the hope behind a claim, then test it.
questions.teaches: The author's own exaggeration shows that enthusiasm, rather than dishonesty, is the usual source of overclaiming for a new method.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A habit researcher lectures on addiction loops yet cannot stop checking their phone. What is the best explanation in the author's spirit?
options: Knowing how a pattern works does not by itself change one's own behaviour inside it
The researcher must not really understand the loops, or the habit would already be gone
Habit loops cannot be changed by anyone, however much they know
Phones are different from the addictions studied, so the lessons do not carry over
optionExplain: Right: understanding and doing are different things.
The author's group understood the structures well and still failed to follow their own advice.
The author does not claim change is impossible, only that knowing is not enough.
The story is that the lessons carried over but were not practised.
questions.explain: The author's group lectured on addiction and could not give up coffee. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Insight into how a system works does not by itself change behaviour inside it, including your own.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Match each pattern the author's group understood to the lapse in their own lives.
pairs: The traps of escalation and shifting the burden
Created them in their own marriages
questions.explain: Each pattern was one the group could explain well and still fell into themselves.
questions.rule: Understanding a trap does not stop you from falling in.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A team hands a hospital an excellent map of its delays and leaves; nothing changes. Which point of the author's best explains this?
options: The map must have been inaccurate, since an accurate map always produces change in a hospital
Hospitals are not systems, so system maps cannot apply to them
The team should have forced the hospital's managers to follow the map
Knowing how to fix a system differs from fixing it, since people and cultures resist
optionExplain: Accuracy does not guarantee action; the author's own group understood and still did not act.
The chapter treats social organisations as systems throughout.
Forcing is the style of implementation the author found shallow and unrealistic.
Right: social systems reflect thinking patterns and human needs, not just structure.
questions.explain: Fixing a system means changing people's needs, emotions and patterns, so an accurate map is not enough. The hospital is our fresh case.
questions.rule: An accurate map does not move a culture.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: True or false: the author says knowing the good does not guarantee doing it, so changing systems takes more than telling people what is right.
questions.explain: He lists trust that he who knows the good shall do the good among the things that make change harder than saying now all change.
questions.rule: Knowing the good is not doing the good.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A workshop leader plans a systems course. Which of her ideas conflict with the author's account of change? Select all that apply.
options: Once managers understand the model, they will change their behaviour
Expect that the course's own teachers will sometimes fall into the traps they teach
Treat implementation as getting other people to follow our advice
Remember that social systems express human needs and cultural patterns
optionExplain: Wrong: this assumes that understanding alone changes behaviour, which the author's own group disproved.
Fine: the author's group did exactly that, so expecting it is realistic.
Wrong: the group meant this by implementation, then found they did not follow their own advice.
Fine: this is the author's reason why change is not simple.
questions.explain: The two flawed ideas assume that understanding moves people. The other two reflect the author's account.
questions.rule: Insight into how a system works does not by itself change behaviour inside it, including your own.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A diet coach hands clients a flawless meal plan and most do not follow it. Where does the author say systems thinking falls short?
options: It can close the gap if the plan is made detailed enough to cover every client
It cannot say anything about the gap, since habits lie outside its subject matter
It can tell us what to do but cannot do it; bridging the gap takes the human spirit
It closes the gap automatically once clients are shown the underlying feedback loops
optionExplain: Detail does not supply willingness; the author says the gap remains between understanding and implementation.
The author uses his own habits as examples, so the gap is within its reach as an observation.
Right: systems thinking leads to the edge of what analysis can do and points beyond.
Showing loops is understanding; the author found understanding did not bring action.
questions.explain: At the chapter's end the author says systems thinking cannot bridge the gap between understanding and implementation by itself. It points beyond analysis to what the human spirit must do.
questions.rule: Analysis can point; people must act.
questions.teaches: The author closes by saying systems thinking cannot by itself bridge the gap between understanding and implementation; it leads to the edge of analysis and points to what the human spirit must do.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A model shows that better information would fix a system, but decision makers ignore it. What question would the author most likely raise next?
options: How can the equations be rewritten so the decision makers cannot ignore them?
How do people decide what information to let in and what to ignore?
How many more variables must be added before the model is accepted?
Which software package would present the same results more persuasively?
optionExplain: This keeps the focus on the model, whereas the author turns to the people receiving the information.
Right: the author asks why people sort and screen information as they do.
A bigger model does not address why people refuse information.
Presentation might help, but the author asks the deeper question about how minds filter.
questions.explain: The author asks how people determine what to reckon with and what to disparage. The card next sets out his examples.
questions.rule: When a systems fix stalls, look for the human question beneath it: how people screen information, what they value, what they fear, and what they believe is possible.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Match each situation from the author's list to the human question it prompted.
pairs: Decision makers ignore the information they need
How do people decide what to let in and what to ignore?
A loop could be aimed at real values
How can a loop be keyed to qualities you cannot measure?
A harmful system that nobody dares sweep away
Why do minimal structure and maximum freedom frighten people?
People put up with harm because they feel powerless
Why are people so easily convinced of their powerlessness?
questions.explain: Each situation led the author from a structural point to a question about human minds, values, fears or beliefs.
questions.rule: Behind each stuck system sits a human question.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: True or false: The author says systems thinkers were the first people to ask questions about the human mind that arise from how systems work.
questions.explain: He says whole disciplines, libraries and histories had asked the same questions and partly answered them.
questions.rule: Systems thinkers joined an old inquiry.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: According to the author, what was unique about the systems search?
options: A tool born of engineering and mechanism leads its users to confront human mysteries
Its answers to questions about values and culture were new to every discipline that had studied them
Its questions about the human mind had never been asked in any library
It showed that computers can settle the question of what people value
optionExplain: Right: the tool's origin makes the destination surprising.
He says the answers were not unique; other disciplines had offered answers.
He says whole libraries were asking the same questions.
The author gives no hint that computers settle such questions.
questions.explain: What was unique, in the author's words, was the route: from a mechanical, predictive tool to the most human questions.
questions.rule: The route was new, not the questions.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Sort these questions: does the author tie it to the human side of systems, or is it a technical modelling matter?

items.t: Why are people so easily convinced of their powerlessness?
What are values, and where do they come from?
Why do different people draw different conclusions from the same information?
Should a stock be drawn as a box or a cloud in this diagram?
How many time steps should the simulation run for?
Which software should we use to run the model?

questions.explain: The first three are questions the author lists or paraphrases. The last three are modelling choices we added as contrasts (our reading).
questions.rule: Human questions sit beneath technical ones.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: An engineer builds a flawless traffic app and finds drivers ignore it. What does the author's conclusion suggest?
options: Flawless engineering should have prevailed, so the drivers must be punished
The app should be abandoned, because technical tools never work with people
The engineer should wait, since drivers will adopt the app in time on their own
Getting along in a world of complex systems needs more than technocracy
optionExplain: The author turns to human minds, not to punishing people.
The author does not reject the tools, only the idea that they are enough.
Waiting passively is not what the author recommends; he asks how people process information.
Right: his conclusion is that even committed technocrats are led beyond technocracy.
questions.explain: He says systems thinking makes clear even to the most committed technocrat that more than technocracy is needed.
questions.rule: Technique is necessary, not sufficient.
questions.teaches: The author concludes that systems thinking makes clear, even to the most committed technocrat, that getting along in a world of complex systems requires more than technocracy.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, complex feedback systems can be understood only in the most general way.
questions.explain: He says they are understandable only in the most general way, and that exact prediction and control are unrealizable. The card next sets out his reasons.
questions.rule: Do not aim at exact prediction, lasting control or optimization of a complex system; aim at general understanding.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: For any but the most trivial objective, the author says we cannot ____ a system, because we do not even know what to aim at.
questions.explain: He says we cannot optimize, and we do not even know what to optimize.
questions.rule: No optimizing without knowing the target.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, success in making a complex system do what you want can last only for a time, at best.
questions.explain: He says the idea of making a complex system do what you want can be achieved only temporarily, at best.
questions.rule: Control, if at all, is temporary.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A government plans twenty years ahead, assuming it can foresee its economy exactly. Which outcome fits the author's claim?
options: The plan succeeds as long as its models include every feedback loop in the whole economy
The plan rests on a goal the author calls unrealizable, so surprises will upset it
The plan works as long as it is revised only when elections are held
The plan fails only if the government deliberately ignores its own data
optionExplain: He says even full models leave the system unpredictable.
Right: exact foresight is unrealizable, so surprises are to be expected.
Nothing links safety to the election cycle; the author doubts exact foresight at all.
Failure here comes from the nature of the system, not from bad faith.
questions.explain: The author calls exact foresight unrealizable. Applying this to a government plan is our fresh case.
questions.rule: Plan for surprise, not for exact foresight.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Sam says: since systems cannot be predicted or controlled, there is no point trying to understand them. What does Sam miss?
options: Such systems are understandable in a general way; what fails is exact foresight and control
The author says understanding systems is possible in full detail, though it takes longer to reach
The author says understanding is pointless, though other benefits might justify the study
The author says predicting is possible, though controlling is not, so the study still pays
optionExplain: Right: understanding is limited, not worthless.
He says only a general understanding is possible.
He does not call understanding pointless.
He says foreseeing exactly is unrealizable as well.
questions.explain: General understanding remains available. Sam moves from no exact control to no understanding.
questions.rule: Limited does not mean useless.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A manager says science will eventually let us know everything about our firm. Which doubt does the author cite against that hope?
options: Science has so far failed to produce reliable models of firms, markets or other organisations
Science is too expensive for firms to apply to their ordinary decisions
Science is limited to the natural world and cannot be applied to human organisations
Science itself, from quantum theory to chaos mathematics, points to irreducible uncertainty
optionExplain: He argues from the nature of science's own findings, not from a record of failures.
Cost is not his argument; the doubt he cites comes from science's own findings about uncertainty.
He treats social systems as systems; the doubt is about certainty, not scope.
Right: he points to science, not just to practical limits.
questions.explain: The author says our science, from quantum theory to chaos, leads into irreducible uncertainty.
questions.rule: Even good science ends in uncertainty.
questions.teaches: The author argues that science itself, from quantum theory to the mathematics of chaos, leads into irreducible uncertainty.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A manager learns that her complex system cannot be controlled. Which response is closest to what the author recommends?
options: Give up trying to influence the system and let it run as it will
Impose firmer rules so that the system is forced to follow the plan
Stay alert, redesign as the system responds, and expect surprises
Hire forecasters so that surprises can be ruled out in advance
optionExplain: The author calls for a different kind of doing, not for giving up.
Imposing will is the stance the author says cannot work.
Right: attentive participation replaces control.
The author says we cannot surge forward into a world of no surprises.
questions.explain: The author says there is plenty to do, of a different sort. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Replace control with attentive participation: envision, design and redesign, expect surprises and listen.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Match what we cannot do with the thing the author says we can do instead.
pairs: Envision it and bring it lovingly into being
Move into a world of no surprises
Expect surprises, learn from them, even profit
Impose our will on a system
Listen to what it tells us
questions.explain: Each lost certainty is paired with a more modest, active alternative.
questions.rule: Trade control for envisioning, redesign, learning and listening.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Sort each action: is it dancing with a system, or trying to conquer it?

items.t: Watching closely and adjusting as feedback arrives
Redesigning structure when the system has shifted
Listening to what the system shows about its own properties
Imposing your will through one fixed plan
Forecasting the exact future and preparing perfectly
Assuming more calculation alone will deliver control

questions.explain: The first three follow the author's description of dancing; the last three are forms of the omniscient-conqueror stance he rejects. The wording of the cases is ours.
questions.rule: Respond to feedback; do not command.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: True or false: The author means by the dance image that we should step back and let systems run themselves.
questions.explain: He says dancing requires staying wide awake, paying close attention and participating flat out.
questions.rule: Dancing means full participation.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: The author says living in a world of systems takes more than calculation. Which does he list among what it requires? Select all that apply.
options: Our rationality and our ability to sort out truth from falsehood
Our intuition, compassion and vision
Greater secrecy about our uncertainties, to keep others confident
Computing power far beyond today's, to model every detail
optionExplain: Right: he names rationality and sorting truth from falsehood.
Right: these are named as part of our full humanity.
He argues the opposite later, in favour of acknowledging uncertainty.
He says no amount of calculation supplies what is needed.
questions.explain: He says the message from every model was that success requires our full humanity: rationality, sorting truth from falsehood, intuition, compassion, vision and morality.
questions.rule: Calculation is only one part of what is needed.
questions.teaches: The author says living successfully with systems requires our full humanity: rationality, sorting truth from falsehood, intuition, compassion, vision and morality.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A new team lead wants to use the author's dance requirements to manage a team. Which behaviour fits?
options: Fix goals for the year and ask the team to avoid adjusting course before the review
Pay close attention to the team and adjust as its feedback arrives
Delegate all decisions to the team and stay clear of the details of their work
Predict each member's output and hold them to the forecast they were given
optionExplain: This is a static stance the dance metaphor argues against.
Right: the same requirements as kayaking, applied to management.
The metaphor asks for taking part flat out, not stepping away.
Prediction and control is the stance the author warns against.
questions.explain: He says the same requirements might apply to intellectual work, management, government and getting along with people.
questions.rule: The skill carries over from sport to management.
questions.teaches: The author had not thought that the requirements of dancing, from kayaking and gardening, also apply to intellectual work, management, government and getting along with people.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A set of rules for living with systems is offered at the end of a book. How would a careful reader treat it?
options: As a starting point from a way of seeing, probably incomplete
As a complete rulebook to be applied step by step, in the order listed
As the only valid way to learn to live with systems in any setting
As a set of tips that is useful only to professional modelers and analysts
optionExplain: Right: that is how the author frames his own list.
The author does not present it as complete or as a procedure.
He says there are many ways to learn to dance.
He says the practices reach beyond one's profession.
questions.explain: The author calls his list a start-off dancing lesson. The card next shows how he frames it.
questions.rule: Read the guidelines as practices that grow out of a systems worldview, not as a finished rulebook.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: True or false: the author says his list of guidelines is probably incomplete and not unique to systems thinking.
questions.explain: He says the list probably is not complete and that there are many ways to learn to dance.
questions.rule: The list is a start, not the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Put these guidelines in the order the author presents them.
items: Get the Beat of the System
Expose Your Mental Models to the Light of Day
Honor, Respect, and Distribute Information
Pay Attention to What Is Important, Not Just What Is Quantifiable
Stay Humble—Stay a Learner
questions.explain: The author starts with watching the system's behaviour and moves from mental models and information to quality, then humility, near the end.
questions.rule: The list begins with watching behaviour.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Match each practice to the guideline it belongs to.
pairs: Plotting ten years of data before changing a policy
Get the Beat of the System
Drawing arrows to show what you think causes what
Expose Your Mental Models to the Light of Day
Publishing emission figures that had been kept private
Speaking up for dignity that cannot be measured
Pay Attention to What Is Important, Not Just What Is Quantifiable
questions.explain: Each practice is the behaviour the named guideline asks for. The practices are our summaries of the author’s advice.
questions.rule: Each guideline names a practice.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A reader treats the guidelines as a rulebook valid only when every one is applied exactly. What does this miss in the author's framing?
options: He insists the guidelines apply in full only to professional modelers and researchers
He says only the first guideline really matters and the rest are optional extras
He says the guidelines are fixed laws derived from computer experiments
He offers them as a start-off lesson, probably incomplete, among many ways to learn
optionExplain: He says they spread to all of life, beyond the profession.
Nothing in the text ranks the first above the rest in this way.
He calls them practices he sees colleagues adopt, not laws.
Right: the guidelines are not a closed procedure.
questions.explain: Treating the list as an exact procedure ignores that the author calls it a start-off lesson, probably incomplete.
questions.rule: A guide, not a procedure.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A school teaches the guidelines only in staff training and not to students. Which point of the author's framing does this overlook?
options: They are meant mostly for children, who still have open minds
They are meant to be written down but not practised until they are fully understood
They are meant to be practised in all of life, beyond one's profession
They are meant to replace the school's disciplines with systems methods
optionExplain: The author does not single out children.
He speaks of practising them, however imperfectly.
Right: he says one begins to practise them beyond one's profession.
He wants to learn across disciplines, not replace them.
questions.explain: The author says the practices come to be used in all of life, not only in one's profession.
questions.rule: The practices reach beyond work.
questions.teaches: The author says the practices penetrate the discipline so deeply that one begins to use them not just in one's profession but in all of life.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: You are asked to improve a firm whose sales swing up and down. What should you do first, per the author?
options: Propose the changes that worked at your previous firm, and measure the result
Watch how sales have actually behaved over time before proposing anything
Interview managers about their theories of why sales swing, then act on them
Run a pilot of the most promising idea to see what happens
optionExplain: This starts from a favourite solution, not from the system's behaviour.
Right: begin with the system's behaviour.
Theories are the thing the guideline asks you not to start with.
Acting first disturbs the system before you know its beat.
questions.explain: The author says to watch before you disturb. The card next gives his reasons.
questions.rule: Watch and record how a system actually behaves over time before you try to change it.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: True or false: according to the author, people’s memories are a dependable guide to the timing of events in a system.
questions.explain: He advises making a time graph of actual data, because memories are not always reliable about timing.
questions.rule: Data over memory for timing.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Sort each response to a neighbour’s claim that local rainfall is declining: does it start from the system’s behaviour, or from belief?

items.t: Collect the rainfall record for many years and plot it
Ask long-time residents what they remember and check it against the records
Compare yearly totals with the spread between wet and dry years
Agree because several neighbours say the same
Plan for drought based on the claim, then look for supporting data
Dismiss the claim because weather impressions are unreliable

questions.explain: The first three look at what the system did; the others rely on belief or on dismissal without data. The cases are ours, built on the author’s rainfall example.
questions.rule: Check beliefs against the record.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: True or false: when the author plots growth rates against tax rates for New Hampshire towns, he finds no discernible relationship.
questions.explain: He reports a scatter as random as the stars in a New Hampshire winter sky, which exploded the selectmen’s belief that growth lowers taxes.
questions.rule: Plot variables together before believing a causal story.
questions.teaches: Plotting growth rates against tax rates for New Hampshire towns showed a random scatter, which exploded the selectmen’s confident belief that growth lowers taxes.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Dana is asked to improve a river's flood management. She spends a week reading experts' theories, then changes the dams. What did she skip?
options: Consulting enough experts about the best-known theories of flood control
Making a detailed plan for the dam changes before carrying them out
Watching how the river system actually behaves and has behaved over time
Waiting until the next flood to see whether the changes were needed
optionExplain: She consulted theories; the guideline asks for facts first.
A plan does not replace watching the system.
Right: she began with theories and acted before watching.
Waiting for a flood is not the same as studying past behaviour.
questions.explain: She started with theories rather than the river's behaviour. The case is our fresh example.
questions.rule: Facts about behaviour come before theories.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A farmer says rainfall has dropped, yet both droughts and floods have worsened. What does the author's rainfall example suggest?
options: Rainfall is decreasing, and the floods are an unrelated local problem that needs separate study
The belief may be wrong; variability may be increasing, with deeper droughts and bigger floods
The farmer's observations are unreliable, so the data should be ignored
The floods and the droughts must each have separate causes with no link
optionExplain: This keeps the belief and ignores the pattern in the data.
Right: the data can show rising variability behind a belief in decline.
The author wants the data checked, not set aside.
The example points to one change in variability, not separate causes.
questions.explain: In the author's example, what people called decreasing rainfall was really increasing variability.
questions.rule: Data can reveal a different pattern than belief.
questions.teaches: In the author's example, people swore rainfall was decreasing, but the data showed variability increasing: deeper droughts and bigger floods.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A committee says: the problem is that we do not have enough salesmen. What is notable about this statement?
options: It defines the problem by a lack of a preferred solution, not by the system's behaviour
It is an accurate description of the firm's behaviour that needs no further check or data
It is a dynamic question that asks how the firm reached its present state
It shows a healthy bias for action that the author recommends
optionExplain: Right: the solution is built into the problem statement.
It names a remedy, not a pattern of behaviour.
Dynamic questions ask how we got here, which this does not.
The author warns against leaping to solutions.
questions.explain: The author warns against defining a problem by the lack of our favorite solution. The card next sets out his reasons.
questions.rule: Define the problem by the system's behaviour over time, and ask how it got there and where it is heading.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Starting with the history of the system directs thought to ____ analysis, not static analysis.
questions.explain: He says starting with behaviour directs thought to dynamic, not static, analysis.
questions.rule: Dynamic means behaviour over time.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Sort each statement: does it define the problem by the system's behaviour, or by a missing favourite solution?

items.t: Orders have swung up and down every six months for three years
The problem is that we need a bigger warehouse
Waiting times have climbed steadily since the booking system changed
The problem is how to attract more growth to this town
Complaints peak every Monday and fall by Friday
The problem is that we need more traffic police

questions.explain: The behaviour statements describe patterns over time. The other three state a wanted solution as the problem; the second is the author's own example, the others are ours.
questions.rule: Describe the pattern, not the wished-for fix.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: Which of these is a dynamic question in the author's sense?
options: Which single part is broken right now and who is to blame for it?
What is the correct size of next year's budget for this department?
Who in the organisation holds the most formal authority over the issue?
If we do not change direction, where are we going to end up?
optionExplain: This is a static question that looks at one point in time.
This is a decision, not a question about behaviour over time.
This is a question about structure of authority at one time.
Right: it looks forward along the system's path.
questions.explain: The author lists how did we get there, what other modes are possible and where will we end up as dynamic questions.
questions.rule: Ask where the path leads.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: True or false: the author says a proposed solution has no place in thinking about a system.
questions.explain: Our reading: he objects to defining the problem by the lack of a favourite solution, not to solutions as such; solutions follow from understanding the behaviour.
questions.rule: Understand the behaviour, then choose the fix.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Get the Beat of the System
questions.q: A family sees its spending creep up. Which question applies the author's attention to strengths?
options: Which family member spends the most and should be asked to cut back this month?
What is the one rule that would stop all overspending from now on in our home?
Which of our spending habits have been keeping us within budget so far?
What will prices be next year, so we can set a plan accordingly?
optionExplain: This looks for blame, not strengths.
This looks for a single fix, not for what already works.
Right: it asks what is working well.
This is a forecast, not a look at the system's strengths.
questions.explain: The author adds that looking to strengths can lead to the question What's working well here? Applied to a household, this is our case.
questions.rule: Ask what is working, as well as what is wrong.
questions.teaches: Looking to a system's strengths adds the question What's working well here? to the dynamic questions about what's wrong and how we got there.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Expose Your Mental Models to the Light of Day
questions.q: You believe a project is late because suppliers are slow. What best helps test that belief?
options: Hold the belief firmly and look for evidence that supports it, ignoring doubts
Draw what you think is connected to what and ask others to challenge it
Ask the suppliers to confirm that they were slow and then act on what they say
Wait for further delays to see whether the pattern becomes obvious over time
optionExplain: This makes you a champion for one explanation.
Right: make the model visible and open to challenge.
One source confirming a view does not expose the whole model.
Waiting leaves the model hidden and untested.
questions.explain: The author says to get models out where they can be viewed. The card next gives his reasons.
questions.rule: Put your model into any visible form, invite challenge, and keep several explanations alive until evidence rules some out.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Expose Your Mental Models to the Light of Day
questions.q: True or false: the author says diagrams and equations are a good practice for exposing a mental model but are not required.
questions.explain: He says you can do it with words, lists, pictures or arrows showing what you think is connected to what.
questions.rule: Any visible form works.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Expose Your Mental Models to the Light of Day
questions.q: A team has competing explanations for falling sign-ups. Sort each response: does it keep models open, or champion one?

items.t: Write all three explanations down and list what evidence would rule each out
Invite colleagues to challenge each explanation’s assumptions
Treat all three as plausible until some evidence eliminates one
Pick the most convincing one and gather support for it
Defend the favourite in meetings and treat doubts as opposition
Let the most senior person choose the explanation

questions.explain: The first three follow the author’s advice to collect explanations and test them; the others make someone a champion for one. The cases are ours.
questions.rule: Hold several models until evidence prunes them.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Expose Your Mental Models to the Light of Day
questions.q: True or false: collecting many plausible explanations keeps you able to accept evidence that rules out one tied to your own identity.
questions.explain: The author says this is why one should not champion a single explanation: you can then see evidence against an assumption entangled with your identity.
questions.rule: Do not tie your identity to one model.
questions.teaches: Keeping many explanations plausible keeps you emotionally able to see evidence that rules out an assumption entangled with your own identity.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Expose Your Mental Models to the Light of Day
questions.q: Lee says on Monday that price drives sales and on Thursday assumes the opposite. No one notices. Which point of the author explains this?
options: Models should be kept hidden so that they can be revised without embarrassment or argument
Lee's mistake was using more than one model, and only one should be held
Mental models are slippery; assumptions slide unless they are made visible and consistent
Meetings should avoid causal claims unless equations have been written
optionExplain: The author wants them in the light of day.
The author advises collecting many models, not one.
Right: writing them out forces consistency.
He does not require equations; writing models out in any clear form makes them visible and consistent.
questions.explain: Lee's two meetings show how unexposed models slide. The case is our fresh example.
questions.rule: Visible models are consistent models.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Expose Your Mental Models to the Light of Day
questions.q: A school board argues from hunches. What does the author call exposing models, testing them and scuttling those the evidence does not support?
options: Practising consensus building, which is done too often in government and business
Practising the scientific method, which is done too seldom even in science
Practising system dynamics, which is done only by trained modelers
Practising devil's advocacy, which is rare only in business
optionExplain: He does not call it consensus building.
Right: he calls it nothing more than the scientific method.
He says it can be done in words, lists or pictures.
The author names the scientific method and says it is rare in many fields.
questions.explain: The author says doing this is the scientific method, done too seldom even in science and hardly at all in social science, management, government or everyday life.
questions.rule: Exposing models is science for everyday life.
questions.teaches: The author says exposing, testing and scuttling models is nothing more than the scientific method, done too seldom even in science and hardly at all in social science, management, government or everyday life.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Which problem does the author guess accounts for most of what goes wrong in systems?
options: Biased, late or missing information
Too few rules governing the people who work in the system
Poor leadership at the top of organisations that run systems
Greedy individuals who put their interest before the system's
optionExplain: Right: this is the author's own guess.
Rules are not his emphasis here.
Leadership is not the cause he names in this guideline.
Self-interest appears in his remarks on power but is not the main cause he guesses.
questions.explain: The author says most of what goes wrong comes from biased, late or missing information. The card next gives his reasoning.
questions.rule: Keep information timely, accurate and complete, and share it with those who must act on it.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Match each flaw in information to what decision makers cannot do with it.
pairs: Respond to it in a timely way
questions.explain: The author names these three flaws and the response each blocks.
questions.rule: Missing, wrong or late information blocks response.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A hospital ward reports its bed shortages to management only once a month. Which flaw from the author's list is at work?
options: Missing information, since the shortages are never reported at all
Inaccurate information, since the monthly figures must be wrong
Excess information, which overwhelms managers with detail
Late information, which cannot be answered in a timely way
optionExplain: The shortages are reported, only late, so missing information is not the flaw here.
Nothing says the monthly figures are wrong; the flaw is that they arrive too late to act on.
The author names flaws of bias, delay and absence, not excess.
Right: delay blocks a timely response.
questions.explain: A monthly report on a fast-changing problem is delayed information. The ward is our case.
questions.rule: Delay is a flaw.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: In 1986 U.S. law required companies to report each factory's hazardous air emissions, and the data became public. What happened within two years?
options: Reported emissions fell about 4 percent, since no penalties were attached to the reports
Reported emissions rose, because companies now reported more fully
Reported emissions fell about 40 percent, with no fines or required cuts
Reported emissions fell about 40 percent, but only after heavy fines were imposed
optionExplain: The fall was about 40 percent, far larger than expected.
The author reports a large decrease.
Right: publication alone produced the drop.
He stresses that there were no lawsuits, fines or penalties.
questions.explain: The reports were not illegal but looked bad when local papers listed the top ten polluters. Within two years emissions fell 40 percent, and some firms aimed at 90 percent.
questions.rule: Publishing withheld information can change a system on its own.
questions.teaches: After the 1986 Toxic Release Inventory made emissions public, reported emissions fell about 40 percent within two years with no lawsuits, fines or required reductions.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: True or false: the author credits the 40 percent fall in reported emissions to lawsuits and fines.
questions.explain: He says there were no lawsuits, required reductions, fines or penalties; the published information alone did it.
questions.rule: Information can act without enforcement.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: The author says some people have far more power over social systems than most realize. Who are they and how do they hold it?
options: Media, PR people, politicians and advertisers, who filter public information
Judges and lawyers, who decide which disputes and court records the public may see
Scientists and engineers, who hold the data that systems depend on for their work
Bankers and investors, who decide which projects receive funds
optionExplain: Right: control of information flow is the source of their power.
The author does not name them in this passage.
Scientists are not named here; the power lies in public information flow.
The power he describes is over information, not funds.
questions.explain: He says information is power, and those who regulate its public flow often filter and channel it for short-term, self-interested purposes.
questions.rule: Whoever controls information holds power.
questions.teaches: The author says that media, public relations people, politicians and advertisers have more power than most realize because they regulate public information, often filtering it for short-term, self-interested ends.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: Why might the words a society uses matter for how it behaves?
options: Words only decorate decisions that are made on other grounds entirely
Words matter only in law, where wording fixes rights and duties
Words matter only when they are spoken aloud, not when written
Language carries the information and models that actions depend on
optionExplain: The author denies this; language shapes what people perceive and do.
His claim covers society broadly.
The claim has nothing to do with speaking.
Right: the author treats language as the stuff of information and models.
questions.explain: The author says information streams are made of language and mental models are mostly verbal. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Say what you mean in concrete, meaningful, truthful words so that information and mental models stay clean.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: A society that talks about productivity but hardly uses the word resilience, the author says, will become productive but not ____.
questions.explain: His example: a society's vocabulary shapes what it achieves.
questions.rule: What we cannot name, we do not build.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: Which sentence is the cleanest use of language by the author's standard?
options: We will rightsize our workforce to align with strategic priorities
We will reallocate human capital to optimise operational outcomes
We will dismiss forty of our three hundred staff in March
We will take a measured approach to talent-related adjustments soon
optionExplain: Vague terms hide what is happening, a form of language pollution.
This refers to nothing in particular.
Right: it names what will happen, concretely and truthfully.
Soft, vague words like talent-related adjustments blur what will actually happen.
questions.explain: Concrete wording keeps the information stream clean; abstractions hide it. The example is our own.
questions.rule: Name the act.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: Sort each phrase: concrete, meaningful and truthful, or tyrannese-style language?

items.t: The river flooded forty houses on Elm Street
We shipped late on twelve of fifty orders
Thirty-one patients waited over two hours on Tuesday
Collateral damage
Ethnic cleansing
A Peacekeeper missile

questions.explain: The last three are the author's own examples of tyrannese; the first three are concrete counterparts we added.
questions.rule: Euphemism hides the thing named.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: Fred Kofman is quoted as saying we do not talk about what we see. What else does he say?
options: We talk about what we see, but language cannot change what we perceive
We see only what we can talk about, as language filters perception
We see what we talk about only when the topic is a technical one
We see everything but talk only about what is allowed by our culture
optionExplain: This is the ordinary view that Kofman reverses.
Right: perception depends on language as well as the nervous system.
He makes a general claim, not a technical one.
His claim is about perception, not about permission to speak.
questions.explain: Kofman says we see only what we can talk about, and language and the nervous system both act as filters.
questions.rule: Language limits what we notice.
questions.teaches: Fred Kofman, quoted by the author, says we do not talk about what we see; we see only what we can talk about, since language filters perception.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: A hospital report calls patient deaths adverse patient outcomes. What does Wendell Berry's account of tyrannese suggest?
options: It is language the user need not stand by or act on; it gives no personal ground
It is helpful, since technical language avoids upsetting families unnecessarily when deaths occur
It is a harmless synonym, since the meaning of the words is clear to all
It is a fair term of art, because every profession needs its own vocabulary
optionExplain: Right: it has no power to designate and asks nothing of the speaker.
Berry attacks such language; it hides the reality of deaths behind a technical phrase.
He says it designates nothing in particular.
He distinguishes tyrannese from honest specialised language.
questions.explain: Berry says tyrannese defines no personal ground for standing or acting; the hospital case is our application.
questions.rule: Euphemism lets speakers avoid responsibility.
questions.teaches: Berry says tyrannese is language the user is not required to stand by or act on, because it defines no personal ground for standing or acting and only supports expert opinion for action already begun.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: As a society begins to deal with complex systems, what is most likely to be needed?
options: Fewer words, so that fewer people are confused by technical language
The same words as before, used more loudly and more often
Only symbols and equations, since ordinary words are too vague
New words and richer meanings for old words to talk about complexity
optionExplain: He asks for an enlarged vocabulary.
Repetition does not supply new concepts.
He treats everyday language as central.
Right: the author says words are having to be enlarged and invented.
questions.explain: The author says the second step of respecting language is to enlarge it. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Learn and use words for systems concepts so that you can talk, and therefore think, about complexity.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: Old words such as carrying capacity, structure, diversity and system are coming to have richer and more ____ meanings.
questions.explain: He says these old words are gaining richer and more precise meanings.
questions.rule: Old words gain precision.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: A water authority has no term for how much demand its aquifer can bear and keeps granting permits. Which step in the guideline would help?
options: Enlarge its language with a term such as carrying capacity, to talk about the limit
Keep its language concrete and truthful, which is the first step and is enough here
Replace the technical word aquifer with an ordinary word that is already in wide use
Wait for a drought to show the limit, since words do not change water use
optionExplain: Right: a word for the limit lets the authority discuss it.
The first step is not wrong, but it does not supply the missing concept.
The gap is a missing concept for the limit, not a technical word.
The author argues that what we can talk about shapes what we notice and do.
questions.explain: The authority lacks a concept for its limit; the second step of the guideline is to add such words. The aquifer case is ours.
questions.rule: Add the word for the limit.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: Why does the author say the Eskimos have many words for snow?
options: Snow is more varied in the Arctic than anywhere else, so it needs far more labels than elsewhere
They studied snow and learned to use it, making it a resource they can dance with
Their language has a simple grammar that creates new words easily
They wanted to keep outsiders from understanding their conversations
optionExplain: He gives use and study as the reason, not variety alone.
Right: the vocabulary follows from use and attention.
He does not discuss grammar; his explanation is that a people who study and use snow develop words for it.
He gives no such motive; the vocabulary comes from use and attention.
questions.explain: A society that studies and uses something develops words for it.
questions.rule: Vocabulary follows use.
questions.teaches: The author says the Eskimos have many words for snow because they studied it and turned it into a resource, a system they can dance with.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: True or false: writing the book, the author had to add feedback, throughput, overshoot, self-organization and sustainability to his word processor’s dictionary.
questions.explain: The anecdote shows how little ordinary language has caught up with systems ideas.
questions.rule: New concepts need new words.
questions.teaches: The author had to add feedback, throughput, overshoot, self-organization and sustainability to his spell-check while writing the book, which shows how new this vocabulary is to ordinary use.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Use Language with Care and Enrich It with Systems Concepts
questions.q: A fishing town does not use the term carrying capacity. By the author's reasoning, what is likely to follow?
options: It will manage its fish stocks well, since no one is distracted by abstractions or jargon
It will remain unaffected by the missing term, since fish ignore what people call things
It will decline only if outsiders introduce the term and its problems
It will exceed its carrying capacity, as a society without the term cannot see the limit
optionExplain: He argues that lack of the term leads to overshoot.
His point is that behaviour follows what people can talk about.
The term does not create the limit; ignoring the term lets it be exceeded.
Right: the author says a society that does not understand or use the term will exceed it.
questions.explain: The author says a society that does not understand or use the term carrying capacity will exceed its carrying capacity.
questions.rule: No word, no awareness, no limit respected.
questions.teaches: The author says a society that does not understand or use the term carrying capacity will exceed its carrying capacity.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Pay Attention to What Is Important, Not Just What Is Quantifiable
questions.q: True or false: A factor that is hard to quantify should be left out of a model, because it cannot be treated scientifically.
questions.explain: The author says pretending something does not exist because it is hard to quantify leads to faulty models. The card next gives his case.
questions.rule: Name and defend qualities that cannot be measured, and do not set goals only around what is easy to count.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Pay Attention to What Is Important, Not Just What Is Quantifiable
questions.q: The author asks us to be a walking, noisy ____ counter that registers the presence or absence of quality.
questions.explain: He compares the quality detector to a noisy Geiger counter.
questions.rule: Detect quality out loud.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Pay Attention to What Is Important, Not Just What Is Quantifiable
questions.q: Someone says: show me figures, or I will not consider the claim that the new office layout is demeaning. What fits the author's guideline?
options: Agree to wait until a survey with numerical scores can be arranged and then decide
Drop the claim, since values that cannot be defined cannot be debated
Say the layout demeans staff, and refuse the measure-it-or-ignore-it ploy
Replace the claim with a figure of annual costs, which is easier to defend in a meeting
optionExplain: This accepts the ploy the author rejects.
He says no one can define or measure any value, and we must still speak for it.
Right: speak up for a quality you cannot easily count.
This swaps quality for what is easily counted.
questions.explain: The author says to refuse the if-you-cannot-measure-it ploy. The meeting is our fresh case.
questions.rule: Speak for what cannot be counted.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Pay Attention to What Is Important, Not Just What Is Quantifiable
questions.q: True or false: when workers in a firm drew the relationship between prejudice and their performance, they produced a nearly straight-line relationship.
questions.explain: They drew one of the most nonlinear relationships the author had seen in a model, and everyone agreed the connection was real.
questions.rule: An arbitrary scale beats an omitted factor.
questions.teaches: In a firm’s model, prejudice was put on an arbitrary numerical scale, and workers drew one of the most nonlinear relationships the author had seen between prejudice and performance.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Pay Attention to What Is Important, Not Just What Is Quantifiable
questions.q: A school ranks teachers only by pupils' test scores, and a head says: quality is whatever shows in the numbers. What does the author warn?
options: If quantity becomes the goal of the loops, quantity will be the result
Test scores are a scientific measure and should be trusted completely
Teachers should not be evaluated at all, since evaluation distorts teaching in schools
The head should replace test scores with an equally easy count
optionExplain: Right: measured goals shape what is produced.
He does not say numbers are bad, only that they are not all that matters.
He does not reject evaluation.
Another easy count repeats the mistake.
questions.explain: The author says what you reward is what you get. The school is our case.
questions.rule: What you count and reward is what you get.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Pay Attention to What Is Important, Not Just What Is Quantifiable
questions.q: A hospital board drops patient dignity from its review because it cannot be measured. Which earlier system trap does the author say this repeats?
options: Shifting the burden to the intervenor, so that the real fix is neglected
Escalation, where each side raises its stakes in response to the other
Success to the successful, where winners gain resources to win again
Setting goals around what is easily measured, not what is important
optionExplain: Shifting the burden is a different trap; the case concerns dropping what cannot be measured.
The case shows no arms-race dynamic.
The case is about what is measured, not about resources.
