Right: the author calls this a system trap he has already shown.
questions.explain: The author reminds the reader he has already shown the trap of setting goals around what is easily measured rather than what is important.
questions.rule: Do not fall into the measured-goal trap.
questions.teaches: The author says that setting goals around what is easily measured, rather than around what is important, is a system trap the reader has already seen.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
questions.q: A city sets a fixed yearly budget for flood defences, whatever the river does. What is the likely weakness?
options: The budget will be too large because fixed budgets always overspend
The budget is too transparent, so the public will lose interest
A fixed policy cannot adjust to a system whose state keeps changing
The budget has no weakness, since predictable policy is always best
optionExplain: Nothing says fixed budgets always overspend; the weakness is that a fixed budget cannot respond to the river.
Transparency is not the problem.
Right: the policy does not respond to the river.
The author says static policy fits poorly with a self-adjusting system.
questions.explain: The author says a self-adjusting system cannot be governed by a static policy. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Tie a policy to the state of the system it governs, and build in loops that let the policy itself be corrected.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
questions.q: True or false: In Carter's proposal, the gasoline tax would fall to zero if oil imports fell to zero.
questions.explain: The tax was proportional to the imported share of consumption, so it would fall with imports.
questions.rule: The tax tracks the problem.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
questions.q: Sort each policy: does it respond to the state of the system, or stay fixed whatever happens?

items.t: A parking fee that rises above 90 percent occupancy and falls below 60 percent
A tax that rises as oil imports rise and falls as they fall
A flood budget raised when the river passes a set level
A parking fee set every January and held all year
A flood budget fixed at the same amount each year
A tax at a set rate whatever the level of imports

questions.explain: The second item is Carter’s example; the others are ours. A feedback policy ties the instrument to the system’s state.
questions.rule: Let the policy follow the state.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
questions.q: On illegal immigration from Mexico, what did Carter suggest should be done?
options: Spend on building the Mexican economy until immigration stopped, not on guards
Spend more on border guards and barriers until the immigration stopped for good
Do nothing at all, since nothing could be done about immigration in any case
Tax employers in proportion to the number of immigrants they employed
optionExplain: Right: aim at the cause until the gap closes.
Carter suggested the opposite: spending on the Mexican economy rather than on guards and barriers.
He said nothing could be done as long as the gap in opportunity remained.
Taxing employers was not his proposal for illegal immigration from Mexico.
questions.explain: His proposal tied spending to the gap in opportunity and continued until the immigration stopped.
questions.rule: Spend until the condition is gone.
questions.teaches: Carter proposed, on immigration, spending money to build the Mexican economy until immigration stopped, because nothing could be done while the gap in opportunity and living standards remained.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
questions.q: Which of these is a meta-feedback loop, as the author describes the term?
options: A thermostat-like rule that adds heat when the temperature falls below a set point
A fixed target that stays in place for the whole of the policy's life, unchanged
A penalty added to the policy when targets are missed by more than a set margin
A rule requiring regular review of the targets, changing them if facts differ
optionExplain: This is an ordinary feedback loop, not one that changes loops.
A fixed target is the opposite of a loop that corrects loops.
A penalty is an ordinary response, not a loop that alters loops.
Right: it alters and corrects the policy's own loops.
questions.explain: Meta-feedback loops alter, correct and expand loops, designing learning into management.
questions.rule: A loop that corrects loops.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
questions.q: A mayor proposes a congestion charge that changes with traffic, and critics call it unpredictable. What does Carter's experience suggest?
options: Feedback policies are always accepted quickly once their logic is explained
Feedback policies cannot work unless the public votes for them
They can be hard to sell to a public that does not think in feedback terms
Feedback policies should be hidden from the public to avoid confusion
optionExplain: Carter's feedback policies were not accepted quickly; they were hard to explain and were not passed.
The author does not say popularity decides whether they work.
Right: Carter had trouble explaining his policies, and they were not passed.
The author gives no such advice; the difficulty was explaining them.
questions.explain: The author says Carter had a hard time explaining his feedback policies to a press and public that did not understand feedback, and the oil tax never passed.
questions.rule: Feedback policies need explaining.
questions.teaches: The author says Carter had a hard time explaining feedback policies to a press and public that did not understand feedback, and neither his oil tax nor his immigration plan was adopted.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
questions.q: A treaty must be signed while the scale of a global danger is still uncertain. Which design is most sensible?
options: Wait to sign until the danger is fully measured, however long that takes
Set targets and require monitoring and a meeting to revise them as evidence arrives
Set one fixed schedule that will not be changed once signed, whatever evidence arrives
Leave all targets to each country with no review of results
optionExplain: Delay leaves the danger unaddressed.
Right: targets plus a way to correct them.
A fixed schedule cannot adapt to new evidence.
Leaving targets to each country with no review gives no monitoring and no shared learning.
questions.explain: The Montreal Protocol set targets and also required monitoring and review. The card next sets it out.
questions.rule: When facts are uncertain, set targets and provide for monitoring and revision of the targets.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
questions.q: In 1990 the phase-out schedule had to be hurried ____, and more chemicals added, because the damage was much greater than foreseen.
questions.explain: The protocol's review process allowed the schedule to be brought forward.
questions.rule: Review lets targets be revised.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
questions.q: Put the steps of the Montreal Protocol's learning process in order.
items: Set targets for phasing down the most damaging chemicals
Monitor the damage to the ozone layer
Reconvene an international congress to review the schedule
Hurry the schedule forward and add more chemicals
questions.explain: The protocol set targets in 1987, required monitoring and a review meeting, and in 1990 the schedule was moved forward and widened.
questions.rule: Target, monitor, review, revise.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
questions.q: True or false: The Montreal Protocol was signed after the danger to the ozone layer had been fully established.
questions.explain: In 1987 there was no certainty about the danger, the rate of degradation or the effect of specific chemicals.
questions.rule: Act under uncertainty, with review.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Make Feedback Policies for Feedback Systems
questions.q: A company launches a safety policy built to be reviewed and revised. Which claim does the author's stance on Montreal support?
options: Being structured for learning does not guarantee success in time
Learning-based policies are guaranteed to succeed because they can be revised
Learning-based policies are valuable only when the danger is already certain
Learning-based policies are pointless, since they will have to be changed anyway
optionExplain: Right: the author says only that he hopes it worked in time.
The author hopes, but does not claim, success.
The example concerns uncertainty.
Change is the purpose, not a sign of failure.
questions.explain: The author calls it a feedback policy structured for learning and says: We all hope that it worked in time.
questions.rule: Structured for learning is not proof of success.
questions.teaches: The author calls the protocol a feedback policy structured for learning but only hopes that it worked in time; he does not claim it did.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Go for the Good of the Whole
questions.q: A firm's sales department hits record numbers by pushing the cost of returns onto operations. How would the author see this?
options: As good management, because each part should pursue its own best result
As a problem only if sales fall in the following year
As irrelevant to systems thinking, since it is a matter of accounting
As maximizing one part of the system while ignoring the whole
optionExplain: The guideline says not to maximize parts while ignoring the whole, so this is not good management.
The problem is the whole system's performance, not next year's figure.
It is a case of part against whole.
Right: the guideline warns against this.
questions.explain: The author says not to maximize parts while ignoring the whole. The card next sets out the guideline.
questions.rule: Judge changes by their effect on the whole system's properties, not by how well one part does.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Go for the Good of the Whole
questions.q: The author says hierarchies exist to serve the ____ layers, not the top.
questions.explain: He says hierarchies exist to serve the bottom layers.
questions.rule: Hierarchy serves the base.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Go for the Good of the Whole
questions.q: Sort each action: does it serve the whole system, or maximize a part?

items.t: Weighing a transport change by its effect on the stability and resilience of the whole town
Judging a plan by how it affects diversity and sustainability in the region
Cutting one ward's costs by moving its patients' delays to the emergency unit
Raising one department's output by drawing on staff from every other department
Asking how a new rule affects the resilience of the organisation as a whole
Boosting one factory's yield at the cost of the shared water supply

questions.explain: The cases are our fresh examples of part versus whole.
questions.rule: Check the whole before the part.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Go for the Good of the Whole
questions.q: Which of these does the author name as total-system properties to enhance? Select all that apply.
options: Resilience
Diversity
Sustainability
Peak output of the best-run department
Efficiency of the largest subsystem
optionExplain: Right: named among total-system properties.
Right: named among total-system properties.
Right: named among total-system properties.
This is a property of a part, not of the whole.
This is a part-level measure.
questions.explain: The author lists growth, stability, diversity, resilience and sustainability.
questions.rule: Whole-system properties, not part measures.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Go for the Good of the Whole
questions.q: A team spends weeks polishing a report's format, then finds nobody reads the report. Which warning does the author quote from Kenneth Boulding?
options: Do not trust any measure of a system that is not a physical quantity
Do not change a system until its history has been fully recorded
Do not go to great trouble to optimize something that should not be done at all
Do not let those at the top of a hierarchy take decisions for those at the bottom
optionExplain: Trusting only physical quantities is not Boulding's remark; his warning is about optimizing what should not be done.
This is related to get-the-beat, not to Boulding's warning here.
Right: improving a pointless task is waste.
Hierarchy and decisions at the top and bottom is a different guideline, not Boulding's remark here.
questions.explain: Boulding warned against optimizing something that never should be done at all.
questions.rule: Ask whether it should be done at all.
questions.teaches: Quoting Kenneth Boulding, the author warns against going to great trouble to optimize something that never should be done at all.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Go for the Good of the Whole
questions.q: A council must decide on a plan. Which aim fits the guideline even though no ledger records it?
options: Only pursue aims that can be recorded as figures in the annual accounts
Raise the town's resilience, though no single figure measures it
Pursue the largest single department's targets, since they can be measured
Delay all decisions until a measure of town-wide resilience has been agreed
optionExplain: The author says to aim at these properties whether easily measured or not.
Right: the author says to aim at these properties whether or not easily measured.
Pursuing the largest department's targets maximizes a part and ignores the whole system's properties.
The guideline does not make action wait for a measure.
questions.explain: The author says to enhance total-system properties whether or not they are easily measured.
questions.rule: Whole-system aims count even when unmeasured.
questions.teaches: The author says to aim to enhance total-system properties such as resilience and sustainability whether or not they are easily measured.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Listen to the Wisdom of the System
questions.q: An agency plans to create jobs in a village by building a factory. What should it do first?
options: Find out what the village already does and what blocks its growth
Survey the investors who might fund a factory and ask what they require
Teach villagers the basics of entrepreneurship in a series of courses
Build the factory quickly so that the benefits arrive before the harvest
optionExplain: Right: look at the existing strengths first.
This starts with outside investors, not with the village.
This assumes villagers lack skills the author says they may already have.
Building the factory first acts before listening to what the village already does and needs.
questions.explain: The author says to pay attention to the value of what is already there. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Find and support what already keeps a system running before you replace or add to it.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Listen to the Wisdom of the System
questions.q: According to the author, many of the forces and structures that help a system run itself are found at the ____ of the hierarchy.
questions.explain: He tells us to notice how many of those forces and structures are at the bottom of the hierarchy.
questions.rule: Look at the bottom.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Listen to the Wisdom of the System
questions.q: A new manager wants to replace the informal peer-mentoring in her team with a corporate scheme. What does the guideline suggest?
options: Replace it at once, since informal structures are less reliable than formal ones
Leave the team entirely alone, since any change will destroy its capacities
Replace it only if a senior committee approves the new scheme
First find out what the mentoring does, since it may be self-maintaining
optionExplain: The author warns against unthinking intervention.
The guideline asks for attention, not for never acting.
Approval is not a test of whether the old structure works.
Right: understand before replacing.
questions.explain: The guideline asks you to check what already works. The mentoring case is our fresh example.
questions.rule: Learn what works before replacing it.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Listen to the Wisdom of the System
questions.q: Agencies arrived in a Guatemalan area to create jobs and increase entrepreneurial abilities. What error did the aid worker Nathan Gray see in them?
options: They failed to bring in enough outside investors to the area
They paid too little attention to teaching the local people to read and write
They walked past a thriving local market where people had made their own jobs
They set up factories without first writing a plan for the work
optionExplain: He concluded that outside investors were not what was needed.
He did recommend literacy classes.
Right: they overlooked existing enterprise.
The error was in overlooking what existed, not in lack of a plan.
questions.explain: The agencies came to create jobs and ignored the market, full of traders who had created jobs for themselves.
questions.rule: Notice what is already thriving.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Listen to the Wisdom of the System
questions.q: True or false: the aid worker Nathan Gray found out what was needed by talking with market traders about their lives and businesses.
questions.explain: He asked about their lives and businesses and learned what stood in the way of expansion and higher incomes.
questions.rule: Ask the people inside the system.
questions.teaches: Nathan Gray spent his time talking with the people in the market, asking about their lives and businesses and learning what stood in the way of expansion and rising incomes.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Listen to the Wisdom of the System
questions.q: A neighbourhood wants more local business. According to Nathan Gray's conclusion, which option is more promising?
options: Small loans at fair interest and bookkeeping classes for existing traders
Bringing in a large chain store to anchor the main shopping street of the district
Attracting an assembly plant whose workers will spend money locally
Offering grants to outside developers to build a new market hall
optionExplain: Right: inside investors, not outside ones.
This is the outside-investor approach he rejected.
He judged that a factory from outside would produce less long-term good.
This replaces the existing market rather than backing it.
questions.explain: Nathan concluded that inside investors, meaning small loans and classes in literacy and accounting, would do more long-term good than bringing in a factory.
questions.rule: Back the insiders.
questions.teaches: Nathan Gray concluded that inside investors, meaning small loans at reasonable interest and classes in literacy and accounting, would do more long-term good than an outside factory or assembly plant.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A shop's queues explode every December, and the manager blames the shoppers. What does the author's guideline warn?
options: The manager should instead blame the staff, who are inside the system
The manager should ignore December, since seasons are not under anyone's control at all
The manager should wait, since queues always settle without action
Blaming outside causes can hide the easier task of fixing how the system responds
optionExplain: Blame is not the point; structure is.
The author says triggers deserve attention.
The guideline asks for action on structure.
Right: look at the system's own part.
questions.explain: The author says blaming an outside influence can blind us to the easier task inside. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Pay attention to outside triggers, but look first for the system's own part in its behaviour.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: True or false: the author says some outside triggering events deserve attention and can sometimes be controlled.
questions.explain: He gives reducing pathogens in drinking water as an example, while adding that some outside events cannot be controlled.
questions.rule: Triggers matter, but not alone.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Sort each item: is it an outside trigger, or part of the system’s own structure that shapes its response?

items.t: A heavy rainstorm on a town
A sudden rumour spreading through a market
A freak cold snap during a harvest
Drains that have been narrowed over the years
A rule that delays reports of shortages for a month
A policy that makes banks lend more when prices rise

questions.explain: The first three bring forth behaviour from outside; the last three are how the system itself responds. The cases are ours.
questions.rule: Trigger and structure both matter.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Which example does the author give of an outside event that can sensibly be controlled?
options: Controlling the weather so that droughts and floods no longer occur in the region
Reducing pathogens in drinking water to keep down infectious disease
Controlling the price of oil so that imports are kept low
Controlling people's opinions so that markets do not panic
optionExplain: He gives no example of controlling the weather; his controllable example is pathogens in drinking water.
Right: his example of a controllable trigger.
This belongs to the feedback-policy discussion.
He gives no example of controlling opinions; the controllable trigger he names is waterborne pathogens.
questions.explain: Some triggers, like waterborne pathogens, can be controlled; some cannot.
questions.rule: Some triggers can be controlled.
questions.teaches: Some outside triggers can be controlled, as when pathogens in drinking water are reduced to keep down infectious disease, though others cannot.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Which statement best sums up the two sides of this guideline?
options: Attend to triggers, but do not let blaming them hide the system's own part
Attend only to the system's own structure, since triggers never matter in practice
Attend only to triggers, since the structure of the system follows from them
Attend to neither, since complex systems cannot be understood at all
optionExplain: Right: both halves.
The author says triggers deserve attention.
This is the view the guideline rejects.
He says they are understandable in a general way.
questions.explain: The guideline combines attention to triggers with a search for responsibility in the system.
questions.rule: Both, in that order.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: The author calls this guideline one for both analysis and design. Which use is design?
options: Studying a failed process to find out which outside event triggered the failure
Writing a report that names who was at fault for a past failure of the process
Counting the failures of the process over the last five years and reporting them
Setting up a new process whose structure sends consequences to those who decide
optionExplain: Finding which outside event triggered a failure is analysis, not design.
Naming who was at fault for a past failure is analysis or blame, not design.
This is description of past behaviour.
Right: building responsibility in.
questions.explain: The author says it is a guideline for analysis and for design. Designing means building responsibility into the structure.
questions.rule: Use it to analyze and to design.
questions.teaches: The author says the guideline serves both analysis, where one looks for the ways the system creates its own behavior, and design, where one builds responsibility into the system.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Why does it matter that a pilot rides in the front of the plane?
options: The pilot can see the passengers and so feels a duty of kindness to each of them
The pilot can reach the controls more easily from the front
The pilot feels the results of decisions directly, so is held responsible
The pilot is shielded from the effects of decisions at the front
optionExplain: The point is consequence, not sympathy.
The author's point is about responsibility.
Right: decision and consequence are joined.
It is the opposite: the pilot experiences them.
questions.explain: The author uses the pilot as his example of intrinsic responsibility. The card next sets it out.
questions.rule: Design systems so that the people who decide also feel the consequences soon and strongly.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Intrinsic responsibility means the system sends feedback about the consequences of decisions to the ____ makers directly and quickly.
questions.explain: The decision makers are the ones who must feel the results.
questions.rule: Send consequences to deciders.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Which design gives a company's staff intrinsic responsibility for software failures?
options: A separate support team handles all failures and reports monthly
The engineers who choose a release carry the pager when it fails
Failures are logged and reviewed in an annual assessment
A manager is held responsible for all releases from a distant office
optionExplain: The deciders feel nothing directly.
Right: deciders feel the consequences quickly.
An annual review is a slow feedback; the deciders do not feel consequences quickly.
The consequences do not reach those who choose.
questions.explain: Giving the pager to the people who choose the release joins decision and consequence. The example is ours.
questions.rule: Close the gap between decision and result.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: What happened when Dartmouth College moved thermostat control to a central computer?
options: Room temperatures swung more, since fixes took hours or days and overcorrected
Room temperatures became steadier, because a central computer is more precise than people
Energy use fell sharply, because staff were no longer able to waste heat in offices
Nothing changed in room temperatures, but costs became easier to audit
optionExplain: Right: the change reduced responsibility and added delay.
The author says the main consequence was greater oscillations.
He mentions that it was an energy-saving measure but reports greater oscillations.
He reports greater oscillations in room temperature.
questions.explain: A professor with an overheated office had to call across campus, and the correction took hours or days and often overcorrected.
questions.rule: Remove the thermostat and responsibility goes too.
questions.teaches: When Dartmouth moved thermostats to a central computer, the author saw greater oscillations in room temperature, because corrections took hours or days and often overcorrected.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Which designs does the author say could build intrinsic responsibility? Select all that apply.
options: Requiring towns and companies to place intake pipes downstream of their own outflow pipes
Forbidding Congress to legislate rules from which it exempts itself
Moving more decisions to a central office far from those affected
Letting rulers declare war without leading troops into battle
optionExplain: Right: they would drink what they discharge.
Right: lawmakers would live under their own rules.
This is the opposite, as with the Dartmouth thermostats.
The author says responsibility was lost when this became the practice.
questions.explain: The author says the first two could mean intrinsic responsibility; the other two reduce it.
questions.rule: Make deciders live with their decisions.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Loan officers sell every loan the same day and do not see defaults. Which loss does the author describe in similar terms?
options: Rulers began leading troops into battle again, which raised the stakes for them
Aid agencies stopped funding local markets, which cut local jobs
Governments began paying for medical costs of smokers, which raised health spending
Warfare grew more irresponsible when a button pushed at a distance hid the damage
optionExplain: This is the earlier arrangement he praises.
This belongs to the listening guideline.
This is a different design example in the section.
Right: distance from consequences removes responsibility.
questions.explain: A great deal of responsibility was lost when rulers no longer led troops and when a button pushed at a distance hid the damage.
questions.rule: Distance from consequences erodes responsibility.
questions.teaches: The author says responsibility was lost when rulers who declared war no longer led the troops, and war became more irresponsible when a button could cause damage at a distance the person pushing it never sees.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: You face a system you do not understand. What does the author advise?
options: Wait until you understand the system fully before you touch it at all
Act confidently and avoid showing any doubt, to keep others calm
Neither bluff nor freeze; experiment in small steps and learn
Copy the policy that worked in a similar system elsewhere
optionExplain: Waiting until you fully understand is freezing, which the author says not to do.
Acting confidently with no doubt is bluffing, which the author says not to do.
Right: act to learn.
This ignores the differences between systems.
questions.explain: The author says the thing to do when you do not know is not to bluff or freeze but to learn. The card next explains.
questions.rule: When uncertain, take small steps, watch the results and change course as you learn.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: The author says that when you do not know, the thing to do is not to bluff and not to ____, but to learn.
questions.explain: Both bluffing and freezing prevent learning.
questions.rule: Neither bluff nor freeze.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A start-up is unsure about a new market. Which plan matches the author's guideline?
options: Commit the full budget to the most likely plan and hold the course for two years
Run small pilots, monitor results and change course as the evidence comes in
Delay launch until market research can remove all uncertainty
Announce a confident forecast to attract investors and then follow it
optionExplain: This is charging ahead with a rigid directive.
Right: small steps, monitoring and willingness to change.
Delaying launch until all uncertainty is gone is freezing, which the author warns against.
Announcing a confident forecast and following it is bluffing, which the author warns against.
questions.explain: Small steps, constant monitoring and willingness to change course are the author's list. The start-up is our case.
questions.rule: Small steps, watch, adjust.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: True or false: the author says pretending to be in control when you are not is a recipe for not learning from mistakes.
questions.explain: He calls it a recipe not only for mistakes but for not learning from them.
questions.rule: Pretence blocks learning.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A leader says Stay the course is the best motto in any circumstance. What does the author say?
options: It is a poor idea in all circumstances, since courses never hold
It is a good idea whenever the leader is confident
It is a good idea only for organisations under outside pressure
It is a good idea only if you are sure you are on course
optionExplain: He allows it when you are sure.
Confidence is not the same as being sure; the author ties the motto to being on course.
He ties it to being sure of the course.
Right: it depends on being sure.
questions.explain: The author qualifies the motto: it fits only when you are sure.
questions.rule: Be sure before you stay the course.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A veteran nurse has an uneasy hunch that conflicts with reassuring numbers on a chart. Which stance matches what systems thinking taught the author?
options: Trust the numbers alone, since a hunch has no standing in a clinical decision
Trust the hunch alone, since numbers cannot capture what is wrong with a patient
Lean on both the hunch and the numbers, and stay ready for surprise
Wait, and do nothing at all until the hunch and the numbers agree
optionExplain: He says he learned to trust intuition more.
He says to lean on both the hunch and the numbers, not on the hunch alone.
Right: trust intuition more, rationality less, but use both.
Waiting until they agree is freezing; the author advises acting while staying ready for surprise.
questions.explain: The author says systems thinking taught him to trust intuition more and figuring-out rationality less, to lean on both, and to be prepared for surprises.
questions.rule: Use both intuition and reasoning.
questions.teaches: Systems thinking taught the author to trust his intuition more and his figuring-out rationality less, to lean on both as much as he can, and still to be prepared for surprises.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: After a project fails, a team quietly buries its review. What do they lose?
options: Nothing, since the project is over and no longer matters to anyone
The information about what went wrong, which learning needs
Only the goodwill of the customers who saw the failure happen
Only the time spent writing the review, which was wasted
optionExplain: Later projects may repeat the failure.
Right: hiding errors blocks learning.
The loss is wider than reputation.
The loss is the lesson, not the time.
questions.explain: The author says error-embracing is the condition for learning. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Seek, use and share information about what went wrong against what you expected.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: True or false: the author says embracing your errors takes a lot of courage.
questions.explain: He says it means making mistakes and, worse, admitting them.
questions.rule: Admitting errors takes courage.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Which unit shows error-embracing?
options: A hospital unit that shares near-miss reports and studies them
A unit that reviews its errors privately and files the reports away
A unit that punishes anyone whose mistake is reported by a colleague
A unit that publishes only its success statistics each quarter
optionExplain: Right: it seeks and shares information about what went wrong.
Reviewing errors privately seeks information but does not share it, so it falls short of error-embracing.
Punishing those whose mistakes are reported discourages the reporting error-embracing needs.
It shares only what went right.
questions.explain: Error-embracing means seeking, using and sharing information about what went wrong. The hospital is our case.
questions.rule: Share the near misses.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Which practices show error-embracing? Select all that apply.
options: A hospital unit shares near-miss reports openly and studies them
A team compares what happened with what it expected and records the gap
A manager punishes anyone whose mistake is reported
A firm publishes only its success statistics
optionExplain: Right: it seeks, uses and shares information about what went wrong.
Right: this is the author’s own wording for the information to seek.
This discourages reporting, so the information is lost.
It shares only what went right.
questions.explain: Error-embracing means seeking, using and sharing information about what went wrong with what you expected. The cases are ours.
questions.rule: Share the near misses.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: True or false: The author says people typically show their vulnerabilities openly to themselves and to others.
questions.explain: He says we typically hide our vulnerabilities from ourselves as well as from others.
questions.rule: We hide our vulnerabilities by habit.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A founder wants to project total certainty to investors about an untested market. What does the author say about accepting responsibility?
options: It requires only a written plan stating who is responsible for each task
It requires hiding doubts so that others are not discouraged by the founder
It requires knowledge of and access to self far beyond most people's
It requires investors who are strong enough to absorb the founder's mistakes
optionExplain: The quotation is about self-knowledge.
He argues against hiding vulnerability.
Right: it takes unusual self-knowledge.
The quotation is about the person.
questions.explain: The author quotes that truly accepting responsibility requires knowledge of and access to self far beyond that of most people.
questions.rule: Accepting responsibility takes self-knowledge.
questions.teaches: Truly accepting responsibility, the author says, requires knowledge of and access to self far beyond that possessed by most people in this society.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: True or false: The author sees the world mainly as a set of neat equilibria that are disturbed now and then.
questions.explain: He says the universe spends its time in transient behaviour on its way to somewhere else. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Welcome self-organization, variety and disorder as the working character of a living world.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: The author says the universe spends its time in ____ behaviour on its way to somewhere else, not in neat equilibria.
questions.explain: Transient behaviour is the normal condition of the world.
questions.rule: The world is in transit.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Sort each response to a changing city: does it celebrate complexity, or push toward tidiness?

items.t: Letting neighbourhoods develop a mix of small shops and homes
Encouraging varied uses and varied building sizes on one street
Supporting groups that organize themselves to run local gardens
Rebuilding every block to a single uniform grid
Banning shop types that do not fit a master plan
Insisting that all buildings be flat-faced boxes

questions.explain: The cases are ours; the first three welcome self-organization and diversity, the last three impose uniformity.
questions.rule: Welcome variety.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: The author quotes Aldo Leopold's land ethic. According to it, when is a thing right?
options: When it tends to maximize the output of the land for those who own, farm and use it
When it preserves the integrity, stability and beauty of the biotic community
When it tends to follow the written rules agreed by landowners and officials
When it tends to return the land to a fixed state of perfect equilibrium
optionExplain: This is the opposite of an ethic of the whole community.
Right: Leopold ties rightness to the community's integrity, stability and beauty.
Leopold's test is the effect on the community.
Leopold speaks of stability and beauty, not of a fixed equilibrium.
questions.explain: Leopold held that a thing is wrong when it tends otherwise. Some people, the author notes, make a moral code of encouraging diversity.
questions.rule: Leopold's test is the whole community.
questions.teaches: The author quotes Aldo Leopold's land ethic: a thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability and beauty of the biotic community, and wrong when it tends otherwise.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: True or false: the author says that preferring straight lines and tidy certainty is wrong in itself.
questions.explain: Our reading: he says part of the human mind is drawn to straight lines and certainty and that another part is drawn to complexity; his advice is to celebrate complexity, not to condemn tidiness.
questions.rule: Welcome complexity without condemning order.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A designer loves straight-line boxes and also delights in cathedral ornament. How does the author explain the two tastes?
options: A recent part of us favours straight lines, while the feedback-system part sees nature's fractals
Straight lines come from training and ornament from instinct, and the two cannot be reconciled in one designer
Both tastes come from the recent part of the mind that designs buildings as boxes with flat surfaces
Ornament is a passing fashion that fades, and straight lines are the lasting human taste in design
optionExplain: Right: two parts of us, one recent and one older.
He describes two tendencies within us rather than training against instinct.
He ties the straight-line taste to the recent part only.
He treats the love of complexity as deep, not as a passing fashion.
questions.explain: The author says part of us, an emerging part, designs boxes with straight lines, while another part, because we ourselves are complex feedback systems, recognises nature's fractals.
questions.rule: We are complex systems ourselves.
questions.teaches: The author says we ourselves evolved out of, and are structured as, complex feedback systems, so one part of us recognises that nature designs in fractals and makes cathedrals, carpets and symphonies, while a recent part builds uncompromising boxes.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A council judges every project by whether it pays back within ten years. What is a likely effect?
options: Short-term effects are ignored, since only the long term counts
All effects are weighed equally, however far ahead they fall
Projects are chosen for their effects on the next generation
Effects beyond the payback period drop out of its decisions
optionExplain: The payback rule does the opposite.
A payback horizon cuts off what lies beyond it.
Payback rules seldom look that far.
Right: the payback test hides the long term.
questions.explain: The author says payback periods give a rational excuse for ignoring the long term. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Look at both the immediate and the long-range effects of a decision, since time scales are nested.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Many Native American cultures, the author says, considered in their decisions the effects on the ____ generation to come.
questions.explain: This is his example of a long time horizon.
questions.rule: Think seven generations ahead.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Sort each decision rule: does it extend the time horizon, or shorten it?

items.t: Weigh a project by its effects on the next several generations
Weigh a project by its effects over the lifetimes of children and grandchildren
Weigh a project by the effects on both the near term and the decades beyond
Weigh a project by its payback within ten years
Weigh a project by how voters will feel at the next election
Weigh a project by the return in the next quarter

questions.explain: The first item echoes the seventh-generation view; the second echoes families’ horizons; the shortening rules are those the author names. The wording is ours.
questions.rule: Stretch the horizon.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: According to Kenneth Boulding, quoted by the author, what happens to a society that loses its identity with posterity and its image of the future?
options: It becomes more practical and so solves its present problems faster than before
It loses its capacity to deal with present problems and falls apart
It keeps its present problems but loses only its interest in art
It becomes stable, since it no longer worries about the future
optionExplain: Boulding argues the opposite: such a society loses its capacity to deal with present problems.
Right: the future image supports present competence.
His claim concerns capacity to deal with present problems.
Boulding says such a society falls apart, not that it becomes stable.
questions.explain: Boulding says this loss of a positive image of the future costs a society its capacity to deal with present problems.
questions.rule: A future image helps with present problems.
questions.teaches: Boulding, quoted by the author, says a society that loses its identity with posterity and its positive image of the future loses its capacity to deal with present problems and soon falls apart.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Ana says: systems thinking tells us to put the long term ahead of the short term. What does the author say?
options: In a strict systems sense there is no such distinction; time scales are nested
Systems thinking tells us the short term should come first because it is more certain
Systems thinking tells us to ignore the short term unless it is a crisis
Systems thinking tells us the long term is knowable and the short term is not
optionExplain: Right: nested time scales.
He does not rank them this way.
He asks us to watch the short term too.
He makes no claim that the long term is knowable and the short term is not.
questions.explain: He says actions have immediate effects and effects that radiate for decades; the whole system includes both.
questions.rule: Watch both.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: In a river basin, slow soil loss seems to do nothing for years, then fast floods dominate. Which point of the author's does this illustrate?
options: Short-term and long-term effects are separate processes that never interact at all
Slow processes are always more important than fast ones in every kind of system
Fast processes can be ignored, since they pass quickly and leave little behind
Nothing seems to happen while slow processes dominate, then fast ones take over
optionExplain: He says short and long term effects are coupled, not separate processes that never interact.
He does not say slow processes are always more important; the balance shifts between slow and fast.
He says they can take over with breathtaking speed.
Right: coupling of fast and slow processes.
questions.explain: Systems are always coupling and uncoupling the large and the small, the fast and the slow.
questions.rule: Fast and slow are coupled.
questions.teaches: The author says that when slow processes dominate nothing seems to be happening, and when fast ones take over things happen with breathtaking speed, because systems are always coupling and uncoupling the fast and the slow.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A study of urban flooding needs economists, engineers and psychologists. How should the team proceed, per the author?
options: Let each discipline study its part and then publish separate reports
Choose the discipline with the best track record and follow its approach
Follow the flooding system across all three fields, learning from each
Wait until a single new discipline of flood science has been established
optionExplain: This is the talking-past-each-other pattern.
This lets one lens limit the study.
Right: follow the system, not the discipline.
The guideline asks for crossing existing lines now.
questions.explain: The author says to follow a system wherever it leads. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Follow the system across disciplines, and take from each field what it honestly sees.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: True or false: the author says putting people from different disciplines together and letting them talk is enough to see systems whole.
questions.explain: He says this is what “interdisciplinary” usually means, and that it often becomes people talking past each other.
questions.rule: Cross lines for a real problem.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Which behaviours fit following a system across disciplines? Select all that apply.
options: Learning the jargon of fields you did not study
Keeping what a field honestly sees and discarding the distortions of its narrowness
Staying within the rules of your own training in order to stay credible
Placing specialists together and trusting that talk will produce insight
optionExplain: Right: the author says to penetrate their jargons.
Right: use each lens with care.
The guideline says to defy the disciplines.
The author says this often produces talk past each other.
questions.explain: The first two are the author's own advice; the last two are the narrow and the merely nominal approaches he warns about.
questions.rule: Cross lines, with care.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Under what conditions does the author say interdisciplinary communication works?
options: When the representatives are all drawn from closely related disciplines of the same school
When there is a real problem and members put solving it above academic correctness
When a respected senior scholar chairs the meeting and sets the agenda for the group
When each discipline keeps strict rules about what counts as evidence in the room
optionExplain: He asks for commitment to the problem, not similarity.
Right: the problem comes first.
He says nothing of chairs or agendas.
He says to be committed to solving the problem rather than being academically correct.
questions.explain: He says interdisciplinary communication works only if there is a real problem and members put it ahead of academic correctness.
questions.rule: A real problem unites disciplines.
questions.teaches: The author says interdisciplinary communication works only if there is a real problem to be solved and the representatives are more committed to solving it than to being academically correct.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A hospital forms a team of doctors, accountants and sociologists to cut waiting times. Which attitude does the author say they need?
options: Learning mode: admit ignorance and be taught by each other and the system
Expert mode: each member defends the standards of their own field against the others
Consensus mode: avoid disputes among the members to keep the project moving
Leadership mode: let the most senior member decide the approach for everyone
optionExplain: Right: the author asks for learning mode.
The author says they must go into learning mode.
He does not ask for avoiding disputes.
He asks them to learn from each other and the system.
questions.explain: The author says they must go into learning mode, admit ignorance and be willing to be taught by each other and by the system.
questions.rule: Learn from each other and the system.
questions.teaches: The author says representatives of different disciplines must go into learning mode: they must admit ignorance and be willing to be taught by each other and by the system.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A company cuts its workers' pay deeply while expecting to prosper. What does the author's guideline say?
options: Its success is separate from its workers' welfare, which is only a moral issue
Its success is safe so long as profits remain high in the short term
Its success depends on the global economy alone, not on its workers
Its success depends on its workers, so their failure would harm the company
optionExplain: The author says the interconnection is practical, not just moral.
The guideline is about interdependence, not short-term profit.
He names company and workers as linked.
Right: the system is interconnected.
questions.explain: The author says the company cannot succeed if its workers fail. The card next explains.
questions.rule: Count more people and parts as your own concern, because in an interconnected system their failure becomes yours.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Match each part the author says cannot succeed with the part whose failure would hurt it.
questions.explain: The author's examples all pair a part with the part it depends on.
questions.rule: Each part depends on another.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: Sort each plan: does it recognise interconnection, or treat parts as separate?

items.t: A town counts the harm to downstream villages when it designs its waste plant
A firm measures the effect of its cost cuts on the people who supply it
A nation sets farm policy with an eye to its effect on the soil and water it shares
A city plans a business district and treats the poorer districts as someone else's matter
A firm pays for growth by moving its costs onto the local environment
A school fixes the staff room and leaves the classrooms for later

questions.explain: The cases are ours; the first three treat the system as connected, the last three as separate.
questions.rule: Count the connections.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: What does the author say about people's knowledge of these interconnections?
options: Most people do not know them and have to be taught by trained specialists first
Most people know them but reject them as a matter of principle
Most people already know them and only have to bring themselves to believe it
Most people know them only in a moral sense, not a practical one
optionExplain: He says people already know these interconnections, so they do not need specialists to teach them first.
The problem is bringing themselves to believe, not principled rejection.
Right: the knowledge exists; the belief is missing.
He says moral and practical rules turn out to be the same.
questions.explain: He says people already know the interconnections that make moral and practical rules the same rules.
questions.rule: Knowing is not yet believing.
questions.teaches: The author says most people already know about the interconnections that make moral and practical rules the same rules; they only have to bring themselves to believe what they know.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A manager says a company can succeed while its workers fail, since their welfare is only a moral matter. What does the author answer?
options: Moral reasons alone are enough, so practical arguments should be left out of the case entirely
The manager is correct, since a company and its workers are separate systems in practice
The company will fail only if its competitors are also run in the same way as it is today
Systems thinking adds practical reasons: the firm cannot succeed if its workers fail
optionExplain: He adds the practical reasons for those not persuaded by morality.
He says no part is separate in the real system.
His claim is about interdependence, not about competitors.
Right: the practical reasons back up the moral ones.
questions.explain: The author says that if moral arguments are not sufficient, systems thinking provides practical reasons, and that the company cannot succeed if its workers fail.
questions.rule: Practical reasons back the moral ones.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.q: A planner widens a project's time horizon and the disciplines consulted, but not whose welfare is counted. Which priority of the author's does this miss?
options: He says time horizons matter most, so the planner's widening is enough to proceed
He says that above all it means widening the horizons of caring
He says disciplines matter most, so the planner has done the essential work already
He says caring is a private matter, not a matter for planning or for design
optionExplain: He says caring matters above all, so widening time horizons alone does not suffice.
Right: caring comes first among the horizons.
He ranks caring above thought horizons.
He says there are practical reasons as well.
questions.explain: The author says living successfully with complex systems means expanding not only time horizons and thought horizons but, above all, the horizons of caring.
questions.rule: Caring comes first among the horizons.
questions.teaches: The author says living successfully in a world of complex systems means expanding time horizons and thought horizons, but above all the horizons of caring.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Don’t Erode the Goal of Goodness
questions.q: Media coverage dwells on bad conduct, and good conduct is treated as not news. What is the long-run effect on expectations?
options: Expectations of behaviour fall, so the standard drifts down
Expectations rise, because people become angry about the bad conduct
Expectations stay the same, since people judge for themselves
Expectations become more varied, with no clear direction
optionExplain: Right: this is how drift to low performance works.
The author says expectations are lowered.
He describes a loop that lowers them.
He describes a downward drift.
questions.explain: The author says this is the classic drift to low performance. The card next sets it out.
questions.rule: Keep standards absolute and give good news its due weight so the goal of goodness is not worn away.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Don’t Erode the Goal of Goodness
questions.q: The author calls the trap that erodes the goal of morality drift to ____ performance.
questions.explain: He names the archetype drift to low performance.
questions.rule: Standards drift down.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Don’t Erode the Goal of Goodness
questions.q: Put the steps of the author's account of moral erosion in order.
items: Examples of bad behaviour are held up as typical
Expectations are lowered
The gap between desired and actual behaviour narrows
Fewer actions are taken to affirm and instill ideals
Public discourse fills with cynicism
questions.explain: The author traces a loop from magnified bad examples to lowered expectations, a narrowing gap, less affirmation of ideals and cynicism.
questions.rule: Bad news up, standards down.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Don’t Erode the Goal of Goodness
questions.q: Joseph Wood Krutch, quoted by the author, describes modern man as confident of his power. What low estimate does he say man holds?
options: Of his wealth: he believes he will soon lose all that he has
Of his power: he doubts that science can do what he sets his mind to
Of his future: he expects that his machines will fail him
Of what he is: for all his wealth and power he is poor in spirit
optionExplain: Krutch says he is complacent about what he has.
Krutch says he is confident of his ability.
The quotation concerns what he is.
Right: the contrast is power without regard for self.
questions.explain: Krutch says man has never been so complacent about what he has, yet never accepted so low an estimate of what he is.
questions.rule: Power without self-regard is poverty of spirit.
questions.teaches: Krutch, quoted by the author, says man was never so confident of his ability and so complacent about what he has, and never accepted so low an estimate of what he is: poor in spirit.

questions.unitTitle: Living in a World of Systems
questions.section: Don’t Erode the Goal of Goodness
questions.q: A school posts a few cheating cases on the wall and does not mention its honest students. Which further effect does the author describe?
options: Honest students are praised more, so honesty rises quickly across the whole school
Students ignore the posters, so nothing changes in the culture of the school
Moral statements become suspect, and it is easier to talk about hate than love
Cheating falls, since it is now visible to everyone and punished more quickly
optionExplain: The author describes the opposite spiral.
He describes a drift, not no change.
Right: cynicism makes idealism seem foolish.
He describes lowered expectations, not deterrence.
questions.explain: The author says idealism is ridiculed, statements of moral belief are suspect, and it is much easier to talk about hate in public than about love.
questions.rule: Cynicism makes ideals sound foolish.
questions.teaches: In the author's account of drift to low performance, idealism is ridiculed, statements of moral belief become suspect, and it is much easier to talk about hate in public than about love.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which claim does Meadows call a central insight of systems theory?
options: A system's behavior is mainly decided by the strength of the outside force that pushes it
A system's own structure holds behavior that outside hands can release or hold back
A system behaves best when its parts are studied one at a time and then added up again
A system's outcomes are best explained by finding the one decision-maker who set them in motion
optionExplain: A common intuition, and it is the view the Slinky and box example is meant to unsettle.
Right: the Slinky shows behavior lying latent in the structure. The card next shows how the book builds on it.
The book does take parts apart, but it says a system is more than the sum of its parts.
The introduction argues against blaming presidents, competitors and other outside agents.
questions.explain: The Slinky drops and bounces, the box does not, though the same hand moves. The hands suppress or release behavior latent in the structure. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Outside events release behavior; structure shapes it.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: The book's third part is titled Creating Change in Systems and in Our ____.
questions.explain: Part Three is called Creating Change, in Systems and in Our Philosophy. Its two chapters are on leverage points and on living in a world of systems.
questions.rule: Part Three: change the system and change how we think.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two hospitals receive the same flu outbreak. One copes and one is overwhelmed. Which reading fits the book's central claim?
options: Look for the stronger virus strain at the overwhelmed hospital, since the cause must be outside it
Look at which hospital had the most energetic manager
Look at the size of the outbreak alone, since a bigger push always means a bigger problem
Look at how each hospital's own staffing, stocks and routines shaped its response
optionExplain: Plausible, but the same outbreak reached both, which points to differences in the systems.
Meadows warns against blaming people before looking at structure.
The Slinky and the box differ under the same push, so push size cannot be the whole story.
Right: the same event applied to a different system is likely to give a different result.
questions.explain: The book's claim is that the system largely causes its own behavior, so a fair comparison starts with the structures that responded to the same event.
questions.rule: Same push, different system, different result.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each part of the book to the question its chapters mainly answer.
pairs: Part One: System Structure and Behavior
What are stocks, flows and loops, and what do they make a system do?
Why do systems work, surprise us and trap us?
Where can we intervene, and how do we live with systems?
questions.explain: The parts follow the book's own titles: structure and behavior, then our encounter with systems, then change. Matching questions to parts is our summary of those titles.
questions.rule: Structure, then our encounter with it, then change.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which summary overstates what Meadows claims in the Introduction about outside events?
options: Outside events play no part, because every pattern of behavior is created from inside the system
Outside events can set off behavior, but the same event on a different system may give a different result
Outside forces can buffet or trigger a system, but its response is characteristic of itself
Leaders and competitors share the blame, since the system itself also helps create its losses
optionExplain: Right: she says an outside event may unleash the behavior, and the system causes it only to a large extent.
This matches her wording: events may unleash behavior that the structure shapes.
She says a system may be buffeted, constricted, triggered or driven, and responds in its own way.
She says a company creates its losses at least in part through its own policies.
questions.explain: The claim is hedged: the system, to a large extent, causes its own behavior. Saying outside events play no part drops that hedge.
questions.rule: Structure is a main cause, not the only one.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A reader hopes the last part will finally give a method to predict and control any system. What does Chapter Seven say?
options: It confirms the hope
It confirms the hope for physical systems and rejects it only for human and social ones
It calls that a terrible mistake, since such systems cannot be predicted or controlled
It says the hope is sound but that the computing power to realize it does not yet exist
optionExplain: Part One supplies understanding of structure, not forecasts; Chapter Seven says otherwise.
The chapter calls self-organizing, nonlinear, feedback systems in general unpredictable.
Right: the chapter opens by calling the hope for prediction and control a mistake of the industrial mind-set.
The chapter says exact foresight is unrealizable, not merely delayed.
questions.explain: Chapter Seven opens by correcting this assumption: self-organizing, nonlinear, feedback systems are inherently unpredictable and not controllable.
questions.rule: The last part withdraws the hope of control.
questions.teaches: Chapter Seven begins by calling the expectation of prediction and control through systems analysis a terrible mistake.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: The same building blocks, chapter after chapter
questions.q: Which pair of ideas from the early chapters would you expect the later chapters to reuse most?
options: Elements and purposes, since every later chapter is mainly about listing a system's visible parts
Graph conventions, since later chapters are mostly about drawing and reading time graphs
Delays and feedback loops, since they explain why systems overshoot, hold steady or run away
Model equations, since later chapters rely on calculating exact values to predict outcomes
optionExplain: Elements are the easy part to see; the later chapters concentrate on connections and loops.
Graphs help, but they are a tool for seeing behavior, not the recurring cause of it.
Right: these keep returning in chapters on surprise, traps and leverage. The card next traces them.
The book stays nontechnical, and puts the equations in an Appendix.
questions.explain: Chapters Four to Six lean on delays and loops again and again, so they are the safest guess. The card shows where.
questions.rule: Delays and loops recur.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: The same building blocks, chapter after chapter
questions.q: Match each chapter to the way it treats delays.
pairs: A delay in a balancing loop makes a dealership's inventory oscillate
Delays are everywhere and are one of the reasons systems surprise us
Delays are item 9 on the list of places to intervene
questions.explain: The same piece is shown first at work, then as a source of surprise, then as a leverage point.
questions.rule: One piece, three jobs.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: The same building blocks, chapter after chapter
questions.q: A restaurant hires cooks when the dining room is full, but training takes four months, so staffing swings. Which piece explains it?
options: A delay in a balancing loop, so the system overshoots and undershoots its goal
A reinforcing loop in which more cooks create more diners who need still more cooks
A badly drawn boundary
A change of purpose, since the restaurant has started to serve a different function
optionExplain: Right: information arrives, the response takes months, and the correction overshoots.
A reinforcing loop would amplify in one direction rather than swing back and forth.
Boundaries matter, but the up-and-down swing is the signature of delay, not of a badly drawn boundary.
Nothing in the case changes what the system is for; the timing of the response is the issue.
questions.explain: Late response inside a balancing loop is the Chapter Two pattern, and it explains swings anywhere stocks are adjusted with delay.
questions.rule: Delay plus correction gives swing.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: The same building blocks, chapter after chapter
questions.q: True or false: Every one of the twelve places to intervene in Chapter Six is a stock, a flow, a delay or a feedback loop.
questions.explain: The top three items, goals, paradigms and transcending paradigms, are about purpose and belief. The building blocks do not cover the whole book.
questions.rule: Know where the blocks stop.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: The same building blocks, chapter after chapter
questions.q: A developer starts building flats when rents are high, but each building takes three years. What pattern should the market show over a decade?
options: A steady match of flats to demand
A steady shortage, because builders can never keep up with the demand that high rents show
Steady growth in flats, because each new building raises the rent that pays for the next
Swings between shortage and surplus, as in the electric power industry
optionExplain: Price is a signal, but a signal that arrives before a three-year delay cannot give a steady match.
A long delay means builders eventually overshoot, not that they always fall short.
Reinforcing growth is possible, but rents fall when supply overshoots, so the balancing loop wins.
Right: long building delays make it hard to match supply to changing demand, so overshoot and undershoot follow.
questions.explain: In the book's power plant case, a plant takes several years to build and lasts about thirty, so electricity industries oscillate between over- and undercapacity. Housing has the same delayed balancing loop.
questions.rule: Long build delays produce long swings.
questions.teaches: Meadows notes that because power plants take years to build, almost every electricity industry swings long between overcapacity and undercapacity.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Why systems work, and what they rest on
questions.q: According to Meadows, what gives a system resilience?
options: One very strong balancing loop that holds the stock at its goal under any shock
Several feedback loops working in different ways, with backups if one fails
A steady, unchanging state that keeps variation to a minimum in every part of the system
A central controller that watches every part and directs the lower layers when trouble comes
optionExplain: A single loop returns a stock to its goal, but one loop fails when it fails.
Right: a rich structure of many loops. The card next adds how it climbs to self-organization.
Holding everything constant is not what resilience means; it is the ability to recover after disturbance.
Chapter Three says overcontrol from the top can damage the whole.
questions.explain: Meadows says resilience arises from many feedback loops operating through different mechanisms, at different time scales and with redundancy. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Resilience is many loops, not one.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Why systems work, and what they rest on
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says resilience comes from several feedback loops that work in different ways, not from one loop.
questions.explain: A single balancing loop brings a stock back to its desired state. Resilience needs several loops operating through different mechanisms, at different time scales and with redundancy.
questions.rule: Resilience needs backup loops.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Why systems work, and what they rest on
questions.q: A town recovers from floods using insurance, volunteers, a reserve fund and building codes. What makes it resilient in Meadows's sense?
options: It has one agency that coordinates every part of flood response from a single office
It has avoided all variation, since floods never change the town's way of life
It has the largest single flood wall that its budget could pay for, built once and left alone
It has several restoring loops acting through different mechanisms and at different speeds
optionExplain: Coordination alone is not what the chapter names; it names many different loops with backups.
Resilience is recovery after disturbance, not avoidance of every change.
One strong defence is a single loop or buffer; the chapter stresses variety and backup.
Right: insurance, volunteers, savings and codes work at different time scales and back each other up.
questions.explain: The town's responses are different loops operating on different time scales, so if one fails another can take over.
questions.rule: Variety and backup give resilience.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Why systems work, and what they rest on
questions.q: Put these levels in the order Meadows climbs them, lowest first.
items: One balancing loop restores a stock to its goal
Several loops with different mechanisms and backups give resilience
Loops that restore or rebuild other loops give meta-resilience
Loops that learn, design and evolve new restorative structures make a system self-organizing
questions.explain: Meadows moves from one loop to many, then to loops that rebuild loops, then to loops that learn and evolve, which is self-organization.
questions.rule: From restoring a stock to restructuring the system.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Why systems work, and what they rest on
questions.q: A student summarizes the chapter. Which sentence gets the hierarchy idea wrong?
options: Hierarchies let subsystems manage themselves while the larger system coordinates them
Hierarchies are built from the top down, and upper layers exist to direct lower ones
Hierarchies grow from the pieces to the whole, as cells became organs and organisms
Hierarchies can fail when a part pursues its own goals over those of the whole
optionExplain: This matches the chapter's description.
Right: Meadows says hierarchies evolve from the bottom up, and upper layers serve the lower ones.
This matches her statement that hierarchies evolve from the lowest level up.
This is the chapter's point about suboptimization.
questions.explain: Hierarchical systems evolve from the bottom up. The purpose of the upper layers is to serve the purposes of the lower layers.
questions.rule: Hierarchy grows from the bottom and serves it.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.section: Why systems work, and what they rest on
questions.q: A farm manager sets one crop, fixed schedules and tight controls to make output perfectly constant. What does Chapter Three's epigraph from ecologist Holling suggest?
options: Constancy is the surest route to resilience
Constancy is harmless, so long as there are several balancing loops somewhere on the farm
Forcing constancy may let fragility evolve, leaving the farm less able to bounce back
Constancy matters only for living systems, so the lesson does not apply to a managed farm
optionExplain: Holling says the opposite; resilience is the ability to recover, not the absence of variation.
Loops help, but forcing constancy on the whole system is what the warning is about.
Right: Holling warns that a straitjacket of constancy can cause fragility to evolve.
The epigraph speaks of placing a system in a straitjacket, which is what the manager does.
questions.explain: Holling's epigraph says that placing a system in a straitjacket of constancy can cause fragility to evolve. Variation is part of how resilience develops.
questions.rule: Do not trade away variation for neatness.
questions.teaches: An epigraph in Chapter Three, from ecologist Holling, warns that placing a system in a straitjacket of constancy can cause fragility to evolve.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: What does Meadows say about surprise once you understand the characteristics of systems?
options: You will be surprised less often, but you will still be surprised
You will no longer be surprised, because each surprise is explained by one of the listed properties
You will be surprised as often as before, because knowing the list changes nothing about the real world
You will be surprised only by human behavior
optionExplain: Right: understanding reduces surprise without removing it. The card next gives her reasons.
She says the opposite: surprise remains.
She says you may be surprised less often, so the list does help.
She names surprises in many kinds of systems, not only human ones.
questions.explain: She puts it as bad news or good news: even knowing these characteristics, you may be surprised less often, but you will still be surprised. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Less surprise, not none.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Meadows says that everything we think we know about the world is a ____.
questions.explain: Words, maps, statistics, books, equations and the pictures in our heads are all models. None of them is the real world.
questions.rule: Everything we know is a model.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
