questions.q: A plant manager forecasts output from machine counts, but output stalls when a scarce chemical runs short. Which warning-list item is this?
options: A limiting factor the model left out, so the scarcest input decides the outcome
A flawed boundary, because the manager forgot to draw the factory walls on the diagram
A delay in perception, because the manager received the count of machines too late
A sign of bounded rationality
optionExplain: Right: models that count only the obvious input miss the one that actually limits.
Boundaries matter, but the case is about a scarce input limiting output, not about the walls.
Nothing in the case concerns slow information; it concerns an input that ran short.
The case does not describe people choosing a locally good but globally bad action.
questions.explain: Counting machines treats one input as the limit, while another input, in short supply, actually sets output. It is the limiting-factor gap in a model.
questions.rule: Find the scarcest input.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each term: is it a reason for surprise in Chapter Four, or a trap named in Chapter Five?

items.t: Delays in feedback loops
Nonlinear relationships
Boundaries drawn in the wrong place
Bounded rationality
Policy resistance
Escalation
Drift to low performance
Success to the successful

questions.explain: Chapter Four lists properties found in nearly any system; Chapter Five names archetypes, structures that produce problem behavior.
questions.rule: Properties surprise us; archetypes trap us.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A manager wants to redesign the firm so that it has no delays and no nonlinearities, to avoid surprises. What does Chapter Five suggest?
options: Go ahead, since delays and nonlinearities are the traps the book wants removed from every system
Remove delays but not nonlinearities
Do not try, since such properties generally should not be changed; learn to expect them
Remove both, but only after a model has shown the exact effect of each change on the firm
optionExplain: They are not the traps; she says these properties are found in just about any system.
She says neither is generally something to change.
Right: she says being less surprised is mainly a matter of learning to expect, appreciate and use complexity.
Her advice is not to try to remove them, whatever the model shows.
questions.explain: Chapter Five says delays, nonlinearities and fuzzy boundaries are found in just about any system. They generally are not properties that can or should be changed.
questions.rule: Expect complexity; do not wish it away.
questions.teaches: Chapter Five says that properties which surprise us, such as delays and nonlinearities, generally cannot or should not be changed; being less surprised means learning to expect and use complexity.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Why does Meadows call the common problem structures of Chapter Five traps?
options: People who understand them are always caught in them anyway, so awareness has no value
Standard responses such as blaming or pushing harder do not fix structural problems
They arise only in poorly run organizations, whose managers have allowed them to form
They cannot be changed at all, because every system keeps its structure for ever
optionExplain: She says traps can be escaped by recognizing them in advance.
Right: the habitual responses leave the structure in place. The card next adds why she also calls them opportunities.
She treats them as common structures, found in many kinds of systems.
She says they can be changed by altering goals and feedback loops.
questions.explain: Blaming, firing, twisting policy levers harder and tinkering at the margins will not fix structural problems, so the structures act as traps. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Trap: the usual responses fail.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Meadows calls the archetypes both traps and ____, because they can be escaped by altering structure.
questions.explain: Her chapter title is System Traps and Opportunities. The opportunity lies in changing goals and feedback loops.
questions.rule: Traps can be redesigned.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Two shops each cut prices to undercut the other's last cut. Using Chapter Five, which response fits best?
options: Blame the owner who cut first and replace that person, so the race can reset itself
Wait, because races between equals level off by themselves when prices reach a limit
Cut prices faster still, so the rival gives way before the loop gathers strength
Break the reinforcing loop: one shop backs off, or both agree new controls
optionExplain: Replacing a player leaves the loop in place.
A reinforcing race does not level off by itself; it ends when someone breaks.
More effort inside the loop feeds it.
Right: escalation is a reinforcing loop, and the ways out interrupt it.
questions.explain: A race in which each side sets its level by the other's is a reinforcing loop. The ways out are to back off or to negotiate new balancing controls.
questions.rule: Interrupt the loop; do not feed it.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A firm replaces every manager inside a trap, but its goals, rules and feedback loops stay the same. What should you expect?
options: A clear improvement, because the new managers will not share the old managers' habits
The same kind of behavior, because the structure that produced it is still there
A worse result, because new managers do not yet know how the loops work
No change at all, because traps fade after a year whoever is in charge
optionExplain: The book says swapping elements rarely changes what a system is while links and purpose survive.
Right: changing players is a low-level move unless goals, information or rules also change.
Nothing in the book predicts it will be worse; it predicts similar behavior.
Traps do not fade by themselves; they persist while the structure does.
questions.explain: Chapter One says swapping elements rarely changes a system if the links and purpose survive, and Chapter Six repeats it for players.
questions.rule: New players, same structure, same pattern.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: According to Chapter Five, match each trap to the structure behind it.
pairs: Actors with different goals pull one stock in opposite directions
Each actor sets its goal by the rival's state and adds a little more
Feedback from the state of the resource to its users is missing or late
The standard falls whenever perceived performance falls
questions.explain: These are the structures the chapter gives for each trap. Our summary groups them as loops and goals from the earlier chapters.
questions.rule: Name the structure, then the way out.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A student says archetypes are rare academic curiosities. What evidence does Meadows give against that?
options: She tested each archetype in a laboratory simulation and found it in every run
She counted that most corporations report at least one trap in their annual reports
She shows that each archetype appears in every system of more than two stocks
She found examples of each archetype in a single week of one newspaper
optionExplain: She does not describe laboratory tests as her evidence here.
No such count of corporate reports appears in the chapter; her evidence is one newspaper week.
She does not claim that every system contains them.
Right: the traps are so prevalent that one week of the International Herald Tribune supplied examples of each.
questions.explain: Meadows says she had no problem finding, in just one week of the International Herald Tribune, enough examples to illustrate each archetype in the chapter.
questions.rule: The traps are common.
questions.teaches: Meadows says she found in a single week of one newspaper enough examples to illustrate every archetype in Chapter Five, showing how prevalent they are.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: On Meadows's list of places to intervene, which kind of change has the least leverage?
options: Adjusting numbers such as taxes, subsidies and standards
Changing the rules that set incentives, punishments and constraints
Adding a new information flow to a decision-maker who lacked feedback
Changing the size of a buffer that stabilizes a stock
optionExplain: Right: numbers are item 12, last on the list. The card next shows why the list is ordered this way.
Rules are item 5, far higher on the list.
Information flows are item 6, a high leverage point.
Buffers are item 11, low but still above numbers.
questions.explain: Meadows ranks numbers dead last on her list of powerful interventions, though most attention goes to them. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Numbers are the lowest lever.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Put these places to intervene in order from lowest leverage to highest.
items: Numbers
Delays
Rules
Goals
Paradigms
questions.explain: On the list they are items 12, 9, 5, 3 and 2. The smaller the number, the greater the leverage.
questions.rule: Read the list upward from 12 to 1.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A school is failing. Which of these changes has the most leverage on Meadows's list?
options: Raising the pass mark from 50 to 55 percent in every subject
Replacing the head teacher while leaving funding rules and aims unchanged
Changing the shared belief that test scores measure what learning is for
Adding two classrooms to ease crowding in the existing building
optionExplain: A number is item 12, the lowest lever.
Changing players is a low-level move if the system stays the same.
Right: a shared assumption is a paradigm, item 2, from which goals and rules arise.
This is a change to physical structure, item 10, far lower than a paradigm.
questions.explain: The belief that scores equal learning is an unstated shared assumption. Meadows places paradigms second from the top.
questions.rule: Beliefs sit above rules and numbers.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: If you move from adjusting a tax rate to changing the shared belief behind the tax system, what should you expect?
options: Smaller effects, because beliefs are vague and a rate is exact
Less resistance, because beliefs cost nothing to change compared with laws
Bigger potential effects, but also stronger resistance from the system
The same effect, because rates and beliefs are equivalent at each level
optionExplain: Meadows says paradigms are the sources of systems, so their effects are larger.
She notes paradigm change is not physical, but whole societies resist challenges to paradigms harder than anything.
Right: the higher the leverage point, the more the system will resist changing it.
The list rests on the point that the levels differ.
questions.explain: Higher leverage means more potential effect and more resistance. Societies resist challenges to their paradigms harder than they resist anything else.
questions.rule: More leverage, more resistance.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Meadows places paradigms at the very bottom of the list because they are the hardest thing to change.
questions.explain: She admits paradigms could be argued to belong at the bottom for how hard they are to change, but she keeps them second from the top because their influence is so great and changing a mind is not physical, expensive or slow.
questions.rule: Leverage is about influence, not ease.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A mayor answers every city problem with more economic growth. Using Forrester's World model in Chapter Six, how would Meadows judge this?
options: Growth is a leverage point, but pushed in the wrong direction, since its costs are uncounted
Growth is the right lever and the mayor pushes the right way, since growth pays for solutions
Growth is not a leverage point at all, since no single variable can shift a whole city
Growth is a low lever like a number, so the mayor's effort changes little either way
optionExplain: Right: she says leaders are pushing with all their might the wrong way on growth.
She says the opposite: growth has costs that we typically do not count.
Forrester's model identified growth as a clear leverage point.
She treats growth as high leverage, which is why pushing it backward matters.
questions.explain: Forrester's World model found growth, both population and economic, to be a leverage point, and its costs are among the problems growth is meant to solve. The leaders push the wrong way.
questions.rule: Check the direction of the push.
questions.teaches: Forrester's World model found that growth, including economic growth, is a leverage point, but that leaders fixated on it push in the wrong direction because its costs are not counted.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which leverage point does Meadows illustrate with the collapse of commercial fisheries?
options: Numbers, because fishing quotas are parameters that could be adjusted each season
Paradigms, because fishing communities share beliefs about the sea's endless supply
Delays, because fish populations take years to recover once they are depleted
Information flows, since little feedback runs from fish stocks to fleet investors
optionExplain: She uses the fishery to show a missing information flow, not a quota.
She does not tie the fishery example to paradigms.
Delays are discussed under another item, not this example.
Right: missing feedback is a common cause of system malfunction. The card next sets this beside the other links.
questions.explain: She says the commons crash because there is little feedback from the state of the fish population to the decision to invest in vessels. Price is not the right signal. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Missing feedback is a lever.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says weakening the reinforcing loops that feed winners beats relying on antipoverty programs, which are weak balancing loops.
questions.explain: She describes the success-to-the-successful loops, calls antipoverty programs weak balancing loops against them, and says weakening the reinforcing loops would be much more effective.
questions.rule: Weaken the loop that feeds winners.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: On a marketplace, top sellers get more visibility, which brings more sales, which keeps them on top. What response fits Meadows's advice for this loop?
options: Give small sellers a monthly cash grant to offset the gap, leaving visibility rules as they are
Weaken the loop that favors winners, for example by capping the visibility any seller can win
Tell the top sellers to show restraint voluntarily, since a call for restraint will limit their gains
Wait for the leading sellers to leave the platform
optionExplain: A grant is a weak balancing patch against a strong reinforcing loop.
Right: it targets the reinforcing loop itself, the move she prefers.
Exhortation does not change the loop, and Chapter Five treats appeals alone as fragile.
Their successors would simply inherit the same loop.
questions.explain: This is the success-to-the-successful trap. Meadows says to weaken the loops that reward winners with the means to win again, not to patch the effects.
questions.rule: Treat the loop, not its symptoms.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Match each case that Chapter Six describes to the leverage point it illustrates.
pairs: Wealthy winners gain the means to win again
Little feedback from fish stocks to fleet investors
A trade system whose rules shut out most of society
questions.explain: Each case is one Meadows herself tells under the named item. Her emphasis is on weakening the loop, restoring the feedback and watching who writes the rules.
questions.rule: Case, then lever.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which statement about the traps and the leverage list goes beyond what Meadows says?
options: She ties the success-to-the-successful trap to the leverage point on reinforcing loops
She uses the commons trap to illustrate the leverage point on information flows
She says missing feedback loops are among the most common causes of system malfunction
She says each of the eight traps has exactly one matching leverage point
optionExplain: She does tie them, in Chapter Six, so this statement is within what she says.
She does, using the fisheries, so this statement is within what she says.
She does, under information flows.
Right: she links some traps to some items but never draws a one-to-one table; the full mapping is inference.
questions.explain: She never says every trap has exactly one lever. Our reading maps the others, and should be labelled as such.
questions.rule: Label inference as inference.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A city reports rising downtown smog to commuters, yet driving keeps growing. What does Meadows's aquifer example suggest would work better?
options: Publish a clearer daily chart of smog levels
Tie a driving charge to the smog level so it rises steeply as air quality worsens
Ask commuters to drive less on bad days, since moral appeals build shared restraint
Stop reporting the smog level, to avoid alarm and to keep drivers from rushing out
optionExplain: She says informing users alone could start a race to the bottom.
Right: feedback should reach decision-makers in a compelling form, as with water priced to climb once pumping exceeds recharge.
Exhortation is fragile, as the commons discussion shows.
Hiding the information removes the very feedback she wants restored.
questions.explain: Meadows says restoring feedback is not enough on its own: it must reach the right place in compelling form, such as a charge that climbs steeply as the harm grows.
questions.rule: Feedback must be placed and made strong.
questions.teaches: Meadows says that merely telling aquifer users the water level is dropping could start a race to the bottom; the feedback should be compelling, such as a water price that rises steeply once pumping exceeds recharge.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: How does Meadows describe the right relationship to complex systems at the end of the book?
options: Commanding them, once the stocks and loops have been modelled accurately enough
Observing them from outside, since any intervention makes complex systems worse
Dancing with them, since they cannot be fully controlled or figured out
Optimizing them, one subsystem at a time
optionExplain: She calls the conqueror's stance a mistake.
She urges participation, not distance.
Right: she says we can dance with systems. The card next shows how the chapter reaches that.
She says we cannot optimize, and do not even know what to optimize.
questions.explain: She writes that we cannot control systems or figure them out, but we can dance with them. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Dance; do not conquer.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: According to Meadows, her own early systems group gave learned lectures on addiction yet could not give up coffee.
questions.explain: She says her group did not follow its own advice: they lectured on addiction and could not give up coffee, and warned about escalation and then created it in their marriages.
questions.rule: Knowing is not doing.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A school board hides test results from teachers to avoid alarm. Which guideline in Chapter Seven does this break?
options: Honor, respect and distribute information, so those who must act can see it
Locate responsibility in the system
Expand the boundary of caring, since the board has ignored students at other schools
Celebrate complexity, since the board has tried to make results simpler than they are
optionExplain: Right: withholding it keeps the feedback from the people who could respond.
That guideline is about looking at a system's own part in its behavior, not at withheld data.
The case concerns information flow, not whom the board counts as its concern.
That guideline is about welcoming variety and disorder, not about reporting results.
questions.explain: Meadows says information should be timely, accurate and complete and shared with those who must act. Hiding it removes feedback.
questions.rule: Feedback needs to reach decision-makers.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: In our reading, match each Chapter Seven practice to the earlier finding it most directly echoes.
pairs: Chapter Four: every model falls short of the real world
Chapters Five and Six: missing feedback is a common cause of malfunction
Chapter Three: self-organization and variety keep systems working
questions.explain: These pairings are our reading. The author says the practices follow from a worldview of feedback, nonlinearity and systems responsible for their own behavior, without printing this table.
questions.rule: Practices grow out of findings.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Which statement misrepresents how Meadows presents the list of systems wisdoms?
options: The list is a complete rulebook that only systems thinking can produce
The practices follow from a worldview of feedback, nonlinearity and self-responsible systems
The author offers the list as a start-off dancing lesson from a still-learning student
Several of the practices are things she saw her colleagues doing, consciously or not
optionExplain: Right: she says it probably is not complete and is not unique to systems thinking.
This is how she describes them.
This matches her wording of a start-off dancing lesson from a still-learning student.
She says these are practices she sees colleagues adopt.
questions.explain: She says the list probably isn't complete and isn't unique to systems thinking, and that there are many ways to learn to dance.
questions.rule: A start, not a rulebook.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A company newsletter reports every error and rarely mentions successes, and expectations are sinking. Which guideline and trap does Chapter Seven link here?
options: Expand time horizons; the trap is a delay between decisions and their results
Defy the disciplines; the trap is a boundary drawn too narrowly around the problem
Do not erode the goal of goodness; the trap is drift to low performance
Stay humble; the trap is escalation between rival departments that report less
optionExplain: Time horizons are a different guideline and no delay is in the case.
The case is about expectations sinking, not about disciplinary boundaries.
Right: she calls eroding morality the most damaging example of drift to low performance.
Nothing in the case is a race between rival departments, so escalation does not fit.
questions.explain: Meadows says the bad is magnified while goodness goes unnoticed, expectations fall and the gap narrows. Her antidote is not to weigh bad news more heavily than good, and to keep standards absolute.
questions.rule: Weigh good news fairly; keep standards absolute.
questions.teaches: Meadows calls the erosion of the goal of morality the most damaging example of drift to low performance, and her antidote is not to weigh bad news more heavily than good, and to keep standards absolute.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Meadows calls her list of leverage points a work in progress rather than a recipe for finding them.
questions.explain: She says it is an invitation to think more broadly about system change. The card next gathers her other admissions.
questions.rule: A guide, not a recipe.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Meadows says her Chapter Two zoo is too ____, because it separates the animals from each other and from their concealing environment.
questions.explain: Real systems occur mixed together and interact with one another, so the zoo is a simplified view.
questions.rule: The zoo is a simplified view.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A consultant says every problem should be tackled at the highest level on the list first. Which caution from Meadows does this ignore?
options: The list covers only four kinds of system, so it cannot guide most problems
The list is tentative and its order slithery, with exceptions for every item
The list is accurate for mathematical models, so it should not be used outside them
The list requires a computer model of the system before any item can be applied
optionExplain: She does not limit the list in that way.
Right: she says an item's place depends on the case.
She offers it as a guide for many kinds of system.
She says one can go a long way without mathematics or computers.
questions.explain: Meadows says it is a tentative list, there are exceptions to every item, and the higher the lever the more the system resists.
questions.rule: Use the order with care.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Because exact prediction is impossible, Meadows concludes that the analysis of systems is of no use.
questions.explain: Her claim is more modest: analysis cannot give exact prediction or control, but systems thinking leads us to the edge of what analysis can do and then points beyond.
questions.rule: Limits do not erase value.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A technocrat argues that a bigger and better model will close the gap between understanding and doing. What does Chapter Seven say of this view?
options: A bigger model would close the gap, provided its builders also learn the human questions
The gap exists only for social systems, so physical models can be made to work as hoped
The gap is a matter of training, so more courses in systems analysis would close it
Systems thinking shows even a committed technocrat that more than technocracy is needed
optionExplain: She says thinking alone cannot bridge the gap.
She says self-organizing, nonlinear, feedback systems are inherently unpredictable.
Her own group was trained in systems analysis and still did not follow its advice.
Right: the chapter says it leads to the most deeply human mysteries.
questions.explain: Systems thinking, born of engineering and mathematics, leads its practitioners to confront the most deeply human mysteries, and requires more than technocracy.
questions.rule: Analysis ends where the human question begins.
questions.teaches: Meadows says systems thinking, born of engineering and computers, leads its practitioners to confront the most deeply human mysteries and shows even the committed technocrat that more than technocracy is needed.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Meadows compares systems thinking to a telescope and a microscope. What claim is she making?
options: That the systems lens replaces the older lenses, which can no longer show anything new
That the systems lens is one more way of seeing, which reveals things the others miss
That the systems lens is a specialist tool, useful only in mathematics and engineering
That the systems lens works only when combined with a computer model of the situation
optionExplain: She says it is not better than reductionist thinking.
Right: each lens shows things that are really there. The card next sets out her conclusion.
She wants it used widely, in daily life as well.
She stresses that you can go far without mathematics or computers.
questions.explain: She calls the systems way of seeing complementary: the more ways of seeing, the better, because everything seen through each lens is actually there. The card next shows why.
questions.rule: Lenses complement one another.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: True or false: Meadows says the systems way of seeing is better than the reductionist way of thinking.
questions.explain: She says she does not think so; she thinks it is complementary, and therefore revealing.
questions.rule: Complementary, not superior.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A hospital board member says that, now the staff have learned systems thinking, detailed department-level analysis can stop. Which view of Meadows does this contradict?
options: That systems thinking can never be applied to hospitals
That systems thinking should be kept to a small group of trained experts
That detailed analysis is the only route to understanding any real system
That the lens complements analysis of the parts and does not replace it
optionExplain: She applies it to many human organizations.
She wrote the book for readers wary of the word systems.
That is the view she says the systems lens complements, not one she holds.
Right: she names understanding parts among the things the lens helps us hone.
questions.explain: The lens helps us hone our abilities to understand parts as well as see interconnections. It adds to analysis, rather than replacing it.
questions.rule: Add the lens; keep the others.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: Sort each claim: does Meadows make it about systems thinking, or does she reject it?

items.t: It is complementary to reductionist analysis
It lets us ask what-if questions about future behavior
It raises deep questions about the human mind and heart
It can lead us to the edge of what analysis can do
It is the key to exact prediction and control
It is better than reductionist thinking
It can optimize a complex system
It removes the gap between understanding and doing

questions.explain: The first four are her claims. The last four are the mistakes she names: control, superiority, optimization and the belief that understanding closes the gap.
questions.rule: Know what she claims and what she rejects.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A team masters the systems lens and still finds that people do not follow the good policy. What does Meadows expect?
options: The gap between understanding and doing remains; closing it lies with the human spirit
The gap will close once the team has built a more detailed model of the people involved
The gap shows that the lens is faulty, so the team should drop it
The gap reflects only a lack of authority, so a stronger manager would remove it
optionExplain: Right: systems thinking can tell us what to do but cannot do it.
Her own group knew the models and still did not follow its advice.
She says the lens is worth more than expected, but not as a tool for control.
She does not trace it to authority; she traces it to human needs and weaknesses.
questions.explain: Her closing says systems thinking by itself cannot bridge that gap, but it points beyond analysis to what the human spirit must do.
questions.rule: Understanding is not yet doing.

questions.unit: Reading the book as a whole
questions.unitTitle: Reading the book as a whole
questions.q: A trainee wants a one-week course to master leverage points. What does the ending of Chapter Six say about mastery?
options: Mastery comes quickly once someone knows the twelve points in order and where each one lies
Mastery is gained by pushing the highest leverage points as hard as possible
There are no cheap tickets to mastery: it takes hard work, then letting go and dancing
Mastery belongs to leaders who can enforce paradigm change across the whole system
optionExplain: She says magical leverage points are not easily accessible, even when known.
She says mastery has less to do with pushing leverage points than with letting go.
Right: she says it is hard work, whether analysing systems or casting off paradigms.
She says systems resist change at high leverage points, often fiercely.
questions.explain: She says there are no cheap tickets to mastery. You have to work hard, whether analysing systems or casting off your own paradigms, and in the end letting go and dancing matter most.
questions.rule: Mastery takes work and then letting go.
questions.teaches: Meadows says there are no cheap tickets to mastery; it takes hard work, whether rigorous analysis of a system or rigorous casting off of one's own paradigms.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: In the diagram, which two quantities set the size of the heat flowing out to the outside?

media.alt: Stock-and-flow diagram with one box, room temperature. A valved pipe brings heat in from a cloud on the left; another valved pipe carries heat out to a cloud on the right. Thin arrows show the inflow valve driven by the gap between thermostat setting and room temperature, and the outflow valve driven by the gap between inside and outside temperature. Both loops are marked balancing.

options: The thermostat setting and the outside temperature
The room temperature and the outside temperature
The thermostat setting and the room temperature
The furnace output and the thermostat setting
questions.explain: The outflow valve is driven by the gap between inside and outside temperature, a loop separate from the thermostat. The thermostat setting drives only the furnace inflow.
optionExplain: The setting only governs the furnace loop; the leak never looks at it.
Right: the cooling loop compares inside with outside temperature, like a coffee cup cooling.
That gap drives the furnace inflow, the other loop.
Furnace output is the inflow, not a driver of the heat leaving.
questions.rule: Each balancing loop on a stock has its own goal and its own gap.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with Two Competing Balancing Loops—a Thermostat
questions.q: In the graph, the room temperature is lowest near hour 13 and then turns upward. At that turning point, what is true of the heat flows?

media.alt: Line graph over 24 hours. The thermostat setting is flat near 18 degrees Celsius. Outside temperature falls from 10 to about minus 5 around hour 12, then recovers toward 10. The room warms to about 16 within two hours, slides down to about 12 near hour 13, then climbs back to about 16 by hour 24.

options: The furnace has shut off, so the room can start to recover
The leak has stopped, so only the furnace is acting
The room has reached the thermostat setting, so the loops are balanced
Furnace inflow equals the leak outflow, so the net change is zero
questions.explain: A stock stops falling and starts rising when inflow catches up with outflow. At the minimum the two are equal for a moment; afterwards the furnace pulls ahead.
optionExplain: The furnace is at full output through the cold spell, so it has not shut off.
The leak only slows as the outside warms; it does not stop.
The room is about 6 degrees below the setting at that point.
Right: at the lowest point inflow equals outflow, then the inflow pulls ahead.
questions.rule: A stock turns around where its inflow and outflow cross.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: In the graph, the curve climbs more steeply decade by decade. What explains the steepening?

media.alt: Line graph of population in billions from about 2005 to 2107, with birth and death rates per person held constant and births above deaths. The curve starts near 6.5 billion and rises throughout, bending upward so that it climbs more steeply in later decades, reaching about 22 billion at the end.

options: Fertility keeps rising each decade while mortality stays put
A fixed number of people is added each year, which adds up faster over time
Births are a share of a growing population, so more are added yearly
Mortality is falling, so fewer people die as the decades pass
questions.explain: With constant rates and fertility above mortality, the reinforcing loop dominates: more people give more births, so the yearly addition itself grows, bending the curve upward.
optionExplain: In this run the rates stay at their 2007 levels; nothing rises.
A fixed yearly addition would give a straight line, not a bending one.
Right: births scale with the population, which is how a reinforcing loop bends the curve.
Mortality is also constant in this run.
questions.rule: A dominant reinforcing loop makes the yearly addition grow with the stock.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: In the graph, the decline gradually flattens as the population shrinks. What best explains this?

media.alt: Line graph of population in billions from about 2005 to 2105, with birth and death rates per person held constant and deaths well above births. The curve starts near 6.5 billion and slopes steadily downward, flattening gradually as it goes, and ends below 3 billion.

options: Births rise as the population falls, which offsets the deaths
The net loss is a share of a shrinking stock, so it falls
The balancing loop weakens as the disease behind it fades away
Mortality rates drop steadily as the population gets smaller
questions.explain: Our reading: births and deaths are each a fixed rate times the population, so the net loss is a fixed share of a shrinking stock. The same rates give a smaller loss each year.
optionExplain: Fertility is constant in this run, so births fall along with the population.
Right: the loss is rate times population, so it gets smaller as the stock does.
The mortality rate stays at the high value; the death loop still dominates.
Mortality is assumed constant here; only the stock changes.
questions.rule: With constant rates, flows shrink and grow with the stock they drain.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Which reading of this graph is mistaken?

media.alt: Line graph of population in billions, 2005 to 2107, with bracketed labels. The curve rises from 6.5 to about 8, flattens from roughly 2030 to 2050, then climbs steeply to about 18.5. Brackets mark the first and last stretches as fertility above mortality, and the flat middle as the two equal.

options: In the flat middle stretch, neither loop dominates
The first climb slows because the reinforcing loop weakens as fertility falls toward mortality
The final climb shows fertility again above mortality
In the flat stretch, mortality exceeds fertility, which holds the stock steady
questions.explain: A flat stock means births equal deaths, not that deaths exceed births; if deaths exceeded births the curve would fall. Dominance shifts as the relative strength of the two loops changes.
optionExplain: Correct reading: with equal strength neither loop dominates.
Correct reading: the growth loop weakens as fertility approaches mortality.
Correct reading: the curve rises again when the growth loop dominates.
Mistaken: if mortality exceeded fertility the curve would decline, not stay level.
questions.rule: Flat means the flows are equal; rising or falling means one loop dominates.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Suppose output per unit of capital rises in the diagram. Which effect follows first along the arrows?

media.alt: Stock-and-flow diagram with one box, capital stock. Investment flows in from a cloud; depreciation flows out to a cloud. Arrows run from capital to annual output, which depends on output per unit capital, and on to investment, which also depends on the investment fraction: a reinforcing loop. A second loop from capital to depreciation, which also depends on capital lifetime, is balancing.

options: Annual output rises, so investment rises, strengthening growth
Depreciation falls, because the capital lasts longer than before
The investment fraction rises, because output is now larger
Capital lifetime rises, because the machines work harder and last
questions.explain: Output per unit capital multiplies capital to give annual output, and investment is a fraction of that output. More output means more investment, strengthening the reinforcing loop.
optionExplain: Right: the arrow runs from output per unit capital to annual output to investment.
Depreciation is set by capital and its lifetime, not by output.
The fraction is a separate setting; output does not change it.
Lifetime is its own input and no arrow reaches it from output.
questions.rule: Follow the arrows from a changed input to the first flow it reaches.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Stock with One Reinforcing Loop and One Balancing Loop—Population and Industrial Economy
questions.q: Suppose the capital in this system lasted 17 years. What would the capital stock do compared with the curves?

media.alt: Line graph over 50 years of capital stock, with every curve starting at 100. One curve, labelled 20-year lifetime, climbs steadily to about 230. A flat line, labelled 15-year lifetime, stays at 100. A third curve, labelled 10-year lifetime, falls steadily to about 20.

options: Grow, but more slowly than the 20-year curve
Stay flat at 100, exactly as the 15-year line does
Fall slowly, like the 10-year curve but less steeply
Grow faster than the 20-year curve
questions.explain: Fifteen years just balances investment against depreciation. Any longer lifetime lets investment win, and the longer the lifetime the faster the growth, so 17 years falls between the flat line and the 20-year curve.
optionExplain: Right: longer than 15 years grows, and shorter than 20 grows more slowly.
Only the 15-year lifetime gives a flat stock.
Decline needs a lifetime shorter than 15 years.
Growth speeds up with lifetime, so 17 years is slower than 20.
questions.rule: Past the balance point, a longer lifetime means faster growth.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Suppose the dealer's model with delays faces the same sales jump as the no-delay run. How does inventory differ?

media.alt: Line graph over 100 days of cars on the lot, for a dealer with no delays. Inventory sits flat at 200 until about day 25, then steps quickly up to about 220 and stays flat at that higher level through day 100, with no swings.

Line graph over 100 days of cars on the lot, for a dealer with three delays. Inventory is flat at 200 until about day 25, then swings around a higher level: dips, rises, falls again, each swing larger than the last. Peaks climb from about 245 to about 290 and troughs fall from about 190 to about 135.

options: It also steps up once and stays flat, since the loops are unchanged
It settles slowly at the new level with no overshoot
It swings around the new level, each swing larger than the last
It swings around the old level and then dies out quickly
questions.explain: Delays in a balancing loop make oscillation likely. Without delays the dealer's inventory moves once to the new level; with three delays it overshoots and undershoots, here with growing swings.
optionExplain: The loops are the same, but the delays change the behavior.
A smooth approach is what the no-delay structure gives, not this run.
Right: the late corrections overshoot and undershoot with growing swings.
The swings are around the new level and they grow here.
questions.rule: Add a delay to a balancing loop and expect oscillation.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: Which readings of this graph are correct? Select all that apply.

media.alt: Graph over 100 days in cars per day. A solid line, orders to the factory, and a dashed line, deliveries, both stay at 20 until day 25, then oscillate with growing swings, from about 30 up to about 50 at the peaks and down to nearly zero in the late troughs. Each dashed peak trails the matching solid peak by a few days.

options: Deliveries trail orders by a few days, as the delivery delay would produce
Orders trail deliveries, because customers decide after cars arrive
The swings in orders grow larger as the days pass
Orders stay flat while only deliveries oscillate
Both curves settle at a steady rate by day 60
questions.explain: Each dashed peak follows the solid one, because cars arrive only after the delivery delay. Both curves swing more widely over time rather than settling.
optionExplain: Correct: an order placed now arrives later.
Orders are the cause and deliveries the effect, so deliveries come second.
Correct: peaks climb to about 50 and troughs fall near zero.
Both lines oscillate together, one a little behind.
They are still swinging widely well past day 60.
questions.rule: A physical delay shows as one curve trailing another.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.q: In the graph the inventory settles at the new target. With ten days of cover and 22 cars sold a day, the target is ____ cars.

media.alt: Line graph over 100 days of cars on the lot, for a dealer whose response delay is lengthened. Inventory is flat at 200 until about day 25, dips to about 185, rises to about 225, and then settles near 220 by about day 70, with only small swings.

questions.explain: Ten days of cover at 22 cars a day is 220 cars, which is where the damped run settles after the sales jump from 20 a day.
questions.rule: Desired inventory is days of cover times the sales rate.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: A Renewable Stock Constrained by a Nonrenewable Stock—an Oil Economy
questions.q: In the graph, the resource falls fastest in the middle years rather than at the start. What explains this?

media.alt: Line graph of the resource stock over 100 years, in a run with constant price and continuing depreciation. The curve starts at 1000 and declines slowly at first, falls fastest between about years 25 and 55, then flattens and sits near zero from about year 65 on. Yield per unit of capital falls as the stock shrinks.

options: Yield per unit of capital is at its highest in the middle years
Capital has grown large by then, so extraction is highest
The price of the resource collapses, which drives demand up
Depreciation has stopped, so extraction is no longer limited
questions.explain: Extraction equals capital times yield. Capital has grown by the middle years, so more is pulled out each year; the greater the capital, the faster the resource is depleted.
optionExplain: Yield falls as the resource shrinks, so it is lowest, not highest, later on.
Right: a large capital stock extracts quickly, and it is largest at that time.
The model holds price constant in this run.
Depreciation goes on throughout the run.
questions.rule: Extraction rate is capital times yield per unit of capital.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: Suppose the link from the resource stock to regeneration were cut, so regeneration stayed steady. Which resource would this resemble?

media.alt: Stock-and-flow diagram of capital and a renewable resource. Capital has investment and depreciation flows with a growth goal, profit and price. The resource stock has a regeneration inflow from a cloud, influenced by the stock itself and by a regeneration rate, and a harvest outflow set by capital and yield per unit capital. Yield feeds price and profit.

options: Fish, which breed from their own existing numbers each year
Trees, which seed from the standing forest around them
Wind, which keeps arriving whatever the current stock
Pasture, which regrows from the grass already growing there
questions.explain: Living resources regenerate through a reinforcing loop from themselves. Nonliving ones such as sunlight, wind and river water are refilled by a steady input regardless of the stock's state.
optionExplain: Fish regenerate through a loop from their own numbers, which the cut link would remove.
Trees also reseed from themselves, a loop.
Right: a steady input that ignores the stock is how nonliving renewables refill.
Grass regrows from existing grass, a loop.
questions.rule: Living resources regenerate through a loop; nonliving ones through a steady input.

questions.unitTitle: A Brief Visit to the Systems Zoo
questions.section: Renewable Stock Constrained by a Renewable Stock—a Fishing Economy
questions.q: In the graph the fish stock oscillates instead of settling. Which explanation matches the author's?

media.alt: Line graph of the fish stock over 150 years, run with slightly better boat technology. A curve starts at 1000, falls to about 320 near year 108, then oscillates between roughly 320 and 430 through year 150 without settling.

options: More efficient boats weakened the controlling balancing loop
The fishing fleet stopped responding to profit once catches fell
Fish stopped reproducing once their numbers were low enough
Faster depreciation wore out the boats and shrank the fleet
questions.explain: Higher yield per unit of capital keeps boats profitable at lower fish numbers, so the controlling balancing loop acts later and less strongly. The result is oscillation instead of smooth leveling.
optionExplain: Right: a slight rise in yield per unit of capital weakens the controlling loop.
The fleet still responds to profit; technology only changes the yield.
Reproduction is not the change in this run; the technology is.
Depreciation is unchanged between the runs.
questions.rule: A small change in a balancing loop's strength can turn smooth leveling into oscillation.

questions.q: Suppose logging stops but tree growth, tree deaths and lumber sales continue. What happens to the lumber inventory in the diagram?
options: It rises, because trees left standing pass more wood along to it
It falls, because sales still drain it and no wood arrives
It stays level, because inventory is fed by tree growth directly
It falls only if tree deaths also stop, since they feed it too
optionExplain: Wood reaches the inventory only through the logging pipe, so unlogged trees add nothing.
Right: the only inflow is logging, and the sales outflow continues.
Tree growth feeds the trees stock, not the inventory.
In the diagram tree deaths end in a cloud, not in the inventory.
questions.explain: The lumber inventory has one inflow, logging, and one outflow, sales. With logging stopped and sales continuing, outflow exceeds inflow and the stock falls.
questions.rule: Follow each pipe to see which stock it feeds before predicting a change.

media.alt: From left to right: a cloud feeds a box of wood in living trees through a tree growth tap. A logging pipe runs from that box into a second box, lumber inventory. A separate tree deaths pipe turns downward from the trees into its own cloud. Lumber sales then drain the inventory to a cloud on the right.

questions.q: Suppose the inflow had levelled off at 3 gallons per minute instead of 5, with outflow staying at 5. What would the water stock do after minute 5?
options: Go flat at its minute-five level, exactly as in the original
Rise slowly, because some water is arriving again
Keep falling, but more gently than in the first minutes
Drop to empty at once, because outflow beats inflow
optionExplain: A flat line needs inflow equal to outflow, and 3 is below 5.
Rising needs inflow above outflow, which is not the case.
Right: outflow still exceeds inflow, by 2 rather than 5, so the fall is slower.
Outflow exceeds inflow, but the stock drains at the gap, not instantly.
questions.explain: The stock changes at the gap between inflow and outflow. A gap of 2 gallons a minute gives a falling but shallower line than the first five minutes' gap of 5.
questions.rule: The slope of a stock equals inflow minus outflow.

media.alt: A graph of flows in gallons per minute over ten minutes. A dashed horizontal line at five marks a constant outflow. The inflow line lies at zero until about minute four, rises steeply to five by minute five, then runs level with the outflow line to minute ten.

A graph of the tub's water stock over ten minutes. The line starts at fifty gallons and falls in a straight line to about twenty-five gallons at minute five, then continues as a flat horizontal line at that level through minute ten.

questions.q: Suppose the desired energy level in the diagram rises while energy available for work stays the same. What follows?
options: The discrepancy shrinks, so coffee intake falls and less energy is mobilized
Nothing changes, since only the available energy feeds the discrepancy
The discrepancy is unchanged, since desired level has no link into it
The discrepancy grows, so coffee intake rises and more energy is mobilized
optionExplain: A higher goal widens the gap rather than closing it.
The desired level has its own information link into the discrepancy.
The picture shows two links into the discrepancy: actual and desired.
Right: a larger gap drives more coffee and more mobilization.
questions.explain: The discrepancy is the desired level minus the actual level. Raising the goal enlarges it, which pushes coffee intake up to pull the stock toward the new goal.
questions.rule: A balancing loop acts on the gap between actual and desired levels.

media.alt: A box of stored energy in the body feeds, through a tap for metabolic mobilization, a box of energy available for work, which drains through an expenditure tap to a cloud. Curved information links run from available energy and from the desired energy level into discrepancy, then to coffee intake, then to the mobilization tap. A B marks the loop.

questions.q: In the graph, each coffee curve is steepest at the start and flattens as the ____ between coffee and room temperature shrinks.
questions.explain: The change in temperature depends on the discrepancy, so the curves are steep when it is large and flatten as it shrinks toward zero, whether coffee is hot or iced.
questions.rule: Balancing loops home in on the goal, fast at first and then slower.

media.alt: A graph of temperature in degrees Celsius over eight minutes, with a dashed line marking room temperature at 18. Three hot-coffee curves start high, near 100, 80 and 60, and fall steeply at first, then flatten toward the dashed line. Three iced-coffee curves start near the bottom, between about 0 and 10, and rise steeply, then level off toward the same line.

questions.q: In the graph, how does the gap between the highest-rate and lowest-rate curves change over twelve years?
options: It widens ever faster, since each balance earns on its own growth
It stays the same, because all five curves start at one hundred
It widens at a steady, constant pace, as straight lines would
It narrows, because the higher curves must slow as they climb
optionExplain: Right: curves bend upward, and the higher rate bends faster.
A shared start does not keep curves together; different rates separate them.
The curves bend upward, so the gap does not grow at a steady pace.
Nothing in the picture slows the top curve; it ends highest.
questions.explain: All five accounts start equal, but interest added to the balance earns further interest, and a higher rate compounds faster, so the fan spreads out faster and faster.
questions.rule: In a reinforcing loop, higher rates compound on larger balances.

media.alt: A graph of dollars over twelve years with five curves, one for each interest rate from two to ten percent. All start together at one hundred dollars and fan out, each bending upward. The highest rate ends near 314 dollars and the lowest near 127, with the other three ordered between.

questions.q: In the diagram, people leave the unemployed stock by hiring or by lapsed registration. What does a hiring-only model miss?
options: The layoff inflow, because hiring and layoffs are one and the same pipe
Nothing, since a lapsed registration is the same event as a hire
A second outflow, so the stock can shrink with no one hired
Only the layoff cloud, since a stock needs a single outflow
optionExplain: Layoffs enter through their own pipe from a cloud; hiring is a separate pipe leaving the stock.
The diagram draws them as two separate pipes with different meanings.
Right: a second outflow means the stock can fall without any hires, so hires alone mislead.
The stock has two outflows here, and ignoring one hides what happens to those people.
questions.explain: Registration lapses are a second pipe out of the stock into a cloud. A model that tracks only hiring cannot say what happens to people whose registration lapses.
questions.rule: Ask what lies behind each cloud before trusting a model.

media.alt: A box labelled registered unemployed. A layoff rate pipe enters it from a cloud on the left. Two pipes leave it to clouds: a hiring rate pipe to the right, and a registration lapses pipe turning downward to a lower cloud.

questions.q: True or false: In the diagram, clouds still end the chain at both sides, so the boundary has reached its final form.
questions.explain: The chain shows more stocks than a single cloud but still ends in clouds, and the boundary can be pushed out further, to chemical plants, landfills and beyond.
questions.rule: Any boundary can be expanded; choose it for the question and time period at hand.

media.alt: A chain of three boxes from left to right: raw materials, inventory, consumers' home stocks, joined by pipes with taps labelled production and sales. A raw materials processing pipe enters from a cloud on the left, and a depreciation or discard pipe leaves the last box to a cloud on the right.
